Maybe i'm pedantic but i can't recommend this game for the full price for the pc platform. If you're not a fanboy, a weeaboo or more of a console player than a pc gamer, then read on, otherwise succumb to your base instincts...
Pros:
- mostly nice graphics 8/10 or so
- wasn't too greedy on my ssd (25something gigs, really low for the quality of the graphics)
- very fast - haven't experienced any glitches etc on my setup (gtx 1060 with both an old bulldozer 8350 and a ryzen 1800x)
- challenging enemies: if you don't spend a bit of time dodging attacks and 'reading' their patterns you're missing on a big part of the game (the biggest i'd say, not much to this game apart from tons of combat), battles can be very strategic. Enemies follow patterns on their attacks, it's fun trying to guess what their stamina is and how to exhaust them/bait their attacks once you understand their programming and defeat them taking minimal damage. There's a couple of enemies that seem to be broken - Boreal Outrider Knight comes to mind, who seem to have endless stamina, with which you need to either use brute force, play very patiently against their patterns or try to use glitches to your advantage (there's tons of glitches you can exploit, narrow passages/corners, half open doors the enemies can't get through etc).
- 'lightweight' rpg, simple mechanics yet not overly simplistic (e.g. witcher3 is an order of magnitude more 'complicated' than ds3, both in fighting/gaming mechanics and everything else really), manages to be fun enough
- has a fun-ish manga tune to it, even though the setting is european (methinks, based on the architecture of buildings etc), you can walk around holding a sword twice your size, smacking things on the head - that's worth something
Cons:
- if you play this game without a controller you'll be frustrated.. alot..
- it's a straight port from console to pc, zero effort has been put into making this game pc friendly, it's not worth the full price if you're buying for your pc and plan to use pc controls occasionally: the first time i used an item from my inventory using my mouse i happened to be standing in front of a npc, using the mouse instead of my controller resulted in the character attacking after using the item, npc almost died and i lost favour with them... It's really frustrating trying to play this game with a keyboard as well, again, zero effort has been put into something that would take minimal coding and would have made the game playable on a pc (while at the same time this game sells for 40£, like a proper pc game). I'm dead serious, steam should have a warning on this game's store page, the rage this game can cause when played with a keyboard/mouse setup is unreal..
- idiotic mechanics at times: if you 'fall' from a step (like a foot high step) on an npc it might damage them/cause aggression
- the control is lacking, if you're used to fast paced games where 100ms of latency is a thing, this game will frustrate you beyond belief, for example:
- 10? npcs, with a combined total of 20 kind of meaningful conversations, maybe about 5 of them present you with a choice, maybe a couple of choices actually have consequences..
- i got the feeling that there's a lot of lore in this game (to be fair, i haven't played the previous souls games), however my main source of understanding what's going on was google.. There's absolutely nothing in the game content wise, compared to witcher the content is 1/100, compared to planescape torment 1/1000, how is this game branded an rpg when trine has a (literally) richer story is beyond me..
- multiplayer is extremely laggy about 30% of the time (typically during invasions...) I live in London, my broadband is 'fibre' bt infinity2, ping times are single digits with anything hosted in the UK, low double digits with anything in europe, no online problems outside ds3

The Good
+ Gameplay is as good as ever
+ Interesting new tactical choices
+ Great mod support
The Bad
- Optimization is terrible
- The overall story is a bit of a wash
XCOM2 is the sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The main gist of the game is that you lost during the first game, and now instead of commanding a global defence you are instead leading a resistance movement. The basics are still the same; command a squad of up to six soldiers with different abilities, fill your ant-farm with rooms back at the base, and do decisions on the geoscape.
Mission gameplay is familiar, but has been expanded somewhat. Two actions per soldier, different skills, full and half cover and overwatch are all there. There are of course improvements into how certain skills behave, but the completely new additions are the Concealment and Turn Timer aspects. Certain missions (and skills that can influence) start with the squad concealed. What this means is that the aliens are none the wiser, and you can move around un-detected as long as you don't run into the aliens (or civilian collaborators) line-of-sight. This is a nice change of pace and opens up some nice tactical possiblities. A well laid-out ambush is the most obvious, but how about doing a mission with a single soldier and not firing a single shot? Yeah, it's pretty great and can be done.
The turn timers are another (apparently somewhat controversial among.. not so skilled individuals?) new feature. Certain mission types have you either completing an objective or the whole mission within a set amount of turns. This was apparently done to discourage the "turtling overwatch" approach to gameplay, and comes as a no surprise after the Meld Canister mechanic from Enemy Within. The limits are generous, but enough to make you keep a steady if not brisk pace through said missions.
Outside of missions the familiar "ant-farm" base awaits. However, there is only half the amount of building slots available compared to the previous installment, and throughout the course of the game you will tend to only build a single (with a duplicate of some) of each type of structure. Compared to the amount of room and buildings in Enemy Within, this is a step backwards.
But with that said, there is at the same time more leverage in how you go about building your base. There is no strict "must do" build order (Like in EU/EW, especially regarding the satellite relays) this time around. You can rush certain building types early to gain their benefits, or opt not to and use the resources elsewehere without any "meta" penalties. This is of course a great thing, and to me slightly outweighs the loss of space.
The Geoscape is much improved. Where aspreviously you had very little actual interaction on the globe, this time around there is a whole lot of it. There are the missions to go to, naturally, but there are also side objectives, opening up new areas, building relays, visiting the black market and HQ. All of this, even flying from one point to another, costs time. And time is not a luxury you have in XCOM2. The interactions and planning involed with the Geoscape are excellent.
Not everything is rosey, of course. The optimization as of launch has been universally terrible. Frames are low and loading times long with some freezing in-between. Some inspecting and .ini tweaking fixed much of it for me personally (and as such said problems can be alleviated), but it's still something that shouldn't be present.
On the gameplay side of things, the overarching campaign story did not hit the same high notes as the previous installment did. However, addons are on the horizon so perhaps this is something that will wrap itself better once we experience the "full" story. As such, the basegame ended somewhat apbrupt and left me unsatisfied. I was also not that pleased with you, the player, being characterized to the degree that the game did. I feel like it's not something that should be done in this genre, unless you get to actually make yourself in the game (like in Jagged Alliance 2).
But with all that said and done, XCOM2 flies with colours blazing. To the fan it is just what we asked, more of that XCOM goodness with a new and fresh twist. To the connosseur of the genre, it is an excellent turn-based squad tactical game. On a final note i must also praise the excellent modding support showed by Firaxis, which should give birth to an excellent modding scene in the not-too-distant future.

Let me just start by saying that, in my honest opinion, this game is great.  I have been on the fence about making this purchase for a while now and I'm so glad I finally did!
I'm not going to go into the whole story and what you're trying to do but I will touch on some of the great points and my one and only criticism of the game.  First off, I love the dark sense of the game.  The setting, the illustration, and especially the narrator all catch the theme very very well.  Second, the upgrade system and differences between the classes are a must for a rogue-like dungeon crawler and Darkest Dungeon nails it!  Not only are there 10+ classes but they all have 8 abilities each.  Each of which can be upgraded up to 4 levels I believe, however you can only utililze 4 at any one given time, which makes the exploring team more precise in regards to the way and style you want to play.  Now, you not only have to worry about your characters and their life bar; you also have to worry about any negative ailments they may receive as well as diseases they may contract.  On top of that, you have to keep a watchful eye on their stress level because if it gets too high they may suffer a heart attack.  Yup, lost my first two warriors to that one lol.  With all of these important factors to keep on top of you'd think there would be a system to deal with that.  And there is, and it's done brilliantly!  You can place your stressed out characters in the Abbey (church) or let them have at it in the Tavern to gamble or even visit the brothel.  I'll touch on that one in a few....  Smh.  And to deal with additional ailments and diseases you can send them to medical wards etc. to get treated.
There are also upgradable places in your town where you can upgrade the characters weapons, armor, skills, all adding to the depth of this game.
Now, to touch on the battle system.  I think this is another strong point for this game.  I've read a few reviews saying that it gets very boring and repetitive.  I can say that, after 16 hours I still don't feel that way.  With the variety of character classes and the amount of abilities they have, the game is still fresh to me.  I should also mention that the character's placement is vital as they can only perform certain skills while in a certain position within the group, all adding to the depth of combat too.  There are a decent number of different enemies though I would like to see more but their abilities and types vary quite a bit, which definitely helps in that regard.  Now, when you meet a big enemy, they are fantastic!  I've faced 3 total so far and each one is so different and challenging that I look forward to the rest of them.  Overall, there are 24 listed enemies of this sort, and let me tell you, the first 3 have been very tough and are hulking beasts!!
So, to give you a little taste of what to expect, this game is not for the faint hearted.  It is very difficult at times and can certainly be unforgiving.  If you take your time and build a good party, you will always stand a chance though.  The computer has had as many bad breaks as I have and I have never felt cheated from the result of my decisions.
One experience I had that I feel compelled to share is when my wife died....  Oh yeah, I forgot to mention that you can change the character names and color or outfit/armor.   Speaking of my wife's death sounds grim, I know but its only a game right???  Anyway, on her second to last run out in the dungeons, I was very close to defeating the bossman known as the Prophet when the tides turned very quickly.  Her stress level skyrocketed but we were able to defeat him and head back to town.  While in town I realized that she contracted some sort of fear from her last battle and the only way I could relieve her stress was to send her to the Brothel..  Yes, my wife in a brothel.  Wasn't crazy about the idea but what was I going to do?   When the time came for her to return  I was notified that, "Andrea's debauchery has reached new heights-whereabouts unknown".  She was missing for an additional week...  The following week I was notified that she had done unspeakable things and that she was no longer allowed in the brothel!  It followed up by saying that she had the time of her life and engaged in pleasures of the flesh and recovered 81 stress but acquired Disease:  Syphilis....  Syphilis!!!  Wtf Andrea!!!  Lol.  Well, I opted not to treat the disease or the fears and onward she went to the next dungeon.  A rough run in with a few vagrants, eldriches, and a bout of poison and the next thing I knew, her untreated stress level got out of control and she suffered a heart attack mid battle.  Now she lies in the cemetary of fallen warriors...  Syphilis and all....
Now for the one criticism I have.  The one and only thing is that I wish certain things were clearer regarding some character stat abbreviations.  I'm still uncertain as to what each and every stat means when choosing the skills I want to equip and which ones to upgrade.  One good thing is in battle, once an enemy target is highlighted, clearer stats are displayed regarding the percentage of a hit or miss and the range of damage a successful hit will cause.
All in all this game is masterfully done.  Difficult but balanced very well and the developers nailed the characters, the upgrade system, overall gameplay and certainly the dark humour.  9.5/10.

I love Darkest Dungeon, personally.

The gameplay may become repetitive at times but all it takes to refresh is to simply retire from playing for abit then return later when you're ready to run into the dungeons once more, have your party stress out and stumble out bloodied before walking into a tavern then walking back out as if nothing happened.
It's an interesting mechanic where it seems your party will stress depending on what occurs, and there's a sort of town aspect. It isn't exactly perfect however, for example, a highwayman of mine developed a love interest but then proceeded to, upon visiting the brothel, called upon three women instead.
For you D&D players out there, you might want to try to make a campaign of this game. I have about 10 people who are currently in this D&D and its a blast. Feel free to talk to me about this if you'd like.
Either way, TL;DR, good game, try D&D with it

Fun game, lots to do and I keep finding things to entertain myself in it.
- Build a House
On your own personal plot of land, I can be moved to new locations with a click
- Build a Club World
On your own personal instanced world serving as a guild hall of sorts for your friends
Both these things serve a real function, crafting benches and a meeting up place for friends in you club. People have created so amazing things so it's worth a look around.
- Go fishing
Relaxing and a good way to make glim/flux/many more (types of in game materials/cash)
- Go Mining
Tad slow at first, but you can craft bombs later and it becomes a fast easy way to collect materials for crafting items and building cool stuff for your House/Club World. Mining is also a great way to collect block recipes as they are randomly hidden in ore node. There are Miners Trove chests that randomly drop from these nodes as well, containing more random ore and even sometimes a Mining pet.
- Collecting recipes
On U1 content and higher (level 10) there are dungeons that have a recipe reward. There are soooooo many recipes, some stupid others very cool.
- Shadow Arena
I have limited experience in them as I'm fairly new but they can be damn hard and take a team to do, best drops in the game as far as I can tell.
- Timed Quests
They pop up and you have 20min to clear 10 bosses for 2 Neon Dragon Chests. Bonuses are available randomly when the quest is given making it easier in certain difficulty settings and with certain classes.
- About paying real money.
You can do it but it's not a huge advantage. I bought the power pack because I wanted to try other classes right away, but normal play will get you enough points to unlock other classes rather quickly.
I think buying something is worth it to support the devs.

Doesn't matter how good your party is.
Doesn't matter what abilities they have or what level they are.
Doesn't matter how many resources you brought.
Doesn't matter how much time and gold you've invested.
Doesn't matter who you have in your party.
They will all die. Painfully.
You'll lose everything… and yet you can't help but love it.
Welcome to
, a brutal and unforgiving turn-based Lovecraftian dungeon-crawler from the team at Red Hook. The rogue-like design makes for near infinite replay value. But your biggest enemy here, however, is RNG and, similar to the
franchise, you'll watch your favourite heroes fall and suffer party wipes again and
Having picked this up a few days after the launch of Early Access last year and knowing very little of it, the level of detail, depth and polish that the small developer team has put into this was instantly engrossing. It wouldn't be that much of a stretch to say that this is one of the most unique games to emerge in recent years, especially from Kickstarter, and
has earned a passionate cult following to show for it, even with a modding community to boot. As one who has never really enjoyed turn-based or strategy games in general, (with exception to
and some cRPGs), I was pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed this, and still do, in fact. Must have sunk hours and hours into it within the first week; it's addictive and can't help but pull you back in for another shot at taking down that seemingly invincible boss.
is, undoubtedly, a great game, with an excellent gothic atmosphere that adds to the bleakness of your heroes' plight. The narration, especially in combat, can be repetitive at times, yet immensely satisfying when you land a game-changing critical hit as your party desperately clings to life. Classes are great and each come with unique and interesting abilities and styles, complementing the gritty and dark design nicely. The micro-management and balancing of resources also adds further to the almost survival-like aspects of general gameplay, so success depends on watching your gold deposits closely and the strength of the torch as you delve deeper still into the heart of darkness..
The most fascinating addition, however, is the stress mechanic which implements psychological, (as well as physical), diseases and maladies to reflect the extremely punishing nature of the game world. These can be alleviated and cured through lore-friendly outlets in your Hamlet, (which acts as the main player hub), such as the Tavern, Abbey and Sanatorium. All these buildings and more can be upgraded, as well as your party's armour and gear in a typical RPG fashion, once again complementing the depth and just how time-consuming this can be.
As you can no doubt imagine, the emphasis on such risk/reward stats in nearly all aspects of gameplay leaves you to the mercy of the random number generation (RNG) and it is this dependency on pure luck rather than skill or tactics that is the game's biggest fault.
While it certainly isn't punishing to the point of being broken or unfair, how much you're willing to endure at the whim of chance is ultimately whether or not I can recommend this game to you personally.
is certainly worth a purchase at full price but is equally crippled for some by the punishing nature of the RNG mechanics.
I am thus torn between both an up and down vote for a recommendation.
If you've played a (traditional) cRPG before or the likes of XCOM, then you should be right at home for an immensely satisfying, albeit hard-core, experience. But for the average, "new age" gamer then it once again comes down to how much you're willing to risk in
to enjoy the gameplay reward. Is it worth it? You must find out for yourself.
Proceed with caution; both treasure and death, friend and foe, await at every turn.

This is a truly terrific game. There is no other way about it.
Let's start with the strategy layer.
It's more than it was in EU/EW. You no longer just wait for things to happen, you need to actually plan accordingly what you are going to do. You can travel across the world in the Avenger in order to complete a multitude of projects and objectives. Everything you choose to do has an impact on the outcome of your game. You can research new technology, build it, build new facilities, upgrade your team, and much more.
The combat layer
Of course XCOM 2 wouldn't be XCOM without the bird's eye style command of your troops on the field. It's a turn based strategic overlay that gives you many choices of what to do. And just like the operations on the Avenger, everything you do has an impact on the outcome of the mission.
The plot
Don't worry, no major spoilers here. The plotline of this game follows the fact that XCOM did not win the first invasion. Maybe this was because of the fact that the majority of people lost their first game in EU/EW, but either way, you still lost. Anyways, it's about taking Earth back now. You must build up XCOM and establish new connections around the world.
Multiplayer
I'll update this later, but I haven't gotten the chance to play it yet. I still have not managed to finish a game, because this game is definitely not easy.
Complaints people have
But ZAAAAAAAAACCH! What about all the optimization problems?
Well, think of it this way. How many different combinations of software, drivers, and hardware can you think of? It's a VERY big number. Testing optimization isn't as easy as it seems. And between people who try to run full settings at the minimum requirments, and those who never bother to update their drivers, there are going to be lots of issues.
But ZAAAAAAAAACCH! The turn limit is impossible!
Believe me, I know the turn limit makes the game a lot more grueling than usual. But that's why XCOM 2 has official mod support! Wait for a mod to come out, or if you're feeling tech savvy, go ahead and see if you can modify the game yourself. The game has open .ini files, so go wild!
But ZAAAAAAAAACCH! My favorite soldier keeps dying and the game is too hard!
Well, there are two answers to this. I can either say lower the dificulty, or just say the following: That's XCOM baby!
Anyways, I give the game a solid 10/10. It's a terrific sequel that took the daunting task to following a plotline that involved you losing the first game.

Updated a wee bit late:
With exception of a few things (which mods take care of) this game finally became the shining jewel it deserved to be. My hat's off to Firaxis for the continued support, and also off to The Long War team for it's mods as well.

Brutal. On many levels.
The Good: More customization of your squadmates, from visuals, to skills, to loadouts. Maps are quite a bit more varied from the previous Xcom game. More events going on so if you are lacking a scientist or engineer, or one of the game currencies (money/intel) you have more chances to get them. A little bit more depth on the main characters in the game.
The Bad:
Technically the game is buggy as hell. Animations not playing, invisible enemies, unable to pick promotion skills unless you exit out of the screen and go to another part of your base and come back.
Performance wise the game is just a mess. You click launch mission, everyone jumps out of the skyranger, and then you sit upwards of 20-30 seconds waiting for the map to finish loading even though you're looking at the map. You will get 5-10 second pauses between the end of one squadmates turn and the next. And performance is all over the place reguardless of what settings you choose (My computer is higher then the recommended specs).
Annoyances:
Your on a mission and the 3 main characters (your support team) will never shut the hell up during a mission. They will constantly nag you OVER and OVER during a mission, which also does NOT allow you to do anything with your squadmates until they are done talking. Have an extra engineer or scientist not assigned to something? Nevermind that there is a little icon in the bottom left corner to let you know that, but you also get the little pop-up video screen being nagged to death about it.
Also you will get story related information from the characters in these little pop-up videos on the Avenger, but if you click on the map you skip them and can't hear them again.
Speaking of the map, you CAN NOT do ANYTHING for 2 mins without getting some sort of mission or contact or SOMETHING. The game is throwing 3-5 missions/events at you constantly. To the point you will actually miss the Minutemen nagging you about another settlement in danger in Fallout 4.
And the game is BRUTAL, even on easy. This is the angry red headed xcom stepchild of Dark Souls.
Maybe with a patch or two, to fix performance and pacing/balance of the game I would recommend this game. Until that time I CAN NOT recommend this game. It was simply rushed out the door without proper QA testing.

A very fun RPG, easy to recommend to strategy fans.  It has very attractive 2D graphics and good music.  The game's themes and mechanics play off each other well, the cosmic horror trappings make for an interesting spin on the classic fantasy formula without being a swoony Lovecraft swansong.
The game revels in chance, as you are given a bottomless reserve of characters to try your hand at the game's dungeon.  Survival is a high-tension boardgame, and circumstances can swing wildly.  Darkest Dungeon expects you to play through (and enjoy) the bad beats until you learn the ways the odds can be tipped in your favor.  Like most strategy games with high chance, the growing pains are suffered immediately, but persistence and mastery are both rewarded.
The game simulates many aspects of the "dungeon crawl" fantasy in one package, so those who like the old Dungeons and Dragons romps will love it.  Each individual mechanic is simple, but the myriad situations that arise from their combination are entertaining.  The game's rules are abstract, it is definitely more a puzzle game than a hardcore simulation.  This is what earns it the "rogue-lite" monicker.
If I had to fault the game, I think that it's a little bit too long for its content.  Though you'll pass many milestones where new elements are introduced, throughout much of the game you'll be in the same few areas, encountering the usual monsters and items.
The game's challenge is good.  Very hard at first, and a difficult concluding episode.  You'll have to play well throughout to prevent bad luck from turning into a costly disaster.
+Good graphics and sound
+Fun dungeon survival mechanics
+Unlimited/disposable/customizable roster of characters
+The game greatly rewards good strategy
-Could use more variety in content for a game of its length
-Middle game is a little too easy, can become a bit grindy to afford expensive upgrades

Ive had my eye on Darkest Dungeons for a long, long time. Its a gorgeous game, with great sound and art direction, but with massive glaring flaws. It would, and I do not exagerate, take me days to go over all the tiny little problems that make this game nothing but a chore to play. I feel it deserves a longer review, but for those who look at Darkest Dugeon and find themselves taken in by the impressive presentation, do not be fooled.
Mechanically the game is poor at best, with few points of creativity among a lackluster and fairly hit-or-miss cast of character classes. Again, I could go on and on and on and on about what this game does right, and what it does wrong, but, and I think that every negative review will reflect this in some way, the problem is singlar and runs throughout the entire game; it is utterly dominated by randomness.
Regardless of your planning, your success is still subject to a poory optomized random-event generator which can see your party go from clean to insane, and having eaten a banquet's worth of food over just three rooms. This would not be such a problem if triumph in the game did not feel incremental and mundane, with the only real catharsis or payoff being when one of your heroes exhibits a virtue and steamrolls the encounter and the dungeon as a result.
After 50 rather irritated, sleepless hours with this game I can firmly say that it isnt really all that good. It isnt bad, and its presentation put it ahead of most other indie games, but whoever made it should really have consulted someone who knew anything about mechanical design.

My general rule of thumb for working out satisfication is £1 for every Hour spent in a game. Spending £10 on a game and only playing for 2 hours in total is generally a sign of me not enjoying a game nor getting my money's worth. You should be able to look at my Fallout 4 play-time and work out how I feel this ratio goes with this game...!
In short, Fallout 4 was a real blast. Along with the Settlement feature, I felt I was really a part of this wasteland and making a difference out there!
The main storyline was good fun,
I definitely enjoyed it.
There is a point with most games, being a game designer/publisher myself, where you start to "see the code" like Neo in one of the Matrix sequels. You know what actions will activate what kind of code, outcomes etc and therefore when it all starts to become "predictable" it's no longer much fun. There are plenty of surprises in Fallout 4 to prevent the core mechanics and repitition from becomming too apparent early on, but that's not to say they don't eventually creep up on you, and nowadays, after so many hours, I find it hard to go back into Fallout 4 and truly enjoy it.
Even when that feeling of "new and exciting" was over, for the first time I decided to give Creation Kit a try, and that probably led to another 150 hours of fun and enjoyment creating mods for the game. I've also started a 2nd playthrough, and there's potential for a 3rd and Survival Mode at some point - so I know there's yet more I can get out of this game. When real life gets you down, this is a game you can jump into and feel some worth again, even if it is just digital, pointless worth! ;)
But clearly, I got my moneys worth, and had heaps of fun. Now I'm waiting patiently for Fallout 5... Therefore, I would say it's absolutely worth every penny, especially if you've enjoyed even just 1 previous 3D Fallout game. For those who have never played a Fallout game, this one should work and be enjoyable. Knowledge of former Fallout games may enlighten you very occasionally here, but it's not a necessity to play and understand. The lore is as fresh as it was previously.
It's a game you can talk about with friends (just general ones) and they know what you're talking about and have stories to share. Companions are great and them liking or disliking your actions is a nice touch. I will admit that more recently, I look back at Fallout 4 wishing there was some kind of multiplayer/co-op mode, which I know would take me back to the game for many hours. But if my review is purely Single Player experience - it excels there. Bethesda know how to make games that will keep me occupied for days, weeks, months... Whether that's a good thing or not is anyone's guess ;)
Highly recommended for anyone who likes a deep and involved story set in an FPS environment. Far Harbour and Nuka World are also excellent DLC additions. I have no problem if this game was not up someone's alley, but it was definitely up mine. Previous Fallout games have been refined here. Whilst I can't decide if I prefer New Vegas's main storyline over this one, I think it still holds up strong and firm. Thank God, I will say, people don't stalk you from across the wasteland (Caesars Men in New Vegas).. I am grateful that mechanic was dropped, because it became a chore after about the 2nd time in New Vegas.
Fallout 4 still has its occasional quirks and annoyances. But this review is about the bigger picture. By my rule, of a pound for every hour spent in game determining whether I'm enjoying it or not, this game blows all the others out the water, with only Skyrim coming close. There's so much to see and do, and on top of that there's also the chance for some great role play, it really is a world and tale you can get lost in.
Highly recommended!

Starbound is an exelent 2D sandbox-explorer-style game. It shares some traits with terraria but apart from that it is a very divrse game. The setting is this: your player leaves their homeworld for some reason, and tries to build a living off the stars. Although many good things are already in this game, it still needs work. But that's good, becasue that means this game will be better and better as time goes on! One interesting thing about the game is that all the planets are individual from another planet, they will have different trees, different dirt, different monsters, everything in the game feels new and refreshing, whereas in terraria you only got one world (although terraria has improved a steady amount). The mining is consistend, you're always looking for coal (the most important mineral in the game) and the mineral of which tier you are at. Each tier unlocks new sets of weapons, armor, tools, and other goodies (including the ability to go to harder regions of the galaxy). At the moment, this is a great game, and with everything planned for it, it may get a "best of 2014" award. Just maybe.

The strongest theme of Darkest Dungeon is responsibility, and whether you accept or reject it.
Do you try and take care of your heroes, keeping them constantly in good health and humour? Do you plan out strategies and tactics? Do you treat the recruits as disposable, dismissing them if they run up too much of a bill after a mission? Do you blame every miss or crit on bad RNG?
Ultimately, if you want to finish the job, you have to carry on one way or another. There is no reloading from a saved game, and restarting won't gain you anything.
From a gameplay perspective: the game is solid with a lot of interesting decisions and high tension due to the potential disasters constantly lurking beneath the surface. While each individual mission isn't too long, the campaign as a whole is very long-form, and strategizing between missions takes time as well. The game starts quickly, but don't expect to complete it in under 40 hours.

Rarely I write a review for a game, but I think this one earned it.
First off: There is a lot of discontent going around, mainly because of the mission timers, doom timer and perfomance issues.
I have a GTX 760 and while some perfomance drops are noticeable they don't really hinder your gameplay experience.
The game certainly doesn't look incredible with AA turned off it's still nice to look at and fun to play. Also, since this is a Firaxis game you can pretty much expect a perfomance patch in the next few weeks or even days.
The timers are a whole different subject. Many people hate them, so do I. From a logical standpoint, the timers are total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Somehow the supply convoy you're about to raid is rigged to explode in a few minutes, despite the fact the enemy doesn't even know you're there. You're concealed after all. Reinforcements under way? Wait what? Reinforcement against whom? The unknown force which nobody knows about?
The alien transmitter only has 8 turns left before it sends out all the data of your operations? It takes hours to get there but the transmitter always finishes a few minutes after your squad drops in. Since these turns would only take seconds in a real scenario this is completely ridiculous.
Sadly however, many players just go ahead and moan all day instead of taking 2 minutes and get the DisableTimers mod from the workshop. (Or the TimerTweaks mod if you still want them but less stressful).
Seriously, it's that easy, your problem is gone with the click of a button. Turn up your difficulty to compensate and you're set for a great experience without any illogical stress.
The doom timer needs editing in the config files of the game which may be an issue for less experienced people but if you're willing to take that step you can tweak those as well. If you don't, no biggie, in my current experience on classic difficulty the doom timer doesn't seem to be that threatening. Don't get me wrong it's fast and really tries to stress you out but it gets much easier after learning how to deal with it.
The doom timer, from a logical standpoint, is again totally illogical of course. It took the aliens 20 years to get there but now they're finishing in a few months.
About the gameplay itself:
If you liked XCOM:EU you will love this one. They took many features from the predecessor and fleshed them out. There are many improvements like the fact that you don't have to fabricate every piece single piece of armor. Instead you get your armor upgrades for everyone while still having to option for unique armor pieces through different means.
All in all a great experience if you're willing to take 2 minutes before starting your campaign.

I played this a fair bit (almost 50h) and in the beginning I loved the game. The artwork, the narrator, the combat system...it is a beautiful game. But here are the two reasons why I do not recommend it:
1. It is too long. What? How can a game be too long? Well...you essentially do the same every mission. It becomes a tedious grind. I love playing FTL and you can finish one game in 90 to 120 mins. Here I played in one playtrough about 30 hours and just reached the "Darkest Dungeon" (the last area). It is just the same over and over again.
You might have several mission types but they play essentially the same. You walk trough the dungeon and kill everything. Sometimes you have to collect stuff, destroy stuff, kill a boss...but these are mere variations on a theme.
2. Champion Level is way too hard. Up to veteran level the difficulty kind of scales with your abilities. On champion level it spikes. You will get crushed...hard! The only way to win is to learn the wiki and use a perfect combo of adventurers and trinkets (something you can't always do). You will loose people. That means you have to hire new adventurers that need to level up. The grind begins anew.
So..with a shorter progression and maybe a smaller difficulty increase this could have been a nice game. As it is...it is too long, too grindy and somewhat too difficult.

Maybe i'm pedantic but i can't recommend this game for the full price for the pc platform. If you're not a fanboy, a weeaboo or more of a console player than a pc gamer, then read on, otherwise succumb to your base instincts...
Pros:
- mostly nice graphics 8/10 or so
- wasn't too greedy on my ssd (25something gigs, really low for the quality of the graphics)
- very fast - haven't experienced any glitches etc on my setup (gtx 1060 with both an old bulldozer 8350 and a ryzen 1800x)
- challenging enemies: if you don't spend a bit of time dodging attacks and 'reading' their patterns you're missing on a big part of the game (the biggest i'd say, not much to this game apart from tons of combat), battles can be very strategic. Enemies follow patterns on their attacks, it's fun trying to guess what their stamina is and how to exhaust them/bait their attacks once you understand their programming and defeat them taking minimal damage. There's a couple of enemies that seem to be broken - Boreal Outrider Knight comes to mind, who seem to have endless stamina, with which you need to either use brute force, play very patiently against their patterns or try to use glitches to your advantage (there's tons of glitches you can exploit, narrow passages/corners, half open doors the enemies can't get through etc).
- 'lightweight' rpg, simple mechanics yet not overly simplistic (e.g. witcher3 is an order of magnitude more 'complicated' than ds3, both in fighting/gaming mechanics and everything else really), manages to be fun enough
- has a fun-ish manga tune to it, even though the setting is european (methinks, based on the architecture of buildings etc), you can walk around holding a sword twice your size, smacking things on the head - that's worth something
Cons:
- if you play this game without a controller you'll be frustrated.. alot..
- it's a straight port from console to pc, zero effort has been put into making this game pc friendly, it's not worth the full price if you're buying for your pc and plan to use pc controls occasionally: the first time i used an item from my inventory using my mouse i happened to be standing in front of a npc, using the mouse instead of my controller resulted in the character attacking after using the item, npc almost died and i lost favour with them... It's really frustrating trying to play this game with a keyboard as well, again, zero effort has been put into something that would take minimal coding and would have made the game playable on a pc (while at the same time this game sells for 40£, like a proper pc game). I'm dead serious, steam should have a warning on this game's store page, the rage this game can cause when played with a keyboard/mouse setup is unreal..
- idiotic mechanics at times: if you 'fall' from a step (like a foot high step) on an npc it might damage them/cause aggression
- the control is lacking, if you're used to fast paced games where 100ms of latency is a thing, this game will frustrate you beyond belief, for example:
- 10? npcs, with a combined total of 20 kind of meaningful conversations, maybe about 5 of them present you with a choice, maybe a couple of choices actually have consequences..
- i got the feeling that there's a lot of lore in this game (to be fair, i haven't played the previous souls games), however my main source of understanding what's going on was google.. There's absolutely nothing in the game content wise, compared to witcher the content is 1/100, compared to planescape torment 1/1000, how is this game branded an rpg when trine has a (literally) richer story is beyond me..
- multiplayer is extremely laggy about 30% of the time (typically during invasions...) I live in London, my broadband is 'fibre' bt infinity2, ping times are single digits with anything hosted in the UK, low double digits with anything in europe, no online problems outside ds3
I liked the Bosses design and the Pets system. I didnt like the repetitive feel of the game though.

To level your equipment you have to gain a ridiculous amount of heat (exp) to level them and when you cap it the items heat you can't move to the next level of the equipment unless you get lucky with the RNG Fire system. Trove, like any other MMO out there, attracts a certain type of audience. In this case, Trove caters to anyone seeking lots of dungeons and loot.
Like,
A LOT of loot.
And that's great, cause its horribly addictive. I've found myself saying "Alright, last dungeon" "Okay, this is the LAST dungeon" "Okay, REALLY REALLY last one" and before I know it its 2 AM and I have work tomorrow. Its embarrassing how many things I've collected in only EIGHT HOURS.
But, what else is there?
Trove presents everything right in front of you in that exact moment. You will be constantly showered with all kinds of hats, and swords,and guns,AND staffs-loot up the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. But in Trove, that's really all that keeps me coming back. I don't find myself caring about cornerstones and huge club worlds and whatnot, as do many people that play this game. I take a look at the chat and all I see is people asking for help with their dungeons and shadow arenas for more and more loot. And honestly, even that gets stale after long enough. you walk, you rapidly click (Or hold, depending on your class), and you get stuff. Rinse and repeat. There's no bigger event, no world building, just more dungeons. That's really the only true substance this game offers and for me, that's not enough. I've been a part of this game since early beta and I thought big things were at some point due to be on their way, but no such thing happened. Of course, a large number of Trove players will argue, saying that cornerstones and club worlds play a large part in the game, and I get that.
But, if you want an MMO with substance, a world of more than dungeons, than I'd pass. Its not everyday I think to write a review, but going back and playing Trove made me realize how empty its world is.

My general rule of thumb for working out satisfication is £1 for every Hour spent in a game. Spending £10 on a game and only playing for 2 hours in total is generally a sign of me not enjoying a game nor getting my money's worth. You should be able to look at my Fallout 4 play-time and work out how I feel this ratio goes with this game...!
In short, Fallout 4 was a real blast. Along with the Settlement feature, I felt I was really a part of this wasteland and making a difference out there!
The main storyline was good fun,
I definitely enjoyed it.
There is a point with most games, being a game designer/publisher myself, where you start to "see the code" like Neo in one of the Matrix sequels. You know what actions will activate what kind of code, outcomes etc and therefore when it all starts to become "predictable" it's no longer much fun. There are plenty of surprises in Fallout 4 to prevent the core mechanics and repitition from becomming too apparent early on, but that's not to say they don't eventually creep up on you, and nowadays, after so many hours, I find it hard to go back into Fallout 4 and truly enjoy it.
Even when that feeling of "new and exciting" was over, for the first time I decided to give Creation Kit a try, and that probably led to another 150 hours of fun and enjoyment creating mods for the game. I've also started a 2nd playthrough, and there's potential for a 3rd and Survival Mode at some point - so I know there's yet more I can get out of this game. When real life gets you down, this is a game you can jump into and feel some worth again, even if it is just digital, pointless worth! ;)
But clearly, I got my moneys worth, and had heaps of fun. Now I'm waiting patiently for Fallout 5... Therefore, I would say it's absolutely worth every penny, especially if you've enjoyed even just 1 previous 3D Fallout game. For those who have never played a Fallout game, this one should work and be enjoyable. Knowledge of former Fallout games may enlighten you very occasionally here, but it's not a necessity to play and understand. The lore is as fresh as it was previously.
It's a game you can talk about with friends (just general ones) and they know what you're talking about and have stories to share. Companions are great and them liking or disliking your actions is a nice touch. I will admit that more recently, I look back at Fallout 4 wishing there was some kind of multiplayer/co-op mode, which I know would take me back to the game for many hours. But if my review is purely Single Player experience - it excels there. Bethesda know how to make games that will keep me occupied for days, weeks, months... Whether that's a good thing or not is anyone's guess ;)
Highly recommended for anyone who likes a deep and involved story set in an FPS environment. Far Harbour and Nuka World are also excellent DLC additions. I have no problem if this game was not up someone's alley, but it was definitely up mine. Previous Fallout games have been refined here. Whilst I can't decide if I prefer New Vegas's main storyline over this one, I think it still holds up strong and firm. Thank God, I will say, people don't stalk you from across the wasteland (Caesars Men in New Vegas).. I am grateful that mechanic was dropped, because it became a chore after about the 2nd time in New Vegas.
Fallout 4 still has its occasional quirks and annoyances. But this review is about the bigger picture. By my rule, of a pound for every hour spent in game determining whether I'm enjoying it or not, this game blows all the others out the water, with only Skyrim coming close. There's so much to see and do, and on top of that there's also the chance for some great role play, it really is a world and tale you can get lost in.
Highly recommended!

Rarely I write a review for a game, but I think this one earned it.
First off: There is a lot of discontent going around, mainly because of the mission timers, doom timer and perfomance issues.
I have a GTX 760 and while some perfomance drops are noticeable they don't really hinder your gameplay experience.
The game certainly doesn't look incredible with AA turned off it's still nice to look at and fun to play. Also, since this is a Firaxis game you can pretty much expect a perfomance patch in the next few weeks or even days.
The timers are a whole different subject. Many people hate them, so do I. From a logical standpoint, the timers are total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Somehow the supply convoy you're about to raid is rigged to explode in a few minutes, despite the fact the enemy doesn't even know you're there. You're concealed after all. Reinforcements under way? Wait what? Reinforcement against whom? The unknown force which nobody knows about?
The alien transmitter only has 8 turns left before it sends out all the data of your operations? It takes hours to get there but the transmitter always finishes a few minutes after your squad drops in. Since these turns would only take seconds in a real scenario this is completely ridiculous.
Sadly however, many players just go ahead and moan all day instead of taking 2 minutes and get the DisableTimers mod from the workshop. (Or the TimerTweaks mod if you still want them but less stressful).
Seriously, it's that easy, your problem is gone with the click of a button. Turn up your difficulty to compensate and you're set for a great experience without any illogical stress.
The doom timer needs editing in the config files of the game which may be an issue for less experienced people but if you're willing to take that step you can tweak those as well. If you don't, no biggie, in my current experience on classic difficulty the doom timer doesn't seem to be that threatening. Don't get me wrong it's fast and really tries to stress you out but it gets much easier after learning how to deal with it.
The doom timer, from a logical standpoint, is again totally illogical of course. It took the aliens 20 years to get there but now they're finishing in a few months.
About the gameplay itself:
If you liked XCOM:EU you will love this one. They took many features from the predecessor and fleshed them out. There are many improvements like the fact that you don't have to fabricate every piece single piece of armor. Instead you get your armor upgrades for everyone while still having to option for unique armor pieces through different means.
All in all a great experience if you're willing to take 2 minutes before starting your campaign.

It's still got that Bethesda clunkiness, but it isn't nearly as clunky as Fallout 3/NV which is a plus in my book, however, it changed the dialogue and perk systems from how they were in Fallout 3/NV, and completely removed the point system (things like putting points into Hacking, Lockpicking, Sneaking, Speech, etc).
Fallout 4 is a fantastic game, but it doesn't quite feel like a Fallout game. The story and lore is interesting enough, but didn't capture me the way New Vegas did. It's about the same as Fallout 3, which I think most people agree isn't as good as New Vegas in terms of writing.
I'm struggling to put in words just how Fallout 4 doesn't feel like a Fallout game, because I can't directly put my finger on it. The biggest two things of course are the voiced protagonist and the writing that I already pointed out, but there are other things that just feel "off" about Fallout 4, despite Fallout 4 being a very great game in it's own right.
Overall, I do highly recommend Fallout 4, but don't jump into it expecting to be captivated like you may have been with Fallout 3 and New Vegas.

I love this game, but there are a few issues you should know before purchasing.
So I guess these will be cons first, then I'll hit up the pros.
CONS:
My biggest gripe with this game (there is another one, we'll get there) has to be the optimization. There's no settings that drastically affect FPS in any real sort of way, aside from resolution and the more prominant, "oh of course these settings will affect FPS". But those are only one or two settings. Textures, shadows, reflections, all of that jazz can be set to medium/high settings and you won't see any difference in FPS if you usually played on low. This sounds good, yes, but if you're wanting to get rid of that constant 40 FPS in one area, you're not going to have any settings to help increase those frames. And frames are important in this game.
The other big gripe I have has to do with the camera. The camera controls have been seemingly downgraded from the past souls games, which I didn't think was entirely possible. Dark Souls 1 had a great lock on system, where you could lock onto an enemy from further away and it KNEW what you were wanting to lock onto. If you were surrounded by enemies in DKS1, changing lock on to a different target was a breeze. But in DKS3, sometimes that changing enemy lock on move just doesn't work. Getting attacked by a giant crab that deals half of your HP while simultaniously being surrounded by tiny crabs that do hardly any? Which do you think lock on SHOULD lock onto? The massive crab or the little one? Apparently it thinks that the little crab is more of a threat, thus ending your character's life with one swift claw strike. Awful!
Pro tip: a lot of bigger enemies have SUPER slow wind up attacks. It's hard to predict a lot of the time, but with practice you should counter it well. It can be very annoying to get hit by slow attacks because you expect them to be faster, but it's okay.
Onto the pros:
I'll keep these short because all the other praise has been said in other reviews.
Bosses are fantastic for the most part. Each boss has a personality and backstory that makes fighting them either extremely exciting or super sad. Each boss has a second (sometimes third) stage which can throw you into a fit of rage, or make you shrug because not that much has changed. But the intensity is fantastic in these stages.
The lore in this game takes after the lore from Dark Souls 1. While you don't need to know exactly what you're doing in order to play and have fun, it's suggested that you either buy and beat Dark Souls 1 (and 2, if you want, but nothing significant really happens there, not from what I can remember). Or watch lore videos on youtube, whichever works for you. Either way, the story unravels in item descriptions and they're probably the most entertaining thing to speculate and hear about when you're not actually playing the game. The story is amazing, you just have to think a little.
And finally, my favorite thing about this game, is the fact that it took everything that I loved from Dark Souls 1 and made it better while also removing everything I hated about it, too. For example, you shouldn't need to know how to toggle escape from a Chaos Zweihander, you shouldn't hate invasions because of backstab fishers and abusers.
I think that's about it for what I have to say.
Tl;DR: it's pretty fun, worth the money, buy it.
PS: Get the Ringed City DLC first if you don't have enough for both DLC's.
PPS: dark souls 3 did invasions right, fight me about it.

The strongest theme of Darkest Dungeon is responsibility, and whether you accept or reject it.
Do you try and take care of your heroes, keeping them constantly in good health and humour? Do you plan out strategies and tactics? Do you treat the recruits as disposable, dismissing them if they run up too much of a bill after a mission? Do you blame every miss or crit on bad RNG?
Ultimately, if you want to finish the job, you have to carry on one way or another. There is no reloading from a saved game, and restarting won't gain you anything.
From a gameplay perspective: the game is solid with a lot of interesting decisions and high tension due to the potential disasters constantly lurking beneath the surface. While each individual mission isn't too long, the campaign as a whole is very long-form, and strategizing between missions takes time as well. The game starts quickly, but don't expect to complete it in under 40 hours.

Yesterday evening I went to the grocery store, and was startled to realize that I was suddenly in a totally different world.
Computer games have difficulty grabbing me these days. I used to like genres like turn-based strategy or adventure that had no time constraints, but those now usually feel too slow-paced to pull me in; whereas pure action action games I've never been particularly good at. (I tried Shadow of Mordor for a bit recently, and quit after a very frustrating two hours where I attempted a simple beginning quest for about a dozen times, only to be killed by the same orc each time.)
Like the previous XCOM remake, Firaxis's XCOM2 managed the magic of transporting me completely elsewhere, in the same way that some of my childhood classics did. I did not even properly realize how deeply I'd become immersed the game, until I went outside, and the sheer _differentness_ of the real world and the game world startled me - somewhat similar to the shock of jumping into cold water, your body suddenly and obviously piercing through a surface that separates two different realms of existence.
A good description of my experience with the game comes, oddly enough, from Michael Vassar​ describing something that's seemingly completely different. He talks about the way that two people, acting together, can achieve such a state of synchrony that they seem to meld into a single being:
> In real-time domains, one rapidly assesses the difficulty of a challenge. If the difficulty seems manageable, one simply does, with no holding back, reflecting, doubting, or trying to figure out how one does. Figuring out how something is done implicitly by a neurological process which is integrated with doing. Under such circumstances, acting intuitively in real time, the question of whether an action is selfish or altruistic or both or neither never comes up, thus in such a flow state one never knows whether one is acting cooperatively, competitively, or predatorily. People with whom you are interacting [...] depend on the fact that you and they are in a flow-state together. In so far as they and you become an integrated process, your actions flow from their agency as well as your own[.]
XCOM2 is not actually a real-time game: it is firmly turn-based. Yet your turns are short and intense, and the game's overall aesthetics reinforce a feeling of rapid action and urgency. There is a sense in which it feels like the player and the game become melded together, there being a constant push-and-pull in which you act and the game responds; the game acts and you respond. A feeling of complete immersion and synchrony with your environment, with a perfect balance between the amount of time that it pays to think and the amount of time that it pays to act, so that the pace neither slows down to a crawl nor becomes one of rushed doing without understanding.
It is in some ways a scary effect: returning to the mundaneness of the real world, there was a strong sense of "it's so sad that all of my existence can't be spent playing games like that", and a corresponding realization of how _dangerous_ that sentiment was. Yet it felt very different from the archetypical addiction: there wasn't that feel of a drug user's understanding of how ultimately dysfunctional the whole thing was, or struggling against something which you knew was harmful and of no real redeeming value. Rather, it felt like a taste of _what human experience should be like_, of how sublime and engaging our daily reality could be, but rarely is.

Starbound is an exelent 2D sandbox-explorer-style game. It shares some traits with terraria but apart from that it is a very divrse game. The setting is this: your player leaves their homeworld for some reason, and tries to build a living off the stars. Although many good things are already in this game, it still needs work. But that's good, becasue that means this game will be better and better as time goes on! One interesting thing about the game is that all the planets are individual from another planet, they will have different trees, different dirt, different monsters, everything in the game feels new and refreshing, whereas in terraria you only got one world (although terraria has improved a steady amount). This review originally did not recommend the game, based on several incomprehensible design choices made by Firaxis. The use of mods has changed my recommendation from very tenuously negative to very tenuously positive. The change from a red to a blue icon may seem dramatic, but in reality it's a very small change that just happened to push the game back into the Recommended zone for me.
I am very appreciative of the feedback, both disagreeing and agreeing, that was put forth in a respectful and reasonable manner, but I do feel obliged to say that none of it convinced me to change my opinion. The decision to very, very cautiously recommend the game was made independently and based solely on more playtime.
Only a fool never revises his opinions.
As a lover of the X-COM series, I've had a very hard time getting to enjoy this game, and the fact that I had to use mods to do so still leaves a bad taste in my mouth. XCOM 2 has a lot of great points going for it, but in some ways, Firaxis sabotaged many players' enjoyment of the game, and this is why I can only very, very caustiously recommend the game, and only to players who know full well what they are getting into.
XCOM 2 is set years after the XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within, and in the time that has passed, the aliens have established a seemingly peaceful (if slightly patronizing) relationship with humanity, creating a global government known as ADVENT. Humanity seems to prosper under the guidance of its alien benefactors, but all is not as it seems, and a hidden Resistance movement, founded from the remains of the old XCOM Project, is determined to expose the aliens for what they really are.
In the vein of its predecessor, XCOM 2 is a turn-based tactical strategy game, where your small squad exchanges fire with a superiour alien force, and only careful guidance from their Commander can help them survive. Once again, the odds are overwhelmingly in the enemy's favour, except this time, the aliens don't give you any breathing room, not even in the beginning.
When you're not commanding your squad, you're constructing your base and researching new technologies, since apparently all the technological advances of the XCOM Project are... misplaced? Forgotten? I don't know. You simply give orders, and the crew of the Avenger, your new mobile base, starts work on the project you've requested, usually taking a set amount of days to complete the effort.
XCOM 2 improves the most - and really, only - glaring problem Enemy Unknown had, which was its extreme reactivity. The aliens always had the initiative, and the player had to chase after events. XCOM 2 fixes this to some degree, allowing you to decide when to strike at alien objectives. You'll still have to respond to missions (and bothersomely often), but you can be a lot more proactive now.
The game looks gorgeous, and plays smoothly when not bugging out. Tactical options are once again legion, and the base and world building aspect is fun if somewhat streamlined. Concealment mode is a nice addition, although hampered by a serious flaw, see below.
Classes were well rebalanced. Snipers got slightly nerfed, going from omnipotent to 'merely' powerful, Supports are now much more useful and even necessary, Heavies are much more fun and versatile to use. Assaults still kill the crap out of everything.
Lastly, it has a lot of the qualities that made XCOM: Enemy Unknown so good, and those should
be understated. XCOM 2 could have been even better than its stellar predecessor, if not for...
Some utterly incomprehensible desicions by Firaxis lie at the base of my ambivalent review of this game, most of which end up making the game actively hampering its own gameplay, especially in the early game.
Firstly, and most importantly, making a turn-based strategy game and then making every single action and movement dependent on a timer is a very questionable decision. I agree, Overwatch Creeping was a lame strategy and had to be discouraged, but stringent timers that require beelining for objectives are a draconic measure. Many “seriously players” absolutely love the timers, and great for them, but
.
A throttling timer is great for Legend difficulty, but on Normal, I want a tough challenge, but I also want to have some leeway, to be able to make one or two mistakes without being instantly brutalized, and to be able to maneuver instead of madly dashing for the objective and evac zone. The timer itself is a good thing, but scaling it to the difficulty would have solved so many problems.
Even when you're not doing missions, you're constantly racing against the clock. Completion on the game-over Avatar Project goes punishingly quick, even on Normal, and you'll find yourself constantly chasing after main objectives to avoid getting strangled by yet another timer. Playing a strategy game on Normal shouldn't involve a feeling of constantly having a muton poking a pitchfork in your back to
Again, great for hardcore players who want to get gut-punched, but not for people who want a challenge without needing to min-max and learn stats by heart.
To exacerbate this problem, some enemies will make your careful positioning irrelevant by teleporting to a flanking position and then getting a free turn to put a soldier in the hospital – or make that the morgue. Faceless enemies are also highly unfair in the early game, revealing themselves whenever they like and then getting a free turn for an automatic hit. Stun Lancers will throw all caution to the wind and dash through withering overwatch fire just to get a hit in. It can be very frustrating in the early game without skills or equipment to counter it, especially with the draconic hospital times of 15 days or more. Sometimes it feels like “computer decides you take 6 points of damage,” and that's a shame.
Also important for a new player, the enemies have been bumped up compared to Enemy Unknown, and the early game can be a brutal meatgrinder. Enemies hit often and hard, even with full cover. Sectoids, encountered from the start, now have 8 health and can Mind Control, Mind Whip and Reanimate right off the bat. There's no occasion to warm up or even get to learn the ropes, you're dropped right onto Hamburger Hill and will have to endure serious punishment before you can start fighting back. Expect to burn through recruits quick in the beginning. A character so much as stubs his toe will spend over fifteen days in the hospital, so it'll be very hard to get any promotions in at first.
Lastly, the game is very poorly tested and this despite its pushed-back release date. Bugs are legion and immensely frustrating, some having serious gameplay consequences including soldier deaths.  The game also does not bother to explain its mechanics, just stacking objectives onto your cart with no explanation as to how or why you should achieve them. And I think only Firaxis know why they removed all the great Second Wave options.
I wish I could gush about this game, I really do, but I find the decision to put stringent timers on all difficulties to seriously chip the paint, making players feel bullwhipped. As it stands, I can only carefully recommend this game, and respectfully advise all non-hardcore players to use mods to make the timer less brutal on standard difficulties. With the timer's grip lessened, the game becomes more enjoyable to many people.
Yes, “you can use mods”, but that's no excuse. Many developers these days have an attitude of “the community will fix it” and it's a bad attitude to have, and not one players shoul defend.

My playtime on steam is only about 25 hrs when I finish this game but my actual playtime is a lot more, maybe more than double that amount and with 159 weeks passed, due to the fact that I had played the game with a pirated copy, it was so great for me that I ended up buying it with my newly made credit card. If anyone doub it, you can check my achivements, about 40 of them was collected at the same time.
Darkest Dungeon has great concept and also executed that concept pretty well, it is very punishing, I must admit, but also exciting and rewarding, seeing your heroes and the Hamlet (your base, sort of) grows makes you yearn for more gold, heirloom and trinkets, pushing you into more expidition, I was once played this game for straight 8 hours non stop because of that.
I didn't plan to make this review far too long so I'll summerize the good and bad of this game for anyone who read this.
***The Good:
- Great concept (stress, resolve, quirk,... all are new to me).
- Great variety of hero with numerous abilities and combat capabilities making every expidition feel fresh, due to diffent strategies apply to different combination of heroes.
- Addictive, the game is quite grindy before the introduction of antiquarian (a new type of hero that sacrifice combat power in exchange for more loot) but it gives you a sense of accomplishment, your heroes grow in power and Hamlet become unlocked with more options.
- Lots of variety in both bosses and enemies, the boss are not that many and got recycled twice but they are well designed and challenging.
***Ok, that's might be all of the good side of the game which I could think of at the moment, now for the bad side:
- Too punishing, every hero cost tons of gold to upgrade and can be reduced to ashes with a critical hit (which happens a lot in champion dungeons), I don't mind the heart attack (which reduce your hero health to 0 or kill them at Death's door) because it usually happens when you don't know when to stop being too greedy.
The thing is, enemy's attack at higher level usually has side effects, like blight and bleed, they also has high speed, making them almost always move first and thus saving your hero become almost impossible.
- Too many trinkets with the same positive and/or negative affects: about 70% of trinket reduce your speed (which determine who move first), there's also a lot of trinkets which increase damage or health, this leads to equiping trinkets a less strategic job and a more grindy job (you have fight more to advance the time and for the perfect trinket to appear as a reward).
- Rely too much on luck, this is perharps what I hated the most, some might argue to it's not, but in my opinion, RNG (random number generator) affects far too much on the game, let's take the boss fights as example:
+ I am going to kill the Prophet, but ended up on a large dungeon with far too many rooms and strong monsters, by the time I reached the boss, my team are already exhausted, thus making the fight far more punishing than normal, on the other time, when I have to kill the Siren, I only encounter a few weak monsters in a small, straightforward dungeon, the boss fight suddenly becomes a  walk in the park.
+ I think some people might say that is fair, at times you get a lot of critical, dodges,... other time enemy got luckier than you,...etc. Well, that might be fair but at least I SHOULD be in control a bit more.
Here's another example: traps cannot be avoided unless you scout the paths first, but how to do that? RNG do that, even when you see the trap, you still need to rely on luck (the hero's percentage of disarming traps).
Why dont they put into a supply item to detect and disarming traps? It will take rooms in the backpack and cost gold in exchange for more safety. And so on, there's still a lot of other examples that the game designers embrace the RNG mechanics too much.
*************************************
Well, time to end this review, in conclusion, I only recommend this game for players who likes turn based combat and RNG based games like Xcom, with an acceptance for loss in mind (you can also be a softcore player like me by turning off the "high difficulty" options in the game, nothing to be ashamed about to me, the default difficulty is mostly require more luck and more grind anyway). Remember though, RNG is a major factor in this game, even more than XCOM, so take your time to considerate.
If you manage to read till this line then please take my thanks and I hope for you made the right decision on buying this game or not, be careful, I didn't take on the New Game+ mode yet and I made the game a bit easier than normal so this review might not reflect the full value of this game.

XCOM 2 is a turn-based strategy developed by Firaxis and published by 2K Games. It is a direct sequel to the previous XCOM: Enemy Unknown and the expansion XCOM: Enemy Within.
In XCOM 2, follows the story where the XCOM lose the war to the alien. The aliens rule Earth, building shining cities that promise a brilliant future for humanity on the surface, while concealing a sinister agenda and eliminating all who dissent from their new order. So they said it, we are now on the offensive on XCOM 2. With only limited resources, XCOM must retake back Earth from the ADVENT.
XCOM 2 gameplay are quite similiar with XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but plays differently. In fact, you feel like you already knew how it plays out until you see the timer. Yes, each mission has a time limit to reach certain objectives. But most people describe it wrong as a turn timer or whatever it is they said. The truth is, it's a turn limit to reach certain objectives such as hacking a device, rescuing VIP or destroying key objectives. Most of them if completed, then the timer is gone and you can have all the time you want to kill the enemy. NOT all missions has this turn limit objectives however. Overwatch in XCOM 2 is even more powerful I think, even if some people didn't like the turn limit, overwatch now doesn't trigger all at once, they trigger one by one that you can be sure every overwatch is count. Base building retains the same element but building adjacent bonuses are gone, instead you get to upgrades with resources. The global map have been changed too. Since you have a mobile headquarters, in the global map, you need to move from place to place to scan for resources, intel or even contacting resistance on other location.
There is this thing called Avatar Project or simply AP by the community, I think, it renders your campaign has time limit which you have to act fast to delay or setback the project progress. You can do this by assaulting alien bases or hacking then kill the alien codex. There's also Dark Event, which some kind of random even that if left unchecked will, I say again WILL give you disadvantage and give the alien an advantage. Like XCOM: Enemy Unknown abduction mission, not all Dark Event mission can't be completed, you have to choose which you think is the best... or the worse. All of this makes your campaign has faster pace then the previous.
Tactical combat also has become more difficult, at least for me. I can see more challenge here. Remember Sectoid? They're not what you remember now, they posses more power and can mess you up if you don't kill them real quick. What about Thin Man? Now you will see the true form of the alien infiltration unit. Soldiers now also has even more useful abilities, some are in fact powerful if you know how to use them. Soldiers can even be upgraded further to gain more advantage, whether it's a weapon or the soldier themselves. Turn limit may be frustrating, but in my opinion they're not as frustrating as some people said.
Customization in XCOM 2 are great, I will say huge if they actually add more content or option into it, nevertheless we have modding support. There is a dedicated place where you can create you characters before you even play the campaign. Characters you created can be set to appear as XCOM soldiers, or VIP which is scientist or engineer, or even Dark VIP which will appear on some mission and you must capture them. With mods, customization will be unlimited.
Firaxis did improve the graphics and effects on XCOM 2. They look prettier than XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The downside XCOM 2 has is the performance. It is unoptimized that I can barely have FPS above 35. Most of the time I get stutters and lags. Mission loading time is quite long. They need to fix this.
Overall, XCOM 2 is a great sequel. Some people don't like the turn limit, but for me, knowing that we are on the offensive with guerilla style warfare, that's just about fair and challenging. With mods support is even better. If only the performance were better on release, I would give XCOM 2 way better score. I recommend XCOM 2.
Rating 7/10
