There's so much good about this game I'm not sure where to start... But I'll do my best.
First of all, the game has fantastic storytelling and narration. The meloncholy voice confessing his sins and warning you about what might be ahead really leaves you in a sense of suspense, and it really keeps that dark, end of the world type of tone in the game, where you otherwise might just think "Oh it's time to skip into the dungeon and loot it again!"
Second of all, the game is, for the most part, very fair. People often complain about RNG, but this often causes their defeat because they become too comfortable with smooth runs, and aren't prepared for the worst when it finally happens. While a hero dying is permanent, you'll often be given so many chances to save them. A hero can
been one-shot, in
circumstance. Instead, they enter death's door, where every hit beyond that has a chance to kill them permanently(If you want to understand this mechanic further, please research it online, there's plenty of info.)
Thirdly, the art. The art looks fantastic! It really drips with that Lovecraftian feel. The characters all look really unique, and the locations are as eerie as ever.
Of course, the game also comes with the unique stress system. While it is the idea that's supposed to keep the game so unique and seperate from others, it actually feels more like a secondary health bar. You try to keep it under control, and it will sometimes require maintenance outside of the dungeon, because your heroes do not instantly go to 0 stress after a mission, while they will fully heal afterwards(odd, eh?)
The only negative thing I can say about the game is that it feels like it hangs around a little longer than neccessary. With a lot of skill, you can clear the game in a reletively short time, but the endgame is
difficult, and unless you find the information online, will probably consist of some trial-and-error. The problem is, because the permadeath, you'll find yourself having to re-train heroes from step 1 to retry the final dungeon. This can make the length feel a bit inflated for anyone unable to overcome that final hurdle.
Overall, I'd say the game is fantastic, though I bought it on sale, I feel it was completely worth $15.
PS: I normally despise turn-based games that don't involve 3D movement.

Oh, this game. This, great yet horrible game.
I've gotten pretty far into the game. I'm finishing up with the 5* Hall of Heroes mission and I think I've seen enough of this game to review it well.
Let's start off with the storyline.
Your nation was in some kind of Morai Wars or something with another nation and nearly went extinct. Considering how the armor on the Spiral Order (your nation) NPCs and yours looks, and how the ranking system works, it's obvious they're militiary. This leads me to believe that it was them that started this war, even though it says nothing of the war's origin. How fun.
Anyways, to escape extinction, the Spiral Order rushes off in space to find some way or somewhere to retreat. While rushing along, their ship's low power is miraculously saved by a planet that has a core with an immense amount of power. Just as they begin to try to locate and extract the power, they get shot down by magical beams coming from the planet.
They send out tons of escape pods down to the planet and those who are left on the ship without the escape pod has stuff happen to them. I don't know. It doesn't say.
Anyways, this is where you come in. you, in one of these escape pods, find yourself in a jungle-ish area, and after getting through a few living jelly cubes and oversized lizards, you meet up with a fellow survivor. Sadly, it's an NPC survivor that does 2% of the work for you and he stays with you for the next 2 or 3 missions.
Anyways, after travelling for a minute you meet up with a captain and two other random people, a mini-boss comes out of nowhere, you again do 90% the work, they commend you after defeating the boss, and you go to this rescue camp.
That's as far as I'm gonna go. You want to see the rest of the story? Good luck. It's extremely drawn out after this.
Next up - Art Style.
The art style for this game is actually pretty good. It's bright and colorful every single time, and yet still somehow is able to put creepy skeleton zombies and ghosts and still be pretty colorful.
The design for the weapons and armor is even better. What's more awesome than pulling out an intense sword with a visible combustion engine? (Yes, COMBUSTION ENGINE)
And then the armor. The actually defensive armor has good-ish looks but once you get into the costume armor, you can really get some awesome looks. What's even better is you can add accessories to your gear that can make it look even more awesome. The awesome thing is that you can make your knight look heavenly with a bright white aura and white/bright blue costume and accessories, all the way to a dark, demonlike look with black/dark purple or red auras with the matching costume and accessories. Fun stuff.
And then the enemies. Some of the enemies look like they just took a shape, recolored it, and called it done (*cough* jelly cubes *cough*) but some look like there was lots of detail put into it, like the once-per-year Tortodrones, the devillites, the wolvers, the gremlins, the mecha-knights, and much more.
Next up - Gameplay.
The gameplay for this game is extremely different than any other, it might seem a bit farmilliar with the up and down camera and with the 1-9 keys doing stuff, but it seperates itself from other gameplay types somehow. the 1-3 keys are kept for the battle sprite abilities. Battle sprites are sort of like your "pets", but instead of being cute and harmless they engulf your enemies with immense fireballs, stick them with tons of needles the size of your character, and incenerate them with godly light beams. And those are only the starter abilities. Scary things, they are.
The core gameplay boils down to three playstyles and four damage systems. The three playstyles are Swording, Gunning, and Bombing. Swordies are the most common because it's the easiest to master and actually has the most balance compared to the others. More on that later. They also have the most variety of weapons. Swords work like swords work. Most swords have a three swipe combo, though faster swords may have larger combos and slower swords have smaller combos. The most I've seen is 2-swipe combo for slowest and 10-swipe combo for fastest. The funny thing is that they both take the same amount of time to complete the combo.
Gunners are the second most common because it's fun to master and sooner or later a massive update is going to be released just for them. The thing is that a year or two ago they promised "Gunner update this November" and at November they said "Release date pushed back" and so far, not much about it from them, other than the occasional "We'll have it soon."
You know what you will have soon? I bet another. Gosh darn. PROMO. Anyways, guns work like, well, guns. Usually the clips are two or three shots big, balanced by unlimited ammo and .5 second reload time.
Then there's the bombers. Since the bombers have boiled down to at least 2 or 3 weapon lines and 1 armor line that barely covers half of their weaknessess, it takes some real dedication to try to be one. Bombs work by charging up the bomb by holding down the attack button, and once it's charged you set it down, and after a second or two, it explodes in a massive AOE spread.
The four basic types of damage are Normal, Shadow, Elemental, and Piercing. Normal damage is what appears most often in the beginning of the game, then it spreads to the other three. The annoying thing is that different monsters are resistant or weak to different damage types, which leaves those who want to always be ready no choice than to get three weapons, three helmets, three armors, and three shields just so they can always be ready. Otherwise there's always that one or two monster types that always get them. And let me tell you, it's hard enough getting one good item in this game. Having to get 9 is nearly impossible.
The different monster types are Slime, Construct, Gremlin, Beast, Fiend, and Undead. Slime and Beast monsters deal Piercing damage, Construct and Gremlin monsters deal Elemental damage, and Fiend and Undead monsters deal Shadow damage. Beast and Fiend monsters are weak to Piercing damage, Construct and Undead monsters are weak to Elemental damage, and Gremlin and Slime monsters are weak to Shadow damage. Slime and Construct monsters are resistant to Piercing damage, Gremlin and Beast monsters are resistant to Elemental damage, and Fiend and Undead are resistant to shadow damage. It's sorta confusing at first, but eventually you memorize it.
Now, for the final aspect - Balancing!
Put in short terms, this game has next to no balancing. Where there is balancing, the balance is overused by players and makes you look like just the common player. Some people are fine with that. I'm not.
Anyways, the leveling system for items in this game is extremely unbalanced. There are two leveling systems - Heating and Upgrading. Heating is a basic level 1-10 system who's only unbalance is its overly encumbering cost. The Upgrading is what I'm looking at here. There's 0-5 stars in upgrading. 0 and 1 star items, even at the levels they're meant to be used at, seem useless. Once you go from 1 star to 2 star though, there's a huge jump in power. Where 1 star items had maybe 1 or 1.5 bars of strength in its stat meter thingy, 2 star items have 3 or so. Huge jump. Then going from 2 to 3 stars is a bit normal, but suddenly where 3 star items had 4 bars or so, 4 stars have around 6. Big jump again. Then going  to five stars in normal again, thankfully. The game tries to explain this by splitting them into tiers, 0-1 star being Tier One, 2-3 star being Tier Two, and 4-5 star being Tier Three, but it still makes me a bit uncomfortable how it jumps so much.
Oh look, I've ran out of room to type. Oh well. No more ranting for me.
TL;DR - Strange story, great art, fun gameplay, horrible balancing. 6.5/10 for me. Still fun. Ish.

This is a review that includes 158 mods that took me three weeks to work in harmony (no crashes). It greatly influences the experience I have with the game so keep that in mind.
I played Fallout 4 on console before and enjoyed the experience, but it felt really monotone half way through. There was little to no challenge and the only moments you died pretty much meant that I overextended and jumped into a fight like a mad person. Not long later I also got the PC version for survival mode (beta) and my jaw dropped down. Fallout 4 just transformed itself into one of the best (if not THE best) singleplayer survival game ever to be released. Yet still... Halfway through the game became monotone. Why? Because the skills in the game make you insanely overpowered and the challenge you feel in the beginning slowely becomes a joke. Combine this with a storyline that rarely makes you feel like you need to make a tough decision, choose sides or kill someone you thought was on your side for a long time. Fallout 4 felt like it had no impact on how I feel about people. Quests felt like chapters with little to no consequenses. Because if you played like an mercenary ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you would actually make it easier on yourself to earn caps and good gear.
So then I waited a few years, let the game evolve (DLC), let modders implement their idea's and try again. Big gameplay overhoal mods like Horizon from Zawinul, Sim Settlements and tons of graphics mods made this game feel like a living world. I tweaked my experience to feel like the most realistic survival game with proper gameplay tweaks to make the game feel like a blast. It worked, Fallout 4 just became the game I put over 600 hours in and probably will add a few hundred more.
I'm the type of gamer who likes the rollercoaster ride of a liniar story, but also want the impact of my descisions whenever possible. Fallout 4 is the mix between the two, yet I understand the critisism it gets because it stepped away from the depth Fallout New Vegas gave. But... This survival options enhanced with a few mods made it that every hour I wasn't playing, I missed playing the game. The gunfights are great, the breaks between fighting and storytelling feel great. Being forced by the mod Horizon to walk back to your town, swap ammo and weapons because you ran out of resources to use one weapon. For me, the trade of a little less depth in story and gameplay makes up entirely by the depth of the survival experience. Having to walk through the entire world (later getting some type of fast travel by Horizon (at the cost of lots of caps) makes for a great experience. It makes me feel like I'm part of a world that I have to adapt too. And the Horizon survival experience makes every choice a tactical choice expecially in the beginning.
Two DLC additions that are really worth mentioning. Automatron and Far Harbor. Automatron is the most fun if you like to tune Curie (companion) into a sweet French speaking death machine who reminds me of the turrets from portal. She doesn't want to, but she will absolutely wreck anything standing in her way if you give her some powerfull tools. Great fun, but not that long. When the story is done you basically have a new base and the option to tweak your robot followers.
Far Harbor... man. This is how the entire game should have been. Powerfull choices, deep and engaging story. Loads of trust and assumptions. An actual detective story. DO NOT forget to bring Nick Valentine with you, he is essential for the full experience. I mean, Far Harbor compared to the Commonwealth (the regular envirionment) looks amazing. The fog, the forest area and the creepy vibe. Combine this with the mod True Storms and you will get attacked by random ghouls during rad storms to keep you on your toes and keep the entire area feel alive eventhough you cleared most of it. If the new Fallout New Vegas 2 is taking the recipe from Fallout 4, they should make it like Far Harbor in a bigger world. It is that great. Even the addition of small hills makes up for an entirely new landscape that is more than some anoying height increase in the commonwealth.
I'm running 158 mods without a crash. This took me three weeks and a lot of patience to work. All I can say is that is was worth it 100%. I have a strong pc, but with this amount of mods I cannot run a ENB (visual enhancer), so I tweaked it in different ways. I have actual flashlights now instead of that weird radiant light. I have thick and heavy storms, my companions actually feel different. There are more trees and there is actual grass. No more health regeneration, but actual preperation (Horizon) before each trip. Weapons that aren't all prestine, but some are entirely♥♥♥♥♥♥so the search for functioning weapons becomes a real thing. Melee being an actual addition of you want (NEED) to save ammo. Having Dogmeat with you with another companion and actually finding out that the game originally was designed that way. I mean, I could talk about it for hours. Good and realistic mods are like the cherry on the cake.
Reading back my review I barely say anything negative. You can read other reviews for that so I won't actually say anything new. More important is that Fallout 4 with DLC and mods is one of my favorite games, maybe even my favorite game of all time. To give the game a rating:
Fallout 4 base game: 7/10
Fallout 4 with (all) DLC: 8/10
(Far Harbor DLC: 9/10)
Fallout 4 with DLC and mods: 9/10
Keep in mind that the story is still the same, and most other things that are a little "meh" are still the same. I stopped looking at Fallout 4 as the RPG I hoped it would be, but as a post apocalyptic Survival game. And really..? It is one of the best experiences out there. Really the only thing it lacks is having a real friend by your side. I really feel like Fallout New Vegas 2 should have a survival option from the get go, because if not... I will go and wait until it has.

There's so much good about this game I'm not sure where to start... But I'll do my best.
First of all, the game has fantastic storytelling and narration. The meloncholy voice confessing his sins and warning you about what might be ahead really leaves you in a sense of suspense, and it really keeps that dark, end of the world type of tone in the game, where you otherwise might just think "Oh it's time to skip into the dungeon and loot it again!"
Second of all, the game is, for the most part, very fair. People often complain about RNG, but this often causes their defeat because they become too comfortable with smooth runs, and aren't prepared for the worst when it finally happens. While a hero dying is permanent, you'll often be given so many chances to save them. A hero can
been one-shot, in
circumstance. Instead, they enter death's door, where every hit beyond that has a chance to kill them permanently(If you want to understand this mechanic further, please research it online, there's plenty of info.)
Thirdly, the art. The art looks fantastic! It really drips with that Lovecraftian feel. The characters all look really unique, and the locations are as eerie as ever.
Of course, the game also comes with the unique stress system. While it is the idea that's supposed to keep the game so unique and seperate from others, it actually feels more like a secondary health bar. You try to keep it under control, and it will sometimes require maintenance outside of the dungeon, because your heroes do not instantly go to 0 stress after a mission, while they will fully heal afterwards(odd, eh?)
The only negative thing I can say about the game is that it feels like it hangs around a little longer than neccessary. With a lot of skill, you can clear the game in a reletively short time, but the endgame is
difficult, and unless you find the information online, will probably consist of some trial-and-error. The problem is, because the permadeath, you'll find yourself having to re-train heroes from step 1 to retry the final dungeon. This can make the length feel a bit inflated for anyone unable to overcome that final hurdle.
Overall, I'd say the game is fantastic, though I bought it on sale, I feel it was completely worth $15.
PS: I normally despise turn-based games that don't involve 3D movement.

I'm gonna tell you right out the gate, fallout 4 is no where near as good as fallout 3 or fallout new Vegas from story standpoint.
I hate the way VATS performs now, I seriously hate it, it's terrible. VATS was something I almost relied upon in previous games, but here I will almost never use it. I also think the Commonwealth is the smallest map yet in a fallout game, which is another con for me. I'm noticing that I can find most of the locations in the Commonwealth in half the time it took me to in fallout 3 and new vegas.
That's the main drawback. I personally feel it also doesn't hold up as well on very specific aspects, but these are just knit picks on my part, not actual problems with the game design. Overall, this game completely anniahlates the previous 2 fallouts graphics wise, without question. That, and the introduction of settlement building are 2 of the strongest points of this game.
Another very nice touch is how they revamped entirely how power armor is utilized. In previous games it was simply a outfit  (a very heavy one) like all other outfits that could be equipped and unequipped at will. However, since it provides the best protection of anything else and was very heavy, it meant that every late game character would most likely be wearing power armor of some form. (Mainly the case of fallout 3. Fallout new Vegas had non power armor options that were on par with them.) However, in fallout 4, power armor is not a outfit, it is more like a vehicle, that needs to be fueled off a consumable power core, but gives you incredible durability and other utilities. In essence. .......power armor now feels exactly how it was meant to feel....like a suit of armor that you take care of and customize,  and take into battle, just like the knights of medieval days. And that is the way it should be from here on out.
The story, while it does carry some weight, is completely forgettable as soon as you get to diamond city. After that, it's either you pursue it further under your own willpower, or..........GATHER RESOURCES, BUILD SETTLEMENT, INSTALL NUDE MODS, EXPLORE, FIND BADASS GEAR........wait, what the F was the main story again?  Oh right,  lul -_- Someone told me this before I bought this game and let me tell you, it will certainly happen like this for most of you, the story is just not very engaging. Sure it's sad and tragic, but it's made even more tragic by the fact that 90% of us forgot about it until sometime around building our 3 settlement and managing a trade caravan empire.
Finally weapon customization, I guess it's alright, and it is time consuming, so is armor building, they are both very well implemented and offers lots of possibilities to fit each playstyle, but as far as creating anything goes, the real highlight of the game.......is settlement building and mods. These 2 things alone are what truly set fallout 4 as a game desErving of great reviews and high recognition as a great game.
Every fallout fan....should be here right now. Every newcomer, should be looking to try fallout 3 and new Vegas first, and then come here. That is the only way to truly appreciate what this game does right in my opinion, otherwise you might take it for granted. I really wish I could say this was the best dark souls game, I really do. Unfortunately, that would be false. My complaints are as follows: It's way too linear for a dark souls game. The location of the coals reduces early-game build variety. Inability to be invaded after bosses makes it harder to invade or do PvP. The FP system makes it harder to survive in PvP as a caster. Roll-Spam is the obvious abundant strategy. Estus drinking is nearly unpunishable. Too many bosses have some gimmick you need to defeat them ex. Yhorm, Ancient Wyvern. Weapon arts are cool, but are mostly useless. There are definitely a few good bosses ex. Nameless King, Soul of Cinder. However, they are, for the most part, fairly average. Covenants are pretty much all the same. Almost every NPC is just a reference to a previous character in the series, which grants me no shortage of dismay. As for graphical quality, the game is very pretty, a lot of work went into Firelink Shrine especially. The enemies are very well designed, you can really see that the world is in a state of regression especially in the Undead Settlement through enemies and environment. The music is prety good, some of the boss battles have very memorable music such as the Soul of Cinder. Both DLC are pretty good, the latter one being a good bit better, but both come together for an overarching story. All in all, it's good, just not as good as previous games in many aspects, while still being more technically impressive.

I adored this game, though be advised it is most certainly not for everyone. It is a very challenging game and the more I played the more i realized how much thought you really have to put into how you form your teams, it's not just a matter of throwing 4 heroes into a dungeon and hoping it works out, there are many synergies between characters that you have to look for, and when you find them, it really pays off. Now as for the story, I personally loved it, but it is a heavily lovecraftian inspired story, and if you don't know what that is, basically it means things are bad, are always going to be bad, and odds are you aren't going to get a super happy and up-beat ending. Despite that, it is a very satisfying game, both in gameplay and story, but you have to be ready for frustration, bad luck, and bad initiative rolls. I can't count how many times a character died to blight or bleed because they happened to go before my healer for the first time in 5 dungeons. So be warned, I highly recommend this game, but it can take a lot of time, effort and tears to beat it, but if you are into lovecraftian lore and story, you will love every moment of it.

A vastly improved and expanded character creation system, a dynamic world map game, and the challenging task of building up the resistance while trying not to be crushed by our new overlords, there's quite a bit to love here and it's enough of it's own game that it doesn't just serve to replace the original.

Welcome to the world of DayZ, hit by a new and presently unknown infection which has wiped out most of the world's population. You are one of the few that have survived and now you must search this new wasteland in order to fight for your life against what is left of the indigenous population now infected with the disease. Go solo, team up with friends or take on the world, as you choose your path in this brutal and chilling landscape using whatever means you stumble upon to survive.
This is DayZ, this is your story.
DayZ is a gritty, authentic, open-world survival horror hybrid-MMO game, in which players follow a single goal: to survive in the harsh post-apocalyptic landscape as long as they can. Players can experience powerful events and emotions arising from the ever-evolving emergent gameplay. There are no superficial tips, waypoints, built in tutorials or help given to players. Every decision matters, there are no save games, no extra lives, every mistake can be lethal. If you fail, you lose everything and you need to play again from the beginning with nothing but your wits, and your two hands. Fight the hostile environment, where every other player can be friend or foe and nothing can be taken for granted.
KEY FEATURES IN ALPHA
Chernarus - 230 sq. km chunk of post soviet state, featuring deep forests, cities, villages, abandoned military bases, and more..
Up to 50 players per server - Rich server / client architecture developed from scratch.
Persistent player profile - Key player data is persistent across all servers.
Inventory – Combine various clothing items, equipment and carry all of the items that you will need to survive the harsh new environment in the open and intuitive inventory system developed to answer the needs of crafting and character customization.
Crafting - In the apocalyptic world of DayZ, resources are sparse and every useful bit should be utilized. Items or equipment can be improved, turned into something else or fixed using the new crafting mechanisms.
Weapon customization – Use customizable firearms with authentic ballistics and weapon characteristics as well as melee weapons to protect yourself against all the dangers a survivor may face.
Customizable clothing – Customize your survivor with a multitude of new clothing items that can be scavenged from the remnants of civilization, which provide various degree of protection against the elements, infected, and other survivors.
Be wary of addiction.

This game is still EA so I'll keep that in mind in my review:
Pros:
-I like the F1, F2 and F3 loadout feature. If you played Ghost In The Shell: SAC then you'll be familiar with it.
You pick a primary, secondary, melee, grenade and other equipment relevant to that playstyle per F slot. During games you can quickly switch between these presets after death to choose a different playstyle.
-Graphically the game looks great.
-The maps are well thought out.
-Based on the amount of firearms in the game, I suspect there will be a lot of choice in the future.
-Blood on the walls after you kill someone.
Cons:
-No sprint option, you have to use a knife to run. This makes me sad. I like my games realistic and with all the other efforts this game chose to make that so, you'd figure this would be too.
-Health is not based on parts of your body, except the head which is an instant kill. I'd very much rather see arms, legs and torso have their own HP with lowering movement speed if legs are damaged and lowering accuracy if arms are damaged.
-No stamina bar, so bunny hoppers run rampant. This will also allow for greater success with aimbots.
tl;dr: This game looks great and plays well. It still has a chance to improve. I'll be checking in on it and suggest you do the same. 7/10 will keep installed.

The second major problem is its pacing. This game has missions with varying levels of diffcults easy, medium, and veteran. if you try to take a group on a medium level mission and your whole group doesnt have atlest level 3 gear and abilities your going to have a really hard time. so now to make it easier your going to have to upgrade them and to do this first you'll have to upgrade the blacksmith and Guild, then you'll have to pay for the gear upgrades and abilities and this is very time consuming and makes the game very grindy. well thats it for negatives lets move to the postives. There are so many good things about this game! Here's a couple of them.
Do you all remember Terraria, where you always ran around building stuff, and eventually running out of space?
Well, Starbound spans across a whole universe, letting you build whatever you want.

These are only a few of the many great things of Starbound, and it's only in Beta! So buy the game, and join the adventure.

Ancient evils of unfathomable dimensions lie within the manor of the ancestor, awoken horrors, ritualized flesh, drowned mariners, gibbering madmen driven insane by a sheer glimpse of what lies beneath - this game has it all.
It is probably one of the best games I have ever played. Period. I started over an over again, because this game holds so much replay value and is so shrewdly designed that one can feel H.P. Lovecraft from the very beginning if one ever read him. (If you want to, start with Dagon, which is where the fish-men in the cove were inspired from.)
As my personal preference of RPGs is clearly in the department of turn-based RPGs, I do know when a game is bad, acceptable or incredibly amazing. This game is probably a 97+ out of 100 in my books.
Sometimes I see that people wouldn't endorse this game and rather give this game a negative review - well, of course, if you are an illiterate bag of mucus and have no idea where the eerie, enchanting atmosphere or the obscure narration comes from, it might not be yours. I reckon you should go back to candy crush then.
As I have mentioned before, this game is brilliant. It is in every single way; there is literally nothing to be held against it. Of course, RNG can get you, but RNG can always get you, it ain't nothing new - if you play Borderlands, Magic: the Gathering, Hearthstone, or Darkest Dungeon, it is all the same - RNG just happens.
This game will punish you for being careless and for not thinking through your turns, it will also punish you for wrong decisions in building up a party or their move sets, but I'd rather have an unforgiving game than I would have a game which is a cakewalk. The so called stress system in the game might be the one feature which is probably affected the most by the RNG, but still, this is not a negative element, it just adds to the experience. I am very happy that the game is very grindy (you need A LOT of heirlooms to upgrade your town buildings), because it guarantees that you will have a lot to do until you are ready to go to see what incomprehensible power of cosmic descent the great old ones have infused the ancestor with.
This is not only a game. This is a piece of ART, dammit. So fondly crafted, it stands as one of its kind; I sincerely doubt there will be a game in this lovecraftian genre which could compete with the picturesque beauty of narration and visualisation. As a lover of classic literature and art, I do know and respect the work of men who are enriching the world with beauty, as the world itself holds so little of it that we can find before we descend back into the earth we emerged from.
"Thus the living, lone and sobbing,
In the throes of anguish throbbing,
With the loathsome Furies robbing
Night and noon of peace and rest.
But beyond the groans and grating
Of abhorrent Life, is waiting
Sweet Oblivion, culminating
All the years of fruitless quest."
- H.P. Lovecraft "Despair"

Well as a gamer and a developer I'm split on my opinion.  I'm a bit disappointed that the game hasn't been fully stabalized before release.  As a developer I understand the huge challenge of this game.  Like as usual 2K tries to takes on a overly ambigious task.  First off.  If your not a developer and just a gamer, you probably think that a turn based game is a simple deal and no where near as complex as a FPS.  And in actuallity you couldn't be more wrong.  Turn based strategies with destructive structures is VERY difficult to build.  Please refer to all the ridiculous bugs that occurred in the original Xcom (DOS) even after patches.  Xcom has a tradition of borderline never being finished long after it's been released.  But the really truly crazy task 2K took on is releasing all 3 PC platforms at once.  Mac, Windows and Linux.  Again sounds like a simple enough deal to do because the Unreal engine supports every platform known.  While it is easy to build all three platforms its incredibly difficult to stablize and optimize all 3 platforms at once.  Normally this task is something you would see a early release indie game maker attempt and hideously get behind schedule on the official release but it doesn't matter because of their early release status.
My original plan for this game was to buy it (bundled with the Steam controller) and just wait for the first round of patches to come out before playing it as I knew a head of time this is a bit ambigious of a project in particular to its release date.  BUT since so many gamer were complaining I had to check it out.  After playing it.  Yeah its got stablization/optimization issues... not huge surprise.  But the game play is actually pretty damn cool.  Building destruct with better realism and can even catch fire.  What a novel challenge to face with my sniper on a roof and trying to stay ahead of the burning and collapsing building.   I believe the original Xcom or  was it Xcom 2 for DOS actually had burning buildings as well but the graphics in the game was hard to read  and was confusing to understand what was going on.   The stealth element in this game adds a huge new aspect to the game.   I found it to be pretty cool and the pace is a lot faster... requires combat strategy not a Rude Goldberg / Sherlock Holmes master mind strategy.
Bottomline... looking forward to when this game stabilizes and don't regret dropping the money on it.  AND it is showing me that a big 3 release is getting pretty close to a real possibility for those releasing on a schedule and that Mac and Linux can and SHOULD be taken serious as a game platform.

I have to say. Firaxis did a pretty good job following up on Enemy Unknown/Within. XCOM 2 is an involved and potentially punishing experience, but its difficulty curve is a huge improvement from EU. No more inverse difficultly curve, and if you screw up, you'll probably have a chance or two to turn things around. I was about to ragequit my first campaign, after a particulary devastating loss followed by a retalation mission, but I was able to take risks to put the campaign back on track, something that may not have been possible to pull off in EU. The game's new classes, items and other features offer a variety of in-depth systems that offer an improvement over the original games, giving the player more choices and combinations to experiment with.
On the less positive side, the game does have opitimzation problems, with a wonky camera and some loading issues, something that I hope patches and driver updates will help fix. However, they tend to only effect the transitions, so the game is perfectly playable, if a bit choppy at times. It still looks better than I expected it to look on my GTX 750ti.
If you're a fan of the series, or of tactical squad-based games in general, I would definitely recommend it. It's an engaging, well designed, pretty looking game that promises more than a hundred hours of playtime, and probably more with mods and DLC. It fixes most of the problems with EU/EW, as well as crafting a novel experience.

This game is indeed hard, but not as hard as people say it is.
Playing cautiously is the key to mastering this game. Chances are, if you dive into the game expecting the fast-paced action of modern games, you will put yourself into the position of being punished by ambushes and traps. Yes, the enemies can be tough to deal with, but there are multiple methods to take care of them.
This is true for single-player experiences. It is a completely different matter in the multiplayer aspect of the game.
Multiplayer:
Take what I said about being cautious, but add enemy players to the mix. Now be extremely cautious.
If you don't want to deal with invaders (players who join your game to kill you), don't be under an ember. Commit suicide to lose your ember. There are many ways to to kill yourslef in firelink shrine which is the safe area.
If you want to play with friends, expect more invasions.
What makes the game fun:
For me, it was the sense of progression. The game is set-up in a way so that as you get through the game, you notice your character getting stronger. Whether it's because you leveled up your stats or found better equipment, enemies that you had trouble with earlier are push-overs later. Not to mention, you get cooler looking equipment the further you go.
Claymore = Basic slow swings --> Greatsword = Still slow, but more damage --> Farron Greatsword = Laws of physics be damned!
Don't be ashamed of using guides for this game. Many items are hidden and require prior knowledge to collect. Quests such as the "Lord of Hollows" do not tell you how to get from point A to point B.
Is the game worth the full price-tag treatment? Well, no. $60 and more for DLC is overpriced for any one game. But, if a sale comes on for the deluxe edition that is less than $60, then you should buy it immediatly.

"Hey, Commander! I recently bought this new strategy game. It is called Chess - The X-Com 2 Edition!"
"An X-Com 2 edition of chess?" the commander replied. "What's different about it, Colonel?"
"I'll teach you. You can be the white knights of X-Com, I shall be the black Advent aliens."
They started playing.
"Ha, I've got you now!" the commander said, grinning, as his knight attacked the colonel's bishop.
"Not so fast! First we need to spin this." The colonel pointed to a roulette wheel that came in the box. "You see, whether a piece can take another piece is random! Fun!"
The commander seemed unsure about this concept. "That makes no sense," he said. "My knight is clearly right in front of that bishop, and he is well trained, so why would he not succeed? Ah, whatever, just spin the damn wheel."
A few minutes later, the commander's peasant moved close to the colonel's queen. Quickly, the colonel moved several pieces out of the way and placed a new knight on the board, which defeated the commander's peasant. The colonel was so into the game that he did all this in slow motion, like a kid playing with action figures.
"What the hell did you just do, soldier?!"
"Oh, that's a rule," the colonel said excitedly. "The black advents get free moves while it's your turn to play, and some newly appearing pieces even get to hit your pieces without the roulette wheel most of the time!"
"Are you kidding me?!" the commander said, an incredulous look on his face. "This is not a strategy game if you have random events like this. And in a turn-based game, pay attention to whose turn it is! Oh, and for the love of advent burgers, stop with the slow motion and killing animations already! You're wasting my time!"
"Sorry, commander, but these are the rules! You chicken? If you'd like, you can just reload your piece and try the same turn again until the outcome suits you. Hmm, come to think of it...basing a game on a probabilistic scheme should always lead people to reload, which means any such system ends up being tedious and no fun for most players. Ha! This is pretty dumb game design, ha ha ha!" The colonel beamed anyway, pretending it was just difficult and challenging.
"I don't need no frickin reload!!"
They continued playing, the commander getting more and more frustrated with the strange rules of the game. Despite all odds, he ended up devising an ingenious strategy, circumnavigating the defenses of his subordinate, when suddenly ...
"Ooh, well," the colonel said. "You lose."
"What?"
"It has been 15 turns, and you have not defeated me yet, so you lose," the colonel explained. "Didn't I tell you? The white knights of X-Com only get a few turns to win the match. I already cheated on your behalf and gave you 7 more turns than normal."
"What in the absolute hell?!" the commander yelled. "That is the dumbest thing I've heard since the incident with the microwave casserole at Black Mesa! On the one hand, I am supposed to devise a strategy to avoid your stupid rules, but on the other hand, you give me no time to do so and waste half of that with roulette! This is not chess, this is not a strategy game, this is a casino!"
The colonel frowned and took a closer look at the box of the game. "Warning: May cause gambling addiction," he read. "Oh, so that's why I'm so hooked on this thing... Anyway, this casino-chess-simulator comes with a story, but it consists of many, many nearly identical matches like this, more time limits and forced gameplay, and I will also be compelled to explain your goal in every match as if you didn't know it already." The colonel smiled brightly. "We can try that, if you like -- you know, for the benefit of the story!"
The commander sighed. "Is the story any good, at least? Proper characters that grow and change as the plot unfolds? A fine ending with a shocking twist, a clever idea at its base and an emotionally significant boss battle?"
"Hmm..." The colonel's face fell a little. "Actually, at the end, I'm just going to throw a large number of pieces on the board for you to defeat, after which I shall act out a meaningless cutscene. The characters have as much personality as a sea slug and come from the planet of hats. Nothing else to it, I'm afraid. On the bright side, these chess pieces and the board are visually really impressive!"
At that moment, a piece glitched through the table and fell in a stuttering motion to the floor.
"Alright, that's it!", the commander yelled as he stood up. "I've had it with you and your badly designed games! We are going to use this one for target practice tomorrow! Star Wars Battlefront - The Board Game Edition, is relieved of this position immediately!"
"Aye, aye, sir!"

Recently finished the game on Commander.
I like it a lot and see it overall as a big improvement.
Short summary:
-Big Step up from Enemy Unknown in difficulty, a lot of people are going to have trouble with it because Enemy Unknown was a cake walk in comparison. It's not as hard as the Long War mod for the original, but its definately up there, just less mindless grinding than long war had is the greatest difference.
-Poor preformance issues all round, I turned down the big killer AA, but otherwise had everything else on high. I have a medium-high end rig, nothing amazing. I had around 40 fps constant, but sometimes it dipped pretty far. Annoying, but will probably be patched. Some people can't play at all which obviously needs to be fixed. The min specs are way below what they should have been given though.
-Much more action packed and tactical than Enemy Unknown, people hate the timers, theres a mod that removes it or gives you four more rounds. Personally I didn't have a problem with it, made me seriously tactically consider things far more than the orginal. I lost three people to timers, holding the line while my squad escaped. Love it. Some people will hate it becuase they want to go 100+ rounds spamming overwatch, doesnt work anymore I'm afraid.
-There are bugs, most definately. And then there are "bugs". The glass window two tiles over from your evac zone breaks due to ambient destruction and your evac point gets moved accross the map causing you to lose the mission. Thats a bug. The Vipers pulling you through walls but they can logically 'target' you and you them is not a bug people, get over it, you positioned poorly. Knocked out units been uncarriable so you lose them in evac is another big bug, happens fairly rarely though in my experience.
Overall I think its a huge leap forward and I really enjoyed it. A few patches for performance and bug fixing and it will be extremely solid. They could 'perhaps' tweak the difficulty on lower settings but I found Commander competitive and hope Legendary will be even more fun.
I'd give it a 8.5/10, 9/10 with a few performance patches.

Welcome to the world of DayZ, hit by a new and presently unknown infection which has wiped out most of the world's population. You are one of the few that have survived and now you must search this new wasteland in order to fight for your life against what is left of the indigenous population now infected with the disease. Go solo, team up with friends or take on the world, as you choose your path in this brutal and chilling landscape using whatever means you stumble upon to survive.
This is DayZ, this is your story.
DayZ is a gritty, authentic, open-world survival horror hybrid-MMO game, in which players follow a single goal: to survive in the harsh post-apocalyptic landscape as long as they can. Players can experience powerful events and emotions arising from the ever-evolving emergent gameplay. There are no superficial tips, waypoints, built in tutorials or help given to players. Every decision matters, there are no save games, no extra lives, every mistake can be lethal. If you fail, you lose everything and you need to play again from the beginning with nothing but your wits, and your two hands. Fight the hostile environment, where every other player can be friend or foe and nothing can be taken for granted.
KEY FEATURES IN ALPHA
Chernarus - 230 sq. km chunk of post soviet state, featuring deep forests, cities, villages, abandoned military bases, and more..
Up to 50 players per server - Rich server / client architecture developed from scratch.
Persistent player profile - Key player data is persistent across all servers.
Inventory – Combine various clothing items, equipment and carry all of the items that you will need to survive the harsh new environment in the open and intuitive inventory system developed to answer the needs of crafting and character customization.
Crafting - In the apocalyptic world of DayZ, resources are sparse and every useful bit should be utilized. Items or equipment can be improved, turned into something else or fixed using the new crafting mechanisms.
Weapon customization – Use customizable firearms with authentic ballistics and weapon characteristics as well as melee weapons to protect yourself against all the dangers a survivor may face.
Customizable clothing – Customize your survivor with a multitude of new clothing items that can be scavenged from the remnants of civilization, which provide various degree of protection against the elements, infected, and other survivors.

Ancient evils of unfathomable dimensions lie within the manor of the ancestor, awoken horrors, ritualized flesh, drowned mariners, gibbering madmen driven insane by a sheer glimpse of what lies beneath - this game has it all.
It is probably one of the best games I have ever played. Period. I started over an over again, because this game holds so much replay value and is so shrewdly designed that one can feel H.P. Lovecraft from the very beginning if one ever read him. (If you want to, start with Dagon, which is where the fish-men in the cove were inspired from.)
As my personal preference of RPGs is clearly in the department of turn-based RPGs, I do know when a game is bad, acceptable or incredibly amazing. This game is probably a 97+ out of 100 in my books.
Sometimes I see that people wouldn't endorse this game and rather give this game a negative review - well, of course, if you are an illiterate bag of mucus and have no idea where the eerie, enchanting atmosphere or the obscure narration comes from, it might not be yours. I reckon you should go back to candy crush then.
As I have mentioned before, this game is brilliant. It is in every single way; there is literally nothing to be held against it. Of course, RNG can get you, but RNG can always get you, it ain't nothing new - if you play Borderlands, Magic: the Gathering, Hearthstone, or Darkest Dungeon, it is all the same - RNG just happens.
This game will punish you for being careless and for not thinking through your turns, it will also punish you for wrong decisions in building up a party or their move sets, but I'd rather have an unforgiving game than I would have a game which is a cakewalk. The so called stress system in the game might be the one feature which is probably affected the most by the RNG, but still, this is not a negative element, it just adds to the experience. I am very happy that the game is very grindy (you need A LOT of heirlooms to upgrade your town buildings), because it guarantees that you will have a lot to do until you are ready to go to see what incomprehensible power of cosmic descent the great old ones have infused the ancestor with.
This is not only a game. This is a piece of ART, dammit. So fondly crafted, it stands as one of its kind; I sincerely doubt there will be a game in this lovecraftian genre which could compete with the picturesque beauty of narration and visualisation. As a lover of classic literature and art, I do know and respect the work of men who are enriching the world with beauty, as the world itself holds so little of it that we can find before we descend back into the earth we emerged from.
"Thus the living, lone and sobbing,
In the throes of anguish throbbing,
With the loathsome Furies robbing
Night and noon of peace and rest.
But beyond the groans and grating
Of abhorrent Life, is waiting
Sweet Oblivion, culminating
All the years of fruitless quest."
- H.P. Lovecraft "Despair"

Let me start by saying this game is overhyped by a rabid fanbase.
It has fun mechanics, hit detection is accurate, the weapon blows are satisfying and you have a decent variety of enemies.
The customization is above average, you can customize your playstyle and appearance somewhat freely except in situations where a certain weapon or gear gives a huge advantage against a specific type of enemy, if you're adamant about the way you look or play you can always summon another player to help you out temporarily.
Online pvp is idiotic as the player that invades your world always has a huge advantage due to being ignored by npcs, popping up in the most unfair and troublesome areas when you're the least prepared, there's the possibility that there are two or more invaders in your world at the same time and on top of it there's no type of skill matchmaking involved so you end up having to put up with the occasional ascended nerd, getting butchered and having to go back and progress through that area again.
The world itself is boring, i was just plowing through monsters for hours without any hint of story development, fans defend this using arguments such as: "you need to read item/souls descriptions", " you need to piece it together", "the lore is what you make of it as its open for interpretation" to me that's just lazy and and insipid i was also told that i needed to play the previous ones to understand the events unfolding in this game which is understandable but bad practice and in my opinion a small recap would help new players get into the series.
The difficulty is at a good level, its usually blown out of proportion but progressing slowly with a little patience and with a good sense of timming will avoid many frustrations.
If you're new to the series, just want a few challenging boss fights and explore distinct regions filled with enemies and smash through them feeling like the top dog, then give it a try when its on sale, otherwise If you're like me and want a proper rpg experience with properly fleshed out world/characters and dont intend to finish the other two games first i cant recommend it.

The game loves to force your hand, apparent from the ticking fail-state clock at the top of the map. You can delay it, but you can't put it off forever. Timed missions are abundant, and taking things safe and slow isn't always an option.
That being said, the game is still lots of fun, and having all of these things stacked agains you makes the reward feel so much sweeter.
The game has some marked improvements over EU: Engineering is done a lot better, the concealment system is nice, albiet lacking, and equipment management is well, manageable.
The game does have a few technical issues, though.
I've experianced some minor animation glitches/bugs, but nothing game breaking. Load times can be sort of long (anywhere from 20 seconds to a full minute, though I installed this to my HDD) and optimization is not the best. I've experienced some rather notable frame chugging during the pre-mission loading screens, and in areas that have a lot of fire/smoke, though lowering shadow detail helped with the latter. Frame-rate on high settings is not entirely consistant on my 2gb GTX 960/ FX 8370 & 16gb RAM, but it is by no means unplayable- though I've seen people with significantly more powerful systems than mine complaining about unplayable frame-rates, even on the lowest settings, so the game seems to be inconsitant.
I've not had the game crash/move into unplayable territory, but I've witnessed a significant number of people note this- so much so that I'd suggest you keep it in mind, though some of these people might be overdramatizing the issue, I would not write it off entirely.
Overall, the game is challenging and fun, and (At least for me) works. Buy it if you like stressing over 98% hit chances missing and leaving your ranger exposed without cover- because obviously your life wasn't already stressful enough.

Let me start by saying this game is overhyped by a rabid fanbase.
It has fun mechanics, hit detection is accurate, the weapon blows are satisfying and you have a decent variety of enemies.
The customization is above average, you can customize your playstyle and appearance somewhat freely except in situations where a certain weapon or gear gives a huge advantage against a specific type of enemy, if you're adamant about the way you look or play you can always summon another player to help you out temporarily.
Online pvp is idiotic as the player that invades your world always has a huge advantage due to being ignored by npcs, popping up in the most unfair and troublesome areas when you're the least prepared, there's the possibility that there are two or more invaders in your world at the same time and on top of it there's no type of skill matchmaking involved so you end up having to put up with the occasional ascended nerd, getting butchered and having to go back and progress through that area again.
The world itself is boring, i was just plowing through monsters for hours without any hint of story development, fans defend this using arguments such as: "you need to read item/souls descriptions", " you need to piece it together", "the lore is what you make of it as its open for interpretation" to me that's just lazy and and insipid i was also told that i needed to play the previous ones to understand the events unfolding in this game which is understandable but bad practice and in my opinion a small recap would help new players get into the series.
The difficulty is at a good level, its usually blown out of proportion but progressing slowly with a little patience and with a good sense of timming will avoid many frustrations.
If you're new to the series, just want a few challenging boss fights and explore distinct regions filled with enemies and smash through them feeling like the top dog, then give it a try when its on sale, otherwise If you're like me and want a proper rpg experience with properly fleshed out world/characters and dont intend to finish the other two games first i cant recommend it.

Pray RNGesus takes pitty on your worthless soul.
Xcom 2 is tense and unforgiving, and accepting failure to some degree is something you'll have to go in with. The game loves to force your hand, apparent from the ticking fail-state clock at the top of the map. You can delay it, but you can't put it off forever. Timed missions are abundant, and taking things safe and slow isn't always an option.
That being said, the game is still lots of fun, and having all of these things stacked agains you makes the reward feel so much sweeter.
The game has some marked improvements over EU: Engineering is done a lot better, the concealment system is nice, albiet lacking, and equipment management is well, manageable.
The game does have a few technical issues, though.
I've experianced some minor animation glitches/bugs, but nothing game breaking. Load times can be sort of long (anywhere from 20 seconds to a full minute, though I installed this to my HDD) and optimization is not the best. I've experienced some rather notable frame chugging during the pre-mission loading screens, and in areas that have a lot of fire/smoke, though lowering shadow detail helped with the latter. Frame-rate on high settings is not entirely consistant on my 2gb GTX 960/ FX 8370 & 16gb RAM, but it is by no means unplayable- though I've seen people with significantly more powerful systems than mine complaining about unplayable frame-rates, even on the lowest settings, so the game seems to be inconsitant.
I've not had the game crash/move into unplayable territory, but I've witnessed a significant number of people note this- so much so that I'd suggest you keep it in mind, though some of these people might be overdramatizing the issue, I would not write it off entirely.
Overall, the game is challenging and fun, and (At least for me) works. Buy it if you like stressing over 98% hit chances missing and leaving your ranger exposed without cover- because obviously your life wasn't already stressful enough.

Poor engine optimization, poor perfromance even on powerful hardware in cities. A poor story that is not on par with previous titles in the franchise, paired with dumbed-down RPG mechanics.
Roleplaying is severely hampered by a grating voiced protagonist who either sounds like a shy soccer mom, or a wacky, bumbling dad. Stats mean nothing in coversation; they will always sound like someone who is scared of what everyone thinks of them, and lacks any self-confidence or backbone.
Weapon and armor designs deviate heavily from previous titles, and are objectively inferior. Art direction following Adam Adamowicz's death just plain sucks.
This was a game that only mods could fix; and two years later, it's still an ongoing process. So naturally, Bethesda decided to effectively declare war on said modding community with a lazy, half-baked system of paid mods, that are totally not paid mods. The Creation Club.
Is the Creation Club paid mods? No, it's worse. It's microtransactions, backed by a premium in-game currency, to pay real money for mods of questionable or mediocre quality at best. Bethesda claims that Creation Club assets have their quality assurance, which mods do not. But given that mods such as various Unofficial Patches are practically essential for many Bethesda games, I find their "quality assurance" unassuring at best.
This is in addition to Creation Club assets being forced downloads onto your data folder, every time the game updates. And if rumor is correct, this means script extender breaking forced updates every time the Creation Club adds new content.
I gave Bethesda, and Fallout 4, the benefit of the doubt for many years. I even stayed quiet during the last paid mods fiasco. I loved this game, and you can clearly see that from my absurdly high playtime. But I cannot, and will not, recommend this game. Go buy New Vegas, Wasteland 2, or even Fallout 3 instead.

Let me start by saying this game is overhyped by a rabid fanbase.
It has fun mechanics, hit detection is accurate, the weapon blows are satisfying and you have a decent variety of enemies.
The customization is above average, you can customize your playstyle and appearance somewhat freely except in situations where a certain weapon or gear gives a huge advantage against a specific type of enemy, if you're adamant about the way you look or play you can always summon another player to help you out temporarily.
Online pvp is idiotic as the player that invades your world always has a huge advantage due to being ignored by npcs, popping up in the most unfair and troublesome areas when you're the least prepared, there's the possibility that there are two or more invaders in your world at the same time and on top of it there's no type of skill matchmaking involved so you end up having to put up with the occasional ascended nerd, getting butchered and having to go back and progress through that area again.
The world itself is boring, i was just plowing through monsters for hours without any hint of story development, fans defend this using arguments such as: "you need to read item/souls descriptions", " you need to piece it together", "the lore is what you make of it as its open for interpretation" to me that's just lazy and and insipid i was also told that i needed to play the previous ones to understand the events unfolding in this game which is understandable but bad practice and in my opinion a small recap would help new players get into the series.
The difficulty is at a good level, its usually blown out of proportion but progressing slowly with a little patience and with a good sense of timming will avoid many frustrations.
If you're new to the series, just want a few challenging boss fights and explore distinct regions filled with enemies and smash through them feeling like the top dog, then give it a try when its on sale, otherwise If you're like me and want a proper rpg experience with properly fleshed out world/characters and dont intend to finish the other two games first i cant recommend it.

Darkest Dungeon is a slow boil, initially off-putting due to its seemingly insane difficulty.  However, if you stick with the game, learn how it works and how to mitigate failure, it is a very rewarding experience.   Visually striking with matching atmospheric music and sound, Darkest Dungeon does a remarkable job of amping up the stress level and making every choice meaningful.  This game incorporates that idea, stress, and runs with it.  Your decisions on who to take on a mission, their positioning, what provisions to take, and what tactics to employ are all amplified by the tone of the game...one of gothic nightmare.  Stress is not only incidental to the theme, but integral to our characters' roles and their effectiveness.  There is a stress meter for each member of the crew and if they get too stressed out can gain afflictions which can seriously affect said effectiveness.  After encountering a few enemies that bring the heat, your heroes could range from an abusive knight that increases others' stress, to a hopeless rogue that refuses medical attention while bleeding out.  The developers have created a turn based rpg that is quite memorable and enjoyable,  The stress mechanic alongside the beautiful art design and challenging enemies, set it apart from the crowd.  Buy this.

I'm writing this review as someone who enjoys RPGs and also as someone who hasn't played Fallout 1 and 2 (although I plan to) but has beat to 100% completion Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas, having hundreds of hours with both games.
Let me tell this to you straight up: Fallout 4 is not an RPG. Fallout 4 is an FPS sprinkled with Fallout themed elements. I will say it is an enjoyable game, and do ultimately recommend it, but under very special conditions.
First, what I didn't like.
-
: Bethesda tends to be really poor when they create main stories for their games. Fallout 3's main quest was poor, Skyrim was debatably worse. However, and as strange as this may look like, I actually think Fallout 4's main quest was the best Bethesda came up with since Fallout 3. Note I wrote Bethesda. Nothing tops New Vegas yet and I doubt that'll change anytime soon.
Why am I saying this though? Well, Fallout 4's story actually has different endings, a first for Bethesda from my experience, and post-game save files, depending on the ending, will have enough changes to be noticeable.
Plot discussion: I will say that
I will say it's a good effort, but not good enough. I feel as though Bethesda could have done so much more with the good concept they had, which ultimately made it disappointing for me.
-
: Why did anyone think this was a good idea? So I can wander around as this seemingly great hero of the wasteland, but if I feel like it, I can just shoot up a random settlement, wipe everyone out (as long as it's not a major settlement, because that has *important* characters, and we can't have them killed), and no one, aside from a few followers, will even bat an eyelash 5 minutes later? When did this become Grand Theft Auto? Fallout used to stand for choices and consequences. Which brings me to my next point.
-
: With the notable exception of some DLC, most quests in Fallout 4 don't offer a lot of choice, it usually boils down to either killing A and sparing B, killing B and sparing A, or killing both. Gone are the inventive, out of the box solutions we've come to expect from these games.
-
: I get that as you move forward in a franchise's history, you'll retcon some things here and there in an attempt to make said franchise more cohesive. But some things just don't make sense. And it has to do with a kid.
That's the most blatant example, but there's others. Just grinds my gears and I can't call this a Fallout game in the true sense of the word.
Those were some of my major gripes. It all makes Fallout 4 more of a shooter than anything else.
-
: If you're gonna go full on shooter, might as well make it good, right? Thankfully, it is. Gunplay's the best it's ever been, and even though there's not a lot of equipment to choose from, the customization you can apply to them is crazy. I approve.
-
: The follower system in Fallout 4 is the best yet, and this time I'm including New Vegas as well. Most, if not all, have a decent enough backstory, with some of the best having their own personal quests. By reaching max affinity with them, (which is achieved by spending time with them, doing what they like, and when applicable, completing their quest) you'll earn a permanent perk benefiting your character throughout the rest of the game. This is excellent since it gives you an extra incentive to go after the other followers and finding all about them, which is usually a good idea since they do provide some of the more interesting stories in Fallout 4. I wish more games would do that, since you usually end up skipping a lot of side characters which at first glance, don't seem like much but when given a chance, can prove to be so much more.
-
: As always with these games, mod support does help out a lot. It won't fix what's wrong at its core, but it can provide a longer and better experience. Always be sure to check out some of the mods in these games, the Unofficial Patch is a must, for example.
-
: I didn't use it all the time, but I sure enjoyed my time turning my first settlement into a major fortress in an ambitious project taking around 4 days. I do think it had a lot of wasted potential, and after my initial effort I had no desire to go back to it, but it was good while it lasted,
I also liked the setting, but that goes without saying, I'm a fan of the franchise and you can see the futuristic 50's influence all around the world and that's always great. Bethesda is still great at crafting a detailed and rich world, with many minute and interesting details in many areas of the game.
I'll go over each DLC real quickly:
- Automatron: Recommend. A fun little adventure, but nothing special.
- Wasteland Workshop and Contraptions Workshop: Barely checked out. I'm including these two because they offer more or less the same content. By the time I got the DLC I had no intention of going back to settlements. Still, a small pack of workshop elements without a story to fit into it wasn't something I liked.
- Far Harbor: Best DLC in the entire game, and I wished the rest of the game could have been like it. The choices were actually multi-layered and engaging.
- Vault-Tec Workshop: Unlike the other two workshop packs, this one had a bit of a side-story! Nothing special, but I did like the whole Vault-Tec manipulative science-y test subject business we've all come to love.
- Nuka-World: A mixed bag. I like that they gave you incentives to be a bad guy, but since there's no karma in the game, it does feel kind of hollow. This whole DLC does, really.

Usually don't write reviews for games but seeing how there are a lot of weirdly pointless negative reviews going around I decided to throw my vote in here.
Not going into full detail, just mentioning a few things people seem to be confused about.
Yes they are a thing, yes about 70% missions have them and yes I like them, if you don't, just disable them
Running the game on a Phenom X6 1100T with a GTX 570 at medium-high settings with 4xFXAA and 4xAF at mostly 60 FPS with dips to 50 when the camera is going all over the place
Small bugs are a thing, characters looking away from the target while shooting at it, the camera, once in a while not noticing that it forgot to make the wall invisible so you can actually see the enemy your character is currently shooting at or other minor annoyances. That's pretty much it though, haven't encountered any game breaking bugs. Also tabbing in and out of the game worked flawlessly on a dual monitor setup.
I noticed that after playing 7 hours straight my overall used system RAM climbed from 3.8GB to 6.9GB.
Tabbed in and out of the game quite a lot though, so that might have something to do with it.
I'm currently 21h in my Veteran campaign and it's a big improvement over XCOM EU/EW.
Aliens are actually dangerous and go out of their way to ruin your life from mission one.
Soldiers are going to die and there's nothing you can change about that.
New skills, good random generated level seeds (these are really well done, not like the XCOM EW ones which always felt really samey) and overall more complex combat offers various strategies to approach any situation and will have me run the campaign a second time, in a higher difficulty, without getting bored of it.
So what else is there to say, I can't argue that the game needs a performance patch, but seeing how it runs at 60 FPS most of the time on my end it personally doesn't affect me that much.

In a game filled with beautiful environments and fun, yet dangerous enemies and hazards... where you can bring a friend along to explore the world, and be ganked over and over by invaders all using the same 3 builds as per watched on various youtube channels. This game is great, I love it. But the over abundance of trolling invaders who simply run away from you or harass you with a great weapon in one hand and a parry in the other gets tiring REALLY fast.
The PVP is a joke, forced upon you in several areas, to which the community responds "Git Gud" or "It's Dark Souls bro". Well, no. That's the community. Developers do their best to balance things in favor of everyone, but in this case it's join them or play offline. To attempt a playthrough without adhering to pvp equipment standards while expecting to have a good time without interference is the same as literally discarding your embers over and over.
Of course, if you still care to play it, be warned. It gets old fast. You may think "Whatever, an invasion here and there is part of the dark souls experience!" Well It was. In Dark souls 1 and 2. In 3, you will be invaded immediately after winning, immediately upon entering a new area, and immediately upon caring to play with your friends.
I don't know if the intention was to completely obliterate any possibility of enjoying the game with a friend without dedicating your characters stats and equipment to being a typical tricked out meme built player killer, but that's what has been accomplished. I enjoyed this game until today, I honestly did. It has great mechanics, it's punishing, and well built. But the community of PVPers has completely wrecked everything I loved about dark souls. Smashing it into the ground with Vordt's Greathammer against my "only as many flasks as I should have for this part of the game" PVE built standard character.
Play this game if you like cheaters. If you win in PVP, good for you. Chances are in the middle of the fight they will just randomly gain invincibility, or perhaps heal maybe once, twice, twenty times more than possible. Maybe they will suddenly begin to "lag" out hard, and get a fre free teleporting backstabs on you. Maybe even point down at your corpse like the cowards they are. I've reported so many players that I still see roaming around, to no avail. If there's nothing that can be done about it, why not join them?
I have more to say. I have a LOT more to say, but this is long enough as it is, and honestly it's a great game, minus the pvp. Completely minus the pvp. There are areas dedicated to it, but that's not enough to keep it from spilling out and ruining any chance of me playing the game for anything but PVP again. I'd rather be the guy with the 2-shot Vordt Build early game slaughtering people than the guy being slaughtered. Try as I might, I just don't see the point in it anymore.

Starbound is the Sandbox Game that you've been looking for. It has everything you could ever imagined packed tightly into a well-organized tier-based progression system. The game is side-scrolling, similar to Terraria and has survival roots, so you'll have to mine and hunt for your resources, similar to Minecraft or Monster Hunter in order to craft items/workbenches to get bigger and better items and boss battles. Did I mention that you can tame and capture creatures like you can in Pokemon and have them fight for you in real time? No? Well, you can. You'll eventually graduate to higher sectors of space which, in turn, make the planets and the creatures/people much more difficult. Starbound is already open to the modding scene and has more mods than most finished games to date, the replay value alone merits the purchase of $14.99. There is so much more I could tell you, but I wouldn't want to ruin it, now would I? Starbound is in Beta right now and is slated to release sometime this year. I will update this review when more has been added to the game!
