This little onlinegame was once a really good one. It had a really nice developer team with friendly gamemasters, a community which was always fun to have a chat with. Regular content updates with bug fixes, where the developers often listened to feedback. New game modes, new levels... but: these times are all over, and I must WARN you about this game.
It started with the acquisition by Sega at the end of 2011. The guys at Three Rings said, there won't be any changes because of this. It was the first lie, because of Sega, there were suddenly EU servers. Although this was positive, everything went VERY slowly downhill since this. I'm not going to cover much gameplay elements, because these are available in other reviews.
A few weeks later in November 2011, they have released a content update with recycled boss levels, which are very same, but only harder. What's the catch? Per level, you needed a "shadow key", and it was findable as a 1% drop in lockboxes, something where you had to spend 2$/€/whatever to open one (if you wanted to of course). For a 1% chance. The community responded by a massive protest, saying that everyone should boycott this. Especially because the developers never did such a rip-off before. One week later, the shadow keys were available for "a limited time", for an energy price of 1800, something around more than 6$. The following weeks they were permanently added for purchase. This was not to be the first money try controlled by Sega.
The next "big" thing was in 2012 a new boss level added as a DLC, for purchase with a 7$ fee. Once again many community members were upset about this, since they had released in 2011 three whole boss and many other levels for free. Although you may say, "but they need to earn money too!", you may be right, but this was abused by an increasing money greed by Sega, slowly completely ruining the future and meaning of the game. I will shorten the next events in 2012: After several other cash grab attempts, the most hilarious attempt happened at the end of 2012. It was the guild hall update, and seriously EVERYTHING was overexpensive. Only people with 24 hour free time, farming the same repetitive levels 100 times per day, or 3 - 4 digit number wallets had the pleasure to burn their cash, or better said, to customize your own guild hall.
Meanwhile, Sega had found out that people don't like DLCs. They like costumes! Which means, the development for all other stuff like from their view pointless things like content updates are completely throttled, and costumes were released and updated regulary, sometimes several times in a month. Usually one costume box was available for "free" if you purchased energy for more than 20$. Later these boxes were available for energy as well, but on the same real-money level.
In December 2012, Three Rings had announced the Battle Sprites, little pets which are a nice help in a battle, but not really necessary. The community was hyped. 7 months later, in July 2013, they had finally released the Battle Sprites. What happened in the meantime? Nothing at all, only tons of cash promos with even more costumes. Please note, most costumes aren't something new. They were simple reskins, a cheap color change. Even a 12 year old could achieve this in programs like
or Gimp with a few clicks. More about these Battle Sprites: If you get your first one for free, the Sprite is level 1, and completely useless. You can level it up until level 100, but this will take a develish amount of time, if you aren't planing to level it up the rest of your life. Here grins the cash grab again: There were plently of purchaseable items to speed up the progress. Veteran players which had a lot of minerals and materials by previous level missions had the best chances to avoid the cash grab as good as possible on their way to level the poor Sprite up to level 100. And there are the next things to facepalm about:
The Battle Sprites are completely unbalanced. The Dragon, which was meant to be an offensive Sprite, is ridiculously weak. The half-offensive-defensive Ghost Sprite has more offensive powers and damage.
Even the defensive Cat Sprite is better than the Dragon, because the skill "Heart Attack" makes it much easier for you to spam your own attacks, if there are heart pickups everywhere. Major balance problems like this aren't fixed; it's still the same today! And there are no signs that they care about this, or the developers are not allowed to care about it. Gameplay bugs, glitches or balance problems have a pathetic high chance to be completely ignored at all, which wasn't the case in 2011. Today they will only issue an emergency patch when one of their cash "promos" stuff has a little texture bug, glitch, or whatever. It became very obvious that it's all about new cash stuff and costumes now, and many veteran members have left the game because of this situation. This online game has too little content to live without content updates, these were an important reason for many people to stay. And since these people have left the game, there are now only these left which think the current situation is perfectly okay and everything is great. Which is another problem:
While you had in 2011 a lot of people free for an adventure or a chat, this is today only partially the case anymore. Many people have developed their own closed-circle-connections in their guilds, like to talk or blaspheme about other people, because of boredom or whatever reasons (I can confirm this with the German community, English could be different). Since there are no new content updates anymore, except one or two simple short missions in ONE year, some people stay there for Social Engineering. The game supports Steam trading, where you could trade energy for games, items from other online games items or more. Which is very attractive for some people. But I have kept the best to the last:
In early months of 2014, someone has hacked the game, and has duplicated items in auctionhouse or had gifted them to other people (as far as I could see it on the forums before it got censored away). They have banned almost everyone who has purchased or accepted such duplicated items in the auctionhouse or via trade, and how are we and other people supposed to see if a virtual item is actually "real" or not (since when are virtual items real anyway?). A friend of mine got such items via a trade, and he gave me some to me and a few guildmates too, because free things are always good, isn't it? From their view obviously not. Many others, including me, got banned in a massive ban wave, with hundreds of other people, and they absolutely don't care about it, nor my massive amount of playtime or invested money. I had contacted their support, which said, "We require a healthy mind from every player", refusing to take off the ban, and indirectly saying I'm a liar. But they´re the liars they already knew about that bug for weeks and didn´t fix it.
Their gamemaster staff became like "brainwashed", handling situations for their profit. In 2011 they have never thought about crazy things like a massive ban wave, just because one bad guy set a fire in the game (metaphorical). It was a time where they have cared about their people very intensively, if people were actually happy about the game progress. And it's all over. No active content development, no mature and friendly community anymore, no new things, no hope at all. This game is for every interested gamer a hopeless case now if you want to play it for a long time. Because Sega treats Spiral Knights like a cashcow, milking it's milk til it's blood and bones. No wonder why one of their lead designers called Nick left Three Rings this year. It was once a very promising and great game, until Sega came in. text:
XCOM 2 is almost the most direct sequel possible, at least in terms of in-mission feel. The gameplay is almost exactly the same as before, with only a few changes in the core mechanics, most of which were added to alleviate the annoyances felt in EU's gameplay. Overwatch being removed on damage and the LOS indicator come to mind.
The geoscape is significantly different, offering a multitude of beneficial scanning opportunities which force you to decide what you need the most. However, mission choice is still almost the same, with the Doom Tracker being replaced by an Avatar Project progress bar, and the abduction mission choices being replaced by Guerrilla Ops missions which each counter a different Dark Event (things the aliens do which are very detrimental to your resistance effort).
Terror missions are still here as the Retaliation missions, in which the aliens attack a Resistance haven, forcing you to rescue at least 6 civilians and clear out any remaining alien forces. From what I can tell, 6 civilians is all that is required to pass the mission without penalty, as countries do not have Panic meters as in EU. You might get better rewards for saving more civilians, but I never bothered to check the end-mission rewards from those missions.
The early game feels a bit rushed, as it's easy to let the Avatar Project's progress get out of hand if you don't do the proper things (assault the Blacksite and get the Resistance Comms facility built) in time. Without Resistance Comms, you won't be able to move on to the regions where new Avatar Project facilities are being built and those facilities will quickly add more blocks to the bar while you rush to build the Comms facility and contact the resistance cells in their regions. This is exacerbated by the fact that excavating and constructing facilities in an effective arrangement (workshops can only provide staffing GREMLINs to adjacent facilities) will take even more time.
The story is a bit disappointing. Some things I was hoping to find out (such as how the Avenger was obtained, what happened to Dr. Vahlen, and how the Avenger/Skyranger can fly about undetected) are not explained, or at least I did not notice them while playing. The ending also seems like a sequel-bait cliffhanger, sadly enough. It left me with more questions than it answered, and didn't answer most of the ones I cared about.
My gripes about the base management and story are easily overshadowed by my good experience with the missions, though. The changes to XCOM:EU's gameplay have made the game a good deal faster and less static. The timers on missions can be irritating, but they work pretty well with the faster tactics you can use with concealment and breaking Overwatch. Melee enemies are quite a bit more dangerous, since melee attacks are now usable after a dash and many of them (including zombies) can move surprisingly far on a dash. On the flip side, this means that your sword-slinging Rangers can pull off some very clutch dash and slashing when everyone else has failed to kill something that needs to die.
Due to the changes made to the combat and the new enemies, holding defensively is less viable, as, for example, Sectoids tend to use Psionic abilities which ignore cover, and ADVENT Officers can Mark your soldiers and cause accompanying Troopers to focus their fire. This can easily lead to wounds or deaths, as a Marked soldier's luck can quickly run out when multiple enemies take shots at them, even when behind full cover. Basically, the enemies have more dice rolls to throw than you do, and plinking at them behind cover usually won't turn out well for you. Pushing up and flanking them will generally provide better results.
One of the best changes is the ability to EVAC units with no actions remaining, which comes very much in handy during the VIP Extraction missions. ADVENT will usually drop squads of troops close to the EVAC zone, and being able to dash to EVAC and extract safely makes simply running away a much more viable strategy.
Soldier customization and loadout choices are pretty good. Equipment is roughly equivalent to EU, with magnetic weapons replacing beam weapons. Pistols are absent on all classes except Sharpshooter, being replaced by Grenade Launchers, Swords, GREMLIN Drones, and Psi Amps for the other four classes. Armor choices are more limited, with Medium and Powered armor being the only options for the most part, with two choices of Medium armor at the highest tier. Weapon customization and PCSes are great, basically allowing you to fill in soldiers' weaknesses or enhance their strengths as you wish.
Soldier customization is varied and detailed, allowing you to change their armor style, armor camo pattern, weapon camo pattern, voice, personality (which changes how they carry themselves and their voice lines), headgear, face (upper and lower) gear, nationality, and biography. That's what I can come up with off the top of my head, there might be more.
I can't speak much on the optimization of the game, as my computer is six years old and roughly equivalent to a potato by today's standards, but on the default detected settings my framerate in-mission is fine, no worse than other contemporary games. That standard is admittedly low and the framerate does drop significantly at some points, but the game is very playable for me. The game even looks decent, though the action cameras on enemies do make the low-res textures I have to use quite apparent. I have run into a few bugs while playing, the biggest of which locked up the AI until I reloaded the game, but none have persisted through a restart or reload.
Overall, I've had a lot of fun with the game. It feels like a proper sequel, offering a similar set of mechanics while making some changes to improve how it plays.
A quick summary:
Pros:
+Faster gameplay
+Good soldier customization
+Good variety of enemies
+Fundamentally similar combat to EU, with some improvements
Cons:
-Mission timers can be annoying
-Early game can feel rushed
-Story isn't all that great

Darkest Dungeon is a slow boil, initially off-putting due to its seemingly insane difficulty.  However, if you stick with the game, learn how it works and how to mitigate failure, it is a very rewarding experience.   Visually striking with matching atmospheric music and sound, Darkest Dungeon does a remarkable job of amping up the stress level and making every choice meaningful.  This game incorporates that idea, stress, and runs with it.  Your decisions on who to take on a mission, their positioning, what provisions to take, and what tactics to employ are all amplified by the tone of the game...one of gothic nightmare.  Stress is not only incidental to the theme, but integral to our characters' roles and their effectiveness.  There is a stress meter for each member of the crew and if they get too stressed out can gain afflictions which can seriously affect said effectiveness.  After encountering a few enemies that bring the heat, your heroes could range from an abusive knight that increases others' stress, to a hopeless rogue that refuses medical attention while bleeding out.  The developers have created a turn based rpg that is quite memorable and enjoyable,  The stress mechanic alongside the beautiful art design and challenging enemies, set it apart from the crowd.  Buy this.

One of your ancestors has died, leaving you a mansion in his will. Before he died, he believed there was treasure buried beneath the mansion, so he hired workers to tunnel underground. But instead of treasure, they unearthed a portal to another dimension, through which many types of monstrous creatures have entered our world. Now its your job to stop them.
The good (tactical combat system)
Each quest involves taking a party of four adventurers into one of five dungeons. There are lots of different characters classes to choose from, each of which has their own unique abilities. Some specialise in melee attacks, some use ranged attacks, some can heal allies, some can attack multiple enemies simultaneously and some can do damage over time through bleed or poison attacks.
As you wander around the dungeons in side scrolling fashion, you'll encounter a variety of monsters. Combat is turn based, and mostly 4v4. The positioning of each character is important, because each ability can only be used in and against specific positions. For example most melee attacks can only be used in the front 2 positions, and can only hit the front 2 enemies. Some enemies have attacks specifically designed to mess up your party's positioning, for example by dragging a ranged specialist to the front, reducing their effectiveness and making you waste a turn changing positions.
There are a couple of unique mechanics related to health and stress meters. There is permadeath, so any hero who dies on a quest, is gone forever. However, when a hero's health reaches zero, they don't die straight away. They're on "death's door", which means the next hit could kill them, or if they're lucky they could still survive by resisting or dodging the attack. If you can heal them before they die, they're no longer in immediate danger, but they do suffer some debuffs until the end of the quest. Some enemies can specifically attack a hero's stress meter. When stress reaches 100, most of the time the hero starts to panic and they'll sometimes ignore your commands, but occasionally if you're lucky, they get a positive perk instead. If stress reaches 200, they suffer a heart attack and either die instantly (even if they were on full health), or go to death's door.
You'll also encounter "curios", which are objects of interest that can be interacted with. These include crates, corpses, coffins, bookcases, and many other things. You can ignore them, but if you choose to examine them, you'll randomly get something positive - some loot, a combat buff, a stress heal - or something negative - a disease (debuffs), stress damage, a bleeding or poisoned wound. This creates a risk/reward situation where you want to find as much loot as possible, but you might end up making things more difficult for yourself.
The bad (repetitive grinding)
The main thing that has hurt my enjoyment of Darkest Dungeon, is the painfully slow progression of levelling up your characters, which eventually makes the game highly repetitive. Each quest has a difficulty level (1,3,5,6), and you need to use adventurers who are the same level, or one level higher than the quest. If a character is two or more levels higher, they refuse to go on the mission (so you can't use a level 5 character on a level 3 quest). You only gain XP from successfully completed quests. You can abandon any quest at any time, which is better than letting heroes die, but you gain no XP for killing monsters, although you do keep whatever loot you'd found.
However, increasing a hero's combat level means nothing by itself, because you have to separately level up their skills, weapons and armour. This firstly requires purchasing upgrades for buildings back at the town, (guildhall for skills, blacksmith for weapons and armour) and secondly requires purchasing the skills/weapons/armour for each individual hero. Building upgrades costs loot (portraits, deeds, sculptures) and everything else costs gold, all of which are found during the quests. But those upgrades are ridiculously expensive compared to the amount of stuff you can collect in each quest.
By the time I'd killed all the level 3 bosses and was ready to make a serious attempt at the level 5 bosses (which are exactly the same bosses that I've killed twice already but with better stats), I had about 16 level 5 heroes, but I was still only using level 3 weapons and armour. Attempting level 5 quests with such underpowered gear was virtually impossible, because the monsters simply did so much more damage than me. It wasn't even competitive, I had people on death's door during the first fight of a dungeon. The only solution was to spend hours and hours and even more hours grinding low level quests to slowly gather the loot required to level up my gear.
And I've not even mentioned yet all the other things that are a drain on your resources. There are six different activities in town (drinking, gambling, praying, etc) which you have to use between quests to reduce adventurers' stress levels - all of those require loot to pay for building upgrades and gold to use the activity itself. And there's a sanatorium that removes diseases and negative perks that requires loot and gold. And there's a stagecoach to recruit new heroes and a survivalist that teaches mid-quest camping skills, both of which requires loot. Every piece of loot and gold spent on those things delays levelling up the stuff you actually want even longer. It also doesn't help that your inventory is too small, so you end up leaving behind some of the loot you find during a quest.
The end result is a requirement to grind the same missions against the same enemies over and over and over again.
The recommendation
Its a shame, I really wanted to give Darkest Dungeon a glowing positive recommendation, because for a long time I really was enjoying the game. However, the constant repetition gradually wore me down and I felt burned out around the 45 hour mark. Even though this does represent good value for money, I don't like leaving games unfinished. But even after a taking a break, I'm struggling to find the motivation to progress further.
This is one of those games that makes me wish the Steam reviews system had a third, neutral option. Darkest Dungeon isn't so bad that it deserves a thumbs down, but I also don't feel comfortable with the thumbs up.
** Update 9 March 16 **
I've seen an article on PC Gamer today which says the developers have planned an update which is designed to reduce some of the late game grind. I don't know how effective it will be, but I thought it was only fair that I should mention it, after spending half my review complaining about the grind. Its possible that new players won't suffer so much from the repetition that annoyed me.
There will be a new character class who is weak in combat but can find more loot, which sounds like another interesting risk/reward situation. Some of the town purchase costs have been reduced (good), but some others have actually been increased (WTF?). Also you will be able to recruit higher level heroes instead of having to start new recruits at level 0.

The sheer level of customization between your character, equipment and how you play the game is a refreshing change compared to the Terarria counterpart, and each race offers a unique take on the world around them based on its backstory. The vast amount of planets, biomes, buildings and codexes to learn more about the world only enhances the immersion of the game and truly demonstrates the care Chucklefish puts into its baby. To me, add what's already implemented, the modding and general community around Starbound and the future updates, and you have a game that's really worth the bang for your buck for now and long into the furture.

And you don't have to wear pants.
You can also pretend to be Samus.
That's a plus.

Dark Souls is a throwback to the days of Dark Souls 1 and guarantees to make you feel nostalgic in so many ways. Its a step up from the second game in the Souls franchise and functions as a perfect apology. As Bloodborne was released before Dark Souls 3, it seems the speed of Bloodborne has latched itself onto Dark Souls 3. Many souls fanboys were very skeptic upon discovery of the fact but, I suppose, they don't like a challenge, eh?
Dark Souls is a series about pushing through the unknown, pressing forward with your shield raised, probing the darkness, and looking for the flicker of the next bonfire. When the fire is lit, the previous area loses its mystique. It is conquered. This same sense of familiarity permeates Dark Souls 3, and it only ever gets you out of your comfort zone by resorting to cheap tricks. Yet despite this, it’s still a beautifully bleak adventure with one of the best combat systems in videogames - it just falls short of the magic of the original. Like the opening cutscene says: the fire fades.
Dark Souls 3 really is amazing, the game mechanics have been polished to the point of perfection regardless of the lacking magic system (feelsbadman). As someone who grew up with Demon Souls and partially Dark Souls 1 it warms my heart to see the spark has returned. Dark Souls 2 was a let down on so many levels that it seemed the spark was gone. But I guarantee you, although this isn't Dark Souls 1 or Demon Souls, this is a Souls game to the core.
The level designs are beautiful along with the designs of the boss arenas and the bosses. The NPCs and the regular enemies. It is all just beautiful.
I know there's been discussions in many Dark Souls communities whether the difficulty of the levels and bosses are suitable. I think, however, the difficulty doesn't matter. Some thoughts of mine, after Dark Souls 2, were that the franchise would soon meet its end, and I think
And I think that what Miyazaki has done is provide us with one heck of a closure, I think FromSoft put less time and effort in the difficulty and more in the graphical and auditorial parts of the game (as much as the parts that made one nostalgic).

Usually don't write reviews for games but seeing how there are a lot of weirdly pointless negative reviews going around I decided to throw my vote in here.
Not going into full detail, just mentioning a few things people seem to be confused about.
Yes they are a thing, yes about 70% missions have them and yes I like them, if you don't, just disable them
Running the game on a Phenom X6 1100T with a GTX 570 at medium-high settings with 4xFXAA and 4xAF at mostly 60 FPS with dips to 50 when the camera is going all over the place
Small bugs are a thing, characters looking away from the target while shooting at it, the camera, once in a while not noticing that it forgot to make the wall invisible so you can actually see the enemy your character is currently shooting at or other minor annoyances. That's pretty much it though, haven't encountered any game breaking bugs. Also tabbing in and out of the game worked flawlessly on a dual monitor setup.
I noticed that after playing 7 hours straight my overall used system RAM climbed from 3.8GB to 6.9GB.
Tabbed in and out of the game quite a lot though, so that might have something to do with it.
I'm currently 21h in my Veteran campaign and it's a big improvement over XCOM EU/EW.
Aliens are actually dangerous and go out of their way to ruin your life from mission one.
Soldiers are going to die and there's nothing you can change about that.
New skills, good random generated level seeds (these are really well done, not like the XCOM EW ones which always felt really samey) and overall more complex combat offers various strategies to approach any situation and will have me run the campaign a second time, in a higher difficulty, without getting bored of it.
So what else is there to say, I can't argue that the game needs a performance patch, but seeing how it runs at 60 FPS most of the time on my end it personally doesn't affect me that much.

TL;DR: 10/10
PROS
-Massive shelf life

-Rich atmosphere

CONS

Probably the best game ever made. Visually stunning, and surprisingly atmospherically rich but still so... empty. Going through the world feels less like a badass rompfest and more like a grueling trek through the ashes of a once-great society. Cursed with immortality, the folk have gone mad after thousands of years of an undending cycle of death and rebirth. The world is so hopelessly entranced in its own cycle of light and dark that even its greatest heroes have given up on it, and it's your job to make sure that they do THEIR job in not allowing the world to fall into darkness.
The controls are responsive and the gameplay much faster than the earlier Dark Souls titles, meaning individual combat encounters are more threatening. While the earlier games were incredible, nothing beats the fast-paced duels against even faster-paced beasts and giants that Dark Souls III provides. The game also encourages exploration and rewards you with items for your troubles, so make sure to check every nook and cranny in every area to uncover items and secrets.
Contrasting the epic, solemn experience of playing through the game alone, is the Dark Souls III community. Of my 334 hours, I have spent probably 200 of them with the sole intent of using the game's multiplayer. Lag is frequent thanks to peer-to-peer connections rather than dedicated servers, but the fact that you can only communicate through gestures makes for an endless amount of memorable and hilarious encounters. The community is also fairly free-flowing. You may find friendship in someone who has invaded your world with the sole intent to kill you, or be tricked by a friendly summoned player to fall into a trap in the area that you haven't discovered yet.
And the difficulty? Yeah, you'll die a lot, but you'll always feel it was because you made a mistake, rather than because the game was toying with you. Little by little, you'll get better, and you might shave that 50-100 hour first playthrough to a 3-5 hour playthrough faster than you'd think. The PvP is almost an entirely separate experience even though it's integrated in the single player game, because PvP combat is so vastly different from boss combat that skills may not even translate. I've spent 200 hours in PvP and know all the ins-and-outs of it, but I still can't beat certain bosses in less than 15 tries.
The DLCs offer a combined extra 10 hours at most, so they aren't necessary, but they offer some of the best boss fights in the entire series and some really cool weapons and well-designed areas, so if you like the game I recommend picking them up.
I do have some issues though. A couple specific areas have massive framedrops even on decent PCs (from 60 in the rest of the game to 20, using an i5 4450 and a gtx 750ti sc, in 1080p on minimum graphics settings). In the rest of the areas the game runs fine on my setup, and as long as you're playing in full resolution, low graphics settings don't take away from the beauty of the world very much at all. If you want to run it on Ultra, however, make sure you have the top-of-the-line parts for the job. Hackers are also not an uncommon sight, but these days they tend to use their hacks to have fun with ridiculous antics rather than to godmode through the game or win PvP fights, likely because most of tthe present playerbase has been playing for a while now and has gotten gud, but there are always exceptions.
Ultimately, the amount of shelf life you're getting is insane, and each hour will feel rewarding and well-spent. Because of its dedicated community offering co-op and PvP and the endless challenges you can impose on yourself in singleplayer, as well as the fact runs don't take too long once you understand the game, you can extend the game's life by as long as the game keeps your interest.

Trove is certainly an interesting concept, as it's basically a voxel-based MMO with a strong emphasis on both adventuring and crafting/building. That being said, is it even any good, or will it fall to the sidelines like so many other voxel-based games released after Minecraft? Let's look at the Pros and Cons
Pros:
+Free-2-Play, not Pay-2-Win. As far as I can tell, there isn't any sort of PvP in this game (correct me if I'm wrong). This means that anything you buy usually only affects your experience, not anyone else's. That being said, the game doesn't force you to buy anything, and most things can be earned (albeit slow) by grinding.
+Procedurally generated worlds. Each time you enter a world, it builds a new one for you and the 10 or so people that spawn there. The biomes are still the same, but the world's shape is quite mixed up. While this theoretically gives the game infinite replayability, it is offset by one of the cons that I will later mention.
+Very Child-Friendly. This is a con to some people, but to me it just means more players playing, which is good for any MMO.
+Intuitive building system. There are many more blocks than Minecraft, including decorations. You get your own portable Cornerstone to customize any way you want, as well as a Club World if you are in a Club.
Cons:
-Very casual and repetitive. This is by no means the next WoW. It doesn't really suck you in, even if you try to force it to. There are different dungeons and raids for each biome, but you will quickly play all of them, and without a proper quest system (save for the yellow box at the top right-hand corner) it really does get repetitive.
-No Auction House, etc. There is a trading post, but you must invite another player to it to use it. There's no market in the game, although there is an economy in the form of Fluxes (I think that's how you spell it).
-Poor Social System for an MMO. There is a friends system, sure, but like I said, the world constant. Even the Hub World is a cerver chosen at random. You can invite your friends to your world, yes, but it's very unlikely that you will make any new ones playing this, because everyone does their own thing.
Conclusion:
It would be a poor game if it was subscription-based, or Pay-2-Win, or even, I would argue, if it charged money up front. Really it is a poor MMO, when it comes down to it. But it's also free. It's a very casual game for an MMO, so you can't really no-life it. Yet it also has a great building and crafting system which sets it apart from other MMOs. In the end, it's up to personal preference. If you're looking for the next 10-year timesuck, or a gritty realistic MMO with a vast open world filled with new structures and monuments around every corner, I'd advise you look elsewhere. However, if you're looking for a fun, casual online experience that basically comes for free, I'd recommend you give it a shot.

(Spoiler free) 40 hours+ gameplay & completed on veteran.  Heres my option about the game.
The games combat has generally been improved with the conceal feature over EU/EW.  Atleast for the first ambush of a fight you are on better footing with your first engagment in a match.  AI felt cleaner, didn't have them doing too many weired things.  That said weird things happen.  For example if you happen to blow the floor from under enough a enemy, and he dies.  His body will hover in air, also if he doesn't die.  There is a chance they will become buggy.  Not show walking / sprinting animations.  Just warp to were they were going for rest of match.  Also if a player troop gets knocked out and falls.  Thier body is not the pick up point, but were they got knocked out.  So that feature is buggy.
The games story picked up smoothly from the last Xcom EU title.  But could have used more backstory with what happend over the 20 years.  An more story on who your research leader is now.  Engineer was pretty well done.
Biggest cons:
1.  Biggest complaint is the experimental equipment.  You can build armors fine, but things for your utilities, ammo and grenades are almost all random on what your going to get.  No way to make more with out spending your resources on a rng system.  Sucks, don't like it.
2.  Dumbed down research tree.  Within the first 15 hours of my play thru, I had everything researched expect story missions.
3.  The ship facilities were dumbed down.  No mechs, genetics labs.  You can upgrade the basic facilities to improve manning and outputs or speed.  But really no new versions of things like EU/EW.  You don't get better power options or coms, ect...
4.  For been a big air ship that travels the world.  You meet very little UFO, the skys are pretty clear.  Every now and than a month special will happen that has a chance to send a ufo after you.  But all they do is emp you out of the air and you fight off a ground assault.  Guess engineers never thought about putting weapons on a mobile base.  That or it was left off because you know, plot boss or lazy boss.
5.  The time VIP missions will make you a save scumlord.  Main reason timer, for go the steady and careful apporach or else you will run out of time.  These missions are a trial and error of moving as fast as you can and sneaking.  I finished a few of these missions within 6 turns, others down to last turn out of 12.  but really I didn't enjoy it.  Wasn't a challenge as more trail and error, reload save.
6.  Enemys get stronger with you, but show no signs of why.  Thier armor will look the same, but thier stats are as good as yours.  Logic, I find none here.
7.  Random performace hits.  Game normally runs fine, but it does suffer some major FPS issues at times.  Espically in transport to and from missions.  I have no idea whats in that shuttle that kills fps, but its there.
So in conclusion:
Solid game.  Its quicker pace, easier to get into.  Combats improved, and upgrades come quick and story is solid.  But game is shallow for old xcom fans.  Research tree is lacking, engineering is a dissappoitment because of the rng.  Lack robotic based troops such has tanks, hover tanks, or mech troops.  An no true base / airbase defense yet again.
But I do recommend this game.  Game is fun, and what bugs that are in the game will probably be patched out in there near future.  Tho none of them or game breaking.

This game is great, I love it. But the over abundance of trolling invaders who simply run away from you or harass you with a great weapon in one hand and a parry in the other gets tiring REALLY fast.
The PVP is a joke, forced upon you in several areas, to which the community responds "Git Gud" or "It's Dark Souls bro". Well, no. That's the community. Developers do their best to balance things in favor of everyone, but in this case it's join them or play offline. To attempt a playthrough without adhering to pvp equipment standards while expecting to have a good time without interference is the same as literally discarding your embers over and over.
Of course, if you still care to play it, be warned. It gets old fast. You may think "Whatever, an invasion here and there is part of the dark souls experience!" Well It was. In Dark souls 1 and 2. In 3, you will be invaded immediately after winning, immediately upon entering a new area, and immediately upon caring to play with your friends.
I don't know if the intention was to completely obliterate any possibility of enjoying the game with a friend without dedicating your characters stats and equipment to being a typical tricked out meme built player killer, but that's what has been accomplished. I enjoyed this game until today, I honestly did. It has great mechanics, it's punishing, and well built. But the community of PVPers has completely wrecked everything I loved about dark souls. Smashing it into the ground with Vordt's Greathammer against my "only as many flasks as I should have for this part of the game" PVE built standard character.
Play this game if you like cheaters. If you win in PVP, good for you. Chances are in the middle of the fight they will just randomly gain invincibility, or perhaps heal maybe once, twice, twenty times more than possible. Maybe they will suddenly begin to "lag" out hard, and get a fre free teleporting backstabs on you. Maybe even point down at your corpse like the cowards they are. I've reported so many players that I still see roaming around, to no avail. If there's nothing that can be done about it, why not join them?
I have more to say. I have a LOT more to say, but this is long enough as it is, and honestly it's a great game, minus the pvp. Completely minus the pvp. There are areas dedicated to it, but that's not enough to keep it from spilling out and ruining any chance of me playing the game for anything but PVP again. I'd rather be the guy with the 2-shot Vordt Build early game slaughtering people than the guy being slaughtered. Try as I might, I just don't see the point in it anymore.

XCOM 2 is great and deserves a much better rating than the 71% it currently has on Steam. Don't be scared away by all the whiners - most people complain about two things:
Yes, the game could have been optimized better. Is this annoying? For sure, since the launch was already postponed from November to February Firaxis should have done better. Is this a game breaking issue? No, not at all. The game runs absolutely stable, I have not experienced a single crash yet. Even tested it on my old machine, that barely meets the minimum requirements (Core2Duo 3,16GHz, GTX560, 4GB Ram) and it still runs stable with 30-40 FPS, only drops for a short time when a lot is going on (explosions, etc.).
There are mods which allow you to edit the turn limits as you like, or switch them off completely, so there is really nothing to complain about here. While I get it that some dislike the timers, I absolutely love them. They bring the action back to the game since you now actually have to rush sometimes. I was never a fan of that
- actually, people call it "tactical" - playstyle where you inch forward every turn, overwatching the sh't out of everything. So if you're like me, you will have no issues with the timers at all. If you prefer a
more tactical playstyle just download one of the mods from the workshop.
The only downside I could possibly think of is, that XCOM 2 does not support actual controllers. Only this weird thing called Steam "Controller" is supported. Since we are on PC we shouldn't discuss this at all and just grab a mouse and keyboard - the way it's meant to be played. If you still need a gamepad, just google PadtoKey, JoytoKey, Xpadder.........
With that being said, XCOM2 is a lot like EU/EW but comes with various improvements and a thrilling new story. Throw the mod support and modding community into the mix and you have a great game that will most likely keep you busy for several hundred hours (I know it will me).

Being a huge nerd for extraplanetary travel, I found Starbound expecting a sort of Terraria with far more world variety. What I got exceeded my expectations. It's not a clone of Terraria by any stretch of the imagination, but it does share a few very fundamental characteristics that probably don't really need mentioning. I has a phenomenal exploration emphasis, as every planet is indeed different, it's actually in a practical and interesting way. I kind of wish there was more content in the way of biomes, but that will come in the future.
That being said, Starbound, while probably passed the halfway point in its production, still has a looooooong way to go. Many mechanics are still unimplemented and even more are stuck as placeholders. Combat is repetetive, as is mining. The tier system needs serious work and more content needs to be made available. All of these and more have been mentioned in blog posts and the like, so much of this will probably be added in the future.
Bottom line is: I recommend this game whole-heartedly, but that comes with a warning. This game needs a lot of work, which is constantly getting done. Unless you have an insatiable desire to explore (as I do) and can handle grinding, you probably should wait until this game is updated further. I can't wait to see where they take this game.

Facts: turn based dungeon crawler, great art style, monsters design, clever mechanics (for example stress, quirks, roster shuffling), synergies, a metric crapton of strategies to succeed. So for mechanics, presentation and overall quality of the game 9/10
Now I want to adress some issues that majority of people seem to have with this game:
1) difficulty spike in champion (and further) dungeons - what people seem to not understand or rather refuse to adapt to is this subtle change of balance in the later game. At the beginning you're good to go with 4 pure damage units, just bashing everything into oblivion. But the further you go, the more it changes to strategy focused game. The battles get longer, enemies get tougher and all you have in your disposal is your creativity and 'on the fly' way of solving these combat puzzles. People seem to think that you just need a crusader or hellion who will crack skulls with sword or axe. That's not the case brother. Think and solve the puzzle or die. That's the name of the game.
2) grind - there are essentially 2 currencies - one for town activities (gold) and others (deeds, crests, etc) for upgrading your town. Again, at first, you need both. But after upgrading the city to the max, you can just abandon the second currency completely. There's no lose state in this game as far as I know, so the only matter here (as I understand) is that you have to go through lower levels dungeons to level up new rosters. Well, isn't it what you like? Playing the game? If not, what the hell are you doing with your life? It's like I would say - 'well, I don't like Disneyland, so let's go to Disneyland and whine about it later'. You don't like to be punished for stupid mistakes that you made? Well, why in the love of ♥♥♥♥ do you play difficult games then...
(not to mention - developers are going to make it easier for people like you and update the game today (08.03.2016) with 'more gold from quests class' and couple of town tweaks to make it less 'tedious' to level up heroes)
Maybe the problem is not in the game, but in the public. People don't like challenge these days, they want to have everything served on a silver platter. This game doesn't do that. It rewards careful planning, thinking and shifting your focus from certain strategies the further in you are. People don't like to think, people don't like to learn on their mistakes. That's why they can't handle the game. Or is it unfair RNG's fault? I'll tell you this - I lost ONE character in about 70 hours of gameplay because I couldn't do anything about it. And it took really unfortunate string of enemy crits and bleed/blight damage combo to make it happen. But it's life man, stuff happens, deal with it :P
Or maybe that's because I'm 80's guy. I was raised on difficult videogames that didn't give a crap about my feelings. They made me tough player that can appreciate cool, merciless gameplay :P And Darkest Dungeon delivers!
Darkest Dungeon ladies and gentlemen - 9/10!

If you have anything less than the
specs, you're done here.  Wait a few months for the game to get performance patches and go on a Steam sale with DLC bundled in before you grab it, and stop reading this review.  I'm not going to sugar coat it: the game is poorly optimized and fairly buggy in its current state.  Do not play on Ironman mode unless you want to lose your game to bugs.
That being said, if you can overlook those issues, this game is the classic we've been waiting for.  XCOM as a series has always been about balancing risk versus reward, diverting scarce resources, forcing yourself to make tough calls, and having your colonels getting one-shot critted in the face through full cover.
The new mechanic, Concealment, plays directly to that strength.  You'll have to decide how far to move before you blow your cover or how much you can afford to move in case a pack is lurking right around the corner.  Deciding whether to sneak past a pack can be agonizing, since when you engage another pack later on the previous pack could activate and trap you in a pincer attack.
Whatever you decide, you'll have to hurry.  Missions are now timed, forcing you to move fast or risk having your squad left behind and captured.  In an interesting twist, later missions will allow you to rescue captured soldiers so they're not lost forever.
The new line of sight indicators next to enemy health bars very clearly let you know what units you'll have line of sight to (and have line of sight back) at a certain position.  This is extremely useful when positioning a revealed squad around a pack visible to a concealed scout Ranger, or simply figuring out whether you can line up a shot.
The Advanced Warfare Center building also gives your soldiers a random chance of gaining an out-of-class perk on level up, which can get you some very interesting combinations.  For example, a Specialist getting a free hunker down when she hasn't fired this turn becomes an absolute defensive monster you can park closer to the front lines with amazing overwatch.
Veteran difficulty, the Normal difficulty “equivalent”, is no cakewalk.  The combination of time pressure and tough new aliens forces you to take your time thinking carefully about every turn.  I'm playing on Commander and unless I play nearly perfectly down to the tile, I'm always at risk of losing the mission or a soldier.  I can't imagine how horrifyingly difficult Legendary is.
Despite all that I've written, the most important reason you'd want to get this game is to watch your last active soldier's 99% Rupture on a Sectopod miss.  The Sectopod turns around to face your soldier, but then you realize too late that it's not a Sectopod, it's been modded into Jake Solomon's face.
“That's XCOM, baby”

One of your ancestors has died, leaving you a mansion in his will. Before he died, he believed there was treasure buried beneath the mansion, so he hired workers to tunnel underground. But instead of treasure, they unearthed a portal to another dimension, through which many types of monstrous creatures have entered our world. Now its your job to stop them.
The good (tactical combat system)
Each quest involves taking a party of four adventurers into one of five dungeons. There are lots of different characters classes to choose from, each of which has their own unique abilities. Some specialise in melee attacks, some use ranged attacks, some can heal allies, some can attack multiple enemies simultaneously and some can do damage over time through bleed or poison attacks.
As you wander around the dungeons in side scrolling fashion, you'll encounter a variety of monsters. Combat is turn based, and mostly 4v4. The positioning of each character is important, because each ability can only be used in and against specific positions. For example most melee attacks can only be used in the front 2 positions, and can only hit the front 2 enemies. Some enemies have attacks specifically designed to mess up your party's positioning, for example by dragging a ranged specialist to the front, reducing their effectiveness and making you waste a turn changing positions.
There are a couple of unique mechanics related to health and stress meters. There is permadeath, so any hero who dies on a quest, is gone forever. However, when a hero's health reaches zero, they don't die straight away. They're on "death's door", which means the next hit could kill them, or if they're lucky they could still survive by resisting or dodging the attack. If you can heal them before they die, they're no longer in immediate danger, but they do suffer some debuffs until the end of the quest. Some enemies can specifically attack a hero's stress meter. When stress reaches 100, most of the time the hero starts to panic and they'll sometimes ignore your commands, but occasionally if you're lucky, they get a positive perk instead. If stress reaches 200, they suffer a heart attack and either die instantly (even if they were on full health), or go to death's door.
You'll also encounter "curios", which are objects of interest that can be interacted with. These include crates, corpses, coffins, bookcases, and many other things. You can ignore them, but if you choose to examine them, you'll randomly get something positive - some loot, a combat buff, a stress heal - or something negative - a disease (debuffs), stress damage, a bleeding or poisoned wound. This creates a risk/reward situation where you want to find as much loot as possible, but you might end up making things more difficult for yourself.
The bad (repetitive grinding)
The main thing that has hurt my enjoyment of Darkest Dungeon, is the painfully slow progression of levelling up your characters, which eventually makes the game highly repetitive. Each quest has a difficulty level (1,3,5,6), and you need to use adventurers who are the same level, or one level higher than the quest. If a character is two or more levels higher, they refuse to go on the mission (so you can't use a level 5 character on a level 3 quest). You only gain XP from successfully completed quests. You can abandon any quest at any time, which is better than letting heroes die, but you gain no XP for killing monsters, although you do keep whatever loot you'd found.
However, increasing a hero's combat level means nothing by itself, because you have to separately level up their skills, weapons and armour. This firstly requires purchasing upgrades for buildings back at the town, (guildhall for skills, blacksmith for weapons and armour) and secondly requires purchasing the skills/weapons/armour for each individual hero. Building upgrades costs loot (portraits, deeds, sculptures) and everything else costs gold, all of which are found during the quests. But those upgrades are ridiculously expensive compared to the amount of stuff you can collect in each quest.
By the time I'd killed all the level 3 bosses and was ready to make a serious attempt at the level 5 bosses (which are exactly the same bosses that I've killed twice already but with better stats), I had about 16 level 5 heroes, but I was still only using level 3 weapons and armour. Attempting level 5 quests with such underpowered gear was virtually impossible, because the monsters simply did so much more damage than me. It wasn't even competitive, I had people on death's door during the first fight of a dungeon. The only solution was to spend hours and hours and even more hours grinding low level quests to slowly gather the loot required to level up my gear.
And I've not even mentioned yet all the other things that are a drain on your resources. There are six different activities in town (drinking, gambling, praying, etc) which you have to use between quests to reduce adventurers' stress levels - all of those require loot to pay for building upgrades and gold to use the activity itself. And there's a sanatorium that removes diseases and negative perks that requires loot and gold. And there's a stagecoach to recruit new heroes and a survivalist that teaches mid-quest camping skills, both of which requires loot. Every piece of loot and gold spent on those things delays levelling up the stuff you actually want even longer. It also doesn't help that your inventory is too small, so you end up leaving behind some of the loot you find during a quest.
The end result is a requirement to grind the same missions against the same enemies over and over and over again.
The recommendation
Its a shame, I really wanted to give Darkest Dungeon a glowing positive recommendation, because for a long time I really was enjoying the game. However, the constant repetition gradually wore me down and I felt burned out around the 45 hour mark. Even though this does represent good value for money, I don't like leaving games unfinished. But even after a taking a break, I'm struggling to find the motivation to progress further.
This is one of those games that makes me wish the Steam reviews system had a third, neutral option. Darkest Dungeon isn't so bad that it deserves a thumbs down, but I also don't feel comfortable with the thumbs up.
** Update 9 March 16 **
I've seen an article on PC Gamer today which says the developers have planned an update which is designed to reduce some of the late game grind. I don't know how effective it will be, but I thought it was only fair that I should mention it, after spending half my review complaining about the grind. Its possible that new players won't suffer so much from the repetition that annoyed me.
There will be a new character class who is weak in combat but can find more loot, which sounds like another interesting risk/reward situation. Some of the town purchase costs have been reduced (good), but some others have actually been increased (WTF?). Also you will be able to recruit higher level heroes instead of having to start new recruits at level 0.

Overall game rating incl. DLCs: 7/10.
Main game
Dark Souls 3 is what you would expect from a Dark Souls game, but it honestly feels a little too much Bloodborn-ish atmosphere wise, mostly in the beginning before it shifts over to classic Dark Souls. Gameplay wise it's fun, but very frustrating at times. Also I don't know why, but basically around every corner there's always something reminding you about Dark Souls 1 which makes it feel more of a game packed with fanservice. Not saying that's a bad thing, it's neat that there's a lot of nods to previous games but I think it should be able to stand on its own for the most part.
The bosses in the main game are fun and challenging, there's plenty of areas to explore and hidden secrets filled with items so I don't have any complaints about that.
DLC 1 - Ashes of Ariandel
I was hoping this DLC would be good for a change, but sadly it's not. You get lost fast in this DLC, and you will probably die a lot in very stupid ways. The main boss of this DLC is pretty good, just not what I was expecting. The optional boss is nothing amazing if you co-op against him, but can be very tough if done solo.
DLC 2 - The Ringed City
A few bosses are a good challenge in this DLC, but some others have are "meh" at best. The only reason I hate this DLC is the optional boss. And having one of the required bosses as an actual player? It's a very clever idea, but I'm not a fan of forced PVP in the story. However, the final boss is probably one of my favorite bosses in the entire game.
Summary
Dark Souls 3, the main game is a great journey and the DLC are alright.

EDIT: After a long and steep learning curve where I really had big trouble with this game, I've decided to change my review to be positive. When you figure out how things work (the game won't explain even half of it!), it gets a lot more manageable and fun. Usually, I always recommend tackling games without a guide. THIS GAME IS AN EXCEPTION! Read all the guides you can possibly find! If you are willing to do so, you will be greatly rewarded with a cool experience.
ORIGINAL REVIEW
I really like many aspects of the game. The general theme is great, the graphics are really cool, and the narrator's voice is awesome and contributes a lot to the atmosphere. It's dark, relentless and unforgiving.
All that sounds really great. The problem is that the amount of randomness in this game is totally out of control. Need some examples?
- Will an attack hit? Random.
- Becoming poisoned, or start to bleed? Random.
- Turn order? Random.
- Is the treasure chest a deadly trap? Random.
- Will the hero die when he's hit while deadly injured? Random.
- Will there be an act of bravery or a mental illness when stress is at max? Random.
- Which party member will fall victim to a trap when you walk into it? Random.
- Which new characters will be available after a dungeon run? What are their skills and stats? All random.
... and worst of all, these random elements absolutely cannot be avoided by the player. The game forces them upon you. There are regular opponents in the game that can  inflict permanent (!) random diseases on your characters with their NORMAL ATTACK (for crying out loud), which cost an awful lot of money to cure. So, literally, if your heroes are unlucky, they WILL die. This is NOT under your control, not even in the slightest. What's more, the game also fails to display any kind of percentages with which an action will succeed, it just happens. Not even turn order is properly displayed when you have to take an action and make a choice which enemy to take down.
To summarize, you can be the greatest tactical genius that ever walked this planet earth, but if you are simply not lucky enough with the random numbers, this game will kick your♥♥♥♥♥without a moment of hesitation. This is just bad game design.

So I'm not exactly a fan of Call of Duty. I used to be but I left the series after Modern Warfare 2. Black Squad feels a lot like Call of Duty to me, and by that I mean you live for 10 - 20 seconds until you have to respawn again. It's a constant respawn fest and very boring since you always  respawn in the exact same location. It feels so repetetive and not in a fun way.
The map design in Black Squad is terrible - unless you like having very short lifespans. If that's the case you'll enjoy it. I don't though, I like to live for a while and not having to constantly be running from the respawn point. One of the worst maps I've ever played is the Cruise Ship level, it's atrociously designed and far too tiny. You basically spawn, run ahead 15 steps, shoot, and either get the kill or get killed. If you die you have to respawn. If you get the kill, right after that you die and have to respawn. So repetetive and incredibly boring.
On top of that, there is no real deathmatch. There is only team stuff. I hate team stuff, I like to do free for all deathmatches and this game does not have that.
While it feels rough and totally not my type of game, I do see how some people could enjoy this. The game is designed to be fun for people who enjoy Call of Duty style FPS rather than Battlefiend or Ghost Recon FPS. There is no time for any strategy at all, it's just run ahead and shoot until you die, then repeat. I also don't know why these games have sniper rifles in them. None of the maps feel like they have any place to set up for sniping at all and even if you were to find somewhere, chances are you will be dead within 5 seconds of finding it.

Highly Recommended.
As a general statement, if you enjoy tactical games that force you to think, stay engaged, reward planning, are challenging, allow significant experimentation and variability and give a strong sense of accomplishment, this is the game for you.
I have played a lot of tactical games over the years, such as both XCOM's, Fire Emblems, Dungeon of the Endless, many playstation era tactics and RPG's, and this game is argueably one of the better ones. While each is different, the aspect I enjoy probably most about Darkest Dungeon is that even when you get later into the game, it will never allow you to go on auto-pilot. By that I mean that I find with many tactic games, once you get a party to a certain point, enemies start to die much quicker and the challenge is gone; it makes you think back to when you first started the game and it was better. Darkest Dungeon captures that enjoyment as each run through a dungeon feels like its own game. Losing champions is definitely frustrating and sometimes it feels like the game is against you, but once you get a feel for it you will be suprised how quickly you can recuit and train up new heroes.

Some context to the above:
- The planning and attacking phases are very well laid out. By this I mean before you enter a dugeon you have a significant control over: Who your party will be, what items they will take, what map size you want, what consumable items you will buy and what skills you will use. Have a short amount of time to play? Play a smaller map.
- The heroes and dungeons are created in such a way that they give you a lot to think about and experiment with. Even 50 hours or so into the game I was still experimenting with party and skill combinations. This helps keep the game fresh as you will likely always have a favorite party, but the mechanics will force you to play will different groups.

I really like many aspects of the game. The general theme is great, the graphics are really cool, and the narrator's voice is awesome and contributes a lot to the atmosphere. It's dark, relentless and unforgiving.
All that sounds really great. The problem is that the amount of randomness in this game is totally out of control. Need some examples?
- Will an attack hit? Random.
- Becoming poisoned, or start to bleed? Random.
- Turn order? Random.
- Is the treasure chest a deadly trap? Random.
- Will the hero die when he's hit while deadly injured? Random.
- Will there be an act of bravery or a mental illness when stress is at max? Random.
- Which party member will fall victim to a trap when you walk into it? Random.
- Which new characters will be available after a dungeon run? What are their skills and stats? All random.
... and worst of all, these random elements absolutely cannot be avoided by the player. The game forces them upon you. There are regular opponents in the game that can  inflict permanent (!) random diseases on your characters with their NORMAL ATTACK (for crying out loud), which cost an awful lot of money to cure. So, literally, if your heroes are unlucky, they WILL die. This is NOT under your control, not even in the slightest. What's more, the game also fails to display any kind of percentages with which an action will succeed, it just happens. Not even turn order is properly displayed when you have to take an action and make a choice which enemy to take down.
To summarize, you can be the greatest tactical genius that ever walked this planet earth, but if you are simply not lucky enough with the random numbers, this game will kick your♥♥♥♥♥without a moment of hesitation. This is just bad game design.

If you have anything less than the
specs, you're done here.  Wait a few months for the game to get performance patches and go on a Steam sale with DLC bundled in before you grab it, and stop reading this review.  I'm not going to sugar coat it: the game is poorly optimized and fairly buggy in its current state.  Do not play on Ironman mode unless you want to lose your game to bugs.
That being said, if you can overlook those issues, this game is the classic we've been waiting for.  XCOM as a series has always been about balancing risk versus reward, diverting scarce resources, forcing yourself to make tough calls, and having your colonels getting one-shot critted in the face through full cover.
The new mechanic, Concealment, plays directly to that strength.  You'll have to decide how far to move before you blow your cover or how much you can afford to move in case a pack is lurking right around the corner.  Deciding whether to sneak past a pack can be agonizing, since when you engage another pack later on the previous pack could activate and trap you in a pincer attack.
Whatever you decide, you'll have to hurry.  Missions are now timed, forcing you to move fast or risk having your squad left behind and captured.  In an interesting twist, later missions will allow you to rescue captured soldiers so they're not lost forever.
The new line of sight indicators next to enemy health bars very clearly let you know what units you'll have line of sight to (and have line of sight back) at a certain position.  This is extremely useful when positioning a revealed squad around a pack visible to a concealed scout Ranger, or simply figuring out whether you can line up a shot.
The Advanced Warfare Center building also gives your soldiers a random chance of gaining an out-of-class perk on level up, which can get you some very interesting combinations.  For example, a Specialist getting a free hunker down when she hasn't fired this turn becomes an absolute defensive monster you can park closer to the front lines with amazing overwatch.
Veteran difficulty, the Normal difficulty “equivalent”, is no cakewalk.  The combination of time pressure and tough new aliens forces you to take your time thinking carefully about every turn.  I'm playing on Commander and unless I play nearly perfectly down to the tile, I'm always at risk of losing the mission or a soldier.  I can't imagine how horrifyingly difficult Legendary is.
Despite all that I've written, the most important reason you'd want to get this game is to watch your last active soldier's 99% Rupture on a Sectopod miss.  The Sectopod turns around to face your soldier, but then you realize too late that it's not a Sectopod, it's been modded into Jake Solomon's face.

As a general statement, if you enjoy tactical games that force you to think, stay engaged, reward planning, are challenging, allow significant experimentation and variability and give a strong sense of accomplishment, this is the game for you.
I have played a lot of tactical games over the years, such as both XCOM's, Fire Emblems, Dungeon of the Endless, many playstation era tactics and RPG's, and this game is argueably one of the better ones. While each is different, the aspect I enjoy probably most about Darkest Dungeon is that even when you get later into the game, it will never allow you to go on auto-pilot. By that I mean that I find with many tactic games, once you get a party to a certain point, enemies start to die much quicker and the challenge is gone; it makes you think back to when you first started the game and it was better. Darkest Dungeon captures that enjoyment as each run through a dungeon feels like its own game. Losing champions is definitely frustrating and sometimes it feels like the game is against you, but once you get a feel for it you will be suprised how quickly you can recuit and train up new heroes.

Some context to the above:
- The planning and attacking phases are very well laid out. By this I mean before you enter a dugeon you have a significant control over: Who your party will be, what items they will take, what map size you want, what consumable items you will buy and what skills you will use. Have a short amount of time to play? Play a smaller map.
- The heroes and dungeons are created in such a way that they give you a lot to think about and experiment with. Even 50 hours or so into the game I was still experimenting with party and skill combinations. This helps keep the game fresh as you will likely always have a favorite party, but the mechanics will force you to play will different groups.

A charming, Zelda-inspired, online RPG. Beautiful art style, great soundtrack, good progression, with fun PvE and PvP.
This is a great game in my opinion, and while it might not be for everyone, it is definitely a 'must-try'.
There is quite a grind mid-game, but it's just enough grind to make you WANT to spend some money, but not so bad you HAVE to spend.
There are not as many end-game dungeons as there should be, but you can go back to previous missions with scaled down stats (with slighty less payout).
The developer (Three Rings) constantly creates new events, with new levels, and usually new costumes armor sets. These incremental updates provide new stuff to do while you wait for the next big level update.
Customization in this game is HUGE, with 'costume armor' sets, and accessories to put on your armor (though you can only afford them towards end-game). It's insane how many different armor combinations you can make. I've played over 1000 hours, and even I can't remember every one!
PvP will provide hours of fun, but at times can be overrun with PvP elitists (trust me, that's no fun).
The "FreeToPlay" system is set up really well, and has greatly improved in a recent update (so if you played it a while ago and hated it, try it again). Currency earned by play is called "Crowns", and currency that you pay real money for is called "Energy". At any time, Crowns can be traded for Energy via the in-game energy market (thus paying real money is completely optional). Of course Energy is more desirable, but when trading with other players, they usually don't mind if you pay in Crowns. You can buy energy to speed up your progression, but is by no means neccessary to reach end-game. I have bought Energy a few times myself, but they were mostly to buy costumes or to pimp out a costume with accessories.
I think my hours spent playing this game tell how fun it is. I love this game, and I would play it at the slightest mention of a new update or event.
It's free, it's fun, and truly FreeToPlay, what more do I need to say? Play it NOW...!

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic roguelike dungeon crawler, with enough content to hook you in (ha), but the flaws reveal themselves as you play. After a few updates though, I would absolutely recommend this now. (there's a tl;dr at the bottom, because this is long.)
Let's start with the art style. I love it. There's no other way to put this - the art is probably what got me interested in the first place. Your party members don't look happy, comfortable, or even well dressed - they just look like they're trying to endure the horrors presented to them when I pick a mission of medium length. Enemies are equally fantastic, with the art style making them look horrific and honestly, almost fearable. The backgrounds are also pretty great, again, builds the atmosphere. The art is dark, gritty, and is incredibly unique. It immerses the player, and it does it well. No complaints.
Speaking of atmosphere, the soundtrack is top-notch. In battles, it's almost like background noise, but that works well when the sound effects of strike after strike on both friend and foe are toned up. In regular areas it serves as ambient music, and when the torch is snuffed, the soundtrack takes a more sinister tone. Presonally, I love playing risky with no torch, and the music just made it more enjoyable.
However, although the creative elements shine through, I have to admit the gameplay just isn't on par.
Battles are decisive and full of risks, do you heal this round to keep your crusader alive or just take the chance that you'll hit the top of your damage range? Do you kill the enemy that hits for lots of stress or the one that can manipulate your party order? It's good fun, but eventually it becomes nearly negligible. I'll address that point later.
The really unique mechanic in this game is stress. As it builds, you begin watching that bar nervously, hoping to not reach 100 too soon. When a party member reaches 100 stress they either gain a virtue and become the paragons of your squad, or, far more likely, stress out and gain some affliction, like masochism or becoming abusive. It encourages you to kill the stress-inducing enemies and it's pretty cool. After they added the heart-attack mechanic which downs a member after 200 stress, it just becomes really annoying later on. Watching my full health Leper suddenly succumb to a heart attack halfway into the level 6 dungeon♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, even more so when he was immediately dealt a deathblow afterwards.

The biggest problem it used to have was the eternal grind, but props to the devs for listening and adding a feature that allows for skilled recruits to arrive as recruits. It saves so much time and was a fantastic addition.
Also, in the dungeons, between the larger rooms, it becomes a boring walk through the corridors. At first you embrace the art and music and it's really cool because you can interact with this and this, but eventually you get bored because you just want to get to the boss without dying too quickly. I just wish my party moved slightly faster.
I could bang on about it's shortcomings for a little longer, but it's getting wordy and i'll skip to my last point - late-game progression. It's long and it sucks.
When you inevitably decide to go to the Darkest Dungeon with your group of 4 legendary heroes, you feel confident, like you'll accomplish something, and you sure as hell will.
So you venture into the dungeon, and after a gruelling battle against some horrors from the void, you realise something.
Something horrific.
Something more terrifying and agonizing than the battle and the beasts themselves.
Your party members won't go back. They'll never go back there again. "Never Again".
EDIT: I have not reached this point again since quite a few updates. Whether or not this is still the case I am unsure.
Yes, after one expedition, they recieve the permanent trait "Never Again". This is supposed to encourage new groups and different approaches to the dungeon and avoid people quickly beating the game. But it doesn't work. Those heroes give a 20% (?) bonus to gained exp when brought on other missions, so you could use them to help your level 1's reach level 2's faster, right?
Wrong. High level units refuse to adventure into lower level dungeons, meaning they're only really viable in level 5 -> 6 grindfests, which is basically pointless. You might as well dismiss them.
Time to spend another playthrough for the same result again.
I like Darkest Dungeon's art, music, immersion, and mechanics.
TL;DR
Don't mind grind? Go for it - it's a great experience.
Hate grind? If you've got nothing else to do, it'll be a good time-passer every once in a while. Still might want to give it a try, like I did, but just don't expect engagement the whole way through.

And since there isnt really any regenerating health from what I can tell or any classes or characters that can throw down medpacks, you have very little chance of surviving more than 3 or 4 gunfights in a life. The map design is fine, but since in TDM the spawns are fixed that makes gameplay (in that mode obviously, I haven't played as much of the others) very repetetive. You walk from your spawn towards the middle of the maps and have gunfights in the same places every time, die to the same people in the same places over and over because everyone is just trying to find the enemy who clump up in maybe 4 locations on each map, then you respawn and do it again. The reason CoD's TDM is so fun and never gets old is because you can spawn pretty much anywhere, and that means you'll probably have gunfights all over the map in one life. Its no fun to just stand in one room in the middle of the map all game and get a kill or two, die to someone who ends up doing the exact same thing, go back, repeat. The objective gamemodes are better suited to the fixed spawns and single lives. There are a couple unique modes but all the players I've come across are next to incompetent and make it no fun to play with or against them. That's not the games problem but it still lessens the experience. The game is very mechanically sound, I haven't come accross any bugs. the only problems I have are with questionable design choices.  I'm not saying this game is bad. I actually think it is capable of being quite good a bit down the road with some balancing and tweaking to certain aspects. But the way it plays right now isn't as fun as I know it could be, so I wont be recommending it. But, I'll definitely keep track of updates and see the progress this game makes. Who knows, a couple patches from now every issue I take with how this game could be completely ironed out. That's the whole point of Early Access; not hating on games just because they have issues and acting like it will never improve, but voicing opinions on those issues so they can be solved for final release.
