My first suggestion in Darkest Dungeon? Don't give up.
At the beginning, the game seems insanely hard.  Your first party will most likely die or go insane.
That's okay.
This isn't a game about keeping heroes safe and healthy.
This isn't a game about keeping heroes at all... not at first anyways.
That's the beauty of the game, It's not just telling a tale of overcoming the grimmest and darkest corners of forgotten labyrinths.  It's a tale of overcoming your own need to constantly bring your people home and defeat those labyrinths and letting a few foolish souls fall to the wayside.  It's a tale of letting go... after all, no matter what you do there's always fresh meat coming on the next stage coach.
That's what was hard for me to grasp initially.  I felt like the game was taking me for a ride, laughing at how weak and pathetic I was... punishing me for trying.
Eventually I figured it out, and it was refreshing.  Some games absolutely punish you for making a fatal mistake.  Losing a powerful character basically is the end in those games -- not so in Darkest Dungeon, let me explain.
Firstly, your adventurers are sent out on quests, quests are tiered.  Some quests are too difficult for new heroes, likewise lesser quests are too easy(and therefore refused) by more experienced heroes.
Lose your favorite Leper tank to a high tier quest? No worries, another one will come along eventully on the stage coach and you'll throw him into the grinder of newbie quests and in short order he'll be hewing all manner of beasties in two... until of course you get careless, he goes insane and he opts to suicidally charge that lurking tentacled thing in the dark.
In essence, this assures that you never accidentally send your fresh meat where they won't make you any money, and that you won't just use overpowered characters to forget the essence of this game, which is managing your party to survive.
Speaking of party management, character position is key, but not always the same.  Character skills are varied though a set of 6 skills, those skills are often favorable in certain party positions, and you can use gold to unlock skills to tailor your character to the position you want them in.  This means if you like a particular class you could potentially have a few of them in a party and each of them would favor a different party position.  If you look at screen shots this concept might make more sense, you'll see the characters stand in a line, reminiscent of 4 - 3 - 2 - 1 .
Beyond mechnics which make this game as strategic as it is a role-playing game, there's also a town which you are also able to upgrade to make it easier on you to keep your heroes happy and healthy, from increasing the pool of heroes you keep on retainer, or how many you can send to the tavern to regain some passable version of sanity.  Thus as you accidently get a few characters killed, or merely let go of their services because they felt useless, you'll have gained resources through their adventures to make future adventurers happy... well as happy as they can be.
The artwork is beautiful, the soundtrack is good, and the narration... well... that has it's own cult following due to how good it is.  Often the narrator will chime in during your adventures with some hopeful(though, more often hope-crushing) phrase, which fits seemlessly with the action.
So all in all, this game is going to initially feel hopeless at first, which is exactly how it's meant to feel.  You'll possibly be frustrated and want to spit and cuss at the screen... but give it a few missions.  Let go of a few adventures.  Send a few to their deaths maliciously simply to gather the ones you want, if you must.  Just give it a chance and you'll find it's an exceptionally rewarding game.

I haven't beaten this game yet (soon though) but from my experience with this game, it's a must-buy if you're into RPGs.
First thing I've gotta say is I almost refunded this game because I wasn't prepared for the difficulty it presented. If you're a newcomer to the series or you've never played a fighting game, you'll most probably feel this game is too difficult and unforgiving. I died more than 15 times fighting against an early NPC (the Swordmaster) outside the first area and asked Steam support for a refund. Fortunately, I did not get it though as I'd already spent 3 hours into the game at that point.
The combat system feels clunky at first but as the game progresses, it's one of the best systems I've ever seen. You can dodge most of the attacks from your opponent if you time it right. There are many types of weapons that fit every play style. Describing the combat system in its full entirety is very hard, you have to play to feel it.
The lore in this game is beautiful. Every boss has their own backstory, all of them are equally interesting and contributes to a well-designed world/story. Level-design in this game although is overall great, but is by no means perfect. Camera angle in some areas is just atrocious, and sometimes you're surrounded by mobs and stucked in a spot where you can only watch yourself die. Nevertheless, it does not happen that often, most of the time, it can be avoided by fleeing to a wider area.
Now about the notorious difficulty of Souls games, many have told that it gets much easier as you progress. I did not believe that at first as I forgot to count how many times I died on my way to the third boss. It took me more than 15 tries to take down Vordt of the Boreal Valley, almost 17 tries to beat Cursed-Rotted Greatwood, I've never even beaten the katana NPC after 2 hours (he accidentally fell to his own death, I'd like to fight him now though). These bosses rank among the easiest bosses in the game according to most Souls players. From then on, I defeated Aldrich and Dancer of the Boreal Valley on my first try. Even Pontiff Sulyvahn, the most difficult boss in the game if you're bad at parrying like me, took me about 10 tries while I was prepared to die for hours and hours.
So you definitely improve as you progress through the game. Difficulty in DS is not an illusion, it's real but it goes down each time you learn your mistakes.

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic Dungeon Crawler in its base form. But it's so much more than that. The game revolves around re-building your Hamlet and forming a roster of heroes to challenge everything the dungeons can throw at you. The stronger and more expansive your Hamlet becomes the easier it is to improve your heroes, but the harder the dungeons become to compensate. So the challenge never diminishes, and the game remains consistently fantastic.
If you enjoy a challenge, and are prepared to fail several times before you succeed this game could be for you.
Turn based combat was never dead, as much as some claim it was. And this is a prime example of exactly how turn based combat is the king of deep tactical combat.
A unique, spectacular art style which extenuates the dark, dismal fate which awaits your unfortunate heroes.
Brilliant Narration is the real champion here, but the sound effects are powerful enough to not be outshone.
Overall, this is definitely a game worth picking up, one of the true Early access success stories.

Where do I begin?
This game has something of a love/hate relationship with many of its players to the point of you wondering whether or not the game is trying to jerk you around between its good and bad qualities. I recommend it merely because of its free to play status, the fact that the good far outshines the bad, and while it does have elements of pay to win, it's actually subverted; you can get all of the best gear (and level it up fully) without a single bit of real-life cash.
Let's look at the good first:
* It looks rather nice, all things considered. Some people complain about the cartoony look, some thing there's too little to look at, but looking at the weapon designs, the armors, the enemies and the interface, everything comes together with a nice finish. It's cartoony and pleasantly kid-friendly, while being fully capable of keeping an adult, or at least a teenager invested in its gameplay.
* It has mix and match items for pretty much any playstyle around. Instead of classes that you're stuck with, you choose weapons (Blades, Guns and Bombs), shields and armors that fit your playstyle, and can switch between multiple ones should you invest enough crowns and items into the gear you have.
* The gameplay is basic, yet fun. Either hack and slash with proper timing, strafe with your gunslinging skills, or plant a bomb at an enemy's feet or in their path and watch the sparks fly. Enemy AI is quite intelligent, but it isn't completely impossible to either avoid or at least block incoming attacks with a proper shield.
* Alchemy. You can craft your own things with the proper recipes. Need I say more?
* The in-game economy is a living, breathing thing with a player-run marketplace that allows buying of very rare items and materials for crafting, and allows you to sell things you don't need for a nice price for very, very easy crowns, the in-game currency.
* Tiers of gameplay difficulty with increasing rewards are very good at helping you grind easily for material drops and crowns while even being able to get specialty items normally found in special shops that use Energy, the secondary currency that's able to be boosted by either trading in crowns for it, or buying it with real money.
* A mission system that allows you to rank up, access new tiers, use stronger gear, and even get free items along the way. Some of the rarest drops are easily gained simply by completing a mission. However, while you can do missions as many times as you'd like, the rewards are a one-time deal, which is a sound choice so people didn't simply milk the system for free items and have the in-game economy crash.
* Not being pay-to-win. For an MMO, that is a crucial part of it that could make or break it. While, on the surface, it does appear to BE pay-to-win, they've since removed play restrictions that have crippled its playability, and added things to subvert that so they can still make money off of it. However? Anything that you "have" to pay for? You can find as a random, though rare, drop. Looking for an item to help you level it up? It's in the dungeon. Looking for an item that allows some high-level alchemy? It's in the dungeon. And the best part is that even if you don't get the items you want, the amount of crowns you get from one dungeon run can be tremendously high, and allow you to simply get the energy to buy it ANYWAYS. Like I said, you don't have to pay a single penny to get the items you need.
On to the bad:
* Forging. To level up your items every single time, from 1 to 10, you need to forge it. You can choose low, medium or high level forging that either has a low, medium or high level of success. This looks good on paper... until you realize how stupidly rare the items you need to actually forge the weapons and armor are, and how absurdly high the amount you need on the highest levels. In example, a 5-star weapon is the highest you can get. To reach level 10? You need over 100 5-star crystals. Which are easily one of the least common drops in the entire game. While I did say that this is very easy to circumvent and prevent the need to pay for these items sold in the Energy shop, it's subverted by being tedious and time-consuming. Which brings me to my next point.
* The higher level difficulties. In Tier 3, the highest tier, the enemies can take down your strongest character... in about three hits. and in some places, two due to elemental damage that sticks to your character like glue, ripping chunks out of your health every second or so. This makes things absurdly high risk and horribly difficult because of how revival works now. Instead of just giving half of your health to a downed player that doesn't have enough energy to revive themselves, you must instead use a "Spark of Life". This is yet another item, much like the Forging crystals, that are stupidly rare drops. Trying to face raid bosses are also a nasty, nasty pain. Expect to die on the second one a few times, expect death to happen with alarming frequency on the third, and the fourth and final one? Good luck. You're going to need it. Because that's the only way you'll win on your first few attempts.
* The lag. The servers are relatively... average. Even if you go in solo, while graphical lag is EXTREMELY rare, server lag is EXTREMELY common. Which is actually, about a third of the time, why your character will get hit/killed. A small, half-second lag that stops the picture... allowing you to run right into an enemy attack. Three Rings needs to upgrade their servers. Badly. About nine times out of ten? Another player in my party will complain about it.
* The lack of variety. Levels are separated into types, and those types are typically denoted by icons. If you've seen a level with a certain icon... you've seen them all. The only ones that have any real solidity and aren't just flip-flopped versions of others, and have solid level design are the raid boss mission levels. And that's 13 levels out of probably nearing 100.
So basically put, it's very fun, yet very hard. Very accessible and easy to learn, but difficult to get past the lag to master it. It's repetitive, but very easy to simply ignore that and get into the actual gameplay. And while it has a pay-to-win mask, you can easily take that off and still get the best stuff without paying a thing.
I recommend it merely as a very good time-waster. Just look at my play record of this game. I wouldn't have that many hours if I didn't enjoy it.

Let me start off by saying that I love the Fallout franchise and for the most part have nothing but good things to say about the franchise as a whole. But in my opinion... Fallout 4 was a massive step in the wrong direction. And here's why.
1) The game is TOO FREAKING EASY.
Fallout 4 really shows a lot of things wrong in the current triple-A gaming market. Over-simplified gameplay, hand-holding, the enemies having a marker to show if they're too hard... It's like the game is treating you like an idiot.
2) THE PLAYER CHARACTER IS FULLY VOICED.
Now, I can give Mass Effect a pass for doing the fully-voiced player character trope since Commander Shepard is a pre-fabricated character, but with a Bethesda RPG like Fallout, that's just not right. The Sole Survivor is YOUR character... Or supposed to be your character anyway. I want to give the player my own voice. Not have to listen to a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥voice actor voice the generic and boring lines that my character speaks. Thankfully, there are mods to remove the character's voice that you can find on Nexus Mods, but I feel like Bethesda would have been wise to just not voice the Sole Survivor.
3) You are forced to join one of the game's four factions on your quest to find your son.
What I miss are the days of the old Fallout games where you could join one of the factions in the game or at the very least do missions for the factions. It made your character feel like they were a part of the wasteland. Like how in New Vegas (*cough* best Fallout game *cough*) you could do missions for the NCR and gain reputation with them without having to join their ranks and upset another faction. You didn't get many bonuses for not joining a faction but I liked the freedom. Here? NOPE.
4)  Mass Effect 3 ending syndrome.
Now, I might go back to finishing the game later once I install the proper mods so I can make my copy of Fallout 4 into a... you know, PROPER FALLOUT GAME. But after watching the "multiple" endings on YouTube let's plays, what felt like a real stab to the back in my opinion was the fact that the game had basically the exact same ending sequence, just with a couple different lines of dialogue and a few different still-frames, so just like Mass Effect 3's "multiple" endings, it ultimately boils down to a matter of "What flavor of the same ending do you want?"
5) Preston Garvey.
"Another settlement needs your-" NO! I don't want to have to do another one of your stupid, unrewarding quests!
6) Marcy Long
Just play the game and you'll find out why I, along with a lot of Fallout 4 players hate her...
Now for the game's positives that I found.
1) The overhaul of VATS
Having everything in bullet-time instead of just time stopping completely made combat feel more intense as you had to be quicker with your decision-making.
2) Being able to romance your companions
Just a fun little feature that adds some fun to the mix and some character development for your companions to feel more like real people.
3) Fighting a Deathclaw in Power Armor with a Minigun
Just. Freaking. Awesome.
Final verdict: With the way Bethesda has been going, I fear they might end up becoming another EA or another Activision. While this is not a horrible game, it certainly is no where near as good as the previous games.

I'm sure other people have come across this feeling too.
I've played all kinds of shooters and put stupid amount of hours in some of those as well. Battlefield, CoD (Mainly played CoDUO and the original CoD4), Titanfall, CSGO, Combat Arms, America's Army...etc etc. Just saying I've played a lot of
shooters.
Now onto Black Squad. I've had my eye on it for a little while but not really looking at it much due to the fact that it really looked like those general rough F2P FPS games...Combat Arms, A.V.A, Warface...And simply put, I really can't get into those types of games. (Anymore)
Black Squad is different though, it's honest (I could not find Any P2W, Devs seem good and communicative) and the actual game is pretty solid.
But my issues stem from what I ment earlier with those general F2P FPS games.
Black Squad is most definitely better then those in my opinion, but it still has this...
Feel to it. I don't honestly know how to explain it properly. This is something that a lot of F2P FPS games have and I know that others have felt the same as I do about those games.
This is something I feel straight off the bat from just the Menu screen, it's very cluttered and has the same style as other F2P FPS games. It's not appealing (At least to me). Obviously with saying this, these things can be changed and the game is an Early Access game, so these things aren't 100% important right now, but it was just my first impression.
The few maps I played didn't feel like anything new...To be honest they felt exactly the same as other maps from other F2P FPS games and even some of the modern CoD maps. 3ish lanes, close quarters, intentional choke points and a couple spots for a sniper to sit. Which you can get away with and still enjoy yourself. (CSGO for instance does this and it's still fun) I don't honestly know if there are other types of maps, larger ones and what not, but really I didn't wait around to find out and didn't really want too.
Movement is really basic (Not always a bad thing). Also I don't mean they need to have sliding, wall running and all that crap. This is proper boots on the ground (GOOD) but the animations, sounds and the general 'Feel' of the movement feels really cheap and just basic...And honestly this is one of the things that have drived me away from games like this.
Gunplay...I didn't notice recoil really, even with another assault rifle I brought (in-game currency) had a lot of recoil, but barely enough to make me need to concentrate on recoil control. This can be a good and bad thing depending on how you like your shooters, I don't mind either...But it did add to that Cheapness feel I was talking about.
I didn't really notice any major overpower-ness with guns, my fights were won to who was quicker or had better awareness, which is what the game is about. It's a twitch shooter for the most part.
Now why the Recommendation? It does sound like I hate the game.
But that's my opinion on MY play of the game. That doesn't mean it's a terrible game.
The game itself is actually quite solid, probably needs some tweaking. Remember it's EA and also it's not exactly easy to balance Multiplayer games straight away.
There doesn't appear to be any P2W (I could be wrong, but I really didn't see anything P2W-ish) which is a massive plus on top of other F2P FPS games which has been plagued with this problem for a long time.
The Devs are actually communicative and in general...Decent. Which is quite rare these days.
I highly recommend at least playing it a bit, it's certainly got an audience...Not me, but certainly has one. It's quick to get in and quick to get out if you're the type of person who likes fast games. Perfect time-killer.
The Good: Solid game, no P2W, Quick gameplay..Good time killer.
The Bad: It can feel cheap and can be pretty generic in areas.
The Ugly: Your mum.
It's anti-cheat is better than Rust's....

Of all the sandbox games like it, Starbound is easily the best one I've seen. It always feels fresh and exploring is a ton of fun. Going to different planets and exploring them will help you lose time quickly. There's so much to do as well, from building to getting your buddies together and forming a band to storming a castle and looting it's residences. Just too much fun. Further updates to the game promise something even better in the future.
Updated 02/01/2015: The massive update to this game has improved it drastically. There's now more progression to the game and it feels like the rpg elements have more pressence. Many of the small annoyances have also been removed, like all the constant survival elements (you no longer need to eat and you no longer get cold unless it's otherwise described on the planet you're going to). Many small things here and there have been tweaked or removed completely, while the combat has been tightened and made more challenging. Where focus for challenge was placed on annoying survival elements, that focus has shifted to challenging quests, enemies, and environments. There's more detail to the game now, ranging in everything from background art and environmental animation to planet descriptions. The update notes contain all the additions and changes, so I don't need to get into every single one, but I will summarize it by saying this: the game is 100% better. Chucklefish have proved to truly respond to the fans of their game and have succeeded in re-crafting an excellent sandbox game that immensly improves upon the original. If ever there was a time to buy this game, it's now.
Update 08/25/15: I once again update my review as this game recieves a new update of it's own. The new content is amazing and only further makes the game a must own. With the addition of being able to build colonies on planets, the game has created a new goal that players can strive for. If desired, you could now build entire cities full of characters. In addition, planets have been made more interesting, with greater variety for improved exploration. I may be exaggerating slightly, but this game has to get some of the best updates I have seen of any game ever. Each major update adds new content and improves the game in some way. This breaths new life into it and is the best way to keep me coming back, even after taking lengthy breaks for some time. I really cannot rave enough about how much this game has improved from when I first started playing it last year. It remains one of my favorites and a core staple of my games list. If there was ever a time to pick this game up, now is that time.

So this game. I can strongly recommend it, and it has had one of my best moments in gaming happen after it being out for a mere 2 days at this point.
What is this event, I hear you ask?
I won't go into too many specifics to avoid spoiling things, but a certain defence mission popped up for me. It was unavoidable, so of course I began it.
I went in expecting a normal mission.
I was so wrong.
This mission was a true struggle. The enemy can reinforce every turn, but a soldier from your reserves was deployed every turn. To win, I had to defend one objective, whilst destroyed another. I decided to do this, my higher ranked soldiers (grenadiers/specialists/sharpshooters) would hold, whilst my experienced ranger Colonel Captain "Commando" Alex would lead 4 rookies forward to destroy the objective.
What resulted was a struggle that resulted in sounds like I was "relieving" myself, as anyone who hear me would have thought I was. Shouts of yes and occasional moans of OH!
Now, poor Alex was killed escorting the rookies to the objectives. I was pressed for time - a rookie was dying every turn. I had one left, and the objective only needed one more hit for me to win.
I sat on the edge of my chair as all 3 enemies w missed this rookie, whilst an explosion failed to kill him. The rookie destroyed the objective, but was promptly killed. I was almost ready to scream in happiness.
But then, I had to extract still. A final rookie ended up being left behind.
An hour later, I completed this mission. What resulted was a total of 46 fallen enemies, and 8 dead soldiers. I realised all 6 surviving soldiers had been gravely wounded, so my fighting force consisted of nothing but rookies.
What I mean by saying all this is - it's a challenging game. But that's it's appeal, nothing comes easy.
Apart from the obvious optimisation problems and a few graphical glitches, I'd recommend this game to anyone looking at trying it. Good luck.

I played this game a ton in early access, enough to beat every available objective at the time. When the game officially came out, I started from scratch, got a full max level roster, maxed out the town, and beat the game. After all this, I cannot recommend this game, which might sound strange given how much I've played.
The game initially appears promising, as you're introduced to a myriad of classes and tasked with crawling through dungeons, acquiring loot, and upgrading your characters and town. It plays very much like an RPG with the hit chance RNG and permadeath of XCOM. The stress mechanic adds an interesting dimension to the game (although, in the end it's really nothing more than a second health bar.)
The problem is the game doesn't add anything new after the first couple hours and becomes a grindfest until the end. Given the way the game is structured, that grindfest is excruciatingly long. To be fair, the early game is refreshingly challenging as you learn the mechanics and try to balance spending gold between hero and town upgrades. However, once you learn how things work and discover a few solid strategies and party compositions, the game becomes a boring routine of:
When a hero needs treatment for a quirk or disease, they need to sit out for a round. This makes it necessary to create multiple teams to rotate in and out of the dungeons. In addition, once any hero completes just one of the end game dungeons, they cannot go into any more end game dungeons, which adds to the number of redundant max level characters you're required to build up. The repetitive grind is partially alleviated by the large number of classes available. Unfortunately, several of the classes end up playing very similarly.
Many of the monsters are simply reskins of existing monsters, with attacks that are essentially the same except for different animations, damage numbers, and sometimes a pick from a limited grab bag of status effects. The dungeons are procedurally generated and also end up looking more or less the same. You walk either left or right from one room to another, fight monsters, and pick up loot. There's no sense of exploration aside from "what's behind that door?"
The RNG nature of the battle system creates a false sense of excitement that sadly vanishes as you learn the range of possible outcomes from each attack and develop strategies to handle worst case scenarios. With some strategies, it is nearly impossible to lose a party member, and you are almost guaranteed to end a dungeon with zero stress. Once you've adopted a set of rules (e.g. if
appears, do
), the game becomes nothing more than carrying out those rules like a mechanical monkey. And although the final dungeon introduces a few new situations, you need only to slightly modify your existing rule set to get through them.
This game starts out interestingly enough with the promise of challenging adventures. As it turns out, the only challenge is staying motivated enough to get through the repetitive grind, which I only endured because I'm a sad OCD completionist. I tried to make the process less painful by listening to podcasts or watching netflix. It helped a little.
Be wary, this game is a slow and insidious killer.

I haven't beaten this game yet (soon though) but from my experience with this game, it's a must-buy if you're into RPGs.
First thing I've gotta say is I almost refunded this game because I wasn't prepared for the difficulty it presented. If you're a newcomer to the series or you've never played a fighting game, you'll most probably feel this game is too difficult and unforgiving. I died more than 15 times fighting against an early NPC (the Swordmaster) outside the first area and asked Steam support for a refund. Fortunately, I did not get it though as I'd already spent 3 hours into the game at that point.
The combat system feels clunky at first but as the game progresses, it's one of the best systems I've ever seen. You can dodge most of the attacks from your opponent if you time it right. There are many types of weapons that fit every play style. Describing the combat system in its full entirety is very hard, you have to play to feel it.
The lore in this game is beautiful. Every boss has their own backstory, all of them are equally interesting and contributes to a well-designed world/story. Level-design in this game although is overall great, but is by no means perfect. Camera angle in some areas is just atrocious, and sometimes you're surrounded by mobs and stucked in a spot where you can only watch yourself die. Nevertheless, it does not happen that often, most of the time, it can be avoided by fleeing to a wider area.
Now about the notorious difficulty of Souls games, many have told that it gets much easier as you progress. I did not believe that at first as I forgot to count how many times I died on my way to the third boss. It took me more than 15 tries to take down Vordt of the Boreal Valley, almost 17 tries to beat Cursed-Rotted Greatwood, I've never even beaten the katana NPC after 2 hours (he accidentally fell to his own death, I'd like to fight him now though). These bosses rank among the easiest bosses in the game according to most Souls players. From then on, I defeated Aldrich and Dancer of the Boreal Valley on my first try. Even Pontiff Sulyvahn, the most difficult boss in the game if you're bad at parrying like me, took me about 10 tries while I was prepared to die for hours and hours.
So you definitely improve as you progress through the game. Difficulty in DS is not an illusion, it's real but it goes down each time you learn your mistakes.

Let's get this one thing out of the way: I have not played the previous games in the Fallout series. I tried once, for five minutes, and found nothing that I liked. Fallout was just a not-for-me-type of game.
Until Fallout 4.
Want to spend hours building houses, arranging beds and decorating? Want to forget about building and just kill stuff?  Want to spend hours wandering around, or follow the storyline and just do the quests? Everything is possible - but your actions do have consequences. The only limitation is that you have to like story-driven games. Otherwise you'll end up skipping a lot of dialogues and getting lost as to why and what you need to do.
The game offers morally and ethically challenging options which, at least for me, made some choices very difficult. You don't always know what decisions are important and what not. This can make it a bit of a guessing game if you want to explore your options before closing any doors. There is of course also humor in the game. You can for example help to free a ship which is crashed on top of a skyscraper. You know, those things can happen to anyone!
One minor issue is that the game can be very repetitive. If you choose to work with a certain faction, you'll end up getting the same quests over and over again. That is not compulsory though, so you can just forget it when a certain NPC tells you AGAIN to liberate some spot you already helped two times with the exact same problem.
All in all, this is a good game for people who like to immerse themselves in a story. Enjoy, have fun and thank you for reading!

Does XCOM 2 build upon its predessecor or is it a mere letdown?
The good:
+The sequel maintains the addictive gameplay of the original, expands features and refines others.
+The campaign now features a doomsday clock which keeps the game going at a much better pace.
+The music is far better and has more personality.
+The graphics have gotten updated and are overall quite pleasant.
The bad:
-Most operation/missions are now set on a hard time limit, which can be frustrating if you're a careful player.
-Even with VO set to a minimum you'll constantly hear Bradford, Tygan and Chen parrot the same lines.
-Base construction has been simplified further and while it does have room for strategy it's a far cry from UFO.
-The launch has been plagued by (potentially) game breaking bugs and a constant frame rate drop even on high end PCs.
Bottom Line:
XCOM 2 expands and improves upon almost every single aspect of the first game and is a great experience for fans of the first game. However, the launch has been a rocky one and potential players should brace themselves for both bugs and frame rate drops.

This is a great final chapter to the Dark Souls series. It's significantly better than the previous one, with great level and environmental design and enemy variety. The pace of the combat is slightly faster this time around, taking some influence from Bloodborne's combat. It's absolutely the most polished of the series, consistent in quality from start to finish. My only criticism is that it's a little uninspired and lacks a clear identity, constantly making references and homages to the previous games. I wish the game had struck out on its own a bit more.
Mechanically in terms of combat this is the best the Souls series has been. If you enjoyed any of the previous games, you must play this game. If you're a newcomer to the series, for PC this is probably the best entry to start with - it's a great port, running well on modern hardware and despite the constant references to previous games, it works well as a standalone title.
A fitting end to one of the best series of the decade.

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic Dungeon Crawler in its base form. But it's so much more than that. The game revolves around re-building your Hamlet and forming a roster of heroes to challenge everything the dungeons can throw at you. The stronger and more expansive your Hamlet becomes the easier it is to improve your heroes, but the harder the dungeons become to compensate. So the challenge never diminishes, and the game remains consistently fantastic.
If you enjoy a challenge, and are prepared to fail several times before you succeed this game could be for you.
Turn based combat was never dead, as much as some claim it was. And this is a prime example of exactly how turn based combat is the king of deep tactical combat.
A unique, spectacular art style which extenuates the dark, dismal fate which awaits your unfortunate heroes.
Brilliant Narration is the real champion here, but the sound effects are powerful enough to not be outshone.
Overall, this is definitely a game worth picking up, one of the true Early access success stories.
EDIT:

Innovation like stress impact on your heroes force you to manage your party instead of just throwing in a team and embarking on a quest, the difficulty could have been a bit less but still this game is fun.
And all the above mentioned aspects will combine together .. to own you.
EDIT:
Okay, this game is quite .. unfair. Its heavy reliance on RNG renders this game unbalanced. Losing a party that you've invested a lot of hours in is too frustrating, which ultimately pushes you to grind more to bring another party to the required level.
I'm not going to change the recommendation, i think this game still needs to be played to appreciate the fantastic gameplay, artwork and voice work / sound effects. I just hope this game is properly balanced in the future.

Does XCOM 2 build upon its predessecor or is it a mere letdown?
The good:
+The sequel maintains the addictive gameplay of the original, expands features and refines others.
+The campaign now features a doomsday clock which keeps the game going at a much better pace.
+The music is far better and has more personality.
+The graphics have gotten updated and are overall quite pleasant.
The bad:
-Most operation/missions are now set on a hard time limit, which can be frustrating if you're a careful player.
-Even with VO set to a minimum you'll constantly hear Bradford, Tygan and Chen parrot the same lines.
-Base construction has been simplified further and while it does have room for strategy it's a far cry from UFO.
-The launch has been plagued by (potentially) game breaking bugs and a constant frame rate drop even on high end PCs.
Bottom Line:
XCOM 2 expands and improves upon almost every single aspect of the first game and is a great experience for fans of the first game. However, the launch has been a rocky one and potential players should brace themselves for both bugs and frame rate drops.

It's pretty much like Warfarm[e], but with even less of a reason to play to the "endgame" given how the game is being updated and developed and the very obvious paywalls. The weapon selection and balancing is also very dubious in a negative way in that some weapons shouldn't even be considered to be sought after because of how terrible they are, even when compared to weapons of the same Rank. This is a huge lack of insight by the developers' part; if you're going to put something in the game, why make it worthless?
The enemies are also similar to that of Warframe's, albeit better, but still shares the same problematic principality. To clarify: the variety of enemies is really good and you can easily decipher which monster is nastier than the basic ones. However, the problem lies in that they are really just those basic enemies but more bullet spongier, hit harder, and maybe have slightly different attacks/attack patterns. That's not to say it's all bad, but it's wasted potential and a little lazy.
Traversing a level could be done a bit better, more specifically when you stumble upon a fork in the road and you end up taking a long path that ultimately leads to treasure rather than the exit. It gets very tedious and boring having to backtrack all the way back at the same dull pace. This might seem a bit nitpicky, but surely the developers could've added a faster way to move about the world when you've already rid a path of enemies.
All-in-all, the latter two issues I addressed aren't much of a big deal, it's the first issues that is the reason for why I do not recommend this game.

For the most part, the game is ok. You go through dungeons, level up your gear and rank up into harder areas, allowing for better gear. But it soon becomes apparent that there is a massive paywall to advance. Although it can be avoided, this leads to IMMEASUREABLE amounts of grinding the same either bosses or Arcade levels constantly to either get enough of the currency, find any orbs required to ccraft new gear to advance to the higher ranks and finding the ridiculous amount of crystals needed to level up your current gear 10 times so you can buy new gear... and the droprates of all of these things is so low you can go through 10s of hours without actually having found a single one.
Another turnoff is that unless you already have them, there are 5 now impossible to get achiements, meaning you can't begin this game and aim to get 100%.
The final downfall of this game though... is there is pretty much no endgame content at all, which hasn't changed for years, and very likely won't change any time soon, or possibly even at all, so once finished it may just seem really pointless trying to continue.
In all seriousness, this game... if you like this sort of genre and you are going in with some friends, or you are great at making online friends, this game can be a lot of fun regardless of the insane grinding as the community is actually very nice for the most part.
Although it has a  redeeming feature of its friendly casual atmosphere;  it can get insanely boring and painful to even bother,
...so I can't recommend this game.

This might be the weakest entry thus far in the Fallout series - it having taken a sharp dive since the transition from 3D isometric to first person open world. Mechanics present in the game have you focusing heavily on crafting, salvaging and scrapping things in order to build structures in settlements - which you then have to babysit.
The story is that you are Vault dweller guy/gal from Vault 111 and some mofos have stolen your baby and murdered your spouse; REVENGE TIME! Not going to spoil the ending for you; but it's a tad lackluster.
Most of the wasteland is exceptionally bland minus two items of note which stuck out to me: Pickman's Gallery and Detective Valentine. There are not as many vaults present and many locations are similar. By mid-to-end game you are immediately thrust into making big decisions (i.e. murder) regarding four factions (Minutemen, Institute, Brotherhood o' Steel & Railroad) in what seems like a sudden way. There isn't anything that has helped to invest you into any of these factions at the end of the day; making the choice of who to support at the end seem pointless.
This is a time waster at best and perhaps hardcore Fallout III / New Vegas fans will dig this. While I got enough time out of it; I can't say I enjoyed that time. Recommend it on sale for $20 or less!

Does XCOM 2 build upon its predessecor or is it a mere letdown?
The good:
+The sequel maintains the addictive gameplay of the original, expands features and refines others.
+The campaign now features a doomsday clock which keeps the game going at a much better pace.
+The music is far better and has more personality.
+The graphics have gotten updated and are overall quite pleasant.
The bad:
-Most operation/missions are now set on a hard time limit, which can be frustrating if you're a careful player.
-Even with VO set to a minimum you'll constantly hear Bradford, Tygan and Chen parrot the same lines.
-Base construction has been simplified further and while it does have room for strategy it's a far cry from UFO.
-The launch has been plagued by (potentially) game breaking bugs and a constant frame rate drop even on high end PCs.
Bottom Line:
XCOM 2 expands and improves upon almost every single aspect of the first game and is a great experience for fans of the first game. However, the launch has been a rocky one and potential players should brace themselves for both bugs and frame rate drops.

Let's get this one thing out of the way: I have not played the previous games in the Fallout series. I tried once, for five minutes, and found nothing that I liked. Fallout was just a not-for-me-type of game.
Until Fallout 4.
Want to spend hours building houses, arranging beds and decorating? Want to forget about building and just kill stuff?  Want to spend hours wandering around, or follow the storyline and just do the quests? Everything is possible - but your actions do have consequences. The only limitation is that you have to like story-driven games. Otherwise you'll end up skipping a lot of dialogues and getting lost as to why and what you need to do.
The game offers morally and ethically challenging options which, at least for me, made some choices very difficult. You don't always know what decisions are important and what not. This can make it a bit of a guessing game if you want to explore your options before closing any doors. There is of course also humor in the game. You can for example help to free a ship which is crashed on top of a skyscraper. You know, those things can happen to anyone!
One minor issue is that the game can be very repetitive. If you choose to work with a certain faction, you'll end up getting the same quests over and over again. That is not compulsory though, so you can just forget it when a certain NPC tells you AGAIN to liberate some spot you already helped two times with the exact same problem.
All in all, this is a good game for people who like to immerse themselves in a story. Enjoy, have fun and thank you for reading!

This game is surprisingly entertaining for thinkers. You assemble a party of 4 adventurers to attack various randomly created dungeons. Thinking is required. You have plenty of characters (20+ at times) but you are always balancing tradeoffs. A given dungeon might have creatures more vulnerable to different attacks. A dungeon might have a boss-monster as the goal, which requires a different strategy from attacking the weaker minions. Different characters have different abilities, but they can only be used from different slots (e.g., warrior-types typically attack from only the front 2- player slots, and can only attack the front-2 of 4 enemy slots). There are numerous class types, and each interacts differently with other class types .
In addition to dungeon tactics, you have to manage your town. Your town has various buildings that allow you to upgrade your characters (guilds for skills, and blacksmith for weapons/armor).
The game is original in its handling of stress and mental disorders. You still have to pay attention to HPs. Run out, and a player is on "Death's door" (which in itself is another interesting dynamic). If your characters get too stressed (from the environment or monster attacks), many many bad things can happen. Anxieties aren't completely random though. As a player, you make choices that affect this. Do I focus my attacks on a melee bruiser that lowers my HPs? Or a drummer that will stress us out?
The game is full of choices, and your choices matter. There are three areas of player skill that will lead you to victory, or make you wallow in misery. Party selection (classes that compliment each other, utilize each of the 4 party spots well, and match up favorably to your dungeon/quest), tactical decisions (which monster do you focus on? Do you try to quickly kill your opponents, or use a slower approach with defensive buffs and more DOTs), and your town decisions. In addition to upgrading your facilities, you must spend precious gold to help characters lower their stress, or remove maladies that are particularly bad for what you are trying to do.
All characters develop quirks, good and bad. To a degree, you can manage them. But every gold you spend removing a quirk means you won't have enough gold to train a character, or equip your party with short-term supplies for expeditions. There are many decisions and tradeoffs with each.
Presentation:
Graphically the game is average. The gothic darkness wears on you after a several hours. The sound effects are entertaining, especially the narrator describing what happens.
For $30, this is a gem.

I came straight from playing XCOM: EW, Long War, and have logged hundreds of hours in that game. That may be why when I started this game at first I felt very frustrated. My first playthrough was on veteren, which I thought should be adequate difficulty for a first time playthorugh. Wow, this game is no joke. I wasn't attempting Iron man or anything first time through, so I  reloaded A LOT at the beginning just to prevent game ending wipes.Unlike LW, the relative cost of recruiting rookies is high, so losing soldiers is NOT fun. Having finished the campaign, I think that's one of my main complaints on balance; the cost of recruits. You WILL lose soldiers in this game. It WILL punish you, much more EW or LW.  As I adjusted to the new difficulty level and quirks of the game, at first I was frustrated by the change in pace.
Then it hit me; This game is not supposed to be a reskin of XCOM 1. It will be different. And it will be harder (we lost the war!). And there are certain tools as the game goes on that will allow you to put the aliens under your foot if you can survive. Looking back, there are things I should've done differently, but I will say this, I LOVE the way the psi ops class is handled. I love the class, I love the abilities, and I love the way you train them. If you're having a bad run but manage to get psi ops guy going, you can turn around your whole game because mind control is such an amazing force multiplier. There is nothing quite as satisfying as mind controlling an Andromedon, a giant metal suit enemy that is an amazing bullet shield for your own troops.
The campaign is story rich, I loved it, it is also long. Expect at least 50 hours for a playthrough, probably closer to 60.  I was on the edge of my seat after I got enough momentum to not be terrified for every single mission.
In sum: This game lived up to its crushing hype and then some. At first I was mad at it because it was flipping hard. Then I was mad because it has some bugs and quirks (beware the VIP missions, they're buggy). Then I just let it go. I let the graphics problems go (not terribly well optimized yet) too. And I had an incredible experience. The soundtrack also is great. This is an incredible game in its own right that makes EW look like a light prelude to some real meat (until LW came around). If you're having any doubts, make sure your computer meets the minimum standards, maybe even higher, then buy it.
To quote Alfred,"Sometimes, people deserve more. Sometimes, people deserve to have their faith rewarded."
My faith has been rewarded. Well done.
*edit* a few weeks in and modders have already made this my favorite strategy game of all time. The community is great here.

Really enjoying it so far. It is pretty much more of the same, only better.
I know some people hate the timer based missions, which do seem to be the majority of the missions, but I'm finding that they keep things nice and tense, and always give you just enough time to make the objective. Also, often, they balanced out by the concealment mechanic - you've got the chance to scout out an area without popping pods, move into flanking positions, and generally get nice and cosy, letting you set up ambushes, which are ~very~ satisying when they pull off.
Performance wise, the game does get choppy during mission loading (cut scenes also seem to be capped at 30fps), and while it does feel shoddy it doesn't particularly impact on the experience in any way (at least on my i5-4690K / R9 290). Currently, I've got it maxed out, apart from dialling back the AA to 2x MSAA (because 8x MSAA, which it autodetected, was actually pretty horrendous), and it runs perfectly fine in game, which is where it counts. Sometimes the camera does go a bit weird, sometimes the game pauses for a few ~seconds~ while the aliens figure out their moves, but none of it feels terrible or immersion breaking. Just a little bit sloppy.
I'm too much of a wuss to try anything above normal difficulty, but so far, five hours in, I haven't had any major setbacks. It's keeping things tense, without feeling horribly unfair. The difficulty, so far, seems fairly balanced.
Oh, and Rangers. Just, Rangers.
Definately recommended.

It is what it is.  It's extremely minimalistic.  It's pretty polished looking and the graphics are neat, but it doesn't seem like there's a lot of depth to it.  It feels like a little homogenized Minecraft / 3D Dot Heroes MMO without all the wonderful amazing features you'd expect. It's free to play and would make a good entry level MMO for a younger kid, but it's not going to blow your mind.  The preview trailers make it look more grandioise than it is.
I admit to only playing a few hours, but if an MMO can't grab me and pull me in during that time then I don't feel like it will at all.  It's easy to get caught up in an MMO's rinse-and-repeat questing, following those bread crumbs to the next level but after trying every MMO on the planet I don't waste much time giving them the benefit of the doubt anymore.
It's free and it's less than a gig to install vs 40 gigs some other MMOs can be so it doesn't take long to install and try yourself.  I can't see myself pressuring any friends to waste their time to check it out alongside me so I can't recommend it in good conscience.

To be blunt, Fallout 4 is the most overwhelming game I have ever played. That's a fantastic problem to have in any RPG game. The amount of content in the base game + that of the DLC is mind boggling. You fill spend hours upon hours questing and scavenging. The main story quest are okay at the least, but the side quest is where things get interesting. You can spend so much time trying to discorver the world, you will sometimes forget after a long night of gaming that it's 7:30am and your job started a half hour ago. The Commenwealth is a place filled with so much depth.  Each building you enter will most likely have a unique story to tell. This coupled with your charcter's own story adds a level of emersion that few games can achieve. If your like me you probably care most about the loot. While the're are lots of unique weapons and mods to discover (which is fantastic). What seems kinda dumb to me is how the legendary items work. While going through the game you will find these legendary enemies. Once killed you can loot a legendary gun or piece of armor from them. These items will have a randomly generated perk. What I find dumb is how often this happens. My first playthrough was on normal. The amount of legendary items I had found at the end was a little insane. Legendaries dropping so often makes them lose their feel as being powerful. The largest negative about this game is its 60fps cap. If your like me and rip out your eyes if you see anything below a 100fps then the cap will probably be the largest bummer. The reason why it is capped is because the Fallout engine cannot functoin if the game is above a certain limit. This causes every thing in the world to move and happen faster. For example picking locks and running become faster. Other than that and some bugs Fallout 4 is a great game. The good drastically outway the bad. So if you like RPG's with a emerive world, solid shooter mechanics, great customization, and a crap ton of content... then buy Fallout 4 now.

Metroidvania style gameplay that rewards exploration and discovery. No character build is useless, unless you're soloing, if that's the case, please don't do a support character like a sorcerer. You will have a bad time.
Dark Souls III is a wonderful experience. It's much closer to the original Dark Souls, rather than Dark Souls 2. Estus is actually useful and the combat is very punchy. Bosses are very creative and quite a lot of fun.
If you enjoyed Dark Souls, get this.

Darkest Dungeon is definitely an interesting game, at least, most of the time. With the idea of having flawed heroes fighting the horrors found in the estate, while struggling with their sanity and their already depleted coffers of gold, DD manages to work in almost every aspect, almost. After a while, the incredible costs of buying upgrades, the amount of heirlooms needed to improve every aspect of your hamlet makes it a long, long grind. This, regrettably, takes another turn when you notice that after a while, you know each and every nook of every dungeon, yes, they change each time you go in, no, after the 50th time in the Cove it won’t matter. On the bright side, the ease with which the game can be modified can certainly increase replayability and decrease the most punishing aspects of the game or at least, reduce grinding to a considerable level. All in all, I found it to be an entertaining game, though we now have to see what does Red Hook intent to do with the game. More characters, more monsters won’t help much with the replayability, but adding a few new dungeons and more interesting things to do and more varied could certainly help.

Darkest Dungeon is legitimately one of the best, most fun games I have played in a long, long time. Every time I shut it down, I count the time until I can pick it up again.
There's something incredibly satisfying about the huge array of classes that all work together in different ways. Customizing your party, their gear, their attacks, etc, for whatever you're set to face and watching them roll through challenges as a well-oiled machine never gets old. But one of the great elements of Darkest Dungeon's design is that there are no guarentees - the strongest party can fall due to a small misstep, a few ill-timed enemy crits, rolling just the wrong encounter at the wrong time.
Some people might dislike this, saying that they don't like 'being screwed by RNG.' Which is fair, but I hold that this constant tension is necessary to the game. Every mission has to have the potential for failure. For example, I once did an extremely beginner mission just to level up a new character, and somehow it turned into a nail-biting war with several near-death encounters, barely scraping my way back to the surface at the mission's end. That, to me, is an important part of the Darkest Dungeon experience, and I love it through and through.
With gameplay spoken for, we get down to the presentation elements - spritework, writing, etc. And they're all phenomenal. Wonderful art, spot-on sound design. The writing can be a bit ostentatious at times, with the narrator using at least two multisyllabic adjectives for every noun he says and item descriptions like gems that are "blue like strangled dreams." But even where it's a bit eye-rolling, it's solid, and the individual character barks flesh out a lot of personality to the classes in very short order.
If I had any complaint, it would be that it is somewhat easy to be stuck between the resources you need: Heirlooms to upgrade your estate, which in turn allows you to use gold to upgrade your characters. I've regularly found myself in surpluss of gold but still waiting for enough heirloom drops to be able to do my next round of character upgrades. It's not a terrible thing - I'll take any excuse to run another dungen - but it can slow the feeling of forward progression a bit.
As it stands, I've played the game for nearly 40 hours. I'll probably complete it around the 50 or 60 mark at this rate, and I'm already thinking of the different class arrangements I want to try the next time I play it. $25 is dirt cheap for the amount of game here.

XCOM for Apple Macs

(also for those looking to know more that the media may miss. There are a lot of reviews online to check out. This is more for the new and those wanting to know more about mac. XCOM 2 takes the idea of a sequel and add's that you didn't win the first XCOM. Earth is now run by the aliens and ADVENT. The storyline is great, but that is just the beginning! The games mechanics are outstanding. This turn based strategy game was great in XCOM and now is legendary in XCOM2.

POST MODERN ALL IN ONE

Did you like the movie Aliens (firebrand takes off and you have a jump ship that brings it all back, "5x5 in the pipe")? or Predator (wooded areas that have sounds that make you feel like its right there)? or Commando (with the DLC there is face paint baby) ? or Farscape (scifi weapons)? or Stargate etc? or Edge of Tomorrow? (exosuit) Its all here. Platoon of military strategy and look of a war is there.

THE SHIP (mobile base)

*contains the skyranger The new base is mobile. Remember when you would look at your ant farm and wish you could see what they really were doing? well in XCOM2 you can zoom and see what is happening. The soldiers and staff including Bradford, will appear in different rooms at different times. If you loose a solider, you may find those that have bonded with your lost solider show up in the bar & memorial. Combat training shows your soldiers work hard at becoming the solider type beyond rookie.

WHAT DID YOU LEARN KIDS?

A lot of flags are in this game to represent your troops nationality. It is there you can get a grasp of who's flags is what country?

CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION

in XCOM you could change the hair and the face and skin. sure. But this, you can create such memorable characters that you find a great emotional attachment to their efforts to regain the world. The loss of a solider is heartbreaking and just what you would expect from an enemy that should put the fear into you! Choose your: *country *m/f *hair *hair color *upper face (glasses etc) *lower face (bandana, cigar, cigarette etc) *hats/helmets *eye color *tattoos (right and left arm separate) *color of tattoos *color of armor (1 for main and 2 for secondary color) *torso armor choice *legs armor choice *arms armor choice *armor pattern *weapon color *weapon pattern Does your character have an attitude? sure why not! *by the book *normal *twitchy *laid back *happy-go-lucky *intense *NOTE: blowout hairstyle is there but none of the helmets from XCOM 1 make their appearance again. oh that isn't all

VOICES

There are a variety to voice packs for this and includes major languages as well. *NOTE: missing Chinese & Japanese (but maybe mods can fill that gap?)

ENEMIES

Fear. Run in Fear, or don't and loose a solider or two, or at least come home with some wounded and be shaken. The enemies of XCOM2 are more lethal and scary. The sectopod is legendary and now is even more intimidating and scary. With more walls and buildings that can fall and collapse, a Sectopod walking through a wall reminds me War of the Worlds with Tom Cruise. Those things scary me to pieces!

MUSIC AND SOUND FX

Tim Wynn is amazing~ The soundtrack is as legendary as Tron Legacy but with all the fanfare of Victory and defeat and foreboding. The emotions and shock that this soundtrack creates is epic and makes the game so much fun as it builds the intensity right along. My favorite is when you land your skyranger and troops are deployed the sound track wraps up like a movie to go silent as the XCOM team readies to engage in their concealed start. (not all mission do you start concealed but most you do) THAT'S NOT ALL! So you remember scientists and engineers that has 'how many you had' and has no image or name in XCOM? in XCOM2 you can name and create your scientists. (see importing for information)

CHARACTER IMPORT AND EXPORT

Yup. you can make your own characters from 80's action shows to your favorite my little pony (for those that want crazy colors its there too). Oh you say you don't want to take that kind of time? Soon there will be downloads for you to put in the game that allow you just load them up! The game offers importing of characters. Scientists and Engineers *NOTE: you can't create either a scientist or engineer. They are called VIP. *NOTE: you can write their back story and biography of not only your soldiers but your VIPS. (Scientists and Engineers)

DARK VIP?

yup. meaning you can actually name your enemies VIP you need to either subdue (hit with a gun butt to knock out and carry to capture) or outright eliminate the Dark VIP causing issues for the ADVENT aliens.

Is this a good game? Yes.
Does it have many flaws compared to previous fallout games? Yes.
First of all radiant quests. Who the hell thought this was a good idea is a fool. Imagine infinite, boring, repetitive, sidequests that the game never tells you "Hey by the way this series of quests have no end." Why are MMO grinds in a single player game? I have no idea.
On top of this in most games if you clear out a building and grab all the items then that area can be crossed off the list.
In this game enemies constantly respawn plus quests keep sending you to the same location over and over.
So even if you have cleared out an area. If you receive a mission to grab an item there then you have to re-do the entire level.
This is a huge time waster compared to telling the NPC, "Hey I already cleared it out and grabbed the item in that building while randomly exploring the wasteland."
Besides those issues we have the writing.
Let's say it is a tad............lackluster.
Compared to New Vegas the whole thing falls apart.
Without spoiling anything. You have 3 main factions. Unlike New Vegas you can't just take over everything on your own and be a "Wild Card".
These groups come off as annoying and have a lot of short term goals but very vague on their long term goals.
When asked of one group, "Hey why are you doing this?"
Their response was simply, "Oh you would not understand it is too complicated."
This is a far cry from new Vegas where certain NPCs would go into a 15 minute debate with the main character about their goals and beliefs.
As the base building aspect of the game is can be pretty fun but expect you houses to come under attack constantly unless you build lots of defenses. Even then with 50 turrets if you are not physically there the whole place can go up in smoke.
About the DLC. Great if you enjoy building stuff but if you are looking for more story I highly suggest point lookout. (Honestly liked it better than the main game.)
The game offers a ton of free mods with a lot of community support.

I won't write a long review as all the details you might desire can be found in other reviews.
Bugs: First up - there are some bugs, in my experience all minor glitches with graphics, with just one exception. One early unit can reposition one of your soldiers with an attack (the snake/tongue) and that may put the soldier into a weird spot - they haven't got the code for where to drop the soldier quite right.  It hasn't caused me any problems - it's just weird.
If you are the kind of person who will find it hard to enjoy the game with some minor graphics glitches - probably best to leave it for the first major fix patch.
Design: It's Xcom - the gameplay design is consistent with Xcom EU/EW - with one major change. There are missions (particularly early in the campaign) with objectives to be met within a certain number of turns. These mean you have to adapt your strategy to meet the objective. It does mean that the gameplay here feels quite different than in Xcom EU/EW ... IF you were a defensive player.  If you were an aggressive player, it won't feel very different. I was a defensive player - I have had to learn a different approach here.
If these time limited objectives will stress you out and make the game unfun - then either give it a miss, or subscribe to one of the mods in the steam workshop that modifies or removes the timers. Personally I expected to find those timers very stressful - I HATED the first bomb mission I faced in Xcom EU.  But, having adapted my gameplay - I find them very good indeed - they add an objective and a challenge and make the fights different.
That's the bad news ...
The good news - it's awesome.
It's already given me a gaming moment that will live with me for a long time.  There is more of everything - and it's all great.
4 months and 250 hours of gameplay later - and the game is still highly enjoyable to me.  I only play ironman and have not encountered any of the game breaking bugs that are supposed to ruin my experience. The new king / queen bosses are great - a completely different challenge, you have to learn to adapt your style for them fast. It gets better and better.

After 159 in-game weeks, I have finally achieved victory, such as it is. I do not regret a single minute I have spent playing Darkest Dungeon. It is a brilliant game. As with everything though, it also has its shortcomings. Here's a short run through all pros and cons of this game:
The good:
+Excellent, dark atmosphere, clearly inspired by the Cthulhu mythos. The difficulty adds to that. You can never feel entirely safe during a dungeon run.
+Stress and disease mechanics. This is such a great, simple idea that I am astonished no one has ever thought of implementing it before (at least no game that I know of). Your characters will stress out and crack, affecting the rest of your party. They will get sick due to all the wounds, blood and vile substances thrown at them. They will need rest and healing. It is not possible to use the same set of characters for the whole game.
+Combat mechanics, which are the meat of the game. At first glance, they are simple. Four characters on one side, max for on the other. That is just the surface. There are 14 classes in the game (with an additional, 15th class being developed) and some combinations simply do not work (or, as with religious classes and the Abomination, refuse to work). Various classes excel at different things and can perform only in specific positions in the party. Different locations, of which there are 5 (Ruins, Weald, Warrens, Cove and the Darkest Dungeon) require different skill sets. Additionally each character has 7 combat skills and 7 camping skills and is only able to use 4 of each at the same time. Also, there are positive and negative quirks, which modify character behaviours. And did I mention trinkets you can equip your characters with?  There are lots of those, each with pros and cons. This whole system is really complex and I love it.
+Challenge. The game is hard. Characters will die. This is a fact. What I found out during my playthrough though is all the character deaths were partially my fault. Sure, bad luck and RNG were a factor, but each and every demise could be traced to an error in my judgement. Overall, I feel Darkest Dungeon is harsh and unforgiving, but fair.
The mediocre:
~Hunger mechanics. I do like the fact that characters need to eat. However, the way this mechanic is implemented is questionable at best. Your characters can get hungry AT RANDOM during a dungeon run. They also eat during camps and can eat to heal themselves. The problem is none of these are connected to each other. For example, you have just made camp where eating is mandatory, and your party gets hungry the moment they step out of the room. The idea is good, but needs polish.
The bad:
-The grind is real. I did not mind it all that much since I enjoy the gameplay, but it can and will be annoying to many. There are 4 types of heirlooms to collect, which are needed to upgrade your hamlet, which in turn allows you to buy better equipment, train better skills etc. There are two problems with it. Firstly, each heirloom is a reward in a specific location. The second problem is you need ridiculous amounts of heirlooms - and the inventory space during expeditions is very limited. This issue is most glaring when it comes to Deeds, which are needed to update the Blacksmith (weapons & armor) and the Stagecoach (additional characters for hire and roster size). Both structures are absolutely crucial to progess in the game. As a result, you need to constantly grind the Weald (where deeds are the quest reward) to even have a shot at the higher difficulty dungeons. The developer has already stated that he will do some rebalancing to solve the issue. Hopefully Red Hook will deliver on their promise.

TL;DR to save everyone some time : low fantasy storyline setting, roguelike settings and difficulty, and turn-based strategic combat make this a must-play for any aspiring strategist on your friends list. Fans of things like DnD, Adventures of the Amazing Screw-On Head, and Lovecraftian-style storytelling will fall in love with the artwork and gameplay.
9/10, a must-have for anyone even remotely interested in strategy, roguelike, or turn-based games.
Personally, I love this game. I'd step up on a rooftop and sing it's praises all day long - it's difficult in a fair way, it's just the right flavor of artstyle and storytelling that I love, and the seething, under-your-skin horror type is one of my absolute favorites around. I love the way this game plays, I love the way it feels, and I love the "easy to learn, difficult to master," aspect of it's gameplay.
Lovecraftian influences aside, this is one of the better games (And a turn-based RPG, at that!) to do the "creeping ethereal horror" trope right. The scenery is dismal, and a damp. You can practically feel your bones ache as you enter your "Hamlet," your hub for all things story and character based. The enemies are dripping with ichor and the floors are marred by dark, mysterious stains - more then often you'll find yourself wondering if you saw something skittering around in the darkness, or if that's just your imagination playing up again.
And, of course, your imagination running wild weighs heavily on how much you'll love the gameplay. I went into this in the "X-Com," style of thinking - I'm going to save the damn world, and I'm going to wind up looking stylish doing it. You will not. Your men will die. They will die screaming; more often then not, they'll die screaming at you. This game makes a habit of telling you not to be prideful of your victories, and it's so gosh-darned right. Pride makes the fall that much more bitter, my friends... And you -will- be falling. Insanity, accidents, religious zealousness, traps - there's a thousand and one ways to die, and I'm constantly finding more. Certainly, you can explore every nook and cranny. You can absolutely run your troops ragged and force them to fight... But they are only human. And, without spoiling too much, you will find that out very, very quickly.
I won't lie - I've died too many times to get the full storyline! Within the intro sequence, you can tell how much love was put into this game... The voices, the artwork - I can tell you that this studio wasn't larger then twenty people without even looking at a wikipedia page. But they loved the work so much, and they sweat and bled for it, and it absolutely shows. Basically, a relative of yours writes to you, telling you that you've inherited the estate that they left behind. Your relative, seeking riches, dug up something... Horrible. Horrible enough for him to put a bullet in his brain rather then deal with the madness that he released upon the world. Let me just say, if any of the devs are reading this? That got my attention within seconds, and I knew that I'd just plopped my money down on something that I was going to be interested in.
I love this game, guys. This is a long review - and my play hours aren't numerous... But if even one person who was on the fence about this game reads this and decides to purchase it? Well, I consider that a victory. This is one of the very few "indie games," that I wholeheartedly feels -deserves- the money that they're getting. I hope the devs do great with this title, and I hope that anyone who's decided to get this game based off this review loves it just as much as I do.

Ok... So I beat it.
I'm writing this review just after FINALLY completing the main quest, so I may be biased. I may be just riding the high... but I don't care. I recommend this game, and I'm gonna now say why.
Darkest Dungeon is an unfair game. Know that before starting. It is unfair and it's chancy, and that's ok. There is no winning strategy here, because the game LOVES to tear things arround you just when you're getting confortable, and that's it's charm, basically. It may make you cry, rage quit, but it'll never feel old. You'll do dozens (in my case, I had to do close to two hundred to beat it, but I did took my time. And I also suck a bit at this game) of dungeons runs and each will feel unique, in some way, so there'll be no boredom in the grindy aspect of this game.
One feature I absolutely love about it, is the final quest. It's awesome. It's all of the game condensed in 4 quests, and it represents a masterful work of the team in terms of balance, ambience and difficulty. You'll both want to see what awaits... and be deathly afraid of what new horror you'll find there.
This is a game that demands patience out of you, to calculate your every move and keep a cool head about you. You won't be able to beat every dungeon and that's ok, knowing when to retreat is crucial here. Sometimes the gods will smile down on you and you'll cruise through it. Other times you'll be down on your knees in the first battle. Perhaps they shuffled your party into a horrible mess and crit you to death. Perhaps you activated a few traps before that particular battle and your party was already fighting at half strength, it doesn't matter. This game both punishes you and gives you ample breathing room to retire, re-plan and re-think your strategy, and that's awesome.
Tl;Dr, it's both a hard and at times unfair game, but it offers enough anti-frustation tools so that you won't curse it's name too loudly.

Let's get this one thing out of the way: I have not played the previous games in the Fallout series. I tried once, for five minutes, and found nothing that I liked. Fallout was just a not-for-me-type of game.
Until Fallout 4.
Want to spend hours building houses, arranging beds and decorating? Want to forget about building and just kill stuff?  Want to spend hours wandering around, or follow the storyline and just do the quests? Everything is possible - but your actions do have consequences. The only limitation is that you have to like story-driven games. Otherwise you'll end up skipping a lot of dialogues and getting lost as to why and what you need to do.
The game offers morally and ethically challenging options which, at least for me, made some choices very difficult. You don't always know what decisions are important and what not. This can make it a bit of a guessing game if you want to explore your options before closing any doors. There is of course also humor in the game. You can for example help to free a ship which is crashed on top of a skyscraper. You know, those things can happen to anyone!
One minor issue is that the game can be very repetitive. If you choose to work with a certain faction, you'll end up getting the same quests over and over again. That is not compulsory though, so you can just forget it when a certain NPC tells you AGAIN to liberate some spot you already helped two times with the exact same problem.
All in all, this is a good game for people who like to immerse themselves in a story. Enjoy, have fun and thank you for reading!

Darkest Dungeon is unique.  That means there isn't really anything else too much like it.  I had fun for the few hours of it I played.
