Did they forget to call this Call of Duty: Wasteland?
Bethesda removed nearly all rpg elements that made the other games great. The world of Fo4 feels empty as you are expected to build most of the settlements throughout Boston. There are two actual cities/towns, and thats Goodneighbor and Diamond City. Of course there are the faction bases, but you're only going to have access to 1 or 2 of them, which at that point amounts to around 4 locations that someone who doesnt like the settlement system can make use of. The settlement system itself feels like a last minute addition as it is very clunky and doesn't work well with inclines or declines in the terrain. Event with the settlement system, the non-settled locations you can find are bland, empty and have no backstory. I feel like they were put there just brag about the amount of locations the game had. Sure, you may find a holotape or two around the area, but thats it. No fun and interesting quest, no deep backstory, just an empty hull of a location that makes the game feel like an early access game. Back to the removal of rpg elements, the skill system is completely gone. No more will you have to worry about building your character uniquely or be able to invest in a certain weapon type or mechanic. Now every character you make will feel the same as most of the unique and interesting perks that were in Fallout 3 and New Vegas are replaced with simple perks such as: "20% more damage with pistols" etc. It seems that Bethesda put most of their time on the graphics, animations and gunplay, and paid little attention to the actual characters, world building, or even the main quest. The main quest is basically Fallout 3's main quest but with a new skin. The motivations of the major factions are poorly written, as when you ask Father in the Institute, he tells you it would take too long to explain. What?!? In New Vegas, Caesar would tell you a long story of how his Legion came to be and why he has the ideaologies he has, while the factions in 4 just do what they do because "they can." Moving on, the dialogue system has been reduced to "yes", "no", sarcastic comment, and more "more info." No longer does it feel like you can actually speak to the characters in game, it now feels like you are a robot pawn being asked to go around killing raiders and super mutants for a reward of caps and no real reason why. The Fallout games have always had interesting side quests that would be memorable for years to come. Fallout 4 has failed in this department as Bethesda has seemed to think, "quantity over quality" as the best side quests are the few that arent fetch quests or "go here and murder these things." I completed the main quest, all side quests, and found every location in game in 110 or so hours, including some of the dlc, on PS4. (Dont even get me started on the DLC, they have no good writing, except for Far Harbor, which was decent, but most of them were settlement building dlc and brought no real content to the game.) Compare this to the 300 or hours I've spent on New Vegas (PS3 and PC gametime combined.) I've tried to get myself to replay Fo4, trust me, I have, but I can't manage to do it due to the lack of decent content and rpg elements in this game. There are 2 endings, none of which show you a slideshow of what you've done has affected everyone else in the wasteland, like how the older 3D Fallout games did. The only real positives this game has over the older ones are the graphics, gunplay, and animations, which are all expected in time from a AAA game company.
If you're looking for a real Fallout experience, play Fallout 3, or better yet, New Vegas.

Now, personally, it's damn rare that I actually fall asleep to
in a videogame. Boredom? Yeah, plenty. Exhaustion, on the other hand, from the frequent 'OH GOD DON'T DIE RESTAULT' moments, among others, is a rarity for me.

Darkest Dungeon lets you assemble a roster of dungeon adventurers and send them into dungeons in order to defeat pestilent creatures that have plagued the land in order to fully restore a hamlet back to its former glory. The game is not so much a pure dungeon crawler, but more of a dungeon crawl management simulator (for lack of a better word). You do not only navigate the heroes through a dungeon. You also take full responsibility for their wellbeing. As heroes go through dungeons, they accumulate stress and could even get diseases, and you have to make sure you bring them back to top shape in between your dungeon runs. You do not just control a single party of heroes. You have to rotate several different heroes around and pick the ones most suitable for the job at hand.
There are 4 areas where you can take your expedition: Ruins, Warrens, Weald, and Cove, and each one has its own dangers and challenges, what means that you need to prepare your team accordingly. The dungeons also come in different lengths (Short, Medium, and Long) and of different difficulty (Apprentice, Veteran, and Champion). As of the final release, the final dungeon has been added too.
The combat is really fun and in my opinion has a lot of tactical depth to it. It's not just a simple turn-based battle system, but each position within your party setup is important. Some hero classes prefer frontal positions in the squad (like the melee tanks), others prefer to hang back (like healers or ranged attackers).
The game has been balanced around loads during Early Access, and though some aspects of it might feel unfair still, overall the gameplay feels pretty solid and requires a lot of strategising and adjusting to the situation when bad things start to happen. The game can be pretty punishing towards those who do not take caution. And even if you do everything right, things can still go wrong at times, and part of the gameplay is also having to deal with that. The game encourages tip-top preparation and contingency planning. That means that the game is easily not for everyone, but those who do enjoy that sort of thing will be up for a real treat.
Art, music, and voice acting are also superb. Easily a cherry on an already delicious cake.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes a good challenge and doesn't mind it when a game occasionally throws them some curve balls. I can't remember the last time a game has kept me interested for 70 hours and counting.

Excellent game if you're into a casual MMORPG. It contains PvE features together with a VERY competitive PvP feature called "Lockdown." As a pro-league Dota 2 player, I felt that Lockdown was really enjoyable to play competitively.
Gameplay:
For short, it's a dungeon crawler. Nothing too shabby, with the birds-eye-view, you're pretty much aware of a decent radius around your character. The game consists of two default controls which focus on keyboard or mouse although fully customizable to your fitting especially if you have a gaming mouse or a gamepad. The game is full of innovative monsters which you're likely to enjoy and many levels which "rotate."
Graphics:
I have to say, I'm rather impressed with the vibrant atmosphere this game has. If you enjoy bright games, you'll love this. The chibi-style avatars are adorable enough to make you have to punch a wall to feel like a man again and the environment is surprisingly detailed. In terms of network-graphics, I'd say they did well enough to avoid graphical-lag - this, I can't explain through words so you'd have to play the game in order to get a feel of fluidity.
Social:
The player-base is small enough for you to socialize and gain deeper friends and wide enough to feel the game's population. Also, being recently implemented to Steam and Steam trading, it's a lot more convenient if you're a Steam gamer due to trade offers whilst offline and such convenient features - only way to get the feel for it is to actually play it and realize.
Support:
Their Spiral Knights Support is mainly based on actually mailing them. Their in-game support lacks and doesn't prioritize the most important aspects of so-called "support." So you can't really expect to get a hold of any "support" whilst in-game because it's not that convenient - only way is to contact them through email, which isn't so bad but could improve.
Overall I give the game an 8/10 - which would've been better if it weren't for their bad tech "support" and I emphasize "SUPPORT," not "filter" team.

So close... but no.
I've been playing the game since early access. A lot of progress has been made, but the game is still deeply flawed. The RNG is just too bad. The developers tried to sell the punishment it dishes to the player as a feature. It's not, just supremely imbalanced. At times you breeze through content... at other times you get smacked in the face no matter how much you strategize, prepare. or equip. Unless you are the kind of player that enjoys mindless safe brings to build up to a chance to really "play" an adventure... I would not recommend the game until it gets fixed.
For example... you can walk into a dungeon and clear it with little effort, with a bunch of trash adventurers... you can spend many days building up a team, train them, equipment them... BOOM.. a worm wipes one of your guys first room... so what do you do? Abandon, lose 15k gold... or move on? Well if you played enough you know that you have to leave. Go back to town run a bunch of trash low level stuff to build back up... and fix the dmg down to your team. This isn't challenging reality... justy grind grind grind. Bad RNG.
The game should force players to face bad luck and make tough choices, but it quite often lets you get away with foolish choices and punishes good ones.... this isn't a feature, a rare result of occasionally rolling a 1 or a 20... this is standard throughout the game. Which is why I must not recommend it, it is SO well done in some aspects and so close to being great... it seems great for much of a play thorugh... you won't notice it at first... but eventually after you have eaten the sandwich you will realize the mayo was rotten. Skip this game, or buy for 2 to 5 dollars.

Honestly Fallout 4 is a mixed bag to me. So I'll list what i think of as the pros and cons of the game
Pros:
Voice acted mc, A blessing so i dont have to read all my own dialog considering how tiny the font is usually in bethesda games.
Companions, they actually feel like characters with some personality instead of just meatshields that follow you and that you can shove your inventory on
Gameplay, *finally* a Falloutgame where I feel confortable attacking things without using VATS constantly. The fact that i am better sniping someone without VATS then using it to snipe someone is rewarding.
Mods, They are good
Setting, everything about synths are cool and no one can convince me otherwise
Cons:
The MC's dialog isn't as well written this time around, there are less options, and your character just isnt as interesting as a person due to those options as prior Fallout Mcs.
The story is probably one of the worst points of this game, it starts off interesting but just kind of drags and a lot of the things that make you go from one place to another seems contrived. Thats not even counting the ending which is just kind of.. Okay. At the end of the day the story isnt BAD it's just OKAY and for a Fallout game it could of been better.
It gets easy after awhile. About halfway into the game I stopped feeling challenged
Settlement building, without mods it drove me insane and only became okay after I downloaded about 5 mods. It feels like it was thrown in because every game has it.
Crafting, its boring and I dont think I ever used it except to color my power armor. Better with mods but yet again you can tell they threw it in because of the idea that all open world games have to have it.
Overall I enjoyed the game though. It's a more casual experience I think compared to New Vegas, and especially Fallout 3, and I appreciate that in some respects. I like what they have done to the actual gameplay and for the first time many of the characters were actually fleshed out and likeable and things were fun enough to keep me interested for the whole story plus some. However there are glaring flaws with the story itself, and there is clearly room for improvement in upcoming Fallout games. I hope the next ones better, and I think overall I enjoyed the story and such of New Vegas more. But if you ever want to snipe someone in the wasteland then go romance a ghoul, this is the Fallout for you.

This game, despite being in early beta, and despite having to start from scratch multiple times from character wipes (which, according to the dev will not happen again), i've never been so happy to start over.
This game takes everything that Terraria popularized, and amps it up many many times over.
Graphics wise, the game is beautiful. Lively, detailed sprites. Incredibly diverse environments. Wonderful lighting effects. I have no complaints at all in the graphics department. As the game gets patched more and more, we will get to see even more things: biomes, cities, planets, and of course, loot.
Sound wise, the music is very minimal, but beautiful. A plethora of instruments, each with their own sounds, make player created music incredibly easy. While the music may not be as iconic or happy as Terrarias, its still good. My only complaint is the combat music. It is constantly fading in and out. In large battles, it isn't as big a deal. However, when you are on a low level planet and are maxed out 1 shotting everything, the constant interruption is kind of annoying. Also, no voices to speak of. It is still early so that may change. I don't expect fully voiced characters, but as of now, the only noises anything makes are when you hit them.... also, why do all the enemies sound like horses or pigs?
Gameplay wise, it is very similar to Terraria (i know the comparison may annoy some gamers, but lets face it, Starbound wears its influence on its sleeve). A very simple "left click foreground, right click background" makes building a breeze. You don't have to build seperate walls and solid blocks anymore!
The biggest gripe for me, game play wise, is combat. It is kinda boring. You can swing a weapon, or shoot a gun/bow... and thats it. No magic. No wands. Guns and swords. Thats it. It isn't even a deep combat system. You have one swing with your weapon. No combos, no alternate attacks, just.... swing. This is the thing i hope changes the most from now.
So far, its early and Chucklefish have shown great interest in player feedback and have great dedication to the product. Every patch release is like a holiday and everyone logs on to see all the shiny new stuff. This is the best early access game i've played and I can't wait to see the direction Chucklefish takes this game. 9/10

This game is quite frankly NOT a sequel to dark souls 1 or 2. Its a sequel to bloodborne.
The art style and the combat style resemble bloodborne MUCH more than darksouls.
The combat especially is total GARBAGE if you liked the slow, methodical, deliberate and defensive souls combat.
This one is ALL about raw speed and reaction times.
Gone is the tradtional slow enemies who unleash combos then have a 2-3 second pause allowing for a punish if you dodged the combo. Now the attacks are incredibly fast (some are almost impossible to dodge since they have no wind up or anything) and relentless with pauses of like 1 second max for retaliation.
Further the enemies now aggressively chase the player, gone are the menacing but slow monsters that would walk up slowly allowing you do catch your breath or gather your thoughts mid fight. Now they will sprint upto you and never give you a second of respite just unleashing combo after combo.
This also makes shields near useless since at anything but ultra late game you wont have the stamina or the shield stability to block these hits, your guard gets broken mid combo and you die.
Gone is the "balanced but fair" souls combat style too, now monsters are much faster than the player and have limitless stamina allowing for chains of attacks even a max level player could never hope to achieve.
Input mapping is also HEAVILY used and some enemies are totally immune to things like leap attacks because they will counter 100% of the time. I have seen enemies leap attack the ground in front of them when i was at right angles on a higher platform because the game read my inputs and knew i would jump down and thus be in the exact spot the leap attack will land by the time its animation is done.
Im not saying its a terrible game but it sure as heck isnt dark souls and doesnt deserve to be called that.
In the original souls games you felt like swordsman, it was all move and counter move, an elegant dance.
Now you will feel like an angry chimp just rushing things and mauling them till they stop moving.
This game is so much fun!!!

There's not that many negative reviews, so I'll give it go.  I'll sing some praise first, since the game is ok.
I won't list everything that's good about Darkest Dungeon (DD), but it does have a lot of goodness tucked away inside.  I really love the artistic style, and turn based combat for example.  These two things drew me to DD.  Stress is a gimicky mechanic, I could take or leave.  It works and adds something to the game play, even though there are times I wish it didn't.
The real problems for me is game pacing, variety, and length.
I've found that pacing is one of those things that rpg's in general have a poor time getting just right.  DD over complicates it by using five different currencies, and then in a rather miserly fashion not giving them out in any quantity.  To add to the worries, bag space is extremely limited, so even if you find some great hoard you might not profit by it.  Oddly enough, the exp gains might be spot on, but without the other resources your party will quickly be outmatched so there's no way I can tell for sure.  Essentially, you'll be forced to start over at some point and rebuild a team with fewer flaws, and hopefully higher earning potential.
The rebuilding of a team isn't bad in itself.  I think it fits the atmosphere the game is going for.  This does lead to problems though.  All of the heroes are rather cookie cutter.  That's not bad presuming that you'll be burning through a lot of expendable characters.  On the downside, there's no reason to be invested in any of them either.  Additionally, every dungeon run is more or less exactly the same.  There are, I don't know, three, four different quest objectives?  Each zone a handful of unique mobs, plus a handful that could appear in any zone.  It leads to dungeon runs where the only objective is to smash and grab while min/maxing the curios and bag space as best you can.  It's too expensive to take stress damage, or risk a negative quirk.  So you find your little strategy, and more or less do the same things in dungeons you could hardly tell apart.
If this game clocked in at 20 hours from start to finish, I'd feel better about it.  It's not.  There are eight bosses, each of which requires some number of zone specific dungeon grinds to open, and has to be killed three times, at slightly more difficult levels.  Why?  just because. . . I'm almost through now, and I like the game enough to finish, and possibly restart it, but come on.  Have some respect for my time.  I've also read some spoilers about the ending.  All I can say is for real?
DD is a good game mired in poor design.  Everything seems to work, which is a big plus.  Guess it's suppose to be hardcore?  There are times it just feels like a hardbore, or a hardchore.  It's not at all bad, it just isn't that great once you get your teeth into it.
Overall, I'd recommend a pass on this one, unless you can get it on sale.  There are some neat things to see, but once you've seen them, you'll see them again and again, and again.

I have deferred this review since the few days that I played it after release as I really didn’t know whether I could recommend it or not. I got Fallout 4 on release day and, as I started to play, my heart began to sink. I wanted to make the best of it and figured the story would pick up and perhaps there would be depth to it that I had yet to discover. I’ve got a spoiler for you: it never happens. Of the 100 some-odd hours that I’ve played, I didn’t even finish the main story nor do I have any inclination to do so. I even bought pretty much all the DLC on sale over a year ago and I still haven’t gone back. Bethesda seems to be taking the approach of dumbing down their titles and streamlining them for maximum profit. Is it a fun shooter? Absolutely. Are there some beautiful, post-apocalyptic environments to enjoy if you can crank your graphics? Without a doubt. But there is no substance beyond a FPS in this game. If you want Fallout 4: The RPG, don’t waste money on this title. I was also one of the fans who managed to get the Fallout Pipboy Edition and I’ll tell you that I was shocked at the quality of that physical memorabilia as well. Took it out of the box, pressed one button lightly, and it broke off into the Pipboy. Same happened for the next buttons I pushed and the knob I turned. Quality control seems to be a thing of the past for good ol’ Bethesda. I’m hesitant to buy the next Fallout game from them, let alone the next Elder Scrolls.

Unturned is a good game at its core, with no shortage of content. However, the public multiplayer is deeply flawed. You're best off getting a couple well-known friends to play, or going your own with singleplayer - unless you enjoy the sound of crying and screaming and having absolutely no chance of cooperation.
+ Balanced vanilla gameplay
+ Plenty to do and see, even in singleplayer
+ Easy to customize gameplay mechanics, allowing you to tailor your experience for a leisurely zombie massacre, a gruelingly difficult survival, or anything in between
+ More than one approach to success - everything in the game has its uses.
+ Flexible and intuitive building mechanics
+Very fair business model - the "Gold" privileges include access to more character customization and cosmetic items, and the ability to join "Gold" servers, which, as far as I can tell, are really just Easy+.
* Highly active modding community
- Many public multiplayer servers are bloated with excessive and unorganized mods and plugins, ruining the balance of the game and confusing players
- Overwhelmingly abysmal multiplayer community, with screeching children and genocidal maniacs in abundance
Overall, Unturned has solid gameplay, is highly customizable,  and will keep you occupied for a while whether you're out to mow down zombies or brave impossible odds. However, if you're hoping to make friends, you'll find yourself knee-deep in high-octane unadulterated cancer. Other than that, as far as free survival games go, it's not at all a bad choice.

Technical issues aside, this is a very solid entry into the XCOM series, but let's go ahead and talk about the performance:
Thankfully, XCOM is not necessary a game where performance can make or break your overall experience, but it is still ridiculous that even though I'm running last year's mid-range specifications (i5-4690k, not overclocked, GTX 970) I'm still seeing constant frame rate drops during gameplay, cutscenes, and even in the menus and Geoscape mode. I average somewhere around 45 across the board, 60 during standard gameplay and combat; 30 in cutscenes and loading screens, and I'm lucky to get 50 when viewing the Avenger carrier.
, with that being said this is still a very good game. Running through the second-lowest difficulty I was able to easily make my way through the campaign and complete it, with moderate losses and a fair share of failed missions. (I played it all night on Friday, all through the day on Saturday, and didn't go to bed until I'd completed the final mission. It was 4:30 Sunday morning when I'd finally done so)
Replay value for this game is amazing. Every decision you make can make or break your playthrough. On its highest difficulty levels, XCOM is as unforgiving as its classic grandfather. I foresee many different playthroughs with this game.
I would give this game my recommendation, but if you're wary of it based on its current performance issues than I don't blame you for wanting to wait a little while longer. Just know that, technical issues aside, this is still a very solid entry in the XCOM series, a worthy follow-up to the Enemy Unknown reboot in 2012.

My opinion on Fallout 4
Fallout 4 takes what Fallout New Vegas did with companions and advances it, allowing you to judge what a companion likes and dislikes by way of the "companion liked this" message that can pop up
Fallout 4 took the idea of weapon customization, which FNV pioneered, and improved it, allowing you to mod your weapon as you like and either buy or build said mods. Fallout 4 also has better graphics and has more vibrant colours, which fits the theme that this game pioneers, that theme being that hope exists in the wasteland, no matter the desolateness of the land, that people can hope to rebuild in a new land, one that, while ravaged by war and american pre-war capitalist values, has plenty to help humanity renew themselves.  The previous fallout games each had different themes, fallout 1's theme being that anyone can make their mark on the land, anyone can be a hero. Fallout 2's theme was that everyone has a destiny to follow, they just have to look inside themselves to find it, and that purity is not a virtuous ideal to behold as a destiny. Fallout 3's theme was that the world has became hell, and people must go against the grain to help each other, Fallout NV's theme being that those who are stuck in the past will lead to the future's endangerment.
One of my personal things i love about fallout 4 is that, despite people complaining about lore breaks, Bethesda actually didnt break any lore besides Jet's origin. What Bethesda did was what is called addition retro-continuity, they added to the lore through a retcon. Fallout 1 and 2 did not talk much about Pre-war power armor and the APA's origin. Fallout 4 states that the X-01 inspired the APA that the Enclave use in Fallout 2. That loadscreen, the one that created the entire argument over X-01's post war or pre war origins, is MISREAD. It doesnt state that X-01 is APA, it says that APA was a design that was used over the older X-01 SERIES models. I use caps to show emphasis, Bethesda added to power armor lore by making each power armor part of a series. Therefore, T-45D is canon, but part of the T-45 Series of powered armor.
And before anyone complains that,"power armor wasnt ever powered in the games", that's a gameplay mechanic that actually fits lore. In Fallout 2, it's stated that the T-51 power armors used a built-in Microfusion Pack, one that would need a start-up, I.E the Fusion Core. In fact, T-45D's had used small energy cells (Microfusion Cells, the ammo for laser rifles) to fuel it's power systems but that the later powerarmors in the T-45 Series had done away with this, preferring the T-51B's power source.
APA is implied to use a micro nuclear reactor as well, as shown by the glowing fan, which X-01 DOESNT HAVE.
Another thing i like is that they did make the BoS as people saw them in Fallout 3. Yes, while it seems like the BoS in Fallout 4 are simply nazis, that's not so. In reality, no one seems to realize that the BoS still actively recruits wastelanders, as proctor Ingram says so if you ask her what she was expecting after she states that you (the player char) werent what she expected. She tells you that she expected a wastelander as the last batch of recruits they picked up were "wastelanders, dirty and beaten-up, looking for a handout". Last has multiple meanings in this case, she either could mean that they were the last batch, as in they werent recruiting anymore, or that they were the last, as in they are recruiting but they were the most recent batch before your recruitment.
Yes the BoS seems to have a Nazi stance against Synths and mutants, but that's easily explainable. The BoS hate mutants because they see mutants as an example of the US pre-war govt's failure to be smart with their tech, The BoS was created in part due to the hatred Roger Maxson held for the scientists in Mariposa who were part of the government project there, which was to test the FEV on P.O.W's and fellow soldiers. On synths and their hatred, the BoS hasnt actually seen a 3rd gen synth, they've only fought the frist 2 generations, who are merely robots bent on fighting under the direction of the Institute. They dont see a 3rd gen until
Synths and the third gen have even sadder stories if you read their creator, Alan Binet's terminal in his quarters in the Institute. You can learn that that Eve, his "personal synth", can dream, and robots can not dream. This is a good reference to Blade Runner and the book that inspired that film, "Do Androids dream of Electric Sheep" by Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥ Synths cant dream, because Synth means robot, but you can also learn from Father's terminal entries that he forced the institute to call their Androids "Synths" because he didnt want them to be acknowledged as beings with free will and rights. And furter more, if you go to the synth retention bureau and talk to Doctor Ayo, he mentions what the SRB does, they mind-wipe synths after Retention, as to make them compliant. This shows that the Institute fully knows that if a thrid gen could, it'd free itself, so they capture them and wipe any idea that the synth could be free. And it's even sadder when you persue the Railroad questline.
Coursers are another example that the synths have free-will. A courser is emotionless, emotions make humans act to save themselves and others, if a killing machine working under a faction that strips the rights of their standing army had emotions, the Institute would be in dire straits.  Third-generation Synths arent robots, they are human clones, if you watch the machine that builds the synths build, you can see that they build a third gen cell by cell.
People that complain that "fallout 4 had no bad guy", yes it might not have, but Bethesda really tried to push the idea that the Institute is a bad faction into your heads.
Do i recommend this game?
Fully, if i could endorse it and get money off of endorsing this game, i would jump at it first chance.
Fallout 4 is a game that has a story that is hidden in every terminal, every note, every person's story, while the main plot of the game might not be well-written, the game does good by fallout standards by making every location have a story that pushes the themes of fallout, be it the story of Vault-tec and their sleazy experiments on unsuspecting people with the permission of the government, or the story of a faction that forces it's own creation, to live in constant fear that their ability to think for themselves will be stripped should they display this ability openly.

XCOM 2 is actually a terrific game, I at first was not sure if I was going to enjoy it or not, the timers being part of it, and the lack of individual targeting areas, and the different if not also similiar format.
After playing the game for several hours, I realized that I did in fact love the game, the combat is enjoyable, the upgrades are fun, the story is exciting, and to be quite honest, I actually like the timers now that I have played with them on. Rather then taking things slow, becoming incredibly risk adverse, and loading up on medkits like I did in XCOM: Enemy Unkown, I've had to change my playstyle up.
Now every single person has some sort of explosive, with my specialists using their gremlin heals, Snipers, being almost the worst class in the first XCOM of this decade, have made a come back with some really amazing abilities and tactics, and every class has a use now that can't be replaced in this very aggressive and high-risk high reward combat style that I have been forced to adopt.
XCOM 2 is an amazing game because of what it is on it's own. The game itself is different enough from XCOM that it doesn't feel anything like an expansion, yet nearly everything in the details has a comparable element in XCOM, the gameplay, even though it's based on the same concept and same rules, is entirely different, yet it is still so fun that I personally can't stop playing the game.
Performance wise the game runs well for me, and it runs on max settings for me with only minor framerate losses in various cinematic parts.
I heavily reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys XCOM style gameplay, as long as they are open enough to understand that just like in real life, tactics have to change with time and the situation.

There are three different aspects a game needs to touch for it to be a considered a great game: the graphics, the gameplay, and the story. Dark Souls III touches every single one of those aspects and nails them perfectly. It's a masterpiece.
1. The graphics: The areas of this game are so diverse and beautifl to look at. Even at a low resolution and graphic options, the areas are astounding. The NPC's, enemies and bosses look realisitc, the textures as well.
2. The story: The story will seem pretty confusing at first, but will be easy to comprehend as you go on. Furthermore, every thing is placed there for a reason, every NPC dialogue needs to mean something, every enemy placement is intentional for lore purposes. The lore behind Dark Souls III is extremely deep, giving backstory to the NPC's, the bosses and the areas as well as giving explanations for anything happenning in the game.
3. The gameplay: This is the main focus of the game. First of all, the combat is extremely diverse. Each weapon has an extremely diverse moveset with attacks from every single possiblity. The choice of weapons itself is extremely diverse as well, giving more replay value to this amazing game. The character builds can be very different as well depending on your playstyle. You can be a melee player weilding a sword, a spear, a katana, a curved sword, a greatsword or claws, a sorcerer or even an archer. When you're not on a killing spree, the huge areas have plenty of space to explore and find new armor, weapons or items (sometimes even new areas).

Dark Souls III is an absolute master piece.  While I'm very disappointed that apparently the Dark Souls franchise has wound down with DSIII being its swan song, part of me slightly happy that the series will go down in history as one of the best of all time.  Dark Souls III gets back to the roots of the franchise by removing some of the less popular additions that were included in Dark Souls II.  DSIII feels very much like a refined, improved and expansive DSI.
The graphics are incredible.  The ambiance is incredible.  Nearly all the boss fights are incredible.  The entire experience is incredible.
The game is easier to navigate single player than DSI or DSII, but still provides a challenging and rewarding experience.  The monsters and bosses are no easier than before, but the lay out of the game - while definitely not linear seems to play out in a way that was easier to figure out where to go and what to do next.  Perhaps I'm just getting more experienced with the Souls series, but DSIII was the easiest blind trip I had through a Souls game and didn't struggle trying to figure out what I had to do to continue the story.
Bottom line is the value you get in this game is nearly unbeatable.  Especially on sale, you can easily spend hundreds of hours playing and replaying this game with a different experience each time.  You won't be disappointed.

While gameplay seems to be appealing from the beginning, the scaling to the later stages of the game is poorly designed. I'd even say it is simply abysmal: every lvl5+ battle turns into RNG fiesta with little to no ability to mitigate or prevent randomness on a side of the player. For example, a group of ~6 SPD monsters all went before any of my 7+ SPD party and killed my lvl6 position 3 hero. Just like that. I was unlucky. But the main problem is that the every high level "unfortunate event" of that type has the only consequence - more boring repetitive grind in leveling up another hero from 1 to 6. This game in its core is just the same old poorly designed RPG with the only way to victory - through tedious, boring, and repetitive grinding of the same content. The only difference is that the old games forced you to grind until your characters are OP enough to beat the game, and here you grind until you happen to be lucky enough to beat the game.

Honestly Fallout 4 is a mixed bag to me. So I'll list what i think of as the pros and cons of the game
Pros:
Voice acted mc, A blessing so i dont have to read all my own dialog considering how tiny the font is usually in bethesda games.
Companions, they actually feel like characters with some personality instead of just meatshields that follow you and that you can shove your inventory on
Gameplay, *finally* a Falloutgame where I feel confortable attacking things without using VATS constantly. The fact that i am better sniping someone without VATS then using it to snipe someone is rewarding.
Mods, They are good
Setting, everything about synths are cool and no one can convince me otherwise
Cons:
The MC's dialog isn't as well written this time around, there are less options, and your character just isnt as interesting as a person due to those options as prior Fallout Mcs.
The story is probably one of the worst points of this game, it starts off interesting but just kind of drags and a lot of the things that make you go from one place to another seems contrived. Thats not even counting the ending which is just kind of.. Okay. At the end of the day the story isnt BAD it's just OKAY and for a Fallout game it could of been better.
It gets easy after awhile. About halfway into the game I stopped feeling challenged
Settlement building, without mods it drove me insane and only became okay after I downloaded about 5 mods. It feels like it was thrown in because every game has it.
Crafting, its boring and I dont think I ever used it except to color my power armor. Better with mods but yet again you can tell they threw it in because of the idea that all open world games have to have it.
Overall I enjoyed the game though. It's a more casual experience I think compared to New Vegas, and especially Fallout 3, and I appreciate that in some respects. I like what they have done to the actual gameplay and for the first time many of the characters were actually fleshed out and likeable and things were fun enough to keep me interested for the whole story plus some. However there are glaring flaws with the story itself, and there is clearly room for improvement in upcoming Fallout games. I hope the next ones better, and I think overall I enjoyed the story and such of New Vegas more. But if you ever want to snipe someone in the wasteland then go romance a ghoul, this is the Fallout for you.

"How hard does a game have to be before I stop enjoying it?" was once a rhetorical question to me. Now it isn't. Dark Souls 3 is legitimately the hardest fair game I've ever played in my life. I know that with practice and patience, some day I can beat the game, start a New Game Plus, and rinse and repeat at my leisure. Many, many other people do, after all. But the truth is that I don't want to. Difficulty is everywhere in DS3. It's in the level design, the enemy design, the path layouts, the combat system, and on and on. Even the menus are harder than they were in Dark Souls 2. Character hair color selection is accessible through about 3 layers of menus during character creation, for example. Whatever it takes to finish this game on principle, I don't have in me, and probably won't have in me in the future. But that's not because it's a bad game. The game itself is gorgeous, fast-paced (by DS standards), and very, very deep. That's why I'm not giving it the thumb down - I don't think anything I've seen in the game is objectively bad. And I've only seen the first few hours of it in any case, which isn't enough time for a fair thumbsing-down of a game of this apparent quality.

Darkest Dungeon is a glorified slot machine disguised with a bloody, wild, dark-fantasy theme. Everything is RNG dependant, as well as being designed to work against you. Your healers barely heal even with trinkets and buffs, your sluggers often miss regardless of traits and buffs, and taking on the actual, literal 'Darkest Dungeon' portion of the game is simply an exercise in sadomasochism.
Many are quick to defend the 'difficulty' of this game because of the current trend in video games (difficult games, ala Dark Souls, Binding of Isaac, etc.), however, the simple fact is that Darkest Dungeon isn't as tough as it is dependant on sheer luck. Crits, dodges, empty rooms and hallways, the discovery of treasure and trinkets that aren't totally useless and the like. Player skill is much less important than simply scoring a critical hit on a cultist with your Crusader or Leper.
Until you struggle through the game and become rich, many of the upgrades to both buildings and equipment are simply too expensive to afford. The hero roster is pitifully small despite how easy it is for them to die, training heroes to their max level takes too long given how tiny said roster is and how quickly they can be killed, trinkets are often as needlessly debilitating as they are helpful, heroes become too stressed too easily (especially in the final dungeon).
The game simply isn't fun to play...but at the same time, the gambling nature of DD makes it addicting. After 100+ hours I've come to realize that I've only been playing this game for those sporadic moments of utter joy that follow criting a tough enemy party three to four times in a row. Those times are wonderful, but they're also far and few between. More often than not, the enemy will be punishing YOU relentlessly, not the other way around.
In summation: buy this game if you like to gamble. It's good for that. The art is fun to look at for a while as well and the narrator is a nice touch...at first. After completing your 20th quest, though, his repeated quips become reminiscent of nails on a chalkboard. The mechanics, however - the actual meat of the game, are rather unenjoyable.

I can't recommend Darkest Dungeon. I feel like there is a number of missed opportunities here, but I concede that a lot of people thoroughly enjoy it. Once you get over the initial difficulty hump the game boils down to using your strongest skill on the most dangerous enemy. There is only superficial synergy between your party members, although there is a lot of classes, the variety feels limited.
On top of this is the repetition. You can't for example hire higher level heroes, expect to nurse low level parties through dungeons over and over.
Now the dungeons themselves. There are some traps, but why aren't there more challenges outside of this? Eg you need to use the grave robber for some specific athletic task to get some extra loot. Instead you wander down the corridors rubbing the correct item on the correct object = reward.
Lastly it has to be said that the aesthetic of the game is amazing, voice acting is great and the art is top notch. I think this game will improve as time goes on and I plan on returning at some time in the future.
Until then for those of you who enjoy it, more power to you!

You purchase the game. You are a naive little casul. You have no idea what kind of pain this will inflict upon you. You start up the game. Big, white letters pop up on your screen: Dark Souls III. You press start. You watch the cutscene. You have a feeling that this is going to be fun. You learn the controls. You fight your way past the firstfew enemies. You reach a big room with a large, armored human-like being kneeling in the middle. You walk up to it, unsure of what to do. As you approach it, on the bottom of your screen it says: (A) : Remove sword. You press (A). You pull out the sword. A sudden rush of panic flows through you. A large red bar appears at the bottom of the screen. You hit the monster a few times with your weapon. The bar gets smaller and smaller. Just when you think you are about to win, the being raises its halberd high above its head. It comes crashing down, along with your health. You are confused. Is this how the entire game is going to be? A cycle of life, death, and progress, only to be sent back to the bonfire again? And the answer is yes. Yes it is. And that's what makes this game so damn good.
Welcome to Dark Souls III.

Okay, so now it’s been a while since my original review and my feelings towards this game have improved quite a bit. There are still some problems, such as the Vipers still occasionally pulling my troops through solid matter and both sides spotting targets through entire buildings with no visual confirmation. The one that really gets me are the moments where your soldier has 100% hit chance and misses his shot from pointblank range.
What really saved this game for me were not the updates and the fixes alone, but the Longest War mode they added into the game. Those familiar with the previous X-com will no doubt remember what I’m talking about. The Longest War adds a gaming mode that will truly challenge you and make almost each battle feel like you’re fighting an actual war against aliens. True, some people will probably find it too difficult, but you can adjust the specifics of the mode’s difficulty to fit your preferences.
The Longest War adds not only new enemies, enemy behavior, weapons and gear, but makes the whole game a lot more exciting. Not that I’m saying the original wasn’t, but this mod really renewed the game and made me want to play it again.
And speaking of mods…get them. Go through the Steam Workshop in the X-Com 2 section and pick some up for yourselves. I’d recommend using Google-search to find the best mods to choose, as some of these mods will improve the gameplay a whole lot. There has even been some attempts to fix the problem with the Vipers pulling your troops through walls and other solid obstacles they logically shouldn’t be able to go through.
The frame rate limit is still there, but I’m no longer bothered by it. I am – however – still quite puzzled why it is there at all. I mean, it’s not like this game is particularly resource heavy, so why the 30 fps limit? I’m sure someone out there knows the answer to this, but I certainly don’t.
My final verdict is that while I haven’t tried the new DLCs yet, but even without them, I would today recommend this game as it is. Just don’t forget to download the Longest War and check out the mods I mentioned above – they will improve your gaming experience quite a lot.

Darkest Dungeon is an excellent, if occasionally key board flippingly frustrating, game. Tasked with defeating the dark god your ancestor awoke, players assemble teams of adventurers and set them to work exploring the monstrous lairs around them, gathering loot, and rebuilding the small town that counts as home.
It could be like many RPGs, except Darkest Dungeon opts to explore the mental as well as physical toll battling an army of fungi-infested zombies or a gigantic demon-pig king might have on human beings. Managing stress, preventing mental breakdowns, and cycling your teams in becomes a careful part of the game. All of this is blended pretty seemlessly into a deep and satisfying combat. The RNG gods can be quite fickle, but post release Red Hook opted to give players some control over parts of the game's difficulty. It mitigates a lot of the grief that cropped up in the Early Access Days.
The presentation is also gorgeous. Pulling more than a few pages from Lovecraft and Mike Mignola, the art style is dynamic, and the voice acting and character designs are all top notch. An easy recommendation for anyone with the patience to dive into this maddening world.

Is XCOM2 better than the last one? Yeah, the game mechanics fit the setting a lot better. The world map is more interesting, even though it just feels like im playing a cheap board game. Darkest Dungeon is a brilliant turn based game loosely based off of lovecraftian lore. You are summoned to your ancestor's home that has fallen in disrepair and corruption to a force that is revealed as you progress through the storyline and fight bosses.
With stunning graphical design and amazing voice acting by Wayne June you'll be instantly drawn in... however.
From the very beginning the player is warned that this game is extremely hard, you will be forced to make tough decisions and not to grow overly attached to characters, THEY WILL DIE. Normally this is not an issue but...
The game mechanics are flawed in many aspects. Your characters have an HP meter and a Stress meter. Once your stress meter reaches 100 out of 200, your characters can and will most of the time develop some sort of side effect from the horrors witnessed throughout combat. Too many times have I witnessed my healer become paranoid and refuse to act all together, and whenever a stressful event happens, ANYTHING at all stress related, all your other companions will get more stress aswell, quickly developing into a failscade, and many times these happen outside of your control. At 200 stress your character has a heartattack and immediately hits 0 HP. This also stresses out the party. I have on multiple occasions seen one character hit 200, heartattack, stressing out everyone else into a heartattack, while all four where under some sort of bleed or poison and watched 4 party members die in one go.
RNG rules this game and will create nightmarish situations for you to witness. The ability for your team to failscade due to bad RNG is all too present, Heals are underwhelming and in no way will keep up with the ludicrous damage monsters put out. Debuffs and buffs dont last long enough, turn order is badly calculated and gives the "House" the advantage, stuns are lackluster and have diminishing returns (which is good) but because of turn order shenanigans, cannot be counted on or managed in any way. Due to these gameplay issues, creating any significant interesting team builds or strategies is highly impossible as nothing can be predicted and even the best team can have a bad day. The most prevalent build is a high spike damage team that is boring to play and takes advantage of the highwayman point blank shot ability.
Characters also need to constantly undergo "psych" treatment to be viable in the next mission which constantly means benching and using a different team. Once a character hits lvl 3 Resolve he cannot ever go back to doing apprentice level missions (Resolve 0-2) which means you can't grind an A-team and go back to do bosses you left so you could grind, you HAVE to fight a boss at the approriate lvl. Character can also level at different speeds, meaning one member of your A-team might have to be benched while others catch up. God forbid one of them dies and you have to level them again...
Ugh what else? I'm already getting tired of writing this review.
Characters have flaws too, those suck and can make a good character turn into a bad one pretty quick, those also need to be managed and purged constantly.
Eating in this game is a terrible mechanic that makes no sense, I've had a completely full character die from hunger.
Overall, fun, crisp, and beautiful game, but an extreme grind fest with no real reward for your work and only a headache when RNG gives you bad luck and wipes your party, there will be a lot of setbacks, be prepared for them.
P.S. Boss fights where designed by a demon from hell itself as they subject you to sadistic forms of actual torture both in real life and in game. Also I broke two mice and a keyboard while playing.

You can really see why this game is named XCOM 2: it shakes up the classic XCOM formula rather than adapting it like Enemy Unknown did.
You know all those games you lost back in Enemy Unknown? Well, they're canon. XCOM 2 takes place 20 years after the aliens won the war against humanity and began remaking the Earth into their image. Your average joe doesn't see the aliens much; they do most of their governing through a human "Speaker" and a human security force known as ADVENT. Meanwhile, XCOM is branded an insurgent organization and shunned by many, and only a few scattered pockets of resistance remain.
You'll start out in a random sector of the world aboard the Avenger, your mobile base. From here you can move from place to place to look for supplies (credits) and make contact with the resistance in other sectors (essentially the satellite meta-game of old). The difference is that your ability to travel to a sector depends on which ones you've already made contact with - think Risk's layout with its connecting lines.
Where classic XCOM had alien abduction missions, XCOM 2 now has Guerrilla Ops. These serve the same basic function - you have several missions available, but can only choose one to complete. The penalties for passing up missions are known as Dark Events, which are ADVENT's responses to your alien slaying. Dark Events can range from increasing enemy reinforcements in missions, decreasing your supply income, or sending a UFO to hunt you down.
The concept of panic is gone. The Doom Tracker is now instead the Avatar Project, a secretive alien agenda with 12 bars that slowly fill up. You can empty bars one at a time and slow the alien's progress by sabotaging Avatar facilities, challenging missions that are akin to large UFO raids from past games. If all 12 Avatar bars are filled, the game goes into a final timer, giving you one last chance to hit an Avatar facility and prevent defeat.
Timers are much more prevalent in XCOM 2, and this is perhaps the biggest controversy I've seen surrounding the game. Though there are still what I call "classic" missions with no turn limit, many of the Guerrilla Ops require you to complete the mission within a certain amount of turns. Terror sites also require you to save a certain number of civilians. If you despised bomb defusals from Enemy Unknown and/or relied on overwatch turtling, you'll definitely need time to adjust to the new pace. Thankfully, for most missions, your squad starts out concealed, a "stealth" mechanic that lets your troops sneak up on enemies and usually take out one hostile squad instantly.
Troop customization is the best it's ever been. XCOM 2 includes color palettes, weapon camos, weapon attachments, soldier biographies, and dozens of choices for appearances. The memorial wall even lets you write epitaphs for your fallen soldiers, which you'll be doing. A lot. Enemy variety is also vastly improved, and pods now contain a mix of enemy species. You'll often find ADVENT troopers patrolling with sectoids, vipers, and more.
The graphics are top quality and the death animations are glorious to see, but multiple reviews have noted that XCOM 2 has several performance issues on some machines. Personally, the game runs fairly well on my computer, although I have experienced freezing and minor glitches. Mission load times are also much longer than before. However, Firaxis has greatly improved these issues with all the patches they've released since February.
And did I mention mod support? Taking a page from Civilization's book, XCOM 2 comes with fully integrated Steam Workshop modding.
While XCOM 2 may not be the top pick for those who want a traditional XCOM experience, it still remains an excellent choice for anyone wanting a fun and challenging turn-based tactical game.

Darkest Dungeon is an excellent, if occasionally key board flippingly frustrating, game. Tasked with defeating the dark god your ancestor awoke, players assemble teams of adventurers and set them to work exploring the monstrous lairs around them, gathering loot, and rebuilding the small town that counts as home.
It could be like many RPGs, except Darkest Dungeon opts to explore the mental as well as physical toll battling an army of fungi-infested zombies or a gigantic demon-pig king might have on human beings. Managing stress, preventing mental breakdowns, and cycling your teams in becomes a careful part of the game. All of this is blended pretty seemlessly into a deep and satisfying combat. The RNG gods can be quite fickle, but post release Red Hook opted to give players some control over parts of the game's difficulty. It mitigates a lot of the grief that cropped up in the Early Access Days.
The presentation is also gorgeous. Pulling more than a few pages from Lovecraft and Mike Mignola, the art style is dynamic, and the voice acting and character designs are all top notch. An easy recommendation for anyone with the patience to dive into this maddening world.

You purchase the game. You are a naive little casul. You have no idea what kind of pain this will inflict upon you. You start up the game. Big, white letters pop up on your screen: Dark Souls III. You press start. You watch the cutscene. You have a feeling that this is going to be fun. You learn the controls. You fight your way past the firstfew enemies. You reach a big room with a large, armored human-like being kneeling in the middle. You walk up to it, unsure of what to do. As you approach it, on the bottom of your screen it says: (A) : Remove sword. You press (A). You pull out the sword. A sudden rush of panic flows through you. A large red bar appears at the bottom of the screen. You hit the monster a few times with your weapon. The bar gets smaller and smaller. Just when you think you are about to win, the being raises its halberd high above its head. It comes crashing down, along with your health. You are confused. Is this how the entire game is going to be? A cycle of life, death, and progress, only to be sent back to the bonfire again? And the answer is yes. Yes it is. And that's what makes this game so damn good.
Welcome to Dark Souls III.

I can't imagine a more mixed set of feelings reviewing a game.  I LOVE the Fallout universe.  Absolutely adore it - my favorite post-apocalyptic universe, bar none.  Besides, the visuals look solid and the sound design is wonderful (including the fully realized score). So why do I not recommend this game?
The fault lies with the publisher.  The issues common to Bethesda open world games are here in full force.  Items can move around when other nearby items are picked up, NPCs seldom act in natural ways (old women and pack animals regularly end up on top of buildings despite not having a way to get up there), it's classic "Bethesda Jank" in all its glory.  But the thing that REALLY ruins the experience is the settlement system (and by extension most of the DLC).  Settlement structure pieces are meant to snap together for ease of building, but it barely works - many building pieces refuse to snap together except in very specific ways, sometimes conflicting with pieces they don't even directly touch.  It's possible to spend hours building up a settlement only to find that your precise arrangement of parts breaks NPC pathfinding, leaving settlers who just stand around 24/7.  In addition, the game allows the dead grass that fills the world to clip through any placed buildings - I hope you like shrubs sticking through your concrete walls, because there's no way to avoid it.
Even without the problems with structures it's pretty awkward.  Many items (including corpses) cannot be removed without console controls - not too bad until you remember that most settlements require you to kill the previous occupants.  Some of the buildable settlement items are noticeably worse than the versions of them you see around the wastelands - the lights, in particular, are often less than half as bright if you placed them yourself compared to the versions found in the wild.
Look, I don't expect perfection from day one - games are HUGE projects with hundreds of people involved.  But Bethesda REFUSES to acknowledge or patch most of these issues.  Forum threads are full of these kinds of issues with no fix in sight, and modders are trying desperately to create unofficial patches that finish the work Bethesda started.  When I buy an indie game made by a team of a couple dozen, I expect to have to mod some things to get them to work as intended.  But when I buy a AAA game by a trusted publisher, I don't want to have to install a dozen unofficial bugfixes because the developer can't be bothered to fix the bugs or acknowledge theeir fans' feedback.
Bethesda - I still love you.  Elder Scrolls and Fallout are a huge part of my gaming identity.  But when a game feels like it shouldn't have left Beta and it's no longer getting patched, I just feel cheated.

After equipping my characters to maximum efforts, the nightmare of what many have described this game as 'unbalanced' has finally rung true, sadly. All time and effort battling with my characters, the last of hard earned gold purchasing much needed upgrades to venture the 5th level dungeons.. All.. for.. null. I have changed my tune and am no longer recommending Darkest Dungeon. I will put DD away until I find there is a much needed update to balance the 5th and 6th level dungeons. I can't imagine why anyone would continue playing this game. What's most upsetting is that I truly wanted to believe the negative reviews wrong..sigh
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
What feels to be a dark side-scrolling dungeon crawler - bringing to mind games of past that I enjoyed, gathering them into one tough ultra strategic D&D RPG of sorts.
I've found Darkest Dungeon (through trial and error) to be very tough on the unprepared. The game is brutal to both seasoned and unseasoned player who dive in with set goal in mind to conquer with a 'record time' mindset. If you do find yourself wanting to give this game a go, then you must know that your characters will die, every time, as long as they aren't developed enough through the lower stages while finding and equipping proper trinkets, leveling, and simply understanding correct placement in the line.
Placement in the line is probably the most important factor to survive and thrive in Darkest Dungeon, as there are 4 spots front to back where you will place your characters, each placement tailored specifically for different characters to maximize their individual strengths. Patience is needed to enjoy this title. If you don't have patience I suggest not purchasing this game as you will have a very difficult and stressful experience. You must study the characters and discover each of their strengths over time, while simultaneously learning by trial and error - dying, and starting over again - until you understand each characters abilities, placements and weaknesses.
The game is fun, I'm sincerely having a blast, and knowing there is permadeath keeps the intensity very high.
I cannot stress enough that Patience, once again, is key to enjoying this game. You cannot rush a game of chess, in Darkest Dungeon you must understand your pieces and respect the unspoken rules of the game first before gaining any glimpse of an advantage. Take it slow and enjoy the game.

Pros
-60 Hour Campaign
-Many more alien types, creating more dynamic encounters.
-UI Cleaned up from Enemy Unknown, quality of life improvements (reload only costing one action now, etc).
-Far more soldier customization options, including weapon customization.
-Game mechanics fit the Guerrilla warfare theme, having to contact cells, stay on the move, tactical insertions.
-Improved story telling and cutscenes.
-Ironman mode returns (requires tutorial to be disabled).
-Graphically gorgeous settings and improved terrain.
-Game now notifies you if you are flanking or being flanked by an enemy.
-Smarter, more aggressive AI. They use their best abilities off cool down and flank hard and often.
-Multiplayer is back and cleaned up/improved.
-Sharing custom characters (can appear randomly through your play through, even as VIPs).
-Weapon customization allows some counters, such as free reloads, increased crit or aim chance, and chance to kill outright.
-Experimental weapon research allowing for random weapon unlocks, including flamethrowers.
-More armor types.
-Armor is now indicated in-game and indicates it's damage reduction, or if it gets shredded.
-Classes redesigned but incredibly balanced with their talent choices, both trees are viable playstyles for all.
-Permadeath
-New event: Base defense, giving you access to ALL your soldiers over time while you defend the Avenger.
-Can EVAC from any mission at anytime, but must deploy and reach your EVAC zone with each soldier.
-Injured soldiers can be EVAC'd if you can't stablize them.
-Line of Sight Indicator now helps tell you in advance if a move gives your soldier line of sight on what targets.
-Concealment and Ambushes, incredibly powerful starts.
-Potentional for PURE stealth missions (incredibly fun).
-Buying Armor or new Weapons no longer require multiple purchases and are instead turned into default equipment.
-High replayability.
-Vast Modding scene.
-Vipers <3
Neutral
-Can lose your 60 hour campaign at anytime (as in the Aliens can win).
-Aliens don't wait around for you to tech up, deploying new aliens very often.
-5x more missions than Enemy Unknown, you will get a ton of random side missions, only a few you can ignore.
-Old mission types are back; UFO Landing Sites, Terror Missions, VIP missions, etc.
-Terror Missions now require that you to save a minimum of 6 civilians out of 13-14, fixing the previous version's mistake.
-Many missions now have turn limits (for objectives), forcing more aggressive play and less Overwatch spam.
-Avatar Project: The Aliens final goal that can make progress incredibly fast if you wait around too long.
-Injured or dead soldiers can be carried to an EVAC zone to return their equipment/weapons.
-Weapon and equipment can be lost if the soldier carrying them dies and is not recovered.
-Can slaughter civilians outside of terror missions with no reprecusions.
-New Geoscape map takes a while to learn but is more streamlined.
-Avenger base building is more streamlined, no adjacant bonuses (just need 1 of everything).
-Can build PSI Operators much more early or rush for unlocking them.
-Many aliens are mini-bosses (Sectoids, Archons, etc) more dangerous mechanics (Mind Control by mission 1).
-Research for Science and Tech upgrades remains the same.
-Only 3 Weapon Types; Standard, Magnetic, Plasma.
-Soldiers can be lightly wounded, wounded, or gravely wounded, putting them out from 3-18 days or more (always occurs if any damage is taken, changed from Enemy Unknown).
-Soldiers can become Shaken (Will reduced to 0), requiring kills or safe missions completion to remove.
-Dark Events: A difficulty modifier where you chose 2 of the 3 debuffs that you want against you.
Cons
-Game difficulty can be overwhelming for new players, even on Rookie (the lowest).
-Central nags at you very often on what needs to be done, even with Beginner VO turned off.
-Missions occur very often, sometimes forcing you to stop scanning to finish something to go do them.
-Avatar Progress can sometimes bump up drastically at random, even after destroying a Black Site.
-Aim chances are lower all around and require heavy use of flanking to increase.
-Hitting or Missing is now PREDETERMINED before you take the shot, and only rerolls when you move (crit not affected).
-Early UFO missions are very overwhelming without more soldiers or equipment.
-Some Launch day performance issues, v-sync, AA, and AO need to be disabled entirely to get or maintain over 60 FPS.
Final Thoughts
-Game is stellar and totally worth the purchase, but might be even more valuable on sale with the small season pass (which adds more customization, more weapons and armor, a new class type, and more story missions). Launch day issues have been very minor at best, my frame rate only seemed to drop during loading screens until the mission was loaded then returned to normal 60+. The customizations, difficulty, alien types all add to the vast replayability to the game and there are different paths you can take early on to determine how you want to play, instead of building satelites. Modding adds even far more to the game, and devs have given the tools they used to make the game to modders to expand upon that (name a dev that does that).

Firstly, I have clocked hundreds of hours in this game (many before I linked it to Steam), so please do not think I dislike this game for no reason.
The biggest problem with the game is the lack of content. Once you reach the end of the missions it all becomes very stale and pointless.
There are very few updates that actually add proper content outside of time limited events in the game. (There has been no actual permanent content in 2014 so far). Every 2 weeks or so they add in time limited grindy lockboxes that you pay real money for a CHANCE to get a cosmetic item. Most of these lockboxes are reskins of existing content ingame, but rarely new models are used that could have been proper content in the game.
It is extremely grindy to level your gear, and all you need to know is that it uses a punishing P2W system, with high paywalls to craft your weapons and armor. You can craft gear without paying money, but it takes an extremely long time. You can convert the normal ingame currency (Crowns) for the currency you pay real money for (Crystal Energy, or CE). The game has a real time fluctuating economy, and the rates of conversion change from time to time. They intentionally pump the game full of lockboxes with reskinned content to make the rates of conversion very high. The game has barely changed since its release in 2011. The only thing that I like about this game now is the art style and mechanics.
The game has PVP, and I do not recommend it at all. It is broken and the PVP community is incredibly toxic.
The devs also never respond to anything on the forums and cannot take constructive criticism without victimizing themselves.

What feels to be a dark side-scrolling dungeon crawler - bringing to mind games of past that I enjoyed, gathering them into one tough ultra strategic D&D RPG of sorts.
I've found Darkest Dungeon (through trial and error) to be very tough on the unprepared. The game is brutal to both seasoned and unseasoned player who dive in with set goal in mind to conquer with a 'record time' mindset. If you do find yourself wanting to give this game a go, then you must know that your characters will die, every time, as long as they aren't developed enough through the lower stages while finding and equipping proper trinkets, leveling, and simply understanding correct placement in the line.
Placement in the line is probably the most important factor to survive and thrive in Darkest Dungeon, as there are 4 spots front to back where you will place your characters, each placement tailored specifically for different characters to maximize their individual strengths. Patience is needed to enjoy this title. If you don't have patience I suggest not purchasing this game as you will have a very difficult and stressful experience. You must study the characters and discover each of their strengths over time, while simultaneously learning by trial and error - dying, and starting over again - until you understand each characters abilities, placements and weaknesses.
The game is fun, I'm sincerely having a blast, and knowing there is permadeath keeps the intensity very high.
I cannot stress enough that Patience, once again, is key to enjoying this game. You cannot rush a game of chess, in Darkest Dungeon you must understand your pieces and respect the unspoken rules of the game first before gaining any glimpse of an advantage. Take it slow and enjoy the game.

Spiral Knights is a fun game to play with friends. My biggest issue with this game is the lag. I had experienced a lot of "rubber-banding" which, of course, becomes incredibly annoying. I liked the Auction House system.
This game is pretty difficult to solo unless you can tank focussed damage as well as deal your own damage all at the same time. I'm talking mainly about boss battles and crowded battles. Teamwork is great.
I'd recommend this game if you like skill-based battle, item crafting, a fair bit of grinding, a guild system, and, of course, if you have a computer/laptop that can handle playing the game without major lag. I think the "rubber-banding" effect would be due to the player's internet connection, so you'd probably need a strong internet connection with relatively high bandwidth to play this game smoothly. The internet-connection-related lag would probably decrease the closer you are to a Spiral Knights server.
So basically, this game is not great performance-wise, especially in my experience of playing the game until around Rank 5-6, but if you manage to deal with the lag or minimise it or even eliminate it, you're going to have some good fun.

Well, what can I say? This game has many things, its good and bad. You'll be thrown into a world that seems Pay-to-Win but soon find out that dedication can get you whatever someone else paid for. Sure, they may get it quicker, but at least you have the satisfaction of achieving it.
The game is a bit grindy, I'm not going to lie. But, that's where the addiction sets in. You'll grind for a few hours, get some good items and money (flux) until you have enough to buy the thing or upgrade the things you wanted. It's well balanced, good for solo players and people who want to play with friends. All of the classes but one are adequate. Gunslinger isn't very good and I definitely would not recommend it for solo players.
There's pretty much one task to achieve in Trove, get the best gear possible on all the characters. As you play you'll get  levels in "Mastery". Collecting mounts, allies, leveling up characters, and virtually doing anything in the game, will level up Mastery. The higher mastery you get, the more benefits you get, such as increased damage and health, along with unlocking mounts, allies, and other goodies. You'll be going through different levels of "Uber" portals to fight harder and harder monsters that require better and better gear and ultimatley achieve the strength to potentially solo the hardest areas in the game.
Now, there's a lot of good to be said about that game, however, there's a few dents in the shiny coin. Such as the amount of bugs. They work hard on removing the bugs from the game, but there're some that are quite persistent and that have been around for awhile; some of them being quite severe.
People can take your items while you try to trade with them if you're not in the hub.
The game gradually loses FPS as you play until you need to restart to get a silky smooth 60
frames again. (Though, the frequent save errors will help you maintain great fps... lol?)
Loading glitches
Save errors
Server Crashes
The game isn't actually difficult. It's all about gear, the higher your gear is, the more trivial it gets. I think the lack of dodging in the game is partly due to this. Though, there is a dodge, its only use is moving away from a boss' power attack.
It's also a bit repetitive, though the areas are randomly generated. I can't help but feel like I've already seen everything there is. (But, hey, that may be 200+ hours talkin')
TL;DR
All in all, it's a great game that I recommend to anyone looking to kill some time. In my case, a lot of time. I'd give it a 7/10. A solid 9/10 if the bugs were less frequent.
