Darkest Dungeon is a 2d turn-based dungeon crawler, created by Red Hook Studios.
Upon starting the game you are greeted with the news that a dear estranged relative of yours has been up to some pretty bad stuff and essentially leaves you to clean up his mess. The mess in question being the multitude of ghouls, horrors and other assorted ne’er-do-wells that now inhabit the family manor and the hamlet that surrounds it. This is the premise of Darkest Dungeon and it works as well as any other to start our adventure.
The bulk of the game revolves around leading a group of four characters through an assortment of randomly generated dungeons and doing battle with the creatures that inhabit them. Characters traverse the dungeons in single file, their position in the line dictating which abilities are able to be used and the enemies on which they are able to use them. For instance some characters will do better on the front line while others will thrive at the back of the group. Setting up your group is key to a successful endeavour. This is where the games hub comes into play.
The Hamlet is a small group of shops and buildings that acts as the games main hub. From here you are able to make use of a wide variety of amenities as you decide which heroes to send out on their next adventure and with what supplies to pack. New heroes are able to be recruited from the stage coach, armour and weapons upgraded at the blacksmith, diseases and quirks cured at the sanatorium as well as many other services being available for the right price. This includes spending money to reduce the effect of one of the games main mechanics - Stress.
Stress is an in-game measurement of a particular hero's mental state, a counter that goes from 0 to 200. If the hero's stress reaches 100 they will gain an affliction or have a chance to become virtuous. While a virtuous hero will only benefit your team with buffs and stress reduction. An afflicted hero has the complete opposite effect, increasing the stress of those around them and sometimes actively putting themselves in danger or ignoring your command completely. If your stress becomes too high, your hero is at risk of a heart attack which may kill them outright. This may be compounded by the games quirk system, where in certain situations a hero will develop a positive or negative quirk that will affect how they act, or how you must treat them. These can range from increased stress gain to a compulsive need to examine every item you come across and many more.

When it comes to presentation, Darkest Dungeon gets full points. The gothic 2d art style oozes personality without being overly busy or confusing and a good use of depth of field stops the game from feeling flat. The interface is incredibly well designed and remains simple, despite the amount of information housed within. There are a few changes I would make to make viewing information a little easier but overall the interface does what it sets out to do very well.  The graphic style of Darkest Dungeon conveys the mood of the game perfectly and only strengthens its theme, ESPECIALY when paired with the terrific audio design and the phenomenal voice acting of the narrator.
The Audio design in this game is on another level when stacked up against its peers. as the light fades so too does the music’s simple nature, giving way to an erratic tune that becomes more maddening the more you venture forth, the weighty sounds of attacks as your group goes toe to toe with all manner of horrors, and of course the absolutely shiver inducing tones of the loquacious narrator as he pontificates about his "Venerable house" and the "arcades of antiquity".
All of these elements come together to make Darkest Dungeon and absolutely unforgettable experience. the feeling of felling an enemy with a perfect strategy leaves you in awe of yourself as a brilliant tactician while other times becoming absolutely downtrodden as you lose the hero you've been cultivating for so very long. Darkest Dungeon is a game about making the best out of what you are given and sometimes when life gives you lemons, well I hope you like lemons.
Overall my Experience with Darkest Dungeon has been incredibly satisfying, having put 40 hours into the game I can see that I am in fact not even close to finishing, nor do I feel the fatigue that I usually would after playing most any other game for such a long period of time. When I first saw it in early access I was itching to play it, but decided to hold off and wait until the developers were confident enough to say that it was a finished product, and I am so glad that I did.
If you are a fan of X-Com, or don’t mind a bit of punishment to get true satisfaction out of your gaming experience then I don't have any problem telling you that

So I am approaching what feels like the end of the game (or at least the point in the story where the player character has fulfilled their purpose and whatnot), and I feel compelled to recommend it.
(I went through a lot of it offline, so the Steam timer isn't accurate)
As someone who now has played both DS2 & 3, I'd tell whoever is interested that while 3 is the better game, you should probably try 2 first, just to warm up to the mindset and see if it's the type of game you'd be interested in, since the game in general is more forgiving, and enemies and bosses are overall less aggressive and combo happy.
Naturally some of the changes between 2 and 3 are better, some are worse, however most of them are very subjective (e.g the addition of the Luck stat, removal of armor upgrades, removing/replacing Powerstances etc.).
For example, as someone who doesn't parry a lot (LT on my gamepad is bugged out or broken, Sulyvahn was rough) the Weapon Skill stuff replacing the end-all-be-all parry button is a really cool change, although the skills my weapons have, like Stance, are too slow for most PvE encounters where it would be worth performing.
The one change that is just an objective flaw is whatever they did to the targeting system. It lets go in the dumbest of conditions! Were you standing close to the Abyss Watcher when he did their forward charge? Goodbye targeting!
This worked fine in the last game, what did you guys even do?
That example is the best case scenario, where it is only an annoying thing, whatever.
Welcome to the lair of Ye Olde Demon King, whose (almost) every attack releases targeting if the player is close to him, aka. the place where most players will spend their time attacking, turning this run o' the mill "big thing with big weapon" style boss into a targeting based nighmare, since retargeting him is almost harder than the boss itself, because sometimes even if the boss is in full view, pressing right stick performs the buttons' secondary function, camera reset.
So now you are no longer targeting the boss, you are facing the wrong direction, and you are confusing the hell out of yourself by frantically mashing R3 to try and retarget the boss. End result is either managing roll out of range and try again, or getting smacked by a flaming mass of bs on a stick.
On a related note, the camera while targeting bosses can get really weird at times. By weird I mostly mean the camera sometimes jacks itself into your characters kneecap during certain boss moves. This was probably is DS2 as well, it just keeps happening here, because guess what - you borderline have to hug the bosses in order to get a swipe in, because due to how aggressive some are and how short their cooldowns are, a melee user is not going to have time to run in, attack, and resume observing/dodging.
Speaking of bosses, you know what's a pretty rad looking boss? The Dancer Of The Boreal Valley.
You know who has a boss fight full of nice details and visual effects? The Dancer Of The Boreal Valley.
You know what boss fight becomes a slideshow (especially during the 2nd phase twirl)? The Dancer Of The Boreal Valley.
I know we've hopped up a generation and that DS2 is far from some elaborate visual masterpiece, but while DS2 almost never went below 30, this game sometimes drops in areas with nothing happening in them, but you can sometimes see the game trying to optimize as best it can. Twirl the camera fast enough and you can sometimes just see the bosses load back in. It's just weird.
Despite that stuff, all in all, great game. Isn't perfect, nor is it for everyone, but I guess that isn't really the point.

I enjoyed Darkest Dungeon enough to spend 45 hours with it.  That should probably be recommendation enough but it does come with a caveat.  Darkest Dungeon is about the grind; the grind is the game.  For the most part it works well enough.  The combat engine feels great.  Your heroes will exchange brutal blows with the enemy and it always feels like you are an inch from death.  Also, it has to be noted that the game nails the atmosphere and the voiceover is brilliant.
The problem is that the game is built in such a way that you can never send an expert party through a low level dungeon.  This means that you will never really feel like your party is getting better.  You will work just as hard at the start of the game as you do at the end and if one of your heroes dies, you have to go back and replace it pretty much from scratch.
When I got to the final dungeon, I was ready for the game to be over, unfortunately, I had a good 10 hours of grind left before I could actually finish the game.  For many people, tthis won't be an issue as long as they enjoy the core gameplay, but for me, I would have preferred a shorter, more streamlined experience.
Despite my reservations, Darkest Dungeon is still a wholly compelling game and well worth a look.

Straight to the point, I really like this game. True, as many have said previously, RPG-wise it feels a lot lighter than previous Fallout incarnations but I'm not holding that against this title. Without the heavier RPG elements, it gives you more time to focus on exploring, combat and just generally mooching around the Commonwealth. To me, Fallout 4 is a quite relaxing exploration rather than a micro-managed RPG.
As for the voiced protagonist, personally, I like it. A good voice actor can make you feel more involved with the character and can insert more of a feeling of emotion in to a situation than you might have felt otherwise. I have played a little over 200 hours in the game and I've been putting off choosing a faction to side with for months now as it means the beginning of the end for my game, plus I really don't want to sever ties with the characters I've fought alongside. Soooo I've basically been bumming around, building settlements, exploring, playing the expansions and generally trying to get everything I can from the game before I make the jump. I would really recommend playing the game with all of the major expansions, whether you get the workshop ones is really extra fluff but I think that Automatron, Far Harbor and Nuka World should definitely be in the mix.

It's a bit fun at first, but it gets old very quickly.
If you wanna try playing something almost identical to it, there's a way to do it for only one cent. Simply flip the coin; if it's heads, you win and everybody is happy. Tails, you lose and you can try again.
Seriously, though, 90% of the game is dictated by dice rolls. There are certainly some levels of strategy, team building, and upgrades, but overall it's just dice rolls. Unlike good RPG's, you can't do much of anything to affect those dice rolls. It's quite possible that it becomes more affected by choice later on, but certainly in the beginning, choices don't matter at all. Why play a game where your choices make no difference? You get just as much enjoyment out of watching someone else play, because choice genuinely doesn't matter.
I had really high hopes for this game, and it looks so great - both the art style, and the gameplay in general. But in practice, the game completely fails to deliver. I wish I had a game that was exactly like Darkest Dungeon in every way, just it punished you for having poor tactics instead of punishing you for simply playing the game. Every time I play, I hope I can find what others apparently see in the game, that same ideal that I had hoped for when I first bought it. Instead, I can't help but feel that the developers are laughing at me for buying their game.

The first thing I'd say is that there are a lot of reports of bugs and optimization problems, even with people with good rigs. I believe them given my own experience.  Given the graphics quality I can't understand why this game is such a resource hog.
As for the game itself, so far I'm enjoying it.  The timers make the missions more interesting, force you to take some risks and that's a good thing, as opposed to the last XCOM where in most missions you would just creep up under overwatch.  Strategically you do have to make decisions, and often urgent necessity interrupts you.  The aliens are generally stronger, right out the front, and you may suffer for the first few missions (I did), till you get a hang of the new scouting systems and the enemy priorities (kill sectoids as priority near the start of the campaign.)
Healing from injuries takes longer, forcing you to keep a larger roster of troops, you can't just use a single super-squad.
Overall I find this more fun than the last XCOM, BUT it is more difficult, there are bugs, and it is badly optimized.  A qualified buy, with the qualificatin being you might wish to wait till some optimization/bug patches are out.
But, given Steam's refunds, I don't see a downside to trying it now and refunding if the bugs/optimization are too much.  Just put aside some time to play it right after purchase.

It's a game I recommend only for people who really have patience to proceed in a game, and like to grind.
At first when I bought this game in it's pre-release stage, it seemed much more fun because of the multiple mechanics having some sort of balance, and opposition in the enemies favor with certain battles. However, when it comes to the clear fact that RNG dictates this game, along with the "forced" party situation with certain areas since the full release/updates, it makes it seem much more limited to bringing a proper party, versus having an advantage/disadvantage to a fully custom party.
What I mean is that the game feels like it forces you to play it's way, but take risk/reward whenever you want. When in fact that the later is a good aspect, it falls flat whenever I must abandon a quest due to enemies that can constantly pair up with other stress inducing ones; those in which force me to carry party members to use forced "move" abilities to get proper adjustment, and cause the game to feel like I must always bring someone to the table who can properly use this.
There's an enemy in the game I think most people can agree on as well that causes the most stress out of everything, and is quite possibly the top of the charts in annoying enemies: The Madman. It doesn't matter which area you go, but the fact that he can pair up with any team of enemies whether they be mostly stress inducers or mostly debilitating enemies; he causes the most frustration with this game since his arrival and forced my argument where I feel forced to bring certain party members. I have to take someone or spend more money into forcing a way to move him ASAP. Which in turn doesn't feel rewarding as it does tedious. The fact that he causes party stress, isn't fun when paired up with Incantations from another enemy in the Ruins.
With the new udpates causing random heartattacks whenever a hero is past 100 stress; it doesn't seem really fair in the aspect as 200 stress was the main culprit in causing the hero's demise. Camping abilities are now feeling more like a tiny buff, rather than a help through the treacherous areas since their nerf, along with deblitiating statuses from recovering from Death's Door? Doesn't help in the slightest of helping the game balance. I know it's supposed to be hard, but where it hinders no progression doesn't bestow clarity on the player rather than giving up.
I did notice the inclusion of hidden passageways leading to new treasures (if you remembered to bring a key that is.) Which make exploring a little more worth it, but only if you feel the chance of running into The Collector or respawning badguys if you must go back a few rooms. Risk and reward is the name, but it's only worth it if you can account for what you lost for.
With all that past, I think the game is a great dungeon crawler, with perhaps way too much on it's plate which bogs it down a little. It wants you to fail and proceed. It wants to see you go on and see if you have what it takes to keep going, which I admire. But the fact of the matter is, it's bogged down with grind-heavy work that makes the game feel more chore-like than a amusing game. The added in factors to make the game harder, don't necessarily make the game harder in a sense of pushing for progression, but more towards the escape key.

Darkest Dungeon is a side scroller  dungeon crawling RPG  with roguelike features such as procedurally generated levels and permadeath. The game is set  in a lovecraftian  universe where your ancestor summoned eldritch creatures through a portal in his manor and asks you to clean his mess.
The soundtrack is amazing, the art style is excellent and as a bonus the game isn't graphically demanding.
The gameplay revolves around doing dungeon runs with four of the (currently) 14 hero classes and managing and upgrading your town.  The main game is based around 4 different areas ( Cove,Ruins, Warrens and Weald) with their own specific types of ennemies and materials ( as quest rewards) to upgrade your town and a final one that serves as endgame content. Each 4 areas are divided in 3 level  ( apprentice (lv 1), veteran(lv3) and champion(lv5)) where ennemies get stronger and have new tricks to their skills. As you level your heroes and go into higher leveled missions, the game punishes more and more carelessy made party compositions and tactics and requires you to plan ahead. This is important to remember because death is permanent.
Combat is different from any other traditional RPGs; heroes have both a hp bar and a stress bar. Some ennemies deal hp damage while others deal stress damage. When your hero hits 100 stress, you have a high chance of getting an affliction ( such as paranoia, abusive, masochistic, etc) that reduces your stats and has a specific negative effect ( refuse heals, heroes damage themselves or give stress to others, etc)  or, if you're lucky, get a virtue ( courageous, stalwart, focused) that gives passive bonuses ( such has buffs, hp/stress heal at the start of a turn). Heroes and ennemies are sorted in ranks ( 1 to 4 ) where ranks 1-2 are usually tanky melee characters and ranks 3-4 ranged heroes /healers. This is important because skills in this game requires to be in a specific rank to be used.  Let's say I'm an arbalest, a ranged class, and try to use my skills while at rank 1. It won't work because most of her skills requires her to be in rank 3-4 and can only the ennemies' rank 2 to 4. Same can be said for most melee heroes. Positioning is crucial in this game and this is why varied party lineups are important ( a mix of melee/ranged heroes).
The game has had a rough Early Access but resulted as a more balanced title in the end. As of the date of the review, there is still more content to come ( 1 hero class and town events). Darkest Dungeon needs around 40-50 hours to complete the game and has a great replay value ( because dungeons are randomly generated ).
I would recommend this game to people that are not affraid to take a beating because, in this game, you will die and you will fail missions. The key is to learn from your mistakes.

Overall, Spiral Knights is a brilliant game and nothing can change that.
All the pros (What I think, anyway...):
+ If you are ready to put in the time, you can get 'anything' for free! (No money cost.)... Spiral Knights is pay to advance/obtain. Not pay to win.
+ You get to create your very own knight! And you can customize it with even cooler clothes later on in the game. You can even become whatever you want later on. Whatever it is, upfront western to outright insane, you name it, you can probably be it in Spiral Knights.
+ You can also be Vegeta! It's over 9000!!!
+ Guns with explosive ammunition!
+ It's got that 'Ability to use OverPowered guns and bombs' feeling, which links to the child-like gameplay.
+ Upgradeable weapons!
+ When you finish off an enemy with a charged attack (especially with a full combo "cutter" attack), it feels goood...
+ You can make your very own 2-item-army loadout, this may not seem much, but when you play and get millions of weapons, there is lots to choose from. It can also be upgraded to 3 or even 4 items.
+ Anime-Heart Eyes are available to purchase later on in the game.
+ Pretty decent soundtracks.
+ Battle Sprites can be chosen to show who you are... Do you want to re-create the Techno-Kitten-Adventure...? Will you use the Draconian and, quite litterally explode your way past enemies? Or will you go stealthy with the maskerwraith...?
+ You get chased by a giant cat in some levels.
+ You are a permanent guest at the ghost hotel.
+ If you have friends that also play, it's a really good game... (Don't worry, I don't have any either.)
+ People can be very friendly, many times they help you out.
+ You can become a samurai... If you wanted...
+ You can use an underpowered and totally-not-worthless shovel in combat (You get it towards the start of the game, too!).
+ You get a message from Saxton Hale. And a free hat for TF2! Can you Friend Request him again?
+ You can own jelly cubes and wear them.

I have very mixed feelings about XCOM 2. GTX 970
i7-4790k
16Gb RAM
Game installed on HDD
The performance is all over the place with my rig. Some settings like ambient occlusion and depth of field actually halved my framerate in some places, I've never seen that happen with any other game. On the ship and in menus the performance usually stays at 50-60fps, but sometimes makes random dips to 30-40fps. This is also the first game I've played that's made my overall RAM usage go over 8Gb, it's bizarre. The game does look pretty good from time to time, but not that good.

In the last ten years I can recall perhaps two or three games that I was this satisfied with.  When I'd purchased the last X-Com, I was rather bored and rightfully so.  It took a year's worth of content to inject that game with enough quality to be great.  XC2 is amazing right out of the gate.
The tone is largely the same as the last game, as is the game's feel.  A discrete group of paramilitary interests must struggle to resist the occupation of Earth by super evil aliens who cured cancer and AIDS for us.  (We'll show THOSE ungrateful turds what happens to the saviors of our species!!)
And so we do.  Now we fly an air-whale around a glowing cyan earth map, instead of squatting in a whole and staring at a cyan glowing earth-map.  It's largely unchanged.  You excavate alien hoard-rooms in your fancy ship rather than boring dirt, but that's largely the same too.  (Of note: it's much better polished now in the base because you can click around and watch your soldiers hit on each other in the bar, or fritter away an afternoon having some smoldering purple beams shot into their skull to make them psionic.  See that, aliens?  We can do WORSE than cancer.)
The staff of your crew are much more verbal this time around, but the conversations are just as aimless.
The real draw of this game, its tactical mode, is why the game is so fantastic.  It's fun, engaging, as interesting as XC:EU, and boasts a couple delightful additions to the mix.  I kinda wish we could tool with the action cam frequency in-game, 'cause I think that camera is mighty fine but mostly unpredictable.  I like watching a dude cut up an alien.
Basically if you're into tactical RPGs, the last X-Com entry, and are aware that game launches haven't had ideal QA since the early 2000s, then buy this game and play it.  In this game, dudes cut up aliens.

As someone who now has played both DS2 & 3, I'd tell whoever is interested that while 3 is the better game, you should probably try 2 first, just to warm up to the mindset and see if it's the type of game you'd be interested in, since the game in general is more forgiving, and enemies and bosses are overall less aggressive and combo happy.
Naturally some of the changes between 2 and 3 are better, some are worse, however most of them are very subjective (e.g the addition of the Luck stat, removal of armor upgrades, removing/replacing Powerstances etc.).
For example, as someone who doesn't parry a lot (LT on my gamepad is bugged out or broken, Sulyvahn was rough) the Weapon Skill stuff replacing the end-all-be-all parry button is a really cool change, although the skills my weapons have, like Stance, are too slow for most PvE encounters where it would be worth performing.
The one change that is just an objective flaw is whatever they did to the targeting system. It lets go in the dumbest of conditions! Were you standing close to the Abyss Watcher when he did their forward charge? Goodbye targeting!
This worked fine in the last game, what did you guys even do?
That example is the best case scenario, where it is only an annoying thing, whatever.
Welcome to the lair of Ye Olde Demon King, whose (almost) every attack releases targeting if the player is close to him, aka. the place where most players will spend their time attacking, turning this run o' the mill "big thing with big weapon" style boss into a targeting based nighmare, since retargeting him is almost harder than the boss itself, because sometimes even if the boss is in full view, pressing right stick performs the buttons' secondary function, camera reset.
So now you are no longer targeting the boss, you are facing the wrong direction, and you are confusing the hell out of yourself by frantically mashing R3 to try and retarget the boss. End result is either managing roll out of range and try again, or getting smacked by a flaming mass of bs on a stick.
On a related note, the camera while targeting bosses can get really weird at times. By weird I mostly mean the camera sometimes jacks itself into your characters kneecap during certain boss moves. This was probably is DS2 as well, it just keeps happening here, because guess what - you borderline have to hug the bosses in order to get a swipe in, because due to how aggressive some are and how short their cooldowns are, a melee user is not going to have time to run in, attack, and resume observing/dodging.
Speaking of bosses, you know what's a pretty rad looking boss? The Dancer Of The Boreal Valley.
You know who has a boss fight full of nice details and visual effects? The Dancer Of The Boreal Valley.
You know what boss fight becomes a slideshow (especially during the 2nd phase twirl)? The Dancer Of The Boreal Valley.
I know we've hopped up a generation and that DS2 is far from some elaborate visual masterpiece, but while DS2 almost never went below 30, this game sometimes drops in areas with nothing happening in them, but you can sometimes see the game trying to optimize as best it can. Twirl the camera fast enough and you can sometimes just see the bosses load back in. It's just weird.
Despite that stuff, all in all, great game. Isn't perfect, nor is it for everyone, but I guess that isn't really the point.

TLDR: If you liked the Borderlands franchise and want more of that only single player, buy this game.  If you are looking for a worthy successor to New Vegas, look elsewhere.
Please understand that this is only superficially a Fallout game.  If you loved the original isometric games, New Vegas, or even Fallout 3, you might want to skip this one.  This iteration has made vast improvements over the previous ones in terms of reliability and playability, however, they have really dropped the ball on writing and quest design.  This is effectively a very pretty Borderlands game, super shallow and infinitely repeating, shoot and loot type gameplay.  I played through the main questline and it was somewhat compelling, and I can appreciate the forced difficult decisions, but the issue is that they were not written in a believable way.  It makes sense that certain factions would wish for you to wipe out another or manipulated them in some way, but what does not make sense is that there is no flexibility in how you accomplish this goal.  Kill so and so and all their friends, period.  There is no shutting them down in other ways, just kill everything, scorched earth, no diplomacy, nothing.  At least some of the factions should have been able to function with the others, and no, the completely irrelevent Minutemen don't count.  I put over 100 hours into this game, and really tried to love it as I have with previous installments, but in the end it just pales in comparison.  Fallout 3 certainly was no masterpiece and I am highly critical of what was done with the story and how they attempted to shoehorn old bits of the originals into it, but that was Bethesda's first go at it, and I expected there to be some issues.  After the amazing and fresh New Vegas installment, I was hopeful and excited that Bethesda had learned from Obsidian's work.  Sadly they saw the success of other open world games and went in a completely different direction.

Darkest Dungeon promised a lot of things that you often see associated with the "Rogue-like" tag; "Challenging", "difficult", "dark", "rewarding of skill", and the usual malarky. It even seemed like it might deliver on these. Playing through its Early Access was usually enjoyable, even when bugs interfered. Still, there was always this nagging feeling that the developers could not quite get the balance of player power versus the game's environment down. There were many times where the game simply decided that you could not win, no matter how well equipped and pre-planned you went in; enemies would land critical strings constantly and dodge far more than they should even after being debuffed, or the foes would relentlessly target one specific unit even when the targeting system is meant to be randomized (aside from certain rare encounters). This feeling grew as release version after release version added more to the enemy's side but did nothing to bring up the player's tools to match. No amount of skill or planning can save you against terrible luck, especially when the abilities available to you just can not measure up to the enemies'.
What I'm trying to say is, the game fell prey to the most common pitfall of the tag: the Random Number God trumps anything you might do, as the developers confused biased dice systems and overpowered enemies with genuine challenge. The early game will let you pass if you use tactics, but the mid and late game are all about praying that the dice land in your favor.
On top of luck being the deciding factor in combat and exploration, the game constantly stacks even the menus against you. Healing higher leveled heroes of stress, illnesses, or mental ailments becomes increasingly expensive just because they are a higher level than the scrubs fresh off the stagecoach; it's an arbitrary punishment for progressing with them! You may get stuck in a cycle of needing to do low level missions to pay for stress relief or illness removal on your higher level characters just so that you can play the missions that actually advance the story. Alternatively, you could just straight up dismiss characters that you already invested money in so that you can hire a fresh batch of heroes off the stagecoach to try again from the start.
Imbalanced gameplay aside, the game does present a very nice... errr, grim atmosphere. The gloomy graphics, subdued sounds, and sudden spikes of noise when something dramatic happens are great at setting the mood. Character animations are rather limited (for example, you get the same animation whether a character dodges or gets hit by something), but they do get the idea of the move or action across. The narrator, your character's ancestor who kicked off the plot, is usually entertaining with his comments, but they do become stale after you've heard every comment many times.
On a final note, major bugs are still seemingly common with the game, as it only recently left Early Access at the time of this review. My patience for it was finally ruined after my saves became corrupted. Such issues may be resolved in time, but until then you're risking all progress if you play in its current state.
TLDR: It's luck-based, and still buggy. Wait to see if it gets fixed and rebalanced before you buy.

I played this a bit when it first came out in early access, and a bit towards the end of EA, and then a bit after the official release.  I can honestly say that on all occasions, I had fun.
The atmosphere that hangs in the writing, art style, and music is amazing, hitting the nail dead on the head for a "Lovecraftian theme" game.  The narrator is phenomenal, and I want to have sex with his voice.  No, seriously.  This guy needs to narrate romance novels.  He'd be a millionaire before the year is out.
The rogue-lite style of game play is punishing while still being fun, but understand that your characters *will* die.  I found myself in the mindset of getting more emotionally attached to the buildings in the hamlet that I upgraded, rather than the disposable characters.
To address a couple of the more prominent complaints:  Is the game reliant on RNG?  Yes it is, but the same can be said of nearly all turn-based dungeon crawler RPGs.  That's the mechanic involved in that genre.  You roll digital dice.  Can your team get unfairly murdered due to bad luck with RNG?  Yes, but the key is to be able to recognize when the dungeon is going badly and cut your losses, retreating back to town.
Final verdict:  If you like horror themed turn-based dungeon crawlers, then you'll almost certainly enjoy this one.  However, if RNG tends to give you a headache, then this game isn't for you.

Black Squad at its current state is very nearly built for a full-fledged Free-To-Play unlike its competitors. There are four different modes to play, a wide assortment of guns to try out, and a variety of different skills to use. In terms of the game development process, this is a breath of fresh air compared to the previous releases over the last year.
Gameplay-wise, the
I personally like being given a little more time to shoot people, and this takes care of that. What I do hope for the future however, is that they will be able to strike a balance on this. You are given an AR, an SMG, and a Sniper Rifle from the start, and at least from Day one, they appear to work pretty well.
There are your run-of-the-mill modes that you can see in any other F2P, TDM, & S&D. They offer 16-player and 10 player modes in S&D, while there is a lesser-seen Escort mode. Our main contender of the game here would probably be their Battle Match, which allows up to 32 players, and has so far been a "Destroy the enemy fort" map.
-- Edit as of 11/23/2017
In playing through some of its patches and shamelessly logging on to receive the attendance rewards, here's what I have to say. A lot of the patches so far have not brought as much depth as I would have hoped. I'm still very much in love with the central premise of Destruction Mode, and hope to see how much more they can extend on it.
Weapons do have recoil, and though it may not feel that way with the default set, you will definitely be able to sense it once you try a QBZ or any of the AKs. Some weapons may have a different category in title, but their weapon recoil/behavior oddly feels the same. This gave me an impression that there hasn't been implementation on it just yet, but we'll have to see what NS does.
Business Model-wise, the game seems pretty fair. There are four main currencies to concern yourself,
The other three currencies so far appear to be for skins. And the skins don't appear to have a benefit to its default counterpart. There appears to be three tiers of GP weapon costs, but allow me to break this down even further.
If I play this game everyday for a week, for probably like one match, ten-fifteen minutes, I can get myself a cheap gun permanently. If I play this game religiously for the week, I can get two average guns or one expensive. As a gun nut, I think I can happily say this is a pretty awesome deal compared to having to play religiously for a month.
I hope NS Studio can stand against having content come out within some kind of schedule. Their release might be successful, but you kind of have to wonder where it will be in three months, like all of the Free-To-Plays that have flopped since. Time will tell whether this game will succeed.

To me, Trove feels like the developers got a few inspirations from Minecraft and a few inspirations from Terraria and applied this to a common MMO formula with a fair business model that is "Play to Win" and "Pay to Look Fabulous" with decent crafting times and a ton of other stuff. Of course you gotta work for all that you have and want to acquire but still, it is very much fair. However, Trove shall not be compared to either of the aforementioned games as Trove poses something inherently different and sets itself apart with multiple features (or the merging of features). But I am getting ahead of myself. If you want to skip the lengthy part of my review, you may skip to the pros and cons I've listed below.
To get us started, what about Trove's lore and story? Well, as far as I am concerned, there is none. A goddess split the world into multiple, infinite realms for you to explore, venture into, slay dangerous foes and collect tons of loot and level up. So Trove has, in my eyes, the nessecary things to be an electronic video game providing fun and entertainment. Also, talking with a few community members revealed that most of the players aren't too concerned about the lack of lore as Trove is almost 100% about gameplay.
So, let's switch to the gameplay!
Trove's gameplay has multiple aspects I'm gonna pick apart one after the other. Starting off with character creation.
And the character creation in Trove is very simple. Pick one out of 11 possible classes at the start of the game and choose a hair style and a race to go with it. However, hair styles and races are purely cosmetic and do neither benefit your character nor do they influence gameplay in any way whatsoever. For instance, I made a female robot Ice Sage-class character, a robotic mage based on ice with a nice, female hair style. Hair- and eye colour may also be chosen, though there are only a few select colours you may choose.
As a new player, you will be most likely concerned with the following: Building, raiding dungeons for loot and XP, leveling up and customizing your character a little more. In terms of building, there are, in every world that is generated and the game throws you in, so-called cornerstones. The cornerstone system works like this: it's a plot of land that is 16x16 blocks in size that you can claim. Upon claiming, a basic starter house with basic equipment spawns. On your cornerstone, you can customize your house any way you want, building up to 150 blocks high (for tower enthusiasts like me) and the stone is the only place (apart from club worlds (clubs are the guilds in this game which have their own world that you can shape the way you want it)) where what you build gets saved and nobody can grief your stuff as it is protected on your little plot of land. And you can switch to another cornerstone, which then triggers the buildup of your house there and the wiping of your house from the previous one. In essence, you got a portable base.
Then there's raiding lairs. There are 3 types of lairs, small, large and recipe lairs (the latter are used to craft furniture). Every lair features a boss (in case of the large lair it is 3 bosses) and every boss drops a chest with loot in it. Speaking loot, there are no armours in this game, only class skins. However, the game has weapons, masks and hats with unique styles based on the biome you've found them in. There are 12 biomes in total with entirely different themes and you are able to build your house around said themes if you wish to.
Anyway, upon getting better weapons you might think "Geez, I sure wish I could keep the style of my previous weapon and apply it to my current weapon!". Well, you can. With the loot collector you can (and kinda must) build to advance your game experience and collecting styles for the multiple items.
Upon collecting styles you get valuable resources (but a lot of resources also have to be mined and acquired through drops or the gardening profession) and mastery points. The mastery rank is a different scale compared to your class's level. You have to level each class you get individually (getting you more mastery points) where as your MR (mastery rank) carries over to your whole game experience.
What do you do with all the resources? Crafting and building!
Trove features multiple crafting stations for multiple professions that either unlock powerful items, stylish new blocks for you to build with and reward you with mastery points upon leveling up your skill. Your MR also rewards you with stuff such as storage currency, stat upgrades that carry over to all of your classes and items.
The professions involve: Ringcrafting, runecrafting, gardening, fishing and building (the latter does not award you MR points however).
Other stuff includes, but is not limited to:
Mounts, allies that give passive bonuses, boats to ride on the seas, sails for your boats, mag riders (another form of mount) and much more.
Now, switching to the term "variety". Here are some gripes I got about Trove.
The enemy variety is barely present. Of course, every biome has its unique enemies and with unique looks and sounds, but the overall variety in terms of attack patterns and abilities of said enemies just isn't there much. Basically you will be fighting the same enemy over and over again with a different skin. Save for the shadow realm bosses of course (which are in more advanced worlds).
Then the class abilities. Each class has four abilitites, two of which have to be unlocked with progression through levels. In my opinion, this is not enough combat variety. But I spoke with some community members and it revealed that the majority of players actually don't mind that too much as Trove's main focus isn't combat. Because to me, Trove has no main focus so to speak, as you can do a myriad of other things within the game.
Another thing that got me disappointed a bit was the music. Don't get me wrong, the music in itself is fine by me. But it is almost never present. When you enter a new biome, the biome specific music plays for a minute, then stops for about half an hour and starts playing again. This is not much for such an explorative game like this I dare say.
What I loved about Trove was the amount of biomes there is and the possibility to style everything, even your character, with a specific biome in mind as well as the amount of possible blocks for building your house. Another thing that I found really neat were the tooltips for almost every item as they, in the majority of cases, reveal how to acquire them. You can view all available items in the game in a certain List (default press Y and check out that stuff) and the tooltips for every item almost all of the time tell you how to get them. This is pretty neat as it reduces the amount of times I have to ask somebody or look it up in a wiki.
One last thing: the devs.
They punch out so many updates and server maintenance to ensure everybody gets a good gaming experience. If they notice there is a persistent issue with even a small percentage of players, they warn us beforehand and then get right to it by shutting down the servers and solving the problems. In my opinion, that's good work.
But now, off to the pros and cons:
Pros:
- Vast world to explore with a lot of variety in landscapes
- Fly, hop on a boat or ride your mount
- Ability to style your equip the way you want
- Ability to have your own, personal WORLD for yourself
- A portable base of operations that you can customize the way you want with a variety of different blocks
- Great development team so far
- Fair business model
Cons:
- Lack in enemy variety
- Lack in musical presence
- Lack in class ability variety
- Getting some resources might get tedious
- Lack of combat variety
Would I recommend this game? I had a ton of fun with it so far, so yes. Totally.
And it's free, it's not like you're paying anything so give Trove a try today!

A fantastic adventure into terror and madness, with a sense of dread and tension perfectly established by its artwork and design, and reinforced by its game mechanics. The gloomy narrator makes grim remarks on everything you do, the art and sound design are bathed in darkness, and everything comes together to absolutely nail the "middle ages Lovecraft" feel it's going for.
, standing as one of the most atmospheric dungeon crawls ever made, and using its basic technical achievements to great effect.
The game itself is an exercise in brutality that sometimes pushes into masochistic territory, but is never insurmountable. Right off the bat, you are told that some heroes will die, and they're gone for good when they do, but you just have to learn to salvage things when they go wrong and figure out how to move on from there. It looks deceptively straightforward at first, involving turn-based combat and a party of four heroes at a time, but
where planning out the perfect party composition, arranged in the right order, with complimentary skills to cover all possible situations all becomes vital to your success. What seems impossibly difficult at first can be reliably crushed once you figure out the proper strategy. Usually.
The most divisive aspect of design is the randomness involved in almost everything. Even the best-laid plans can suddenly take a turn for the disastrous, all thanks to a particularly nasty turn of the invisible dice. A valuable hero might get wrecked by a monstrous critical hit, or a vitally important attack might miss or fail to do enough damage to bring down the target in time, and etc. Things can also go in your favour suddenly when they seem to be going horribly wrong, but more often than not it seems,
.
These moments can be immensely frustrating and may very well cause some players to drop the game entirely, but in a great many cases, the disaster struck because of some failure in planning that occurred somewhere down the line. You took that massive crit because you allowed the enemy to take a swing at you, because it wasn't stunned/debuffed/killed efficiently and your attacks were poorly chosen. So, while luck plays a definite factor in the game, it's not just a matter of pressing "go!" and hoping for the best. It's all about determining the odds, and knowing when to choose the safe course of action, when to gamble, and of course planning well ahead and being ready for anything. The game isn't remotely fair sometimes, and it gleefully embraces the players who want to suffer and feel miserable, but
, even if you can never fully guarantee it.
All this harsh, punishing game design goes hand in hand with the overall feel of the game, which plays its gratuitously dark tone almost completely straight-faced, embracing the ridiculousness and drama of it all. Though the game lacks a sense of ongoing plot or character development,

I can't imagine a more mixed set of feelings reviewing a game.  I LOVE the Fallout universe.  Absolutely adore it - my favorite post-apocalyptic universe, bar none.  Besides, the visuals look solid and the sound design is wonderful (including the fully realized score). So why do I not recommend this game?
The fault lies with the publisher.  The issues common to Bethesda open world games are here in full force.  Items can move around when other nearby items are picked up, NPCs seldom act in natural ways (old women and pack animals regularly end up on top of buildings despite not having a way to get up there), it's classic "Bethesda Jank" in all its glory.  But the thing that REALLY ruins the experience is the settlement system (and by extension most of the DLC).  Settlement structure pieces are meant to snap together for ease of building, but it barely works - many building pieces refuse to snap together except in very specific ways, sometimes conflicting with pieces they don't even directly touch.  It's possible to spend hours building up a settlement only to find that your precise arrangement of parts breaks NPC pathfinding, leaving settlers who just stand around 24/7.  In addition, the game allows the dead grass that fills the world to clip through any placed buildings - I hope you like shrubs sticking through your concrete walls, because there's no way to avoid it.
Even without the problems with structures it's pretty awkward.  Many items (including corpses) cannot be removed without console controls - not too bad until you remember that most settlements require you to kill the previous occupants.  Some of the buildable settlement items are noticeably worse than the versions of them you see around the wastelands - the lights, in particular, are often less than half as bright if you placed them yourself compared to the versions found in the wild.
Look, I don't expect perfection from day one - games are HUGE projects with hundreds of people involved.  But Bethesda REFUSES to acknowledge or patch most of these issues.  Forum threads are full of these kinds of issues with no fix in sight, and modders are trying desperately to create unofficial patches that finish the work Bethesda started.  When I buy an indie game made by a team of a couple dozen, I expect to have to mod some things to get them to work as intended.  But when I buy a AAA game by a trusted publisher, I don't want to have to install a dozen unofficial bugfixes because the developer can't be bothered to fix the bugs or acknowledge theeir fans' feedback.

It´s a very good looking, turn based, game featuring the "rebels against the world".
You are fighting a guerrilla war against the Aliens and their puppet government ADVENT, in which you are the hunted prey.

Performance:
The game runs with the Unreal Engine 3.5. It looks great but it needs quite some power for this.
The biggest fps killers are vsync, smooth framerate and MSAA. Especially MSAA eats a lot fps and even a 980ti can´t currently handle MSAA 8x.

Okay, I wrote a review as a long-time Bethesda fan who just recently got the game. Now that I punched over 700 hrs, I have a better view of it, but I will still use other Bethesda games as comparatives.
RPG: This not really an RPG. Your RP options are quite narrow, and is pretty much limited to followers, whose limited and repetitive lines will certainly get on your nerves. Your character's background or reactions in the main quest is effectively limited. It is an open-world building and shooting game, let it be clear.
Combat and skills: The best compromise so far: Instead of eliminating attributes, like in Skyrim, they eliminated the skill system: your character is "average" in everything up until he gains perks, not unlike Fallout 3 and N-Vegas, that he places according to the player's choice. It's working good, and pretty much removes the level cap or make it incredibly high. The combat is now excellent, with "bullet-time" VATS and more control on criticals. Melee is still a bit frustrating as it seems ennemies can still block and attack at the same time, like in previous Fallout games.
Crafting: This is big thing in this game, and it will eat a lot of your playing time, so be advised: There are zones when one can literally build whole settlements, with a system that's limited in scope but efficient. Happy settlements provide the player with more ressources with which he upgrades said settlements, or his own personal weapons and protections.
You gear does not, like in previous Fallouts, degrade with use: They just get obsolete as you progress unless you upgrade them, a very pleasant system that takes the best of both worlds. There are numerous workbenches that let you do chemicals, provisions and stuff. The components required for crafting will pretty much makes the bulk of your loot: Teddy bears, office fans, coffee cups...
Ambiance and immersion: This is very important to me, and lies beyond the complex technicalities. First off, the textures are too pale, too bright. Fallout 4 is a colourful, sunny world, not the bleak, even depressive landscape of Fallout 3. The music, some Fallout classics with a tendency towards rockabilly, doesn't help too much. These song didn't have the melancolic nostalgia that matched so well with the brilliant art deco civilisation they elaborated before destroying it. The games' original music is solid as it always been, thought. It is kinda fun to walk in Business District, with its aerial highways and creaking metal sounds.
I can't tell much about the infamous Creation Club - I mod my own game myself, and so can you. All and all, this is quite a vast amount of hours for the "investment". Althought it isn't a perfect game, nor the absolutre classic that Fallout 3 was, Fallout 4 is a satisfying advance in the serie. They are on the good track here, as at the end of "Skyrim" I wasn't so sure. Good work, Beth - just check out for the gimmicks, mmmhh? - 8/10.

The game is very good in that it endlessly generates new situations to confront you and your resistance force. It has that RPG flavor that gives you a sense of accomplishment as well as direction.

However I think the difficulty dictates the longevity, as it was back in the old era of video games. If you haven't completed a single campaign, then the game is not over.

Darkest Dungeon is a fun game to delve right into. It's only about after you finish your first (mini?) boss and see how the progression works in this game to understand how much of a grindfest this game forces you to partake in order to finish it. What I mean is when you've established a party that has hit the next level tier (such as level 3) you will have quests that those characters will ONLY go to (so a tier 2 [level 3-4] level hero would not be able to go into a tier 1 [level 0-2] mission). Its understandable why the developers put this feature in as to avoid easily farming money and loot from the lower tier missions; however, when you're party is exhausted from a mid-high tier fight with a boss, with even deaths accumulating from your higher level characters, the time it takes to recover, go to the stage coach and recruit new heroes, send on quests to farm heirlooms and gold, and upgrade your hamlet and characters can be quite daunting if you're not patient, especially when upgrades (whether character or hamlet) take up a ton of resources. For Instance in my playthrough I thought I was doing well with 20,000 gold pieces, but then after i upgraded the equipment of just four members of my roster I ended up with 600 and not being able to afford torches and food for my next adventure without having to sell items that i've gained throughout my adventure.
The dungeon delving in this game and the boss fights I feel are the best part about this game, with even the lower level dungeons requiring some careful planning and preparation for in order to be successful. With a Narrator who does a decent enough job of setting the atmosphere of the game, along with characters who have their own subtle traits that can spring up at anytime (i.e. kleptomaniacs end up stealing loot out of the blue) it can be a quite entertaining and immersive experience. I also enjoy the camping system and that each character can bring certain skills to the campfire such as mending wounds, cheering others up, etc. with some pretty cheeky dialogue as well. The only thing I dislike about it is that each dungeon gets repetitive because the game forces you to grind the same missions over and over again to gain the necessary resources and in order for you to level up your lower level heroes (even more so when your higher level people die).
I would have to recommend this game still even though it gets quite repetitive and the difficulty can spike with certain bosses as some of the characters you've leveled up may not be suited for the encounter all because even at the most frustrating of times (such as a whole high level party dying to a boss) the game never felt unfair or unwinnable. Much like XCom, it can even be quite entertaining to see how badly a poor decision could end up causing severe consequences such as a healer gaining an affliction and not following directions when your party is about to die.
I give this game 7/10 and possibly higher when I've beaten more bosses.

FALLOUT 4 (2015)
Bethesda Studios
As someone who has never played a Fallout game, the hype surrounding Fallout 4 seemed to make a compelling argument to hop into the latest game first. I'd be playing alongside an active community, finding and sharing secrets with everyone else, and enjoying the most up-to-date version of the systems in the series. To my own surprise, the game played and flowed a lot like Skyrim. The RPG mechanics were almost identical. Given how much freedom Skyrim's systems allow you, I thought this spelled great things for the game. My final thoughts wouldn't quite match up with that.
The Post Nuclear Wasteland of the Commonwealth is rich with things to do and explore, but damn if it doesn't become repetitive at some point. The gameplay philosophy with Fallout 4 is very much quantity over quality.. you'll come across the same level interiors, the same raiders and super mutant enemies, the same loot and guns, the same fetch quests, the same dialogue quips and encounters, over and over to the point of fatigue. You feel the urge to continue out of the possibility that you'll eventually find an interesting location, an interesting enemy, an interesting weapon, an interesting quest, or an interesting moment, but they are too far and few in between to warrant putting so much time in the game. Because of this, Fallout 4 feels like a game that never really starts and never really ends, you either take it for what it is or play a more interesting game.
So is there a saving grace to Fallout 4? Yes, and no, depending on how much you value it.
Fallout 4 has a cool 1950s style aesthetic to everything in the world. The radio plays 1950s tunes, billboards and corporate products boast trends that might've existed during the 50s, the design and architecture for clothing and robotics feels like a sci-fi tale written in the 50s, and the cultural values of that era ring throughout the game. Being set in Boston also allows the game to juggle with American history, and overall the blend makes Fallout feel like a world that's somehow pleasant to live within.
There's a few other problems with Fallout 4, such as a dialogue wheel that often fails to let my character say something I'm thinking, or a settlement system that doesn't go as deep or as complex as building systems in other games, but a lot of these problems can be overlooked if you find what the game is giving you genuinely fun. Personally I didn't, and I feel like there's other games in this genre that accomplish what Fallout 4 goes for way better. I do realize Bethesda Studios put a lot of work into this game, but the corners are cut in far too many places for it to called a well-designed game.
Conclusion: 5 / 10
Would Not Recommend (until you've played basically most other Besthesda games)

This game is fantastic. Before you read this review, get it downloading so it'll be ready when you're done.
Of all the Free-to-Play games to choose from (and there are a lot of them), Trove is one of the best. It has an incredible amount of content, which has kept me busy for over 350 hours at the time of writing, and I'm not even close to running out of things to do.
Right now there are 11 classes (with another on the way), and I own 9 of them at varying levels. Every class I've tried so far has been unique and fun to play, with an interesting theme and personality to each one.
Alongside the adventuring content is the building. You get your own little 16x16 plot, or 'cornerstone', that you can teleport to any cornerstone location you find. This cornerstone can be your own little slice of home, with all the amenities an adventurer could ever need. You can also use it to show off your building skills to the world at large!
There are also club worlds. These are expandable worlds, much larger than the cornerstone plots, on which you can build to your heart's content.
All I've spoken about in this review so far is just a small portion of what you'll experience when playing Trove. There are also tons of mounts, wings, boats, allies (pets), and equipment styles to collect, the community is top-notch, and the devs are constantly adding new content to the game.
Now, I hope your download has finished so you can go and check out this excellent game for yourself!

If you like games that will make you miserable.....
I have to strongly warn any and all interested that it will produce in the player massive levels of anger, frustration, and salt the likes of which you would not even find playing the likes of Dark Souls on a bad day. At least in a game like Dark Souls skill takes precedence and makes the game gradually more enjoyable. In this game, you are never not a victim to the RNG. When things go well, they go very well. But when things go bad, it honestly feels like the developers are giving you the finger and kicking you in the balls with a smug smirk for good measure.
I've pushed on through this game and managed to defeat every beginner and veteran boss with two of the intermediate bosses (the dreaded Swine God and the Hag Witch) under my belt. But I've recently thrown in the towel and decided I can't push myself any further. It isn't simply a matter of the RNG either; the intermediate dungeons are too difficult with enemies that will frequently have both high dodging AND protection stats making each battle a slow grind and a fight for your life. That there are ways to mitigate the enemies ability to survive your attacks with debuffs barely helps when the debuffs tragically miss, making that character's turn wasted, or when you simply don't have anyone on your team available to do such a thing. It doesn't help that you can't ever go anywhere without a healer, whose healing skills are so hit and miss you're constantly on the edge of your seat whenever they attempt to patch your crumbling team together.
Where the difficulty goes overboard is with an enemy called The Collector that you are guaranteed to fight at least once randomly in EVERY intermediate level dungeon. These enemies are the biggest asshats due to their ability to continually respawn allies which can either heal or protect it while it too heals itself by draining life from your team to refresh its already huge pool of helth. The reward for defeating this enemy, an item worth a lot of gold, won't even cover your losses at the end of the quest when you have to send your team to the tavern or the abbey to undo their accumulated stress (assuming you can even survive).
Where I quit was in a dungeon where I had just barely survived an encounter with this most dreaded of foes only for TWO of my high level heroes whom I had already invested much money into upgrading, BOTH died, in a game with perma death no less. That brought the toll of dead heroes to ten and caused me to delete my save file in frustration. I don't mind (too much) if a hero dies valiantly while fighting a boss which I then proceed to defeat, but when it happens randomly due to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t RNG it brings my blood to a boil and I have to fight not to hurl my laptop across the room.
It's sad, because I like this game. I really, truly do. But it is TOO F&%#ing hard!!! Would it honestly kill them to dial down the difficulty just a bit? Even to allow you to purchase disposable healing items so you're not constantly relying on healers who can only heal during battle? When every quest becomes a desperate roll of the dice not just to progress the game but to just get yourself out of the black so you can invest in hero upgrades then it becomes more of a painful chore than a thrill. Especially when you see all that hard work go down the drain due to some random trick of the RNG. (Like missing four times in a row when trying to kill even a single enemy!)
I like hard games but I'm getting sick and tired of this meat-head "git gud" mentality which is plaguing games lately and making people feel ashamed for just wanting to have fun.
This game is too hard. Not hard but rewarding kind of hard, but hard and painful, like the worst day of your life at the worst job you've ever had and when deep in debt to boot. Would it be such a bad thing if they just make it a little more forgiving?????

Darkest Dungeon is a roguelike dungeon crawler game, developed by Red Hook Studios. The game was initially released in Early access in January 2015, before leaving Early Access in January 2016.
Gameplay in Darkest Dungeon leaves you in control of a roster of heroes; you control almost every aspect of your hero’s journey throughout the game. Initially you start out with two heroes from the tutorial, and you can expand your roster by visiting the stage coach in the main game hub, here you can select from at least two heroes and have them join your group. The central hub of the game also includes various other useful locations too, such as an armour smith, weapon smith, a tavern, hospital, and many more. Each of these locations becomes key to the progression in Darkest Dungeon.  The dungeon crawling side of the game is done from a side scrolling perspective, as you explore randomly generated dungeons in search for loot and treasure. The combat in this game is turn based, and very tactical. Each of your party of 5 heroes will have their own preferred location in your group and will only be able to use certain attacks based on their location too. Each of your characters has 4 active abilities they can use in a dungeon; you can swap and change them as you please in the main hub provided you have learned the skill beforehand.  Your party will also contract diseases, afflictions, blights and wounds throughout their journey and most will probably even die or become useless. You can cure these by visiting the hospital in the hub, but some may render your character pointless to have around. Like the game says at the very start, you really have to make the best out of a bad situation most of the time.
Graphically, it isn’t very intense; however the art style which is presented is just wonderful. The art style is really important to this game, as it shows the essence and feel of the game perfectly. The hand drawn look to the game is one of my favourite styles in gaming at the moment, and Darkest Dungeon wets my appetite beautifully there.   What is really important here though, would be the game’s user interface. As there is a lot of information needed to be able to progress successfully through the game, you are obviously going to need a clean and clear interface to show that information. The game’s tutorial at the start of the game explains a lot of it quite nicely. However a lot of the information is left for you to find out for yourself.  All of your characters information, stats and equipment are all a click away, as well as your map and inventory screen. I was really happy with the interface, a few changes I would of made is to add a lot of information to show right on the screen straight away, rather than having to hover over the item, or bar – it just felt like an unneeded hoop to jump through to get the information I wanted. The ordering of the turns can be quite difficult to keep track of as well; I still have no idea how it is worked out, but I would of liked to have seen maybe a time line of the battle somewhere on the screen to make it a little easier for you to plan your attacks; maybe this was considered already but was specifically not added so the game is all that much harder, that to me is the only logical reason for not having something like that included.
The audio in Darkest Dungeon is also spot on as well. First of all, the narrator is just plain awesome. His rusty voice sent shivers down my spine at times; it is very much on par with other great narrations like Bastion and Transistor. Sound effects are all really nicely designed too; the attack noises and monster sound effects are very nice and add an extra level of immersion to your game play.
This may be the hardest video game I have ever played. The game is so unforgiving and you will get screwed over, and you will probably die from your own stupid mistakes over and over again; but that is the whole point of this game. The aim to finish the game is very hard to hit and when you do hit it, you will be able to give yourself a very well earned pat on the back, because you will have just completed a monster difficulty game. I have never actually completed lost all of my party members, there seems to be an endless supply of them in the game’s hub, so you will never “lose the game” so to speak, you can just keep retrying (all be it with lower level characters).  This is one of those games where I had to spend a sufficient amount of time outside of the game, in the wiki and on forums just to give me that little extra edge over the unforgiving game play; I am not ashamed to admit and you shouldn’t be too if you have to check little bits of information out.
Due to playing the game a lot offline this week due to PC problems, a lot of my time has not been tracked, but I have put in roughly 30 hours of gameplay. I have still not finished the game, I have managed to hit max level with about 6 of my characters but I have been spending quite a while farming and grinding money for me to upgrade them more before taking on the final stages of the game. Due to the game’s randomness, the replay ability is extremely high even when you manage to finish it the once. This is a game you can easily get at least 100 hours out of without growing bored of it.
Technically I had no issues what so ever. It is definitely a game you have to use a keyboard and mouse on, just because of the amount of information you require access to. There aren’t any graphical options available sadly but it should run on just about anything as it isn’t graphically intensive. Although it isn’t exactly a technical talking point, but a nice added feature here was that you can actually turn off some of the game mechanics right out of an options menu, yes this may make the gam experience differ and may even decrease the difficulty, but I personally don’t see this as a real issue in a single player game.
My conclusion on Darkest Dungeon is that it is one of the best games to come out via the Early Access system. Even when it was first released, it was a better game than most, but now it has been fully released this year it is an absolute must play title. All other devs looking to release a game into early access really need to pay attention to these guys as it was done so perfectly and hassle free. I can easily say that it is my up most favourite roguelike game ever. The game’s regular price on Steam for £18, 99 is a good price point, there is tons of content and extremely high production values put into this game. Do not hesitate for a second more and pick this game up.

I know people will just vote this down without reading it, but I really don't care.
Darkest Dungeon is not a game I can bring myself to recommend, but I still find it to be an incredibly earnest videogame on the merit of how much effort went into making it -- at least as far as general production goes. The visual polish is incredible, even though it lacks variety. The core ideas are very interesting and some choices were good, such as the ability to leave a dungeon at any time to prevent loss of recruits, at a cost. The narrator is amazing and the addition of a section in the options menu which lets the player toggle certain systems such as corpses was a very good decision.
That said, while this breaks my heart to say, this is easily one of the most disappointing games I've ever played.
As it stands, progression-wise, Darkest Dungeon's design is very akin to your standard mobile game. Perform task, then perform task again, then perform same task again. As you do this, your funds may rise and you may inch yourself closer to... Whatever objectives the game throws at you. At its core, the game asks you to pick a party, throw the party into a dungeon where they'll hopefully succeed. After this, the player will receive funds in return for a good performance, promptly wasting said funds recovering party members from basically unavoidable mental injury and funding the next expedition's quasi-mandatory set of supplies. This will / may leave the player with a very, very small margin of profit. Since money is so important to progress, half of the game will feel like a constant grind to stay just above debt. Losing out will often imply a huge scuffle just to recover from debt. Running out of funds will almost always mean the player will be losing recruits or a great deal of time just to get back on the treadmill, let alone back to progressing.
The core design doesn't help this. I love turn-based RPGs and I particularly love tough ones. My favourite RPG series ever is Shin Megami Tensei, for example. The difference is that, in those games, the player has more going on that they don't feel like all they're doing is fighting. That's more or less what I felt while playing this. I fight, then I fight some more, and then I fight a little bit more, and in the end I hope that I made slightly more money than I wasted.
I'd also like to add that for a game whose narrative is based around eldritch horror, it certainly is pretty safe with its monster designs.
Combat-wise, each and every enemy encounter feels designed specifically to kill or maim the player's progression as fast as possible. Some enemies are dedicated solely to inflicting large amounts of stress damage and they're often protected by beasts with over-inflated health bars and sometimes even spells to protect other members from direct harm. On paper this might sound alright, but in practice, since practically every move a player makes is subject to RNG, it's hard for the player to feel like they can control their fate.
The game is too reliant on dice rolls and that's fine, in theory. However, the enemies are not under the same pressure that the player is, so they can easily form all-out attack parties and stack debuffs on your recruits because losing their ranks doesn't matter. They are more-or-less subject to the same kind of dice roll the player is, so to some players that might feel fair. But since the AI has no sense of self-preservation, they can easily throw themselves at your party until it breaks.
This would also be okay, would it not be for the overwhelming odds. The developer has gone on record to state that they wish this game to feel like the player is constantly in a bad spot. I understand this mentality, but I think it didn't work out for them.
The game becomes grueling to the point of frustration and tedium -- where things happen completely outside of your control and you're somehow being asked to feel responsible for something you couldn't possibly prevent. It's like saying you worked hard to win the lottery.This is one example of a new genre I call "Badge of Honour" games. Games which live and die through unfairly punishing design and are extremely contingent on clicking with the audience -- being able to say you've "beaten" Darkest Dungeon will become a badge of honour and very few people want to admit they won because they got lucky, so it creates this aura about it wherein the audience is divided by "people who got good", and "people who don't get it". Plainly, I disagree both of these are the case, so I don't feel the game should be recognized in this manner. There's nothing quite as infuriating as knowing a game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and yet being told it was intended.
I'm sorry, but I can't possibly recommend Darkest Dungeon. There are those who say people like me "didn't get it", but I'm sorry. I systematically play bullethell games, I've done challenge runs in games like Contra and Megaman and I often engage in challenge runs in more modern games like Dark Souls or Bloodborne. I do get 'punishing but fair', and this is CERTAINLY not it.
Seen as I'm told all of this was intended, I'll make sure to not recommend this. I can forgive awful balancing work and poor overall design due to inexperience, but if this was the vision the creator had, then they'll have to accept those consequences -- ironically.
Did I enjoy my time with Darkest Dungeon so far? To some extent, sure. And I'll be playing more of it. That said, I am fully aware that this is a game a lot of people will not enjoy for this price.
Once the price drops to 5€ or thereabouts, I'll edit my review. Until then, again, I'm sorry, but at this price, a glorified mobile turn-based badge of honour game isn't worth your time or investment. I've said this before and I'll say it again: Videogames are a past time. Designing a videogame explicitly to make the player feel like crap on a constant basis is counterproductive at best, and just plain stupid design at worst.
If you're not convinced, then I would highly recommend downloading the Lighter Dungeon mod and then going into the game's files and adjusting the parameters to better fit your criteria. Bumping down the cost of supply items can go a long way toward making the experience bearable at best.

Right now, I sadly can't recommend the game; there are simply too many bugs ,and a few design decisions, that make this game more frustrating than enjoyable.
The random numbers are pre-generated whenever a new map is loaded. Meaning, sometimes your units WILL miss four times in a row. No matter how you position them, if it's overwatch or not, if the displayed chance to hit 100% or if the enemy is flanked, they will miss four times. So, if you use bad tactics and reload to try something different, you just wasting time because the outcome is already determined.
And sometimes the aliens WILL hit, no matter what you do. Even through walls and floors, without them having seen your doomed units previously.
Speaking of walls, it seems that they don't block the line of sight very reliable. It's very frustrating if you set up a nice ambush (in the rare case the map doesn't have a VERY tight turn limit), and the aliens notice your units through a wall or door, kill one or two, and poison the rest though the wall without even opening the door.
Also, my first campaign save suddenly couldn't be loaded any more; it just crashed the game without any error.
I hope Firaxis will fix them eventually, but until then you should better play something less frustrating.
