Spiral Knights is an alright MMO, alright for free at least. It's definitely worth a try, seeing as how the initial pricetag is agreeable. For me, however, it's more of a social platform than a real kind of game. Allow me to explain as to why I see it as I do.
Spiral Knight's selection of equippable gear is quite wide at first glance, there are plenty of different resistances and weaknesses to all kinds of armor, all of which can be interchanged at a moment's notice, but the variety is wasted upon especially superior gear that provides a kind of range that none other can provide. For example, if you were to choose between say, a Seraphic set or a Wolver set, the seraphic would give a damage buff equal to that of the wolver. However, the Wolver set gives a universal buff to swords, meaning that it does what the seraphic does, but can go beyond that, as well. It's armors like those that begin to break down the options available through common sense and unfair stats. Why anyone would go with an armor so selective versus an armor completely open-ended is beyond me, and most likely anyone else.
An even better case is when it comes to early-game bombers and bombers overall. Bombs themselves are fairly underpowered items when working up, so it's more likely people go Gunner or Swordsman, for better attack and whatnot. Bombers overall that strictly follow the bomber line can choose the Mad Bomber Gear, giving them amazing stats for bombs, but horrible defense. There's another armor that does this, surprisingly, but, get this,
Whoever decided that was a good idea must've thought pretty lowly of bombers, as it completely voids the Mad Bomber gear, allowing for sidearms and whatnot to be used in conjunction with bombs. All in all, the gear doesn't stop there, and most likely won't as the game progresses.
You'd think with the previously mentioned, they'd begin working on balancing armors and fixing things up, right? Hah, no. You want some costumes? Here's a few hundred. You want some reskins? Here's a box of 'em, have fun. Balancing the game is about as much of a lie as Santa. As while it's not real content, some people still love ripping open the new boxes and slapping whatever colorful paper that was inside right onto their character. I can understand dishing out some cash for a thing to make you look snazzy, but why feed a company more money when their game's pretty darn broken? I understand wanting to make the most out of the overpowered gear, but seeing one team of adventurers run into a dungeon all brandishing the same kind of gear is boring, stale, and just sad. There is no unique quality among players, no matter what little accessory they slap onto their armor, it's still the same cookie-cutter formula. I had more fun running into a dungeon with some close friends of whom we all chose oddjob gear, it was complex, it was different, it was confusing, and most of all, it was fun. Don't even begin on promised "updates" that hold new gear, as they delay for as long as they can. I'd get more in-depth with it, but I'll have to get back to you on that one. (Pun intended.)
So say you've finished the endgame, you've beat Vanaduke, heated your gear as far as you please, and have successfully reached the coveted rank of Vanguard. What's left? Apparently not much, if you don't have a guild, some good Spiral Knights friends, or anything immediately tying to it. The endgame leaves very little left, sure you have PvP, sure you have Blast Network, sure you might have guildruns, but why bother? PvP offers gear that has an alternative spin on some of your favorite (not-by-choice) weapons, with some stats made exceptionally worse, or some still a bit broken. But what's that to you? You've spent all this time grinding through repetitive missions for the things necessary to create your god-tier gear, so why bother struggling through all of that again? And don't try to play the card that PvP is interesting, it's usually the people with the broken gear using the broken swords. More often than not it's always Skolver wearing Strikers with the occasional Gunner or Snarbolax wearing Striker. Blast Network's just a bomberman port, playable by all skill levels no matter what, and to be fair, it's fairly fun. However, the lack of discrimination between skill levels can make it harsh on those who try it out, and more experienced players could potentially offset newcomers who'd like to begin playing as well.
Don't think it's just endgame, either, as the monotony can set in as immediately as when you first begin to start. The missions assigned to you to gain rank feel incredibly scripted and not as free as they could be. It feels more like a chore than anything else, and nowhere near as fun as the random generation of the Clockworks (Which seems to be, for the most part, swept under the rug.). The Clockworks now takes discovering on your own to find, which the game already doesn't reward, making it harder to want to do so. Missions are also more likely to have the boxes you need to find to use for the drop system to give you the main crafting materials that you need for better gear, so that's another hit against the Clockworks. If you find that grinding much to your distaste, don't worry, the online store will be happy to help, for the right price, of course. Online store not your cup of tea either? The Auction House sells them at prices only a "few" monotonous boss runs can pay for!
Spiral Knights is an okay MMO, not great under any means, but it's not horrible. The only shining light that keeps this game from a true dark abyss would have to be it's community. The community has it's fair share of mean customers and nice folk. You can find some pretty good friends, and some truly cool people on this game. All it takes is a little bit of chatting, and you've found one heck of a pal. The missions and so are more tolerable with a fun group, as the dulling world can take on a new sense of rejuvenation with good talks, funny dialogue, and crazy moments. This game is saved by it's community, whether it be a good or bad thing. I only ever come back to Spiral Knights more for the people than the actual game, truth be told.
All in all, Spiral Knights receives a 6/10 from me, for what it's worth. The game has alot to fix, and sadly, they haven't done much fixing. The experience can only really be fulfilled with friends, as going alone can dull the sense of wonderment you'll receive initially. I say you take some time out and find a little clique of sorts that you do things with, and you'll make it one great of an experience.

I've had never been a huge Minecraft fan and I've never played Terraria....like ever.  So I bought this game based entirely on the fact that, "everyone else is doing it so it must be good."  I know, dad always said just because everyone else is jumping off a cliff doesn't mean I have to do it too....... But sometimes it's fun to jump off the cliff with everyone else.  With that known, this review will be from a non-Minecraft/Terraria fan and what my impressions are.
My first game play into Starbound was solo.  After all, I didn't want to look like a complete n00b when I start playing with friends.  I think I was expecting some sort of 2D Minecraft, to which I wasn't let down in that aspect.  There was mining, crafting, building your home/base all those things that make Minecraft interesting.  Then I see one of those cute little aliens and I'm like, "oh cool, hopefully it won't attack me at a snail’s pace like the monsters in Minecraft.........ohh, oohh.. WTF it's spraying some sort of fire barf all over me and jumping at me.  Good gods get it off... I'm dead."  It would take me another few fights similar to that to get the hang of the combat system which thankfully is much more active than Minecrafts.  Being one who likes challenging game play, (my favorite game series is Monster Hunter after all,) this was the first thing in Starbound that made me want to play more.  Hanging out more in the game, discovering that different mobs do have different attacks and there are boss monsters, I've not been let down in this area.
After reading a bit online about how to get a good start, (if you’re a game player that likes to be lead by the nose to everything you need to do in a game then you may not enjoy this game as much...) I felt I was ready for multi-player.  A friend of mine asked if I'd like to join him and off we went.  After playing a bit I've seen that multiplayer is certainly where it’s at in this game.  Don’t' get me wrong, solo was fun but there's just something about teaming up and traveling to other planets, building fancy bases, exploring random dungeons, it's all much more fun when you've got a friend to hang out with.  Throw in some Skype so you can hear each other panic as some monster from hell rips though your group and your set for some very fun times.
Overall I enjoy the game a lot.  Even in early access there's a ton of content and things to do and well worth the money spent to buy it.  I eagerly look forward to what the future holds for this game.

Firaxis knocked it out of the park with XCOM 2. They took everything that made EU and EW a smash hit, fixed all the niggling problems--namely the overly simplified strategic world campaign and the repetitiveness of the tactical combat--and added a great story to create a masterpiece of a strategy game.
There are no formulas to win in XCOM 2. Every battle is fresh, thanks to the procedural map generator and the dynamic goals. Some missions you'll have all the time in the world to kill each and every alien; other missions are a frantic rush across the map from cover to cover to beat the objective timer (an idea perhaps borrowed by another great game, Invisible, Inc.) Some scenarios drop you into the map in stealth mode, allowing you to perform those gorgeously cinematic ambushes; other times you have to slog through the map fully visible, taking care as you go not to leave your squadmembers exposed out of cover. Sometimes an enemy reinforcement drop winds up in the perfect place, other times it impedes your progress towards the objective. The hacking towers might offer something up of use now, or maybe halfway through the battle, or perhaps not at all.
The best part about XCOM 2 is that you're allowed to lose in the smaller scope of things--something I think was missing in XCOM 1, particularly mid-to-late game. In XCOM 2 you're expected to fail missions. There's even a built-in function to call up the SkyRanger for an emergency evac for those times a battle goes south, or when you realize you're not going to make the timer-based objective.
You'll be using that evac a LOT.
The squadmember customization options are also fantastic. Each of your squadmembers can take on as much character as you want to give them, from the color of their gear to the swagger in their walk. You'll spend dozens of minutes doctoring up a squadmember (best to do it in the main menu roster so it saves the soldier for future use) only to have him or her gunned down after 8 missions.
The game has a handful of quirky bugs, but most are minor nuisances (except for the bug where the view of the various floors of a building gets stuck on or off--it makes it quite impossible to see where you're moving.) I've heard there are performance issues, but they're easily remedied by turning off your anti-aliasing. All these bugs will probably be ironed out in patches during the next few months, but until then this game is still 110% worth the buy.
Many die, would recommend!

Darkest Dungeon is a fun game to delve right into. It's only about after you finish your first (mini?) boss and see how the progression works in this game to understand how much of a grindfest this game forces you to partake in order to finish it. What I mean is when you've established a party that has hit the next level tier (such as level 3) you will have quests that those characters will ONLY go to (so a tier 2 [level 3-4] level hero would not be able to go into a tier 1 [level 0-2] mission). Its understandable why the developers put this feature in as to avoid easily farming money and loot from the lower tier missions; however, when you're party is exhausted from a mid-high tier fight with a boss, with even deaths accumulating from your higher level characters, the time it takes to recover, go to the stage coach and recruit new heroes, send on quests to farm heirlooms and gold, and upgrade your hamlet and characters can be quite daunting if you're not patient, especially when upgrades (whether character or hamlet) take up a ton of resources. For Instance in my playthrough I thought I was doing well with 20,000 gold pieces, but then after i upgraded the equipment of just four members of my roster I ended up with 600 and not being able to afford torches and food for my next adventure without having to sell items that i've gained throughout my adventure.
The dungeon delving in this game and the boss fights I feel are the best part about this game, with even the lower level dungeons requiring some careful planning and preparation for in order to be successful. With a Narrator who does a decent enough job of setting the atmosphere of the game, along with characters who have their own subtle traits that can spring up at anytime (i.e. kleptomaniacs end up stealing loot out of the blue) it can be a quite entertaining and immersive experience. I also enjoy the camping system and that each character can bring certain skills to the campfire such as mending wounds, cheering others up, etc. with some pretty cheeky dialogue as well. The only thing I dislike about it is that each dungeon gets repetitive because the game forces you to grind the same missions over and over again to gain the necessary resources and in order for you to level up your lower level heroes (even more so when your higher level people die).
I would have to recommend this game still even though it gets quite repetitive and the difficulty can spike with certain bosses as some of the characters you've leveled up may not be suited for the encounter all because even at the most frustrating of times (such as a whole high level party dying to a boss) the game never felt unfair or unwinnable. Much like XCom, it can even be quite entertaining to see how badly a poor decision could end up causing severe consequences such as a healer gaining an affliction and not following directions when your party is about to die.
I give this game 7/10 and possibly higher when I've beaten more bosses.

TLDR: If you liked the Borderlands franchise and want more of that only single player, buy this game.  If you are looking for a worthy successor to New Vegas, look elsewhere.
Please understand that this is only superficially a Fallout game.  If you loved the original isometric games, New Vegas, or even Fallout 3, you might want to skip this one.  This iteration has made vast improvements over the previous ones in terms of reliability and playability, however, they have really dropped the ball on writing and quest design.  This is effectively a very pretty Borderlands game, super shallow and infinitely repeating, shoot and loot type gameplay.  I played through the main questline and it was somewhat compelling, and I can appreciate the forced difficult decisions, but the issue is that they were not written in a believable way.  It makes sense that certain factions would wish for you to wipe out another or manipulated them in some way, but what does not make sense is that there is no flexibility in how you accomplish this goal.  Kill so and so and all their friends, period.  There is no shutting them down in other ways, just kill everything, scorched earth, no diplomacy, nothing.  At least some of the factions should have been able to function with the others, and no, the completely irrelevent Minutemen don't count.  I put over 100 hours into this game, and really tried to love it as I have with previous installments, but in the end it just pales in comparison.  Fallout 3 certainly was no masterpiece and I am highly critical of what was done with the story and how they attempted to shoehorn old bits of the originals into it, but that was Bethesda's first go at it, and I expected there to be some issues.  After the amazing and fresh New Vegas installment, I was hopeful and excited that Bethesda had learned from Obsidian's work.  Sadly they saw the success of other open world games and went in a completely different direction.

The Darkest Dungeon is a classic dungeon crawler, with brutal difficulty, yet very carefully balanced mechanics. It is extraordinarily hard but never to a point of being unfair. However, you will have to go through a certain amount of grind in order to reach the endgame dungeons. Despite being slightly repetitive, I enjoy this kind of gameplay which reminds me of the days when games were not a widely spread form of entertainment such as it is today. The Darkest Dungeon gives a tribute to this bygone era, and on top of that provides fresh and crisp visuals that stand out in comparison with other roguelike indie games which prefer the "x"bit visual styles. The audio is superb quality, with an atmospheric soundtrack and a punctual narration. I would reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys dungeon crawlers, challenging games and gothic horror atmosphere. This is not for the faint of heart, or for people with no patience.

What happened to this game?
After a long break, I came back to Spiral Knights hoping for the charming, cute and relaxing atmosphere it once had. A simple yet rewarding game. Go down the clockworks, level up your weapons, hope Basil has something awesome, kill some bosses, get deeper, trade at the auction house, buy energy through the market at the right time, and so on. The game was so fun yet simple that it lured me back over a year later without even being reminded of it.
So what is this game now? A grindfest. The main reason for this is because you can no longer level up your equipment more than once in a single Clockworks run, you need to grind for (sometimes ridiculous amounts of) Fire Crystals, waste Heat (experience) and "forge" them even then with a chance of failure.
Adding to this, the mission system feels completely detached from the game itself, in fact a lot of the modes are. Everything just doesn't meld together, it feels like a mix of gameplay ideas all accessed from a mess of a menu system. Zero immersion unlike before.
I can overlook the poor performance because it's a game written in
. Which in itself is huge feet. Optimising games in Java is hard, especially to look like Spiral Knights does.
The music is relaxing and exilerating at the right times. The enemies, though lacking in variety, are well designed much like the rest of the characters and stages.
It's just sad that Three Rings decided to take the game in this direction. Though, with the servers still being somewhat dodgy,  it's probably a choice of what we have now or nothing at all.

All the great elements you loved in the first game a present

The Darkest Dungeon is a classic dungeon crawler, with brutal difficulty, yet very carefully balanced mechanics. It is extraordinarily hard but never to a point of being unfair. However, you will have to go through a certain amount of grind in order to reach the endgame dungeons. Despite being slightly repetitive, I enjoy this kind of gameplay which reminds me of the days when games were not a widely spread form of entertainment such as it is today. The Darkest Dungeon gives a tribute to this bygone era, and on top of that provides fresh and crisp visuals that stand out in comparison with other roguelike indie games which prefer the "x"bit visual styles. The audio is superb quality, with an atmospheric soundtrack and a punctual narration. I would reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys dungeon crawlers, challenging games and gothic horror atmosphere. This is not for the faint of heart, or for people with no patience.

INGREDIENTS:
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon baking soda
1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature
1/2 cup granulated sugar
1 cup packed light-brown sugar
1 teaspoon salt
2 teaspoons pure vanilla extract
2 large eggs
2 cups (about 12 ounces) semisweet and/or milk chocolate chips
DIRECTIONS:
1:  Preheat oven to 350 degrees. In a small bowl, whisk together the flour and baking soda; set aside. In the bowl of an electric mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, combine the butter with both sugars; beat on medium speed until light and fluffy. Reduce speed to low; add the salt, vanilla, and eggs. Beat until well mixed, about 1 minute. Add flour mixture; mix until just combined. Stir in the chocolate chips.
2: Drop heaping tablespoon-size balls of dough about 2 inches apart on baking sheets lined with parchment paper.
3: Bake until cookies are golden around the edges, but still soft in the center, 8 to 10 minutes. Remove from oven, and let cool on baking sheet 1 to 2 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack, and let cool completely. Store cookies in an airtight container at room temperature up to 1 week.

TLDR: If you liked the Borderlands franchise and want more of that only single player, buy this game.  If you are looking for a worthy successor to New Vegas, look elsewhere.
Please understand that this is only superficially a Fallout game.  If you loved the original isometric games, New Vegas, or even Fallout 3, you might want to skip this one.  This iteration has made vast improvements over the previous ones in terms of reliability and playability, however, they have really dropped the ball on writing and quest design.  This is effectively a very pretty Borderlands game, super shallow and infinitely repeating, shoot and loot type gameplay.  I played through the main questline and it was somewhat compelling, and I can appreciate the forced difficult decisions, but the issue is that they were not written in a believable way.  It makes sense that certain factions would wish for you to wipe out another or manipulated them in some way, but what does not make sense is that there is no flexibility in how you accomplish this goal.  Kill so and so and all their friends, period.  There is no shutting them down in other ways, just kill everything, scorched earth, no diplomacy, nothing.  At least some of the factions should have been able to function with the others, and no, the completely irrelevent Minutemen don't count.  I put over 100 hours into this game, and really tried to love it as I have with previous installments, but in the end it just pales in comparison.  Fallout 3 certainly was no masterpiece and I am highly critical of what was done with the story and how they attempted to shoehorn old bits of the originals into it, but that was Bethesda's first go at it, and I expected there to be some issues.  After the amazing and fresh New Vegas installment, I was hopeful and excited that Bethesda had learned from Obsidian's work.  Sadly they saw the success of other open world games and went in a completely different direction.

First thing's first.  Don't buy the game if you don't want a challenge.  Don't buy the game if you hate a little bit of grinding.  Don't buy the game if you hate turn based strategy games (they really should include strategy as a tag).  Don't buy the game if you want an immersive storyline.  Don't buy this game if you're not willing to invest a little time failing in order to learn.  RPG's are my genre.  I don't think I would call this an RPG.  It's something else.  Difficult is obviously a very subjective word.  If you plan to buy this, assume that it will be very hard.  If it fails to live up to your difficulty expectation, then you're in a very small minority I think.
There's been a lot of bad reviews gaining traction for this game since the full release.  I never played it in EA, but I've enjoyed the game thoroughly since I've had it.  I can't say whether or not the quality of the game was affected since EA ended, but I've definately got my money's worth out of the final release, and enjoyed every moment of it.
The only reason I'm wrting this review is because I agree with what everyone has to say about the game's positive attributes.  Most of the the negative reviews bring up luck, RNG, grinding, and "unfair".  I don't know what to say to that.  I've never once thought the RNG was out of balance or that the game was unfair.  However, the game is pretty tough.  There's a decent learning curve as well.  Once you know which party compositions fit your playstyle, who to bring where, how to interact with dungeon objects, when to kick a hero to the curb, which trinkets are worth finding and using, and how to manage the different enemies in the game..... There's no more problem.  The game remains a challenge, especially the final end game push, but once you're familiar with the game, the farming that is necessary is almost risk proof.
The game did ruin my night once, but it was my fault.  I chose to engage a champion level mini-boss.  It didn't go well.  It didn't go great on Veteran the first time I fought him either.  He wiped my party in the Champion level dungeon.  I lost 8 ancestral trinkets.  All gone.  4 resolve level 6 heros.  Gone.  However, it was my fault, and I learned from it.  It was not "unfair".  Also, crits happen.  I'm not sure why people complain about a string of crits against their party that snowballs into disaster.  I mean, think of all the monsters that constantly get wrecked by your heros.  Over and over and over again.  Surely they should be able to ruin your day every once in a while.  That's what I think.
Yes, farming is necessary.  Yes, there is grinding.  I've enjoyed every minute of it.  I enjoy the dungeon crawls.  I think if one were to approach this game as a turn based strategy game, there would be less hate.  Also, the game isn't as random as people have stated.  You can mitigate the chance of just about anything happening as long as you use the right trinkets and skills.  Mitigate, not prevent.  But you can't mitigate everything at once.  As the player, you need to decide what would be best to prepare for depending on your group composition and dungeon.
Full disclosure:  I haven't finished the game, but I'm close enough to have a full oppinion of the game.  I will finish this first run with strict (default) settings, with all caretaker goals completed.  I have two final pushes on the Darkest Dungeon itself left, and one boss left in the Cove.
Final note:  If you find yourself truly finding this game "unfair", try running vestal, plague doctor, hound master/ crusader/man at arms.  Now you've become the one who is playing unfair.
Very final note:  You don't have to play the game the way the dev's intended.  Most things can be toggled on or off in the menu.  I urge you to try to play with strict rules, but If you truly dislike them, then by all means turn some of that stuff off.

My Original Review can be found below this, I'm adding this segment in to voice my extreme displeasure after the Creation Club update. I've played around about 60 hours of this game on PS4, and now a further 43 hours on PC, so I've got quite a bit of experience with the game, I've done about 4 different characters, following different paths and such and completely plan on doing more. The game is highly replayable, with tons of different options with how you approach and carry out the questlines, and some of the quests really tickle you morally. The combat works really well, it's probably my favourite in recent Fallout games, though a bit reliant on rifles, in many cases. Otherwise, here is a pro's and cons list:
PROS:
Excellent combat
Some really good quests and scenes
Dogmeat
Very stable
Some great mods if you're interested in changing your experience.
Settlement building
CONS:
Some performance issues in dense urban areas
Having all the options for character development and being stuck to the whole parent narrative
Some repetitive side quests
Fetch quests
"Another Settlement Needs your help"
TL;DR A great, immersive atmospheric game with a few issues, many of which can be fixed by mods, and one of those games I'll remember enjoying in about 10 years.

I decided to review this game because I played extensivly and I have a feeling I can write a review based on my knowledge. Anyways this is my first review so if I make some sort of mistake let it slide.
So this game is Spiral Knights, a MMORPG that has a kinda in depth story, the story goes as follows apparently you are in a ship it's attacked, its about to blow up and you and all of your shipmates land on the Clockworks where monsters and creatures live in some hostile but some friendly. Spiral Knights also has a rank system which grants you the ability to make and weild/use better equipment. They are 10 ranks each with their own quests. But a big turn-down though is that sometimes there is a Hall of Heroes quest which requires you to have _ * Equipment...All of it. This leads to grinding for materials and Orbs of Alchemy, different types. Sometimes you can get stuck in this game because of this so the only choice you got is to save up those orbs. you are gonna need at least 15 orbs of whatever type to make the armor alongside other materials. However you eventually get this creature called a Battle Sprite which can help you fight but it wont attack by itself with default attacks, in fact it doesn't have a default attack which means you are responsible for any losses you have which can be a pain if you suck. Luckily it is pretty fun in general. Leveling up your Battle Sprite so it's stronger, getting new armor, weapons and sheilds, doing a quest for the first time, finding rare items. But it all boils down to do you like MMORPG's in general.
My ending note is this, Spiral Knights can be fun (and in some casses addicting) but it is much more fun with friends and when you are part of a guild. Either way making Armor and weapons aren't that fun and grinding can really be annoying but the amount of fun I have in each quest backs it up, if anything I think the best part for me is my Battle Sprite... Since this doesn't really have a rating system (Kinda but not really) I would give it a rating of 7/10. Its fun if you like RPGs and Doing quests and MMOs so. If you like these things I reccomend it, it is free so go for it if you wanna.

This game is a lovely refresher to the modern FPS genre. Black Squad takes firing mechanics similar to the Counter-Strike series, alongside weapons that function similar to that of Call of Duty and Battlefield. The maps layouts are believable and play out very well. The guns feel good (though some are tricky to master), and each have their own specific playstyles.
The gamemodes are fun, the maps work out pretty well. The graphics are pleasing and the animations are smooth and clean.
So far the game seems promising. There doesn't seem to be any pay-to-win elements to Black Squad whatsoever. Sure, there's paid content, but it's only for cosmetic skins and character playermodels.
However, I am not impressed with the crate system. I paid $0.99 (which is a good amount, to be fair) for a crate which contains the chance to get a weapon skin, in-game rare currency or standard currency. It's absurd that $0.99 gives you the chance to get standard currency which you can literally earn in one match. The standard currency should not be an available reward in paid crates whatsoever.
In summary, Black Squad is a fun game and is very unique. Best played with friends.

If i could give this game something between a thumbs up and a thumbs down i would.
It has great use of art style, narration, dungeon crawling, and the lovecraftian theme. The dark world you need to traverse affects your heroes on an emotinal and mental level. It really helps you feel the impact of the insane situation you find yourself in, watching your party slowly lose their minds from the horror they face.
Every battle and dungeon expedition is narrated by excellent voice acting, and going into dungeons forces you to think about what supplies to bring and what to throw away for space. Sometimes bandages are more valuable than gold.
I have a great deal of respect for what this game tries to do
However...
Many pivotal moments in this game come down to a throw of the dice. No matter how hard you preapre, no matter how well thought out your stratagy, everything can fall apart at a instant. A poorly timed miss, a weak heal, or a well placed crit can spell out death for the party youve spent a long time preparing, and there is nothing you can do about it. Hours of progress can be wiped in an instant.
This unfortunately can and will lead to large amounts of grinding, whether for money or levels, through the same dungeons youve been to time and time again. Progress in this game is slow, painfully so, and the final darkest dungeon requires many heroes to be max level. Fully upgraded max level heroes that can die at a moments notice.
I imagine the devolpers of this game wanted the player to feel as stressed as the party they are playing as, because every fight is a challenge, and the fear of losing it all will put you on edge, but when you lose a full team (or even a half team) of level 6 heroes, it can be depressing to the point of game quitting especially near the end game. Its like putting 50 hours into a big game youre trying to 100% only to have your file deleted.
This game absolutely has its merits and you can tell the developer put much time into it. However, the heavy focus on RNG and the repetative grind hold this game back from being something truly special.

A momentary lapse of concentration can lead to a death, and subsequent failure of a mission. You'll find yourself reverting to previous saves and playing out the scenario over and over again until you get the optimum outcome, but eventually you'll just learn to toughen up and power though the losses.
This game is good. Really good. A great step up from the previous title, it's more refined and content full. New features such as the concealment mechanic and the procedural levels really make this game stand out from its predecessor, and the new character creation and character pool really adds to the experience and influences how you play. It’s soul crushing to watch your favourite soldier who you spent ages making and writing a witty bio for die to the hands of ADVENT scum... The memorial and customisable epitaph are a really neat touch to display all the tens of soldiers you're inevitably going to lose. There will always be casualties, it's unavoidable.
I can't recommend this game enough, even as someone like myself who isn't the biggest fan of turn-based strategy games, I find myself glued to my desk urging to play Xcom at all times. It's a fantastic game, and a real game of the year contender already at this early stage.
I'd also quickly like to mention the mod support, it seems like modding is going to become a big deal in this game, and I'm excited to see where it ends up. I so far haven’t dabbled in the current workshop content, but as soon as I've completed a couple of campaigns I'll dive right in.
I have faith that this game will get the long term support and content that it so strongly deserves.
Okay, no more rambling, time to get back to saving the earth. Just give this game a go, you won’t be disappointed.

The amount of passion, talent, and knowledge going into this game is incredible. The art is stunning, the gameplay is seamless, the systems are interesting and fun, the characters are imaginative and diverse (their commentary helps make the time spent between dungeons feel more like interacting with your fellow adventurers and less like menu hopping). And of course, the writing is masterful. They've found the perfect blend of familiar monster horror dungeon mythos and their own creepy classic folk tale twist. In tone and visuals, it feels like a book written collectively by Edgar Allen Poe, H.P. Lovecraft, Bram Stoker, and Mary Shelley (but less forgiving for the reader) and the darkly humorous narration adds a literary element that ties all of those strings together. The difficulty of the game itself is well-balanced and gives very real consequences to your decisions, making the experience that much more rewarding.
So buy the game and support the developers, we need teams like this making games.
Thank you, Red Hook. You guys are awesome.

Far too difficult and unforgiving.
Now I understand that this game was intended to be challenging so it is by design that the game is as brutal as it is, but brutally challenging does not, a good game make.
First I'll go over what I like about the game.
-The setting is pretty cool. Now, I've not gotten very far into the game, as it just constantly makes me frustrated and unhappy, But from what I've seen of it, it's a pretty neat setting and I just wish that I could enjoy it more.
-The art style is pretty fantastic, I love the art style and look of the game.
-There are quite a variety of heroe types to choose from and there seems to be a great deal of customizability to the game.
Now what I don't like.
-Stress is incredibly difficult to manage. Stress causes all kinds of negative stuff to your heroes, some times devestating stuff, it's expensive to get rid of and is accumulated all of the damn time. The more stress your heroes have, the more bat♥♥♥♥♥♥insane they get and the more stat penalties they incur. Stat penalties are also expensive to get rid of.
-The torch system in this game is also very difficult to manage. You have to buy torches at the beginning of an expedition and you have to use them to recharge your light as you make your way through the dungeon. My issue with them is that the lower your light gets the more stress your heroes suffer from and the more difficult the monsters become, and torches do not last long at all, I often times will have to use up two of them just to get between rooms.
-My biggest complaint and the primary reason I keep quitting out of frustration, is how you constantly have to micromanage your expenses. You get gold from completing expeditions and you must spend that gold on upgrading the abilities and gear for your heroes, providing leasure activities for your heroes so they don't go bat♥♥♥♥♥♥insane and on consumable items used during expeditions.
Not that big of a deal, the problem for me is specifically in reguard to the consumable items, you have to do some major guess work(or clever statistical calculation) in order to make sure you have enough to keep your party from dying horribly or going insane. Now, I am not a statistician so I cannot do the clever statistical calculating to make sure I have enough to stay alive and even if I could, there's a very serious randomness to the entire game. Even if you math out the most efficient use of your gold to gear to abilities to leasure to items, you still will probably get screwed over during the expedition. Perhaps you didn't pack enough food to feed your heroes(yes you have to feed your heroes at least a couple times, if not more, during an expedition) and the RNG didn't provide you with food as treasure, or perhaps you didn't pack enough torches so you run out of torches and your heroes either go totally bonkers or die horribly in battle. Maybe you couldn't afford enough bandages and that damn pig creature just kept making your heroes bleed and they died of blood loss. Maybe you couldn't afford enough antivenom to heal the poison(or blight as it's called) that the mushroom mutants constantly cause. There is no item to heal the huge stress that the undead inflict to your heroes, the only time you can do that is when you spend gold and keep the hero out of the following expedition(and you must attempt an expedition every single day(or week as they call it), you can't skip weeks!).
Every time I play I feel like I'm beating my head endlessly against a wall. It is very stressful to have to guess so much about what to expect or plan for in a given dungeon because more often than not, the random number generator will completely screw you over. In fact, everything about this game seems to be random, everything from what heroes you get to pick from after the introduction to how much and of what types of loot you aquire in a dungeon. Everything from what happens to your heroes during combat to what groups of enemies you run into. Even the effects of stress on your heroes is random. Sometimes you just get an amusing phobia, other times your hero gets a debilitating debuff that will have a real, sometimes crippling effect in game.
I understand that the developers wanted to create a challenging game, I understand that they wanted to create a game that elicits a sense of crushing hopelessness. They very much succeeded, perhaps they succeeded a too well. The randomness coupled with the micromanagment this game expects just overwhelms and frustrates me to the point where I simply don't enjoy myself and enjoyment is the whole reason one plays a video game.
I'd play the hell out of this game if they just allowed us to customize the difficulty, but the only way to make the game less difficult is through a mod that alters the game files and that mod doesn't really do much to lessen the cruelty built into this game.

My actual review though, if you at the very least liked XCOM EU/EW then you will feel the same about XCOM2, it's more of the same - but not for one second in a negative way.
Firaxis has done what it seems that no other dev can do these days and managed to remove what was bad, and improved on what was good from the previous iteration, XCOM2 is by no means a revolutionary new experience or idea, but simply a very polished upgrade, and if you're into turn based thrillrides that includes the whole spectrum of negative emotions - again, somehow, not in a negative way. - then this is most certainly for you.
The story is in my opinion a lot better than it was in EU/EW, still that being said; it could really have been a lot longer than it was, there's an achievement for finishing the game really fast on Commander+ difficulty and at first I thought "How?" but after soon starting my third playthrough I no longer have my doubts, only about actual survival.
The new mechanics of sneaking and setting up ambushes is fun to no end, you can do incredibly brutal overwatch ambushes (That execute in sequence now, and not all at once on one enemy.) now that just make you jump in your seat and giggle like the sad manchild you are. If your soldiers land their shots that is. [Git gud] The new classes are warped versions of the previous ones, but they're spectacular and playing a very agressive Ranger makes my manparts shift.
The game also looks really good, I've seen a lot of people complain about performance issues (That I'm sure will be adressed.) but I've had none and I'm playing on a mid-to-high-tier LAPTOP (Screw you /vg/) (GTX770M/2.4GHX 16GB RAM) on Ultra settings, loadtimes are at about a minute or so for missions and give me the occasional sputter in FPS but after that it's smooth sailing.
Negatively though, if you're a - Muh immurshun - kinda person you should be aware that the very same graphical glitches and oddities are still in the sequel, floating debris, soldiers taking aim not-at-all-at-what-you're-aiming-at and shooting out of their necks and the occasional very odd spawn point of pods, although the latter could be in part to the randomly generated maps, which is a fantastic improvement due to the fact that this time around you never know for sure where a pod will be and all maps will in the end feel familiar but never the same.
So, should you buy it?
If you loved EU/EW you will love this one, I'm sure of it.
If you liked EU/EW, you will most likely feel the same about XCOM2, but maybe you should wait for a sale or until you've got money to burn.
If you hated EU/EW, then what are you even doing here? It's the same, but much better, for those who enjoy the core of XCOM EU/EW.
If you disliked that, you will, sadly, dislike this great game too.

EDIT: There has been some misunderstanding stemming from my opening lines. The key point is that the development team behind the game has tuned the game to target a unique player experience that makes Darkest Dungeon unique and rewarding to play.
Darkest Dungeon isn't just another RPG, and I don't blame anyone for approaching it like one. There are plenty of on-screen cues and tips that guide the player, but for players who have played since the beginnings of Early Access, it's easy to overlook them and not start from square one. Players who are completely new to Darkest Dungeon are likely to heed these in-game suggestions and warnings at face value, and may have a better experience as a result.
I do not think the game is perfect, but it's pretty great and worth your time and money to experience.
There are a lot of negative reviews gaining traction with a severe misunderstanding of the way the game is currently intended to be played, and I want to shed some light on why this game is actually AMAZING, and has CHANGED over time to become BETTER. There aren't going to be ANY story spoilers here, just basic mechanics--more or less just the hamlet's features and how they interact with the core gameplay.
It is a difficult game, and it is an RPG. When the going gets tough in a traditional RPG, there's usually a couple ways to deal with that: grinding monsters for money, gear, and experience, completing sidequests, and so on.
In Darkest Dungeon, you have a variety of resources at your disposal.
You have Heirlooms (used to upgrade your Hamlet facilities), you have Gold (required to use your Hamlet facilities and stock up on supplies before an expedition), you have trinkets(a way of customizing your heroes and buffing their abilities), and you have the Heroes themselves--a renewable resource. Each of your heroes has their own set of resources and attributes: Resolve Level, Sanity, Quirks, Disease, Equipment, and Spells.
Here's the part where people go wrong: they try to min-max, they try to save their heroes, they'll make sure their heroes have all of their gear and spells upgraded before sending them out. This game restricts your resources far too hard for that, and makes your gains from doing so miniscule--you do make a profit, but its tiny and takes a long time. The profit margin of gold on maintaining perfectly geared heroes and sending them on optimal missions is almost non-existent, and players see this as being the 'grindfest' as they slowly approach the endgame, often trying to circumvent this game's difficult mechanics (popular Steam guides are guilty of this!) by 'grinding it out,' using strategies such as suicide-gold runs (which are a time sink in and of themselves, adding to the grind illusion)...
Those narrow margins of profit? The seemingly unending grind? Its a losing strategy that was made worse by the developers to discourage that style of play, and those players aren't adjusting their gameplay.
Progression through this game's intense difficulty isn't made by grinding out the perfect heroes, its by taking what you have and going for it. You're going to fail. You're going to lose heroes. You're going to hit brickwalls. But you're going to learn the absolute limits of every hero, the absolute limits of your style of play, and you'll push those limits. Your profit margins will double or triple as you start to play every situation perfectly, taking advantage of good luck and avoiding the bad luck from having an opportunity to take you down.
Brute-forcing a grind through the game is technically possible. But you shouldn't do it.
This game wants you to face its depths head-on, and as soon as you do, it drags you further down and constricts you even more.
When you finally get it though--when you finally make your way through the most difficult sequences of the game--there is very little more rewarding. It doesn't happen because you grind. It doesn't happen because you followed a strategy--it happens because you got dealt a hand of cards and made the absolute best of it.

This game starts off great but becomes borderline unplayable mid- to late game.
Artstyle, narration and atmosphere are pretty much 10/10 and the first maybe 10-20 hours of the game (though I'm generally a slow player) are a ton of fun. The dungeons are hard but also rewarding and interesting, your characters grow or die, develop their individual traits and get on your nerves with their quirks (in a good way).
The fun ends once your characters level up to the higher quest tiers. There are level 1, 3, 5 and with the Darkest Dungeon presumably level 6 quests. Once your characters reach the respective level, they refuse to go on lower level quests, which generally would be fine. The problem is that the difficulty scaling from one tier to the other is insane and level ups themselves don't do anything for the characters. You will therefore be massively "underleveled", if you haven't been extremely successfull in upgrading your guild and your smithy and getting loads of money to then actually upgrade your heroes. You can then either send your best guys on runs they're not prepared for and either see them die or spend most of the money you get on their recovery OR you grind ridiculously small rewards with new arrivals.
A lot of people are complaining about the RNG but I honestly didn't have any issues with that. Yes, sometimes it can feel unfair and your party gets ♥♥♥♥ed because of a series of terrible rolls, but other times you'll see them destroy a boss with him barely being able to get a hit in, so... yeah, that's RNG for you.
What really ruins this game for me is its insane difficulty scaling and artificially stretched length. I have started a couple of runs and have never gotten past the level 3 quests. To be fair, I can be pretty bad at video games but it seems like a lot of people are having similar experiences, so I don't think it's just entirely that.
The game still has a lot of good elements and I can't say I completely advice people not to buy it. It's just that actually finishing it is an enormous pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and I'd reckon most people won't actually see the end if they're not extremely determined and have a very high tolerance for frustration.
Makes for great streams though.

UPDATE: Since I wrote this review, Firaxis has fixed a lot of the bugs, and the modding community has come out with a myriad of ways to make the game more balanced and fun. I finished the vanilla version of the game after a patch dropped that allowed me to proceed, and did enjoy myself quite a bit. Switching my recommendation to "YES", now that you can play the game you wanted, instead of the buggy mess that was first released.
ORGINAL REVIEW (Feb 2016):
I honestly want to know what version of the game the highlighted reviewers above were playing. I would swear it's different from the one that got downloaded to my system.
Serious balance issues, buggy, performance is really below where it should be. With graphics turned all the way down, or all the way up, it still chugs and lags so bad on my system that I can hardly play. Delivers the same frustrations as the previous game with little of the novelty. Enemy reinforcements are frequent and punishing, even on lower difficulty levels. Overpowered enemy units show up early in campaign and make some required missions nearly impossible to complete. You will run out of soldiers frequently through attrition or when everybody is in sickbay for a month.
EVERYTHING has a time limit, or a timer, or a progress bar, or some hidden event that will push you to the brink of ruin. Tactics and choice are truly very limited, the concealment idea is nice but poorly executed- how can I put my units where I want them AND engage overwatch, etc when there are so many detection zones, and I have just a handful of turns to complete my objective? No time really given to let you learn things, I guess the idea is you will fail in your first game somewhere, give up, and play again with all your "training" in place.
Apparently there is a "correct" tech path to take in order to go very far in the game- don't deviate or you will quickly be outmatched and outgunned to the point of abandoning the game. DONT USE MODS UNTIL EVERYTHING IS PATCHED- they seem to corrupt your savegames :). That was a fun discovery.
This could all be done in a fun way, but it isn't. If XCom was Civ 5, XCom 2 is Beyond Earth. Somebody at Firaxis needs to sit down and figure out what they used to do right, and do that, instead of whatever they're doing now.
Definitely not worth full price. DLC is dangled out there in Summer (really?), so if you want to finish the game and then wait four months to play it again WITH A NEW HAT, grab it now. Knowing what I do now, I'd pick it up when it's on sale and patched, or when mods are out that help balance the game and make it enjoyable.

I will review this game in context of it being a free game. Black Squad just released today and has already diplayed itself as a strong competitor for other f2p fps games. It's style reminds me that of cod black ops with a few spices from csgo. It's game mechanics make it very fast paced and fun combat. You can shoot while jumping, running, or just hold and angle to have a great time. It's casual yet quick combat makes it very fun if you like f2p games.
I'm going to cover some features that I believe the devs should keep through early access. I of course found some issues that need to be covered as well.
First off the the gameplay and weapons. Every gun is awesome and fun to use. I like that I can screw around with my favorite guns that has cool optics and features. The experience is so badass that I can't help but scratch my head over which gun I want to use. Combat is fun and engaging. Only complaint is even on my NA servers, I'm seeing people where populated lobbies contain 80% or more with users clocking over 100ping. This is very frustrating at times as they do have an advatage peeking and killing me even when I have 30-40 ping. I expect that they will change their netcode in the future is have a more desireable experience for low ping and punish higher ping users.
The common question of a f2p game is that is it really a pay2win game? Thankfully it is not showing any signs of one so far. All guns are permanat which I absolutely love. Grenades are timed for some reason which I find a little strange. They limit how many you can use ingame which is brilliant. I applaud them for that. You may also buy skins of the same guns which do not alter any stats so they are purely cosmetic. The only black sheep is the medal shop. I'm hoping this pay wall area doesn't become the meta for this game to start being pay2win. So far I haven't seen any game breaking guns in this area so I plead to the devs to never do so.
My biggest complaint is the graphics. I cannot use my native resolution 1920x1080 for some reason. The highest I can use is 1440x1050. This is pretty annoying but I hope this is fixed soon.
One last minor complaint is the voice acting and some dialog. I strongly suggest you hire a proper translator because some of the english lines are off by a mile. Add some more diversity to the ingame dialog as well. "Tactical reload! Tactical reload! Tactical reload! Tactical reload!" gets a bit irritating over time.
Overall I love what the game has to offer for being free. If you want a very fun game to play and your wallet is looking really shy, this game is definately worth the shot. I doubt I personally will play it more as I prefer more of my paid games over this. I only pray that the development of this game doesn't take a dark turn. Keep it up guys.
Thanks for reading.

Performance wise, I was having some choppy fps here and there until I changed the AA from MSAA to FXAA. It's been smooth and solid ever since. I have everything else set to max and am running it on a GTX 960 w/ 4gb of ram.
Gameplay wise, It's a fantastic sequel to Enemy Unknown. If you enjoyed the previous entry in the Xcom series, and are looking for a challenge, here it is. In the previous game players would delay doing certain things so they could have more time do research and build up their squads. That's no longer an option, Sitting still and doing nothing will ensure failure.
On top of that, the enemies have all evolved. Sectoids have been spliced with humans and now have more HP and psionic abilities, Thin Men are now snakes that can grab you from across the map and slowly squeeze the life out of you, Chrysallids have more HP, are armored, move faster, and poison you with one hit.  You know what that poison does? makes your people turn into a giant pod that spawns more Chrsyallids.
The skill trees have changed a bit too, but for the most part it's the same. Rangers, formerly assault now carry swords and can dash across the map and cut people down. they start with this instead of run and gun, but you can get run and gun later in addition. Feels very similar anyways. Weapon mods like scopes are permanently added to guns, and can't be shared or removed, only replaced.
In conclusion I would recommend this game to anyone who likes tactical turn based games. I'd highly recommend it to people who liked the previous game.

BY FAR, THE MOST BUGGED GAME EVER PLAYED
Played hours and hours on PC and even more on PS4.
Great concept, free roaming, huge world, unfortunately is EXTREMELY bugged, and even after official and custom patches, it remains riddled with problems.
Optimized by some blind guys, no matter how powerful your rig will be , you will run into absurd frame drops,  100 fps one second and unplayable the next one.
Broken quests, clumsy npcs, clumsy character movements.
Fallout 4 is actually a pre-alpha that has been released as gold version.
Therefore the main reason why you will die or fail missions in this game is because you get stuck somewhere, you fall through solid floors, npc shoots you through walls, or even for no reason at all...
Fortunately there are plenty of mods to minimize the horrible game engine and mechanics problems, but the fact that there are all these third party fixing speaks loud about the game overall quality.
After around 150 mods installed, my game is starting to be playable and entertaining, basically a whole new game made by the community.
To give you an example of the "skills" of Bethesda developers (which are completely random amatorials from my point of view) , texture packs from common modders, kids mainly, are visually far better than vanilla ones, AND will make the game run with double frames per second too...
The only real plus about Bethesda games are the stories and atmosphere they create in their games (they should write books and make movies maybe ?), and even more importantly the possibility to have these games completely re-worked by common people, to have them run decently.
Years are passing by, and the overall quality of Bethesda games remain very low at vanilla.
They want to develop big games, with big concepts, filled with things to do, and in the end these games are frequently  just a big mess of broken mechanics left to the community to be fixed.
Fallout 4 anyway is, hands down, the worst of the Fallout franchise.
A special mention goes to:
Whoever designed the editor tools for this game.
He/she should be incarcerated for crimes against humanity or, at the very least, kept far away from any software related company for life.
Do I reccomend the purchase of this game ?
No, but if you want to do it, equip yourself with lot of patience, because you are in for many frustrating gaming moments.

"Infinite Universe, Infinite Possibilities..."
10 / 10

To start this off, I understand the hate.
You need to upgrade town buildings to upgrade your heroes. To do this, you need to collect "heirlooms" from dungeons, using up your precious inventory space which could be used for gold, or food.
Now the other problem is that heroes refuse to go on dungeons that are two or more levels below them. This creates the problem where heroes want to do high level dungeons, but are severly under-geared for those dungeons, making them worthless. New players who don't know this information will be screwed, since they won't know to prioritize deeds and crests. I personally haven't run into this problem, but I've been playing for a while and know what to do.
With that out of the way, I love this game. It's a lot like old tabletop RPGs, where you are always at the mercy of dice rolls. Sometimes, you'll keep rolling high, destroying everything in the dungeon. Sometimes you'll just roll low, stabbing yourself in the foot repeatedly. But it's not what the dice rolls give you. It's what you do with those. Will you keep pushing on, praying that your heroes will finish this last room battle alive and (mostly) unbroken? Or do you retreat, and let them live to fight another day.
Speaking of unbroken, your heroes need to deal with stress. In every other game, your heroes deal with zombies and skeletons and demons, without blinking an eye. In Darkest Dungeon, your heroes deal with them as well, but your heroes are all just regular people. Sometimes seeing walking bones and mushroom people and being vomited on by pig people is too much to bear, and they will go insane. Or they might become virtuous and carry the party to victory. Of course, you can relieve the stress in town, for a price of course.
Crawling through dungeons in this game isn't anything too special. You walk from room to room by hallways, and in those hallways you'll find different interactable objects. You can use consumables on them to get loot, or relieve stress, or combat buffs etc. In rooms there are sometimes chests, or more powerful interactable objects, but they are always guarded by enemies. Each dungeon is randomly generated of course, and there are eight different bosses for you to fight.
Combat in this game is interesting. Moves can only be used from certain positions in your party, and can only target certain postions in the enemy party. Therefore, party composition and positioning is very important to a successful run. Enemies, on death, drop corpses that stop others from moving towards your party, and into more targetable positions. People were adverse to this at first, but I enjoy it. It adds another layer of strategy to battles. Really, battles are kind of hard to describe succinctly, as there is a lot going on.
Finally the aesthetics of this game. I love the artstyle, it really sets this game apart from others. You can see from the pictures what I mean. The sound design is also incredible. Every single attack has a distinct sound for when it hits, and when it misses. The music is lovely. I constantly have the Warrens battle theme stuck in my head. But most of all, there is a narrator voiced by Wayne June. Look him up, as he has an awesome voice, and I couldn't imagine this game without him.
Final thoughts? I'd give it a 9/10. There are some glaring issues with the deed grind and heroes levelling too quickly. But this game is just so much god damn fun, that I can't help but feel pumped up when I kill an enemy and hear "PRESS THIS ADVANTAGE. GIVE THEM NO QUARTER".
TL;DR if you like tabletop RPGs and dice rolls, this game is for you. If you don't, I would still suggest picking it up. I never played D&D before picking this game up (when it first released in Early Access in February of 2015) and I adore this game.
P.S. Watch out for spiders, they throughly enjoy ♥♥♥♥ing your day up.
P.S.S Remember that overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer.

You were allowed up to have up to 100 mist each day which would be used for crafting, elevator fees to get to missions, and revives. As much as I complained about the old system to my friends, it still had a nice balance to the f2p model, since if you went into the dungeons others can help pay the fees and other players can revive teamates by giving them part of their health. This idea allowed for more cooperative play with others and made the community more nice. Even though some may argue the idea that restrcting time played was a bad thing, I think it was a good idea, especially considering that those who play games for hours on end eventually get bored of playing them. Think of how the horrible android and ios games keep others playing, because they don't tire out the game the whole day through charging towards beating it. Besides if you liked the game and wated to continue playing for as much as one wants you could support the devs and pay real life money for energy (ingame currency) for as low as 2 bucks!

I don't really like this type of game; I normally play 3D open world RPGs or action games but I do like some good lore. I wasn't even going to play it until I listened to a podcast with one of the creators (Chris Bourassa). 10 minutes in I was sold. The amount of passion, talent, and knowledge going into this game is incredible. The art is stunning, the gameplay is seamless, the systems are interesting and fun, the characters are imaginative and diverse (their commentary helps make the time spent between dungeons feel more like interacting with your fellow adventurers and less like menu hopping). And of course, the writing is masterful. They've found the perfect blend of familiar monster horror dungeon mythos and their own creepy classic folk tale twist. In tone and visuals, it feels like a book written collectively by Edgar Allen Poe, H.P. Lovecraft, Bram Stoker, and Mary Shelley (but less forgiving for the reader) and the darkly humorous narration adds a literary element that ties all of those strings together. The difficulty of the game itself is well-balanced and gives very real consequences to your decisions, making the experience that much more rewarding.
So buy the game and support the developers, we need teams like this making games.
Thank you, Red Hook. You guys are awesome.

-My biggest complaint and the primary reason I keep quitting out of frustration, is how you constantly have to micromanage your expenses. You get gold from completing expeditions and you must spend that gold on upgrading the abilities and gear for your heroes, providing leasure activities for your heroes so they don't go bat♥♥♥♥♥♥insane and on consumable items used during expeditions.
Not that big of a deal, the problem for me is specifically in reguard to the consumable items, you have to do some major guess work(or clever statistical calculation) in order to make sure you have enough to keep your party from dying horribly or going insane. Now, I am not a statistician so I cannot do the clever statistical calculating to make sure I have enough to stay alive and even if I could, there's a very serious randomness to the entire game. Even if you math out the most efficient use of your gold to gear to abilities to leasure to items, you still will probably get screwed over during the expedition. Perhaps you didn't pack enough food to feed your heroes(yes you have to feed your heroes at least a couple times, if not more, during an expedition) and the RNG didn't provide you with food as treasure, or perhaps you didn't pack enough torches so you run out of torches and your heroes either go totally bonkers or die horribly in battle. Maybe you couldn't afford enough bandages and that damn pig creature just kept making your heroes bleed and they died of blood loss. Maybe you couldn't afford enough antivenom to heal the poison(or blight as it's called) that the mushroom mutants constantly cause. There is no item to heal the huge stress that the undead inflict to your heroes, the only time you can do that is when you spend gold and keep the hero out of the following expedition(and you must attempt an expedition every single day(or week as they call it), you can't skip weeks!).
Every time I play I feel like I'm beating my head endlessly against a wall. It is very stressful to have to guess so much about what to expect or plan for in a given dungeon because more often than not, the random number generator will completely screw you over. In fact, everything about this game seems to be random, everything from what heroes you get to pick from after the introduction to how much and of what types of loot you aquire in a dungeon. Everything from what happens to your heroes during combat to what groups of enemies you run into. Even the effects of stress on your heroes is random. Sometimes you just get an amusing phobia, other times your hero gets a debilitating debuff that will have a real, sometimes crippling effect in game.
I understand that the developers wanted to create a challenging game, I understand that they wanted to create a game that elicits a sense of crushing hopelessness. They very much succeeded, perhaps they succeeded a too well. The randomness coupled with the micromanagment this game expects just overwhelms and frustrates me to the point where I simply don't enjoy myself and enjoyment is the whole reason one plays a video game.
I'd play the hell out of this game if they just allowed us to customize the difficulty, but the only way to make the game less difficult is through a mod that alters the game files and that mod doesn't really do much to lessen the cruelty built into this game.

XCOM 2, like it's predecessor, is a top down, turn based, tactical game. In the previous game, XCOM: Enemy Unknown (EU from here on out), earth got invaded by aliens and it was up to the XCOM organization to put the invasion to a stop. In XCOM:EU, you were the defending force of Earth. You control a squad of 4-6 units and take turns. Missions varied from saving civilians, defusing a bomb, taking out all enemy forces etc. Besides the turn based gameplay there is also your base of operations you had to run. Constructing certain facilities to do research and build items and weapons to further aid you in the battle against the aliens.
XCOM 2 keeps the core of XCOM:EU intact. However, the roles have reversed this time. The aliens have taken over earth completely and there is little left of the XCOM organization. You, the Commander, have been captured and the first mission (which also serves as the tutorial mission) revolves around freeing you so you can get back to work. Once that is done, it's time to get into the real game. You are taken to the new base of operation: The Avenger. A large airborne ship. From here you construct various facilities which aid you in alien research, constructing weapons, searching out rebels, start your mission etc. To research and build you need currency which comes in the form of supplies. You get supplies every month from rebels you made contact with and you can get some from clearing debris in your base when expanding, from missions or searching out points of interest on the map.
Once you go on a mission, you get a squad of soldiers. They all start out as rookies and level up as you put them to use in the field. The amound of kills and damage done increases their XP (more for kills) which promotes the soldiers. They randomly are assigned to a class. Leveling up even further, provides 2 skills and you can only pick one. The classes are:
Ranger: Can focus on stealth and has a blade which deals a nice amount of damage.
Sharpshooter: The sniper class, useful from long distances for great cover of the rest of team.
Grenadier: The Heavy class, outfitted with a minigun and a grenade launcher, they are a formidable force.
Specialist: Has a drone which can focus on offense or defense and healing depending on you skill choice.
Then there is the Psi-Operative which can only be obtained by building a Psi Lab and let a rookie soldier undergo some training. They use Psionic powers to buff allies or damage foes. Psi is a power some aliens posess. They use it to reanimate the dead, send your troops into a panic attack or mind control them.
Once you get into the field you start to notice the difference between XCOM: EU and XCOM 2 immediately. There are a lot of missions which have a turn counter: Retrieve this object within 8 turns, extract this VIP within 10 turns, etc. Where you could take your time in most of the missions in XCOM: EU, you are now pressured to move and stay on top of your game. This makes the game feel way more hectic and makes your every move count. This fits the game perfectly since you are the force that is invading this time instead of defending. This also results into aliens having a more relaxed stance. They are often guarding the objectives. This adds a new feature called concealment. You start most missions with your team concealed. The aliens don't know you are there and you can set up an ambush before alarming them. It's a very useful phase. Once concealment is broken only the ranger (when picked the right skill) is able to conceal itself again.
I think XCOM 2 is a perfect sequel to a great game. The pressure puts you in front of some difficult decisions. It will force you to do things you wouldn't do in the previous game. Time is pushing you to think outside the box which result in table flipping frustration or a surprised look on your face and a feeling of happines that your team made it out despite the horrible situation you were in. I will certainly have a great time with this game. The amount of modification you can make to the game is also stunningly large. It's a very open game so expect a ton of mods. It's also easy to change certain options yourself through some lines of text. Simply look it up and change the values to tinker with certain mechanichs and tweak them to your liking.
The only 2 cons in this game is how it runs. on an i5 3570k @ 4.3GHZ, GTX970, 8GB RAM, W10, I have some weird frame drops from time to time no matter on what settings I play. And the aim percentage can really spark some frustration. A guy right in front of you? 50% chance to hit!? What? 99% chance to hit and still miss.... That's some table flipping, keyboard smashing stuff right there. Luckily it tends to keep it to a minimum (for me at least).
To be honest, Fallout 4 is a great game & Franchise, but the graphics aren't that good for the Steam Version. -5/10

Ever seen a soldier smash in a laser-grid window, shattering glas everywhere? You will see that a lot in XCOM 2.
Displayed information for actions is occasionally incorrect or doesn't contain any info at all (like missing damage/percentage numbers). Occasionally Explosives that clearly outline the enemey units as affected, don't to jack to them.
The action cam repeatedly shows a black screen with red bars - so you won't even directly see what the ADVENT soldier right in front of you is doing. And when you can see something, the soldiers usually hold the guns to each others heads or walk though obstacles to shoot at the enemy. Same stuff they did in Enemy Unknown.
Also, the mission occasionally lets stuff go boom next to your squad for no discernable reason, killing off your dudes without you ever having a chance to have prevented it.
It's now all bad though. On the plus side, you can customize soldiers and weapons and even augment most of them with mods. Loads of maps are randomized now, so you won't likely see the same levels multiple times. And you have concealment now. Which basically means you don't have to creep ahead one space at a time as enemies are now unware of you until you get the drop on them. But don't worry, after that first fight, you get right back on your knees and crawl at a snails pace again as Enemy Pods are the way to go in the sequel as well...
But you have turn limits on most missions now, so the game acitvely FORCES you to run into Pods head on as you wouldn't be able to complete the missions elsewise.

So, I am not a fan.

UPDATE: Since I wrote this review, Firaxis has fixed a lot of the bugs, and the modding community has come out with a myriad of ways to make the game more balanced and fun. I finished the vanilla version of the game after a patch dropped that allowed me to proceed, and did enjoy myself quite a bit. Switching my recommendation to "YES", now that you can play the game you wanted, instead of the buggy mess that was first released.
ORGINAL REVIEW (Feb 2016):
I honestly want to know what version of the game the highlighted reviewers above were playing. I would swear it's different from the one that got downloaded to my system.
Serious balance issues, buggy, performance is really below where it should be. With graphics turned all the way down, or all the way up, it still chugs and lags so bad on my system that I can hardly play. Delivers the same frustrations as the previous game with little of the novelty. Enemy reinforcements are frequent and punishing, even on lower difficulty levels. Overpowered enemy units show up early in campaign and make some required missions nearly impossible to complete. You will run out of soldiers frequently through attrition or when everybody is in sickbay for a month.
EVERYTHING has a time limit, or a timer, or a progress bar, or some hidden event that will push you to the brink of ruin. Tactics and choice are truly very limited, the concealment idea is nice but poorly executed- how can I put my units where I want them AND engage overwatch, etc when there are so many detection zones, and I have just a handful of turns to complete my objective? No time really given to let you learn things, I guess the idea is you will fail in your first game somewhere, give up, and play again with all your "training" in place.
Apparently there is a "correct" tech path to take in order to go very far in the game- don't deviate or you will quickly be outmatched and outgunned to the point of abandoning the game. DONT USE MODS UNTIL EVERYTHING IS PATCHED- they seem to corrupt your savegames :). That was a fun discovery.
This could all be done in a fun way, but it isn't. If XCom was Civ 5, XCom 2 is Beyond Earth. Somebody at Firaxis needs to sit down and figure out what they used to do right, and do that, instead of whatever they're doing now.
Definitely not worth full price. DLC is dangled out there in Summer (really?), so if you want to finish the game and then wait four months to play it again WITH A NEW HAT, grab it now. Knowing what I do now, I'd pick it up when it's on sale and patched, or when mods are out that help balance the game and make it enjoyable.
