War... war never changes
Or at least thats the game's motto, as per Bethesda. But by no means whatsoever is that true of this game. They changed just about everything that made fallout...fallout.
Enjoy the lore and history of the fallout universe? Too bad, everything has been retconned and contradicted to the point of being almost unrecognisable from original lore.
Enjoy the rugged and unique aesthetic of the fallout universe? Too bad, nearly everything has been remade into cartoony almost steampunk-esque nonsense that doesn't mesh with the other games.
Enjoy the fleshed out characters and factions of the fallout series? Too bad, none of the characters or factions are really that fleshed out or have clear motives and are just kind of there to give you things to shoot.
Enjoy the choices and freedom to role play of the fallout series? Too bad, there are no real, distinct, consequential choices, and your character is already predetermined to be a generic hero.
Enjoy the raw and clever writing, satire, and commentary of the fallout series? Too bad, the game is void of raw subject mattter or clever writing and is EXTREMELY embellished.
Its a decent, but only decent open-world adventure game like Far Cry or something, and a good modding platform I suppose. The game relies too heavily on new ideas to Bethesda that are not executed well enought to actually carry the game, while also stripping all the essentials to the foundation of a fallout game or even a role playing game. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy the game. Heck, I have almost 600 hours at the time of writing. But its a disappointment and in some ways a betrayal.
I have a feeling the game may have been screwed over by a mixture of Bethesda wanting to experiment and the suits in the company pushing the game to be more accessible and profitable. I just wish they did that with a new series instead of violating Fallout with this installation in the series. Experimentation is really a very good process in game development and I am not against it at all, but this wasn't the right time or the right series to totally redefine. Like I said, if they wanted to do new things, they should have defined a new series instead of redefining an old one. Does anything but sequels even come out anymore? I know Bethesda has the creativity to make something else, they didn't have to hijack fallout.
Like has been said before, go play Fallout New Vegas instead. It holds up even after seven years and is incredibly fun and well-executed. Some things like gunplay and graphics are undeniably dated, but you get used to it, even learn to love it. Fingers crossed that Bethesda signs Obsidian to make another Fallout on this engine, that would truly be something.

A review of this game can be summed up by my most recent experience with it:
I was in a dungeon with 2 camps, very large dungeon.  Everything was going perfectly, but about 80% of the way through, I ran out of food and blight potions.  My team was also slowly wearing down from accumulated fights with blight and bleed casting enemies.  I got to the very end of the dungeon, and my team was on its last legs.  I had to explore just one more room and win the fight, and I get the big quest reward.
I had someone at death's door, and they just fell into a blight in the final hallway.  I had two choices:  Abandon the long quest to preserve that party member, or press on and risk death from the blight.
I chose to press on, and paid a heavy price.  He was a member of my primary party, a Jester to be exact.  While he wasn't the most important member, I rely on Jesters for stress relief so I don't have to do it in town.
People who write negative reviews for this game don't understand how it's played.  This isn't a game where you get attached to characters.  It's a game where every single hero, regardless of investment in him, is expendable for greater reward.  You'll grow attachments to some and yes, you will lose some, which will take a few duneons to get someone of that same class back up there, but the main game is about an entire roster of heroes and the upgrades and services available to them.
The big downside to this game isn't the difficulty, it's that it gets a little bit repetitive and there's not a lot of depth.  The addiction to this game drags me in to do a quest or two every now and then, but the repetitiveness of it makes it so I've had enough after that, and not really any motivation to sit and play for long hours.
But if you're a roguelike masochist and love to be punished by games and believe in the saying "losing is fun," then you'll probably enjoy this game.

Darkest Dungeon stands out with its hauntingly beautiful art design and its harsh difficulty, but it also has some serious flaws.
The game's most apparent problem is that its qualities as a strategic game are vastly limited by the factor of randomness.
For someone who hasn't played Darkest Dungeon yet, it is most easily demonstrated by the Occultist, a hero class which has arguably the strongest healing spell in the game - and at the same time the weakest: his "Wyrd Reconstruction" replenishes 0-15 hit points. In the final dungeon I once got a crit for around 60 HP (which is about the total health of heroes of the highest experience level), while the next turn the spell would produce a flat zero. Needless to say that this may not only cause major aggravation for players, but also instantly turn the tide in a battle.
The Occultist's healing spell might be an extreme example, but the game is full of such annoyances: a lucky streak of dice throws will carry you through almost any encounter, while your favourite hero may just fall prey to the blades of some weak foes just because they happened to roll a few crits in a row.
The number of enemies and explorable regions is rather limited, but the game manages to hide this fairly well - at first. Unfortunately, the game drags out massively once your heroes start to reach the higher experience tiers, which culminates with reaching the final stage - the eponymous Darkest Dungeon:  even after a successful expedition, your characters will refuse to brave this lair again, and you will have to raise a new batch.
What is wrong with that, one may ask?
In short, the game punishes you for being successful, and this is not the only time it does so: fleeing from a losing battle instead of dying is often a worse option than letting your characters die, as time in the hamlet (i.e. the nexus point of your expeditions) will not advance - meaning that you might have to send your already tattered party in battle again instead of getting new recruits. IWhile frightened heroes unwilling to return to a horrible dungeon may make sense from the perspective of the story, gameplay-wise it is pure stupidity: of course you'll want to have exact replacements for your A-Team, so this achieves nothing but forcing the player to invest time in meaningless grinding.
Despite all its balance issues and the horrible drag towards the endgame, I would still recommend Darkest Dungeon - it may have some rough edges, but I still enjoyed playing it at large. It may however be wise to wait for a few future patches before buying it, as the game could certainly be much better with some rebalancing.

I played a lot of Starbound two/three years ago and I just started playing (a lot) of it recently. So here is my two cents about it.
At its core, Starbound is pretty much Minecraft in 2D and in space. It's an open-world survival sandbox game that lets you visit 18 quintillions star systems (lol). The big feature here is the fact that you can visit 80-90% of the planets in these systems. Each one has a dominant biom, a level of threat and specific day and night cycle. Each planet can spawn a variety of monsters mostly procedurally created. And each planet has its own set of, backgrounds trees, vines, dirt etc. Each planet can also be inhabited by one of the races you can start the game as. All these races have two sets of NPCs you can meet on the planets: an aggressive one that you encounter mostly in procedurally generated dungeons, and a friendly one that will give you small quests, that you meet in villages.
-Regrets from the past:
I would say that the early access builds were heavier on the procedurally generated content and sandbox gameplay. The planets were not systematically inhabited, the dungeons where less identical, and there were not much interactions with NPCs. Now you have the pre-made monsters that you can find in systems far away from each other which is bizarre, the main quest that "forces" you to find and analyse each civilization (even when you already met them before the main quest arrives at that point) and it's almost impossible to find a planet without at least one camp with NPCs in it.
That last one in particular is kind of jarring because part of the fun of exploring in Starbound came from the unknown; you were not sure you would find something, so finding something was a big deal in itself. Now it's more about finding exactly what you are searching for, not about finding something at all.
-Enjoyment from the present:
On the other hand, I think the team did a pretty good job balancing the light traditional rpg aspect of the game with the sandbox game-design of the beginning. The content is still plethoric and wether you are more about trading goods to make money, farming (litterally), exploring, building, Starbound is a great playground for all of this. The main-story, though a bit (to be nice) shallow makes for nice little pouches of more linear gameplay from time to time, with dungeons and bosses made by the devs themselves; even though I don't like the fact that you can't mine in these dungeon, they can give an enjoyable break. They also bring in more backstory for the races which can help for roleplayers that like the scientific part of the game. In that type of game, I love to make a huge base where I catalog all my findings; with a gigantic greenhouse for the trees and plants, a zoo for the monsters, a museum of natural history...and I can do that in that game. One thing that I really enjoy in that regard is the excavation mini-game that lets you find a variety of fossils you can then put in you own little display stands. I always get a kick out of finding one while mining, because you can't know what you will find until you get it out of the wall. And getting it out of the wall is not always easy. It adds to the exploration and gives me one more reason to go down caverns to mine stuff.
And the interactions with NPCs, that can accompany you in your ship or that you can put in colony, or that you can work for in some (admittedly) mmoesque fetching and killing quests, all these helps having interest in the lore of the game. If it isn't a priority for you, you don't have to do it  except for the very start of the game that will give you a couple of interesting abilities. Once you have your double jump, your morph-ball and dash, you can do whatever you want. I think the main quest is overall a good addition for people who need a bit of focus to evolve and start doing stuff in that type of open games. And since it isn't required at all (weapons and upgrades can be found anywhere else while exploring) it's not much of a problem for the rest of the players.
So the game still is really system heavy, and roleplaying comes both from the player's realm of possibilities and from the traditional, surely a bit bland, narrative and social interactive part of the game.
Oh and did I mention that you can capture the unique creatures of the game and use them in combat? That's pretty fun too!
TL;DR
Though I don't know if I love Starbound now for the exact same reasons I loved it when I first played it two years ago, I still thinks it's a fantastic game. A couple of things bothers me in the released game, it still is my favorite Minecraft-like game. There is so much to do I just lose track of time, and playing it with friends is an absolute blast. I whole-heartedly recommand it!

I love the entire XCOM and UFO franchise. I played all previous games, I preordered XCOM2, I was waiting like for the goddamn christmas.
But no. I'm disappointed, I'm very disappointed.
Because it's not strategy right now. It's "rush forward and wish for lucky shot or reload latest save if you miss".
Timers, timers everywhere. Every mission crucial for the plot is on timer, main quest on strategic map is on timer, but that's not the problem. Problem is that these timers are set up so you have no tactical or strategical options other that mindlessly rushing forward. Only other choise is defeat from running out of time. You can't outflank enemies, you can't set up ambushes, you can't walk around them because CLOCK IS TICKING.
Why? First XCOM didn't have those (yeah, terror misions, but they make sense. It's either aliens kill everyone around, or you manage to kill aliens faster, no issue here). Technically you could take all the time you wanted. But the aliens were also growing and advancing, they were attacking, they were getting new units and new toys. There was no clock but the pressure was there all the time. That's the difference between enjoying the challenge the games gives you and just being worried seeing diminishing turn counter. I want a game where I have to worry about long term decisions and about outsmarting enemies on tactical level, not go Call of Duty dakka-dakka style.
Then there is performance issues. It's not even about FPS drops. New games always have issues like that, they will probably patch it soon.
But visible animation issues? You can see where animation of soldier running ends and animation of sticking to cover begins. And after you complete some action the game just waits for several seconds like it is thinking what to do now. Or my soldiers lands a shot at the enemy even if he is looking in COMPLETELY different direction.
THOSE WERE ALL PRESENT IN FIRST XCOM. HOW MANY YEARS YOU HAD TO CORRECT THOSE?
And this feature of editing how your soldiers look and behave? You advertised this as best thing since sliced bread. It's just few options more than first XCOM. And what logic allows you to edit those only after soldier get higher ranks?
If I had to rate the game.
As a standalone game, not looking at the title - 6/10.
Big game, lot of content, good graphics, complex, yet annoying mechanics. Still much better than most other on the market.
As one of the XCOM series - 2/10. A disgrace to to the brand for reasons mentioned above.

This game is simply amazing. This sandbox game has attempted to go over an obstacle that most sandbox games suffer from, the feeling that you have nothing left to do. And let me just say, the developers have done this beautifully, instead leaving you thinking of what to do next. The best thing about this game is that the developers are willing to listen to suggestions from the community, something as a game developer you need to take advantage of.  If you enjoy games like Minecraft and Terraria, you NEED to check out this game.

So, the first twenty hours were pretty great. The art is the best thing ever, the writing is good, the combat very thoughtfully created and fun and nailbiting to play through.
However, I lost interested and stopped playing after a while. The end objective is never really clarified (presumably, a tentacled Lovecraftian monster awaits in the Darkest Dungeon, the purpose is never really spelled out. You need to close a portal by... getting your guys to a high enough level to handle entering the final dungeon area? There's not even a "gather four keys" subplot.)  The game presumes the existence of repetive grinds is enough to pull you forward, but it's not really. Contrary to what you might think, there's not much RPG elements. You don't come across randomized loot, or make key decisions in how to permanently upgrading a character. What would make me want to grind up to level five or six?
The game sells itself as a game where character death is frequent and permanent, but this is kind of misleading. You have an inexhaustable supply of heroes, you can rename them, recolor them, respec them at any time, and when they die, you can take their items off their corpse. So if your favorite Grave Robber dies, nothing happens other than you having to spend three hours leveling another Grave Robber to your current highest level and spending gold to upgrade them. Without limited numbers of heroes, or unique characters, death felt pretty meaningless. Why not just have them recuperate for three campaign turns? Or, maybe better yet, make the campaign itself more rougue-like, and shorter, so you have to make more consequential decisions on who to recruit.
In the end, I'm really pumped for Darkest Dungeon 2. This game felt complete, but it felt like the prelude to a much more fun sequal -- it needed more plot, more environments, more hallway variations, some tweaks to the gameplay. And it needs support to make the late game involving, with more rewards with the harder difficulty.

I've put a lot of time into the game, almost as much as I have Factorio (That might not be true much longer, my hours just keep going up for that game.) and is just as addictive. Everything about it is great, especially the way Nelson handled the premium thing. Some games make their game totally P2W and that a terrible way to treat a community, especially if your game is getting a decent amount of media attention. Other games try and minimize the bonus, and hurt their income by just using cosmetic suits. Nelson took those ideas and had an entirely new one (At least not one I have seen before.), he added the cosmetic stuff and added a game mode, Gold, which makes the game easier and less gritty. Now, only people with gold can use this, so nobody is ever at a disadvantage. The simple way he did this so perfectly astounds me. Nelson is a developer that others should look at for ideas. Ok 30 hours of gaming later, I have one finished campaign. Overall opinion? Holy hell this is a GREAT sequel!!!
What you WON'T get... Fighters, Skyranger Upgrades, UFO Intercepts, Gene tweaked soldiers, Tanks/Vehicles, MEC Troopers, EXALT, or The same 6 maps over and over and over again.
What WILL you get? PLOT! XCOM 2 actually has a story to the campaign, the mechanics of it can make some elements frustrating, but overall this is a VAST improvement. Did you hate Meld timers in EW? Well brace yourself, XCOM 2 makes a LOT of use of timers, albeit much more generous ones. Aside from the elements mentioned, almost everything else traditional about "XCOM" and similar titles is here, and generally improved upon. Soldier customization, for example, goes beyond what most MMOs will allow you to do with your character.
The game creates all the maps you play on right before loading so you will never see the exact same map twice. While awesome, this feature seems to result in load times that are just a hair on the longish side for modern games. Maps still generally take less than 1 minute to load and, imo, its WELL worth it to have different maps EACH mission. Which brings me to the next "issue" with XCOM 2, if you want to nitpick, this thing pushes your cpu cores and gpu FAR FAR harder than its predecessor ever dreamt of. I don't know if this is due to sloppy optimization or just that they crammed that much more under the hood, but my GTX 650ti still handled the game rather well, if on some seriously low end settings. Interestingly, the game still looks better than the previous title even on these lower settings.
One thing I am on the fence about is that, in this title, you are pushed to move. Your enemy is working on its ultimate 'I win' project and it cannot be stopped by you during game play, only delayed. This removes the option to go everywhere, do all the side missions, and finish the "Alien Menace" at your whim. While, at times, it can seem that the enemy will finish long before you are prepared, 2K was very good about balancing out pacing, and your ability to reduce their progress. For example: At one point they were nearly 3/4 the way finished before I did several major missions back to back and pushed them back to zero. As normal, once you begin the endgame you no longer have access to most of the game features and you have to make do with your soldiers as they are with whatever gear you have in your inventory. On the upside, if you are REALLY short handed for some reason, critical missions will allow you to bring wounded soldiers.
Construction order is a bit trickier in this title than others in the same vein, I nearly screwed myself by ignoring the radio room while pursuing psionic tech and soldiers. You WILL spend a lot more time thinking out the consequences of what to build and when. The developers did a fabulous job of simulating the difference between XCOM as a super-black op with funding from around the globe versus XCOM as a barely existent guerrilla force only marginally better equipped than a militia.
There are tons and tons of little things in this game that make it an absolutely fantastic TBS, and entry into the XCOM franchise. The addition of a story and some very RPG elements bring the game to the next level, especially when combined with the amazingly robust modding tools 2K provided. The possibilities are mind blowing, and if the mod authors embrace this title, its one we will still be playing 10 years from now and enjoying new stories and user made content. Obviously this also lends itself to giving 2K a huge opportunity for tons of DLC which can help keep the game fresh, interesting and new for years to come.
This one is definitely a "must own" for fans of TBS or XCOM.

What is it?
Somehow Bethesda combined the Simulation, FPS, and RPG genres with a dash of anxiety all into one package in Fallout 4.  In the world of Fallout 4, a Nuclear war has left the inhabitants of Boston Massachusetts to fend for themselves without a central government.  In this post-apocalyptic part of the Commonwealth, you play the role of a widowed husband or wife, who’s looking for their child Shaun after being frozen in a Vault for a couple hundred years.
You’ll be building, crafting, shooting and surviving.
The Good and the Ugly.
Giving EA a run for their money, Fallout 4 introduced an entire new mechanic to the Fallout series: Settlements; I’d argue this game is ALL about Settlements. Think of it like a dumbed down Sims, but instead of using Simoleons to purchase buildings and furniture, you’re gathering supplies all across the Commonwealth from the remnants of Boston like Hot Plates, Hacksaws, and more.  Basically you’re going to MacGyver the crap out of this.  Each Settlement has several needs: Food, Water, Defense, and Beds; and they can populated by Settlers, and Companions (companions accompany you in-game & have side stories).  Anyone who likes Simulation games will accidently carry themselves into the wee early-morning building….and building until you run out of resources and are forced back into the wasteland to scavenge more.
The Settlement system can feel pretty beta at times.  Even with all the expansions added, furniture and structures are limited in number.  Placement of objects can be odd as there isn’t always a snap system to have things completely symmetric like walls (Gaps are never a good thing in any scenario).  It’s not always totally clear where an object goes after you choose to “store” it.  Almost none of the placeable objects have tooltips, and the ones that do are not descriptive enough; for example, it’s almost impossible to tell what Bathtubs do unless you googled it, or you’re a Brahim whisperer.  All objects that can be built always have a “just went through nuclear holocaust” aesthetic, even though you just built it from scratch.  Why am I building a brand new glass door, if the glass is going to be broken already?  Who broke that glass?  WE JUST BUILT IT!
Despite all its flaws, I wouldn’t be playing Fallout 4 as much as I have been without Settlements.  They provide a way to get away from all the gloom and doom and reinstate that “life flourishes in the darkness” sorta thing.  The game feels alive in your settlements, and you can customize a house of your own, for your settlers, heck even Dogmeat’s.  Fast-traveling into one of your Settlements can trigger a dynamic event that usually pitt you and your comrades against Gunmen, Ghouls, and others. Tl;dr
This game is incredible and you’re getting a lot for a great price
If you liked the last game, buy it.
If you had issues with the last game, this probably fixes them.
It’s the future and this game is on sale and you’ve heard about but never tried it? Definitely give it a shot. It’s a pretty unique experience that you can have a lot of fun with.
I love strategy games that are super randomized for maximum replayability and this games does that with a lot of heart.
This game isn’t made to make money it’s made for the fans.
The Review:
I really don’t say this lightly. Xcom 2 is a 10/10 for me
And to explain that I need to briefly mention it’s predecessor. Xcom, EU was quite a good game because above all else it had a lot of heart. There isn’t really another game that gets you quite as attached to your characters the way xcom does. And the system around that is great, you personalize them and they can die and be gone forever for you to mourn.
It’s really because of this that anyone’s experience with xcom is going to be positive.
So the reason xcom 2 is classified as ‘perfect’ is because they improve every element of the previous game for the better and they went extremely above and beyond in those improvements.
That’s not to say this game doesn’t have flaws, but relative to the mount of things it does well it vastly outweighs them. For one I would say this game has a stiff learning curve, and for a game that punishes mistakes that’s kind of hard to balance. If I hadn’t been paying a ton of attention to this game pre launch it would’ve been rough. Although, sometimes the learning curve can be a cool experience (see below)
The Core Gameplay:
The way the grand strategy aspects are set up this time are fantastic and a very obvious step up from the original. It’s also decently intuitive when you get the hang of it it’s fun to try and master it. And the core combat is addicting and satisfying. It really has a great flow of mentally preparing yourself for a mission, dropping in as well equipped as you can be and then playing a complex game of chess against the aliens and then just barely scraping out of there and allowing yourself to relax at base. If you do poorly on a mission it’s significant and you have to push on. But if you complete a mission flawlessly it’s deeply satisfying.
I think one of the most important aspects for this game as a strategy game is pacing. If you play a lot of other strategy games you know this is a very hard thing to get right because they have to balance difficulty with mistakes/losses and power upgrades you can unlock to counter the difficulty. I know plenty of games where the early game is extremely challenging in a very fun way but the middle and late game is stupidly easy. And let me say: this game NAILS it’s pacing. The initial challenge of the early game feels great and the transition to the mid game is just as good. My experience was how I slowly felt like I was getting outgunned as the aliens got stronger and my odds felt slimmer but once I finally got some better armor and weapons researched and invested in them on top of some proving grounds and it helped level the playing field and further gave me more abilities/counters and there’s just a great amount of depth in general.
This game is really friendly for mods! So what that means is there is a huge opportunity for free content that totally changes things or just to do what you want. And mods is weird to consider for a review but in this case it adds to the list of “great things the developer did to make the game better for the community” as opposed to a game where the base game is subpar but mods can make astounding.
Sound/Graphics:
Of the many things, one thing I really enjoy about xcom 2 is the sound design and art design. The guns and explosions just sound so good and everything looks so cool which really helps make it a game you can play a lot. Like I just love hearing the conventional weapons and the magnetic guns fire. Also dynamic destruction and ragdolls again make every encounter fun and never get old.
The aesthetic and personalization of this game is great as well. The memorial and character biographies and just seeing your units move around the base in the variety of locations is something I love a lot.
This is again not something that really goes in a review but the dlc for this game is also very well done. It’s just a simple season pass pack that’s $15-$20 and is just going to add a bit more for a small price. And when a game is already this good it’s always nice to have a few new additions. In a world where so many games are shipped short and the dlc is the rest of the package it’s nice to be able to purchase the dlc for this game and just feel like I’m supporting a great developer.
Story/Lore:
The game is filled with lore that adds a great amount of depth and nuance if you want it. It can’t be said enough but the setting for this game being “you lost the first game because that game was hard as hell” is really unique and on top of that the way it’s built into the story is great. You find remnants of what xcom could’ve been in little story bits. “This is an old ruined xcom base, you search through the files and find data about old autopsies of what appears to be a smaller sectoid, ect…” I really enjoy this callback to the first game, it’s a really indescribable feeling, you know what they were building to, and trying to do but it just never happened and you have to make do with what you have.
The story is good. There’s something to enjoy about a game that isn’t trying to build to some twist like “the aliens were the good guys the whole time! :O” it’s just a straightforward story that’s slightly melodramatic in a fun way. And that type of intelligent simplicity is good for a game that’s replayable because you’re not sitting there going “oh, here’s the part where I get betrayed by this character even though this time I can totally see it coming.”
Personal Experience:
I really enjoy the spirit of this game in regards to the learning curve. Not to be a save scummer but if I miss click or stumble myself into the worst situation imagineable that will lose the mission I’ll reload. But when mistakes happen authentically I'll keep them.
Here’s a little excerpt of one of the coolest and cinematic missions I ever undertook.
When I first fought a codex it was on the first blacksite mission. Hit me with that psionic bubble and it disabled my weapons and I was already outnumbered and being pinned down by a turret with one squad member poisoned. So instead of moving my two units hit with the bubble, not knowing what it did, i reloaded and covered my squad. And low and behold that bubble exploded and blew out half of a building taking half of my squad with it. I sat there in shock but on one hand this was a complicated battle and their sacrifice saved everyone else. So now I’m on a blacksite mission with three soldiers one on the verge of death. I find the final squad and engage in a very cautious skirmish and I made a move for some cover and an advent trooper I couldn’t see that was in overwatch took the shot and killed that unit. Down to two men, a sectoid panicked one of my guys, down to 1 guy with one shot. He takes it, hits and saves his friends life. We secure the target and go for extraction. Advent reinforcements drop in. We overwatch and take out a trooper but there’s too many. I look at the evac zone and both of my guys can make it one square inside. We book it and I evac my troops. That story wasn’t scripted, it happened on it’s own. Now in my eyes those two soldiers are like brothers and one of the soldiers who died in the psionic explosion was a member of he original xcom project. It was heavy stuff.

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic game, however I cannot recommend it to everybody. To truly play Darkest Dungeon you must be prepared to be flogged, punished and beaten to a pulp by the game and it's harsh rules. I cannot recommend Darkest Dungeon to everybody, because not everybody is a flagellant who revels in abuse and hardship, who can withstand the stress and push on with their resolve tested and steadfast but be wary, as your great ancestor says triumphant pride precipitates a dizzying fall.
A big part of Darkest Dungeon, and another reason why I cannot recommend it to everybody, is that you must learn harshly from your mistakes and correct them in future endeavors. Not everybody has the stubbornness, not everybody can get over a setback, because after all failure tests the mettle of heart, brain and body but heart most of all. I consider myself masochistic enough to enjoy this game but even I have had moments of quiet contemplation wondering whether it really was worth it to continue.
There is another component of Darkest Dungeon which will shy a lot of weaker-willed people away. Luck. I don't consider myself a gambler, and I don't get thrills from playing the numbers, so personally, I'm not a huge fan of the way that luck is used in Darkest Dungeon. If you are not prepared to take risks, to compromise for chance and to expect the worst Darkest Dungeon is going to walk all over you. Almost literally every factor in the entire game is dictated by a roll of the dice and dice being the fickle ivory cuboids that they are, have no allegiance. One dungeon you might roll full sixes with a great layout and constant critical hits but in another, snake eyes.
Now that I have outlined what makes this game challenging I would like to address the other reviews for Darkest Dungeon. You may be confused when you see the amount of negative reviews in the helpful section. I don't want to say that they're salty and that the people who vote them as helpful are salty, but what I will say is that many of them call for a rebalance patch, quite often on the grounds that the game used to be easier, now it's harder or it's just difficult or unreasonable or a grindfest and therefore not fun. Personally I don't believe that darkest dungeon is meant to be fun, at least not to everybody. Darkest Dungeon is meant to be a challenge, an obstacle to overcome something to work at. The game is far from impossible and if you lack the mettle, courage and perserverance to withstand the effort to triumph, you need to try harder and learn from your mistakes before slapping a "boo-hoo I failed and had to restart but I refuse to learn from my mistakes and improve" negative review on it
TLDR: The game isn't meant to be fun for everybody get over yourself and realize not every game is tailor made to your preferred difficulty cap before you post a heavily opinionated review that doesn't help anybody understand jack.
Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic, hellish experience which will push you to your limits and beyond, but be warned that it is not for everybody, as the Old Road will take you to Hell, but in that gaping abyss, you will find your redemption. So, steel yourself, and remember, there can be no bravery without madness, because truly, this is the Darkest Dungeon
Pros

I'm not going to tell you what Darkest Dungeon is about in terms of gameplay, since that's something that you can easily learn from the store page, of course. I just want to express my conclusions on the game after beating it.
It's wonderful, really, especially if you love Lovecraft like I do. The overall aesthetic, the sound design, the narrative, everything looks great and polished. Combat feels very satisfying and has you literally scream in joy and terror in front of the screen. It's awesome. There's a ton of content too, it took me more than 70 hours to beat the game (though it's also very possible to do it in a much shorter time).
But this can be quite a stressful experience aswell, not just for your heroes but for you, the player. While I found most of the campaign to be very enjoyable, the endgame really killed most of my enthusiasm and almost got me to the point of giving up playing to just watch the ending on YouTube. This is because the game gets very grindy during the final quests: the Darkest Dungeon is a pretty rough place, and it will probably kill many of your heroes. And unless you send legendary heroes, your party will be dead long before it can explore the dungeon enough to give a clear notion of how the various mobs and bosses fight. And remember that there can be no retreat from that place without at least one dead hero.
The grinding aspect kicks in when you realize that you don't have the legendary heroes you need for a particular quest and that you have to train new ones up to level six in order to get a single chance to succeed. Even if you win a Darkest Dungeon quest, the survivors will permanently refuse to embark on the following ones, thus becoming useless.
Yet the game does actually provide you with some hints so that you can immediately guess which heroes you should bring in a particular quest in the Dungeon. (let's imagine that you are tasked with killing a boss, and that maybe the name of said boss can help you plan your party composition before you start the mission...)
But since I was too dumb to notice such hints, I finally decided to use a guide to beat the last missions of the game. I guess I'm just not that good with this kind of games, I can't come up with particularly good strategies in terms of party composition, so that my chances of victory often depend on RNG and luck. Plus, this is not Dark Souls or Super Meat Boy, you WILL be punished even though you don't deserve it. Many have criticized the importance of RNG in Darkest Dungeon, but it's a necessary element in a game that wants you to feel stressed whenever your heroes do.
That said, I did beat the game with default difficulty options: you can toggle off some mechanics in order to make your experience less frustrating if you feel you can't stand the overall difficulty of the game. You'll probably be labelled a "casual" from hardcore players and you won't be given a particular achievement when you beat the game, but who cares. Your heroes will go crazy during the adventure, make sure you don't. The fact that you are given an option to customize the overall difficulty of the experience is the main reason why I would recommend Darkest Dungeon to anyone, even those who are not familiar with the genre. It's probably still going to hit you hard even in "casual mode" but, as the game tells you, there can be no victory without madness.
EDIT (12 March 2016): the Antiquarian Update solved most of the issues I had with the endgame. So most of what I said above about grinding should no longer be of concern. Great job, developers!

What is it?
Somehow Bethesda combined the Simulation, FPS, and RPG genres with a dash of anxiety all into one package in Fallout 4.  In the world of Fallout 4, a Nuclear war has left the inhabitants of Boston Massachusetts to fend for themselves without a central government.  In this post-apocalyptic part of the Commonwealth, you play the role of a widowed husband or wife, who’s looking for their child Shaun after being frozen in a Vault for a couple hundred years.
You’ll be building, crafting, shooting and surviving.
The Good and the Ugly.
Giving EA a run for their money, Fallout 4 introduced an entire new mechanic to the Fallout series: Settlements; I’d argue this game is ALL about Settlements. Think of it like a dumbed down Sims, but instead of using Simoleons to purchase buildings and furniture, you’re gathering supplies all across the Commonwealth from the remnants of Boston like Hot Plates, Hacksaws, and more.  Basically you’re going to MacGyver the crap out of this.  Each Settlement has several needs: Food, Water, Defense, and Beds; and they can populated by Settlers, and Companions (companions accompany you in-game & have side stories).  Anyone who likes Simulation games will accidently carry themselves into the wee early-morning building….and building until you run out of resources and are forced back into the wasteland to scavenge more.
The Settlement system can feel pretty beta at times.  Even with all the expansions added, furniture and structures are limited in number.  Placement of objects can be odd as there isn’t always a snap system to have things completely symmetric like walls (Gaps are never a good thing in any scenario).  It’s not always totally clear where an object goes after you choose to “store” it.  Almost none of the placeable objects have tooltips, and the ones that do are not descriptive enough; for example, it’s almost impossible to tell what Bathtubs do unless you googled it, or you’re a Brahim whisperer.  All objects that can be built always have a “just went through nuclear holocaust” aesthetic, even though you just built it from scratch.  Why am I building a brand new glass door, if the glass is going to be broken already?  Who broke that glass?  WE JUST BUILT IT!
Despite all its flaws, I wouldn’t be playing Fallout 4 as much as I have been without Settlements.  They provide a way to get away from all the gloom and doom and reinstate that “life flourishes in the darkness” sorta thing.  The game feels alive in your settlements, and you can customize a house of your own, for your settlers, heck even Dogmeat’s.  Fast-traveling into one of your Settlements can trigger a dynamic event that usually pitt you and your comrades against Gunmen, Ghouls, and others.  It’s very rewarding, and literally having the shirt off of someone’s back come straight to your door is very useful. (You can loot those em up’)
Love it or hate it, Settlements are what makes Fallout 4 a unique first person shooter and role playing game & definitely worth investing in if you’re a fan of those genres.  Simulation lovers beware, all the kinks haven’t been worked out yet; Fallout 4 is a ginormous game & maybe a little too big for it’s own good (tons of things I haven’t even mentioned yet, like Power Armor)  however it may be worth checking out.  You may just end up loving it like I did!

This game is really a FPS, when given "decisions" of RPG games, the outcome is usually solved by killing all the bad guys.  Unlike the previous Fallout games where good and evil are blurred and lets you make decisions, this game simply has you killing everybody and everything to finish each quest.
Overall, I still had lots of fun with the game.  It really is a FPS game set in the Fallout universe, but it really doesn't play like the RPG of it's predicessors.

First let's get the 1st elephant in the room out the way: this game is not fully optimized atm. And why should it be? Considering that there are litterally millions of possible pc combinations to build for, no game will be 100% optimized right out the gates unless its a "simple" game.
Second elephant which everyone and their mother is complaining about currantly. Timed missions. First of all, yes, a majority of the missions you will be in will have them. HOWEVER! The majority of these timers are for a portion of the mission. For example:
VIP extraction = entire mission
hack/secure/destroy terminal = timed until primary objective complete OR after objective and you need to escape
Story missions = Varies
every other mission type = no timer
The saddest part about all these complaints? It's from people who A: want to use XCOM 1 turtle force tactics and B: people who didn't pay attention to the main plot.
*******Story (no spoilers)*****
20 years after the events of XCOM 1. Earth has fallen under the control of the invaders. The XCOM project is now a shell of its former self, a guerilla warfare unit fight alongside the last of the human resistance. There is no council, there is no army, no air force... mearly a handful of underequiped soldiers, scientist, and engineers fighting for survival. Most of humanity has been moved to massive cities spanning entire swaths of territory. The aliens control all forms of mass transit, and mass propaganda promotes paranoia and self-reporting. Times are dark for humanities future.
***What I liked***
****Cons****
****Summary****
In short, XCOM 2 takes the majority of the tactics and strategies you learned from the first game, shoves them down the toilet, and makes you start from the begining. The story makes sense, the gameplay fits the story, and the challenge at higher difficulties teaches you the meaning of tears and pain.
All in all I have to give XCOM 2 a solid 9/10 which will easily get 10/10 once its a tad bit more optimized.

I originally had this game thumbs down in protest over the rather glitchy release.  But I am a die-hard XCOM and Long War fan.  So I kept at it trying to fix the game on my end.
It is done and it was worth it.  If you are an XCOM fan, then GET THIS GAME!  I'll skip the rah rah and just give you the skinny on the performance and how you can prep for a glitch free start.  Learn from me!
1.  the game is NOT optimized very well.  Fact.
So..  a.  Don't expect to run it at particularly high specs.  Turn on the little Steam FPS tracker and tweak the settings till you get the rate you like.  Humans can't see faster than 30fps, but since it reports a running average, shoot for at least 50-60 to minimize frame drops.  You may have to turn off some things that make you sad unless your card is uber.  (I am on GeForce 660, so it doesn't have to be)
b.  It will run HOT!  If you don't have a temp monitor then go into the cabinet and maximize the cooling.  Clean it, raise it off carpets, point a room fan at it..  all the tricks.  You'll know its too hot if you get sound glitches that lead to hard freezes.
c.  Wait for patch.  There will be one, every game gets one.  Unfortunately.
2.  the game is tougher than XCOM: EW.  The mechanics are also a little different.  Swallow your pride and start at least one difficulty setting lower than you would for EW/EU.  You can always call me a wuss after pwning the first several missions and increase it.  I won't mind.
3.  Get you some mods!  I don't mean game change mods at least not at first.  But check out the mod community with lots of neat stuff like camera tweaks, some things from the Long War folks, and some new countries.  You can also load a ton of nerf mods (but don't!).. try lower difficulty first.  I mean, you don't expect the aliens to just give the Earth back, do you?  That being said if you think there is something terrible unfair, odds are someone has tweaked it already.
4. Kill aliens.
Very happy to change my review and accepting a good amount or responsibility.  Sorry?  Sheesh XCOM, stop teaching me so hard.

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic game, however I cannot recommend it to everybody. To truly play Darkest Dungeon you must be prepared to be flogged, punished and beaten to a pulp by the game and it's harsh rules. I cannot recommend Darkest Dungeon to everybody, because not everybody is a flagellant who revels in abuse and hardship, who can withstand the stress and push on with their resolve tested and steadfast but be wary, as your great ancestor says triumphant pride precipitates a dizzying fall.
A big part of Darkest Dungeon, and another reason why I cannot recommend it to everybody, is that you must learn harshly from your mistakes and correct them in future endeavors. Not everybody has the stubbornness, not everybody can get over a setback, because after all failure tests the mettle of heart, brain and body but heart most of all. I consider myself masochistic enough to enjoy this game but even I have had moments of quiet contemplation wondering whether it really was worth it to continue.
There is another component of Darkest Dungeon which will shy a lot of weaker-willed people away. Luck. I don't consider myself a gambler, and I don't get thrills from playing the numbers, so personally, I'm not a huge fan of the way that luck is used in Darkest Dungeon. If you are not prepared to take risks, to compromise for chance and to expect the worst Darkest Dungeon is going to walk all over you. Almost literally every factor in the entire game is dictated by a roll of the dice and dice being the fickle ivory cuboids that they are, have no allegiance. One dungeon you might roll full sixes with a great layout and constant critical hits but in another, snake eyes.
Now that I have outlined what makes this game challenging I would like to address the other reviews for Darkest Dungeon. You may be confused when you see the amount of negative reviews in the helpful section. I don't want to say that they're salty and that the people who vote them as helpful are salty, but what I will say is that many of them call for a rebalance patch, quite often on the grounds that the game used to be easier, now it's harder or it's just difficult or unreasonable or a grindfest and therefore not fun. Personally I don't believe that darkest dungeon is meant to be fun, at least not to everybody. Darkest Dungeon is meant to be a challenge, an obstacle to overcome something to work at. The game is far from impossible and if you lack the mettle, courage and perserverance to withstand the effort to triumph, you need to try harder and learn from your mistakes before slapping a "boo-hoo I failed and had to restart but I refuse to learn from my mistakes and improve" negative review on it
TLDR: The game isn't meant to be fun for everybody get over yourself and realize not every game is tailor made to your preferred difficulty cap before you post a heavily opinionated review that doesn't help anybody understand jack.
Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic, hellish experience which will push you to your limits and beyond, but be warned that it is not for everybody, as the Old Road will take you to Hell, but in that gaping abyss, you will find your redemption. So, steel yourself, and remember, there can be no bravery without madness, because truly, this is the Darkest Dungeon

I'm not going to tell you what Darkest Dungeon is about in terms of gameplay, since that's something that you can easily learn from the store page, of course. I just want to express my conclusions on the game after beating it.
It's wonderful, really, especially if you love Lovecraft like I do. The overall aesthetic, the sound design, the narrative, everything looks great and polished. Combat feels very satisfying and has you literally scream in joy and terror in front of the screen. It's awesome. There's a ton of content too, it took me more than 70 hours to beat the game (though it's also very possible to do it in a much shorter time).
But this can be quite a stressful experience aswell, not just for your heroes but for you, the player. While I found most of the campaign to be very enjoyable, the endgame really killed most of my enthusiasm and almost got me to the point of giving up playing to just watch the ending on YouTube. This is because the game gets very grindy during the final quests: the Darkest Dungeon is a pretty rough place, and it will probably kill many of your heroes. And unless you send legendary heroes, your party will be dead long before it can explore the dungeon enough to give a clear notion of how the various mobs and bosses fight. And remember that there can be no retreat from that place without at least one dead hero.
The grinding aspect kicks in when you realize that you don't have the legendary heroes you need for a particular quest and that you have to train new ones up to level six in order to get a single chance to succeed. Even if you win a Darkest Dungeon quest, the survivors will permanently refuse to embark on the following ones, thus becoming useless.
Yet the game does actually provide you with some hints so that you can immediately guess which heroes you should bring in a particular quest in the Dungeon. (let's imagine that you are tasked with killing a boss, and that maybe the name of said boss can help you plan your party composition before you start the mission...)
But since I was too dumb to notice such hints, I finally decided to use a guide to beat the last missions of the game. I guess I'm just not that good with this kind of games, I can't come up with particularly good strategies in terms of party composition, so that my chances of victory often depend on RNG and luck. Plus, this is not Dark Souls or Super Meat Boy, you WILL be punished even though you don't deserve it. Many have criticized the importance of RNG in Darkest Dungeon, but it's a necessary element in a game that wants you to feel stressed whenever your heroes do.
That said, I did beat the game with default difficulty options: you can toggle off some mechanics in order to make your experience less frustrating if you feel you can't stand the overall difficulty of the game. You'll probably be labelled a "casual" from hardcore players and you won't be given a particular achievement when you beat the game, but who cares. Your heroes will go crazy during the adventure, make sure you don't. The fact that you are given an option to customize the overall difficulty of the experience is the main reason why I would recommend Darkest Dungeon to anyone, even those who are not familiar with the genre. It's probably still going to hit you hard even in "casual mode" but, as the game tells you, there can be no victory without madness.
EDIT (12 March 2016): the Antiquarian Update solved most of the issues I had with the endgame. So most of what I said above about grinding should no longer be of concern. Great job, developers!

70% rating? Come on, this game is fantastic. I've played 10 hours of this game so far, and I haven't enjoyed a game so much in this way since, well, XCOM EU.

So if someone complains that the game is too hard, they're missing the point. I mean, jeez guys. We're liberating the human race from technologically superior aliens. Why did you expect it to be easy?
Anyways, half the fun of XCOM is when everything goes to hell and yet, somehow, you scrape together a victory.

Hey, Vsauce. Michael here. Skeletons are scary and spooky, but you know what else is? Teenagers. Their attitude, the way they dress and the music they listen to. Can you even call it music? Pff, kids these days.
But what are kids these days? What's with all the concern and what's a generation? Why do we think that coevals, groups of people of roughly the same age, act so much alike?
The sheer number of articles and papers and internet posts published daily comparing then and now, both sincerely and ironically, is astonishing. We can't seem to get enough about kids these days and just how different and awesome it was to be a kid back in the good old days. Generational labels make human history look ordered and discreet, instead of scary and messy. They also have a delightfully suspicious tendency to flatter those using them. George Orwell put it well. "Every generation imagines itself to be more intelligent than the one that went before it, and wiser than the one that comes after it." There's a name for this sentiment. Juvenoia.
Sociologist David Finkelhor coined the term. It means "an exaggerated fear about the things that influence kids these days." Juvenoia is a concerned disappointment that because of iPhones or the Internet or TV or rock music or those pesky horseless carriages the world just isn't fit for kids like it used to be. Generational conflict really has been going on for that long. After all, "honor thy [your] father and thy [your] mother" was an ancient commandant for a reason. In the 4th century BC, Aristotle remarked that youth’s mistakes are due to excess and vehemence, they think they know everything. Here's an engraving from 1627 admonishing the 'now,' compared to the ways of 'old.' In the early 1900's Romain Rolland complained that the new generation of young people were, quote, "passionately in love with pleasure and violent games, easily duped." New people and the direction society is headed in has always been seen with some disapproval. Xkcd famously collected a brief history of juicy examples.
In 1871, the Sunday Magazine published a line that may as well have been written today about texting. "Now we fire off a multitude of rapid and short notes, instead of sitting down to have a good talk over a real sheet of paper." And the Journal of Education in 1907 lamented that at a modern family gathering, silent around the fire, each individual has his head buried in his favorite magazine. The point is there's nothing new under the Sun. Not even the Sun, in fact. The Sun is believed to be a third generation star. This constant cycle of generation clashing can sometimes sound like a broken record. Are these commentaries really providing insight into the minds of future leaders or prematurely judging a coeval based on how it acts as teens? Despite the incessant concerns otherwise, the proverbial 'kids these days' seem to be better off than ever before. Drug use is down, exercising is up, math and writing proficiency have increased, crimes committed by young people have decreased, hate comments reported by children have dropped, the number of 9th to 12th graders who have been in fights has dropped, and the number of teens who fear attacks at school has dropped. But still, juvenoia persists. But why?
Well, it kinda makes sense. I mean, children are the future of a species, so it's reasonable to assume that nature would select for features in a species that cause adult members to prefer the way they were raised and distrust anything different. After all, parents, by definition, were a reproductive success for the species. They made new members. So whatever choices and influences brought them to that point must have been good enough. Any deviation from that could be a problem. So worrying about the young may have been naturally selected, just like eyes and fingers and breathing air and pooping. But here's the thing. Our brains don't accurately remember the past or apply memories fairly or rationally. That kind of thinking has a plethora of interesting causes.
First, at a social level, concerns for and about the youth are often exaggerated, because exaggerating is effective. You'll generate greater mobilization around the cause if you can convince people that we're on the cusp of a crisis here, folks. Also, our increasingly connected world means more potential contacts with people outside the family, the tribe, the neighborhood. Even though juvenile problems often involve people the juvenile already knows, stranger danger is a more powerful fear. "My kids have good friends, who are good influences, so why should I worry?" can be replaced today with "even so, people you don't know are threats, so worry."
Other reasons for juvenoia are personal and often it's not so much the world that's changed, it's you. Are drivers today really worse than they were when you were young or do you simply have new responsibilities and experience that makes you more aware of dangers that were always there? We remember the past abstractly. There just isn't enough room in our brains or a vital need for complete voracity when recalling things. Thus, we are more likely to remember the general way we felt in the past, without the petty annoyances, more salient still, for the present.
Secondly, loss aversion and the endowment effect. People perceive a loss as greater than an equal gain. In one famous study, when asked how much they would pay for a coffee mug, people gave prices that were significantly lower than what people given the mug first said they'd be willing to sell it for. This may play a role in how we value what we already have - our memories and favorites - over what's new. There's even neuroscience backing up why new stuff seems so bad to you. It's called the reminiscence bump. Storage of autobiographical memories, memories about yourself, increases during times of change. Incidentally, this is why you remember exciting things as lasting longer than they really did, but rarely remember times of boredom in detail. I've discussed before the ways in which this causes us to feel like time slowed down during particularly quick but significant events.
Anyway, adolescence and early adulthood, particularly ages 10 to 30, are major times of change. Many important things happened during those years that define your identity. So, it's no surprise that along with things that have happened recently, memories from this bump period are greater in number and more emotional. The books and songs and movies and slang words and behaviour you loved and used during this time correlates quite well with what you will, when you're older, remember the most fondly.
As we can see, juvenoia is natural. In fact, a healthy dose of it is important. There are plenty of things we should be fired up about improving. What's sometimes lost though, when explaining that juvenoia occurs in every generation is the fact that the nature of juvenoia hasn't always been the same. The generation gap of antiquity, or of the 1300's, wasn't the same as it is today. The more rapid speed of change may be one reason, but another is the appearance of a new type of creature around the turn of the last century - the teenager. The word teenager wasn't even used as a stage of life until 1922. John Savage's 'Teenage' is a fantastic read on how human society sort of accidentally invented the teenager.
You see, as factories generated new unskilled jobs, young people could acquire something neat - their own money. Suddenly, marketers realized that products could be made for the youth. They were no longer stuck with what their parents decided on. Also, the surge in immigration at the time highlighted for a new generation the view that identity wasn't something you're stuck with. It's fluid, personal, decided.

-the world. its not very great. the people in it are mostly uninteresting. the terrible dialogue system of the game doesnt help this. its hard to learn about anything and get invested. in new vegas i walked into the crimson caravan and talked with their leader for like 10 minutes and grew very interested in working with them. i talked to the people and learned how it was working there. the world felt alive. in fallout 4 you get 4 dialogue options at all times. just 2 ways of saying no one yes and a what? i cant talk to a random guy on the street and learn about how there settlement is. in new vegas this was alot easier to do. fallout 4 fumbled the ball on this one. i can't go and learn about the world at these big places. people that are there feel like they are only for shops, quests, or just space fillers. most people just have one line thats it. new vegas was much better about this. it had a lot of people to talk to who had a lot to say. not here. the world feels like paper.
The Good:
-the combat. excellent. much improved. the gunplay is great. the melee combat is so much more than skyrims was. timed blocks are awesome. weapon bashing is awesome. aiming and shooting feels awesome. explosives are great. everything here was absolutely nailed. it feels like the best bethesda combat yet. much better than fo3. and new vegas. i have a few caveats. no throwing items is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. no poision is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. they should have included that stuff. it limits gameplay styles. yet the combat feels so much better than other games ill barely forgive it. plus you can mod in that stuff anyway. with the inclusion of cratable traps from the dlc and build your own robots it makes everything fall into place much more solidly. i never want to not have this combat system now in a fallout game. i dont want the skyrim melee system for the next elder scrolls either if they make another one(which they will i guarentee. skyrim sold too well.)
-the world(atmoshphereic) while the characters and culture of the people is lacking the worlds atmosphere and visuals are not. this is the best looking fallout game. period. not just in graphics. the art direction here was fantastic. the city feels like an apoctolyptic playground. it rocks. the sandy beaches of that big island. the crowded ruins with so much going on in them to the more peaceful suberb areas. the artists deserve a big raise on this one.
- the gameplay. it is solid overall. the whole loop of exploration combat and crafting feels right. it works very well. simply as that. crafting is amazingly cool. customizing your guns is superb. crafting armor upgrades is good. it gives you alot to do. and it doesnt feel like a chore. i like that.
In conclusion:
this game is worth your time and money. but its not a fallout game. it is missing the core staples of a fallout game. that makes me sad because this game is so fun. but its a good game. very solid and worth a buy.

I'm very sad to report that XCOM 2 is just not worth the hassle as the games state is right now, below this little essay i will list observations that i've made that will be useful to know prior to purchase.
First and foremost I'm a fan of the series and both XCOM ORI and XCOM EW, but this one has, not captured the same fun elements of seemingly unending and important research, interresting buildings and the general planing between the team, the engineers and the scientists.
Engineering and the building of facilities is extremely boring, no depth or intruiguing or important bonuses to adjacent rooms. Scientists are just exponentielly decreasing, yet flat, science speed upgrades with names. (Yes somewhat similair to XCOM EWs, I just personally expected more)
The worst however is the boring absence of pre-planing required to be successful, and by the time you get anywhere with a plan, some random, un-ignorable, mission interrupts your work + plan.
Worst of all though, is the extreme amount of animation time you will be wasting watching an AI doing nothing, before and after it has done anything, for no visible reason, as if it went afk to fix a lamp mid fight.
Below here is a list of observations, one or two could be considered spoilers, but they're rather important. Also they're obvious.
*Locked 30~ Fps? Odd decision since the game runs like excremation from a donkey.
*Only outtro cinematic is 60fps, intro menu 1-48 fps (wtf?)
*Numerous performence issues, mainly removing all lighting features and filtering will fix the fps from 16 to 30, sometimes.
*Crashes upon launch, crashes upon certain actions in certain areas (shotgunning an avatar on the last mission), crashes randomly, crashes upon reloading certain load files (curropts all related MISSION autosaves and quicksaves).
Unreliable movement control, misinformative movement in certain circumstances (VIPs for instance block paths, but aren't shown to do so), On higher difficulty my own statistics show that the aim your soldiers pretend they have, is somewhere around 37% worse than it says, multiplicative.
*Artificial difficulty – over the board.
*Information needed from the f1 function in xcom Eu/EW surprisingly missing.
*General sudden missing imformation.
*Boring streamlining of stats in classes, boring abilities.
*Annoying mission interruption (constant interruptions).
*Research and building boring and linear.
*Overused Cliché “you’re the hero” ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (with a character looking directly at ‘you’ saying “you’re the one”).
*Too short (<- more of a personal thing)
*All the other "minor" glitches and buggs from XCOM EW, such as wallhacking units, glitching and shooting through them.

There are missions that are time sensitive. As in you have 10 turns to finish the mission or to complete some objective. I particullary like those. Not every mission is time critical. You will probably fail your first time mission trying to figure out stuff, just the same you will loose a soldier that encounter a Faceless for the first time ever. But overall are quite balance. Anyway, if you are a winny baby, and think that the aliens should give you infinite time before they bomb you to oblivion there is already a mod that does that.
Costumization level is ok, but I would had prefer more faces, or been able to modify the face directly, over dresses or armor patterns.
The experimental weapon system is quite nice and it force you to have a variaty of tactics. Although I'm not sure why some stuff is avaible to build from the engineer menu, and other from the advance props room. You still need to do research anyway, so is not like a filter for mid-end game props.
The first run it will give you many surprises. Mostly bad surprises in the form of something exploding in the face of your colonel, or teleporting behind the cover of the important VIP. But I guess that part of the charm of the game. I haven't find anything that is unfair for an experience player. Even after finishing the normal campaing for the first time, in a de-facto ironman run, I don't have any complain about any fail mission, or any soldier dead that it wasn't partly my fault.
Story wise is quite similar to XCOM:EU and EW. I liked the cheesy scify theme, you will like this one too. My only issue is that I would prefer for them to stop making references to future content. Or at least make it more subtle. Finally, I'm reserving my opinion about the ending until the expansions are publish.
The only bad things that I had encountered are random camera and animation glitches. They happen now and then but is not really an issue for me. There are not Beteshda level of glitches.

You might think this game is about dungeon-crawling and combat, and while combat might be a large portion of the game, these are not what turn out to be the primary focuses.
This game is essentially a management simulator. Your crew of rude dudes will undergo constant stress, which will no doubt cause them to lose their damn marbles and start doing stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥like marking themselves, skipping turns, changing their position in the group, and denying healings/buffs/order changes. These do not heal when you return from the dungeon and into town. These will stay with them until you start giving them stress treatment, like drinking, gambling, ♥♥♥♥♥-♥♥♥♥ing, prayer, meditation, or flagelation; and while they are engaged in these activities (which cost money), they will be unavailable for weapon/armor upgrades, training, and more importantly, dungeon-crawling. If you let their stress levels get too high, they'll start having heart attacks.
You can get new heroes in off the stagecoach, and you will need to keep more in your roster than just the 4 you have in a party. The thing is, these guys are level 0, so they're going to be weaker than your experienced dungeon crew. At least until you send them out and have them return successfully.
This game is brutal, and also has city management elements, but it's more "here are your buildings, upgrade them if you want." You can get better armor, upgrade skills to higher levels, etc. You will always have to make a decision between taking some new guy on a tough quest, or take the crazy/borderline crazy guy with you.
Also, why the hell are there achievements for losing or general failure? That's just idiotic.

I'm very sad to report that XCOM 2 is just not worth the hassle as the games state is right now, below this little essay i will list observations that i've made that will be useful to know prior to purchase.
First and foremost I'm a fan of the series and both XCOM ORI and XCOM EW, but this one has, not captured the same fun elements of seemingly unending and important research, interresting buildings and the general planing between the team, the engineers and the scientists.
Engineering and the building of facilities is extremely boring, no depth or intruiguing or important bonuses to adjacent rooms. Scientists are just exponentielly decreasing, yet flat, science speed upgrades with names. (Yes somewhat similair to XCOM EWs, I just personally expected more)
The worst however is the boring absence of pre-planing required to be successful, and by the time you get anywhere with a plan, some random, un-ignorable, mission interrupts your work + plan.
Worst of all though, is the extreme amount of animation time you will be wasting watching an AI doing nothing, before and after it has done anything, for no visible reason, as if it went afk to fix a lamp mid fight.
Below here is a list of observations, one or two could be considered spoilers, but they're rather important. Also they're obvious.
*Locked 30~ Fps? Odd decision since the game runs like excremation from a donkey.
*Only outtro cinematic is 60fps, intro menu 1-48 fps (wtf?)
*Numerous performence issues, mainly removing all lighting features and filtering will fix the fps from 16 to 30, sometimes.
*Crashes upon launch, crashes upon certain actions in certain areas (shotgunning an avatar on the last mission), crashes randomly, crashes upon reloading certain load files (curropts all related MISSION autosaves and quicksaves).
Unreliable movement control, misinformative movement in certain circumstances (VIPs for instance block paths, but aren't shown to do so), On higher difficulty my own statistics show that the aim your soldiers pretend they have, is somewhere around 37% worse than it says, multiplicative.
*Artificial difficulty – over the board.
*Information needed from the f1 function in xcom Eu/EW surprisingly missing.
*General sudden missing imformation.
*Boring streamlining of stats in classes, boring abilities.
*Annoying mission interruption (constant interruptions).
*Research and building boring and linear.
*Overused Cliché “you’re the hero” ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (with a character looking directly at ‘you’ saying “you’re the one”).
*Too short (<- more of a personal thing)
*All the other "minor" glitches and buggs from XCOM EW, such as wallhacking units, glitching and shooting through them.

There are missions that are time sensitive. As in you have 10 turns to finish the mission or to complete some objective. I particullary like those. Not every mission is time critical. Darkest Dungeon is a game that follows the HP Lovecraft theme and it has the writing, voice acting and art style to match it perfectly. You will have to work with the abilities (and disabilities) of the heroes you recruit in order to build a strong enough army of adventureres to conquer the Darkest Dungeon.
A lot people will say that the game has too much RNG, but the truth is the game has a lot of tactical and practical decision-making that is required for you to safely bring your band of heroes through each dungeon with minimal casualties and stress.
This is not a game where you were meant to win by default just because youu have higher stats. If you want to win, you're going to have to put some thought into your actions and decisions and that might include retreating and abandoning a dungeon run before you lose your most powerful party.
I can't relate to those who have a hard time with the game. I did my homework and haven't had a single death in my first 135 weeks of play and I've been having fun making calculated risks to see what I could get away with without sacrificing any heroes. As of writing this I'm preparing my teams to go into the final dungeon. For better or for worse, I know I'm going to have a lot of fun throwing my legendary heroes into the maw of this final challenge.
Get the game... and see you in Hell.
