XCOM 2 isn't a bad sequel.
XCOM 2 is a clumsy sequel.
Enemy Unknown showed us that this team could capture the original spirit of XCOM and refine it to appeal to the palette of XCOM fans and the world at large. This has showed us that there's a significant challenge to be faced when the systems that make up XCOM are expanded. It's unfortunate that on the surface that it looks like not much has been changed. What's even more unfortunate is those changes are what cause the game to fail hardest.
No, this isn't about timers. Okay, it's partially about timers, but it's more about a direction, a tone almost, to how the new XCOM 2 plays out. To steal a phrase, "I knew something was very wrong, just by the way it started." XCOM 2 starts with an intro that kills two squadmates one after another. Which felt a little odd, because that doesn't attach us to the characters--something XCOM is known for. The only other game that focuses this much on customization is The Sims, after all.
No, this is for the purpose of detachment. I'm convinced this scene is there to set the stage for you to feel less about the NPC's you personalize than ever before. Your squad will die, and it won't be your fault. You won't even be able to make decisions to prevent it from happening. The game will roll a die, ruin your squad, and you won't be able to stop it from happening. Again. And again. And again.  This isn't due to the core of the XCOM experience, but due to the changes that they've made to it.
For whatever reason, it seems like they want to make the XCOM experience more active. Ambushes aren't something that you have time to prepare 99% of the time. They seem to be there for the purpose of adding more movement to the maps. The new class, Ranger, is entirely close-ranged. Sharpshooters have been re-tooled with a separate pistol tree as opposed to an alternative tree for alternative sniper skills. The specialist has to be in fairly close range to make the shots that it needs to, and the grenadier has this same problem to a far greater extent. Timers make it so that you're almost always on the move and not setting up and enacting a strategy. You're more reacting. You do what you need to do--move everyone as fast as you can to one particular spot--and you deal with the rest as best you can, as you go. You can see how this makes the game feel clumsy.
You were never meant to rush forward in XCOM, because you're meant to be afraid of uncovering enemies without enough actions to counter the fortified positions that they'd instantly slip into. XCOM is about thinking about who to move, where to move them, and when. Advancing in a particular direction had to be planned carefully to avoid hanging part of your squad out to dry, spreading them too thin to take down oncoming enemies, or clumping them together so that they could be grenaded or get in each other's way. So what winds up happening is that you are forced to do what other XCOM games painfully beat into you to avoid doing: charging forward and hoping there aren't any enemies there at worst, or at best, be far more reckless than tactical.
Not only is the XCOM combat system as a whole not geared for this, but the classes aren't either, other than the Ranger. A more close-quarters combat focus on the whole is still dragged down by the traditions of each class's role that the game strives to fulfill on top of that, and each near always feels like the worst sort of hybrid--too inept to fulfill either potential option you could try to make it into. Sharpshooters fare the worst. The pistol tree was clearly them recognizing that you needed to be more mobile in the sequel and allowing players to mix in some skills to make the class have more utility. In practice, it only just keeps them from becoming dead weight, with little real value when compared to other classes.
Granted, this seems to be a function of the randomly generated maps when combined with the timers,  as plenty of missions gave me more than enough time to feel things out without making me feel the pressure of the clock. Others, however, did seem next to impossible, if not actually unwinnable with a squad that was well-geared and leveled for the stage of the game I was in. They were rarely as bad as that, and certainly in the minority, but the distribution leaves much to be desired. Even for XCOM, some parts of the game should have a sense of structure and clear progression.
It does make me feel a little better to think that while these are substantial problems, the mods to fix them will likely only need to change little. I'm not sure that adding more turns onto each timer is the right solution, as becoming too easy is as much of a problem as being too difficult, but it'd not take much to simply activate the timer only at a certain point in the mission. Skill trees can be changes and rebalanced, with new trees added or the old ones simply rebalanced. I just wish they weren't seemingly mandatory to fix some structural flaws that should have been evident early in development.
There are some improvements. This isn't a bad game, or necessarily a worse game than XCOM Enemy Unknown.
The only way XCOM could have had a less intuitive interface would be if Randy Pitchford came over to work at Firaxis, but that doesn't mean I don't appreciate what it does, so to see it revamped is satisfying. It no longer feels like diving into the depths of an inky-black ocean and feeling around for whatever is inside. It's fairly simple and straightforward. Much of that is due to clearing out the clutter of resources and the amount of things to research and build. As a result, I never felt lost or unsure of what I was doing or why. Unlike the original, I felt like I had a solid understanding of the choices I was making in advancing my tech, and I could even keep track of how to move it in a certain direction.
Research was the most impenetrable and unenjoyable part of the original XCOM to me until I played it enough to know what to do by memory, and there's a part of me that wants to give the game a gold star for fixing that alone. There's nothing quite like feeling that you can explore the game without a guide, that you'll be able to catch on and not feel like a total moron for the first three playthroughs. It's simple to plan, to take actions to bring that plan to fruition, and to adapt to changes in the situation, and all without losing much of anything other than needless complexity. That could never be said about XCOM before. Although I suppose some would say XCOM is nothing without needless complexity, I don't miss it.
Whoever was in charge of sound design on this game should win an award, as I didn't know it was possible to feel so satisfied by the way something sounds in a game. It was something I found myself continually drawn to as I babbled to my friends while playing without noticing. There's something innately right about the weight that they lend to the combat that demands to be  appreciated. It's not often you can say that something as mundane as how something sounds. You could say the same thing about the animations and the voice acting to a lesser degree. The sense of style to each never fail to make me smile with the repetitive, but always fun, odd moments of badassery by one of my squad members.
It feels like things have been streamlined and made more stylish and grandiose for the sequel, but a few missteps bring down the whole experience. This is a game that aims to expand upon its predecessor, but it all-too-often feels like the ideas that that original game was based on are still miles ahead of where the developers are trying to lead it. All the same, it isn't an bad experience, and with a few tweaks, it'll go from a 'good' experience bordering on 'great', to a 'great' experience borderling on the excellent. It's just a shame that the original XCOM will still overshadow it. Ah well. Better luck with XCOM 3, guys.

If you can accept that death, being frustrated and failing are essentially the main activities in this game it has a lot to offer.
The random number generator can (and will!) screw you over and you rarely feel like things are going well.
The experience as a whole is a lot of fun though and all that difficulty together with the art style and the awesome narrator really do a good job of drowning you in a sea of desperation full of diseases, death, traps, psychological problems and many other nice things.
The combat system and skill options are not overly complex but there is a huge amount of classes available, each with its own quirks, so this simplicity is actually quite comforting.
Unfortunately i did experience a few crashes with this game, as well as some issues with streaming. I did not see any other bugs though and fortunately the game autosaves often enough so i never felt i lost progress.
It DOES have some similarity to Dark Souls even: Unless you accept that you might fail over and over again you will have a very hard time surviving in this game, if you let go and enjoy the experience instead of looking for min maxing options you will have a lot of fun.

Hey, Vsauce. Michael here. Skeletons are scary and spooky, but you know what else is? Teenagers. Their attitude, the way they dress and the music they listen to. Can you even call it music? Pff, kids these days.
But what are kids these days? What's with all the concern and what's a generation? Why do we think that coevals, groups of people of roughly the same age, act so much alike?
The sheer number of articles and papers and internet posts published daily comparing then and now, both sincerely and ironically, is astonishing. We can't seem to get enough about kids these days and just how different and awesome it was to be a kid back in the good old days. Generational labels make human history look ordered and discreet, instead of scary and messy. They also have a delightfully suspicious tendency to flatter those using them. George Orwell put it well. "Every generation imagines itself to be more intelligent than the one that went before it, and wiser than the one that comes after it." There's a name for this sentiment. Juvenoia.
Sociologist David Finkelhor coined the term. It means "an exaggerated fear about the things that influence kids these days." Juvenoia is a concerned disappointment that because of iPhones or the Internet or TV or rock music or those pesky horseless carriages the world just isn't fit for kids like it used to be. Generational conflict really has been going on for that long. After all, "honor thy [your] father and thy [your] mother" was an ancient commandant for a reason. In the 4th century BC, Aristotle remarked that youth’s mistakes are due to excess and vehemence, they think they know everything. Here's an engraving from 1627 admonishing the 'now,' compared to the ways of 'old.' In the early 1900's Romain Rolland complained that the new generation of young people were, quote, "passionately in love with pleasure and violent games, easily duped." New people and the direction society is headed in has always been seen with some disapproval. Xkcd famously collected a brief history of juicy examples.
In 1871, the Sunday Magazine published a line that may as well have been written today about texting. "Now we fire off a multitude of rapid and short notes, instead of sitting down to have a good talk over a real sheet of paper." And the Journal of Education in 1907 lamented that at a modern family gathering, silent around the fire, each individual has his head buried in his favorite magazine. The point is there's nothing new under the Sun. Not even the Sun, in fact. The Sun is believed to be a third generation star. This constant cycle of generation clashing can sometimes sound like a broken record. Are these commentaries really providing insight into the minds of future leaders or prematurely judging a coeval based on how it acts as teens? Despite the incessant concerns otherwise, the proverbial 'kids these days' seem to be better off than ever before. Drug use is down, exercising is up, math and writing proficiency have increased, crimes committed by young people have decreased, hate comments reported by children have dropped, the number of 9th to 12th graders who have been in fights has dropped, and the number of teens who fear attacks at school has dropped. But still, juvenoia persists. But why?
Well, it kinda makes sense. I mean, children are the future of a species, so it's reasonable to assume that nature would select for features in a species that cause adult members to prefer the way they were raised and distrust anything different. After all, parents, by definition, were a reproductive success for the species. They made new members. So whatever choices and influences brought them to that point must have been good enough. Any deviation from that could be a problem. So worrying about the young may have been naturally selected, just like eyes and fingers and breathing air and pooping. But here's the thing. Our brains don't accurately remember the past or apply memories fairly or rationally. That kind of thinking has a plethora of interesting causes.
First, at a social level, concerns for and about the youth are often exaggerated, because exaggerating is effective. You'll generate greater mobilization around the cause if you can convince people that we're on the cusp of a crisis here, folks. Also, our increasingly connected world means more potential contacts with people outside the family, the tribe, the neighborhood. Even though juvenile problems often involve people the juvenile already knows, stranger danger is a more powerful fear. "My kids have good friends, who are good influences, so why should I worry?" can be replaced today with "even so, people you don't know are threats, so worry."
Other reasons for juvenoia are personal and often it's not so much the world that's changed, it's you. Are drivers today really worse than they were when you were young or do you simply have new responsibilities and experience that makes you more aware of dangers that were always there? We remember the past abstractly. There just isn't enough room in our brains or a vital need for complete voracity when recalling things. Thus, we are more likely to remember the general way we felt in the past, without the petty annoyances, more salient still, for the present.
Secondly, loss aversion and the endowment effect. People perceive a loss as greater than an equal gain. In one famous study, when asked how much they would pay for a coffee mug, people gave prices that were significantly lower than what people given the mug first said they'd be willing to sell it for. This may play a role in how we value what we already have - our memories and favorites - over what's new. There's even neuroscience backing up why new stuff seems so bad to you. It's called the reminiscence bump. Storage of autobiographical memories, memories about yourself, increases during times of change. Incidentally, this is why you remember exciting things as lasting longer than they really did, but rarely remember times of boredom in detail. I've discussed before the ways in which this causes us to feel like time slowed down during particularly quick but significant events.
Anyway, adolescence and early adulthood, particularly ages 10 to 30, are major times of change. Many important things happened during those years that define your identity. So, it's no surprise that along with things that have happened recently, memories from this bump period are greater in number and more emotional. The books and songs and movies and slang words and behaviour you loved and used during this time correlates quite well with what you will, when you're older, remember the most fondly.
As we can see, juvenoia is natural. In fact, a healthy dose of it is important. There are plenty of things we should be fired up about improving. What's sometimes lost though, when explaining that juvenoia occurs in every generation is the fact that the nature of juvenoia hasn't always been the same. The generation gap of antiquity, or of the 1300's, wasn't the same as it is today. The more rapid speed of change may be one reason, but another is the appearance of a new type of creature around the turn of the last century - the teenager. The word teenager wasn't even used as a stage of life until 1922. John Savage's 'Teenage' is a fantastic read on how human society sort of accidentally invented the teenager.
You see, as factories generated new unskilled jobs, young people could acquire something neat - their own money. Suddenly, marketers realized that products could be made for the youth. They were no longer stuck with what their parents decided on. Also, the surge in immigration at the time highlighted for a new generation the view that identity wasn't something you're stuck with. It's fluid, personal, decided.

Darkest Dungeon is a game that follows the HP Lovecraft theme and it has the writing, voice acting and art style to match it perfectly. You will have to work with the abilities (and disabilities) of the heroes you recruit in order to build a strong enough army of adventureres to conquer the Darkest Dungeon.
A lot people will say that the game has too much RNG, but the truth is the game has a lot of tactical and practical decision-making that is required for you to safely bring your band of heroes through each dungeon with minimal casualties and stress.
This is not a game where you were meant to win by default just because youu have higher stats. If you want to win, you're going to have to put some thought into your actions and decisions and that might include retreating and abandoning a dungeon run before you lose your most powerful party.
I can't relate to those who have a hard time with the game. I did my homework and haven't had a single death in my first 135 weeks of play and I've been having fun making calculated risks to see what I could get away with without sacrificing any heroes. As of writing this I'm preparing my teams to go into the final dungeon. For better or for worse, I know I'm going to have a lot of fun throwing my legendary heroes into the maw of this final challenge.
Get the game... and see you in Hell.

I'd like to begin by saying that this review is long overdo.  I've owned and played this game for quite some time, put a lot of hours into it as I'm sure many others have.  I'd like to break down my review by the different aspects of the game.
Gameplay - 7/10
The UI is simple enough, and the FPS style is also basic but efficient.  There's a but of a lack of actual variety to the weapon choices, the stronger gun wins, there aren't really any alternatives in shootouts other than sniping, which can be pretty fun, especially with the kill cam (which also can be extremely annoying).  Interaction with other characters is also a bit basic and at times rather cumbersome as the controls do tend to be a bit clunky.
Story - 6/10
A pretty heartfelt origin story followed by (without spoilers) a bit of a letdown twist.  Without ruining anything, the main story is kind of hollow, after following what feels like an actual storyline, you just seem to start following a series of mini quests into a very anti-climactic set of "choices" which are basically just glorified factions.  Each has their own charm and are extreme in their differences, and all seem to lead to sort of dead ends and extremely open ended gameplay.
Character interaction - 5/10
Very very bland.  The only reason I rate it as high as I did was because at the start, there is a lot of interaction when you first meet your companion choices, with the exception of one big brute who you just basicaly pick up for no reason.  But after their initial interactions and a very small amount of pointless side quests they just become some light background noise.  Even the romance is completely bland and pointless.  Just a series of one liners that change in the quick talking dialogue you can do if you want to kill 10 seconds.
Graphics - 7/10
The graphics are decent, a little unpolished, but in the higher graphics settings things can be quite beautiful even in a setting as dreary as fallout's radiated post apocalyptic world.  My main concern is with the characters.  For the most part, they are quite basic and also for the most part quite ugly.  The design of the characters seemed to be a secondary thought when in developement.
Settlements - 9/10
This is where I'm sure many will disagree with me on principle alone, but I truly did enjoy building settlements.  While I do wish there was a nicer interface and simpler method to putting it together, the concept is really quite enjoyable.  It's also nice to see just how my string of turrets and traps took down the horde of invading mutants.  While I wish there was more of a user friendly menu system or interface in general for building, it still did the trick.
Mods - 10/10
What's not to love about our modding community?  They take everything wrong with a game and make it right again (or.. just weird sometimes)
For everything wrong I've stated above, there's basically a mod for it.  Support your modders, download, upvote, donate, and if you're new to the scene, or just curious, check it out, you won't regret it!
Overall - 7/10
The overall experience of the game was pretty pleasant.  I mod heavily so the shortcomings of the vanilla version are mostly taken care of, and I get to build some fun things in my settlements.  The game is a worthy play, and if you don't go in expecting a masterpiece and want a fun sandbox shooter, have at it and play away!
Sidenote about DLC - This is where I get very, very frustrated.  The DLC for Fallout 4 is decent, but the prices for it leave a lot to be desired.  To download all of the extra content not released with the initial game, you have to pay for the game two times more over.  If you have the money go for it, but be forwarned, the prices are not equivalent to the quality of the product.

I feel like i've played enough of this game to compare it to the other fallout games.
Fallout 4 is very different from New Vegas and Fallout 3, that much goes without saying. People dislike Fallout 4 because it "dumbs downt he RPG part of the game" which is true to an extended. Perks are still there but it's the dialogue choices that people (probably) refer to. Fallout 4 consist of usually 4 choices, a straight honest one, a sarcastic one, a questioning one, and a snarky mean choice. The other fallout games revealed the lore through dialogue that consist in different checks, FO4 reveals lore through the computers that are in the game.
Another thing that Bethesda changed in this game is the power armor, see, in the previous Fallout games you needed a perk for moving in the power armor, FO4 doesn't care about that and instead gives you your first suit in about an hour into the game. However FO4 also makes the power armor a literal suit of armor, some people hate this, i personally loved it. See, the previous games the power armor was similar to...let's say Heavy Armor from Skyrim. You could put it on at any time so a lot of people had a suit of power armor and normal clothes in which to sneak in. The same people that hate this new mechanic always talked about how New Vegas was
.  That's a dumb reason to dislike a mechanic in a game. This sh*t made more sense to me, i just wished Bethesda had made a better HUD for when you're in the suit.
Now let's talk about the story, it amuses me that people talk about how FO3's story is so much better cause you can blow up Megaton and all of this other nonsense but that really doesn't impact the main story of that game. The dad of the lone wanderer simply tells you "I'm disappointed that you blew up Megaton" and nothing happens. There is no difference between what happened there and what happens in this game. Fallout New Vegas on the other hand is very different. New Vegas's story is much more complex with a lot more ramifications, also the DLC in New Vegas tie in to the story line, that's good for some but I disliked that sh*t. Let me explain why. Once you're done with the main story in FO4 and FO3 you can simply do the DLC, they're a standalone stories. Once you do the final mission for New Vegas that's it. No more DLC you can still wander the wasteland but you missed out on some great DLC (Dead Money is my favorite one).
Back to FO4's story. at the third act of the story you come to a decision on who to side with, there are basically five endings to the game, Railroad, Institute, Brotherhood, Minutemen, and Railroad + Minutemen. For me the best ending is the railroad + minutemen, because you HAVE TO destroy the other factions. There is no going around it. People b*tch about how that's so unrealistic and that you should be able to have a perfect ending that let's all the factions solve their problems by "talking it out." That's horse sh*t. Only the minutemen and railroad have a somewhat similar ideology, everyone else is pretty bad. The brotherhood is very much like a gang of raiders (Nuka World DLC companion talks about this). The institute wants to ♥♥♥♥ everyone over. The Minutemen just want to protect people, and the Railroad wants to help Synths. There really isn't some peaceful solution.
Honestly, for me, this game is a hell of a lot better than New Vegas and FO3, simply because of the mechanics and graphics. People that say that "graphics don't matter it's all in the gameplay" are idiots. Graphics do matter, you spend hours upon hours staring at the characters, watching your courier/wonderer/survivor run around the wasteland.

Darkest Dungeon was a game that came to my attention almost as soon as it came into steam. The concept seemed interesting to me and I indulged in watching a few streams and YouTube videos of the game. Turned off by the early access label I decided to withhold my purchase and buy it some other time.
Recently it came to my attention that the game had been "finished." I had seen numinous glowing reviews from critics I trust and I was convinced to make the purchase. To me the game looked like Xcom: the RPG with a dark graphic novel H.P. Lovecraft aesthetic.
I am a fan of HP's stories and the narrative to me is clearly inspired by 'The statement of Randolph Carter' and of course the classic 'The call of Cthulhu.' I even encountered a rather on the nose reference to HP's work as my rambling arbalest asked my crusader "have you ever seen a colour out of space?" Referencing the HP Lovercraft story of the same name.
I didn't even have any truck with the controversial ending (that I spoiled for myself, more on that later) it's as hopeless and grim as many a Lovecaftian tale.
The visual and sound design are excellent, The character sprites are very graphic novel-ly and well-drawn, the music is well composed and the disheartening ambiance that gets louder the darker the torch gets is a nice atmospheric touch.
These well done aspects of the game added to the exclusively positive media i had heard up to that point convinced me to buy the game. While this did not cross my mind when i first made my purchase I now remember a certain youtuber saying something along the lines of 'those people who played for 300 hours and hate it.'
This should have sent off warning signs in my head but sadly I did not research enough. I made my purchase and began playing. I did well (I think) initially and had a good time. I only lost 3 party members in 15 hours and I managed to beat 4 bosses and both the encounter bosses. I'm not exactly sure if I did anything wrong or if I was just unlucky but I started lousing, lots. Most of the time I would lose one or two level 3 party members and flee, But then I had my first party wipe, I lost one level 4, three level 5 heroes and some incredibly rare trinkets (including the drop I received of my hard won shambler fight).
Up to this point I had played the game akin to the way I play Xcom. I had named each hero after someone I know in real life and had upgraded all my heroes as much as possible in an attempt for them to stop dying. This caused my string of losses to be quite costly both emotionally and financially, I understand that I may have been playing it wrong but the way the game punishes you for losing high level heroes breaks the fun of the game for me.
Falling back on my Xcom instincts I started a new save file and started playing that. At this point my friend linked a video showing why he wouldn’t be purchasing the game after I had stated I had a good time with the first 10 to 15 hours and I realised why I would not be revisiting this game until it is significantly patched.
The game is SUPER grind focused. Not only that but the core gameplay loop is repetitive. The same missions: scout(search almost all rooms), exterminate(finish all room battles), and an item mission where you must find 3 'curios' and interact with them with 3 provided items repeat over and over.
For some reason Red Hook have padded out the game with completely unnecessary repetition and a slow progression system that will set you back HOURS of grinding a replacement hero if you are unlucky and lose even one or 2 party members.
Boss fights are repeated 2 more times at harder difficulties for seemingly no reason and the final straw was seeing what was in store for me in the final missions of the game.
One your party beats an incredibly hard level in the Darkest Dungeon they will all refuse to ever go there again forcing you to grind even more on easier levels to produce max level and well equipped heroes in order to stand a chance.
This revelation I had has killed any desire for me to play the game. I am familiar with challenging games, even ones with RNG tied to them, I beat Xcom on ironman classic.
But Darkest Dungeon is not 'challenging'. It's not really. You can’t even lose. It just takes up your time to make it feel like its challenging. If the game was shorter, had more variation in the core gameplay loop and removed unnecessary features like the 'Never Again' mechanic then I may of recommended this game.
But in its current unfairly grindy state I do not recommend. Hopefully with the alleged addition of the steam workshop soon someone may just fix the game instead of the devs.

Despite some issues of framerate and glitches, this is a fantastic expansion to the previous Firaxis XCOM. Most of what has been done to the game is possitive, and even some of the more divisive of changes, such as the inclusion of so many mission timers, are at worst minor complaints. True, it would be nice to have a few more un-timed missions for the sake of sniper focusing and setting up elaborate ambushes, but for many missions the added drive to move helps the feel of this game as a leaner, meaner child of Enemy Unknown/Within.
Mechanically, it plays much like it's predecessor, and I can see anyone who played and enjoyed the first game being easily about to do so again, even if some of the more esoteric additions don't quite click. The tactical game is fantastic, with simple controls and a clean UI. At the stretegy level, things are a little less clear, likely due to this being the more experimental side of things. The way missions are presented can be distracting, and while functionaly the satelite system from the first game the territory system is less well presented and explained in-game. It all works, but be ready to make some mistakes and poor choices in your first game.
The real problem is in stability. I've not had a single crash as of hour 5, but certain missions have suffered from stuttering and bugs. It's easy to assign this to 'new game jank' but after being held back several months, you have to wonder how broken the game was when it was first meant to be released. Given Firaxis' history with XCOM, I can only assume it will be dealt with, or mitigated soon. Still, if you're not desperate to play right now, it may be worth waiting for a patch or two before getting started.

Is this a good game? Yes.
Is it a good fallout? No.
Do I recommend you play it? Yes.
Do I recommend you play Fallout: New Vegas first? Yes.
My go-to for Fallout games and the one I would suggest anyone to play as their first experience of the Fallout world is, and will likely continue to be, Fallout: New Vegas.
Whilst Fallout 4 is not a terrible game it has problems; I will summarise my main issues with Fallout 4 below:
- Whilst I think the power armor mechanic in Fallout 4 is great (i.e. the way it requires fusion cores to power, the customisation and the way it's treated more as a vehicle than just another set of armor), the manner in which you get the power armor is disappointing. You just get it right at the start at the game. In other Fallouts you need to work for it, gain trust in one of the power armor using factions, and learn the Power Armor training skill. It was a big reward. Not in Fallout 4. Just jump in and away you go. Yes, the fusion cores limit how much you can use the suit in the early game but it's not long until you can find them pretty regularly.
- The leveling is basic. Gone are the skill points of all previous Fallout games and now you just pick a level perk. Makes all your characters feel basically the same, albeit the different weapons your characters may or may not be using.
- Simplified. Now it has become almost Mass Effect like. They give you a singular word or phrase that you're meant to choose, but it may not be wholly representative of what you character actually says. Gone are the science, small guns, lockpicking and charisma conversation options. Most you'll have is charisma option, a sarcastic option and a couple of other options - all of which end up being 5 or 6 different ways of saying the exact same thing. None of the conversations are particularly deep and some are just boring and unhelpful.
The new conversation camera makes the conversations more natural and allows a conversation with multiple NPCs but has a tendency to glitch out or get stuck on scenery or other NPCs. Sometimes important conversations happen as you stare at a wall or the inside of another NPC’s head.
- Competent amongst the NPCs and the player character, however unwanted on the latter. In previous games the fact that your character was silent meant you could make up a voice in order to fit the specific character you had in mind. Not in this, your evil character will sound the same as your saint character. Also, the fact that the emotion in the player character's voice changes so frequently, especially during the main questline dialogues, is jarring.
- Not going to lie, I honestly don't care for the 'stolen child / murder wife' story line. We met them for the whole of 5mins, I didn't get attached. I'd rather loot these ruined buildings for scrap or have interesting side quests.
- Honestly, it is fun to build up a settlement but the UI and mechanics for it are just plain bad. I also dislike that you can start tearing down Sanctuary and rebuilding it as soon as you start the game. It would make more sense for it to be gated, perhaps behind the minutemen quests, and be more integrated into the world. Maybe instead of building building instantly, you place everything and then it takes "X" in-game days to build? I'm not sure. But the instant 'Minecraft Light' building style doesn't fit the fallout world in my opinion.
- Gone. Your actions seem to have little effect on the world as a whole - excluding the main quests. There also seems to be very few ways, outside of straight up murdering people, of being evil. Unless you play the Nuka Cola World DLC where you can be nothing but. It seems like you can be either good or evil but the game doesn’t give you a choice of which. Also, Bethesda: being sarcastic knob is not being evil and is not a satisfying conversation option.
- The game is being ported to VR headsets but they still haven’t officially patched in support for ultra wide resolutions. Therefore I have to use a mod from Nexus Mods and Flawless Widescreen, but even with these the Power Armor HUD still breaks.
- Can’t comment on all of it yet in detail. I bought the season pass when it was on sale as it is far too expensive otherwise. From what I’ve played it is one good DLC (Far Harbor), one mediocre (Nuka Cola World) and a load of broken mod-like component packs for the settlement building. I.e. skip all of them but Far Harbor, unless you are REALLY into the settlement building.
- Looking for a post-apocalyptic RPG with interesting lore, really good environmental storytelling that is cheap and has amazing DLC? Play Fallout: New Vegas. I guess you could play this, but New Vegas is more deserving of your time and the Game of Year version of New Vegas is cheaper (£14.99 vs. £59.98).

The apparent commercial success of this title is the best example of style over substance I have ever seen in the context of PC gaming. There's a lot of style in this game and it is compellingly presented. However, the game that lies beneath the presentation layer is tedious and grindy. It's not a difficult game; it doesn't particularly challenge your intelligence, or memory, or reflexes or anything like that. What it is is a tedious and frustrating game. There is a difference.
If you are easily amused and like shiny things you may like this game. If you are easily bowled over by a slick presentation, and don't notice or care that you've been doing the same thing again and again and again - for hours - then you may like this game. A lot of people seem to. But if you are a more discerning person, well... I'll say no more. I just wish I had gotten a poster for my 20 dollars instead of what is essentially a gothic-reskinned version of Cookie Clicker.

TL;DR I imagine Darkest Dungeon is Dark Souls the RPG.
Man, this game is not meant for me. I don't know how people like TotalBiscet or NorthernLion make it look so fun. Maybe it's because I'm not the one playing. Maybe it is because they make it look easy. I don't know.
I just start a game and I'm already having a salty time. Getting constistently hit by crits and consistently missing attacks makes combat feel very unnatural, despite the fact you're combating supernatural beings but that is not the point. It doesn't feel like I'm being slowly whittled down bit by bit like a #2 pencil in a hand-cranked sharpener, but more like I'm a #2 pencil being snapped in half for funsies.
I feel no sense of escalation. Like instead of throwing monster fodder at me at the beginning like most RPGs do, it's more like every fight is a mini-boss, which means that one team of skeletons at the beginning of a mission will end you if RNGesus doesn't particularly like you that day.
I can't settle in on one save file because I can't trust the game on anything, like gambling since my luck is about as reliable as getting kicked in the groin. I know there are options in the setting menu that will decrease the risk, but I'm afraid that will decrease the authenticity of the experience of what the game is suppose to provide. Which is a delema to me. Do I want to enjoy PLAYING the game, or enjoy playing the GAME? I'll probably just leave it in my Steam library and leave it alone ad infinium.
Darkest Dungeon is a game about making the best out of a bad situation. But if the best I can make out of a bad situation is effectively nothing (poor roster selection, essentially no gold, bad luck with RNG) or worse, what is the point in trying?

Before I say anything else, this was my first Souls experience, including Bloodborne.
People have said you need a controller, and that's absolutely not true - I started the game with M/KB thinking I'd get as far as I could at least, and wound up beating the whole thing without being annoyed about controls, including the endgame optional boss with keyboard and mouse. For those who like controllers, go for it obviously, but for those of us who strongly prefer M/KB, it's a perfectly servicable option. That said, control labels will be off, so you'll need to remember that X and Y correspond to E and F, respectively, and a few other oddities. Oh, and you have to exit to main menu and press a button to exit the game. Or Alt+F4, which it complains about, but I did it anyway.
In every other regard, it's a great PC port, and I had no performance issues, etc, and the mouse movement felt great to me. Mouse support in menus was a welcome surprise.
The game itself is a masterpiece. I can't remember the last time I played a game that was able to make me this frustrated but keep me playing. The difficulty curve is a little all over the place - I found the last few bosses much easier than some of the midgame bosses - but the whole "Dark Souls is hard" narrative is pretty correct. There's very little room for error in most fights, and it gets harder as you go on, for the most part. What's interesting is that they managed to make the progression of your character feel meaningful while increasing that difficulty, which is a place many games screw up, either by making the player overpowered or by having to pull a macguffin and remove abilities to make boss fights hard or something. This game does none of that, but you do feel like you're getting somewhere as you level up.
The enemy design is pretty spectacular, although there's some "oh, Japan..." moments. It's fun to see a Japanese game set in Western fantasy, though. It's an interesting cultural perspective.
In terms of the game design, there's some obtuse stuff; unhelpfully named items, a number of poorly-explained mechanics (parrying, damage scaling, weapon upgrades), arcane NPC plots, and quest-crucial stuff being hidden will all have you looking things up online. Let's just say this is a good game to have a second monitor for. I can't imagine what people playing this on their living room TV would have done. I guess iPads are a thing now.
Speaking of which, while I can see this being the kind of game that would appeal to people who want to find out everything on their own no matter how long it takes, for the rest of us there are some really excellent walkthroughs and guides out there. Without that kind of assistance, I would never have gotten through the game; I would have missed something important, gotten frustrated, and done something else.
I feel like a lot of diehard fans are going to look at me like a casual tourist scrub, and you know, they're not wrong. I don't really play games to prove something, but for entertainment, and while this game did force me to step up my game, and did make me really frustrated in parts (Dancer of the Boreal Valley was a personal low point) being able to finally get past something that's been stumping you for an hour or two is really satisfying. Despite all the flaws - and I DO view the obtuse stuff as flaws - I enjoyed the heck out of this game. I would recommend this game to anyone who thinks they're up for a challenge.
Also, for what is technically a JRPG, this game is amazingly light on cutscenes, even by Western standards. Like damn. Still had a full-DBZ-mode moment or two in it, though. And no shortage of helmets worn so far forward they're actually blindfolds.
Final opinion:

Even though it doesn't have a storyline, or any kind of structure for that matter, that's what gives Trove the edge it needs. Because you have so many options, and nothing but a small suggestion that calls itself a quest to really work on, you're free to set up goals on your own for things that you want to do.
Want to work to get a new mount? Go for it.
Want to make a checklist and see every biome personally? Easy to do.
Want to get the fastest mount in the game and run as far as possible in any direction? Sure, why the hell not.
Granted, there are things like server stability issues, queue time problems, and a few hiccups surrounding things like updates, the game is still good, and thankfully it's still being worked on unlike quite a few of the F2P games on the Steam Store. Above all that, I can personally say that even though I have an absolutely crap computer, I can still run this game without too much of a problem, save for the fact that the resolution changer is stubborn and won't show up.
Overall, 8.5/10 for a game with some very serious potential, if worked on properly. Though you can take what I say with a grain of salt, it's worth giving this game a shot at least once. You never know, you might find something enjoyable.

Darkest Dungeon was a game that came to my attention almost as soon as it came into steam. The concept seemed interesting to me and I indulged in watching a few streams and YouTube videos of the game. Turned off by the early access label I decided to withhold my purchase and buy it some other time.
Recently it came to my attention that the game had been "finished." I had seen numinous glowing reviews from critics I trust and I was convinced to make the purchase. To me the game looked like Xcom: the RPG with a dark graphic novel H.P. Lovecraft aesthetic.
I am a fan of HP's stories and the narrative to me is clearly inspired by 'The statement of Randolph Carter' and of course the classic 'The call of Cthulhu.' I even encountered a rather on the nose reference to HP's work as my rambling arbalest asked my crusader "have you ever seen a colour out of space?" Referencing the HP Lovercraft story of the same name.
I didn't even have any truck with the controversial ending (that I spoiled for myself, more on that later) it's as hopeless and grim as many a Lovecaftian tale.
The visual and sound design are excellent, The character sprites are very graphic novel-ly and well-drawn, the music is well composed and the disheartening ambiance that gets louder the darker the torch gets is a nice atmospheric touch.
These well done aspects of the game added to the exclusively positive media i had heard up to that point convinced me to buy the game. While this did not cross my mind when i first made my purchase I now remember a certain youtuber saying something along the lines of 'those people who played for 300 hours and hate it.'
This should have sent off warning signs in my head but sadly I did not research enough. I made my purchase and began playing. I did well (I think) initially and had a good time. I only lost 3 party members in 15 hours and I managed to beat 4 bosses and both the encounter bosses. I'm not exactly sure if I did anything wrong or if I was just unlucky but I started lousing, lots. Most of the time I would lose one or two level 3 party members and flee, But then I had my first party wipe, I lost one level 4, three level 5 heroes and some incredibly rare trinkets (including the drop I received of my hard won shambler fight).
Up to this point I had played the game akin to the way I play Xcom. I had named each hero after someone I know in real life and had upgraded all my heroes as much as possible in an attempt for them to stop dying. This caused my string of losses to be quite costly both emotionally and financially, I understand that I may have been playing it wrong but the way the game punishes you for losing high level heroes breaks the fun of the game for me.
Falling back on my Xcom instincts I started a new save file and started playing that. At this point my friend linked a video showing why he wouldn’t be purchasing the game after I had stated I had a good time with the first 10 to 15 hours and I realised why I would not be revisiting this game until it is significantly patched.
The game is SUPER grind focused. Not only that but the core gameplay loop is repetitive. The same missions: scout(search almost all rooms), exterminate(finish all room battles), and an item mission where you must find 3 'curios' and interact with them with 3 provided items repeat over and over.
For some reason Red Hook have padded out the game with completely unnecessary repetition and a slow progression system that will set you back HOURS of grinding a replacement hero if you are unlucky and lose even one or 2 party members.
Boss fights are repeated 2 more times at harder difficulties for seemingly no reason and the final straw was seeing what was in store for me in the final missions of the game.
One your party beats an incredibly hard level in the Darkest Dungeon they will all refuse to ever go there again forcing you to grind even more on easier levels to produce max level and well equipped heroes in order to stand a chance.
This revelation I had has killed any desire for me to play the game. I am familiar with challenging games, even ones with RNG tied to them, I beat Xcom on ironman classic.
But Darkest Dungeon is not 'challenging'. It's not really. You can’t even lose. It just takes up your time to make it feel like its challenging. If the game was shorter, had more variation in the core gameplay loop and removed unnecessary features like the 'Never Again' mechanic then I may of recommended this game.
But in its current unfairly grindy state I do not recommend. Hopefully with the alleged addition of the steam workshop soon someone may just fix the game instead of the devs.
No other game can send you into crippling depression like this one.

I'd like to begin by saying that this review is long overdo.  I've owned and played this game for quite some time, put a lot of hours into it as I'm sure many others have.  I'd like to break down my review by the different aspects of the game.
Gameplay - 7/10
The UI is simple enough, and the FPS style is also basic but efficient.  There's a but of a lack of actual variety to the weapon choices, the stronger gun wins, there aren't really any alternatives in shootouts other than sniping, which can be pretty fun, especially with the kill cam (which also can be extremely annoying).  Interaction with other characters is also a bit basic and at times rather cumbersome as the controls do tend to be a bit clunky.
Story - 6/10
A pretty heartfelt origin story followed by (without spoilers) a bit of a letdown twist.  Without ruining anything, the main story is kind of hollow, after following what feels like an actual storyline, you just seem to start following a series of mini quests into a very anti-climactic set of "choices" which are basically just glorified factions.  Each has their own charm and are extreme in their differences, and all seem to lead to sort of dead ends and extremely open ended gameplay.
Character interaction - 5/10
Very very bland.  The only reason I rate it as high as I did was because at the start, there is a lot of interaction when you first meet your companion choices, with the exception of one big brute who you just basicaly pick up for no reason.  But after their initial interactions and a very small amount of pointless side quests they just become some light background noise.  Even the romance is completely bland and pointless.  Just a series of one liners that change in the quick talking dialogue you can do if you want to kill 10 seconds.
Graphics - 7/10
The graphics are decent, a little unpolished, but in the higher graphics settings things can be quite beautiful even in a setting as dreary as fallout's radiated post apocalyptic world.  My main concern is with the characters.  For the most part, they are quite basic and also for the most part quite ugly.  The design of the characters seemed to be a secondary thought when in developement.
Settlements - 9/10
This is where I'm sure many will disagree with me on principle alone, but I truly did enjoy building settlements.  While I do wish there was a nicer interface and simpler method to putting it together, the concept is really quite enjoyable.  It's also nice to see just how my string of turrets and traps took down the horde of invading mutants.  While I wish there was more of a user friendly menu system or interface in general for building, it still did the trick.
Mods - 10/10
What's not to love about our modding community?  They take everything wrong with a game and make it right again (or.. just weird sometimes)
For everything wrong I've stated above, there's basically a mod for it.  Support your modders, download, upvote, donate, and if you're new to the scene, or just curious, check it out, you won't regret it!
Overall - 7/10
The overall experience of the game was pretty pleasant.  I mod heavily so the shortcomings of the vanilla version are mostly taken care of, and I get to build some fun things in my settlements.  The game is a worthy play, and if you don't go in expecting a masterpiece and want a fun sandbox shooter, have at it and play away!
Sidenote about DLC - This is where I get very, very frustrated.  The DLC for Fallout 4 is decent, but the prices for it leave a lot to be desired.  To download all of the extra content not released with the initial game, you have to pay for the game two times more over.  If you have the money go for it, but be forwarned, the prices are not equivalent to the quality of the product.
Imagine Terraria, but better, with space travel, and aliens!

Before I say anything else, this was my first Souls experience, including Bloodborne.
People have said you need a controller, and that's absolutely not true - I started the game with M/KB thinking I'd get as far as I could at least, and wound up beating the whole thing without being annoyed about controls, including the endgame optional boss with keyboard and mouse. For those who like controllers, go for it obviously, but for those of us who strongly prefer M/KB, it's a perfectly servicable option. That said, control labels will be off, so you'll need to remember that X and Y correspond to E and F, respectively, and a few other oddities. Oh, and you have to exit to main menu and press a button to exit the game. Or Alt+F4, which it complains about, but I did it anyway.
In every other regard, it's a great PC port, and I had no performance issues, etc, and the mouse movement felt great to me. Mouse support in menus was a welcome surprise.
The game itself is a masterpiece. I can't remember the last time I played a game that was able to make me this frustrated but keep me playing. The difficulty curve is a little all over the place - I found the last few bosses much easier than some of the midgame bosses - but the whole "Dark Souls is hard" narrative is pretty correct. There's very little room for error in most fights, and it gets harder as you go on, for the most part. What's interesting is that they managed to make the progression of your character feel meaningful while increasing that difficulty, which is a place many games screw up, either by making the player overpowered or by having to pull a macguffin and remove abilities to make boss fights hard or something. This game does none of that, but you do feel like you're getting somewhere as you level up.
The enemy design is pretty spectacular, although there's some "oh, Japan..." moments. It's fun to see a Japanese game set in Western fantasy, though. It's an interesting cultural perspective.
In terms of the game design, there's some obtuse stuff; unhelpfully named items, a number of poorly-explained mechanics (parrying, damage scaling, weapon upgrades), arcane NPC plots, and quest-crucial stuff being hidden will all have you looking things up online. Let's just say this is a good game to have a second monitor for. I can't imagine what people playing this on their living room TV would have done. I guess iPads are a thing now.
Speaking of which, while I can see this being the kind of game that would appeal to people who want to find out everything on their own no matter how long it takes, for the rest of us there are some really excellent walkthroughs and guides out there. Without that kind of assistance, I would never have gotten through the game; I would have missed something important, gotten frustrated, and done something else.
I feel like a lot of diehard fans are going to look at me like a casual tourist scrub, and you know, they're not wrong. I don't really play games to prove something, but for entertainment, and while this game did force me to step up my game, and did make me really frustrated in parts (Dancer of the Boreal Valley was a personal low point) being able to finally get past something that's been stumping you for an hour or two is really satisfying. Despite all the flaws - and I DO view the obtuse stuff as flaws - I enjoyed the heck out of this game. I would recommend this game to anyone who thinks they're up for a challenge.
Also, for what is technically a JRPG, this game is amazingly light on cutscenes, even by Western standards. Like damn. Still had a full-DBZ-mode moment or two in it, though. And no shortage of helmets worn so far forward they're actually blindfolds.
Final opinion:

This is one of my favorite games, but I'm gonna start out with countering some common complaints I hear before getting onto my own opinions.
People complain that "there's not enough content", or that "there's too much content". I'm someone who usually believes that the more content, the better, and if someone believes something other than that, I respect that, because it's entirely valid. The arguement I'm not OK with? The arguement that it's impossible to advance in the game without paying!
Here's the thing: people flip out about how this game is "pay-to-win" and how it's impossible to get past 4* gear without paying real world money.
Alrighty, I'll admit, back in the day when Mist Energy was still a thing, the game was definatly leaning on pay-to-win. But even then, you could in theory do everything with enough grinding. Post-update, the only thing you'd really pay real world money to get is cosmetic items, which, again, in theory you could save up crowns for to trade for. No one's forcing you to buy them, and now one is forcing you to buy weapons either.
Anyway, my main complaint with the game is that sadly, there's a ton of balancing issues, especially in PVP. PVP is usually just a bunch of dudes with the same old swords and armor tearing each other up with the occasional guy with the Polaris. Bombers can't do much other than spread status, which is dubiously helpful at best. In the clockworks, everything's for the most part good, except certain weapon lines are totally outclassed. I feel kinda bad for the people who went for the Cautery Sword, the Deconstructor, the Pepperbox, the Spur, and other abruptly ending or dubiously useful lines. My other problem is that players don't know what items are good unless they ask others. Perhaps there should be a feature that allows players to try out different weapons without buying them, or at least something that shows how far weapon lines extend, star wise.
Now for my positive stuff: the game is an amazing hack-and-slash MMO that plays really well. It actually gives me vague memories of the Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicals games, which were some of my old favorites. The enemies are creative: with things somewhat familiar, like Gremlins and Zombies, to things that are totally cool and never-before-seen, including most of the Fiend family. The Slime family deserves a special mention for putting a cool new twist on the concept of "gelatinous cube". The bosses are fun and engaging: the epic feeling I got as a new player when I fought the Snarbolax alone for the first time was something I'll remember for a long time. The seasonal events are great too - as rather bothersome as parts of it are, the Apocrea event is probably one of my favorites. The player base is for the most part friendly. Guild life is fun, and most players will help you out with missions if you need them to.
In conclusion, Spiral Knights is one of the few MMOs that I actually enjoy, and while it does have some issues, it's still fun, and those issues could be fixed. This is my first review pretty much, so hopefully I did everything right.

Is this a good game? Yes.
Is it a good fallout? No.
Do I recommend you play it? Yes.
Do I recommend you play Fallout: New Vegas first? Yes.
My go-to for Fallout games and the one I would suggest anyone to play as their first experience of the Fallout world is, and will likely continue to be, Fallout: New Vegas.
Whilst Fallout 4 is not a terrible game it has problems; I will summarise my main issues with Fallout 4 below:
- Whilst I think the power armor mechanic in Fallout 4 is great (i.e. the way it requires fusion cores to power, the customisation and the way it's treated more as a vehicle than just another set of armor), the manner in which you get the power armor is disappointing. You just get it right at the start at the game. In other Fallouts you need to work for it, gain trust in one of the power armor using factions, and learn the Power Armor training skill. It was a big reward. Not in Fallout 4. Just jump in and away you go. Yes, the fusion cores limit how much you can use the suit in the early game but it's not long until you can find them pretty regularly.
- The leveling is basic. Gone are the skill points of all previous Fallout games and now you just pick a level perk. Makes all your characters feel basically the same, albeit the different weapons your characters may or may not be using.
- Simplified. Now it has become almost Mass Effect like. They give you a singular word or phrase that you're meant to choose, but it may not be wholly representative of what you character actually says. Gone are the science, small guns, lockpicking and charisma conversation options. Most you'll have is charisma option, a sarcastic option and a couple of other options - all of which end up being 5 or 6 different ways of saying the exact same thing. None of the conversations are particularly deep and some are just boring and unhelpful.
The new conversation camera makes the conversations more natural and allows a conversation with multiple NPCs but has a tendency to glitch out or get stuck on scenery or other NPCs. Sometimes important conversations happen as you stare at a wall or the inside of another NPC’s head.
- Competent amongst the NPCs and the player character, however unwanted on the latter. In previous games the fact that your character was silent meant you could make up a voice in order to fit the specific character you had in mind. Not in this, your evil character will sound the same as your saint character. Also, the fact that the emotion in the player character's voice changes so frequently, especially during the main questline dialogues, is jarring.
- Not going to lie, I honestly don't care for the 'stolen child / murder wife' story line. We met them for the whole of 5mins, I didn't get attached. I'd rather loot these ruined buildings for scrap or have interesting side quests.
- Honestly, it is fun to build up a settlement but the UI and mechanics for it are just plain bad. I also dislike that you can start tearing down Sanctuary and rebuilding it as soon as you start the game. It would make more sense for it to be gated, perhaps behind the minutemen quests, and be more integrated into the world. Maybe instead of building building instantly, you place everything and then it takes "X" in-game days to build? I'm not sure. But the instant 'Minecraft Light' building style doesn't fit the fallout world in my opinion.
- Gone. Your actions seem to have little effect on the world as a whole - excluding the main quests. There also seems to be very few ways, outside of straight up murdering people, of being evil. Unless you play the Nuka Cola World DLC where you can be nothing but. It seems like you can be either good or evil but the game doesn’t give you a choice of which. Also, Bethesda: being sarcastic knob is not being evil and is not a satisfying conversation option.
- The game is being ported to VR headsets but they still haven’t officially patched in support for ultra wide resolutions. Therefore I have to use a mod from Nexus Mods and Flawless Widescreen, but even with these the Power Armor HUD still breaks.
- Can’t comment on all of it yet in detail. I bought the season pass when it was on sale as it is far too expensive otherwise. From what I’ve played it is one good DLC (Far Harbor), one mediocre (Nuka Cola World) and a load of broken mod-like component packs for the settlement building. I.e. skip all of them but Far Harbor, unless you are REALLY into the settlement building.
- Looking for a post-apocalyptic RPG with interesting lore, really good environmental storytelling that is cheap and has amazing DLC? Play Fallout: New Vegas. I guess you could play this, but New Vegas is more deserving of your time and the Game of Year version of New Vegas is cheaper (£14.99 vs. £59.98).

Before I say anything else, this was my first Souls experience, including Bloodborne.
People have said you need a controller, and that's absolutely not true - I started the game with M/KB thinking I'd get as far as I could at least, and wound up beating the whole thing without being annoyed about controls, including the endgame optional boss with keyboard and mouse. For those who like controllers, go for it obviously, but for those of us who strongly prefer M/KB, it's a perfectly servicable option. That said, control labels will be off, so you'll need to remember that X and Y correspond to E and F, respectively, and a few other oddities. Oh, and you have to exit to main menu and press a button to exit the game. Or Alt+F4, which it complains about, but I did it anyway.
In every other regard, it's a great PC port, and I had no performance issues, etc, and the mouse movement felt great to me. Mouse support in menus was a welcome surprise.
The game itself is a masterpiece. I can't remember the last time I played a game that was able to make me this frustrated but keep me playing. The difficulty curve is a little all over the place - I found the last few bosses much easier than some of the midgame bosses - but the whole "Dark Souls is hard" narrative is pretty correct. There's very little room for error in most fights, and it gets harder as you go on, for the most part. What's interesting is that they managed to make the progression of your character feel meaningful while increasing that difficulty, which is a place many games screw up, either by making the player overpowered or by having to pull a macguffin and remove abilities to make boss fights hard or something. This game does none of that, but you do feel like you're getting somewhere as you level up.
The enemy design is pretty spectacular, although there's some "oh, Japan..." moments. It's fun to see a Japanese game set in Western fantasy, though. It's an interesting cultural perspective.
In terms of the game design, there's some obtuse stuff; unhelpfully named items, a number of poorly-explained mechanics (parrying, damage scaling, weapon upgrades), arcane NPC plots, and quest-crucial stuff being hidden will all have you looking things up online. Let's just say this is a good game to have a second monitor for. I can't imagine what people playing this on their living room TV would have done. I guess iPads are a thing now.
Speaking of which, while I can see this being the kind of game that would appeal to people who want to find out everything on their own no matter how long it takes, for the rest of us there are some really excellent walkthroughs and guides out there. Without that kind of assistance, I would never have gotten through the game; I would have missed something important, gotten frustrated, and done something else.
I feel like a lot of diehard fans are going to look at me like a casual tourist scrub, and you know, they're not wrong. I don't really play games to prove something, but for entertainment, and while this game did force me to step up my game, and did make me really frustrated in parts (Dancer of the Boreal Valley was a personal low point) being able to finally get past something that's been stumping you for an hour or two is really satisfying. Despite all the flaws - and I DO view the obtuse stuff as flaws - I enjoyed the heck out of this game. I would recommend this game to anyone who thinks they're up for a challenge.
Also, for what is technically a JRPG, this game is amazingly light on cutscenes, even by Western standards. Like damn. Still had a full-DBZ-mode moment or two in it, though. And no shortage of helmets worn so far forward they're actually blindfolds.
Final opinion:

Fantastic Firaxis.  Fantastic.
Love it.  If you enjoyed XCOM and hoped for a second helping, Firaxis has largely outdone themselves. That's not to say XCOM 2 isn't without some odds and issues, but it largely addresses the biggest complaints levied at the original and does so with gusto.  In many ways it's a different game, and that might take some adjustment if you were particularly well-versed in the original (I had ~200 hours).  The strategic layer has been entirely revamped and you'll spend quite a bit more time managing time as you fly around the world establishing contacts, protecting innocents and assaulting enemy resources.  There's just so much more to manage and be involved with.  It's more punishing, hateful and depressing, and I wouldn't want it any other way.
To be honest I can't fault much in the main game outside of some camera issues but I have to mention performance.  It can be pretty demanding even at low settings.  I get frame rates ~30 in some areas of maps and the base.  And mind you, I played Rise of the Tomb Raider at High settings with 60fps.  That said, I get nearly the SAME performance regardless of graphical settings so if you aren't running a fairly beefy system your mileage may vary and this could be a problem for many users if the game doesn't scale to your system.

I'm sorry, I just cannot like this game. I've been a massive fan of both Fallout 3 and NV, yet Fallout 4 is the worst experience I've had in the franchise. I don't have the time to go extremely in depth with my issues with the game, but the most notable ones I do remember:
- The amount of unique quests in this game is horribly abysmal. Throughout my playthrough I have found next to no memorable side quests. Barring quests like the USS Constitution, every other was a fetch/radiant quest that was shoved into my face as if it were actual respectable content. Even the main quests incorporated a shockingly high amount of radiant quests, which I can tell were only there to create fake substance to the game's lacking quest infrastructure.
- The locations in the world have suffered, specifically regarding settlements. No, not the settlement system, but actual settlements with a backstory behind them and unique NPCs within them. There is a huge gap in the number of settlements between Fo4 and FoNV. Even if I were to include faction locations as "settlements", they're all so concentrated around downtown Boston that the rest of the map feels completely empty. They disregarded a huge portion of the map and just slapped settlement locations there for you to build up. Does that provide any meaningful NPC dialogue, exploration or quest content? NO.
- Dialogue is dead. Absolutely dead. Without a skills system, the only "unique" conversation chioces are unlocked through speech. Otherwise, every dialogue option feels bland and playing with the visible dialogue option mod, I can see how uncreative Bethesda was with it. Situations arose where several of the options were the exact same, worded differently. People say that you can't say no in this game because it truly does not give you the option to. Even if I object to an NPC's remark or ask with "skepticism", the NPCs respond in the exact same way almost every time. There is no meaningful way to change the outcome of quests through your dialogue. Please prove me wrong if there are situations where dialogue truly matters on a fundamental level (as in changing the quest outcome drastically or altering an NPC's choices, etc). I would LOVE to see some of that after I found little to none in my playthrough of the game.
Bethesda has put a stain on the Fallout franchise with this game. I fell in love with the Fallout games because of the intriguing aspects of post-apocalypse politics and civilization. Fallout 4 puts on a mask that makes you think it's in the Fallout world, sure. But if you try to dig deeper you hit the barrier that is Bethesda's incompetence. The world is barren in most areas, with most areas inhabited by raiders/hostiles and others preserved for a settlement system that lacks true substance in terms of content. The politics and morality are heavily dumbed down. Every Super Mutant is a brainless monster that kills on sight. The Gunners, despite being a mercenary group, target you for no explainable reason. The Institute gives no meaningful reasons for their actions, which turns the entire faction into the obvious antagonist (the same cannot be said for the Legion in Fallout NV). The Minutemen show no flaws past their starting numbers, which makes them the obvious choice for a "good" ending.
I tried so hard to like this game. I modded out major flaws such as the dialogue wheel and a player voice that limited character creation. Yet, no mod can truly fix the absolutely shallow attempt at a Fallout game that is Fallout 4.
