I'm disappointed in Firaxis. I'm disappointed in the development team. I can't imagine that there isn't at least a few of the developers, whether writers artists or programmers who didn't think "Man, there's going to be a lot of really angry players."
This game is a reskin. That's it. That's the entire review. Everything else is just exposition and nuance.
Satellites are now Listening Posts. The Council timer is now the ADVENT timer. You excavate a starship like you excavate a bunker (amazingly straight down only. No, you can't excavate starting from the bottom or sides ignore the areas of the ship around this smaller-base-than-XCOM-1 you must excavate down). The Terror Missions are now named Retaliation Missions. The Classes are still split into Heavy, Sniper, Support and Assault but there's been some rebalancing to remove certain abilities players were abusing and name-changes to protect the innocent.
Combat is the same. The AI is different, but also in a strange way, the same. Did you play Long War? Did you listen to Long War talk about what was wrong with XCOM1? Congratulations. You've already played XCOM2's combat.
It looks the same, it plays the same beyond minor tweaks (if the enemy getting free moves bothered you then you'll be happy to note: its now an essential gameplay mechanic). This is the same engine. Same content. Same everything. Its ctrl+c; ctrl+v. Its lazy... and amazingly it doesn't have things that we find in the first XCOM like Second Wave mechanics. The cynic in me says that Second Wave will be released under a new name as DLC. Again.
It feels like an expansion pack. No, it doesn't. Scratch that. It feels like the Blue Shift or Opposing Force campaigns. Allow me explanation on that one in case you're not familiar with the examples. In Half-Life1 you had some alternate campaigns that were released as expansions. Same game, same engine, obvious recycles the whole nine yards. You just played the same story from a different perspective. The same happened in a lot of older video games. You got two campaigns. Usually an Allieds and Axis, or Rebellion and Empire. That sorta thing. This feels like a Blue Shift campaign being marketed as a sequel in hopes that the playerbase is too stupid to notice. That's what you get here. Not a game in its own right, because you've already played it and this game is so identical that you could probably mod in XCOM2 back into XCOM1 without a whole lot of work.
And you know what pisses me off? What really angers me the most about this? This isn't like the trailer. This game doesn't even reflect the main menu (for those of you who haven't seen it, its one of your soldiers in the suburbs about to ambush alien police officers). You don't build up multiple fronts of cells. You don't fight and take cities. There's no thought or complexity in this beyond "hack the thing and shoot everything in the face". There's no campaign beyond flimsy goalposts of "research this" or "stun a Sectoid Commander for interrogation" (in XCOM2 its stabbing ADVENT Commanders in the face with a probe to interrogate their faces directly) but that's one of the requirements.
Obviously there's a lot of money in the XCOM franchise. XCOM1 sold well. The DLC sold well. The Enemy Within expansion sold well. There's a lot of people like myself who bought the second game with little more than a trailer and some hope. The press releases for XCOM2 were... quiet, but what was released promised something more than just a reskin and taking notes out of a modding community's playbook.
If I had to sum it up: XCOM2 was a♥♥♥♥♥♥move, Firaxis. You should be ashamed.

First, a disclosure: In about two years, I had clocked in about 130 hours of playtime in Terraria, a game that has been endearing to me in many levels and will hold fond memories for me.
However, when I picked up Starbound, I've already clocked in over 200 hours
.
Starbound holds on to the 2D sandbox core that Terraria started and kicks it up to another level in many different vectors. For starters, it has lore/logical in-gameplay explenations for the necessity to explore multiple planets for riches and resources instead of having to exit and re-create a world in Terraria, which I found to more appealing than I thought it would be.
Crafting is expanded upon, with more varied flavor items (many unique cooking recipes that vary from race) and a simplified system for those who love decorating but only are able to retrieve so many things from a dungeon run, thanks to a lampshaded currency-to-object item replication system. And there are MANY themes of decor, ranging from 1960's totalitarianesque dormitories, high tech matter-fabrication doompyramids, and even pseudo-mideval greasepunk robotics. If you can encounter a theme in the game, you can replicate the look for your own homebase. The game developers even hint at the prospect of being able to terraform planets you conquer, so you can truly take decorating your home base to a new level.
There's game lore and interesting race dynamics. Vendors and villages and an almost Skyrim-esque question in whether or not to destroy peaceful settlements or lord over their resources. Dungeons are many and highly rewarding. Weapons, while highly random in traits, have extremely fun design elements. A grenade launcher that fires a small pig with dynamite bundled to it and hones in to your target, shotguns that shoot white fire orbs that either explode on target impact or detonate on the ground later on, and giant Teslea coil staves that shoot lightning are some potentiates for your arsenal.
Progression through the various armor sets and planetary sectors is completely on your own terms. You won't face your first boss until you're set and ready for it -- which may, for some, be a complaint for those who would use sandboxing to wall off dangerous attacks. On the other hand, you won't suddenly have a structure-destroying UFO blowing up your home just because you happened to aquire a lot of health boosts on a digging run. Your first planet even has quests that assist you in figure out what is going on around you and how crafting and survival works. A hunger and warmth system puts the torch to your backside to help you keep motivated in your construction, production and exploration.
One of the biggest pluses for this over Terraria, however, is that this game was made with modding in mind, even with the official site having a mod hub ready for sharing community creations. Already with this game only being a few months old in the hands of fans, there is already a thriving modding community. If there is something I could point to that I would say boosts the life of any sandbox game to epic amounts, it would have to be good modding support and this game
While plain that the game is very unfinished (some items lack descriptions still, semi-frequent crashes, and item/monster strength issues that crop up fairly often) and still adding in many features, the game as it is now is a joyous experience. If you had enjoyed Terraria, or even Minecraft, to any degree you will love Starbound.

I still bought it and playing to my heart's content, and i certanly don't care if my fps can suddenly drop in bloody turn-based game. I spent some time looking for a fix that makes fps drop to the bottom because of bloody USB MODEM connected. And this bug is present since BORDERLANDS 2 and was never fixed (something about 2K online integration and stuff). Majority of Enemy Within performance issues were never fixed and  you expected a clean lubed start with this one? This is like buying Total War or Paradox games and expect them to work.
Yes, PC games' quality control is dire nowadays, there's no actual testing, wide variety of PC configurations can not work with the game for mystical reasons, publishers always push devs to release SOONER AND SOONER, it's not a reason to discard the game if the game is good. You should have a vague idea that making games is pretty hard, right? Or do you think throwing a tantrum about having 59 fps isntead of 60 will somehow change the world?
Second of all, people complaining about game being TOO HARD, TIMED MISSIONS ARE TOO FAST, INTEL INCOME TOO LOW... Is it official IGN embassy or what? It's XCOM, bro, make up your mind. You are supposed to care about every single rookie in your barraks and to know how to damage control your every failure. You are supposed to have squad wipes because of bad luck, massive panic from unlucky crit, scarce resources and you have to know how to work with what you got, unless you like to be a whimp and save scum your every failed shot. Tactical combat is much more compelling, geoscape gameplay makes much more sense, base management is somewhat nonexistent, but i don't really care that much. To be fair, this thing about single base was stupid in the first place, so making mobile base is pretty much right decision, considering that introducing multiple bases would only spawn more "too difficult >:(" whine at this point. Being a fan of RPG games, I started playing SK with an open mind.. when I started I wasn't too sure how much I would enjoy the gameplay, but after a while (and a few rank-ups and gear changes) I really started enjoying Spiral Knights.
Based on a Micro-transaction income model, this Free-to-play RPG is exactly what is says. Free-To-Play.
Meaning, you CAN play for free.. but a lot of the beginning grind can be removed with a few small purchases of the ingame "Energy", which can help you develop your gear faster and start earning more of the ingame currency, "Crowns".
Saying that, the game CAN be completely Free-to-Play if you choose. Be prepaired to run some of the lower levels quite a lot as you try and rank your gear up.
I would recommend researching different types of weapons and armor in the game. At the beginning you are provided a large variety of weapons via Missions, which reflect the different weapon types, and different variations of each weapon (Swords, Guns and Bombs).
-Pro's:
Easy going, Fun, and the community is generally very friendly.
-Con's:
can take a little while to get started, and at the beginning earning Crowns can seem very difficult. this is all part of the learning curve of the game, and any necessary purchases in the game will correlate to the mission rewards that you get. If you don't waste your crowns when you start, then you will be fine... But it's very important to not waste crowns on useless things you do not need at the beginning.
Overall, I have played SK for around 2 months now. I started playing standalone, and then switched my account to the Steam version. I managed to reach the highest rank, Vanguard, and STILL enjoy playing the game. That's a hard thing for a game to achieve in my eyes, and I believe they have been successful with this.

I have been playing this game since the FIRST DAY of early access. Many things have changed since then but DD is still a great game. A lot of the reviews you will read on here that give this title a thumbs DOWN are mostly due to the difficulty which revolves around the RNG (Random Number Generator) of the game. While this is true that many things in the game revolve around computer generated "dice rolls" that does not mean in ANY WAY that this game is bad and as such I will NOT be docking points because people walked in here thinking that this game will hold your hand and give you a pat on the back (Pete's sake in the intro Red Hook even says that DD is about making the MOST of a BAD situation). I personally feel that there is nothing wrong with an RNG and that is actually one of the reasons I love D&D which is almost ENTIRELY based off dice rolls. *sigh*...It's all thanks to these MOBA-douches that are all about "My skills as a player should not be dependent on bad rolls HUH HUH" *stomps away disdainfully* Anyway..
Well my first inclination is to say go cry to your mommy you console peasant BUT...there are game play configuration options found in the game menu that you can turn off and on, things like enemies doing only max damage for crits instead of multipliers, turning off battle length penalties and so on. Now that all the crap is out of the way let's begin...
"Ha ha ha! Let those dirty beasts worship the mud now!"
Thus are the words of the Ancestor. Your Ancestor.
In Darkest Dungeon you play as the Descendant who's Ancestor left a rich and prestigious estate...which has now been completely overrun by tenticle demons that came through a portal conveniently opened by your (now DEAD) Ancestor that sent a letter to you so you could clean up his mess.... GEE! WHAT A GUY!
So you go to the manor and the estate, which is in complete shambles, and start rebuilding. As you go as a party of 4 into different dungeons and complete missions you will begin to rebuild that forsaken ground that was entrusted to you. You will recruit new hirelings and I say hirelings because even though Red Hook has said this game is a bit like XCOM it is NOTHING like XCOM. Your hirelings will die. They will die OVER AND OVER again.
So let's get down to the *Nacho Libre voice* nhiitty grriiitey
Pros:
+AWESOME ARTWORK. Beautifully drawn characters which are VERY reminiscent to Mike Mignola's work on Hellboy. I don't think that was a coincendence either.
+BRUTAL GAMEPLAY. Like I've been trying to tell you guys a million times: this game was made for masochists. It will punish you SEVERLY for even trying to step foot out of the Estate. But at the same time getting those crits or barely completing that mission with only one survivor makes it so worth.
+GREAT SOUNDTRACK. It really is, lot's of drums and deep horns. Each dungeon has a unique theme song. The Warrens' is warlike and orcish sounding while the Weald's is more on the horrific side.
+NARRATOR IS 10/10. I mean "EXECUTED WITH IMPUNITY!" doesn't grant an auto-thumb up?
Now the Cons
-FOOD. Food is a needed thing especially for long trips in a dungeon, manually healing your party and also for countering starving events which pop-up randomly. The thing is even if you feed your heroes manually and then move one space you might still be hit with a starving event. Would be nice to at least have a way to manually avoid that instead of wasting food on healing your team (you can't even feed them a ton of food because it will say they are full) to only be hit by a starving event.
-STORY. A bit weak. Almost none at all. I guess the bosses have their own mini plot's but all in all it's not SUPER compelling. That's where the gameplay comes in to pick up the slack.
-BRUTAL GAMEPLAY. Funny how this is a con and a pro right? I put it as a con as well because this is not a game for everyone. It's for those sick creatures that like to cut themselves with pencils and other slightly blunt but mostly sharp objects. It is very tough for players that are looking for a fair game as this is NOT a fair game and it most likely will stay unfair. I guess I'm one of those that likes the crazy difficulty.
TL;DR
Fun, dungeon crawler that's based around dice-rolled combat and brutal difficulty which is backed up by great artwork and a stellar narrator.
Final Score?: 8/10

I'm not the biggest strategy fan most of the time. I don't rule those games out, but I don't often go searching for them either. I took a pretty big risk on XCOM 2, I didn't play much of the reboot, Enemy Unknown, but I decided to give this a try. I have to say, its one of the most frustrating, but fufulling gaming experiences I've had in a while.
The game has a large RNG component, first of all. If you have a problem with that, just don't play it, you'll go into so much RNG induced rage, you might never recover. If you didn't like Darkest Dungeon or Enemy Unknown, don't bother with this.
Now, XCOM 2 takes place 20(?) years after the events of Enemy Unknown, and you lost. The aliens won and took over the planet and now your on the attack, which is reflected in the missions since most of the time you work on timers and your attacking from flanked positions and cover. You really feel like you percieved the aliens in the firts game, and it adds a new element that really separates this game from the first. The maps are better(for the most part, there are some that kinda screwed me on full cover), the gameplay is improved with little tweaks here and there, and even the story is a bit more engaging.
I have yet to beat the game, obviously since I'm at 10 hours reviewing this, but even though I'm not super into tactical gameplay, I find myself launching it and playing a few missions at least every 2 or 3 hours. Its very engaging and I think thats all that needs to be said. If your into strategy games and liked Enemy Unknown, its a must buy, just be wary of Performance issues at launch. You do have a 2 hour refund window, it should be enough time to know if your going to have performance drops. Firaxis, fix your game please, some people can't even play it.
For everyone else though, its a great game, very difficult but a lot of fun.

When I first heard about this game it was pretty early on in its developmental stage of life. I will tell everyone in all honesty that I deeply regret not paying into the kickstarter for this awesome little game.
Besides the excellent voice acting, amazing soundtrack, phenomenal artwork, and simple controls, the game boasts a degree of difficulty and complexity I haven't seen in a game of this type for a while.
For lack of any better definition the game is a rogue-like dungeon crawler with emphasis not on direct player control but on giving the player more of a management position over these adventurers. To explain quickly you hire them, equip them, upgrade them, but for the sake of running missions you only tell them how to attack or use abilities. Part of the management aspect is choosing the right group for the task. There really is no 'one party fits all' in this game as most units mesh well and perform well in the Ruins, but will completely be at a disadvantage in the Weald, Warrens, or Cove. On top of managing what groups go where you also have two status bars to manage. A majority of the game is well within the players hands. You either get too greedy, get caught unprepared, or make poor combat or exploratory decisions and lose a team.
I could go into extreme detail but no one wants another TL:DR review. Instead I'll just give you all the bottom line.

*** EDIT 6/08/2016 ***
Game has had a new update that didn't really do the game any favors. Explained below.
Things it did right
- Added new class
- Added new events
- Balanced current classes out
Things it did wrong
- Added a useless and boring class
- New event is a♥♥♥♥♥♥show
THE NEW CLASS
---------------------------
New class! Yay! Don't celebrate just yet. Antiquarian has some nice perks that should have really made it exciting to have. It looks like a mix between the plague doctor and the grave robber.
The two best moves it has are Festering Vapours (Max level deals -75% damage but adds a -39% blight resist to target and does 4 DOT) and Protect Me (Forces ally to guard her but adds +5 dodge and 30% protection to the ally guarding you). The next best ability is outclassed by the Plague Doctors Battlefield Medicine because it has status recovery, but it's called  Fortifying Vapors and really doesn't give you a reason to bring her over a Plague Doctor.
Her skillset makes her literally the weakest character on the roster damage-wise however she has a passive ability that isn't really defined in-game. Antiquarian boosts your income by enabling your inventory to stack gold to 2k instead of 1.5k, and when you make her loot objects she has a change of recovering antiques which stack to 20 and are worth 275 a piece. And rarer loot which is worth 1k a piece.
The second bonus comes with her camp perks, she has two abilities that don't cost much and can do you some favors. Trinket scrounger and Resupply. Trinket scrounger generates a trinket on command, the rarity is based on chance, but you CAN get a rare or legendary trinket. It's like 1/25 chance. This is actually kinda cool. Resupply is the same thing only it generates a random supply item. It never hurts to generate a Key, extra torches, food or bandages.
Now all this sounds wonderful but this character is NOT built for late game. Taking her into a tier 5 or 6 dungeon is idiocy. She cannot pull her own weight at all and is only useful in dealing blight damage and buffing your tanks protection. If they add additional utility to her existing skills or replace some of them she would be very viable to take into end game fights.
THE NEW EVENT
---------------------------
The new event is a total♥♥♥♥♥♥show. After you hit 40 weeks into your game you have a percentage chance to spawn a bandit attack on your hamlet. The chance is relatively low but since it released I've had it spawn almost every time it comes off its cooldown (2 weeks).
The issue is that you aren't given a way out of this event. When it spawns you have two choices: 1.) Ignore it, and next turn you lose 2 upgrades on a building in your hamlet.
2.) Risk a team and beat it.
Now I'm all for difficulty in my games. I love this game. I enjoy having a challenge. This one just seems to defy how they've done it so far though. You don'y really have any options here. The dungeon itself is really really hard like a Darkest Dungeon run and operates the same way. You quit? Lose one member randomly. Choose to stay and you're likely to lose a team. A dungeon that is THIS hard shouldn't be forced on people and give them negative outcomes if they can't or won't do it. Right now at my level I can choose to just ignore it and rebuild what they destroy but new players or people who have teams able to do it but are unfieldable are going to be faced with having to eat a setback. It's just a RNG roulette where all options are♥♥♥♥♥♥but only one of them is less♥♥♥♥♥♥than the rest.
The boss is not extremely difficult by any stretch of the imagination. He has the standard 200-ish health with average resistances you find in bosses at that level. He summons minions and behaves almost like the 9 Pounder fight. Explosive barrel in place of someone lighting the fuse and whatnot.
A lot of the difficulty comes in the minions he spawns and the minions you fight on your way TO him. They have highwaymen who do the usual blanket fire but this blanket fire does severe damage AND causes stress. They have a lot of fast units to support these highwaymen that cause a lot of bleeds as well. So what you end up with is a lot of stress racking up quickly and if you fail to find the boss after a few rooms you're likely screwed.
The dungeon is classified as SHORT so you can't camp to reduce stress, thus your only option is to bring a jester which isn't bad, but you really need almost an exact party comp to succeed.
I beat it using Jester, Vestal, Arbalest and Leper. Each of these classes is fairly self-sufficient and can heal itself. Leper can self-heal HP and Stress and apply resistances, Vestal is best healer period, Arbalest is a goddamn must against the boss, and if you don't bring a Jester you're not going to win period. And even then I BARELY beat it.
Unlike every other difficult dungeon in the game I did not feel a sense of accomplishment or pride in beating the event. I just felt like I completed an escort mission for a break-even on my monetary rewards and a setback on my roster from all the damn rabies and stress levels. Cue the 'feels bad man' image because doing the event felt... Really bad. If they're going to make something like that totally random they better tone down the difficulty to tier 5 so it's still not a cake-walk but it's not total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If they want to give end-game players something to do maybe add a new area or two that spawn tier 6 dungeons.

Fallout 4 is a great game. Unfortunately for many long-time fans of the Fallout series, it is not a great FALLOUT game. Combat is great and vastly improved over previous games, but the role-playing "actions have an effect on the world" are all but been stripped out.
Fallout 3 was actually pretty weak on role-playing, despite it being one my favorite titles of all time. New Vegas was a far better role-playing game, with many choices to make as far as main story line. But your actions in different terrorities in the game had a serious effect on a number of factors. Prices at stores, hostility, and so on. A lot of those subtler elements of reputation and so on, don't exist in Fallout 4. There are a bunch of choices for allies and endings, but ultimately, they're not all that different. It's hard to really play a "bad guy" in Fallout 4, whereas in New Vegas, you had different and clear "moral" choices you could make as far as story-line, eg siding with Caesar's Legion.
Is Fallout 4 a ton of fun? Yes. Will it probably give you many hours of enjoyment, and is it therefore worth the purchase price? I say yes. But if you ARE a long-time fan of the Fallout series, you need to understand that you will likely be disappointed in regards to the RPG elements of this game. But if you're fine with a more "arcade" style Fallout game, then this is still a really solid title that I think the majority of people out there will still enjoy.

People say time is money, so let's interpret that as this; the money you spend on something is worth a specific amount of time that you use said item for, and if you dont wind up using that item for a specific amount of time (in ratio to the cost) then the item wasn't worth buying. So lets see if Fallout 4 is worth buying then, shall we? Let's start with the cost, which is $30.00 dollars. Let's say that for each penny spent, the ratio dictates that we must spend around one minute in the game. that means that to make fallout 4 worth buying, we would need to spend 3,000 minutes in the game, or 50 hours. A rough estimation says that the main story is around 40 hours long, all sidequests are about 40 to 50 hours alltogether, and exploration of the map as well as any other activities you could do would take about 60 hours to complete. Now, you may ask, "what if I just get bored?", Well, this is a bethesda game, and that means that you will contstantly be wanting more and more until there's just nothing left. at which point you will most likely turn to mods, which will add another 30 to 40 hours, take me for example, iv'e only played for 11 hours at the time of this review, and I already intend to add at least 200 more to that. So in conclusion, is Fallout 4 worth buying?...Yes, Hell yes it is.
P.S. How do I know all this? I bought Skyrim, so trust me, I know how these things go.

I have decided to give this game a qualified thumbs up. For the record, I would have given XCOM Enemy Unknown an unqualified thumbs up.
There are some bugs, and some major optimization problems. Personally, however, I haven't (in 16 hours) come across any game breaking bug (such as a CTD) . Also, I'm lucky enough that the game works fine on my system, although I did have to turn off V-sync and AA, but that doesn't seem to have a negative impact on any other aspect of the game.
The other thing is the infamous turn timer. I don't like this feature, and I have to tell you that my own personal experience is that it's in over 80% of the missions (although others seem to report lower percentages). For many people the turn timers are a deal-breaker, and they're close to being a deal-breaker for me to (although they can be modded out).
However, so many other things about the game are pure XCOM EU/EW, but better. New story. New techs. New equipment. New mechanics (including ******* turn timers!). So there's a lot to love about the new game, and a few things to dislike.
On balance, if your system can run the game, and if you can put up with (or even enjoy) the turn timers, you're probably going to really enjoy this game. Behind the flaws, there is a good game in there.
PS if my system couldn't run the game, I may not have been so charitable!

TL DR: A fascinating game turns into a boring grindfest, skip or wait for rebalance patch
--------------------------------------------------
...And it's a pity, cause I really like this game! The combat is awesome and diverse, the dark atmosphere is perfect, the random nature of the game makes the dungeon runs very fun every single time - overall, this is a great game, let down by two major factors:
1) The Catch-22 equipment upgrades, caused by the fact that your characters level far faster than you generate the necessary money for their upgrades.
so, let's say you've leveled four of your characters from level four to level five. There's a game mechanic where high level characters will refuse to go to low level dungeons (which are beneath their dignity).
So, the four champions can only do level 5 dungeons.
But you can't beat a level 5 dungeon without the equipment upgrades.
But equipment upgrades costs money.
But to get the money you need to beat the level 5 dungeon.
But the champions cannot beat it!
So to solve it, you get a B-team doing the dungeons as well, but then you need to spend money on the B-team! The only solution is to recruit new characters (recruiting level 0 characters is free) and duing suicide runs with them, which is extremely grindy and boring.
But this is nothing compared to...
2) The Endgame
Basically, once your team of four best characters of the highest level, the finest characters, goes into the first level of the final dungeon and beats it...
They can never go there again!
So you level four more best characters for level two of the dungeon.
And they also can't go there again!
So you do it again for level three, and level four.
Assuming no one dies (which is impossible), this is 16 CHARACTERS you need to level up to level 6!
This is the worst game restriction I've ever seen, I don't even know what to compare it with - it's like in Skyrim you would have to start a new character from scratch for every single boss fight.
And for people saying "this is hardcore" - no, this is not hardcore, stupid restrictions to artifically prolong the game's life by making you do a ton of unnesessary work and grindfest are not hardcore!
With these two factors, I cannot recommend the game in its current state.

Darkest Dungeon is a great game, but not for everyone. If you enjoy a game that forces you to figure out mechanics or fail spectacularly this is the game for you. Alternatively you can watch videos / read wikis / whatever, but the fun in it, for me at least, was the game + needing to figure out the ins and outs of all the different skill and battle mechanics to succeed. The only issue I have with this is that it is just sort of dropped on you at the end.
It essentialy goes:
Easy dungeons: You can get through with almost any party comp given you aren't particularly unlucky
Medium dungeons: You generally need to understand what team comps work and play the classes to their advantages OR have weapons / armor / skills fully upgraded.
Hard dungeons: Bad luck can ruin a run the first or second battle, but the key is to always retreat when this is the case. Other than that you have to be a lot smarter about how you maintain your heroes health and sanity by using down turns to keep everyone healthy and to strategically use camping and items.
The Darkest Dungeon: Pending you don't read a tutorial before hand you will almost inevitably fail your first few attempts at each of the four levels simply because you really do need to understand all your heroes, the enemies, and the bosses to do well.
One thing you'll notice about the hardest and end game dungeon is that it sounds like you will likely lose heroes. You probably will. If you get really into the games you play and attached the characters you build up or realy just want to use specific heroes and play only one particular way, you will get angry at the game and you probably won't enjoy it. If you are also prone to rage quitting the game probably isn't for you. Bad things will happen and half the game is figuring out how to salvage the situation or in the worst cases how to build back up to where you were in the most efficient way possible.
All that said, I love Darkest Dungeon. It was everything I hoped it would be when I first saw the original trailer.

Genre - Roguelike Gothic Fantasy
I waited until the full release to post a review as there were a few key things missing from early access like achievements. Now after playing the game some more I can safely recommend it.
Although it is roguelike it plays as a side scrolling dungeon crawler with parties of four. You are situated in a village allowing for weapon and skill upgrades as well as the recruiting of new adventurers (expect some to die along the way). There are quite varied classes, although maybe another tyoe of party healer is required, as there are only two classes that do this role effectively. As you complete each dungeon you get heirlooms, these can then be used to upgrade your village amenites. You can choose out of a few areas at once with bosses along the way to fight, meaning you won't get stuck in just one area with the smae baddies for ages. The combat can be challenging but not impossible (as far as I know, I am still near the start).
What makes this game stand out is the stress effect on your characters as you explore each dungeon. Some are positive but most are negative. For instance they might become abusive to other adventurers increasing their stress or paranoid and avoid being healed etc. To help with this you use the tavern or the abbey to calm them down. Meaning you will constantly be rotating your party for each mission. There are also disease effects to account for and sometimes personal preference like being god fearing etc.
The art style itself is fairly unique and very atmospheric and the voice acting of the plot driver is fantastic.
It is a fun game that pushes the boundaries of the genre and can be played in short doses with persistent progression to your village and characters, if they survive that is...

Fallout 4 is a massive disappointment, and a hard kick in the nads to fans of the earlier games in the series. Bethesda claims that player freedom is their number one priority, in spite of the fact that Fallout 4 has even less freedom than any of the previous games.
None of your actions come with consequences, all you do is kill, get told to kill, fetch, and get told to fetch. Hell, I even remember Bethesda stating that Fallout 4 will support pacifistic playthroughs. Whatever happened to that? One of the earliest missions REQUIRES you to kill a number of raiders. You can't draw them away, you can't make a deal with them, you just kill them. How bland.
Not to mention that it has the worst graphics of any triple-A game from 2015. Compare it to games like The Witcher 3, Mad Max, and even Batman: Arkham Knight. All beautiful games, and Fallout 4, while it has a few good-looking environments, overall looks very ugly. In spite of its overall lack of graphical fidelity, it runs worse than any of the aforementioned games. This is due to the fact that while the textures are lacking in quality, they have been upscaled to a very high resolution. They look no better at 2048x2048 than the 512x512 textures featured in Bethesda's previous title, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. The volumetric lighting system and god rays are also at fault for bad performance, in spite of the fact that they just look average at best.
One of the advertised merits of Fallout 4 is that the player can be whoever they want. This is false. The player can be one of two characters. A pre-war American ex-army soldier who was frozen in a vault for 210 years, or his wife, a woman with a law degree who was frozen in a vault for 210 years. In Fallout: New Vegas, while it was certain that you were a courier who had carried at least two deliveries, your backstory was otherwise vague. You could have been a BoS deserter, a prospector, or even an ex-marine/woman with a law degree who was frozen in a vault. The choice was yours. Bethesda should never have restricted the player's freedom.
The dialogue system has also been stunted, as Bethesda shoehorned in voice acting for the protagonist for no proper reason. Because of this, there are only four dialogue options at any given time. Most of the time, they are just variations of the same answer. At one point I even remember that literally walking away at one point had the same effect as saying yes. Absolutely stupid.
Not to mention that Bethesda has retconned or ignored so much obvious lore in many places. You've probably heard of the whole pre-war jet fiasco and the kid-in-the-fridge quest, so I don't need to expand this much futher.
Fallout 1 and 2 are hardcore turn-based roleplaying games. New Vegas is a roleplaying game with a few shooter aspects. Fallout 4, however is a mindless shooter with few aspects of a roleplaying game. It does not fit in with the rest of the series, and is overall just a bad game. Every time I try playing it I just get bored and give up. The world doesn't react to me. It feels like I'm just watching it. Because of this, I don't recommend Fallout 4 at all.
That's being generous.
In all honesty, it's garbage. Unless they pull some serious magic out of their asses, I'm never buying a game made by Bethesda Game Studios again.
Seeing as making a crappy pandering game like Fallout 4 can only rack in billions from deceived consumers, Bethesda has decided to add microtransactions to A FREAKING SINGLE-PLAYER GAME. Yes, Creation Club addons are not just paid mods, they're microtransactions. Pay a little bit of real-world money for some ingame currency to spend on little pieces of content.
Typical for a big AAA company that doesn't care about core gamers to add features that are purely for profit. Five bucks for a gun. Five bucks for a backpack. Just stupid. It hasn't changed my opinion of the base game one bit, though. I always thought it was trash. Now it's just trash with microtransactions.

The overall gameplay is fun, exciting, engulfing. The turn based style fits it well and the abilities and classes are all different so you can feel the excitement of leveling up and making progress in dungeons. The stress mechanic is an interesting and overall good concept. It really adds another level to the game. The RNG ( Random Number Generator, which is what determines what happens, if you hit, how much damage you give or receive etc. etc. etc.) however is something that needs a bit of work, especially in combat. The RNG seems to favor bad things happening to you. Traps going off, enemies getting multiple turns before your party gets any, often times resulting in enemy teams getting all of its hits in and you getting 2-3 instead of 4. Your strikes often tend to miss and your teammates turn into idiots when the stress mechanic and the RNG combine. When they get stressed they often times won’t do anything, will hurt themselves despite low health or being on deaths door (which is the games version of the next hit you receive has a RNG chance of killing you) and refusing any sort of help from the rest of your team, whether that be healing or switching places or buffing. This is an issue because you can only heal and get stress down while in combat. Outside of the dungeon your party automatically heals and there are "stress relief options" but the stress relief options cost an insane amount of money often meaning you have to throw your idiots with high stress right back into a dungeon to doom themselves and everyone else and that’s only if they made it out in the first place. There is a way to upgrade things in your town to be cheaper and easier but the problem is you need items from dungeons to do this and to enter dungeons and get money and treasure you need a bit of money in the first place. So between upgrades for the town and the cost of entering dungeons and the cost of stress relief so your party is useful, you can often times run out of money and have to send a party into a dungeon with no supplies. This can work but often times gets you killed. This makes it so unforgiving that I had to put the game down for a while to calm down and come back. Arguably the game is supposed to be this unforgiving and stressful.
Overall: This game is great fun, even if it manages to ♥♥♥♥ you off constantly with the "it can and will get worse RNG"
It is definitely replayable and it is a game that you can just sink hours and hours into, it is a game that I want to sink hours and hours into, but if the RNG is just against you it makes it hard.
I would give the game an 9.0 out of 10.

REVIEW AS OF 9/5/2015: Version Pleased Giraffe
SUMMARY: A universe-exploring and building game with procedurally generated worlds, crafting, construction, colonization - and a sense of humor.  Even in its Early Access state it offers an incredible amount of content and things to do.  Worth purchasing, worth supporting - and worth enjoying - for any fan of adventure/crafting games.
Starbound is a procedurally-generated space adventure where an entire galaxy is created randomly (don't worry, you can swap planet coordinates with friends or game together).  A refugee of one of six races, you end up in a broken-down, out-of-fuel spaceship above a random world, and your adventure begins.  Early quests lead you through surviving in a kind of "Robinson Curose in space" adventure, where you learn to craft, build, mine, and so on. Once you've got your ship in some state of repair, you hook up with an outpost full of refugees, and your adventure's scope encompasses the universe.
You can take on quests, kick around, or do whatever you want - though following quests does unlock more equipment and options so you'll want to chase those down.  As you adventure, you'll travel a proceduraly-generated galaxy, wander over randomly-generated 2D worlds, encounter various environments, find towns, build buildings, fight monsters (unique to each world), and try and unlock the mystery of the game.
Crafting and farming are a big part of the game, and Starbound delivers.  You unlock various pieces of technology, raise a variety of crops, and build structures for whatever reason you want.  Customize your character with clothes, weapons,  armor, equipment, and special "Tech" abilities.  There's always something new to try or find, and it gets addictive to keep experimenting; making an item may unlock new items, raising a new crop can unlock recipies, new equipment leads to new items.
Feel lonlely? Then you can even add characters to the setting.  Find a nice planet, set up some buildings, place electronic "Colony Deeds", and populate your new world (and enjoy the benefits of rent).  Or maybe your farrmstead isn't something you live out of, so get a colony deed and get yourself a buddy to watch the place when you're gone.
Maybe you don't want to settle down or want to travel in style?  Work on expanding your ship by doing missions and getting the Outpost shipyard to help you out.  With more space you can build kitchens, rec rooms, labs, and more.  If you want a crew, you can post Colony Deeds inside your own craft and summon up your own crew of hackers, merchants, scientists, cultits, or whatever you want.  Plus they pay rent to live onboard!
Because of the procedural generation, the game also has some magic moments that can surprise you.  Travel a savanna as a gas giant fills the sky at night.  Discover a peaceful village . . . right as a meteor shower strikes.   Mine into a cavern filled with valuable materials.  Find a forest of beautiful trees unlike any other you've seen.   Dig underground and find hidden complexes. There's always a wonder awaiting you.
"Always something new" really describes all of Starbound.
The game as of this review has now implemented plot progression, story, and colonization, so there's now something "going on" for the game.  Yes, it's not finished, but you may not even notice when you're building your space farm, mining deep into a planet, colonizing a planet, or turning your ship into a flying town.
For the price, Starbound already provides an absolutely grand adventure.  But when you pick it up, you can also participate in the active, passionate community.  The devs are backing this game and always listening.  For a "not done yet" game it's amazing - it's worth your time, your money, and your support.
Starbound is one of the few games I consider a "must buy" for anyone into this genre.

Spiral Knights.....what have you turned into. Spiral Knights is a top-down, 2.5D (Can you call it 2.5D? Maybe it's more 3D than anything...) P2P Er I mean *Cough* F2P MMORPG where you run around and kick some monster butt like you did back in the days of the SNES with Legend of Zelda...but with a much better combat system (you would think). Lets start with the basics.
(Read farther if you please. Basic Synopsis- Casual gamer=SK is a good choice. Want more polish? Keep looking.
1; Graphics 7.5/10
Not exactly the greatest but not the worst either. What really makes this game so inviting is it's art style which is btw AMAZING! Everything looks awesome even though textures, models, and shading aren't top notch.
2; Community ?/?
I never really had anything to do with the community...maybe played every once 'n a while with strangers but I never really traded with anyone and that crap. Maybe someone else could answer that for you Mr/Ms viewer of my review (Really? I had to break the 4th wall?)
3; Soundtrack/SoundEffects 8/10
The sound track is really good. It has this feel of going on an adventure and discovering things like what a game like this should be. Every level has a nice theme that plays well with it, from volcanic forests to frozen devilite business offices to a ruin full of slimes. The sound effects are good too. Not much else to say for the sounds.
4;Leveling system.... Doesn't even need a rating....
First off, WHY DOES TAKE ME A YEAR JUST SO I CAN GO UP ONE GOD DARN RANK!?!?!? Before that I was zipping through the ranks like it was nothing! Then I got stuck trying to get to 4*, and I had to play for what like ages just so i could get my 5* armor.  I'm not saying that having to work to get to your rank is bad, but they way it has been implemented in this present edition of SK is ridiculous. Before (I'm sure most of you already know this who have been reading the reviews for hours now) the game had you collect heat (exp) that leveled up you're gear. What happened when it capped? IT LEVELED UP! WOW! IT CAN LEVEL UP! What happens now? You cap...and have to play for another 3 months just so you can get some stupid fire cyrstals to level up your gear BUT WAIT THERE'S MORE! NOT ONLY DO YOU HAVE TO GRIND FOREVER, YOU HAVE A CHANCE TO FAIL IN THE FORGE AND HAVE TO DO IT ALL OVER AGAIN! Isn't that just the sweetest thing ever.....NO! And the only thing you can do to make it work is have so much fire crystals for a 100% chance rate of working. I hate it so much. Oh and if you think I'm lying about spending months leveling up you just wait until you're Knight Elite...you just wait.
5; Gameplay 8/10
The gameplay is pretty solid. Basic 123 slash with pistol and a choice of using an explosive (which are overpowered if used with the right loadout). You can dogde and shield bash and defend and is relativley solid. Now, don't get GAMEPLAY confused with "Difficulty." In reality, the game isn't that hard, and it functions well. Now...for the really negative stuff.
6; "Difficulty" 2/10
.....Where do I start...Hm...I know. You know those things called defenses on your armor, like elemental defense, pierce defense, shadow defense, those things? Yeah um...those don't matter at all. If you play the game on normal you "should" be fine, advanced you might need some help, and expert you're going to need a really good loadout with lightning reflexes and friends who have a ton of sparks (I'll get to sparks soon enough). Now, why did I say "should" for normal....well here's the thing.....All difficulties, have the same amount of enemies....and there are ALOT of enemies...and they do the SAME amount of damage no matter what difficulty...the difficulty just decides how much health they have. They do the same amount of damage because of the game's elevator and depths. The elevator is your level transition, and you're depths are you're "difficulty." That little slide bar does nothing except make a tier 1 gremlin take 3 hits instead of 2 and alter the spawn rate of certain drops. So you will constantly be having to fight what looks like 15 zombies at all times that do the same amount of damage at that specific depth. Forgot to mention why you're defenses don't matter...they don't matter because of what has just been stated and, you don't just face the enemies specified in the level, you fight ALTERED enemies as well. So instead of fighting a Elemental only Gremlin, you'll fight an Elemental Shadow Gremlin. O_o What? But...I have the armor? Nope. Doesn't matter. The only difference is instead of taking half a health bar they take like a quarter. The only thing I have to say is awesome is being able to live with 1% health. If you are MLG enough to play this game with 1% health I salute you! You can't get 1 shotted by enemies because of this, all you need is above 1% to land in that "Crisis mode."
7; Enemyvariaty/Enemies  8/10-1/10
Lets just get this straight, there are alot of creative enemies with alot uniqueness to them. They are pretty darn cool. First, a disclosure: In about two years, I had clocked in about 130 hours of playtime in Terraria, a game that has been endearing to me in many levels and will hold fond memories for me.
However, when I picked up Starbound, I've already clocked in over 200 hours
.
Starbound holds on to the 2D sandbox core that Terraria started and kicks it up to another level in many different vectors. For starters, it has lore/logical in-gameplay explenations for the necessity to explore multiple planets for riches and resources instead of having to exit and re-create a world in Terraria, which I found to more appealing than I thought it would be.
Crafting is expanded upon, with more varied flavor items (many unique cooking recipes that vary from race) and a simplified system for those who love decorating but only are able to retrieve so many things from a dungeon run, thanks to a lampshaded currency-to-object item replication system. And there are MANY themes of decor, ranging from 1960's totalitarianesque dormitories, high tech matter-fabrication doompyramids, and even pseudo-mideval greasepunk robotics. If you can encounter a theme in the game, you can replicate the look for your own homebase. The game developers even hint at the prospect of being able to terraform planets you conquer, so you can truly take decorating your home base to a new level.
There's game lore and interesting race dynamics. Vendors and villages and an almost Skyrim-esque question in whether or not to destroy peaceful settlements or lord over their resources. Dungeons are many and highly rewarding. Weapons, while highly random in traits, have extremely fun design elements. A grenade launcher that fires a small pig with dynamite bundled to it and hones in to your target, shotguns that shoot white fire orbs that either explode on target impact or detonate on the ground later on, and giant Teslea coil staves that shoot lightning are some potentiates for your arsenal.
Progression through the various armor sets and planetary sectors is completely on your own terms. You won't face your first boss until you're set and ready for it -- which may, for some, be a complaint for those who would use sandboxing to wall off dangerous attacks. On the other hand, you won't suddenly have a structure-destroying UFO blowing up your home just because you happened to aquire a lot of health boosts on a digging run. Your first planet even has quests that assist you in figure out what is going on around you and how crafting and survival works. A hunger and warmth system puts the torch to your backside to help you keep motivated in your construction, production and exploration.
One of the biggest pluses for this over Terraria, however, is that this game was made with modding in mind, even with the official site having a mod hub ready for sharing community creations. Already with this game only being a few months old in the hands of fans, there is already a thriving modding community. If there is something I could point to that I would say boosts the life of any sandbox game to epic amounts, it would have to be good modding support and this game
While plain that the game is very unfinished (some items lack descriptions still, semi-frequent crashes, and item/monster strength issues that crop up fairly often) and still adding in many features, the game as it is now is a joyous experience. If you had enjoyed Terraria, or even Minecraft, to any degree you will love Starbound.

I have decided to give this game a qualified thumbs up. For the record, I would have given XCOM Enemy Unknown an unqualified thumbs up.
There are some bugs, and some major optimization problems. Personally, however, I haven't (in 16 hours) come across any game breaking bug (such as a CTD) . Also, I'm lucky enough that the game works fine on my system, although I did have to turn off V-sync and AA, but that doesn't seem to have a negative impact on any other aspect of the game.
The other thing is the infamous turn timer. I don't like this feature, and I have to tell you that my own personal experience is that it's in over 80% of the missions (although others seem to report lower percentages). For many people the turn timers are a deal-breaker, and they're close to being a deal-breaker for me to (although they can be modded out).
However, so many other things about the game are pure XCOM EU/EW, but better. New story. New techs. New equipment. New mechanics (including ******* turn timers!). So there's a lot to love about the new game, and a few things to dislike.
On balance, if your system can run the game, and if you can put up with (or even enjoy) the turn timers, you're probably going to really enjoy this game. Behind the flaws, there is a good game in there.
PS if my system couldn't run the game, I may not have been so charitable!

"There is no such thing as difficulty in a game which requires no skill." -ldubx
The RNG is so horrible in this game it isn't funny and puts BloodBowl to shame. Typical bad luck in games is failing a few rolls in a row. Darkest Dungeon bad luck is 6 fails, 5 enemy crits, 4 bleeds, 3 stuns, 2 characters going insane/skipping their turns, and a 1 point heal in a pear tree.
Darkest Dungeon is essentially a board game with only one player where you play against the DM, you may or may not reach the end, and put the game back into the box when you're done. No real surprises, repetitve gameplay, lack of multiplayer etc. It's only worth it if you're a compulsive gambler who's content the prize is absolutely nothing and the odds are heavily in favor of the house. It cheats worse than the NES games I grew up with which is saying a hell'vea lot.
My first run ever for instance resulted in 3 party members developing paranoia, skipping 4 entire turns in a row, the same monster critting 3x in a row during a single fight, and 3 out of 4 party member deaths by the 4th room. If I wasn't warned about the horrible balance and randomness of this game in advance I would uninstall and get a refund asap. The lack of multiplayer is another strike against it, because I feel it would be perfect if an opposing human player could controll the monster NPCs during encounters like a genuine Dungeon Master.
On the up side at the price of $19.99 I feel that's worth it for the hand drawn art and superp narration to an otherwise frustrating, generic dungeon crawler that players only sink high amounts of time into due to the cruel and unfair RNG system forcing them to start over again and again. If there was a neutral way to recommend this game I would, but Steam requires only positive or negative so this game's getting a NEGATIVE review due to the poor first impression it left.
Even after sinking more hours into Darkest Dungeon, I'm not impressed with how poor the RNG algorythms and they detract from the rest of the game's enjoyment to the point there will be absolutely no reasons to replay this title once a player slogs through it the first time. This game is one of those stamps onto the man-card that millennials are going nuts for, yet the irony is it's one big inside joke to watch fanboys squeel with joy over a game that takes absolutely no skill at all and simply plays out like a choose your own mis-adventure graphic novel.

The reviews here that I looked over are thick with fanboyism, it's time to be honest about Starbound. (TLDR version included at bottom).
Starbound has a lot of great ideas and the future of the game is moderately promising. However, it seems the game creators bit off more than they can chew, and are a bit more concerned with being silly than making a great game.
Starbound touts endless planets. The problem is that the planets don't differ from one another apart from cosmetics. Sure, you may run into a prison facility on one planet, but quickly find everything there to be useless and not interesting. Go on to the next planet and you find an egyptian-like tomb. Anything of value there? Sorry but no. The only nice things about these places is you can demolish them to take the materials to build your own house (which of course is pretty neat, but still not a great consolation prize). Sidequests? Story? These things really aren't in the game yet, despite fanboys claiming they are.
Starbound updates have fixed the combat system since beta release, so it's decent now (hooray!) but most of the other additions have been minor. EXPORATION IS STILL MOSTLY POINTLESS. For example: you can build a tower up into space and find astroids, but there is nothing in the astroids to harvest. This is an example of exploration everywhere: you will find cool looking things that serve no purpose.
The item system is annoying as well. Starbound operates in a tiered system, which creates an endless quest of: Find ore 1, make armor 1, go to planet 2, find ore 2, make armor 2, go to planet 3 and so on. This makes exploraton even less exciting, because there are very few things to find which are more valuable than the next ore for the next armor you need. Recent reviews with Tiy (one of the lead devs) show that the tier system is here to stay. SOURCE:

Granted, much in that interview does sound exciting, but so far the developers have delievered on a very minor fraction of what they have promised, so don't expect to see any of those ideas come into the game for at least a year.
The upside is that this game is still in Beta, and though I DO NOT recommend it now, give it a couple years and it will probably have most of the cool things promised which will actually make it worthwhile. I look forward to this game as being even better than Terraria, but for now, it's pretty pointless.
TLDR: The Beta for starbound shows the fetal stages of promise, but ultimately fails to deliver on important mechanics, such as planetary differences, and rewards for adventuring/exploring. They made a large world, then filled it with a whole lot of nothing.

You will either love or hate this game. The timer mechanic is fantastic if you like gritty missions where failure and complete squad loss occurs (best played with Ironman). If you liked to go through every mission near-flawlessly and perfectly level up your squad and seldom lose soldiers or missions, you probably won't like X-COM 2. It's tone is substantially changed from the first one due to the inclusion of the timer mechanic. Or you can save your soilders by aborting the mission, which is my current go-to option. The gritty pace extends to base management and the global map, and in terms of that, I'm much more lukewarm, because it almost requires you to play the game multiple times to know the importance of timing of plot events. But that kind of existed in X-COM 1 as well - i.e. the base attack.
On the downside, the graphics are basically the same as X-COM 1 (trivial improvements) and the performance is much worse, probably because of some random default graphics setting that I haven't yet tried to tweak. Edit: I tried tweaking a few settings, and the game still stutters on a i7-6700k@4.5Ghz, 980gtx, 16gb ram, ssd. There are also a few graphical glitches and a few minor but noticeable bugs here and there. Definitely less polished than earlier releases.
Still, a great game. Oh, and a word of advice: Don't be afriad to call in an emergency evac - despite the mission objectives - sometimes is necessary to overcome spikes in difficulty due to random generation of terrain and alien patrols. Overall, I'd rank this game as better than Enemy Unknown, but somewhat less than Enemy Within.

Bought this because of the hype and good reviews, wasn't like what I expected
Played this on Legendary and these are my opinions:
The turn based was confusing, you have two actions per turn for each of your soldier so you can move to another position and then shoot, sounds normal right? The problem is, you can't do it vice versa. If you didn't move to a new position, but chose to shoot, that will count as 2 actions and you will have to move on to the next soldier. No 2 actions for ya! And they didn't mention this in the tutorial, you have to figure it out yourself.
Second is the range, you have and got no idea how further out is your soldiers' and enemies' range. You just have to estimate it. Once I have a soldier in overwatch and he shot across the whole screen and other times didnt even trigger it. This also applies to how far they can move, you just really have to go with all the highlighted areas appear on the map.
Third is the fog of war, way too confusing, there are times you can see the enemies behind a wall or cover way across the map, but some times you can't. I didn't know how this works, it's just really unreliable.
Fourth, I don't know if this was a bug or anything but once it was my turn and I moved next to a red highlighted area but didnt touch it or moved pass it but I got detected right off the bat, keep in mind I still have two soldiers left to move. Also I made some characters in the characters pool and they appeared in the game with only the same name and appearance but not the classes I chose.
Fifth is the chance system, I know it's supposed to be realistic when nothing is guaranteed 100% but this sometimes may just ruined your stategy. Like one time I have two soldiers couldn't hit an officer with 60% chance but that same officer killed both within two shots and they were both in cover, and no I didn't got flanked either. I just have really bad luck.
Finally, the game did a really bad job in showing the aliens' abilities. You don't know what the hell their abilities are the first time you meet them. Maybe they showed it in the prequel but new players like me had a hard time dealing with it.
There are other small things like, you're not sure if some material in the game can be destroyed or not. Bullets go through wall, other times not. Sometimes my soldier caught on fire standing near a fire some other times not. It's just really really unreliable.
In conclusion, this game was a bit of a disapointment for me. Not because I failed to play on Legendary but because of the inconsistent, unreliable and confusing gameplay mechanics.

so i have finished the game together with all dlcs and i have one thing to say, i am hoocked. this game was kinda my life for a week or two. now i am preparing to go into ng+
so, seem as though i guess i am not so much a casual player anymore lemme start a more serious and in depth review.
-for mouse and keyboard users such as myself, this game shouldn't pose a challenge. it is easy to get the hang of the controls and i found no need to make any changes myself
-now this game is the type of easy to learn, hard to master. the basic controls are easy to learn, but throughout the game new little mechanics will pop up, helping or hindering you against new foes.
-speaking of which, the enemies in this game are amazing. each area has new enemies with different attacks, making memorising attack patterns a must. of course there are exceptions, like rats been in every sewer like area and some ram like creature been in 2 areas (can someone pls eplain why they are in such different enviroments?)
-there are many weapons and armor sets you can collect. but armor is pretty useless in this game, at least that is what many people and i have discovered. just put on the armor that makes you look the most badass. all weapons have a special move that vary from healing to defense to damage and buffs. (i am not including magic because i have yet to actually make such a character)
-the multiplayer of this game can be a real upgrade to the game or a real downside. there are 2 gamemodes (3 if you own any of the two dlc). there is the friendly phantom, which is used for players that want help with a boss or area in general and there is pvp, which is self explenatory. now there is a feature called invasion, which is when a red phantom (the pvp guy) invades your world. they will try to kill you. note that invasions happen only when you are embered, something that you will find out in the game. point is, you are safe as long as you not embered.
-there are also covenants. these can either act as ways to assist the player (with bosses or against invaders) or they are pvp covenants, which is where you are summoned to another world as an invader to kill the "tresspasser" of an area. doing these covenant "duties" rewards you with ites and spells. please note that the following covenants, some of which are pvp and others co-op take quite a while for you to be summoned to various reason. the covenants watchdogs of farron, darkmoon blades and blue sentinels.
-bosses are all very nicely designed and all have their own unique patterns and fighting styles. where as others might be slow but strong, others can be fast and nimble, but still strong as all hell.
-now the thing that casuals like me are waiting for in this review. is the game hard? yes, yes it is. is it as hard as it shows in most youtube videos? no by dear god it is not. the game is difficult, and will leave you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at many points, but none of the bosses are impossible to beat. even if they are for whatever reason, you can summon other players to help you out with the boss. it is what most soul veterans on youtube say, tough but fair.
-a few words for the dlc. in my opinion, it isn't worth it full price, but if you can grab them at a discount or the season pass at a discount it really is. one dlc adds an area which is a very different but welcome change in enviroment, taking you to a snowy mountain type area, where as the other dlc takes you to a more familiar setting. both dlcs add quite a few new spells, weapons and armor sets with their own unique abilities.
overall i will give this game a 9/10.

I love this game. It's easily my favorite of all the Fallout series (and I have played every one, except Brotherhood of Steel).
The main plot centers around your quest to find your missing son. I found this a lot more motivating than 'hey, the colony needs you to fetch a widget'. You have a personal reason for being out there, other than your own survival. During the course of the main question, you will find four main factions that you can ally with in order to accomplish your goals. Each faction has different motivations and perks, so they actually have more personality than some other games, where factions are essentially enemies two armies vying to control everything.
While similar to previous fallout games, the mechanics have changed quite a bit. While some people don't like them, I think that they work very well, and I was pleased with the changes overall. (I think some people are just resistant to change.)
One big difference is the perk system, which completely replaces the skill system. (No more skills.) I love this system. There are a ton of perks that you can put points into to make you better at certain things, or give you special abilities. Each perk is linked to an attribute, so you have to have certain attribute levels to unlock certain perks. This makes logical sense. Endurance perks make you tougher, strength perks help melee combat, agility helps stealth, etc... (I like one luck perk that gives extra experience to stupid people.)
Another major difference is in the way power armor works. Power armor now functions like a vehicle. You can enter and exit at any time, you have to supply it fuel, and you have to repair it. But, you can customize it quite a bit, mixing and matching parts, and even giving it custom paint schemes. The fuel requirements means that you won't spend the entire game in power armor, but certain perks can help you use fuel more efficiently, allowing you to use it more often.
The gun mod system from Fallout NV is back, and better than ever, IMHO. Guns are assembled from different parts, so you can take the parts you want off of guns you find and use them to assemble a weapon of your choice. It gives a huge amount of variety to the weapons. Even melee weapons can be modded, but to a smaller extent than guns.
One new system I don't like is the ability to run settlements. You can help settlers establish settlements and protect them against raiders, and even construct buildings. I found that this was too much work for too little reward, so I generally skip this facet. (Like most everything in the game, it's entirely optional.)
The game is set around Boston. I found the setting similar to Fallout 3, with a main city area and a lot of outlying rural areas. (I didn't like the setting of Fallout NV much. It seemed mostly empty, but the civilized places were TOO civilized.) It seems to be a good mix or rural/urban, and wild/civilized. There are some historic landmarks to visit, although nothing comparable to the DC setting of Fallout 3. The good thing is that you don't have to go through a subway system to access the Boston interior, like you did in Fallout 3. You can just walk straight in.
Overall, I love this game, and consider it the best in the series. The DLC is good, too, particularly Far Harbor and Nuka World. I highly recommend it.

As a bored college student, I have two very limited factors in my life: time and money. As such, I try to find games that are cheap, have plenty of content, and can be picked up and put down in a small amount of time. Darkest Dungeon delivers all of these aspects as well as a great setting that is only bolstered by the art, music, and narration.
Gameplay:
Darkest Dungeon is a Rouge-lite 3rd person horror rpg that puts an emphasis on struggling for resources and the mortality of your party members. Combat is turn based, and offers a ton of challenge due to the game's stress feature which can cause your party members to gain quirks, or have heart attacks and die.
Art and Music:
Darkest Dungeon's art fits the name quite well: gritty and dark motif that takes ideas and concepts from the likes of H.P. Lovecraft and Clive Barker. Not a moment is spent without a sort of grotesque abomination, or some sort of foreboding scene. The music is hard to describe, but it does its job perfectly. In your town, the music gives a desolate feeling, while in one of the dungeons the music is non existant until a fight happens at which point the music is grating and fast paced, giving a sense of urgency.
Narration:
All of the games story is done through narration in the style of Bastion. The narrator's voice is beyond a perfect fit for the setting, and there is no shortage of lines he says to either make you feel empowered, or hopeless in the middle of a battle.
Length of Play:
Each dungeon takes about 10-20 minutes to complete depending on what level of dungeon it is and what the objective is. This is perfect as it allows for breaks to be taken and ample opportunities to quit without losing any progess.
Price:
The game is $20, which I think is a good price for this game as it holds many hours of quality content. If it's on sale, then it's just even more value right there.

Although I may have only played Fallout 4 for 100+ hours, I should mention that I got a physical copy of the game near its initial release. And I am not too impressed with the game.
At first impression, I was amazed by the new graphics the game sported, a weather system and better gun play. But those were the only good things until I encountered multiple glaring issues. The game doesn't have much progression to it. You basically start at Sanctuary. And very early in the game, you fight a Deathclaw, whilst also being equipped with a full power armour suit and a minigun. This defeats any feeling of progression that the other Fallout games had, where you had to work to get very powerful weapons and armor. The new S.P.E.C.I.A.L system is nice but it completely forgets about being able to have specific character traits based on their skills like in Fallout 3 and New Vegas. For the sake of example, you could have your character be extremely lucky but not very intelligent. But here, it becomes pointless since you can obtain all 70 perks in the game. This completely defeats the purpose of creating an unique character as you will always make a character with these perks: Armorer, Gun Nut, Locksmith and Hacker.
Additionally, the dialogue elements in Fallout 4 are a complete joke. You are only given 4 options for dialogue, it's either asking a question about a specific quest or persuasion option, Yes, No or Sarcastic (yes). Basically this removes a major part of the RPG elements that the other Fallout games had, since the game becomes very linear.

In other words, the story is extremely lazy, linear and dissapointing. Completely removing the options for multiple endings that the other Fallout games had is inexcusable.
Lastly, the building system in Fallout 4 is very clunky and a pain to use. But on a positive note, if you get it work you can build almost anything creative or unique. With the use of mods, you can get other building types to make other kind of creations that the base game doesn't allow and also improves the building system to make it less clunky and allows to clip through the ground or make them float. Modding is the only feature that will help keep Fallout 4 alive for another year or two and the DLC that is released for the game are also very boring and waste of money. The DLC Vault-Tec Workshop gives you a few, very short quests and the option to build a vault anywhere, only for the price of $4.99. Whilst with a mod "Build your own Vault" (you can find it at Nexus mods), you get to build a vault as well but you get to do it underground, which makes more sense than having all of the buildable pieces sitting around outside, looking ugly. All for the price of free.
But overall, as a base game, Fallout 4 is a very flawed and dissapointing game that lacks in a lot of areas that made Fallout 3 and New Vegas very replayable and enjoyable. If you want to play a good Fallout game, I suggest buying Fallout New Vegas, or get Fallout 4 at a very cheap price. I cannot recommend this game to anyone except for die-hard fans of the series.

If you’re into difficult, fantasy heavy RPGs – this is an absolutely fantastic game. Brilliant atmosphere, stellar writing and deep, strategic mechanics makes every victory more rewarding and every defeat another puzzle to solve. Yes, like many turn-based games, there is a bunch of RNG thrown at you but don’t let that deter you. The UI is fantastic and every step is shown to the player with clarity and precision. And like a good poker game, it’s all about playing your luck to your advantage and knowing when to fold your hand and retreat.
With 14 varied classes, all with their pros and cons – you will find your daily thoughts getting lost into ideal combinations and positions for your characters. Unique mechanics like stress, light levels and camping skills all serve to enhance your connection with these 2D characters that feel more alive than whatever AAA publishers have come up with in the last few years.
It is definitely worth trying out – and you’ll know if this game is for you in the first hour so refunding is always an option. A highly recommended game and one of the most fun experiences I’ve had in a long time.
