Having played this for some time now I could not recommend it in good taste. There is simply too many times where the games major mechanics are shown to be shallow and unfinished, or enemy types bland and uninteresting. The stress system seems interesting at first but quickly devolves into a second health bar that you can't reliably heal back to acceptable levels, combined with every other enemy having massive stress damage attacks makes progression painful and unrewarding.
Another issue is player control. In one of Valves in game commentaries for Half-Life 2 they stated that the best thing a developer can do is to never take control away from the player, even if they aren't actually in control they should at least feel as if they have some say in what happens in a situation. Darkest Dungeon takes player control away so often that it's bordering on absurdity. Randomly given quirks randomly cause your character to make random arbitrary choices in combat and at town, making it seem like you have no say at all in what happens in your party. Even if you complete a hard dungeon with 0 stress across the board theres still a hefty chance of your characters gaining up to two character destroying traits that make them dead weight and functionally dead to you.
The next issue is the diversity and balance of each of the dungeons. There's a forest, a ruin, a cove, and a city for the main dungeons. Each of these supposedly has a diverse set of enemies and challenges to face, but if you examine them closely they are nearly carbon copies of one another. The ruins has skeletons that act the same as the coves fish people, the cultists have a spellcaster that has nearly the same spells as the coves fish spellcaster, the pigs have the same support abilities as the fungal growths in the forest.
The main cause of all this sameness stems from the games shallow combat system, there are only two DOT's, one stun type, forced movement attacks and then normal damage with crits. This is not a recipe for replayability at all. There are simply too few ways for the enemy to fight the player, leading to stagnation. The game tries to add another layer of complexity in its stress system, but it falls flat, with it being a near unmanagable mess of too much stress and too few ways to mitigate it within the dungeon itself. The few characters that can mend stress heal it for so little as to not be worth it, why waste turns stress healing when you could be killing the enemy to stop the stress from being placed to begin with? The stress system is also very bottom heavy, it mostly affects newer characters and seems to dissappear by level 2-3, mostly serving to kill off fresh characters by having a skeleton splash wine on them for 10 rounds.
The stat system is also very oddly designed. Dodge works like in most games, by serving as a way to completely mitigate damage in echange for reliability, but most characters will not high high enough dodge stats to take advantage of it, and will instead opt in for the much more realiable and plentiful PROT stat which functions as a flat damage reduction. Most enemies also seems to have either 100% accuracy attacks, or attacks that hit so hard that even taking the chance of focusing on dodge and having it fail makes prot all the more worth while. Why even have the chance of taking a 20 damage attack on a 22 Health character when you can always reduce that 20 damage to 10 or less?
Sadly Darkest Dungeon is a trainwreck of balance issues and poorly implemented game mechanics overlaid with amazing art and stellar sound and voice work. It simply isn't worth the $20 in its current state, and likely never will be.

Where can I even begin with the Dark Souls story-line? The world is so big, so expansive, it's like reading a book to understand the whole lore of what has happened in this universe. Words cannot describe how beautifully written this whole series is, the gothic feeling of it all. The feeling of despair, loss, and regret fills this universe up. The way the world has been sapped of so much, how it's former glory is no more, especially in this third installment.
If you have an itch for a gritty lonesome tale, Dark Souls will fulfill that desire to the fullest. For in the Dark Souls universe, you are not a known hero, you are not constantly praised, you are simply placed in this universe to fulfill your duty. To continue the vicious cycle of "Life". You may find out various pieces of lore within item descriptions, and some pieces can be linked together to tell a full tale. If you wish to look further into the lore, it is simply spread out through-out gameplay, you must look closer to reveal it. All in all, the tale of Dark Souls is a dark, lonely and treacherous road. To those who have played Dark Souls 1, an old foe returns during the final fight of this game..I'll let you figure out who.
As said in the other Dark Souls games, Dark Souls 3 continues it's lock on & dodge system of course. However in Dark Souls 3, the combat is very much polished. The pacing of the combat is quite fast as well, much faster than the previous Dark Souls games, excellent timing is required to dodge some of the later game's bosses. As with previous games, "Trial & Error" is still very much applied to the third installment - you
die. Now, I've noticed that during PvP it seems hitboxes are effected in a certain way - For instance, if you swing just as someone is duck-rolling, it would make the sound effect & blood splatter as if you hit them when in reality, you did not!
I would not recommend PvPing to new-comers to this game, train a little and get a feel of what can happen with the enemies that are shown before you. Until recently I've noticed that Dark Souls 3 has a meta, and some can say the previous games have not had this before. For instance, if you're just becoming a high enough level to where most people PvP, you will see nothing but Ultra-Greatswords & Hyperarmour! But alas, if you're feeling up to it, proceed with PvP! A good tip for new-comers when PvPing is if an opponent comes at you, count their swings, this will give you a good idea when they will not have enough stamina to attack back/dodge away!
The soundtrack is incredibly epic in this installment, the vibes that come from the music really hit home with what you're fighting. In some cases, these tales are told with the music that is being played when you are fighting them. The lyrics, the opera, is all so dramatic and that's exactly what the game is going for - It's dramatic and dark, even epic! Yuka Kitamura & Motoi Sakuraba knew what they were doing when composing such tracks. I
suggest buying the soundtrack for this game!

SUMMARY: A universe-exploring and building game with procedurally generated worlds, crafting, construction, colonization - and a sense of humor.  Even in its Early Access state it offers an incredible amount of content and things to do.  Worth purchasing, worth supporting - and worth enjoying - for any fan of adventure/crafting games.
Starbound is a procedurally-generated space adventure where an entire galaxy is created randomly (don't worry, you can swap planet coordinates with friends or game together).  A refugee of one of six races, you end up in a broken-down, out-of-fuel spaceship above a random world, and your adventure begins.  Early quests lead you through surviving in a kind of "Robinson Curose in space" adventure, where you learn to craft, build, mine, and so on. Once you've got your ship in some state of repair, you hook up with an outpost full of refugees, and your adventure's scope encompasses the universe.
You can take on quests, kick around, or do whatever you want - though following quests does unlock more equipment and options so you'll want to chase those down.  As you adventure, you'll travel a proceduraly-generated galaxy, wander over randomly-generated 2D worlds, encounter various environments, find towns, build buildings, fight monsters (unique to each world), and try and unlock the mystery of the game.
Crafting and farming are a big part of the game, and Starbound delivers.  You unlock various pieces of technology, raise a variety of crops, and build structures for whatever reason you want.  Customize your character with clothes, weapons,  armor, equipment, and special "Tech" abilities.  There's always something new to try or find, and it gets addictive to keep experimenting; making an item may unlock new items, raising a new crop can unlock recipies, new equipment leads to new items.
Feel lonlely? Then you can even add characters to the setting.  Find a nice planet, set up some buildings, place electronic "Colony Deeds", and populate your new world (and enjoy the benefits of rent).  Or maybe your farrmstead isn't something you live out of, so get a colony deed and get yourself a buddy to watch the place when you're gone.
Maybe you don't want to settle down or want to travel in style?  Work on expanding your ship by doing missions and getting the Outpost shipyard to help you out.  With more space you can build kitchens, rec rooms, labs, and more.  If you want a crew, you can post Colony Deeds inside your own craft and summon up your own crew of hackers, merchants, scientists, cultits, or whatever you want.  Plus they pay rent to live onboard!
Because of the procedural generation, the game also has some magic moments that can surprise you.  Travel a savanna as a gas giant fills the sky at night.  Discover a peaceful village . . . right as a meteor shower strikes.   Mine into a cavern filled with valuable materials.  Find a forest of beautiful trees unlike any other you've seen.   Dig underground and find hidden complexes. There's always a wonder awaiting you.
"Always something new" really describes all of Starbound.
The game as of this review has now implemented plot progression, story, and colonization, so there's now something "going on" for the game.  Yes, it's not finished, but you may not even notice when you're building your space farm, mining deep into a planet, colonizing a planet, or turning your ship into a flying town.
For the price, Starbound already provides an absolutely grand adventure.  But when you pick it up, you can also participate in the active, passionate community.  The devs are backing this game and always listening.  For a "not done yet" game it's amazing - it's worth your time, your money, and your support.
Starbound is one of the few games I consider a "must buy" for anyone into this genre.

If you are into MMOs, or are interested in getting into one, definitely give Spiral Knights a try.
Many MMOs follow the same format, consisting of endless numbers of "fetch" or "collect" quests, where all you do is grind against monsters, hoping that they will drop the item you need progressively more ridiculous amounts of.
In Spiral Knights, there actually is a good amount of variety in the available missions. The story also provides a healthy amount of cutscenes if and text if you are looking for that. Missions typically involve you progressing through a dungeon littered with enemies and different types of square voxels of differing types (ex: wall voxel or explosive voxel). There are sometimes gates that require you to pick up a key (you cannot attack while carrying it) and bring it to the padlock in order to open it. You might also have to pick up a pot object and throw it at another object in order to clear obstacles, allowing for further access into a dungeon.
The combat and controls are pretty easy to become familiar with. Left click to attack, right click to use your shield. Holding the attack down allows you to charge up your weapon (a gauge will appear). You may also use the mouse wheel to alternate between weapons. There is a dash/evade mechanic you can execute by holding shift and pressing right click.
The dungeons can become fairly challenging if playing solo, however, it is still viable if you are careful and do not rush right into enemy spawns. The rewards from completing missions and item drops are reasonable. The loot automatically is attracted to your character like a magnet, so you do not need to click on dropped items.
Aesthetics are nice, the dungeons and enemies are decently detailed. Like many MMOs, there can be a lot of clutter in the interface, especially when you first log into the game and access the game hub - you will need to get used to this orientation if you have not played many MMOs.
The minimap can be expanded to cover the center of your screen by pressing B (do not press tab, that brings up the character stats/info panel), however, be advised that the border of the map is a bold blue, making it noticeably difficult to play while keeping the minimap expanded (compared to games like Path of Exile, or Diablo, where the minimap is translucent enough for you to see most things easily.
Overall, the game seems pretty fleshed out, with quite a bit to do. Definitely recommend trying it out if you are interested and/or not already playing other MMOs  (or have the extra time to spare).

Having played this for some time now I could not recommend it in good taste. There is simply too many times where the games major mechanics are shown to be shallow and unfinished, or enemy types bland and uninteresting. The stress system seems interesting at first but quickly devolves into a second health bar that you can't reliably heal back to acceptable levels, combined with every other enemy having massive stress damage attacks makes progression painful and unrewarding.
Another issue is player control. In one of Valves in game commentaries for Half-Life 2 they stated that the best thing a developer can do is to never take control away from the player, even if they aren't actually in control they should at least feel as if they have some say in what happens in a situation. Darkest Dungeon takes player control away so often that it's bordering on absurdity. Randomly given quirks randomly cause your character to make random arbitrary choices in combat and at town, making it seem like you have no say at all in what happens in your party. Even if you complete a hard dungeon with 0 stress across the board theres still a hefty chance of your characters gaining up to two character destroying traits that make them dead weight and functionally dead to you.
The next issue is the diversity and balance of each of the dungeons. There's a forest, a ruin, a cove, and a city for the main dungeons. Each of these supposedly has a diverse set of enemies and challenges to face, but if you examine them closely they are nearly carbon copies of one another. The ruins has skeletons that act the same as the coves fish people, the cultists have a spellcaster that has nearly the same spells as the coves fish spellcaster, the pigs have the same support abilities as the fungal growths in the forest.
The main cause of all this sameness stems from the games shallow combat system, there are only two DOT's, one stun type, forced movement attacks and then normal damage with crits. This is not a recipe for replayability at all. There are simply too few ways for the enemy to fight the player, leading to stagnation. The game tries to add another layer of complexity in its stress system, but it falls flat, with it being a near unmanagable mess of too much stress and too few ways to mitigate it within the dungeon itself. The few characters that can mend stress heal it for so little as to not be worth it, why waste turns stress healing when you could be killing the enemy to stop the stress from being placed to begin with? The stress system is also very bottom heavy, it mostly affects newer characters and seems to dissappear by level 2-3, mostly serving to kill off fresh characters by having a skeleton splash wine on them for 10 rounds.
The stat system is also very oddly designed. Dodge works like in most games, by serving as a way to completely mitigate damage in echange for reliability, but most characters will not high high enough dodge stats to take advantage of it, and will instead opt in for the much more realiable and plentiful PROT stat which functions as a flat damage reduction. Most enemies also seems to have either 100% accuracy attacks, or attacks that hit so hard that even taking the chance of focusing on dodge and having it fail makes prot all the more worth while. Why even have the chance of taking a 20 damage attack on a 22 Health character when you can always reduce that 20 damage to 10 or less?
Sadly Darkest Dungeon is a trainwreck of balance issues and poorly implemented game mechanics overlaid with amazing art and stellar sound and voice work. It simply isn't worth the $20 in its current state, and likely never will be.

As a bored college student, I have two very limited factors in my life: time and money. As such, I try to find games that are cheap, have plenty of content, and can be picked up and put down in a small amount of time. Darkest Dungeon delivers all of these aspects as well as a great setting that is only bolstered by the art, music, and narration.
Gameplay:
Darkest Dungeon is a Rouge-lite 3rd person horror rpg that puts an emphasis on struggling for resources and the mortality of your party members. Combat is turn based, and offers a ton of challenge due to the game's stress feature which can cause your party members to gain quirks, or have heart attacks and die.
Art and Music:
Darkest Dungeon's art fits the name quite well: gritty and dark motif that takes ideas and concepts from the likes of H.P. Lovecraft and Clive Barker. Not a moment is spent without a sort of grotesque abomination, or some sort of foreboding scene. The music is hard to describe, but it does its job perfectly. In your town, the music gives a desolate feeling, while in one of the dungeons the music is non existant until a fight happens at which point the music is grating and fast paced, giving a sense of urgency.
Narration:
All of the games story is done through narration in the style of Bastion. The narrator's voice is beyond a perfect fit for the setting, and there is no shortage of lines he says to either make you feel empowered, or hopeless in the middle of a battle.
Length of Play:
Each dungeon takes about 10-20 minutes to complete depending on what level of dungeon it is and what the objective is. This is perfect as it allows for breaks to be taken and ample opportunities to quit without losing any progess.
Price:
The game is $20, which I think is a good price for this game as it holds many hours of quality content. If it's on sale, then it's just even more value right there.

Given the alternatives, Earth is a pretty cool place to live. (although with pollution and global warming it sometimes seems we're doing our best to change that).
It's just as well Earth meets our needs so perfectly because we don't have the ability to travel anywhere else to set up camp anyway... at least not yet (unless you count the moon, but we haven't been back there in nearly 50 years, governments would rather spend their money sending planes to drop bombs on deserts than sending rockets into space to benefit all mankind.)
One day, we will have the technological capability to travel to the stars, which will come in handy when the Earth becomes a less hospitable place to live.
It's inevitable, whether it's climate change, lack of resources or the death throes of the Sun itself, eventually, if we want to survive as a species, we're going to need  to get off this rock and find a new one.
The problem is, even if everything works out for us, if we survive long enough and develop the technology to travel on mass to the stars, we're still going to need to find another Earth-like planet with all the amenities (running water, central heating, oxygen, etc.) that we're accustomed to.
Whatever happens, however we ruin our planet, for the moment, we're all stuck here so we have to make the most of it..
Do you know why life evolved on earth?
It was because we have all of those lovely luxuries here already.
There's a chance that if we did manage to find another planet that can sustain oxygen sucking life like ourselves, that it is already doing just that, sustaining some alien oxygen suckers that are perfectly happy where they are and have no interest in moving out and letting us move in.
Sure, we could ask nicely, but if they didn't want to share there's always another option.
We've been turning sandy deserts into glassy craters on Earth for a while now, why not just use our military might to clear a path for our forlorn colonists? Desperate times call for desperate measures. We can justify anything if we need it badly enough.
If the native nuisance is still trapped on their own evolutionary cradle and we have the capability to get there, we're probably going to be more technologically advanced than they are (we'll have bigger bombs) so it shouldn't be too much of a problem.
But what if the tables were turned?
We're still happy here on Earth, things are ticking over nicely, we've still got petrol for our cars, food for our bellies and oxygen for our lungs, then some alien eyes start to peer greedily at our planet.
We'd be unlikely to roll over and give it to them, no matter how big their bombs are.
It'd be a fight we'd likely lose (unless Jeff Goldblum and his trusty laptop are around to save us with a timely upload of a computer virus).
But assuming this technological war or the worlds fluke doesn't come to pass, we'd be screwed.
It'd take a long time to eradicate all of us though and a submissive populace might fit better with the aliens plans, besides, why make war when propaganda can enslave a people just as easily.
That's where XCOM 2 comes in.
It's been 20 years since the brief "war" against the invaders was lost, their propaganda machine has been in full swing for decades brainwashing the masses. The aliens are entrenched and the people cowed.
But there is still hope. Pockets of resistance strike against our alien masters, there are remnants from the war, from the group that was meant to defend us from this alien menace.
The survivors of the original XCOM project haven't forgotten the world before the overlords arrival and they want it back.
Picking up the pieces of the devastated XCOM initiative, you are tasked with the job of unifying a global resistance against the insidious interlopers.
If you've played any of the other XCOM games, especially the excellent 2012 title "XCOM: Enemy Unknown" then you're going to be on familiar, if somewhat prettier, ground.
Starting with a small band of rookie recruits and a bare bones facility which serves as your headquarters (It's mobile this time around too!) you'll need to send out your team to engage in various hit and run missions against the aliens.
In Enemy Unknown you were defending Earth against the alien incursions, the tables are turned this time as you strike out against the entrenched invaders, attacking them where and when you think it'll hurt them the most.
Before each strike against the enemy you'll need to select your squad from the pool of able bodied recruits you have available.
They're all pretty green when you first start out, but the ones that you manage to keep alive will learn new skills and become adept at using different weapon types.
You'll end up with heavy ordinance specialists, medics, snipers, etc. all of which will play a vital role in the often punishing tactical battles that you're going to find yourself engaged in.
Again, just as with "Enemy Unknown" there's a promotion system to reward your best performing operatives, they'll even earn nicknames (which you can edit to suit your tastes if you're the sort that likes to tinker with these things).
Talking of tinkering, the level of customisation and attention to detail with regards to editing your team is exceptional.
You can edit their names and nicknames to make them more memorable (Duncan 'McBig' Donald for instance) , engage in a little plastic surgery to make them look how you want, customise the colours of each individuals armour (I like to use different colours to represent different skill sets, heavy weapons guys in yellow, snipers in black, that sort of thing.)
You can even select their nationalities (Their nations flag is displayed on their armour) and the language they speak, which you'll get to hear whilst they're chattering (or screaming) out in the field.
It's not limited to languages  (English, German, Spanish, etc.) either, there are also accents to choose from.
Under the British voices for example, you'll find Scottish and Irish accents available to really personalise your resistance fighters.
Of course, this customisation serves to increase your attachment to the little guys, which makes it all the more painful when you inevitably lose one of them in battle, especially if it's someone you've come to rely on, some you've been watching climb the ranks for a while, someone like my first major loss in the game... (You're sacrifice will not be forgotten Sergeant 'McBig').
As well as the emotional loss of losing 'McBig' to hostile fire,  (I'll make the alien ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s pay for that!) there's also the strategic loss of losing a seasoned vet and likely having to replace him with a wide eyed rookie who will take several missions to become useful or more likely, wet his pants and get shot the first time he sees an alien.
The aliens have been busy in the twenty years following "Enemy Unknown" too, their genetic tinkering has continued so you're going to find new and improved alien types terrorising the down trodden humans, which means new specimens to capture and fresh autopsies to perform.
Researching alien tech (and biology) found in the field is vital, you're... [snip]

It has been stated before, but i just have to say it again.
The game is basically a nice improvement over the first part, but two very annoying issues drive the fun out very quickly.
The first one is the mission timers. Timed missions were the curse of the first part, because all the nice setups you can plan in this kind of game just need to be hurried and you cannot explore with a timer. This happens almost every single mission now. The entire laid-back feeling that made the XCOM series great for all that time is gone with this single change. It wouldnt be so bad if this happened to b the occasional odd-one-out timed mission. But it is almost every single one.
The same principle applies to the whole campaign by the way. Your only have the illusion of choosing your goals in the campaign, because the very narrow time limit has you chasing after primary objectives and the means necessary to acces them (contacts/intel) all the time. This always hectic feeling really squelches the fun out of what could be a prime gaming experience.
The second issue is the ridicoulous low performance and memory leaks.
The in-combat performance is really low on default settings, but can actually be tweaked via lowering graphic options to manageable levels. The bigger problem here is a kind of stuttering that is introduced after you run the game for some time. Usually starts with slightly longer breaks between turns, missions or changing a screen on the campaign map. The longer you play, the longer the pauses, until you feel like the game freezes every couple of seconds.
Now this feels like something that could be patched in time, so the question remains: why on gods green earth does every premium developer nowadays resort to releasing half baked products?

At the moment, that's all I can think of, but it's definitely a game I'm loving so far. This game is gonna eat up all my time, and I won't regret it!

So, a month ago, I wrote a rather scathing review for a pre-release patch for the Darkest Dungeon. I was really passionate about the game, and that made the review (if you could even call it that) pretty bad. So I figured I'd write a more succinct, and less flamebaity review for the final release.
Darkest dungeon and I have a sordid history. I've loved it, hated it, marathoned it, and rage quit it many a time. Its art style is gorgous, presentation captivating, and narration excellent. The mechanics are simple and have a fairly high skill cap. There's a massive amount of replayability. But I cannot wholeheartedly reccomend this game.
Why? Darkest Dungeon is a game at odds with itself. On one hand, the game demands a great deal of skill and planning to succeed. On the other, the game contains a very large amount of frustrating RNG. RNG can add some engaging elements to gameplay, but games with a heavy amount of RNG are often designed around it. In ways Darkest Dungeon is not.
For example, FTL is notorius for its brutal random encounters. But the developers made this work by keeping the gameplay loop short: you've only wasted minutes, not hours. Another game, X-COM, has RNG similar to that of Darkest Dungeon. But if you're absolutley annihilated by the dice, you can always load (assuming you haven't opted into ironman mode).
But in Darkest Dungeon, you will (often) lose members of your party. Characters you have invested hours of time and small mountains of gold into upgrading. Maybe they were crit several times in a row, maybe they got a really unlucky deathblow, or perhaps you just couldn't escape an encounter. It's just unavoidable.
At first, you'll get over it. It was just bad luck, right? But as you get into higher level dungeons, the more brutal the game gets, and the more often your party will die. It won't be every dungeon, mind you, but often enough that it will really sting. Eventually, one of two things will happen:
A. You'll rage quit, and maybe never play the game again.
B. You'll stop giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥about your party members, and by extension, the game.
Most people reading this review simply will not beat Darkest Dungeon. Hell, you'll probably not even get to the final tier of dungeons. It'll end up being one of 'those' games, the ones sitting in your library that you tell yourself you'll beat one day. But you won't.
Maybe the devs will lower the RNG by adding crit resistance, or by increasing deathblow resist. But as of now, Darkest Dungeon demands too much investment for a game so reliant on RNG.
If you're looking for a game that uses roguelike elements like Darkest Dungeon, consider buying FTL, X-COM, or X-COM 2 coming out later this month.

, further separating player base for these missions alone.

If you have a group of friends willing to play then by all means, go ahead, I really wouldn't recommend starting now by yourself.

TL;DR: Good, but buggy, not recommended for now - as good as the core game is, the bugs make it too frustrating
Mechanically, the game is fine - plays like the first one for the most part, with a few changes I would consider improvements, such as the "Concealment" system which - at least to some extent - makes overwatch crawling unnecesary for the first part of most missions.
I, for one, like the "dumbed down" base building, seeing as in the first one, it didn't feel deep, it just felt needlessly complicated, but of course that's a matter of opinion.
However, I've run into a lot of really annoying problems, mostly with the UI - not only does it seem poorly designed in a lot of cases, it also flat out breaks a lot. This includes stuff like not being able to click on buttons or icons for skills and mismatched tooltips.
But I could deal with that stuff - it's just annoying, not really game ending.
I will not recommend though, not until the number of bugs I (and apparently quite a few others) have run into.
In my last session, all of a sudden, research and buildings stopped popping up when done. I didn't think much of it - the UI does a terrible job of conveying information at other times, so I figured I'd just misunderstood, and they simply weren't complete after all.
But then I went to look, and construction timers and wound timers had gone into negative values - I had a facilty with a due time of "-195 hours", and soldiers with "-4 days" recovery, and I couldn't do anything with it, until all of a sudden I got spammed with alerts of completed stuff all over the place.
In a game with fairly strict time and resource management, that's just not okay.
Other than that, I frequently get "blackouts" during missions, where the screen turns grey with a red outline and only the HUD visible. The game still runs, and it will recover after a short while, but I just can't see what the enemy is doing, even though they're in my vision range.
Then there's the framerate tanking, which I've seen quite a few people report here and there - it's simply atrocious. I'm running on a high end rig, I should not be seeing 15-20 frames.
And whose brilliant idea was it to keep excessive screen shake in the game. One mission had a very strong shake throughout several of my turns. I kept my cursor completely still, but the shake of the screen meant that I was switching between 4 seperate tiles at random, making it really difficult to throw a grenade properly to hit 3 enemies.
A lot of people are reporting crashes and shader errors, and the inability to quit the game without it crashing and mocking about - I get around this issue through the magic of Alt + F4.
I want to keep playing, because the game is good. But the bugs are making it really annoying, and I will therefore in stead recommend picking it up at a later date.
Edit: As a lot of people have pointed out, the game involves a lot of "timed" missions - many more than the first one. I'd be okay with that, if it didn't feel like there were just slightly too few turns to do stuff - if you step out in the wrong direction, you'll likely simply not have enough turns to get to the objective.
I've rushed through missions, putting my soldiers in really dangerous positions and taking out targets as quickly as I could, but a lot of the time, they get reinforcements at the last second. So even when I rush, I usually get to the objective with 1 or 2 turns left, which is just barely enough for me to also "activate" the objective.
The very highest I've had left (and I save-scummed on that one) was 4. The margin for error relative to the price of failure just seems off on many of the timed missions. But hey, maybe you're into that, in which case: Go nuts, you'll love it.

GAME IS A GREAT ADDITION, IMPROVING ON EU/EW. I ADDRESS THE GAME TIMER ISSUES.
I've been looking forward to this game for a long time and it does not disappoint. They've vastly improved upon everything that EU/EW had going good already. Although there are a few bugs and issues that need to be resolved, overwatch not initiating after an enemy moves under supression (for me), enemies scanned by the battle scanner remain opaque and red and a little bit of a framerate issue even though I'm running a high end pc. But this doesn't diminish the quality of the game by any means. The extensive customisation options, the variety of missions, the new geoscape and being able to prioritize certain resources or objectives is all great. I will talk about a major issue, most of the negative reviewers are complaining about, and that is the mission timers. Personally, I think it's all hogwash. I'm playing on Commander-Ironman difficulty (legend might be a different story altogether as I may agree timers would be unfair on that difficulty) but I''ve had no issues on commander difficulty. "Timers are too short, it make you walk in a straight line to objective. I can't take my time in planning and thinking of strategies." Please, it forces you to think about your moves going forward. It doesn't give you all the time in the world for you to quickly outmanouver enemies and flank them, ultimately rinsing pods with extreme prejudice. I think of it as an aggressive breach, offensively moving forward each turn, overelapping overwatches, attack and move - rather than attack and camp (which so many players wish it would be like, considering they think they don't have enough time to move.) All in the meanwhile, my soldier with phantom is scouting ahead, still in concealment, waiting to pop and flank. Most of the time, I leave the missions on 1-2 turns left on timer, or just in time. Sometimes I do have to sacrifice the safety of a soldier, or ultimately lose someone in order to fulfill the objective. It's all part of the fact that you are the resistance. You are the attackers, the invaders in a well-armed, alert military occupation of Earth. Additionally, if you feel like you can't cope with the timers, there is a mod that increases them or completely removes them. Even that is an issue, even if there are more crazy issues people are complaining about, XCOM 2 is a fully moddable game and I believe that all future content will continue to bolster everyone's experience - positive or negative - and even fix some of the minor issues that are currently present.
I feel that the great features of this game speaks for itself, as many reviewers have elaborated on, this is the first time I've done a review on steam, mainly because I wanted to address the reviews that had the mission timers are their main negative focus. Commander is by no means an easy walkthrough, and I can understand that the timers are very short for legend, so if you were to attempt legend, I would suggest increasing the timers by 2-3 turns (there is a mod for that).

Since I am a massive XCOM fan I assumed I would absolutely love Darkest Dungeon and for the first few hours I did.
The combat seemed deep and varied. There are so many character classes such that I have not used them all let alone try all possible permutations of a four adventurer party. Managing your hamlet is just as stressful as combat when deciding where to spend your hard earned resources. I opted to boost the strength of my party by focusing on the guild and blacksmith but every so often I had to throw some resources to help my adventures recover from all the horrors they had seen.
It felt like I had a rich game that I was going to lose myself in for days.
But after those first few hours I realized that I felt I wasn't making any real progress. Sure I had a few adventures at level two but I wasn't really making enough money to actually upgrade their skills and equipment. I also never seemed to be sending out the same party composition more than once. The stress would be too great or some malady was would afflict an adventure and they would have to miss a week of adventuring while I spent some gold healing them up. The caravan never really seemed to bring me much variety (could I please have more than one Arbalst?) so it forced me to put together so many patchwork party compositions because I just didn't have the ones I wanted to try. Also, every time I came back from a quest I didn't really have enough money to do any major upgrades to my characters such that I felt I was ready for the next challenge.
It was at this time that I had realized I had already entered the grind of the game. I had only been doing lvl 1 short quests (either complete every room battle or explore 90% of rooms) and I was already at a point where I felt like I needed to grind for hours to make enough progress to even attempt the first boss of the game.
But OK this is a hardcore game right? Maybe I'm just playing it wrong. I set myself a goal of attempting one of the first bosses, the Swine Prince, and I picked out a party that I thought would work well and aimed to get them to level two with level one skills and armor (since my guild or blacksmith was not upgraded enough to get everything to level two). I grinded for four more hours and got exactly what I wanted and equiped my party with the best trinkets I had, provisioned them to the gills and out I went. I explored the dungeon and didn't even need to camp before I scouted the boss's lair. It was at this point where things went completely sideways. I managed to kill the boss but I lost three of my four party members. All of that time and energy was gone without much to show for it. All the gold I got for beating the boss was essentially a moot point because I would need to spend it all again to upgrade new adventurers to have that same level of skill and equipment. With respect to the boss battle I felt like I could have retreated and gone back to the hamlet with my spoils. But I would have to spend a lot of gold to reduce the stress and afflictions they had acrued on the quest so it feels like it would have been a moot point.
But again this is a hardcore game! I just gotta git gud! I mean I made progress right? Killing one of those first bosses means something does it not? Let's pick out a second boss and try again. So I picked out the Wizened Hag, put together a team, grinded for two hours to get them where they needed to be (some this time had level two armor because I finally got enough freakin' deeds) and set out into the dungeon. It went every much like the first where I got to the boss without needing to camp and I made my attempt. This time only two of my four adventurers died, although the other two came back with such high stress that they won't ever been quite the same.
And so I am back again to where I was before I decided it was time to attempt my first boss. I have a stable of adventurers that are in no shape to make any attempt on the next boss let alone an attempt at a level three dungeon. None of my healers are above level zero since they've all died so I'll need to grind them up again. But I could do it. I could pick a boss, pick a party composition, grind 2-4 more hours doing the level one dungeons and make another attempt. Odds are I'll lose some adventurers again but thats a point of the game. How does a player deal with such great loss? To me though the grind is just far too obvious that it makes it much easier to just put down the mouse and keyboard and walk away. Its far too clear that I'll have to just grind the same dungeons over and over again, kill the same creatures and then go into another boss battle completely blind where I am likely to come away with some heavy losses. And after I kill all four of the starting bosses I'll be essentially in the same position as I was before with the exception of my hamlet being a little more upgraded. But at that point I'll have to do all of this over again for level three dungeons and I think that I need something else to pull me throught his grind.

Well, decided to add my 2 cents since reviews are mixed. Just a note, I'm no casual scrub like 90% the reviewers here. Fan of all the roguelikes.
TL;DR
-Great atmosphere
-Simple yet not boring combat
-Very addictive first hours
-Gets way too easy once you l2p and grasp locations themes
-Lack of shorter and more roguelikish mode - campaign feels more like a VERY long tutorial
-endgame may get a bit dull and grindy (though it's possible to speedrun it np)
The game's okay. Though in all honesty I feel disapointed. After everyone told me how hard it is I decided to buy it (since earlier I heard it gets too easy lategame). When you start out it's moderately chalenging, not too easy, not too hard (though rather on the easy scale still, after all it's  just a small scale turn based combat, but there was enough stuff to keep you entertained). Problem comes after 15-30 hours when you already know what every location's theme is. Then the game simply becomes too easy since you know what party compositions to use and whom to focus (not to mention all kinds of strange stuff works once you get good at the game). There may be a short moment where it gets hard again (transition from veteran to champion lvl, though it's only because you may have lower tier equipment for a while). Then you can either grind all the bosses and trinkets or go fast for the endgame. The dungs there are scripted so even if you fail for the 1st time you got the general idea what to do in your next attempt.
Despite what most people say RNG can't really screw you (maybe 1 in 100 chance but still not really). If you fail that's most likely your fault and once you get a good grip at the game you shouldn't really come close to losing people if you play safe. Thus lategame may be a bit repelling. So if you are difficult junkie in single player, like me, you will be dissapointed in this sphere. It's the same case as in FTL reviews and discussions. People will cry about everything but not their horrible skill, while there were dozens of evidences of semi decent players being able to win on hard difficulty on very regular basis.
So how I feel about campaign? It feels like it's just a longer tutorial for some better, competitive, more roguelikish mode. Unfortunately there's none (yet, I've read somewhere that developpers mentioned some ''competitive'' mode with leaderboards). Despite all that the game is still somewhat fun for its great style and possibility to still lose some party members if you do some stupid stuff (in that sense it feels to me like vanilla Binding of Isaac - after 30-40 hours you were able to stomp 100% runs but it still felt good to play it for some reason).
So what's the verdict? At the current state the game is worth it at 50% discount I'd say. I'm selecting the recommend option for I believe the devs will deliver the actually chalenging, refreshing game mode. If the difficulty gets boosted and game gets less grindy I'd say it can easily be a pretender for game of first half 2016.

I played this game like 30 hours to reach the end of the beta version, and another 20 hours after it's fully released.
In my opinion, this game is not for everyone. However, if this type of games are your things, you just cannot stop playing. There're 3 reasons that I don't recommend it to everyone.
First, If you don't like cast away your heros like a spent torch, this is not your game.
Sometimes you have to send them away because they're useless, or they just meet their fate on the quests,
or you even have to recruit heros to farm a bit of golds, and throw them away.
It's all about expendable heros clearing their(or future heros') path to the success.
Second, the battle system is not for everyone. So it is all about planning your attacks.

The in-game narrative that proclaims "over-confidence is an insidious killer" should not be taken light-heartedly. This one short sentence is the truest statement in the entire game.
Darkest Dungeon is a rogue-like, turn-based combat RPG that is heavily inspired by the darkest depths of the Cthulhu Mythos and various other Lovecraft writings. The story, while rather vague at the beginning, sets you up for what the ultimate end goal will be; exploring the darkest dungeon of a decrepit manor that has been infested by monsters thanks to a dark ritual. You will be facing an onslaught of Eldritch horrors during every skirmish and adventure, to which if you are not prepared... you WILL die. As is the case with rogue-likes, when you die you stay dead.
Now let me just get this next bit out of the way. I've seen dozens of people in both the Steam forums and the review section complaining and whining about how Darkest Dungeon is "too hard". Yes, this game is quite difficult and it is absolutely not for the casual gamer, or those who get frustrated quickly. That being said, there are also outs to every bad situation that you may face, but they come with a price. Over-exploring above and beyond meeting a quest goal is almost always certain death, and an under-provisioned party is almost always doomed. Do not go into this game expecting to clear it quickly, easily, or without losing party members.
This leads me to the gameplay. There's a slight learning curve to the game itself, which is why I suggest a trial run prior to beginning a serious game file. At all times, you will have 4 members in your party, and throughout the game you will be able to expand and fill your roster. Your roster houses your party members that you can acquire after every quest, and believe me... the more roster members you have, the better off you are, but we'll get into why in a moment. When you begin a quest, you pick 4 members from your roster to participate and the rest will simply stay in town. There is a large variety of classes within the game, such as the Highwayman, Crusader, Man-at-Arms, Occultist, Grave Robber, Houndsman, and Jester. Each class has their preferred spot on the party list, strengths, weaknesses, skills, buffs, debuffs, and effects.
So, why would you want a huge roster of characters to pick from? A huge part of Darkest Dungeon is the stress mechanic, which kind of acts like an insanity meter. Every time that you are in a dungeon, the members of the party get progressively more stressed out. If their stress meter gets high enough, the party member freaks out and will either gain a negative stress effect, or if you're lucky a positive one; the latter are, of course, rare. If their stress meter fills a second time, they'll have a heart attack and face potential death. Once you complete a quest and go back to town, the party members will be healed but their stress levels will remain the same, and so you must de-stress them by sending them to the tavern or church. No matter how long you wait in town, the members that you've sent to these places will only progress with de-stressing after you complete another quest, with another set of party members. It's basically a never ending cycle of quest/de-stress last party members/pick new ones/quest/etc.
These game play mechanics are rather unique, and at times hard to master. Many things can cause your characters to become stressed out, and a good deal of Darkest Dungeon relies on RNG. Some dungeons may only cause minor stress, while others will have characters reeling in a matter of just a few rooms. The combat factors are also heavily RNG based, as there are many effects to take into account; bleed and blight effects are your DOTs (damage over time), which can be placed on an enemy with the right skill, or an enemy can place it on you. There are of course counters and cures to these like bandages and potions, but enemies can also inflict diseases on your characters; such as crooping cough and rabies, and all diseases have different negative effects like -20% damage or -20% HP. Diseases must be healed in town, only after you've completed your quest and if you have enough gold to do so. Otherwise, the inflicted character is stuck with it until you have enough funds.
After each completed quest, the characters that you've had in your party gain Resolve XP. A character will max out at level 6 Resolve, and the higher this level is determines the next skills and upgrades that you will be able to buy for them. It will also determine which quests they are best suited for. As you can tell, I've mentioned that you need gold (and a lot of it) for just about everything you'll want to do in town. A huge factor that causes Darkest Dungeon to be as hard as it is, aside from RNG, is the fact that gold is NOT plentiful. If you get a bad dungeon, you'll come out with 3k gold at best, while a good dungeon will grant you about 7k.
Darkest Dungeon is a rough, vicious cycle game. You will constantly be skrimping and saving gold where and if you can. What is worse, more RNG elements come in when your characters are de-stressing. Sometimes they have such a grand time they just decide to throw away 1k+ on gambling or prayer donations. Sometimes these de-stressing programs do not work enough, and the character must go back a second time. The good thing is, upgrading places in town does not require gold; instead, it requires various artifacts that you will find while completing quests and exploring dungeons. The more you upgrade places such as the tavern, guild, and blacksmith, the cheaper it will be for you to de-stress your characters and upgrade their armor.
Death is permanent. That is why this game is called a rogue-like. If you get a rough dungeon, your favorite and most long-term characters can die. With bad enough RNG, characters can die on extremely easy fights. However, the game does grant you a chance before death to redeem a character. If a character is taken down to 0 HP, they will then be "at death's door". They can even take hits while at this stage, but too many hits will cause them to die. If you can manage to heal a character while they're at death's door, and before they take too many hits, they will live. There is also a "flee" button in game, indicated by a white flag, that allows you to leave any given fight and abandon any quest/dungeon. Doing so will cause your characters to experience stress, but it may in turn save their lives. This is why I said that there is an out to any given bad situation, but yes... it does come with a price.
While everything I've just stated might sound like I'm going negative on Darkest Dungeon, I'm not. It's just the reality of the game itself, and the game is a very harsh, grueling, negative title. That being said, it's extremely fun and addictive. Party and financial management are the biggest concerns that players will face, along with hefty doses of RNG. While regular battles are tough, boss fights are genuinely dreaded. The visuals are also absolutely amazing, the heavy-lined comic sketch inspired drawings are as fantastic as they are grim. The audio is just okay, this is a title that is better suited to your own personal playlist of tracks, as the in-game soundtrack is repetitive. I highly recommend Darkest Dungeon, but ONLY to the toughest of gamers.

Darkest Dungeon is a 2-D roguelike dungeon crawler that tasks you to put together a rag-tag group of misfits, crusaders and bandits to raid neighboring areas in preparation for the largest raid into the Darkest Dungeon, which is narratively built to be a festering, climatic and brutal playground of destructive beasts and traps. The title's core gameplay involves 3 pillars at various stages of your raiding excursions: preparation, exploration and combat, supplanting these core aspects with a variety of nuanced systems that enhance its difficulty, strategic necessity and more. You prepare for your dungeon raids in Hamlet, a small, decrepit town of hollowed out buildings and decaying structures. These buildings serve various roles to your team, from recruiting new team members, buying new equipment, visiting saloons and cathedrals for stress relief and blacksmith and guild workshops to upgrade their talents. You pay gold to obtain their services and utilize other collectable trinkets to permanently upgrade their efficiency, cost and number of teammates that can be serviced at once. It’s also in Hamlet where you do pre-mission preparation and provisioning for items you’ll need for the upcoming mission. Party order and composition are extremely important here, since particular characters are skilled at building basecamps, healing and even scouting rooms at random to give you a better sense of the challenges headed your way. Since there is no chest system for storing items you don’t use on missions either, you can quickly spend yourself dry on key items if you don’t carefully micromanage your gold.
Once you embark on a mission, you’ll begin in a random room in the chosen dungeon. It’s at this point you’ll walk right on a 2-D plane and explore, coming across different optional items, obstacles as well as traps and enemy encounters. These items range from chests, corpses, old books, torches and many more, and each occasion you can choose whether to interact with them or not, and each object could hurt or hinder your team, from a sudden bleeding or poison effect or even a new permanent characteristic or loot/gold. Barricade obstacles are unpassable and must either be removed with a shovel or with your team’s bare hands (taking some health away as well). Traps can often be spotted on the ground, but are invisible depending on your constantly draining torch meter at the top of the screen, which dictates your visibility and can confer advantages or disadvantages depending on its level (ranging from pitch black to radiant brightness). Opposing teams can even get the jump on you and attack first if they attack with no torch equipped. It also affects how much stress your team will accumulate, which is an actual statistic the game keeps track of for each party member and will often affect their combat abilities, their quotes and even their performance off the battlefield. If left unchecked, a character with a tremendous stress level may begin to disobey your orders, loot a booby trap without you clicking and several other unintended negative effects. You must complete the objective in order to leave the dungeon, with the goal often being exploring the majority of the dungeon, clearing every room or even defeating a particularly strong adversary.
Finally, once you run into a combat scenario, the game’s varied and cinematic combat begins. Your team stands in a row, with the one farthest to the right typically your melee fighters to stay up close, and the one on the far left your ranged fighters who prefer to keep their distance, although you can choose and party members placement to your hearts content. However, their placement affects what abilities can and cannot be used. There is a speed stat in the game but often times it is random who will strike first¬¬¬. Enemies often have additional attributes to their attacks, like poison damage, stun and knockback/shuffle, which forcefully displaces the party member’s original position to a different spot, often putting melee fighters far away and so on. Other moves can heal, buff or de-buff characters on screen and even do a much stronger attack in exchange for detrimental effects in upcoming turns.  Once an enemy is defeated, corpses are left on the battlefield that can either be destroyed for easier access to the remaining foes or left to loot later for additional rewards. Taking a major hit, being cursed by certain incantations or certain party members being near a particular type of foe will stack stress on your character. Stress affects combat in a number of ways, but the most nefarious ones are characters at high stress levels receiving afflictions, which instill random negative effects like auto-attacking a random target, passing or even shouting to stress out neighboring party members. At its worse, stress can even result in a character permanently dying from a heart attack mid-battle, removing them entirely from your game.
Darkest Dungeon offers a grim but striking and appealing Gothic art style, with every corner of its game world dripping with disgusting monster effects and sounds, occasionally disturbing character dialogue and an atmosphere of brutality. The art style perfectly captures this feeling, with even the character designs feeling worn down and battle-torn, from the healing cleric’s tattered robe to the abominations vulgar appearance. Everything feels well placed and methodically tuned to deliver a mood of foreboding. The dungeons as well feel aged and mysterious, although repetitious at times with their similar setups of traps and set hallway lengths. This tone is complimented further by a bombastic and epic narrator who voices many of the proceedings, whether it be the end of a battle or key event, a particularly gruesome kill or just a well written quip of battlefield dialogue to enhance the mood. The narrator greatly accented my enjoyment with the game because he always made the events transpiring more interesting and eventful. There are tons of other smaller touches you may use to personalize your quest as well, not least of which being able to name each member of your party. While a small touch, I ended up naming the best of my squad the names of some of my closest family and friends, which in some ways was quite a mistake as I approached higher difficulty areas. My most palpable moment of dread and overwhelming exertion with Darkest Dungeon came with my encounter with that first boss, who due to my drastic underestimation of his abilities was able to decimate my entire team, with the 4 members lost consisting of the real life names of my sister, cousin and 2 best friends, all while my self-named character was resting comfortably back in Hamlet. It’s a shocking effectively blow to my morale, self-perceived skill level and pride, never feeling so defeated when I returned to Hamlet knowing that I had gotten several of my “family and friends” killed. I even started building my own stories on how my remaining party members would be reacting knowing the losses we had incurred. While not everyone may end up having that experience, it was one of the most sincere moments of shock I felt while playing.
Darkest Dungeon hits all the rights notes with its methodical combat, Victorian gothic visual style and its sense of mystery in exploration. Preparing for missions felt worthwhile and necessary, with optimum planning essential to keeping party members alive and as unstressed as possible. The story was a bit disappointing but creating my own narrative and character personalities by naming my characters gave the fledgling tale much more weight and personal depth. The number of options and factors at play in any given gameplay scenario is often breathtaking and overwhelming, but remains fun and challenging in all the right ways. Darkest Dungeon is a superb title and a truly fantastic start to 2016 for me. I highly recommend it.

TL;DR: Good, but buggy, not recommended for now - as good as the core game is, the bugs make it too frustrating
Mechanically, the game is fine - plays like the first one for the most part, with a few changes I would consider improvements, such as the "Concealment" system which - at least to some extent - makes overwatch crawling unnecesary for the first part of most missions.
I, for one, like the "dumbed down" base building, seeing as in the first one, it didn't feel deep, it just felt needlessly complicated, but of course that's a matter of opinion.
However, I've run into a lot of really annoying problems, mostly with the UI - not only does it seem poorly designed in a lot of cases, it also flat out breaks a lot. This includes stuff like not being able to click on buttons or icons for skills and mismatched tooltips.
But I could deal with that stuff - it's just annoying, not really game ending.
I will not recommend though, not until the number of bugs I (and apparently quite a few others) have run into.
In my last session, all of a sudden, research and buildings stopped popping up when done. I didn't think much of it - the UI does a terrible job of conveying information at other times, so I figured I'd just misunderstood, and they simply weren't complete after all.
But then I went to look, and construction timers and wound timers had gone into negative values - I had a facilty with a due time of "-195 hours", and soldiers with "-4 days" recovery, and I couldn't do anything with it, until all of a sudden I got spammed with alerts of completed stuff all over the place.
In a game with fairly strict time and resource management, that's just not okay.
Other than that, I frequently get "blackouts" during missions, where the screen turns grey with a red outline and only the HUD visible. The game still runs, and it will recover after a short while, but I just can't see what the enemy is doing, even though they're in my vision range.
Then there's the framerate tanking, which I've seen quite a few people report here and there - it's simply atrocious. I'm running on a high end rig, I should not be seeing 15-20 frames.
And whose brilliant idea was it to keep excessive screen shake in the game. One mission had a very strong shake throughout several of my turns. I kept my cursor completely still, but the shake of the screen meant that I was switching between 4 seperate tiles at random, making it really difficult to throw a grenade properly to hit 3 enemies.
A lot of people are reporting crashes and shader errors, and the inability to quit the game without it crashing and mocking about - I get around this issue through the magic of Alt + F4.
I want to keep playing, because the game is good. But the bugs are making it really annoying, and I will therefore in stead recommend picking it up at a later date.
Edit: As a lot of people have pointed out, the game involves a lot of "timed" missions - many more than the first one. I'd be okay with that, if it didn't feel like there were just slightly too few turns to do stuff - if you step out in the wrong direction, you'll likely simply not have enough turns to get to the objective.
I've rushed through missions, putting my soldiers in really dangerous positions and taking out targets as quickly as I could, but a lot of the time, they get reinforcements at the last second. So even when I rush, I usually get to the objective with 1 or 2 turns left, which is just barely enough for me to also "activate" the objective.
The very highest I've had left (and I save-scummed on that one) was 4. The margin for error relative to the price of failure just seems off on many of the timed missions. But hey, maybe you're into that, in which case: Go nuts, you'll love it.

Although there are a few bugs and issues that need to be resolved, overwatch not initiating after an enemy moves under supression (for me), enemies scanned by the battle scanner remain opaque and red and a little bit of a framerate issue even though I'm running a high end pc. But this doesn't diminish the quality of the game by any means. The extensive customisation options, the variety of missions, the new geoscape and being able to prioritize certain resources or objectives is all great. I will talk about a major issue, most of the negative reviewers are complaining about, and that is the mission timers. Personally, I think it's all hogwash. I'm playing on Commander-Ironman difficulty (legend might be a different story altogether as I may agree timers would be unfair on that difficulty) but I''ve had no issues on commander difficulty. "Timers are too short, it make you walk in a straight line to objective. I can't take my time in planning and thinking of strategies." Please, it forces you to think about your moves going forward. It doesn't give you all the time in the world for you to quickly outmanouver enemies and flank them, ultimately rinsing pods with extreme prejudice. I think of it as an aggressive breach, offensively moving forward each turn, overelapping overwatches, attack and move - rather than attack and camp (which so many players wish it would be like, considering they think they don't have enough time to move.) All in the meanwhile, my soldier with phantom is scouting ahead, still in concealment, waiting to pop and flank. Most of the time, I leave the missions on 1-2 turns left on timer, or just in time. Sometimes I do have to sacrifice the safety of a soldier, or ultimately lose someone in order to fulfill the objective. It's all part of the fact that you are the resistance. You are the attackers, the invaders in a well-armed, alert military occupation of Earth. Additionally, if you feel like you can't cope with the timers, there is a mod that increases them or completely removes them. Even that is an issue, even if there are more crazy issues people are complaining about, XCOM 2 is a fully moddable game and I believe that all future content will continue to bolster everyone's experience - positive or negative - and even fix some of the minor issues that are currently present.
I feel that the great features of this game speaks for itself, as many reviewers have elaborated on, this is the first time I've done a review on steam, mainly because I wanted to address the reviews that had the mission timers are their main negative focus. Commander is by no means an easy walkthrough, and I can understand that the timers are very short for legend, so if you were to attempt legend, I would suggest increasing the timers by 2-3 turns (there is a mod for that).

Since I am a massive XCOM fan I assumed I would absolutely love Darkest Dungeon and for the first few hours I did.
The combat seemed deep and varied. There are so many character classes such that I have not used them all let alone try all possible permutations of a four adventurer party. Managing your hamlet is just as stressful as combat when deciding where to spend your hard earned resources. I opted to boost the strength of my party by focusing on the guild and blacksmith but every so often I had to throw some resources to help my adventures recover from all the horrors they had seen.
It felt like I had a rich game that I was going to lose myself in for days.
But after those first few hours I realized that I felt I wasn't making any real progress. Sure I had a few adventures at level two but I wasn't really making enough money to actually upgrade their skills and equipment. I also never seemed to be sending out the same party composition more than once. The stress would be too great or some malady was would afflict an adventure and they would have to miss a week of adventuring while I spent some gold healing them up. The caravan never really seemed to bring me much variety (could I please have more than one Arbalst?) so it forced me to put together so many patchwork party compositions because I just didn't have the ones I wanted to try. Also, every time I came back from a quest I didn't really have enough money to do any major upgrades to my characters such that I felt I was ready for the next challenge.
It was at this time that I had realized I had already entered the grind of the game. I had only been doing lvl 1 short quests (either complete every room battle or explore 90% of rooms) and I was already at a point where I felt like I needed to grind for hours to make enough progress to even attempt the first boss of the game.
But OK this is a hardcore game right? Maybe I'm just playing it wrong. I set myself a goal of attempting one of the first bosses, the Swine Prince, and I picked out a party that I thought would work well and aimed to get them to level two with level one skills and armor (since my guild or blacksmith was not upgraded enough to get everything to level two). I grinded for four more hours and got exactly what I wanted and equiped my party with the best trinkets I had, provisioned them to the gills and out I went. I explored the dungeon and didn't even need to camp before I scouted the boss's lair. It was at this point where things went completely sideways. I managed to kill the boss but I lost three of my four party members. All of that time and energy was gone without much to show for it. All the gold I got for beating the boss was essentially a moot point because I would need to spend it all again to upgrade new adventurers to have that same level of skill and equipment. With respect to the boss battle I felt like I could have retreated and gone back to the hamlet with my spoils. But I would have to spend a lot of gold to reduce the stress and afflictions they had acrued on the quest so it feels like it would have been a moot point.
But again this is a hardcore game! I just gotta git gud! I mean I made progress right? Killing one of those first bosses means something does it not? Let's pick out a second boss and try again. So I picked out the Wizened Hag, put together a team, grinded for two hours to get them where they needed to be (some this time had level two armor because I finally got enough freakin' deeds) and set out into the dungeon. It went every much like the first where I got to the boss without needing to camp and I made my attempt. This time only two of my four adventurers died, although the other two came back with such high stress that they won't ever been quite the same.
And so I am back again to where I was before I decided it was time to attempt my first boss. I have a stable of adventurers that are in no shape to make any attempt on the next boss let alone an attempt at a level three dungeon. None of my healers are above level zero since they've all died so I'll need to grind them up again. But I could do it. I could pick a boss, pick a party composition, grind 2-4 more hours doing the level one dungeons and make another attempt. Odds are I'll lose some adventurers again but thats a point of the game. How does a player deal with such great loss? To me though the grind is just far too obvious that it makes it much easier to just put down the mouse and keyboard and walk away. Its far too clear that I'll have to just grind the same dungeons over and over again, kill the same creatures and then go into another boss battle completely blind where I am likely to come away with some heavy losses. And after I kill all four of the starting bosses I'll be essentially in the same position as I was before with the exception of my hamlet being a little more upgraded. But at that point I'll have to do all of this over again for level three dungeons and I think that I need something else to pull me throught his grind.

Well, decided to add my 2 cents since reviews are mixed. Just a note, I'm no casual scrub like 90% the reviewers here. Fan of all the roguelikes.
TL;DR
-Great atmosphere
-Simple yet not boring combat
-Very addictive first hours
-Gets way too easy once you l2p and grasp locations themes
-Lack of shorter and more roguelikish mode - campaign feels more like a VERY long tutorial
-endgame may get a bit dull and grindy (though it's possible to speedrun it np)
The game's okay. Though in all honesty I feel disapointed. After everyone told me how hard it is I decided to buy it (since earlier I heard it gets too easy lategame). When you start out it's moderately chalenging, not too easy, not too hard (though rather on the easy scale still, after all it's  just a small scale turn based combat, but there was enough stuff to keep you entertained). Problem comes after 15-30 hours when you already know what every location's theme is. Then the game simply becomes too easy since you know what party compositions to use and whom to focus (not to mention all kinds of strange stuff works once you get good at the game). There may be a short moment where it gets hard again (transition from veteran to champion lvl, though it's only because you may have lower tier equipment for a while). Then you can either grind all the bosses and trinkets or go fast for the endgame. The dungs there are scripted so even if you fail for the 1st time you got the general idea what to do in your next attempt.
Despite what most people say RNG can't really screw you (maybe 1 in 100 chance but still not really). If you fail that's most likely your fault and once you get a good grip at the game you shouldn't really come close to losing people if you play safe. Thus lategame may be a bit repelling. So if you are difficult junkie in single player, like me, you will be dissapointed in this sphere. It's the same case as in FTL reviews and discussions. People will cry about everything but not their horrible skill, while there were dozens of evidences of semi decent players being able to win on hard difficulty on very regular basis.
So how I feel about campaign? It feels like it's just a longer tutorial for some better, competitive, more roguelikish mode. Unfortunately there's none (yet, I've read somewhere that developpers mentioned some ''competitive'' mode with leaderboards). Despite all that the game is still somewhat fun for its great style and possibility to still lose some party members if you do some stupid stuff (in that sense it feels to me like vanilla Binding of Isaac - after 30-40 hours you were able to stomp 100% runs but it still felt good to play it for some reason).
So what's the verdict? At the current state the game is worth it at 50% discount I'd say. I'm selecting the recommend option for I believe the devs will deliver the actually chalenging, refreshing game mode. If the difficulty gets boosted and game gets less grindy I'd say it can easily be a pretender for game of first half 2016.
