The in-game narrative that proclaims "over-confidence is an insidious killer" should not be taken light-heartedly. This one short sentence is the truest statement in the entire game.
Darkest Dungeon is a rogue-like, turn-based combat RPG that is heavily inspired by the darkest depths of the Cthulhu Mythos and various other Lovecraft writings. The story, while rather vague at the beginning, sets you up for what the ultimate end goal will be; exploring the darkest dungeon of a decrepit manor that has been infested by monsters thanks to a dark ritual. You will be facing an onslaught of Eldritch horrors during every skirmish and adventure, to which if you are not prepared... you WILL die. As is the case with rogue-likes, when you die you stay dead.
Now let me just get this next bit out of the way. I've seen dozens of people in both the Steam forums and the review section complaining and whining about how Darkest Dungeon is "too hard". Yes, this game is quite difficult and it is absolutely not for the casual gamer, or those who get frustrated quickly. That being said, there are also outs to every bad situation that you may face, but they come with a price. Over-exploring above and beyond meeting a quest goal is almost always certain death, and an under-provisioned party is almost always doomed. Do not go into this game expecting to clear it quickly, easily, or without losing party members.
This leads me to the gameplay. There's a slight learning curve to the game itself, which is why I suggest a trial run prior to beginning a serious game file. At all times, you will have 4 members in your party, and throughout the game you will be able to expand and fill your roster. Your roster houses your party members that you can acquire after every quest, and believe me... the more roster members you have, the better off you are, but we'll get into why in a moment. When you begin a quest, you pick 4 members from your roster to participate and the rest will simply stay in town. There is a large variety of classes within the game, such as the Highwayman, Crusader, Man-at-Arms, Occultist, Grave Robber, Houndsman, and Jester. Each class has their preferred spot on the party list, strengths, weaknesses, skills, buffs, debuffs, and effects.
So, why would you want a huge roster of characters to pick from? A huge part of Darkest Dungeon is the stress mechanic, which kind of acts like an insanity meter. Every time that you are in a dungeon, the members of the party get progressively more stressed out. If their stress meter gets high enough, the party member freaks out and will either gain a negative stress effect, or if you're lucky a positive one; the latter are, of course, rare. If their stress meter fills a second time, they'll have a heart attack and face potential death. Once you complete a quest and go back to town, the party members will be healed but their stress levels will remain the same, and so you must de-stress them by sending them to the tavern or church. No matter how long you wait in town, the members that you've sent to these places will only progress with de-stressing after you complete another quest, with another set of party members. It's basically a never ending cycle of quest/de-stress last party members/pick new ones/quest/etc.
These game play mechanics are rather unique, and at times hard to master. Many things can cause your characters to become stressed out, and a good deal of Darkest Dungeon relies on RNG. Some dungeons may only cause minor stress, while others will have characters reeling in a matter of just a few rooms. The combat factors are also heavily RNG based, as there are many effects to take into account; bleed and blight effects are your DOTs (damage over time), which can be placed on an enemy with the right skill, or an enemy can place it on you. There are of course counters and cures to these like bandages and potions, but enemies can also inflict diseases on your characters; such as crooping cough and rabies, and all diseases have different negative effects like -20% damage or -20% HP. Diseases must be healed in town, only after you've completed your quest and if you have enough gold to do so. Otherwise, the inflicted character is stuck with it until you have enough funds.
After each completed quest, the characters that you've had in your party gain Resolve XP. A character will max out at level 6 Resolve, and the higher this level is determines the next skills and upgrades that you will be able to buy for them. It will also determine which quests they are best suited for. As you can tell, I've mentioned that you need gold (and a lot of it) for just about everything you'll want to do in town. A huge factor that causes Darkest Dungeon to be as hard as it is, aside from RNG, is the fact that gold is NOT plentiful. If you get a bad dungeon, you'll come out with 3k gold at best, while a good dungeon will grant you about 7k.
Darkest Dungeon is a rough, vicious cycle game. You will constantly be skrimping and saving gold where and if you can. What is worse, more RNG elements come in when your characters are de-stressing. Sometimes they have such a grand time they just decide to throw away 1k+ on gambling or prayer donations. Sometimes these de-stressing programs do not work enough, and the character must go back a second time. The good thing is, upgrading places in town does not require gold; instead, it requires various artifacts that you will find while completing quests and exploring dungeons. The more you upgrade places such as the tavern, guild, and blacksmith, the cheaper it will be for you to de-stress your characters and upgrade their armor.
Death is permanent. That is why this game is called a rogue-like. If you get a rough dungeon, your favorite and most long-term characters can die. With bad enough RNG, characters can die on extremely easy fights. However, the game does grant you a chance before death to redeem a character. If a character is taken down to 0 HP, they will then be "at death's door". They can even take hits while at this stage, but too many hits will cause them to die. If you can manage to heal a character while they're at death's door, and before they take too many hits, they will live. There is also a "flee" button in game, indicated by a white flag, that allows you to leave any given fight and abandon any quest/dungeon. Doing so will cause your characters to experience stress, but it may in turn save their lives. This is why I said that there is an out to any given bad situation, but yes... it does come with a price.
While everything I've just stated might sound like I'm going negative on Darkest Dungeon, I'm not. It's just the reality of the game itself, and the game is a very harsh, grueling, negative title. That being said, it's extremely fun and addictive. Party and financial management are the biggest concerns that players will face, along with hefty doses of RNG. While regular battles are tough, boss fights are genuinely dreaded. The visuals are also absolutely amazing, the heavy-lined comic sketch inspired drawings are as fantastic as they are grim. The audio is just okay, this is a title that is better suited to your own personal playlist of tracks, as the in-game soundtrack is repetitive. I highly recommend Darkest Dungeon, but ONLY to the toughest of gamers.

I will talk about a major issue, most of the negative reviewers are complaining about, and that is the mission timers. Personally, I think it's all hogwash. I'm playing on Commander-Ironman difficulty (legend might be a different story altogether as I may agree timers would be unfair on that difficulty) but I''ve had no issues on commander difficulty. "Timers are too short, it make you walk in a straight line to objective. I can't take my time in planning and thinking of strategies." Please, it forces you to think about your moves going forward. It doesn't give you all the time in the world for you to quickly outmanouver enemies and flank them, ultimately rinsing pods with extreme prejudice. I think of it as an aggressive breach, offensively moving forward each turn, overelapping overwatches, attack and move - rather than attack and camp (which so many players wish it would be like, considering they think they don't have enough time to move.) Sometimes I do have to sacrifice the safety of a soldier, or ultimately lose someone in order to fulfill the objective. It's all part of the fact that you are the resistance. TLDR: Fun hard game let down by a few oversights/bugs which if are fixed I would recommend.
This game can be quite a challenge, it embraces the 'losing is fun' motto, you learn how to play and can progress further and further, it's as much about your decisions as it is team composition and skills.
After 11ish hours of play, restarting a few times, reading reviews and guides I can say the game defiantly stacked against the player, you WILL have to 'Make the best of a bad situation', which is not really a bad thing- it does appeal to some, you will have moments where your party will fail or thrive at the whim of RNG and no amount of preparation from placement/items/skill can mitigate that. (Again not a bad thing).
The game is let down in a few areas that totally break immersion or seem just plain unfair/wrong.
The following bugs/oversights have tipped the balance far too many times and I feel I cannot recommend this game until they are all fixed, it really feels like laziness or poorly thought out mechanics during gameplay which takes all the fun out of it (losing can be fun, but not from bugs/poor dev decisions)
1) Party requires 4 food randomly to eat, even if you have 3, too bad take full penalty
2) Party sometimes requires food only 2 rooms after just eating- or even after a camping feast(seriously devs did you even code in checks for this?)
3) Traps listed at 100% have failed- my record 6 times in a row at 110%... list the value properly please.
4) You can run out low level dungeons to crawl through, at this point you MUST restart your entire game (I feel this is intended but poorly implemented at best, if it was intended it is incredibly sloppy and lazy- add more feedback to the user to show this)
5) Crashes often- typically at the end of a level after camping when receiving the final reward (lucky it saves progress quite well)
Just to be clear- the games difficulty has nothing to do with my non-recommendation of the game.

I have to give this game a negative review. Mainly because it's so much missed potential and some major design decisions that ruin the experience. Don't get me wrong, it's a decent game, but I feel it does not deserve all the credit it's getting from official reviewers, and frankly giving this game anything higher than 7/10 just proves that they have no real grasp of game design or game mechanics.
At a first glance the game looks and plays very much like the previous game, I recon this is why it's getting good reviews from a lot of reviewers who haven't really spent that much time playing. I played this on iron-man, and veteran settings because that's how I believe X-Com should be played to offer an interesting challenge. If you play it on easy settings your soldiers will have some unfair bonuses to your aim and damage.
The Good:
- Upgraded graphics
- More events, locations, enemies, gadgets and weapons
- The random map generator. (Adds some degree of replayability to the regular missions)
- The mod support
- Addition of "stealth"
The Bad:
- Too much randomness, random events that screw up the most carefully planned mission. Events that you as a player could not have had any chance of predicting. It's just too much.
- "Unfair" rules, say that you sneak past a group of enemies and think you were smart, think again. If you complete the main objective all enemies that have not been activated might be activated at once and rush you.
- Timed missions, most missions have a timer attached forcing you to have to sprint forward in order to reach the objective in time, This in turn makes stealth tactics or any tactics for that matter pretty useless.
- Enemy behaviours don't match their roles. As an example zombie aliens can move about as far as your soldiers per turn, even though they look and are animated like they should be far slower.
- Lack of unique soldiers/recruits. They are so obviously randomly generated that they sort of lose their "personality". Lazily written descriptions where there could have been hundreds of stories for the soldiers making them seem more real.

This game is fantastic.
You round up a team of heroes and send them into a dungeon to kill horrors and bring back loot.  However, these aren't godly JRPG superhumans you're sending in, your heroes are fragile both in mind and body.  This is reinforced both through the Mignola-esque art style and through the gameplay.  Even if you are well-prepared and cautious, you are always a handle of unlucky rolls from disaster.  The fact that you can and will lose heroes is mitigated by the fact that fresh recruits are freely available, and the upgrades to your hamlet are permanent once unlocked.
The game design ensures that you will feel tense as you explore the dungeon.  Your stocks of food and torches slowly run out, and the dungeon becomes more menacing as the light level dims (even so, these dangers are balanced by greater rewards).  Encounters and traps will whittle away at your health and sanity, and much of the time you will have only limited means to recover.  If things go badly, it is often best to cut your losses and run away.  However, it's all too easy to say 'just a little bit further' and before you know it you've been ambushed and are being cut down.
The devs have said that they are considering future balance tweaks, and I trust them to do a good job.  The gameplay is more polished compared to the initial EA release and the difficulty is very-well calibrated.  Combat is tactical due to the positioning mechanics and yet feels visceral given the possibility of huge swings of luck.  I have put hours and hours into this game and it still gets my heart pounding every time.  I'm still not at the titular 'Darkest Dungeon' but I already feel that this has been one of my favorite games of all time.

It's too random, way too luck-based, more than before, to the point it becomes aggrevating. Countless of times I found myself yelling at the screen when my squad mate misses a target at point blank range with 90% hit chance, only to be gunned down with ease by another enemy 30 yards away. People say "that's XCOM", but I say it's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The beginning missions are ridiculously difficult, even at an easier difficulty, your squad mates die constantly, so you have no promoted soldiers and therefore no edge against the enemies. When you complete an objective with barely your squad intact, more reinforcements show up to kill you. I had a scenario where 1 enemy with a stun sword killed my entire team. It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's even worse when you have to complete an objective in X amound of turns, forcing you to hurry and dropping your guard, so you have absolutely no way to plan a careful approach, which is what XCOM is supposed to be all about. Instead, you have some annoying ♥♥♥♥ back at the HQ barking orders at you while he's eating a donut, telling that the Alien relay is closing down, as if you didn't know why you're there in the first place.
XCOM 2 is like playing Mount & Blade and selecting "Auto-fight" before every encounter and getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by the computer. You can maneuver, yes, but ultimately it all comes down to a dice roll and you will die in situations that would never happen in real life, like missing a shot, when the gun barrel is literally at the enemy's stupid face.
There's just so much frustration in this game. Creating a squad of friends and seeing them all die during the first mission is beyond infuriating. To me there's nothing more annoying than an unfair challenge and that's what this game boils down to. Some people get easier missions and scenarios early on so they can build their team, but if you're like me, you just get humiliated again, again, again and again. You start feeling like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, because you paid full price for a game that makes fun of you at every turn, and forces you to turn down the difficulty, because you're too much of a ♥♥♥♥♥ to play on Ironman like you did in the previous game.

I can't recommend this game.  It's no longer a strategy game, just a race against XCOM's legendary rage-inducing RNG.
There's so much here to build on, and that's part of that makes this so disappointing.  There's a great stealth mechanic...that you can't use because of the turn timer, so you blow it on the opening group of enemies you see.  It's neat, fun to play with for a few (failed) missions, then you leave it alone because the turn timer invalidates a piece of great design.
There's awesome classes with neat abilities...except sharpshooters are worthless since using them like the sniper they're supposed to be means that you lose them when the evac timer runs out.  Once again, the turn timer invalidates another piece of some really good class/game design.
You could always counter the whims of the RNG in XCOM: EU/EW by playing safe with overwatch and setting up a good sniper position, and you can see the design intent to stop that with the turn timer.  But that turn timer coupled with the whimsical RNG turns the game from a "series of interesting decisions" into a series of bad ones and worse ones.
It's really close to being the GOTY candidate so many reviewers are making it out to be.  But without a balance pass, it's just an overengineered race against a timer full of nigh-impossible missions.  Any strategy is invalidated by the timer, so you just roll your shots and hope they hit, because if they don't, you're dead.
This is XCOM.  They don't hit often enough to stop you from dying.

TLDR: Fun hard game let down by a few oversights/bugs which if are fixed I would recommend.
This game can be quite a challenge, it embraces the 'losing is fun' motto, you learn how to play and can progress further and further, it's as much about your decisions as it is team composition and skills.
After 11ish hours of play, restarting a few times, reading reviews and guides I can say the game defiantly stacked against the player, you WILL have to 'Make the best of a bad situation', which is not really a bad thing- it does appeal to some, you will have moments where your party will fail or thrive at the whim of RNG and no amount of preparation from placement/items/skill can mitigate that. (Again not a bad thing).
The game is let down in a few areas that totally break immersion or seem just plain unfair/wrong.
The following bugs/oversights have tipped the balance far too many times and I feel I cannot recommend this game until they are all fixed, it really feels like laziness or poorly thought out mechanics during gameplay which takes all the fun out of it (losing can be fun, but not from bugs/poor dev decisions)
1) Party requires 4 food randomly to eat, even if you have 3, too bad take full penalty
2) Party sometimes requires food only 2 rooms after just eating- or even after a camping feast(seriously devs did you even code in checks for this?)
3) Traps listed at 100% have failed- my record 6 times in a row at 110%... list the value properly please.
4) You can run out low level dungeons to crawl through, at this point you MUST restart your entire game (I feel this is intended but poorly implemented at best, if it was intended it is incredibly sloppy and lazy- add more feedback to the user to show this)
5) Crashes often- typically at the end of a level after camping when receiving the final reward (lucky it saves progress quite well)
Just to be clear- the games difficulty has nothing to do with my non-recommendation of the game.

Years after finishing Enemy Unknown and loving it, I couldn't wait to get XCOM 2. However, after many dozens of failed missions and restarted campaigns later, I just can't recommend this game. It's too random, way too luck-based, more than before, to the point it becomes aggrevating. Countless of times I found myself yelling at the screen when my squad mate misses a target at point blank range with 90% hit chance, only to be gunned down with ease by another enemy 30 yards away. People say "that's XCOM", but I say it's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The beginning missions are ridiculously difficult, even at an easier difficulty, your squad mates die constantly, so you have no promoted soldiers and therefore no edge against the enemies. When you complete an objective with barely your squad intact, more reinforcements show up to kill you. I had a scenario where 1 enemy with a stun sword killed my entire team. It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's even worse when you have to complete an objective in X amound of turns, forcing you to hurry and dropping your guard, so you have absolutely no way to plan a careful approach, which is what XCOM is supposed to be all about. Instead, you have some annoying ♥♥♥♥ back at the HQ barking orders at you while he's eating a donut, telling that the Alien relay is closing down, as if you didn't know why you're there in the first place.
XCOM 2 is like playing Mount & Blade and selecting "Auto-fight" before every encounter and getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by the computer. You can maneuver, yes, but ultimately it all comes down to a dice roll and you will die in situations that would never happen in real life, like missing a shot, when the gun barrel is literally at the enemy's stupid face.
There's just so much frustration in this game. Creating a squad of friends and seeing them all die during the first mission is beyond infuriating. To me there's nothing more annoying than an unfair challenge and that's what this game boils down to. Some people get easier missions and scenarios early on so they can build their team, but if you're like me, you just get humiliated again, again, again and again. You start feeling like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, because you paid full price for a game that makes fun of you at every turn, and forces you to turn down the difficulty, because you're too much of a ♥♥♥♥♥ to play on Ironman like you did in the previous game.
It was also plagued with weird gamebreaking bugs, like a zombie ragdoll glitching through the floor and flying around the map, preventing the game from progressing. I have never seen a game, where a round continuing is dependent on whether a random ragdoll is stationary or not. Astounding.
Overall, I felt like I was going insane while playing this game, I almost broke my mouse and my keyboard. If you buy this game, you might have an easier time, but I'd rather shove a pineapple up my♥♥♥♥♥than play it again.

I can't recommend this game.  It's no longer a strategy game, just a race against XCOM's legendary rage-inducing RNG.
There's so much here to build on, and that's part of that makes this so disappointing.  There's a great stealth mechanic...that you can't use because of the turn timer, so you blow it on the opening group of enemies you see.  It's neat, fun to play with for a few (failed) missions, then you leave it alone because the turn timer invalidates a piece of great design.
There's awesome classes with neat abilities...except sharpshooters are worthless since using them like the sniper they're supposed to be means that you lose them when the evac timer runs out.  Once again, the turn timer invalidates another piece of some really good class/game design.
You could always counter the whims of the RNG in XCOM: EU/EW by playing safe with overwatch and setting up a good sniper position, and you can see the design intent to stop that with the turn timer.  But that turn timer coupled with the whimsical RNG turns the game from a "series of interesting decisions" into a series of bad ones and worse ones.
It's really close to being the GOTY candidate so many reviewers are making it out to be.  But without a balance pass, it's just an overengineered race against a timer full of nigh-impossible missions.  Any strategy is invalidated by the timer, so you just roll your shots and hope they hit, because if they don't, you're dead.
This is XCOM.  They don't hit often enough to stop you from dying.

TLDR: Fun hard game let down by a few oversights/bugs which if are fixed I would recommend.
This game can be quite a challenge, it embraces the 'losing is fun' motto, you learn how to play and can progress further and further, it's as much about your decisions as it is team composition and skills.
After 11ish hours of play, restarting a few times, reading reviews and guides I can say the game defiantly stacked against the player, you WILL have to 'Make the best of a bad situation', which is not really a bad thing- it does appeal to some, you will have moments where your party will fail or thrive at the whim of RNG and no amount of preparation from placement/items/skill can mitigate that. (Again not a bad thing).
The game is let down in a few areas that totally break immersion or seem just plain unfair/wrong.
The following bugs/oversights have tipped the balance far too many times and I feel I cannot recommend this game until they are all fixed, it really feels like laziness or poorly thought out mechanics during gameplay which takes all the fun out of it (losing can be fun, but not from bugs/poor dev decisions)
1) Party requires 4 food randomly to eat, even if you have 3, too bad take full penalty
2) Party sometimes requires food only 2 rooms after just eating- or even after a camping feast(seriously devs did you even code in checks for this?)
3) Traps listed at 100% have failed- my record 6 times in a row at 110%... list the value properly please.
4) You can run out low level dungeons to crawl through, at this point you MUST restart your entire game (I feel this is intended but poorly implemented at best, if it was intended it is incredibly sloppy and lazy- add more feedback to the user to show this)
5) Crashes often- typically at the end of a level after camping when receiving the final reward (lucky it saves progress quite well)
Just to be clear- the games difficulty has nothing to do with my non-recommendation of the game.

Years after finishing Enemy Unknown and loving it, I couldn't wait to get XCOM 2. However, after many dozens of failed missions and restarted campaigns later, I just can't recommend this game. It's too random, way too luck-based, more than before, to the point it becomes aggrevating. Countless of times I found myself yelling at the screen when my squad mate misses a target at point blank range with 90% hit chance, only to be gunned down with ease by another enemy 30 yards away. People say "that's XCOM", but I say it's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The beginning missions are ridiculously difficult, even at an easier difficulty, your squad mates die constantly, so you have no promoted soldiers and therefore no edge against the enemies. When you complete an objective with barely your squad intact, more reinforcements show up to kill you. I had a scenario where 1 enemy with a stun sword killed my entire team. It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's even worse when you have to complete an objective in X amound of turns, forcing you to hurry and dropping your guard, so you have absolutely no way to plan a careful approach, which is what XCOM is supposed to be all about. Instead, you have some annoying ♥♥♥♥ back at the HQ barking orders at you while he's eating a donut, telling that the Alien relay is closing down, as if you didn't know why you're there in the first place.
XCOM 2 is like playing Mount & Blade and selecting "Auto-fight" before every encounter and getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by the computer. You can maneuver, yes, but ultimately it all comes down to a dice roll and you will die in situations that would never happen in real life, like missing a shot, when the gun barrel is literally at the enemy's stupid face.
There's just so much frustration in this game. Creating a squad of friends and seeing them all die during the first mission is beyond infuriating. To me there's nothing more annoying than an unfair challenge and that's what this game boils down to. Some people get easier missions and scenarios early on so they can build their team, but if you're like me, you just get humiliated again, again, again and again. You start feeling like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, because you paid full price for a game that makes fun of you at every turn, and forces you to turn down the difficulty, because you're too much of a ♥♥♥♥♥ to play on Ironman like you did in the previous game.

I can't recommend this game.  It's no longer a strategy game, just a race against XCOM's legendary rage-inducing RNG.
There's so much here to build on, and that's part of that makes this so disappointing.  There's a great stealth mechanic...that you can't use because of the turn timer, so you blow it on the opening group of enemies you see.  It's neat, fun to play with for a few (failed) missions, then you leave it alone because the turn timer invalidates a piece of great design.
There's awesome classes with neat abilities...except sharpshooters are worthless since using them like the sniper they're supposed to be means that you lose them when the evac timer runs out.  Once again, the turn timer invalidates another piece of some really good class/game design.
You could always counter the whims of the RNG in XCOM: EU/EW by playing safe with overwatch and setting up a good sniper position, and you can see the design intent to stop that with the turn timer.  But that turn timer coupled with the whimsical RNG turns the game from a "series of interesting decisions" into a series of bad ones and worse ones.
It's really close to being the GOTY candidate so many reviewers are making it out to be.  But without a balance pass, it's just an overengineered race against a timer full of nigh-impossible missions.  Any strategy is invalidated by the timer, so you just roll your shots and hope they hit, because if they don't, you're dead.
This is XCOM.  They don't hit often enough to stop you from dying.

This game is fantastic.
You round up a team of heroes and send them into a dungeon to kill horrors and bring back loot.  However, these aren't godly JRPG superhumans you're sending in, your heroes are fragile both in mind and body.  This is reinforced both through the Mignola-esque art style and through the gameplay.  Even if you are well-prepared and cautious, you are always a handle of unlucky rolls from disaster.  The fact that you can and will lose heroes is mitigated by the fact that fresh recruits are freely available, and the upgrades to your hamlet are permanent once unlocked.
The game design ensures that you will feel tense as you explore the dungeon.  Your stocks of food and torches slowly run out, and the dungeon becomes more menacing as the light level dims (even so, these dangers are balanced by greater rewards).  Encounters and traps will whittle away at your health and sanity, and much of the time you will have only limited means to recover.  If things go badly, it is often best to cut your losses and run away.  However, it's all too easy to say 'just a little bit further' and before you know it you've been ambushed and are being cut down.
The devs have said that they are considering future balance tweaks, and I trust them to do a good job.  The gameplay is more polished compared to the initial EA release and the difficulty is very-well calibrated.  Combat is tactical due to the positioning mechanics and yet feels visceral given the possibility of huge swings of luck.  I have put hours and hours into this game and it still gets my heart pounding every time.  I'm still not at the titular 'Darkest Dungeon' but I already feel that this has been one of my favorite games of all time.

I recommend this game with a MASSIVE qualification:  Get it, but get a mod that reduces the difficulty.  This game is too hard.  It's insanely fun and addicting, but as you get farther, your motivation to slog against the "random" number generator (which is only random if being stacked in the foe's favor still counts as "random", which I suppose only does through the most clinical definition of the term) that continually punishes you for doing poorly and punishes you HARDER for doing well will wane.  Soon as your guys hit level 3, they will refuse "Tier 1" dungeons (represented by green icons), and even STARTING the "Tier 2" dungeons is ridiculously hard, even with release notes saying monsters there have been nerfed.  They haven't. Or rather, they haven't been so enough.  I have ventured to Tier 2 dungeons several times, both during Early Access (supported this game, and it merits mentioning I don't regret it) and after this full release, and three of those times were Total Party Wipes, and the remainder had two survivors at most.  I can't even IMAGINE the Tier 3 dungeons.  I have been playing video games for most of my life, consisting mainly of strategy and tactical games, and I am no stranger to roguelikes. This game is ridiculously difficult for me, which suggests that for your average gamer, they won't complete it.  Hell, *I* probably won't; certainly not without a difficulty mod.
The good news is that the construction is relatively simple, meaning anyone with a text editor can screw with values, probabilities, everything that makes up how the game works and how combat goes.
I really don't want to whine like a broken turbofan, and I really want to make it clear that I am not johnning here.  I honestly believe (and I am confident I am not alone) that they catered to a very vocal minority that holds difficulty in almost fetishistic regard (wishing no offense to those people, it's just that most of us nerds, ya know, AREN'T like that).  Most people I talk to claim that they play until it becomes  a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and then call it a "full experience".  What's depressing is that that seems to be about maybe ten hours in, when your guys have gained three levels (they start at 0) and then it just becomes an exercise in head-against-brick-wall.
It's lots of fun; its only fatal flaw is that it's super fun until it super isn't, and that "super isn't" time hits WAY too fast.  I maintain that this can be averted by finding a competent mod that makes it hard without making it masochistic, so, yes, recommended.  Just seriously qualified recommendation.  Pick it up on a discount, see where it takes you.  Don't feel shame if you end up ♥♥♥♥ing with the game's internal files, though.  You aren't alone, friend.
Happy hunting, kiddies.

The games will often get you my overpowering you with enormous amounts of enemies and a lack of hearts/pill drops to make your adventure that much more painful. Spiral Knights is a fun game that I believe should be played for leisure and avoid obsessing over it, it is not a game worth spending money on because it just gets harder with a difficult learning curve. In tier 2 and 3 of the game, 'Normal' difficulty loses its meaning, the entire game in itself becomes horribly difficult with enemies that can hit you from 2 yards away  and, often, bite right through your shield in a single chomp. This review is from the perspective of an MMO veteran who has wasted countless hours of his life on a wide range of online RPGs from Ultima Online to World of Warcraft and now Trove.
Good:
- Free but polished
- Gorgeous graphics
- Excellent real-time combat system
- Vibrant, active community
- Wide range of unconventional and interesting classes. No Warriors and rogues here, instead you choose between classes such as the Candy barbarian, Dracolyte or Gunslinger
- Great new concepts such as cornerstones (little home plots that you build up and take with you as you adventure or chill in the central hub world), and club worlds (basically guilds, but with instanced plots of land that members can expand and build on minecraft style)
- Frequent content updates. The devs keep the patches rolling
Bad:
- Lack of true party system is unfortunate.
- While the sound isn't terrible, some of the music and enemy emotes can become very repetitive.
- The economy is a little wild right now. With no true currency or in-game auction system, hardcore players are able to easily prey on newcomers who don't know what the trade value is on particular items. This may appeal to some people but I prefer the visibility an auction house provides.
- Endgame is lacking at the moment. Basically boils down to leveling a new class, or farm. Although the devs have some endgame content coming in the near future
Ugly:
- Server issues! As with any new and popular online game, Trove has it's share of issues. And in it's defense, things have been steadily improving each week since launch, but there are still many issues at the moment. Weird lag and long queues during prime hours, server crashes, random disconnects, emergency patches that keep the servers down for hours at a time. If you have ever experienced a popular online game at launch, you know what to expect here.
- Real money shop has lots of overpriced crap on it but what else did you expect in a F2P MMORPG, right?
Conclusion:
Trove is a good game that is currently going through a rough post launch phase. But the server issues are steadily improving, so there is no reason why any action/RPG/minecraft-like fan shouldn't check this out.

Overall: I strongly dislike this game and if you're heavily into roleplaying games and/or Fallout lore you probably won't either. Bethesda was clearly trying to widen their audience base with this game by adding elements to attract everyone and anyone, but as a result, the game lacks depth and it's difficult (for me anyway) to get invested in the main storyline.
+better lighting and general graphics
+character creator and bodyslider allow for both unique looking player characters and a more diverse and interesting wasteland
+combat has been cleaned up; UI is more responsive
+power armor finally feels and functions the way it should according to lore
+companions are better written and more interactive
+AI and pathing has been improved
+huge range of new voice actors with repeats far less often
+aid items heal over time and have timers so things like stimpaks aren't totally abusable
-complete scrapping of skills; perks now have to do the boring number work (damage increases, lockpicking and hacking abilities, etc) that skills did
-levelling up is dumbed down and unrewarding
-RADIANT QUESTS JESUS CHRIST
-no ending slideshow to show how your decisions changed the wasteland, just a boring cinematic
-dialogue "wheel" is clunky and hard to manage and even Bethesda admits this
-lots of retconning and lore breaking that makes no sense in the Fallout universe and even breaks other games' questlines and history, including FO3, a game the Bethesda ALSO made
-no serious decision making is ever really required of the player
-factions continue to make baffling decisions
-player character has a pre-set background which suppresses roleplaying
-no more skill or perk checks in dialogue
-speech checks are based on a diceroll and not the bare numbers so even with a maxed out charisma stat you can still fail
-bad, overpriced DLC
-main questline is short and convoluted
-most quests in general are uninteresting and unengaging
-world building makes no sense (how are there so many weapons just laying around in the open, untouched for 200 years?)
-why would you do this to me, Todd?
Just play the original isometric games or F:NV. Hell, even FO3, which I am very critical of, was at least more engaging and fun to play than FO4.

Right now the big question is "Should I buy this game."
As someone who loved XCOM, and Long War, the answer is yes for me. I have a pretty decent computer, and there are only a few hangups and longish loading screen. I run on full graphics settings, and there's nothing a patch won't fix in the near future. The base game is great (not outstanding), but I have faith it will only get better with time - both with player mods and official patches and DLC.
People who might want to hold off on this game are people who only meet the minimum requirements for this game. I'm sure they will optimize it soon, but it might be frustrating with the stuttering. Also, if you like easy turn-based tactics games where you don't actually need to apply tactics (grinding games to level up and dominate later), then this might not be the game for you. The enemy is always one step ahead of you and the difficulty so far has only increased each mission. Just when you think you have the advantage, a new enemy will pop out and destroy your squad.
Pre TL/DR:
Pros:
- The MUSIC (I haven't seen this in other reviews, but the music is great)
- The story is actually really good.
- Customization - you can now customize, mod, and name weapons! (in addition to the characters)
- No $%&$ing rock/paper/scissors ufo missions (so far)
- Really good graphics (now with cinematic misses!)
- Improved destructible environment (blow up enemies on the roof, the roof collapses, they die to the falling damage)
- Improved difficulty (this may be a con to some people)
Cons:
(Nothing that can't be patched or modded out in the future)
-Some stuttering (maybe once or twice a mission for me)  and long loading screens
- Timed Missions (Hopefully a mission pack will be released with some traditional missions to mix up the tedium)
- Poor interface (similar to previous xcom, but a little clunkier imo)
- Balance Tweaks Needed (some enemies are a bit strong; some classes are under-utilized)
- Lack of weapon/class variety (I say this coming from playing LW....the LW team is working on a mod for this game though)
That said, this game is different - for better or worse, and you must change your tactics. Using the same tactics from XCOM EW will eat you up and spit you out. Learn to use up both movements instead of just dashing once. Only set up overwatch on your point man, while other characters catch up and move forward. Overwatch actually has a decent chance to hit this game. Focus fire on "certain" enemies - flank them even if it leaves you vulnerable. Certain enemies must die asap (grenades or swords) or you will spend too much time later on. Small tactical adjustments like this will help you acclimate from the previous XCOM.
This type of gameplay is different, and classes like sharpshooter are now somewhat worthless on many levels. Just give me 2 rangers and 2 grenadiers and I can clear a map in half the time limit. That said, all classes have their place and can be used well. A sharpshooter with full pistol upgrades is better in some missions than the actual sniper rifle.
One of the best parts about this game is you now MUST be creative in completing missions, or you will fail many times. I was stuck in the middle of a building with 2 turns to reach the evac zone. There was no way I could reach the door in time. So I just blew the wall up, creating an exit point and rushed my squad out. Moments like this make up for a lot of the bad RNG. The deck is stacked against you the whole game. You must be creative and take advantage of every opportunity to succeed. If you are returning back to base with all your secondary items....you will not succeed later (I like to conserve grenades/ammo, but you don't have the luxury to do that in this game).
If you like turn based, tactics games, then this is a must-buy for you at some point. If you are worried about not meeting the specs, just wait a week or two until some of these performance bugs are fixed and check back.
If you enjoy playing these games (like I do) then you will probably like Xcom 2 -
XCOM:EW (Long War)
Divinity Original Sin
Pillars of Eternity
Dragon Age: Origin
Wasteland 2

I think the best way to describe this game is by saying what Darkest Dungeon
Darkest Dungeon isn't a RPG that gives you much freedom. It's a roguelike dungeon crawler that gives you limited resources which you need to make the best of. Choice is limited and skill customization is very rudimentary. The more important thing is managing your stats, quirks and positioning.
Darkest Dungeon isn't something that will praise and reward you for progress. Instead, it will remind you that overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer - either through narration that has really been nailed spot-on; or through throwing a curvebal at you right when you thought you've earned yourself a break. One slip-up or one unlucky roll, and the star of your squad will be pushing up daisies. Your victories will be taken from you if you are not careful.
Darkest Dungeon isn't something you can min-max an A team for and blow the content away. It will hit you with mechanics that will make you rotate your teams and building a sufficiently large and healthy roster is required if you want to have a chance.
Darkest Dungeon isn't fair. It withholds information, and it doesn't telegraph its intentions to you. Sometimes, you'll get lucky. Sometimes the cards will be stacked against you. There are toggles you can use to remove some of the more frustrating elements from the game, but that takes away from the experience.
Darkest Dungeon isn't about you or your path to glory. You don't get to save the world. You don't get a happy ending with a cigar in one hand, and a lovely tavern lass in your lap. You get thrown into a desperate situation and the world doesn't care about you or about what you want to achieve. What you have to decide is whether to ragequit or to make your stand for as long as you can.
The one choice that Darkest Dungeon does give you is this: When the frustration of the game is building up, are you going to fall into affliction and let the stress take you down, or call on virtue and push on in face of overwhelming odds? Your heroes do not get to make this choice. You do.
If what's been said above doesn't appeal to you, then Darkest Dungeon isn't for you. But I do know that it

This game is about if heroes in RPG games were more human. Characters get stressed out if attacked or if its dark. There is a bar that is called the stress bar. If this fills up you can become afflicted (most likely) or virtuous (rare). This is one of the main draws.
Another main draw is permadeath. Like real life, if you die, there is no respawning. If a character dies they are DEAD.
Also there is the torch. This mechanic is my favorite draw. If the torch is darker that means you get more stressed out, get surprised, and even get crits if the torch is low enough.
The combat system is siple yet complex. You pick an abilty and it has a certain amout of damage, targets, and special feature. Like the Vestal's judgement: it heals her after hitting an enemy.
There is just so much charm to this game and more things i can't write down.

Right now the big question is "Should I buy this game."
As someone who loved XCOM, and Long War, the answer is yes for me. I have a pretty decent computer, and there are only a few hangups and longish loading screen. I run on full graphics settings, and there's nothing a patch won't fix in the near future. The base game is great (not outstanding), but I have faith it will only get better with time - both with player mods and official patches and DLC.
People who might want to hold off on this game are people who only meet the minimum requirements for this game. I'm sure they will optimize it soon, but it might be frustrating with the stuttering. Also, if you like easy turn-based tactics games where you don't actually need to apply tactics (grinding games to level up and dominate later), then this might not be the game for you. The enemy is always one step ahead of you and the difficulty so far has only increased each mission. Just when you think you have the advantage, a new enemy will pop out and destroy your squad.
Pre TL/DR:
Pros:
- The MUSIC (I haven't seen this in other reviews, but the music is great)
- The story is actually really good.
- Customization - you can now customize, mod, and name weapons! (in addition to the characters)
- No $%&$ing rock/paper/scissors ufo missions (so far)
- Really good graphics (now with cinematic misses!)
- Improved destructible environment (blow up enemies on the roof, the roof collapses, they die to the falling damage)
- Improved difficulty (this may be a con to some people)
Cons:
(Nothing that can't be patched or modded out in the future)
-Some stuttering (maybe once or twice a mission for me)  and long loading screens
- Timed Missions (Hopefully a mission pack will be released with some traditional missions to mix up the tedium)
- Poor interface (similar to previous xcom, but a little clunkier imo)
- Balance Tweaks Needed (some enemies are a bit strong; some classes are under-utilized)
- Lack of weapon/class variety (I say this coming from playing LW....the LW team is working on a mod for this game though)
That said, this game is different - for better or worse, and you must change your tactics. Using the same tactics from XCOM EW will eat you up and spit you out. Learn to use up both movements instead of just dashing once. Only set up overwatch on your point man, while other characters catch up and move forward. Overwatch actually has a decent chance to hit this game. Focus fire on "certain" enemies - flank them even if it leaves you vulnerable. Certain enemies must die asap (grenades or swords) or you will spend too much time later on. Small tactical adjustments like this will help you acclimate from the previous XCOM.
This type of gameplay is different, and classes like sharpshooter are now somewhat worthless on many levels. Just give me 2 rangers and 2 grenadiers and I can clear a map in half the time limit. That said, all classes have their place and can be used well. A sharpshooter with full pistol upgrades is better in some missions than the actual sniper rifle.
One of the best parts about this game is you now MUST be creative in completing missions, or you will fail many times. I was stuck in the middle of a building with 2 turns to reach the evac zone. There was no way I could reach the door in time. So I just blew the wall up, creating an exit point and rushed my squad out. Moments like this make up for a lot of the bad RNG. The deck is stacked against you the whole game. You must be creative and take advantage of every opportunity to succeed. If you are returning back to base with all your secondary items....you will not succeed later (I like to conserve grenades/ammo, but you don't have the luxury to do that in this game).
If you like turn based, tactics games, then this is a must-buy for you at some point. If you are worried about not meeting the specs, just wait a week or two until some of these performance bugs are fixed and check back.
If you enjoy playing these games (like I do) then you will probably like Xcom 2 -
XCOM:EW (Long War)
Divinity Original Sin
Pillars of Eternity
Dragon Age: Origin
Wasteland 2
Valkyria Chronicles

The game follows the endeavours of knights from the Spiral Order marooned on the mysterious planet Cradle, and their battles against the monsters living in the Clockworks underground. Fantastic game...with bugs.
If you enjoyed XCOM then XCOM 2 is a no brainer. It's a fantastic game that changes just enough to make it new and fresh without screwing over it's fanbase with a crappy sequel. However, at this time there are some very annoying bugs and performance issues that bring it's appeal down a little. The performance issues I can live with, I have a fairly strong rig (4790k @ 4.7 ghz, R9 290 Tri-X, 8GB of RAM, game installed on 850 EVO SSD) but load times seem quite a bit longer than they should be (especially being on an SSD) and graphical performance seems quite a bit less than it should be. I'm playing on medium settings at 1440p and I'm getting some crunchy frame drops. It's definitely playable but it just seems like I should be getting more fps for the visuals.
The bugs are what are annoying me the most. In particular I've been experiencing random freezes that force me to hard restart my computer. The game autosaves after each turn (at least at my current difficulty setting) so that helps a little, but the last time it froze I had just spent a good while customizing my "A Team" to perfection, only to have all those customizations wiped out by a game freeze. Bummer.
Bottom Line: Even with the issues listed above, I would still recommend it. It's been so much fun and while the performance seems lower than it should be, it's still a very good looking game. I'm really hoping a patch will come down the pipe soon to fix some of the problems I listed. Have fun!

Darkest Dungeon is a about managing the quirks, traumas, wounds, diseases and failings of adventuring. You manage small parties of heroes, who quest against the horrors that lurk beneath your estate and manor. It is difficult, but very atmospheric. If you like a challenging turn-based dungeon crawler, reminiscent of old pen-and-paper horror RPGs, then I can thoroughly recommend this to you.
Your task is to clear the ruins, woods and caverns beneath your estate of all manner of unspeakable horrors and evil abominations. This is done with parties of 4, who are drawn from a roster of adventurers who you keep in town. These hapless heroes are fallible and suffer diseases, blights, wounds, afflictions, quirks and... stress. Part of the game is about improving their skills and upgrading their weapons. But much of it is about healing them, managing their stress, dealing with their phobias and coping when they die.
The game play is unforgiving and difficult, but it does reward careful planning and adaptability. Yet you need to face the fact that there will be losses and that sometimes you simply need to dismiss an adventurer who has become incurable or hopeless to the cause. Knowing when to retreat and when to push on is a critical part of this game. For some, this adversity proves too much, and there are many negative reviews about how hard it is or how unrelenting the game can be. Sure... it is not for everyone. But for those who relish that type of dark challenge, this game does it exceptionally well.
The game mechanics are straight forward, but with no set "best way" to use them. Different skills and abilities change the ideal configuration and different locations and enemies each require different approaches. There is no one perfect group and players must be prepared too re-arrange and adapt their heroes to accommodate the foul monsters that await them. The dungeon layouts are simple, but effective. A scouting ability sometimes gives you some warning of what lies ahead and there are occasions where taking a separate path is advisable.
There are a large number of achievements to collect. Although these are pretty straight forward, they do give a measure of progress and spur on your determination. Unusual party compositions are titled and actions and afflictions are cleverly labelled. Comments from the adventurers are witty and raise a smile, despite the forlorn predicament that has resulted in them.
The noir artwork and foreboding narration provide a rich and deeply atmospheric setting. All the graphics fit together seamlessly and with a unique convincing style. The voice-over is particularly appealing, and conveys the horrors and adversities without being depressing or morose. The terminology and setting is rich and deep, reminiscent of the works of Walter de la Mare, Howard Lovecraft or Edgar Poe. For those who like this level of linguistic sophistication, you will find much to smile at here. It is not often you hear the phrase
!
Challenging, polished and deeply atmospheric. Righteous traits for a computer game!

Darkest Dungeon is a about managing the quirks, traumas, wounds, diseases and failings of adventuring. You manage small parties of heroes, who quest against the horrors that lurk beneath your estate and manor. It is difficult, but very atmospheric. If you like a challenging turn-based dungeon crawler, reminiscent of old pen-and-paper horror RPGs, then I can thoroughly recommend this to you.
Your task is to clear the ruins, woods and caverns beneath your estate of all manner of unspeakable horrors and evil abominations. This is done with parties of 4, who are drawn from a roster of adventurers who you keep in town. These hapless heroes are fallible and suffer diseases, blights, wounds, afflictions, quirks and... stress. Part of the game is about improving their skills and upgrading their weapons. But much of it is about healing them, managing their stress, dealing with their phobias and coping when they die.
The game play is unforgiving and difficult, but it does reward careful planning and adaptability. Yet you need to face the fact that there will be losses and that sometimes you simply need to dismiss an adventurer who has become incurable or hopeless to the cause. Knowing when to retreat and when to push on is a critical part of this game. For some, this adversity proves too much, and there are many negative reviews about how hard it is or how unrelenting the game can be. Sure... it is not for everyone. But for those who relish that type of dark challenge, this game does it exceptionally well.
The game mechanics are straight forward, but with no set "best way" to use them. Different skills and abilities change the ideal configuration and different locations and enemies each require different approaches. There is no one perfect group and players must be prepared too re-arrange and adapt their heroes to accommodate the foul monsters that await them. The dungeon layouts are simple, but effective. A scouting ability sometimes gives you some warning of what lies ahead and there are occasions where taking a separate path is advisable.
There are a large number of achievements to collect. Although these are pretty straight forward, they do give a measure of progress and spur on your determination. Unusual party compositions are titled and actions and afflictions are cleverly labelled. Comments from the adventurers are witty and raise a smile, despite the forlorn predicament that has resulted in them.
The noir artwork and foreboding narration provide a rich and deeply atmospheric setting. All the graphics fit together seamlessly and with a unique convincing style. The voice-over is particularly appealing, and conveys the horrors and adversities without being depressing or morose. The terminology and setting is rich and deep, reminiscent of the works of Walter de la Mare, Howard Lovecraft or Edgar Poe. For those who like this level of linguistic sophistication, you will find much to smile at here. It is not often you hear the phrase

Awesome addition to the XCOM games! Quick rundown:
+ Graphics look good & unit customization is great
+ Solder pool allows you to save favorite looking solders, or import other people's solders. One from the pool may show up in game as a solder, engineer that has to be rescused, or even an enemy informant you need to kidnap or kill!
+ Maps look great, and are all of a good size, as well as variety
+ Enemies are varied, with more types than before. Aliens are actually a threat!
+ Tons of different items for solders to use (various granades, ammo types, gun mods)
+ Turn based missions make overwatch turtling an impossible strategy, which was pretty much the I-Win-Button for XCOM EU/EW. Also adds a sense of urgency.
+ Ranged heals
+ New classes are well designed and have some neat perks
- Some performance issues. Sometimes there's a 5 - 10 second pause at the start of the enemy turn. Sometimes on the enemy turn the screen will go black. Sometimes FPS tanks for no discernible reason.
- Navigating multi-floored buildings just as much of a pain as XCOM:EU/EW
- While I find the time limit missions (which seem to be about 50% of them) fine, I think extending the timer by two turns on a mission would help out the casual XCOM players.
- Russian & Polish languages missing. These were added in Enemy Within (along with localization), and should have remained. Even if Firaxis didn't localise there for XCOM 2, I'm sure a copy/paste of sound files from EW would have pleased those overseas. Though I am of neither nationality, I did like my Russian & Polish solders speaking their language, and hope this is implemented in the future.

Yeah, so this game is something else.
Is it hard? You betcha.
This isn't a game for people who get really connected to their characters, because they WILL die. But that's part of the mechanics. Your adventerers die and become insane, but (hopefully) your hamlet slowly starts to develop, making things just a little easier every time. It's a battle of inches and sometimes, you'll feel robbed and cheated and angry, but then suddenly, you were able to clear a whole dungeon without retreating, or you came across a big cache of loot. All those frustrations add up, but every success feels monumental.
Oh, and don't be afraid to retreat. Like in poker, you've gotta know when to fold 'em.
One of my favorite aspects of the game is the art. There's something uniquely compelling about it. The animations are not elaborate, but they are effective. It vaguely reminds me of games like Card Hunter or Paper Mario, except its aesthetic is grim and gothic and surreal.
The turn-based combat is simple enough to wrap one's head around. Pretty intuitive stuff. There are some minor details that took me a little time to figure out, like that each hero has preferred combat positions.
But it's simple enough that you'll get the hang of the mechanics after a few fights.
Looting, saving up money and stocking up before an adventure is a difficult balance, though I do appreciate the game designer's decision to use different collectibles for the various upgrades around the hamlet, rather than the coin you need for potions, bandages and such.
It feels rather grindy/repetitive, but as long as I keep a degree of narrative going in my head (the frequent character comments/changing sanity levels do help in that respect), it prevents the gameplay from getting too stale.
8/10.
Very interesting setting/themes/aesthetics
Stress/sanity levels are generally well done, though it often does seem too easy to push a hero to high stress. I get that they're seeing scary things, having their comrades die and fighting monsters, but a lot of these guys seem like they've done this sort of thing before. Two or three fights in, and new guy is already a kleptomaniac.
There are many personality types for the heroes. I had one guy who was super gung-ho when he arrived, all like, "when can I go? When can I go? When can I go?" and then after one quest that went a little sour, he refused to go back.
The music and narration also help keep things interesting.
The combat system itself is solid, if a little uninspired.
Overall, a very engaging game.

With with more than 300 hours on Fallout 4(Seperate system), I have finally come to a conclusion, summarized in a Steam review.
PREVIEW:
In case you didn't know, Fallout 4 takes place in an alternative future, where America (and most likely other countries) have been all but destroyed by atomic bombs launched on October 23rd, 2077. After this event, about 200 years later, your character (Which is fully customizable) is thrown into the Commonwealth (What's left of Boston). At this point you can basically do whatever you want. Build a settlement, fight for one of the 4 factions in their seemingly endless struggle for control over Boston, or you can just scavenge. The list goes on.
DIALOGUE:
In Fallout 4, you have slightly less choice than the previous Fallout games. For example, the dialogue system, though good, doesn't even compare to Fallout New Vegas, which had a unique dialogue choice for almost every perk/S.P.E.C.I.A.L. rank. Also, most dialogue options in-game will almost always lead in the same outcome as the other choices. It gives you the illusion of choice, but it really doesn't have an effect on anything (Unless you have a companion).

CHARACTERS:
Speaking of, it's time to move on to characters. In Fallout 4, there are so many characters to meet. Like the Minuteman "good-guy" Preston Garvey, or the tough as nails Cait. these colorful people make the Commonwealth feel alive, it seems almost every character has a story. It's amazing how fleshed out the huge world is. An average Raider can have an entire story hidden behind notes and terminals, giving more insight and information on the world you're traveling thorugh.
PLOT/STORY:

Sadly, the "main story" of Fallout 4 is the usual "I need to find my ..." sort of thing. Although it does pick up very greatly in the late game, though many people might be put off by the boring old formula. I highly recommend you sit through the shaky beginning, because once you get into the story, it'll stay in your mind until it's finished. It's based on finding your son, Shaun who was kidnapped by masked men. With nothing else but the name of your child, you venture into the wasteland, in search of him. Which turns over even more questions which leads to an explosive finale, where you play a key role in a questline for a faction that you choose.
S.P.E.C.I.A.L.

I was originally going to include this in the "dialogue" segment, but I've decided that this is too big of a problem to ignore. This Fallout 4's S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system is VERY lacking. In past games, your S.P.E.C.I.A.L. would change the game for you, with dialogue choices to defuse the situation (High Charisma), or to have a good shot at an enemy's head from far away (High Perception). But sadly, in Fallout 4, the RPG elements are basically thrown out the window. All your  S.P.E.C.I.A.L. does in this game is decide what perks you're able to get at that  S.P.E.C.I.A.L. level. It's very upsetting to see such a unique and interesting system be trashed. I truly hope that it is brought back in Fallout 5.
ENDING NOTES:
Many people will ask, "Is Fallout 4 a good game?" In short. yes fallout 4 is a good game, it improves on the gameplay issues the previous games had and it provides a immersive experience throughout that supports and implies multiple playthroughs. Fallout 4 is a good game, but it's not a good Fallout game. The very watered down dialogue system and Perk/ S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system takes away the charm the games had since the first Fallout game was released. Without these features, Fallout 4 is just another generic shooter, And I wish I could say otherwise. I recommend this game because of it's amazing in-game world and great gameplay (Excluding RPG elements).
P.S.:
I highly recommend you play the previous Fallout games to see the true potential of the  S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, also. The older games may have aged, but they're still classics that deserve your attention. (Personal recommendation: Fallout New Vegas)

XCOM 2 is a great sequel improving upon many aspects of the original game and the EW expansion. It took some great ideas from The Long War mod and the new concealment system allows for actual stealth gameplay. Even has great Day 1 mod support. But I cannot recommend XCOM 2 as it is right now due to a lot of bugs and optimization issues.
Sometimes the game seems to hang when enemies make decisions, not an actual system hang but the game almost pauses for an odd amount of time. Sometimes when on higher elevations above the enemy, you still are revealed even if you're not in their "tile of vision", which completely wrecks your game and tactics.  I think the timer is fine, but needs a lot of tweaking for later difficulties as even with a mod that increases the timer, I still barely passed a mission with a mere 2 turns remaining on Commander difficulty.
I also clearly meet the recommended requirements (FX 6300 and GTX 770 2GB), but still run into serious performance issues, dropping FPS down to the teens. This is not just me, nearly everyone even with better specs than me are experiencing this. Being as this is not a fast paced game, it doesn't really affect gameplay but this is still an issue that needs fixing nonetheless.
In conclusion, I would not recommend buying XCOM 2 right now at full price. Wait until they release a few patches to fix the current problems that burden this great game.

This wont be an incredibly detailed Review, I want to offer a simple "everygamer" perspective on the game. Plenty of people allready went into the deep, mechanical stuff, numbercrunching and the like, so I'll try to simply offer my thoughts on DD.
First of all, Darkest Dungeon is, in my opinion, very much a "hit or miss" game. Getting into it with the wrong expectations may ruin it for a lot of people. So keep this in mind if you're thinking about making a purchase:
If you can't handle loss of any sort, do NOT buy it.
I wont call it "hardcore", because I dont like the term. Like any other game, once you go deep enough even DD can be mastered, and played in a way that minimizes loss and renders some of the challenge less impactful.
Combat may seem very random at first. The game does not tell you the order in which participants move, and damage has a rather wide range, especially for Crits. Depending on how much RNGJesus loves you, the initial experience can thus either be "Why do they call this hard?" and obliterating your monitor with your keyboard. Additional frustration can (And in my experience will) arise for people that don't look anything up Online. Both Items and Bossfights can screw the uninformed in major ways, and it's easy to just quit the game out of frustration because of it.
However, the deeper you go, the more the game unravels. The dark, lovecraftian atmosphere is great right away. But becomes even more cool once you discover some tidbits about the Lore and how everything is connected. Combat also becomes easier the longer you play, as you learn the ups and downs of each class, strengths and weaknesses of enemies and the proper use of items and curios. Bosses and higher difficulty missions become more manageable, the more you play. I can't stress this enough: Give the game and yourself time to settle in.
The best way to play it, is to treat each of your guys as expendable. They are ressources, just like the Gold, Trinkets and Upgradematerial. If you treat that Crusader like a Pawn instead of a King, you're gonna have a much easier time dealing with the ocassional backlash the game throws at you.
The bottom line is, at least for me: Yes the game is an a**hole from time to time. Yes it takes some investment to get into it. But the atmosphere, class design, fantastic music and the feeling from finally downing that one Boss, makes it worth it in the end.

Awesome addition to the XCOM games! Quick rundown:
+ Graphics look good & unit customization is great
+ Solder pool allows you to save favorite looking solders, or import other people's solders. One from the pool may show up in game as a solder, engineer that has to be rescused, or even an enemy informant you need to kidnap or kill!
+ Maps look great, and are all of a good size, as well as variety
+ Enemies are varied, with more types than before. Aliens are actually a threat!
+ Tons of different items for solders to use (various granades, ammo types, gun mods)
+ Turn based missions make overwatch turtling an impossible strategy, which was pretty much the I-Win-Button for XCOM EU/EW. Also adds a sense of urgency.
+ Ranged heals
+ New classes are well designed and have some neat perks
- Some performance issues. Sometimes there's a 5 - 10 second pause at the start of the enemy turn. Sometimes on the enemy turn the screen will go black. Sometimes FPS tanks for no discernible reason.
- Navigating multi-floored buildings just as much of a pain as XCOM:EU/EW
- While I find the time limit missions (which seem to be about 50% of them) fine, I think extending the timer by two turns on a mission would help out the casual XCOM players.
- Russian & Polish languages missing. These were added in Enemy Within (along with localization), and should have remained. Even if Firaxis didn't localise there for XCOM 2, I'm sure a copy/paste of sound files from EW would have pleased those overseas. Though I am of neither nationality, I did like my Russian & Polish solders speaking their language, and hope this is implemented in the future.

If you've played a X-Com game on anything above easy or normal, keep in mind that the difficulty is increased for X-Com2. The difficulty on Veteran level is closer to Classic. If you liked Long War, you'll find the combat to be more challenging.
The four initial classes are diversified based on soldier perks to more resemble the eight class system of the long war system. This is a refined mechanic that allows you to customize your soldiers greatly.
Performance wise, on two year old built computer, the game ran smoothly with no hiccups.
The shooting through walls animation issues have been greatly reduced between 1 and 2.
Tactically, you have far more options than X-COM EW or EU.
Waypoints are essential for sucess. You can use them to avoid many situations that would otherwise break your squad.
Overwatch is still a key mechanic but there are many times you will take the risky option to get to the objective and you will fail. Every shot will miss, beause of the order you took them in. This is okay, the war is not over yet.
There will be the one time everybody makes the shot against incredible odds and you go home with a everyone alive. Treasure it.
This game will make you sob when your squad gets wiped out in one turn because you misjudged pod locations and triggered four of them. But your small squad of soldiers will go down fighting, and the war against the aliens will go on.
Your small band of soldiers is doing their best to save the planet and there will be casualties along the way.

With the upgrade paths in the different buildings being so linear, I feel like there's actually very little variance in this game and it's purely a matter of endurance instead of randomness: max everything out and go for the final dungeon. The problem is that this form of progression just isn't masked well enough to make the game endearing to play until the end, and being able to see what skills you'll get for each character makes it more of a chore and less of a reward.

I don't normally write reviews for games, but seeing all the negative things people are saying about this game, I just wanted to take the time to post my opinion of XCOM 2 so far.
I think it is far better than Enemy Unknown.  I see people complaining about how buggy XCOM 2 is, but I was dealing with worse bugs in Enemy Unknown after it had been out for a year or two.  Granted, I haven't run into any game breaking bugs in XCOM 2, but I can not say the same of Enemy Unknown.  XCOM 2 has also only been out for a couple days, so really I don't think that most people had realistic expectations of what the state of the game was going to be on release.  Sure, it has some bugs, but not more than many other games have on release.
I'm also seeing people complain about how difficult XCOM 2 is.  If you don't want to play a difficult game, then what are you doing playing XCOM?  Perhaps it is not that the developers made the game too difficult, but it is you who are playing the wrong game...
People are also complaining about having to complete certain missions within a certain number of turns.  This was also an element in Enemy Unknown, so it isn't anything new.  I also have yet to be able to complete said missions within the given number of turns, so it does not seem to be that difficult to do.
Anyway, my opinion so far is that this game is a great step forward for the XCOM series.  Sure, some people are having performance issues, so try turning the graphics all the way down, or buying a better computer.  Newer games don't run well on low-end PCs.  My PC is not anywhere near top of the line, and I can run the game fine on mid-to-high graphics settings.
Additionally, this game is definitely more difficult than Enemy Unknown, and if you don't like that, then go play an easier game.
Some thing to also keep in mind is that many people are going to complain no matter what.  It seems to have become part of gamer culture to bash any new games that come out, in order for the individual to make themselves feel good or somehow superior.  My suggestion is watch some videos of people playing the game to find out if you would like it.  And if you don't like difficult games you will not like this game.  As far as performance goes, you can always buy the game, and if your computer is not capable of running this game, you can get a refund.

I'm writing this review as someone who has never played any XCOM game or had any former knowledge until a few days ago.
I watched a friend play on Steam broadcast for about 3-4 hours, and was really enjoying watching and decided to get the game.
Simply impressed with the gameplay, I'm not a big fan of turn based games typically but this is SO well done - the mechanics are usually spot on minus a few discrepencies with blowing up cover by accident or the animation issues which are apparent.
The game makes you value every choice, time is on the clock and if you don't move and stagnate the game will punish you or you'll miss out. Its the very best combination of a turn-based shooter and a global map based game with a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of roguelike and random elements.
You can fully customize your soldiers, save them into a character pool and you'll see them again forever. You can edit people you already have completely gender, nationality, colors, names, nicknames etc on the fly. Get invested in your squad mates then sadly watch them all die. Soldiers die, never to return, get wounded and require turns to heal.
You have to carefully balance between helping yourself, helping the resistance, and fighting back against alien forces. You will make tough choices with every bit of supplies, intelligence and items you have. Things go very wrong and you must scrape things together or your whole team will die.
I recall a mission where I had to choose to save one guy, or have them all die. So I chose for a person to toss a grenade at a soldier who was "binded" by an enemy and couldn't move. That saved him and allowed him to evac and live.
TLDR Pros/Cons
PROS:
Great story even if you've never played an XCOM game before
Amazing attatchment to characters / customization of them
Well done combat system
Random maps so I've never seen the same layout ever in my first ten hours
Lengthy and Difficulty campaign if you so desire it to be difficult
Things like music are very spot on and add great atmosphere to winning, losing, and even the downtime
Random events that are both positive and negative add a lot of depth and replayability
CONS:
Animations are wonky. Battle animations bug out and sometimes it slows down the turn pace of the game because you are waiting on someone to shoot/be hit.
Minor performance gripes, had some issues with the game hanging a bit while loading and it doesn't get the greatest of frames maxed out without AA/AO
Some mechanics aren't really hidden per se, but aren't explained. Like soldiers gaining their XP from kills, or when you break concealment all enemies in LOS will have LOS on you and move in/engage.
All in all this game was a major surprise and I say its worth the price tag. Most suspenseful game I've ever played!
