Having looked forward to this since completing the first X-Com: Enemy Unknown, I'm left underwhelmed.
The improvements and tweaks to how much you can personalize your Squaddies are great, as are the suble nods to the previous game and the tie-ins to Enemy Within... but... sigh... the GUI is even more twitchy than the previous incarnation, RNGeezus still blesses your enemies more often than you and worst of all, the concealment system, the big gameplay improvement Firaxis touted, is rigged. Enemy patrols WILL gravitate towards your hiding position despite their "obliviousness" of where you are.
This has some pretty disappointing concequences. Whatever tactical elements concealment could've added are undermined, as all it really enables you to do is ambush the first group of mobs you enounter and even then in a fairly clunky way.
Thinking of creating a squad of stealthed up Rangers for infiltrating and planting bombs in sabotage missions? Nope. Not possible. Well the all Ranger squad is, but the stealth approach isn't. I found this out the hard way. It's not so bad that your squad HAS to go in the front door, but if they aren't, they're meerely going in through the front window instead.
The other disappointment is the optimization; it's baaaaaad. Even with a Quad core, i7 and 980Ti, I'm seeing stuttery framerates at the begining and end of missions and noticable framerate drops in the armory menu. Hoping this eventually gets patched, but still sad to see it on release.
Overall, XCom 2 is a good game, and I'll happily recommend it, but compared to Enemy Unknown it's one step forward and one step back.  7.5/10

This wont be an incredibly detailed Review, I want to offer a simple "everygamer" perspective on the game. Plenty of people allready went into the deep, mechanical stuff, numbercrunching and the like, so I'll try to simply offer my thoughts on DD.
First of all, Darkest Dungeon is, in my opinion, very much a "hit or miss" game. Getting into it with the wrong expectations may ruin it for a lot of people. So keep this in mind if you're thinking about making a purchase:
If you can't handle loss of any sort, do NOT buy it.
I wont call it "hardcore", because I dont like the term. Like any other game, once you go deep enough even DD can be mastered, and played in a way that minimizes loss and renders some of the challenge less impactful.
Combat may seem very random at first. The game does not tell you the order in which participants move, and damage has a rather wide range, especially for Crits. Depending on how much RNGJesus loves you, the initial experience can thus either be "Why do they call this hard?" and obliterating your monitor with your keyboard. Additional frustration can (And in my experience will) arise for people that don't look anything up Online. Both Items and Bossfights can screw the uninformed in major ways, and it's easy to just quit the game out of frustration because of it.
However, the deeper you go, the more the game unravels. The dark, lovecraftian atmosphere is great right away. But becomes even more cool once you discover some tidbits about the Lore and how everything is connected. Combat also becomes easier the longer you play, as you learn the ups and downs of each class, strengths and weaknesses of enemies and the proper use of items and curios. Bosses and higher difficulty missions become more manageable, the more you play. I can't stress this enough: Give the game and yourself time to settle in.
The best way to play it, is to treat each of your guys as expendable. They are ressources, just like the Gold, Trinkets and Upgradematerial. If you treat that Crusader like a Pawn instead of a King, you're gonna have a much easier time dealing with the ocassional backlash the game throws at you.
The bottom line is, at least for me: Yes the game is an a**hole from time to time. Yes it takes some investment to get into it. But the atmosphere, class design, fantastic music and the feeling from finally downing that one Boss, makes it worth it in the end.

Fallout, as a game in general, is one of, if not the best, open world games that I have ever played. I somehow never got bored of it after several playthroughs across almost 500 hours of gameplay.
The graphics are completely different from Fallout 3 and New Vegas, so if you really like Fallout but hated the graphics from those games, you're in for a real treat!
The mechanics of the game are awesome. Bethesda drastically improved the gameplay from Fallout 3 with their new engine, making everything from the combat to general movement so much more enjoyable. The combat adapted to be more like a modern FPS, which means you don't have to rely on the VATS system all the time. Also, VATS is a little different than Fallout 3 and New Vegas in that everything switches to slow motion, giving the need to keep the quick thinking in mind, but only a little slower than it is out of VATS. Some people might not like this, but I think it makes the combat a little more challenging and immersive. Back to when I mentioned "general movement", walking around doesn't feel so clunky, and they added a much needed feature... SPRINTING! Skyrim had sprinting, but it still felt a little clunky and didn't have full 360 degree rotational movement in third person. That's another thing, third person view has been improved so that you can point the camera in one direction, and are able to smoothly run in a full circle without doing a weird square-dancing move, which makes playing in third person a lot more fun. Despite all those nice mechanics, one thing I was disappointed with was that the old Karma System has been removed. The Karma System allowed you to perform good and evil actions that will affect the game world, whether it's a physical change like, say, blowing up an entire settlement with a previously inactive nuclear bomb, or a change in somebody's view of you. In New Vegas, if you weren't in good with the NCR, they might make a negative remark towards you, saying something like "You should probably leave" or "You're a disgrace to us". Nuka World sort of let you be evil since the main characters were raiders, but it wasn't the same. You could also get unique perks, unique items, and unique companions for having a certain overall karma level, which added more depth to the roleplay. Karma was one of the main factors to roleplaying in Fallout and it doesn't feel as satisfying as it did in Fallout 3 and New Vegas.
Another huge change is the settlement building. Apparently, mods that allow you to build houses and♥♥♥♥♥♥was really popular, so Bethesda, being the great bunch of devs they are, decided to make their own system for it and put it into this game. Settlement building is a really fun addition that you can easily ignore if you don't want to have anything to do with it. Though, there are some parts in the story where you'll need to build a few things, but it's super easy and shouldn't take more than a few minutes if you have all the materials. By the way, the building does require specific materials (i.e. wood, steel, electronics, etc.) Scavenging for materials is easy, since pretty much every item in the game can be recycled into materials, but it can be hard to find a certain material that you need. Luckily, there's merchants that sell materials, but they might now always have what you need.
I could go on and on about the new gameplay features, but it's more fun to play it for yourself and see what the hell is so amazing about them. Moving on, the story wasn't great. A lot of the characters were ♥♥♥♥♥♥, and the story was very similar to Fallout 3 (minor spoilers, sorry.) They definitely could've written a better story, but thankfully they made up for it by making two awesome DLCs, Far Harbor and Nuka World. In my opinion, the DLC stories are a lot better, and the settings are really cool.
I give this game a 9.5/10 for the gameplay and a 5/10 for the story (of the base game). The gameplay could definitely be a little more polished with building; sometimes it's hard to place objects exactly how you want it and it can be a bit janky at times. And as I said, the story was pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Recommended, buy it if you want a great new open world adventure! Also, definitely get the DLCs, you won't be disappointed!

As of right now the free camera rotation mod has broken my save games (5-6 missions in) and the game performs questionably* even on powerful hardware.
*When I say questionably I mean fluctuations between (edit: Game seems to running more intensive maps at a lower FPS, still not breaking the fun) 30-60fps on a rig made from the following:
i7-4790 @ 3.6ghz
24gb DDR3 RAM
GTX 970
I've also stuck through about 3 or 4 texture loading problems which results in the game being TOTALLY unplayable until it has been restarted. The FPS problems are a patch or two away, they can and WILL be dealt with. Remember this is a turn based strategy game with absolutely NO twitch skill required. So even if the game drops to 30fps it will not affect the gameplay at all. If you are unfortunate enough to be suffering worse than that then that's unlucky for you but in this day and age, most Triple-A games have issues at launch due to the way publishers climb on top of developers to push out products that still need some polish to gain profit (I would advise not buying any games on day 1 in future).
This game despite those fixable issues is incredibly fun and rewarding so far. It's essentially the same thing as you'll find in XCOM:EU but with a few neat new features that make it all the more interesting. Performing ambushes will make you smile from smile from ear to ear! You will spend the first turn or two putting your squad into place and then laugh relentlessly as a sectoid walks into the line of sight of an overwatched minigunner to be shred into pieces in slowmo. The building is all much the same as before, as is the research.
DOOM TIMERS! Now this seems to be a touchy subject. I for one am playing with the Timer Tweaks mod as I'm not incredibly good at the game and like the extra few turns at hand just incase I screw up really bad (which I have done, it resulted in my minigun soldier and medic being captured :( and killed). I can understand how this might annoy some initially, but it was a design decision made to combat slow pace and help force the player into making more difficult decisions. I respect this and think it works quite well, if you don't then there is the timer remover mod :).
The enemies I have encountered so far have proven to be absolutely relentless and the sectoids are a genuine enemy to be afraid of now! As of now this is a huge recommdation by me. The bugs are a shame, but hey-ho that's how it is, they will be fixed but as it stands this IS a better game than XCOM:EU. Absolutely buy this if you enjoyed the first game!

PROs
- Tactical gameplay and options top notch: improved LOS markers, not all actions end the turn, more actions to choose from, stealth game play is tremendous

- Story is more interesting this time round, with more cut scenes
- Procedurally generated environments
- Perfectly balanced encuonters
- Destructible environments - including roofs
- Power curve of the aliens is also very well balanced
- Deep customisation on soldiers, and weapons
- Long War mods (free) at launch that are really well handled
- Great creature design
- Old aliens are revamped and made to be more interesting and/or powerful, yet it's tied neatly into the narrative.
- Good long campaign (20hrs in at time of writing this and no sign of being even halfway)
- Deluxe edition: the resistance armor skin pack is very cool: sending your soldiers out in jeans and t-shirts is bad♥♥♥♥♥
CONS (niggles)
- As per the last XCOM: models clipping through the environment, shooting through walls - zero effect on gaemplay, and less of a concern now with the improved LOS markers
- Occassional graphical glitches: model animations getting stuck (ranger got bound by snake man, but had bladeward, so killed it as a reactiom - but the ranger model stayed in the bound animation), or cut scenes hitching/skipping.

Trove is a classic grinding MMO, with an option to fast-forward the grinding with real money. The game is fun, the different classes lend some diversity to an otherwise routine game. The enemies balance well with the player level, and the game is paced so as to offer the player a reward at intervals that make it fun and keep the game feeling like an adventure. One of the greatest features is the "cornerstone"- your own plot of ground that you can build and outfit as you see fit and move with you as you move from biome to biome.
The downside is that grinding MMO's require functional servers to enjoy, and the developers can't seem to maintain a server or push a patch successfully to save their life. In the past two weeks since I began playing, with 48.5 hrs on record, there was not a day that passed  without the servers going down. Disruptions of less than an hour or 2 do not make the forum ( I think the dev's see them as common) but looking at the forum you can see that the server goes down for long periods at approximately 2 day intervals.
.

fun biomes to explore

What an amazing improvement on an already incredible tactical squad game. Must buy.
PROs
- Tactical gameplay and options top notch: improved LOS markers, not all actions end the turn, more actions to choose from, stealth game play is tremendous
- Ambushes
- Global strategy game absorbing and challenging (XCOMs and trhe aliens)
- Story is more interesting this time round, with more cut scenes
- Procedurally generated environments
- Perfectly balanced encuonters
- Destructible environments - including roofs
- Power curve of the aliens is also very well balanced
- Deep customisation on soldiers, and weapons
- Long War mods (free) at launch that are really well handled
- Great creature design
- Old aliens are revamped and made to be more interesting and/or powerful, yet it's tied neatly into the narrative.
- Good long campaign (20hrs in at time of writing this and no sign of being even halfway)
- Deluxe edition: the resistance armor skin pack is very cool: sending your soldiers out in jeans and t-shirts is bad♥♥♥♥♥
CONS (niggles)
- As per the last XCOM: models clipping through the environment, shooting through walls - zero effect on gaemplay, and less of a concern now with the improved LOS markers
- Occassional graphical glitches: model animations getting stuck (ranger got bound by snake man, but had bladeward, so killed it as a reactiom - but the ranger model stayed in the bound animation), or cut scenes hitching/skipping.
- Crashed to desktop once, when trying to use an xbox 360 controller in the menues
Highly recommend this title.

Great story, great gameplay and great graphics.
Regarding graphics:
SLI currently not supported.
But if you have Nvidia graphic cards try installing 'Nvidia Inspector', you can force SLI with this software.
I have 2 GTX 780 SC EVGA, before I installed 'Nvidia Inspector' I was getting around 30 FPS (at 1080p max settings). One GPU was at 95-99% load while the other was idle. (as I said, SLI is not supported by default)
After tweaking a few settings in 'Nvidia Inspector' I managed to get both GPUs working at 95-99% and now I have around  55-60FPS. (with the exact the same settings as before)
Having in mind it is a strategy game and not a shooter 55-60 is quite acceptable.
Another issue regarding graphics is the amount of RAM this game eats.
And by eating I mean constant RAM load at about 7.5 GB and peaks at close to 12 GB.
Keep in mind that this is again at max settings.
Hope my review helps anyone thinking of buying.
Would definetly recommend it.

When I first purchased Starbound, I really didn't expect it to be that amazing. But lo and behold, IT IS. You play as one of six races, a bird (Avian), a plant-thing (Floran), an ape (Apex), a human, a fish (Hyolt), or a robot (Glitch) that has fled your home planet. Your ship runs out of fuel, forcing you to search the nearby planet for supplies. That's when the fun starts! When you finally acquire enough fuel to travel to another planet, you realize that the Starbound universe is HUGE. Starbound has an abosolutely enormous universe filled with a planets in a variety of biomes and sizes.
Not wanting to spoil much, but in Starbound you'll encounter bosses, dungeons, a variety of hostile monsters, and many friendly villages. What's also great is that each planet is randomly generated, so you won't find a planet that's exactly the same as the next.
I will admit, I was first overwhelmed by all of the features the games has, but I was happy to keep playing... for 50+ hours...
TL;DR: Do I recommend this game? Yes! But no. Remember, Starbound is still in early access, so bugs and crashes are expected. As of the most recent patch, Furious Koala, the developers has informed the community that there will be no more character wipes. This does have a possibility of changing, though. If you can live with that, ABSOLUTELY buy Starbound. As long as you're into survival type games, Starbound will keep you happy for a long time.

What can I add to some of the great reviews available on this game?
Well, nothing really but the message to all potential buyers that here is one of those games that really satisfies in every aspect of gaming.
I found the difficulty a breaking point at first but once I  kept at it and learned more and more about the games features (and there are many!!) it became more and more addictive.
Lead a party of different warriors into the locations and you will have to deal with all their flawed character traits (they all have some traits to discover that can seriously impact their performance) and rising fear (up till heartattack level) plus fight enemies in turnbased combat.
Luckily you have numerous ways to keep those things in check if prepared well and used well. Potions, bandages, spells and weapon upgades will all be available once you level up and when you're back in town there's all those buildings where you can restore the health, weapons and fear or morale issues. (visit a tavern, gamble away or sneak to a brothel, find blessings and conquer fear in the monastery)
This is all just the tip of the iceberg.
The whole game is drenched in atmosphere, the art work is sublime and dark, there are no bugs that I have found and the music is perfectly suited for some dangerous adventuring to find out the curse of the manor.

Pros:
+ Nice graphics style
+ Great narrator
+ many classes with overall good balance and many posibilities for tactics
+ Party management matters
+ Inventory management
+ Many items (gear) which makes you think about them, not only +stat increase
+ Constant fixes/patches mean that developers care about balance
Cons:
- Horrible progress system throughout the game which punishes your leveled up characters, the game is harder the more experienced your heroes are (who refuse to come to lower levels missions)
- extremely overtuned creatures/enemies on end level dungeons (for example and ogre with more health in total than your whole group who one shot your characters, oh ye and he isnt alone of course and it is not boss, just regular fight)
- randomness in things that just doesnt make sense (how can hunger be random is beyond me)
- extremely hard grind for gold, everything costs gold, the more your characters are leveled up, the more every treatement costs, which ultimately doesnt make any sense (why level 1 character pays 1000g for brothel services while level 6 character pays 2500g?), not to mention that removing and locking quirks are behaving the same
- no matter how well you end your mission, you will almost always get punished (for example negative quirks, diseases)
- treating your characters punishes you aswell (lost money in gambling, getting negative quirks while reducing stress, etc.)
- I see no point in buying trinkets (items), i barely scratch money for treatement for my "champions", you must also take in consideration that your characters will need upgrade weapons and skills which also costs plenty of gold, maybe after 150+ hours of grind I will finally get to buy something
- future DLCs?, I cant imagine jumping into this game again just because they add 1 - 2 new classes, it is just too much of a grind
Buy if you like turn-based, management games, but beware, the grind on higher levels is real, you will lose things you feel like you didnt deserve, i would compare this game to playing diablo on hardcore, if you lose, you lose everything and you can start from over again, on the other hand, this game is very atmospheric and very enjoyable on apprentice - veteran levels
After a while ive decided to change the review to positive, i keep coming back to it, it has both originality and solid gameplay in genre that is not that popular anymore, it has its flaws, but it was love on first sight back then, but if you buy it, you wont keep your sanity, negative points above still stands though

It happened first about 7 hours in. I had just started feeling good about my chances with this game. I had learned the main mechanics, put together a party I was confident in, and was on the way to beating my most difficult quest to date.
Then, something unexpected happened. The boss, exploiting a mechanic I had not seen yet, decimited the health of all my heros in one round.
One. Round.
In an instant my entire situation had flipped. From full health to everyone suddenly knocking at deaths door. From feeling optomisticly confident, to feeling like I had no chance in hell. One, round.
The next few rounds I tried diligently to staunch the bleeding that had occured to no avail, my whole party wiped, as I could never recover. And not only did I lose the time and money invested in grooming those heros, I lost the few pieces of legendary gear I had that had enabled most of my smooth progress. It was a beyond devestating defeat.
This is normally the point of a game where I reload, start from scratch, or begin a new save to correct refine my tactics and correct my failure. The magic of this game is the fact that the way it is designed, reloading and restarting is completely un-necessary. You gain exctly nothing from starting over a new campaign, which I think is a brilliant design point to make. And since there is no way to reload, you have to learn how to accept defeat and move on.
Brilliant.
There's only one problem. That wouldn't be my first wipe.
The next day, I got back on the proverbial horse and started again. I groomed fresh troops to go back to the same mission and eventually avenge my original fallen party. It took a few days, but I did it. The confidence was back, the swagger regained.
And unfortunately, sadly, pathetically, the same unavoidable cycle repetead itself 2 more times, each failure successively more demoralizing than the one before it. 3 total times, my party wiped from some previously unforseen mechanic activating that totally flipped the tables no matter how well provisoned and prepared I might have been. The very last wipe I slammed my desk and haven't opened the game since.
Herein lies the question.
Ultimately, is the game at times gorgeous, wonder-inducing, challenging, and terror-invoking?
Yes. Without question, yes.
And at other times, is the game gimmicky, niche, and disengenuous in the sense that, it may lead to believe that you are prepared for what lies ahead, but unless you sink hours into trial in error wipes or research fights in advance, you will ultimately have the tables turned upside-down on you no matter what, because the developers specifically want you to fail in such a devestating way? In other words, are you okay with walking into a trap that you have no way to counter without some research and some good rng? Some people may not like the feeling of being setup, as I certainly did not. In fact, I haven't re-opened the game since that last wipe. And while I might one day muster up the pride to go back, I could also very well choose not to and maybe live a life better off for it.
Only time can tell.
For now, though it is a great game, I'm advising no as a reccomendation simply because I've had it, after 27hrs. Maybe I'll go back one day and get to 100, and then in terms of value I will change the review to yes. Maybe other reviewers got their moneys worth already despite all I've said and will put yes.
For me, and my rng karma though, the answer for now is no.

Although this game has a lot of perks, I will admit, it still has a lot of flaws.  However, if you are a fan of quick, twitchy fighting that is heavily inspired by old-school Zelda, you will be a fan of this game.  This game is 90% skill and 10% strategy. Equipment is the strategy in this game instead of the main motivation.  Most MMO's of any kind make you completely reliant on having the best equipment to fight, this game makes you only use equipment of the proper type to fight in the levels that need it.  Other than that, it is largely aesthetic.
Plot:  You are a knight crashed on a strange planet with others of your kind trying to survive the inner part of the planet called the Clockworks.  Unfortunately, the game has not advanced much there for a couple years, other than some interesting side missions.
Art: This is part of where the game truly shines, as the art in this game is very fun and somewhat unique.  You will find yourself creating diverse armors for the sake of a costume to use, and the levels are fun to run around in (although they can get repetitive)
Music:  The soundtrack is reminiscent of older 8-bit with a dose of electronica, and definitely fits the style of the game.
Give this game a try, it might not be for everybody, but you might find it a good fit!  And with the monetary system, it costs a lot less than other MMO's of it's type, especially since you don't need to pay to play.

I've been a fan of the game for quite a while, and I have about 65 recorded hours at the time of writing. This fact alone should tell you how I feel about this game- fantastic! I am very happy with the full release, many issues that people complained about that needed to addressed were indeed addressed in the full version. Things that needed to be toned down were, and little cheapskate things that even I was guilty of doing were also addressed.
As I read some of the reviews talking about droves of heroes dying within just ~5 hours of gameplay, that will indeed probably happen as you're learning how to play. The game isn't always that hard, and I promise that the rng isn't as run-destroying as some make it out to be. I can only speak from my personal experience, but in the new game I started at release and have since gotten several top tier characters, only two characters total have died. Those two died at the same time due to my not knowing that they removed being able to go back to town while camping and making the mistake of not preventing ambush... whoops. I also have never needed or read any guides and I don't min/max teams or whatever. I don't even have teams.
However, it doesn't really matter either way, because a point I want to make is that it honestly doesn't matter how many of your characters die or how good or bad you are at the game- this is because the gameplay is largely the same no matter your "progress". All the core mechanics are present at the start. My advice is: don't pick up this game if your only enjoyment from it will come from "beating" it. I'll just go ahead and be cliche and say that it's the journey that matters here. The game is entirely designed around being hard, many people are meant to die, and I personally feel that they've achieved a good balance.
Also as an artist I have to put in a word for the artwork, design, and image that this game has created, that's what drew me in and that alone makes it worth it to me!

There is a lack of 'hard' games on the market. Most games treat the player like he/she is an idiot. So when a hard game is released its something to be celebrated, but being 'hard' does not automatically make a game 'good'.
Problems with this game:
Line of site is just broken: I frequently kill aliens by shooting through several feet of concrete, steel, and large metal obstacles from overwatch. The animation shows that my bullets hit the wall and yet the alien dies. On the other hand, I can be standing 20 feet from an alien with only a few pixels of some obstacle possibly in view and some how not have line of site when I am controlling units.
Terrible performance: I have an overclocked Ivybridge-E processor with 16GB of memory and two Nvidia 670's in SLI. Not the fastest gaming PC, but the Witcher 3 ran on this system at mostly max settings. XCOM 2 even on all LOW settings freezes and lags terribly. This is something wrong with this game's optimization.
Very poor design: The begining of the game is crushingly difficult even on Rookie, but the middle of the game is too easy. This is the exact OPPOSITE of how it should be. Timer limits on most missions means you are going to be zerging through almost EVERY mission to complete it. Occasionally that would be nice, but how about allowing for some variety in strategy from mission to mission?
Bugs: Secondary control settings delete themselves, enemies frequently clip through walls, etc...
AI is dumb as rocks: If you look what the AI units choose to do, they are terribly stupid. The only reason the game is 'hard' is because the missions are designed to be one sided and the AI cheats terribly. They basically are allowed to ignore all the rules of combat. I like it when smart AI makes a game difficult. Allowing the game to cheat makes the game seem just arbitrary. Loosing units has no meaning once you realize the game is designed for you to use soliders like paper clips.
Base building is busy work: It becomes obvious after one or two play throughs that there is a best path to build your base. Devs, if you are not going to add strategic complexity to a part of the game, leave it out.
I anticipate the MOD community will correct most of these problems, but you shouldn't have to depend on the community to fix a game you are paying for.

Starbound is a 2D Sidescrolling Sandbox Game with a lot of potential, and is more complete than most games today. It is completely procedurally generated in almost every aspect, bringing a fresh experience each time.
Here's what I think about it (At the time of Beta V. Furious Koala):
First of all, the aesthetics: This is a beautiful game, with amazing looks, on both the ships and the planets. It has a lot to see and it has no problem showing it all off.
Secondly, the optimization: The optimization isn't very good at the current state, it's quite buggy and takes a while to load. It lags on High-End computers, and I hope this will be sorted out in the future.
The gameplay, on the otherhand is simple, build, create, explore. They call it Sandbox for a reason, it doesn't limit you like some other games (such as Terraria) and is very fun. It is sure to keep you interested for a long time, and it's just in early beta.
This game is great, with frequent updates and a nice community. I hope they continue to expand it as they see fit and I will definentely still be playing when it's released. 9/10

It happened first about 7 hours in. I had just started feeling good about my chances with this game. I had learned the main mechanics, put together a party I was confident in, and was on the way to beating my most difficult quest to date.
Then, something unexpected happened. The boss, exploiting a mechanic I had not seen yet, decimited the health of all my heros in one round.
One. Round.
In an instant my entire situation had flipped. From full health to everyone suddenly knocking at deaths door. From feeling optomisticly confident, to feeling like I had no chance in hell. One, round.
The next few rounds I tried diligently to staunch the bleeding that had occured to no avail, my whole party wiped, as I could never recover. And not only did I lose the time and money invested in grooming those heros, I lost the few pieces of legendary gear I had that had enabled most of my smooth progress. It was a beyond devestating defeat.
This is normally the point of a game where I reload, start from scratch, or begin a new save to correct refine my tactics and correct my failure. The magic of this game is the fact that the way it is designed, reloading and restarting is completely un-necessary. You gain exctly nothing from starting over a new campaign, which I think is a brilliant design point to make. And since there is no way to reload, you have to learn how to accept defeat and move on.
Brilliant.
There's only one problem. That wouldn't be my first wipe.
The next day, I got back on the proverbial horse and started again. I groomed fresh troops to go back to the same mission and eventually avenge my original fallen party. It took a few days, but I did it. The confidence was back, the swagger regained.
And unfortunately, sadly, pathetically, the same unavoidable cycle repetead itself 2 more times, each failure successively more demoralizing than the one before it. 3 total times, my party wiped from some previously unforseen mechanic activating that totally flipped the tables no matter how well provisoned and prepared I might have been. The very last wipe I slammed my desk and haven't opened the game since.
Herein lies the question.
Ultimately, is the game at times gorgeous, wonder-inducing, challenging, and terror-invoking?
Yes. Without question, yes.
And at other times, is the game gimmicky, niche, and disengenuous in the sense that, it may lead to believe that you are prepared for what lies ahead, but unless you sink hours into trial in error wipes or research fights in advance, you will ultimately have the tables turned upside-down on you no matter what, because the developers specifically want you to fail in such a devestating way? In other words, are you okay with walking into a trap that you have no way to counter without some research and some good rng? Some people may not like the feeling of being setup, as I certainly did not. In fact, I haven't re-opened the game since that last wipe. And while I might one day muster up the pride to go back, I could also very well choose not to and maybe live a life better off for it.
Only time can tell.
For now, though it is a great game, I'm advising no as a reccomendation simply because I've had it, after 27hrs. Maybe I'll go back one day and get to 100, and then in terms of value I will change the review to yes. Maybe other reviewers got their moneys worth already despite all I've said and will put yes.
For me, and my rng karma though, the answer for now is no.

I've been a fan of the game for quite a while, and I have about 65 recorded hours at the time of writing. This fact alone should tell you how I feel about this game- fantastic! I am very happy with the full release, many issues that people complained about that needed to addressed were indeed addressed in the full version. Things that needed to be toned down were, and little cheapskate things that even I was guilty of doing were also addressed.
As I read some of the reviews talking about droves of heroes dying within just ~5 hours of gameplay, that will indeed probably happen as you're learning how to play. The game isn't always that hard, and I promise that the rng isn't as run-destroying as some make it out to be. I can only speak from my personal experience, but in the new game I started at release and have since gotten several top tier characters, only two characters total have died. Those two died at the same time due to my not knowing that they removed being able to go back to town while camping and making the mistake of not preventing ambush... whoops. I also have never needed or read any guides and I don't min/max teams or whatever. I don't even have teams.
However, it doesn't really matter either way, because a point I want to make is that it honestly doesn't matter how many of your characters die or how good or bad you are at the game- this is because the gameplay is largely the same no matter your "progress". All the core mechanics are present at the start. My advice is: don't pick up this game if your only enjoyment from it will come from "beating" it. Darkest Dungeon (a Lovecraft inspired dungeon RPG) is a  turn-based battler with an overarching structure, and one idea that lifts it way above the ordinary. This is stress, the idea that people subjected to the kind of horrors that dungeon explorers go through might crack under the pressure. Each hero has their own stress meter, which is regularly added to by everything from it being too dark to the presence of a killer god, and when a tipping point is reached their mental fortitude is tested. In some cases they’ll respond favorably and inspire their compatriots but, far more often, the mind breaks.
The game begins with a foreboding admonition. It’s a game about making the most of a bad situation, you’re told from the outset. Your actions are permanent, therefore the quests you embark upon will often end in failure. “Heroes will die,” it says. “And when they die they stay dead.” That's what is one of the most striking thing, how the rampant and merciless randomness always keeps one off balance, struggling to stay alive. It comes in both the usual accuracy percentages for various attacks and dodges, but also unexpected and unusual places - even the turn order is mixed up by behind-the-scenes dice rolls. So you’re never quite sure, for example, if your Vestal healer will be able to patch up your Crusader tank before the enemy can deal a killing blow, permanently removing that character and all his progress from your roster. By robbing you of the certainty and predictability you usually see in a turn-based tactics game of this nature, Darkest Dungeon creates tense and terrifying battles where you’re never sure what will happen next.
Then there are quirks, which can positively or negatively impact a hero’s effectiveness in certain dungeons, or against certain enemies, or cause them to independently perform actions, including stealing any money you see in the case of Kleptomania, and each hero can have up to five positive and five negative traits. Keeping track of them all – your stable can hold up to 25 of them at once – is a big task.
Consider Lovecraft. No, consider the anglerfish, that Lovecraftian nightmare of the deep with its sickly glowing lightbulb luring you in before the wretched face becomes visible. The tiny, melted eyes, the cruel underbite, and the thatch, not of hair, but of teeth. This is Darkest Dungeon, even before the fish people turn up and are troublingly untroubled by bleeding. This is a game that's horrid in a way that means that you can't look away, a game of exhaustion and luridness and of terrible things happening in an awful, awful place. In other words, it's just lovely.

Darkest Dungeon is an amazing game... Until you start doing lv. 5 dungeons, at which point it becomes an unbearable, incredibly unfair, RNG-filled, chaotic grindfest. Mobs get absolutely insane buffs, while your heroes remain the same. Even when you win an encounter, there's no sense of accomplishment since even with best trinkets and "meta" party composition, you still depend on good rolls in order to succeed. Don't even bother experimenting or trying to "play for fun" at that point - you'll just lose your best heroes and then it's back to the beginning.
Just because the early game is so good, and the style and the atmosphere are so cool, i've started the campaign multiple times - only to abandon it after a couple of days. I even bought the DLC hoping that it will somehow make the game more entertaining. But guess what - it actually makes things worse. After you kill the first boss in the Crimson Court - the Baron  - your game is practically over. Lv.5 mobs from the Court are even more ridiculously overpowered than the regular ones, and you basically have no choice but to keep trying to fight them, or else eventually your entire roster gets infested with the Curse and dies.
I'm really sorry to say this, but i think this time i'm done with DD. I tried to "git gud", but it just isn't fun anymore. And i'm not switching to "ez mode" just because some people don't know how to balance their own game.

I love how many of the old systems from the last Xcom have been carried over but in some cases improved. Having reload of your weapon not end your turn for example.

The will loss (from taking damage?) that recovers from doing well at a future mission is annoying. Thankfully panic is much less of a mission ender.

The only saving grace is that the aliens won't damage mind controlled teammates, so sometimes it actually saves you. My biggest beef with the game is how the timed missions with random maps work. You will have X amount of time to do something and get to a certain point. However, because the maps are random, sometimes that point can be so hard to get to that even if you ignored the aliens and dashed right for it your cutting it close. I don't mind the rush effect sometimes, but I like to take my time and do things systematically. They need to have at least one more turn added to them across the board.
Moving units to different levels is STILL a pain. I have had units run to the wrong point because it's hard to tell exactly what level your selecting your space on. A couple of pods activated through walls too.
It's overall a good game. It needs to be tweaked somewhat however. Thankfully it's supposed to be super mod friendly, so we will see. I suggest to anyone who loved the last XCOM, to get this one. It is good game overall.

The first Dark Souls game introduced many staple mechanics in the BloodSouls/SoulsBorne/Whatever the hell you want to call this franchise. Hard as nails level design to the average player, stamina and durability to have the player manage things other than their own life force, so many good things were in that game but a lot of odd choices like with calculating damage from supposedly holy weapons.
Fast forward to Dark Souls II, the more awkward middle child of the franchise (in my opinion) with a lot of diverging design choises that aren't all bad but lead to a very different experience. Changes in how estus, the essential healing item, works. Level design seems to revolve around placing the player in a field-like area full of enemies. Humanity can be restored away from a bonfire, and has a direct influence on how difficult the game potentially is by giving you less health.
Everything good from these games seems to be present in the latest installment in the series, and now that the DLC is all out and the game is on sale, now is as good a time as any to sing its praises. Faster combat, a new management bar to use abilities with, weapons now having unique things they can do and special attacks, and varied and interesting bosses all lead to probably the best installment of the franchise. I don't entirely know for sure just because I don't have the money for a PS4 for Bloodborne, but this is definitely up there. Just like the first game, many of the ambushes and traps are designed in a way where if the player stops for a moment, maybe looking around them, can find reasoning behind anywhere they run to being a trap. Maybe the developers want me to grab this item, with the animation taking just long enough to aggro a horde of magical crow people. Maybe walking through this cavern will have giant ballistae shoot at me, or a giant worm burst from the ground to kill me, or hey why not both. It is Dark Souls after all, you never know what traps lie ahead.
Many points like this are similar to the good design aspects of the first game, with an open journey and picking which boss to chase after next being similar to the second game in the series. Maybe you'll go after the god-eating blob living in the ruins of the most famous city from the first game. Maybe you'll face a now crazy yet once noble giant living just beyond a hellish jail, or perhaps say screw it, kill an old lady to fight a lady icy knight monster and make your way through the grandest castle in the land early. It's literally all up to you, this is your journey.
As far as the DLC, the first, Ashes of Ariandel, isn't actually all that amazing. It does include an arena mode to use, as well as a variety of interesting weapons and spells, but the actual level/world added just doesn't quite make it entirely worth it, in my opinion. It starts you off in a large snowy field with enemies everywhere, a choice that just doesn't seem to fit terribly well with the mechanics of the Dark Souls games. A maze-like hill and a final boss that has just a tad too fast of timing leaves a bit of a bitter taste, before moving on to the final DLC.
The Ringed City does what Dark Souls is best at, which is using difficulty to make the player observe the world around them to advance. The locations of the vulnerable spots for the laser shooting angel enemies, the path forward past a legion of spectral archers, the way through the titular Ringed City, all of these are examples of how The Ringed City takes the best aspects of this kind of level and amps it up, making the player feel extremely satisfied even at more minor accomplishements. Just running after a specific item can cause you to die several times just from a singular enemy.
Overall the final installment of the Dark Souls series of games is probably for the best as a final game, since all the effort put into it makes it very difficult to make a much better game than this, and it still be Dark Souls.

There are two major gripes with this game currently. Turn limits on some missions and poor performance. First let me say that as a general rule I HATE with an undying passion timers or turn limiters in my gaming experience. With that being said the turn limits in this game actually work quite well. are fairly generous, don't force you to do nothing but sprint and are thematically correct for the situations you are in. Before playing I was genuinely concerned about this design decision. My fears IMO were incorrect and so far It's keeping the game moving at a nice pace. In XCOM EU I didn't realize how much I "turtled" and it actually was preventing me from having as much fun and excitement as I could.
As for the second issue, it kinda sucks right now performance wise. Most people are having FPS issues and the game really isn't graphically intensive. It looks good but this isn't Crysis or Witcher 3. It's most likely just an optimization issue that Firaxis will hopefully address with a hotfix patch sooner rather than later.
Long story short don't be scared off by the negative reviews about the turn timers and wait until the game is patched.

This game gets alot of flak. And yeah, some of it is deserved.
Progress in updates has been slow
Not all the new updates are nececarily good ones
The game STILL feels unfinished
BUT THIS IS STILL A GOOD GAME!
In the latest update, I feel that the game has been taken many steps closer to its origna; promise: An open world space exploration game. The update, while creating some new problems, has at least fixed some of the more major errors:
-Combat is now more fun than it was before. Skill and timeing are now needed rather than simply cowering behind a shield untill enemies let their guard down. 2 handed weapons are now just as viable as any other weaopn type
-The new race, Novakids, are one of the more unique races with a new progression system. Plus, they get guns to start with, so thats cool.
-Whlie I may be alone in this opinion, I think that the way the bosses are now built into missions is a cool adition. It makes your victory feel earned, rather than summoning the box inside a cube with a small hole in it and taknig potshots at it.
-The new progression system feels much beter than the old method of sectors.
-New weapons/items. It helps make the game feel more full.
But, there are some things that have been wronged in this update.
-Hunger and temprature have been removed. I understand this is because they were fundamentaly broken in the new update, but they were cool features. I hope they get added again soon.
-Guns are still way too rare to make them a viable choice. Novakids get them as default cradting options, and so far they are the only race i've used guns over swords in
-The codexes, one of the best features in the orignal version, seem even more rare than before. Not a horrible thing, but it makes finding the full story almost impossible.
-There is no motivation to build houses. Sure, the new teleporters mean it is at least viable to build a base on a planet, but it's much easier to simply build everything in your ship.
Starbound, to me at least, is the prime example of why developers should think very, very hard about early access. Starbound told a story of grand adventures in the stars, and at first playes were satisfied with the taste they got in early access. Then they got slightly annoyed at the lack of updates. And when they were told that the winter update was THE BIG one, they seemed to expect a finished game. When it still wasn't enough, the negative review poured in.
So I suppose there realy isn't a way to convince you to buy this. The game is better, but still far from perfect. But I still love it. When I land on a planet, explore it, find a random dungeon, get something from it, finaly get enough titanium to complete the armour set, go on a new quest, and when that all gets boring, simply set in random co-ordinates and see where it takes me. And yes, more often than not it will take me to a random planet that has nothing on it except trees and more trees. But every now and again, the game grabs my attention and convinces me it was worth buying it.
At this point, the best thing you can do is keep in mind that if you buy it now, you are not buying THE starbound. In fact, it may take awhile before you get that. But I can guarantee that you will at least get a taste of it. So, pick it up in a sale. Find a friend who owns it, see if you like it. Or do as I did, and take a chance on a game that, imperfect as it is, still keeps me engrossed. The new update makes the game a million times better. And this is one player who is willing to wait as long as it takes to get the finished product.

My review of this game was quite negative during early acess.  Now that I've come back to it after release, my opinion has changed.
My biggest complaint of this game was the difficulty, and this has now been addressed.  Extra game options allow you to tweak things from crit severity, to corpses once again.  This has brought the game to a level I can enjoy again.
PROS:
1 ) Atmosphere.  The darkest dungeon is infact a dark dungeon that is darkly dark, and you will feel the darkness encroaching on you!
2 ) Music/Voice.  Still as good as ever.
3 ) Graphics.  Relatively simple but they get the job done with style
4 ) Difficulty.  It is much more tweakable now so can cater to more tastes.
CONS:
1 ) RNG is still crazy as ever, but with the difficulty tweaks, they're less likely to make you want to pull your hair out.
2 ) Low level grind.  The game still suffers from low level grind as your recruits become too good for dungeons you need to go to.  Unfortunately I don't see this getting fixed as the game would be too short otherwise I suspect.
Overall?  I'm much happier with the game now and will gladly give it a yes!

Do you like minecraft and RPG games? Then this game is not for you...
Do you like repetitive gameplay, gear grinding, few skills and building games with boring block colors and no materials? This game is absolutely for you.
Pros
+ You can vary your home in many different ways.
+ Classes are different and varies in skills ans spells.
+ Many build items like fences, bookshelves, campfire and lots more.

+ Crafting systems seems alright.

Cons
- You only get one little plot to build on. Not bog enough to make cool or fantastic structures.
- No quests.
- Same game play over and over and over and over and over and...
- No materials to build with, only colored blocks.
- To few skills. Every class only have 2 skills except main and second attack.

- I like block games but with nothing more than different colors and no textures this is not very compelling or attractive.
- Again, next to no skills. I write it again because this makes games like this extremely boring and repetitive.
- No skills system.

Support Mojang/Microsoft instead and buy Minecraft. The later versions have RPG elements that are better than this and not to mention textures and a way better build system. XCOM 2 is a sequel that kept what was awesome about the previous iterations, and only expanded and improved on many of those features. My computer is by no means amazing (2 year old, 600 dollar CyberPower), but even on the "Low" settings, it is a beautiful game. The environments have a very pleasing aesthetic, and most characters/soldiers are only ugly looking if you choose to make them so.
The customization is incredible, and though there could ALWAYS be more options, what they have is enough to create an amazing variety of soldiers and possible VIPs. Every map is different, with many options in terms of verticality and ambush spots, as well as an array of areas where your soldiers get their asses whooped.
Combat is more or less the same, though this time around every specialty feels equally powerful and helpful. The Sharpshooter starting off the class with Squadsight is one of my favorite new things about the change to the classes. Everyone is useful, and every enemy is incredibly deadly. Starting off most of the combat situations in "Concealment" (Where your soldiers are temporarily hidden from enemies and can allow you to set up the perfect ambush) is an interesting and helpful addition to the game, allowing you to take a moment to gain an advantage before realizing that you are completely outnumbered, one of the most exciting parts about the game.
To many people's dismay, there is a feeling of being rushed through many of the missions in the game. A turn timer gives you a reason to push further into a map quicker than you ever would have in the previous games. Sometimes it causes you to step into an enemy's zone of sight, and other times it can mean getting many of your soldiers killed as you move too much and shoot too little. While it makes the game sound nearly impossible, I believe it has added so much more strategy to the game. No more moving everyone up one space and then overwatching. No waiting out for enemies to wander into your path of fire. Every single move you make is critical, as every move can position someone incorrectly or too far away from an objective. I've had to leave some soldiers behind since they were too far from Evac on many occasions.
The strategy layer of the game feels a lot more deep, with a lot going on at once that you can choose to ignore or prioritize. There is still much to research and create in the game, with everything helping to push you closer to your goal.
There are some ****minor**** performance issues (not everyone will agree, of course), like it taking a few seconds longer than it should to move the camera away from a dead enemy or soldiers firing through walls, but none of this takes away from what makes this a great game: The fact that the gameplay itself is fun. Lots of fun. It is much more challenging than Enemy Unknown, but every mission leaves you feeling either accomplished, or crushed. Just the way I like it!

The first Dark Souls game introduced many staple mechanics in the BloodSouls/SoulsBorne/Whatever the hell you want to call this franchise. Hard as nails level design to the average player, stamina and durability to have the player manage things other than their own life force, so many good things were in that game but a lot of odd choices like with calculating damage from supposedly holy weapons.
Fast forward to Dark Souls II, the more awkward middle child of the franchise (in my opinion) with a lot of diverging design choises that aren't all bad but lead to a very different experience. Changes in how estus, the essential healing item, works. Level design seems to revolve around placing the player in a field-like area full of enemies. Humanity can be restored away from a bonfire, and has a direct influence on how difficult the game potentially is by giving you less health.
Everything good from these games seems to be present in the latest installment in the series, and now that the DLC is all out and the game is on sale, now is as good a time as any to sing its praises. Faster combat, a new management bar to use abilities with, weapons now having unique things they can do and special attacks, and varied and interesting bosses all lead to probably the best installment of the franchise. I don't entirely know for sure just because I don't have the money for a PS4 for Bloodborne, but this is definitely up there. Just like the first game, many of the ambushes and traps are designed in a way where if the player stops for a moment, maybe looking around them, can find reasoning behind anywhere they run to being a trap. Maybe the developers want me to grab this item, with the animation taking just long enough to aggro a horde of magical crow people. Maybe walking through this cavern will have giant ballistae shoot at me, or a giant worm burst from the ground to kill me, or hey why not both. It is Dark Souls after all, you never know what traps lie ahead.
Many points like this are similar to the good design aspects of the first game, with an open journey and picking which boss to chase after next being similar to the second game in the series. Maybe you'll go after the god-eating blob living in the ruins of the most famous city from the first game. Maybe you'll face a now crazy yet once noble giant living just beyond a hellish jail, or perhaps say screw it, kill an old lady to fight a lady icy knight monster and make your way through the grandest castle in the land early. It's literally all up to you, this is your journey.
As far as the DLC, the first, Ashes of Ariandel, isn't actually all that amazing. It does include an arena mode to use, as well as a variety of interesting weapons and spells, but the actual level/world added just doesn't quite make it entirely worth it, in my opinion. It starts you off in a large snowy field with enemies everywhere, a choice that just doesn't seem to fit terribly well with the mechanics of the Dark Souls games. A maze-like hill and a final boss that has just a tad too fast of timing leaves a bit of a bitter taste, before moving on to the final DLC.
The Ringed City does what Dark Souls is best at, which is using difficulty to make the player observe the world around them to advance. The locations of the vulnerable spots for the laser shooting angel enemies, the path forward past a legion of spectral archers, the way through the titular Ringed City, all of these are examples of how The Ringed City takes the best aspects of this kind of level and amps it up, making the player feel extremely satisfied even at more minor accomplishements. Just running after a specific item can cause you to die several times just from a singular enemy.
Overall the final installment of the Dark Souls series of games is probably for the best as a final game, since all the effort put into it makes it very difficult to make a much better game than this, and it still be Dark Souls.

1 ) Atmosphere.  The darkest dungeon is infact a dark dungeon that is darkly dark, and you will feel the darkness encroaching on you!

CONS:
1 ) RNG is still crazy as ever, but with the difficulty tweaks, they're less likely to make you want to pull your hair out.

Overall?  I'm much happier with the game now and will gladly give it a yes!

Very rarely have I seen a sequel build and improve on its original this consistently. A masterclass in polishing an existing game design to its absolute best form.
The overworld gameplay still has the same feeling of building a base and managing regions, but a number of key improvements add much more strategic depth and a real sense of urgency. Where Enemy Unknown had this awkward phase where you didn't really want to progress time, but you had to in order to continue the game, and you were just sort of sitting there waiting for the game to throw things at you, the new mechanic of scanning points of interest for goodies and upgrades means there is
something you want to be doing, and the alien attacks truly feel like the unwelcome interruptions to your operations that they are supposed to feel like.
The core principles of the tactical combat are largely unchanged, but the new classes all feel much more unique in their gameplay and the abilities you can gain will have you salivating at the new tactical opportunities they grant you. They took an already great combat system and polished the heck out of the content. The environments and general graphics also look much improved now that the game has decided it might be nice to have colors!
Finally, the game manages to simultaneously be
than its predecessor, while also seeming entirely more
than it. The special enemies have been given strong unique abilities that have to be played around on a tactical level, instead of the original game's "THIN MAN GONNA CRIT YOU NOW" level of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
I cannot recommend this game enough as a culmination of the entire XCOM experience.

The problems with the Darkest Dungeon since it got its full release is not that it's harder. Or that the RNG is against you. For me, the problem is if you don't look up youtube videos and read the wiki cover to cover, the gameplay sucks. There's no trial and error, because your party will be wiped out, your gold reserves emptied and you'll have to start again and go through the painfully long tutorial. There are so many times where I've found a boss, tried to fight them only to realise that they endlessly summon. By the time you've worked out that this is indeed a bossfight, you've lost. I'm all for no hand holding, but DD seems to delibrately deny you any clues on what the hell is going on until it's too late.
EDIT: I wrote this review quite late and upon looking at it again, see I've left off the end. There IS a good game, once you get past the ridiculous learning wall. The aesthetic is brilliant, the difficulty, once you've thoroughly read the wiki, is just right to be always challenging. The gear upgrade is a bit pointless, as are the skill levels. However, it's rather made up for by the plethora of trinkets you can equip to tweak your characters' stats.
Overall, this is a good game if you have the patience to persevere, but I couldn't recommend it as it is with so much vital information witheld from the player.

I recommend this game fairly strongly. I'm enjoying the game a lot, the story is better, the core gameplay feel like "Enemy Within, but better", and overall I'm having a blast. However, I am going to list a few things that irk me and may irk some people looking to buy. Basically, I'm saying "I recommend this game unless any of the following deeply bother you."
1. Performance issues abound. Turning off AA and AO kill off most of the performance issues for me, and allows me to run the game are max settings at a pretty decent FPS most of the time. However, there is severe FPS drops during common cutscences (Skyranger landing and taking off) as well as moving from room to room on the base. This is pretty unfortunate, and I hope this is ironed out soon as I think this is the game's most pressing issue.
2. Mission timers. Mission timers are surprisingly divisive. In my opinion, the mission timers works with one of the reoccuring themes of the game, which is "time is a resource". The tried and true method of crawling across the map slowly in overwatch still works in some missions, but now there are more trade-offs between going slow and going fast. With that said, mission timers could be improved. I feel like some missions begin a countdown before what I consider reasonable. If the aliens discover there's a hack, or there's a broken down convoy, then I understand the countdown.
But what about a mission where you have to extract a VIP and Advent doesn't know you're coming? Or missions where you have to kidnap a dark VIP that, again, the Advent don't know you're coming for? I feel like these countdowns shouldn't begin until concealment is broken. Otherwise though, I don't have a problem with mission timers. For anyone that does though, there is a mod that increases mission timers and another one that gets rid of them altogether.
3. [MINOR ISSUE ALERT] Lower face props like the striped bandana should match your soldier's color scheme better. This is so minor that I'm only putting it here in the off chance that a developer read this and tweaks it so bandanas match your soldiers' color schemes.
4. [MINOR ISSUE ALERT] No Second Wave options? But what about my marathon? :(
5. Camera is garbage. If there is one mod besides SMGs that I wholeheartedly recommend, it is the one that improves the camera so you can look at the battlefield from more than four angles.
Overall, I recommend the game (which is what Steam is asking for in these reviews by the way people). If you want to get a better impression, I strongly recommend TotalBiscuit's "WTF is XCOM 2?" on Youtube.

Beware before you buy this game Darkest Dungeon. Now do not misunderstand I love this game, but this is not for the faint of heart. This game is made to screw you over, and put you in the most terrible of situations, it all depends on how you prepare for it. Half this game is about planning, what to bring for the mission. Beware at naming your characters friends and family, as you’ll get attached and they will sometimes die. I mean heck I do it and I felt like a horrible person if I had to dismiss them or they were gruesomely killed. As I rewrite this I felt I wrote it unfairly. So getting further into the game, I will admit this is one game. There can be some improvements to the items and the cost of some upgrades.  It’s a brilliant game and just be careful. This is a gold standard to early access games, an exemplar, of the formula working. I love this game, even if it is a abusive relationship. odd I know but heck I love hard games.
Positives
+ Innovative gameplay, each class puts different talents on the table. Want a finesse fencing fighter, that can dodge blows and critical like mad; but is also flexible? Get a Grave Robber. Want a character who can both tank and heal? Grab a Crusader. Etc
+ Art is exquisite, it fits the lovecraftian dark theme of hopelessness of it all. It has some inspiration from X-com meets dark souls. It has a dark graphic novel esthetic.
+ Sound design is great. It really has the disparity of it all.
+ Battle is refined, its form following function with every piece and detail, there is a huge amount of strategy, and you are forced to try out new classes, strategize. It’s satisfying. Be prepared to think on the fly.
+ It has a high risk high reward game play, the further you are on the edge, the higher the intensity. You get this adrenaline rush when you succeed and get the epic loot at the end
+ That announcer, I swear when he says: Confidence surges as the enemy crumbles. Makes me just bloodthirsty when you crit.
+It fits the dungeon theme right, they are terrifying, full of risks, and they are the dark secrets of the world. Those whom dare to explore them they will find great relics and wonders, but also the world’s greatest horrors. A dungeon is not a place to get free riches, they are a test of your perseverance and will.
Negatives
-    This Game is not fair, it will put you in the most horrible situations that are unwinnable
-    A lot of your attacks is a roll of the dice, same as the enemies so they can one hit kill you. Combat can be just risky at times.
-    Have no emotional attachments to your team, it will only lead up to disappointment
-    Be prepared to restart the game a lot….A lot. Salt will be common here
-    Later weeks will become impossibly hard I got to week 70 and everyone died. No money and I am screwed.
-    Dodging is a farce, as there will be moves that cannot dodge even with high dodge
-    The enemies will always get initiative before you, and will always go first and sometimes they will cheat and hit you twice even if you have more speed. Yes I looked my perks and none of them were slow draw.
-    There will be plenty of B.S parts where even common enemies will one hit kill you, no deaths door where you have a chance to save them, nope, they die
-    Money and treasures are fickle, at times you will get almost nothing at times for going through a dungeon where surviving is your treasure, along with your team to be mentally intact.
-    Bosses have instant one hit kill team wipes, they cannot be interrupted. Bypasses all armor and causes max stress.
-    Even if you come prepared, you will still get your butt handed to you
-    Stress is B.S at times where having a great virtue when maxed out stress and getting a good virtue is rare. There are times where a hero will refuse to be healed, as negative perks when max stressed will always happen. He is about to die and just gives up, the team then gets maxed out stress and one of them gets a heart attack.
-    Murphy’s Law, the game. What Can go wrong will go horribly wrong.
-    Enemies level up with you to rookie to veteran and they will always have better stats then you, I know a challenge to one thing but I feel that this game spikes up from hey let’s start you easy, to punching you in the stomach and shoving your face in the mud telling you: Know your place human. This game is Bipolar like that

Starbound is a 2D Sidescrolling Sandbox Game with a lot of potential, and is more complete than most games today. It is completely procedurally generated in almost every aspect, bringing a fresh experience each time.
Here's what I think about it (At the time of Beta V. Furious Koala):
First of all, the aesthetics: This is a beautiful game, with amazing looks, on both the ships and the planets. It has a lot to see and it has no problem showing it all off.
Secondly, the optimization: The optimization isn't very good at the current state, it's quite buggy and takes a while to load. It lags on High-End computers, and I hope this will be sorted out in the future.
The gameplay, on the otherhand is simple, build, create, explore. They call it Sandbox for a reason, it doesn't limit you like some other games (such as Terraria) and is very fun. It is sure to keep you interested for a long time, and it's just in early beta.
This game is great, with frequent updates and a nice community. I hope they continue to expand it as they see fit and I will definentely still be playing when it's released. 9/10

If you like permadeath, RPGs that have much tactical depth without a steep learning curve, and gorgeous, if slightly static, art, Darkest Dungeon will not disappoint you. It's punishing and difficult, but these nightmarish creatures
be felled, they
be beaten.

Throughout Early Access, people's opinions on the game have shifted harder than a Cultist being bombarded by a Bounty Hunter's Flash Bang, which is the main reason you'll still see negative reviews, but the solution the developers finally settled on has been the absolute best one, and people not updating their reviews to reflect this is the main reason some reviews are still negative.
Darkest Dungeon is a dark dungeon crawler (heh), where you lead a party of four heroes and the items you provide for them into the depths, time and again, hoping every time they'll make it out alive, knowing the possibility is very real that they won't - and if they do, they might be so traumatized and mentally scarred that you decide to let them spend the rest of their lives wandering, impoverished and unhinged.
The entire game balances on the question, 'what are your heroes worth'? Given the constant influx of new hopefuls, it'll be very tempting to dismiss heroes or send them on a suicide mission to recover as much loot as possible, simply because you can't afford to take care of them. Because while wounds of the body heal, wounds of the mind do not, at least not without a sizeable cost in gold.
That is not to say all your heroes are doomed. They can win fights and clear dungeons, grow stronger and become Heroes worthy of a capital 'H', champions honed and trained for one purpose: to brave the depths of the eponymous Darkest Dungeon.
When your characters aren't delving in the depths of the Dankest Dungeon, you have 'free' time to upgrade the hamlet, adding some modest but interesting base building to the mix. With the heirlooms your heroes collect from the dungeons, you can upgrade buildings, whose functions range from upgrading weapons and armour to curing stress and disease or selling trinkets. Unless of course, the heirlooms remain forever in the dark, clutched in the dead hands of your adventurers.
You will get attached to your heroes, and the threat of them dying when they set out into the depths is always very real, but good preparation can minimize that risk. Darkest Dungeon uses a Random Number God who may throw a wrench in even the best-laid plans, but with the game's immensely clever and dynamic combat system, good planning and calculated responses to unexpected circumstances will do much to win the day.
So no, you have no direct control over the numbers, but yes, you can make a very significant difference as the player without success or failure hinging on die rolls. Character classes are so diverse (and individually customizable) that the possibilities of combining them are endless, and a good combination and positioning of characters is a fun challenge every time you assemble a team, as is a clear-headed response when enemies mess up your formation and heroes start having to fight in positions they're not accustomed to.
The base building aspect, while slightly grindy, is a streamlined but functional and efficient element, and seeing your hamlet get restored from a ruined ghost town to a thriving community is a joy to watch - even though the graveyards are packed with heroes who died to make it happen.
All this takes place in a world full of gothic, dark beauty, with an art style that never bores, even though the game consists mostly of still images, animated and moved to reflect what happens. This isn't to say that the game is a boring slideshow - the camera moves and pans, visual effects splatter off the screen, and thanks to good animation, the entire world is moving and alive.
Add a highly evocative narrator, Wayne June, who provides tons of atmosphere while hamming it up to just the right levels, and you've got a gripping experience that'll keep you engaged during every moment.
If you like high-poly 3D-models, motion capped animations and lighting that makes your 980TI Titan chug, then you'll probably want to pass on this. But it would be your loss, since the amazing art style and execution is more efficient and powerful than any amount of realism could ever be. The animators did a wonderful job too, making the still images come alive as the action unfolds.
Also, be aware that Darkest Dungeon is difficult. You'll need to stay focused if you wish to survive, because even trash mobs (and there aren't many of those) can devastate a party if the player's concentration lapses. Because of this, heroes will die. If you get attached to your heroes, like I do, this can be difficult to deal with. All players so far consider Darkest Dungeon's difficulty to be a plus, but if you want to just play a game and have fun without thinking too much, you might consider the difficulty a stumbling block.
Be aware that you can - and probably should - turn off many difficulty options introduced by the devs in Early Access to discourage certain tactics or make the game more hardcore, and that's a good thing. Some of those options were, with good reason, seriously disliked by most EA players, including myself, for making the game unfairly difficult.
Darkest Dungeon is a must have for any role player, save-scum hater, tactics fan, or really anyone who likes a solid challenge (s)he can overcome with clever and tactical thinking. In fact, I can recommend it to everyone except people who play video games purely as a relaxing distraction after a hard work day, because it does require concentration and active thinking.

How would you like to talk to strangers, attack wild animals, attack mutant cakes, ruin an office party, destroy some one elses work, beat up 2 entities of royal decent, play with scissors, have fights to the death with your friends, and all while having fun in the process??? Spiral Knights a game that lets you do all that and more.
It's a free-to-play game that's easy to learn, but becomes addicting and is challenging to master. Also, you'll get a free hat for TF2 in the process (who doesn't like to have a freebie provided from a free game)!
You play as a personally (or randomly) created rookie knight that has crash landed on a mysterious mechanical planet called Cradle. The mission given is simple to understand: Find your way to the core and harness the power inside....but that is easier said than done. You must enter battle with Gremlins, Fiends, Jellies, Constructs, and Beasts in order to go deeper into the planet that has a ever changing enviroment.
Your arsenal consists of a wide variety of guns, swords, and bombs each designed to fight the onslaught, as well as a variety of armors, helms, and shields to withstand their attacks.
You'll also be provided with a Battle Sprite, 3 floating creatures with unique abilities that can help fight enemies or protect you from further harm. However, choose wisely as you can only choose 1 to start off with for free (you can have them all, but you'll have to pay for the rest).
There are 2 currencies here:
1) Crowns obtained by selling goods, breaking item boxes, or killing enemies.
2) Energy which can be obtained from real money or converting crowns in a trade system that adjusts value based on the demand from other players.
There are 4 ways to buy stuff in Spiral Knights:
1) The Auction House which lets you spend crowns to buy someone elses discarded gear.
2) Vendors that also ask for crowns but give you new gear or recipes for you to make them yourself.
