Incredibly tough, even on just "Veteran" setting. Much more like classic XCOM in that you'll be churning through legions of rookies. Contrast this to XCOM:EU/EW, where the loss of anybody during a mission feels like preventable odds--in XCOM2, some missions will leave you thanking RNGesus you managed to evac with anybody.
Note that the guerrilla themes apply beyond just the aesthetics. A lot of missions will be on tight timer limits, forcing you to scramble. Fighters will also be affected by PTSD, and Will reductions are more frequent than the previous installment. They're hammering home the fact that you're making do with civilian volunteers, rather than trained pros, but this adherence to thematic cohesion does often come across as a gameplay burden.
Finally, in terms of performance: until Firaxis provides an optimization patch, expect a lot of lag. Turning off anti-aliasing can help, as does canceling cinematics, but there's going to be a lot of unavoidable stall-outs as the game processes combat results. Once spent a solid minute waiting for a single grenade result to register--between the odd angles, the burn damage, and everything else, the enemy unit ultimately clipped through a wall. Weird.
Past the optimization problem, the game is very pretty, very deep, and VERY fun. I trust Firaxis to do what they need to do to make it shine. In the meantime, there's bug-eyed alien ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to gun down.
Good hunting, Commander.

However, it's rather made up for by the plethora of trinkets you can equip to tweak your characters' stats.
Overall, this is a good game if you have the patience to persevere, but I couldn't recommend it as it is with so much vital information witheld from the player.

+ Sure, you'll get boned ruthlessly by RNG from time to time but it's not terribly unfair at all and it does goes both ways. A challenging game with unforgiving consequences of actions. In Darkest Dungeon, you'll find that your characters grow over time and develop their skills to succeed in certain situations. You'll need to figure out the right chemistry and balance of four party members. Many of your team will die in the process, but finally completing a mission and obtaining gobs of treasure and experience will be your reward. It is exciting and addictive in the beginning and through into the late game because of that sense of completion.
However, I have found that sense of excitement has worn off once the late game has been established. Developing characters will peak, and then it's down to a test of will to keep going. Perhaps it embraces what the developers want - to test the resolve of in-game characters, and also the player.
With consistent late game character deaths and the eventual need to build up more charcters from level 1, the game starts the repetitive process over without the reward of new story content in an attempt complete the last few mission quests. For some, this is enjoyable and worth the effort. However, I found that I just lost interest in actually completing the game quests and moved on. Even so, I'd recommend this game for anyone who likes the grind.
On another note, Wayne June is now my favorite narrator. He makes the game special.

Darkest Dungeon is definitely recommendable. The idea is simple and fun. The art is great. The voice-over is good. The challenge is... well challenging. The games takes awhile to work through, because you won't be able to simply plow through.
Now while I do recommend the game there are a few elements that would turn away some people. Two of the biggest factors that may turn would be players away are: Substantial RNG and the amount of Grinding. In order to make the game challenging it uses RNG to produce varying results, some horribly unfavorable, and others hilariously fortunate. If you plan well enough you can limit the tragedy caused by the RNG. You can't see everything bad headed your way, and how could you. PLus that would take some of the challenge away. But, after about 15 hours you will have gone back and done the same dungeons multiple times (I say this with heavy multiples). Whether, it's because to sent your adventurers to the slaughter house and needed a new crew, you needed some money, or even wanted to pass time before your A team recuperated.
Now I know this sounds like it should be a negative review, but it's not. I find it fair to point out the flaws, and if you can get past them then you've found a good game to play. If these are a complete dealbreaker then I've saved you the time of refunding for your money.

Now don't get me wrong, Spiral Knights USE to be a good game until they made it a real free to play. It is quite obvious that the developers wanted as much money as they could get, so they added Spark's of life, and those heat things that level up your weapons, and made the elevators free just to remove the good co-op in the game. (No shared coins, can't revive party members) God. Why. I actually enjoyed the co-op and even contributed to the game and bought things with money, that won't be happening anytime soon again, unless they fix this terrible new co-op, and new free to play feature)
There are still *some* good things in the game, but it is beaten down by the new features. The art style is great, and well done. The fighting is fun, or use to be fun until they removed reviving. The weapons have their own up's and downs, balancing most out. Some things are set up nicely, but the new features do ruin them. There is an auction house to buy things that you want when you can't get them, but have the crowns to get them. That is really all I can think of.
The bad features? Well all of the new features. The "mini" monsters. Those things are devils and will ALWAYS kill you. No reviving, little co-op. Coins aren't shared in levels anymore. Sparks of life which cost energy to buy. No more mist energy. Elevators are free, and addition that came with the new features, which means no more elevator passes (I liked the elevator pass system, changed the game into a non-free to play, but now it is a complete free to play, and you can't get out of it). New heat system where leveling up weapons requires crystals which cost money too. Gaining heat on your weapons was hard enough, and now there is a CHANCE for it to level up when you use crystals (Unless you use a load of them which costs even more money)?! The repetitive arena levels and the missions to get to new tiers are really useless. The old tier system was better where you would have to go through a group of levels, not boring missions, and have the correct armor and weapons.
As an old player, I DO NOT recommend this game, it was hard enough before, and now they made it even HARDER.

Aside from being a game filled with hazardous paywalls (which can be easily averted), and other nasties with the ingame economy, I really don't see why this title gets so much flak from the community.
Solid Multiplayer RPG, four man dungeon crawling. Wearing armor and items while you complete levels allows you to gain EXP (Known as Heat) to further level the items to a maximum of level 10. From there you can transmute and pick different branches that you want to evolve your weapon for a cost of in-game currency.
The game used to employ a revive system where you would share your HP to revive them, and uses now items known as Spark of Life.  The game used to be much more limited in terms of how much you could play per day, your Knight would store "Mist Energy" in their armor as time passes, and you could use this energy to power the Elevators (which help you advance to lower dungeons in the specific dungeon series).
The dungeons in general are randomly generated based on user contributions to that specific elevator, by adding different crystals (which you can find in almost every level), you may influence how the next dungeon will be generated.
I believe it is a nice addition to the randomness of the stages, and it forces you to be prepared for the dungeons you go into.
The netcode is rather solid, I have not had many problems with my connection and playing the game, aside from the occasional lag spike between other players.
The themes and atmosphere are well designed, and the music compliments said environments.
All in all I would very much recommend this game to my friends and family, even though my opinion may be unpopular.

at a first glance this game might remind one of Minecraft, but in my opinion the two can't really be compared. while Minecraft seems mostly building-based, Trove is focused a lot more on combat.  it embeds many elements from your average fantasy (MMO)RPG and that makes it a fun game to play.
Pros:
+ many elements from different types of games
+ interesting art style (3D pixel/fantasy)
+ combat (and abilities) are very easy to grasp
+ cool takes on classes, like the 'Boomeranger' (a rogue-like archer or swordsperson), the 'Candy Barbarian' (warrior with candy-styled combat and armour), or the 'Fae Trickster' (mage specialised in 'illusion' magic), and a bunch more.
+ you can customise your character to play as a tank, dps, mage, or whatever you want, depending on the gear you choose.
+ as a community member you can get rewards for designing gear items and there are contests for designing enemy bosses (and probably a lot more community-stuff, but i haven't really gotten into that)
+ while in many MMOs i get the feeling that you
to buy items/currency with real life money to progress or to make the game decently playable (especially in free MMOs), i don't really get this feeling in Trove. you can choose to buy store items/currency with 'credits' that you paid for IRL, but it's not really necessary. i haven't bought anything and so far i didn't feel like i needed to, or felt like i was missing out on something. in case you do need something and you don't want to spend IRL money, you might trade with other players.
+ every player can make use of 'cornerstones', which are 16x16x200 blocks sized pieces of land where you can build your base. spread throughout the biomes, you can put down your base wherever you go, as long as there's a cornerstone available. when you leave, you don't have to pick your base up, you can just go to the next cornerstone and put your base down again.
+ building is fun. it's similar to Minecraft's building system, i think. i haven't played Minecraft in a while. there's base blocks that you can build with, and you can collect biome-styled recipes for decorative items, like barrels, torches, etc. (making a private club and then using the club grounds is very convenient for building).
+ i can play as a girl! yay!
Cons:
- despite the amount of classes one can choose from, the playing style doesn't really change with it. you might change your playing style with the use of your gear (whether you play tank, dps, mage, etc.), but generally it's mostly the same.
- the game is based on combat, where a lot of what you're doing is just grinding (which can get repetitive quickly)
- quest system isn't very elaborate. every player gets the same questline and it's mostly just 'Kill this', 'Go here', 'Find this' (which is probably what it is in most MMORPGs, but anyway).
- the large amount of masks and hats can be a bit overwhelming at times. (though i do love how much there is to explore. there are many cool and crazy items.)
- no story at all. not really any lore or background information either.
- there's only a few NPCs! i'd love to see more of them.
i've probably forgotten a bunch of things in this review, but TL;DR:
for a free game, it is very good and it's fun to play when you just want something casual.

A challenging game with unforgiving consequences of actions. In Darkest Dungeon, you'll find that your characters grow over time and develop their skills to succeed in certain situations. You'll need to figure out the right chemistry and balance of four party members. Many of your team will die in the process, but finally completing a mission and obtaining gobs of treasure and experience will be your reward. It is exciting and addictive in the beginning and through into the late game because of that sense of completion.
However, I have found that sense of excitement has worn off once the late game has been established. Developing characters will peak, and then it's down to a test of will to keep going. Perhaps it embraces what the developers want - to test the resolve of in-game characters, and also the player.
With consistent late game character deaths and the eventual need to build up more charcters from level 1, the game starts the repetitive process over without the reward of new story content in an attempt complete the last few mission quests. For some, this is enjoyable and worth the effort. However, I found that I just lost interest in actually completing the game quests and moved on. Even so, I'd recommend this game for anyone who likes the grind.
On another note, Wayne June is now my favorite narrator. He makes the game special.

I will try to keep it simple and clear. Yes, X-COM 2 could be better. Yes, it has a few issues. By that logic, any game with more funding could (but not necessarily would) be better. Truth is firaxis did a damn good job on this sequel. If you are a fan of strategy games, this is a must have. Like any hyped release, a lot of empty reviews and hate will come down. People are already trying to put the game down because of a few issues and difficulty. It's their right to express what they feel, but I'll tell you why you need to ignore those reviews and play the game yourself: flexibility.
Flexibility? Yes. You can tweak almost every setting on the game to your preferences. If you don't want to change difficulty but feels a certain mechanic is too punishing, you can probably tone it down easily. If you don't want to do it, people will do it for you. You know why? flexibility. X-COM 2 is made so that modding can make pretty much anything happen. Firaxis didn't only give us an already great sequel, they gave us a COMMUNITY. And skyrim and dota (among others) are living proof of what can happen with modding! If you ever played ROTK or DA:I and Mass Effect, you can only imagine how great those games would be with modding support. If anything, firaxis took a step on the right direction by offering modding support of this level. All game developers could learn from it. The PROS and CONS:
PRO
+ Expands on the already great Enemy Unknown without changing what was good about it.
+ True tactical and strategy layers: multiple choices. Your choices really matter. You can win or lose an entire campaign in a single mission. Learn when to give up and when to take risks. No playthrough will be the same, ever.
+ Procedural maps: With as many combinations there already are, more can be added through modding or dlc. So far no map feels the same.
+ Much better customization;
+ Better graphics: I don't understand the hate on this. If you expected Tera level graphics on this type of game, sorry but that's on you. Game looks gorgeous to me, and will look even better once the community gets their hands on it.
+ Virtually infinte potential through modding: More customization, maps, mission types, enemies, change of mechanics, new mechanics, new AI .. really, what else would I want?
CONS
- Difficulty can be a turn off for some people. To me, it's challenging. If I ever get frustrated I'll change it or tweak the game (I liked on EU to let soldiers level faster). Right now I'm playing on Commander, and its just right.
- Timers: A lot of people aren't happy with this mechanic. I didn't like it, but got used to it and now I see it as great. It makes you take risks, and not just turtle your way through every mission. It can be changed through the mod tools, and there are already mods that increase or remove it.
- Steep learning curve: you won't master this game in a day. There is no shame in taking it easy and climbing your way up. Play to enjoy. This game can be very frustrating, That's just how it is.
- Performance issues: To me it plays fine. I don't try to play on max through. There will be patches and new drivers, but even if there weren't any, this would be no reason not to get this game. Hell I'd play it on minimum, but I would never skip it.
TL;DR: Great game. Near infinite potential through modding. Even if I didn't like it I would consider buying it to encourage more developers supporting modding. A few issues, the worst one being perfomance, as with every other game, but nothing game breaking so far. Definitely worth it.

I cannot recommend this game anymore due to several reasons.  With the forge update, crafting has become much much more expensive, and the game much more grindy.  Now i'm fine with grinding but the only missions worth your time grinding for profit is soley 1 dungeon/mission whatever you want to call it.  Gameplay gets repetitive really quickly.
To put this in perspective, crafting a regular equip from 1* to its final 5* form would cost you between 10-11k CE.  This is not including additonal cost/time to get materials and in game currencies.
To get enough in game currency for 10-11k (based on in game economy at time of writing) would require around 900k cr.
Say you grind the most profitable dungeon faster than average time (~30 minutes);
(900k/9k per run)*30 min = 50 HRS of straight grinding.
While this is not totally ludicious for an mmo, the method(s) to gain money is.  If you opt not to grind the most profitable dungeon, then be prepared to spend 3-5x the time to get the same amount.
I understand this is free to play and new content shouldn't be expected, but it is disappointing there have been no new missions (or plans made publically known) added over the past few years (overpriced, low profit, barren-of-players DLC not included).

Darkest Dungeon is definitely recommendable. The idea is simple and fun. The art is great. The voice-over is good. The challenge is... well challenging. The games takes awhile to work through, because you won't be able to simply plow through.
Now while I do recommend the game there are a few elements that would turn away some people. Two of the biggest factors that may turn would be players away are: Substantial RNG and the amount of Grinding. In order to make the game challenging it uses RNG to produce varying results, some horribly unfavorable, and others hilariously fortunate. If you plan well enough you can limit the tragedy caused by the RNG. You can't see everything bad headed your way, and how could you. PLus that would take some of the challenge away. But, after about 15 hours you will have gone back and done the same dungeons multiple times (I say this with heavy multiples). Whether, it's because to sent your adventurers to the slaughter house and needed a new crew, you needed some money, or even wanted to pass time before your A team recuperated.
Now I know this sounds like it should be a negative review, but it's not. I find it fair to point out the flaws, and if you can get past them then you've found a good game to play. If these are a complete dealbreaker then I've saved you the time of refunding for your money.

Let me start by saying that this game appeals to a specific audience; an audience that likes difficult, frustrating, and at times downright unfair dungeon crawlers.
This is a dungeon crawler that involves not only HP and specific movesets and all of the other typical SRPG elements, it also comes with a 'stress' mechanic added in. When members of your team get stressed, they may obtain 'afflictions' that hinder themselves, or the team as a whole.
The dungeon crawling aspect is fun for me, as I find dungeon crawlers to be incredibly entertaining, but to some this game is too difficult.
You will spend hours grinding and building up an awesome team, just to have one of them (or all of them if you're unlucky) die and you have to start from square one and level a whole new team up. It can be irritating and frustrating and you may have to shut the game off and come back to it a few days later if you get really frustrated, but that - to me - is a satisfying game.
I think many of those giving this game a negative rating, are the type that like to sit down and play a game until they finish it, or they type that want a game to progress linearly from start to finish, and they can enjoy it start to finish. This game involves a lot of back-track, a lot of accepting loss and moving on, learning to say, "that sucked, but I have to get back up and try again.". Some people may find that really unenjoyable. Others, however, will love the reward of overcomming something they've tried 10,000 times to overcome, and finally achieve.
I love this game and if you enjoy games that will drive you nuts, frustrate you, but eventually give you rewards, you'll like the game. If you like to devour games start-to-finish in 40 hours or less, this may not be the right game for you.

Dang♥♥♥♥♥Dungeon is a gritty dungeon crawler thats appealed to a person that usually doesn't like turn based games. The artwork is talented and disturbing, the music fits the atmosphere (I love how daunting and 'uphill battle' the combat music sounds) and the game design is clever in its own unique ways.
As a game dev myself I especially enjoyed the clever game design to keep the player challenged. The game clearly has an agenda to break any sort of easy routine and strategy in managing your roster and money, and makes sure the player knows this through mechanics. For example, in the game you are forced to send a party out each week to advance time. However to prevent the player from endlessly farming easy quests with the same heroes, to prevent them from advancing a week with no effort, your heroes will eventually grow bored of the apprentice quests and refuse to take part, so you will have to spend resources to send out rookies which won't be able to easily roll those quests as much as your vets.
While the game has a lot going for it for game design, there are still a few flaws. It feels like the game's difficulty agenda gets ahead of itself, and bad stuff can happen to you for seemingly no reason just to throw you for a loop. This would be fine if the game would outright state its trying to ♥♥♥♥ you, but instead it does it in ways that seem to resist its own rules. For example, for no reason at all, even without being Marked, the 4-creature party will continually focus one of your squishier heroes into the ground. You can try using a Man-At-Arms or Crusader to mark themselves, but when this is happening it usually doesn't help and they'll continue to slaughter the one character. You have all of these abilities but occasionally the game refuses to listen and will throw any advantages you have from those abilities out the window.
Despite the negative reviews, a frustrating set back once in a while should not really overshadow the game's polish, well thought out game play and clear love the developers have for it. A game is not bad because you can't beat it.
I haven't been too far along yet but I'll definitely play more, however I've seen some complaints about the end-game and it sounds incredibly unpleasant, so unless something REALLY clicks I only really see myself playing this until I succeed in my first assault.

I still recommend this game, although I enjoyed the older versions much more.
This game was once a unique masterpiece.  Everything just worked.  The prices, the balance, and especially the content.
Then the updates got worse.
Buggy, hardly-tested updates were released, one after another, each one taking away from this game's uniqueness.  For example, just about every monster in the game has been "nerfed" to oblivion.  Fighting the monsters was once a challenge.  You could expect that construct to turn to face you when he attacked.  Instead, watch as he swings at the air and accomplishes nothing.  Nowadays, the only challenge is avoiding the hazards that the latency loves driving you into.
The economy.  Originally, the energy prices were decent.  Then, they spiked up to ridiculous prices.  Once this game was brought to steam, the prices basically reset.  Then, the prices slowly began to increase past the once thought to be insane price.  Updates increased and decreased the prices, but one idea sure did it.  Flash sales on accessories which do nothing except make you look shinier spiked the prices past the ten thousand mark.  Now, the prices just go as they please, usually always too high for players just starting to accomplish anything.  While energy isn't as crucial as before, it's still worth mentioning the economy.
And finally, the game's content itself.  What was once a beautiful, unique work of art became a shadow of it's former self.
I'll start on the UI.  The old one was perfection.  It fitted the classic style of this game, and along with most of the glory in this game, was laid to rest.  In the year or so I've played after the GUI update, I can say I still never figured out most of it.  While the new UI wasn't popular, it still made it into the game, and remains to this day.
As I mentioned earlier, each type of monster had the difficulty toned down on them.  This made the game itself a lot less challenging, taking some of the fun out of it.
A lot of of updates were simply promotions at this point.  Costumes and accessories which had no effect on gameplay could be obtained through boxes the player had to buy.
Not too long after this, the game basically changed entirely.  While the new UI stayed, the crafting system received a complete overhaul.  Energy wasn't the main component in actual gameplay anymore.  Elevators were free.  Crafting advanced gear was free.  The game was free.  While it was always "free-to-play", Spiral Knights had run mostly on energy before this, and new players wouldn't be able to accomplish much at the very start.  Now, new players could progress.  This was a step in the right direction.
Some new updates showed up, including some eerie content, and a festive Holiday update.  An update geared toward gunners is also still in the works.
Despite all of the bad things I have said, this game isn't bad.  It's just terrible compared to the old days, and I'll always try to remember Spiral Knights for how it once was.  A treasure.  A unique land of fun.
A legend.

The word gay arrived in English during the 12th century from Old French gai, most likely deriving ultimately from a Germanic source.[1] For most of its life in English, the word's primary meaning was "joyful", "carefree", "bright and showy", and the word was very commonly used with this meaning in speech and literature. For example, the optimistic 1890s are still often referred to as the Gay Nineties. The title of the 1938 French ballet Gaîté Parisienne ("Parisian Gaiety"), which became the 1941 Warner Brothers movie, The Gay Parisian,[7] also illustrates this connotation. It was apparently not until the 20th century that the word began to be used to mean specifically "homosexual", although it had earlier acquired sexual connotations.[1]
The derived abstract noun gaiety remains largely free of sexual connotations, and has, in the past, been used in the names of places of entertainment; for example W.B. Yeats heard Oscar Wilde lecture at the Gaiety Theatre in Dublin.[8]
Sexualization
Usage statistics from English books, according to Google Ngram Viewer.
The word may have started to acquire associations of immorality as early as the 14th century, and had certainly acquired them by the 17th.[1] By the late 17th century it had acquired the specific meaning of "addicted to pleasures and dissipations",[9] an extension of its primary meaning of "carefree" implying "uninhibited by moral constraints." A gay woman was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, a gay man a womanizer and a gay house a brothel.[1]
The use of gay to mean "homosexual" was in origin merely an extension of the word's sexualised connotation of "carefree and uninhibited", which implied a willingness to disregard conventional or respectable sexual mores. Such usage is documented as early as the 1920s, and there is evidence for it before the 20th century,[1] although it was initially more commonly used to imply heterosexually unconstrained lifestyles, as in the once-common phrase "gay Lothario",[10] or in the title of the book and film The Gay Falcon (1941), which concerns a womanizing detective whose first name is "Gay." Similarly, Gilbert and MacDermott's music hall song of the 1880s, "Charlie Dilke Upset the Milk" – "Master Dilke upset the milk/When taking it home to Chelsea;/ The papers say that Charlie's gay/Rather a wilful wag!" – referred to Sir Charles Dilke's alleged heterosexual impropriety.[11] Well into the mid 20th century a middle-aged bachelor could be described as "gay", indicating that he was unattached and therefore free, without any implication of homosexuality. This usage could apply to women too. The British comic strip Jane was first published in the 1930s and described the adventures of Jane Gay. Far from implying homosexuality, it referred to her free-wheeling lifestyle with plenty of boyfriends (while also punning on Lady Jane Grey).
A passage from Gertrude Stein's Miss Furr & Miss Skeene (1922) is possibly the first traceable published use of the word to refer to a homosexual relationship. According to Linda Wagner-Martin (Favored Strangers: Gertrude Stein and her Family (1995)) the portrait, "featured the sly repetition of the word gay, used with sexual intent for one of the first times in linguistic history," and Edmund Wilson (1951, quoted by James Mellow in Charmed Circle (1974)) agreed.[12] For example:
They were ...gay, they learned little things that are things in being gay, ... they were quite regularly gay.
—Gertrude Stein, 1922
Through the mid 20th century, the term "gay" commonly referred to "carefree", as illustrated in the Astaire and Rogers film The Gay Divorcee. (See detailed discussion in article.)
Bringing Up Baby (1938) was the first film to use the word gay in apparent reference to homosexuality. In a scene in which the Cary Grant character's clothes have been sent to the cleaners, he is forced to wear a woman’s feather-trimmed robe. When another character asks about his robe, he responds, "Because I just went gay all of a sudden!" Since this was a mainstream film at a time when the use of the word to refer to homosexuality would still be unfamiliar to most film-goers, the line can also be interpreted to mean "I just decided to do something frivolous."[13]
The word continued to be used with the dominant meaning of "carefree", as evidenced by the title of The Gay Divorcee (1934), a musical film about a heterosexual couple.
Shift to homosexual
By the mid-20th century, gay was well established in reference to hedonistic and uninhibited lifestyles[9] and its antonym straight, which had long had connotations of seriousness, respectability, and conventionality, had now acquired specific connotations of heterosexuality.[14] In the case of gay, other connotations of frivolousness and showiness in dress ("gay apparel") led to association with camp and effeminacy. This association no doubt helped the gradual narrowing in scope of the term towards its current dominant meaning, which was at first confined to subcultures. Gay was the preferred term since other terms, such as queer, were felt to be derogatory.[15] Homosexual is perceived as excessively clinical,[16][17][18] since the sexual orientation now commonly referred to as "homosexuality" was at that time a mental illness diagnosis in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM).
In mid-20th century Britain, where male homosexuality was illegal until the Sexual Offences Act 1967, to openly identify someone as homosexual was considered very offensive and an accusation of serious criminal activity. Additionally, none of the words describing any aspect of homosexuality were considered suitable for polite society. Consequently, a number of euphemisms were used to hint at suspected homosexuality. Examples include "sporty" girls and "artistic" boys,[19] all with the stress deliberately on the otherwise completely innocent adjective.
The sixties marked the transition in the predominant meaning of the word gay from that of "carefree" to the current "homosexual".
In the British comedy-drama film Light Up The Sky! (1960) directed by Lewis Gilbert about the antics of a British Army searchlight squad during World War II, there is a scene in the mess hut where the character played by Benny Hill proposes an after dinner toast. He begins, "I'd lke to propose..." at which point a fellow diner, played by Sidney Tafler, interjects "Who to?", suggesting a proposal of marriage. The Benny Hill character responds, "Not to you for start, you ain't my type". He then adds in mock doubt, "Oh, I don't know, you're rather gay on the quiet."
By 1963, a new sense of the word gay was known well enough to be used by Albert Ellis in his book The Intelligent Woman's Guide to Man-Hunting. Similarly, Hubert Selby, Jr. in his 1964 novel Last Exit to Brooklyn, could write that a character "took pride in being a homosexual by feeling intellectually and esthetically superior to those (especially women) who weren't gay..."[20] Later examples of the original meaning of the word being used in popular culture include the theme song to the 1960–1966 animated TV series The Flintstones, whereby viewers are assured that they will "have a gay old time." Similarly, the 1966 Herman's Hermits song "No Milk Today", which became a Top 10 hit in the UK and a Top 40 hit in the U.S. and included the lyric "No milk today, it was not always so / The company was gay, we'd turn night into day."[21] In June 1967, the headline of the review of the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band album in the British daily newspaper The Times stated, "The Beatles revive hopes of progress in pop music with their gay new LP".[22] Yet in the same year, The Kinks recorded "David Watts".[23] Ostensibly about schoolboy envy, the song also operated as an in-joke, as related in Jon Savage's "The Kinks: The Official Biography", because the song took its name from a homosexual promoter they'd encountered who'd had romantic designs on songwriter

I just lost my party in an adventuring forray i've done a half dozen times before, because the enemy happened to crit me one time too many and at the same time have a string of 5+ dodges, which should be statistically impossible, which led to utter annihilation. Nothing to do with skill, with party makeup, with preparation, nothing. I actually am going to uninstall the game now, not out of some kind of angst, but because of a lack of total reward. Mind you, to this point in 40 hours of gameplay, I had lost 1 hero. When RNG strikes, it strikes hard.
The concept of constant saves and losing heros is great, not against that - but when your actual gaming ability , preperation, perception - anything that normally would work against a games inherent "difficulty" have almost nothing to do with success, it just becomes an excercise in frustration. Also, keep in mind the game is not on a linear scale, if you were to say, take the same party of 4 and level them together straight through, you could in no way shape or form afford to outfit them and level their skills (nevermind level the town itself) based on your quest rewards. You would have to run multiple groups multiple times to outfit 1 group in accordance with their level. So you end up putting alot into it.
Games have moved away from RNG for the most part, or at least from drastic examples of it, and for good reason. I haven't even mentioned the arbitrary disease / virtue "rewards" at the end of battles, or how between stress (somewhat random but manageable) or random disease in battles, you could end up not only losing entire adventures worth of gold "healing" a hero, but disable them for 2,3,4,5 adventuers at a time, based on the back end RNG of "lol they arent done praying this week! oh also they developed a bad trait from praying lol!"
For a satisfying gaming experience, I just can't recommend this game. Great concept, great execution, good balancing, but a total waste of time based on the battle system, and all of the outside player control RNG that just crushes this game in a very bad way.

Darkest Dungeon was very nearly one of the big wins from Kickstarter alongside Divinity Original Sin, and Wasteland 2 (though opinions do remain a bit divided on that one from time to time). How best to describe it? It's basically the grown up version of Warhammer Quest, except it's the grown up version *done right*. This is probably as close as you'll likely get to a pen and paper roleplaying experience on your computer without actually rolling the dice yourself.
The game follows two distinct beats, the first takes place in your hamlet, known simply as the estate - insert the name of your save file between 'the' and 'estate', this leads to all kinds of possible creative humour if you stop to consider the implications, for people over here in Britain, the obvious choices such as "The Darkest Leeds Council estate" are going to be too easy to pass up - the estate serves as your hub to manage your roster of adventurers, and it will be a roster, a sizable bunch of misfits drawn from a wide class pool, easily as diverse as you could possibly wish for, and all of them have a slightly grim twist upon their usual fantasy tropes upon which they are based.
For example, in normal roleplay games, one would ordinarily expect the adventuring party to be made up of the holy trinity, that is to say - tanking, damage and healing. Those tenets are more or less followed here within reason, two of the classes offer up healing options in the guise of the Vestal, a priestess who is decked out in more metal than robocop, and the occultist, who can mend with dark powers whilst raining down curses upon his foes. Tanks include a crusader, possibly the only unambiguously "good" moral choice in the bunch, and even he can be easily brought down from grace if you send him to the brothel (yes, there's a brothel, and yes, you can get people -banned- from it for "deviant tastes"), and a leper, a hulking brute of a tank who wears a mask reminiscent of the guy from V for Vendetta.
All of the classes have their own unique twist on the usual trope, and their own backstory, a reason for visiting this utterly forsaken place, and as a result you'll likely get attatched to your favourite classes and heroes, all of whom you can name and provide trinkets to adjust their stats a touch here and there. Gear can be upgraded, naturally (though as of the current build, there doesn't seem to be a visual reflection of upgrades, which is a bit saddening, though the art style more than makes up for it), and additional skills can be bought and then shuffled around from the guild hall. Each character gets seven skills, but you can only take four into battle, and some skills are usable only from specific places and only UPON specific targets in the opponents position order, so choose carefully and ensure you have a good spread.
Once you've settled upon your choice of party, skills and core kit, you then move to the provisioning stage, where you select the mission you wish to take on, you then buy up any consumables you wish to take with you for the mission ahead and then deploy, and the game proper begins. You move about between rooms on a map, following "corridors" made up of little mapsquares that can contain encounters, loot and other interesting things, the rooms too can contain multiple items and enemy groups, and over time, fighting can build up stress in the group, and as wounds pile up and the group gets taxed, so too does their minds.
That's when the stress mechanic begins to take it's toll, eventually as the minds of the adventurers begin to fracture, you'll find they get more... talkative, and less co-operative. Sometimes they'll act on their own, sometimes they'll pass their turn, sometimes they'll refuse healing. It adds a random factor into proceedings that can make the difference between life and death, and combined with the death's door mechanic, can create some genuinely tense and hair raising fights.
In this game, death is permanent, and boy will you go through adventurers, even getting one to level -3- is considered a feat in itself, most will die before they even see level 2 or even level 1, and the graveyard will likely be full to bursting within a few months. This is not a game to play if you are expecting to develop long lasting relationships with a lot of heroes, you may get to preserve a select few over time, but most will be as moths to the flame. Thankfully the cart comes weekly, loaded with fresh meat for the grinder, and recruitment is free, so that's nice!
The art style is -glorious-, and the sound and overall design back this up, creating a genuine Tabletop RPG feel that perhaps could only be provided for by a computer, though if there ever was a proper pen and paper version of this game created, I could imagine as a first edition, it'd sell amazingly well. It has all the ingredients for a fantastic atmosphere, and a great evening in, much like a great night with Dungeons and Dragons. The cherry on the cake is the narrator, who lends a thick, grim air to proceedings, and even when things go well, seems to live to take what little hope you have, and smother it in a layer of soot and grime.
Did I say this game is grim and contained adult themes? Oh it does. Much flagellation and deviancy await, along with unspeakable horrors that will cause many an adventurer's mind to turn in on itself.
There is a but...
The endgame however, pulls the most mighty of penile moves. A hardcoded debuff called "Never again" applies a ban to heroes that enter the Darkest Dungeon, preventing them from returning. This forcibly extends the playtime of the game by forcing you to grind out a minimum of four complete teams, depending on how your parties have evolved, this may take you significantly longer than you expect.
There's very little reason for this other than to pad out the game and to prevent you from blasting the Dungeon with your "A-team", but nonetheless, here we are. A lot of needless grind put into the game simply to stop you from finishing the game when the time is right.
This turns the game from being fun, to being frustrating. All the work you do up to the Darkest Dungeon gets thrown in your face and you wind up staring down the barrels of long trudge after long trudge. A ceaseless grind that simply exists to make you stick your face in the dirt.
I'm sorry, but that's no longer "fun". As it stands, it's not fixable either by users. I looked.
For this very reason, this game loses it's positive Early Access rating from me, and gains a negative rating, with a final verdict that's much less positive in it's standing.
Verdict :
..what is there not to love about Starbound, seriously? Buy it.

Here's the thing, the game is fun, it's unique, it has an interesting premise (the darker side of adventuring) it's well narrated and the ambience is awesome and authentic feeling.
However, the game is just punishingly difficult - and "difficult" doesn't even really apply. It's just punishing to play. The entire thing is based on RNG. I just lost my party in an adventuring forray i've done a half dozen times before, because the enemy happened to crit me one time too many and at the same time have a string of 5+ dodges, which should be statistically impossible, which led to utter annihilation. Nothing to do with skill, with party makeup, with preparation, nothing. I actually am going to uninstall the game now, not out of some kind of angst, but because of a lack of total reward. Mind you, to this point in 40 hours of gameplay, I had lost 1 hero. When RNG strikes, it strikes hard.
The concept of constant saves and losing heros is great, not against that - but when your actual gaming ability , preperation, perception - anything that normally would work against a games inherent "difficulty" have almost nothing to do with success, it just becomes an excercise in frustration. Also, keep in mind the game is not on a linear scale, if you were to say, take the same party of 4 and level them together straight through, you could in no way shape or form afford to outfit them and level their skills (nevermind level the town itself) based on your quest rewards. You would have to run multiple groups multiple times to outfit 1 group in accordance with their level. So you end up putting alot into it.
Games have moved away from RNG for the most part, or at least from drastic examples of it, and for good reason. I haven't even mentioned the arbitrary disease / virtue "rewards" at the end of battles, or how between stress (somewhat random but manageable) or random disease in battles, you could end up not only losing entire adventures worth of gold "healing" a hero, but disable them for 2,3,4,5 adventuers at a time, based on the back end RNG of "lol they arent done praying this week! oh also they developed a bad trait from praying lol!"
For a satisfying gaming experience, I just can't recommend this game. Great concept, great execution, good balancing, but a total waste of time based on the battle system, and all of the outside player control RNG that just crushes this game in a very bad way.

First off I have and will always an avid fan of the Fallout series and I truly believe that each one that has released only gets better. Now, with that out of the way I would like to delve into my review of Fallout 4. The game looks absolutely amazing if you have it running on ultra, the gunplay is absolutely fantastic and in my honest opinion the best change coming from FO3 and FNV. However, I must admit that the settlement building is my absolute favorite part of the entire game. I love being able to create city like settlements in the middle of a wasteland and turn them into thriving little towns.
Now for the bad part:
1. The guns look great, the animations are absolutely awful. Bethesda got extremely lazy when it came to making the animations for these guns. Not only does most of the weapons use a left handed bolt pull (looking @ you hunting rifle) but most of the reloads are just so simple. There is no gun that catches your eye and makes you enjoy using it because hell half of the vanilla guns just use the Assault rifle animation over and over.
2. The base game + DLC's settlement objects are a♥♥♥♥♥♥take. Granted there was some nice stuff that did come with it, however, most of it was just stuff that honestly should've released with the base game.
3. There are only two "story" DLC's: Now for me I wasn't as bothered by this, although, a ton of people were which I can completely understand. I will admit though that both story DLC's are absolutely fantastic.
[ Good News ]
Now luckily for you if you decide to buy and play this game you can remedy every bad thing about it by installing FREE mods off the Fallout 4 Nexus. Not only does it come with a simple mod manager that is just one button press - it also has an extremely helpful and easy to use UI. Want that Assault Carbine from New Vegas with badass animations and leveled list injection? Boom. Go to the Nexus and you got yourself a nice custom gun. This will negate the awful vanilla guns (Hell there are even mods that fix them!). Want more settlement building objects? Look up something like Vanilla Extensions, SOE workshop, G2M workshop, Sim Settlements, etc. Not only does this add lore friendly settlement objects, it also adds a ton of variability and uniquness to the settlement building. Now you can make settlements feel unique without having to use the same objects over and over.
Do you like the concept of settlements but hate baby sitting? Then Sim Settlements would be perfect in fixing that. It is a unique settlement mod that allows you to place plots and assign settlers and those settlers do their jobs, while building their houses up while living in them. So each time you come to your settlement it will not only look different but feel more alive.
Also while Fallout 4 Vanilla looks amazing it can ALWAYS look better. You can download a multitude of texture packs + ENB's and have the game looking like a new release (assuming your computer can run it).
For any mod questions or if you are interested in getting into them I would highly recommend Gopher's modding tutorials on youtube. Within a few hours you could have you game not only looking ten times better, but also playing ten times better.
[ Final Thoughts ]
If you have been on the fence for a while this would be the perfect time to buy the game + season pass since it is on sale during the Steam Summer sale (honestly would recommend buying the whole bundle and getting every game in the serieis for an incredible price). While the season pass DLC was kind of lacking the two story DLC's more than make up for it. Also if you do decide to mod a lot of mods REQUIRE all DLC. So having the season pass will help you more in the long run and prevent you from having to trouble shoot mods because you are missing a DLC or two.
TL;DR: The gunplay is amazing, the story is captiviating for the first two or three playthroughs, and the settlement building is great and can always be made better. Graphics are really nice on higher settings. RPG elements have been somewhat netuered since previous Fallout's but you can still roleplay with easy, and mods completely change the game.

I was there when the hype was being built. The years of waiting. Hoax after hoax. When the game was announce, I went online to see when that pip boy edition was being released. I bought it♥♥♥♥♥soon as I could and waited patiently. When I popped the game in, and played the game, I was more than happy. the wait was over and the reward was well recieved.
The world in Fallout 4 initially is full of things to do. Completing each main questline felt rewarding. Exploring each ruin that was open felt fantastic. The characters are memorable, and the memes this game generated are also the dankest. However there is a problem. After 200+ hours of playing, a patter evolves. Unlike in other fallout games such as NV, you begin to realize you have one main choice in the game. Do what the game wants you to do. An example would be if you are given a quest, you are presented with 4 options. Yes, No, why, what. This then comes to 2 options, yes and no.  You either do the quest the game tells you to, or you dont do it at all. Going back to NV, this is not as common. WHile at camp Mccaran, investigating a spy in the NCR, you choose how to find out who the spy is, and how to deal justice. The only thing you are given, is a clue. While simplicity is great, choice in a RPG is more what I wanted.
After saying this, you may be thinking that I dislike the game. I dont. I actually think it is one of my favorite games. The combat is fantastic, and the world is just waiting to be explored. The problem is, this game is not a full blown RPG. you are guided between decisions with very little to choose from. I highly recommend this game if you are a fan of the lore, want better combat from a fallout game, and you also want to play through a solid story line with many side quests and locations to discover. Just dont go into this game expecting the best fallout game ever. Obsidion is hopefully working on topping themselves on that one.

Let me start by saying XCOM 2 is a triumph. XCOM EU and EW paid homage to UFO Defence's difficulty and fear factor by making sure the game was truly difficult, but in a mostly rewarding way. In some ways they compromised on those principles - having your best squad wiped a few weeks in and losing a critical mission was basically game over, so half the time losses felt frustrating rather than just punishing and reinvigorating. In my first XCOM 2 run, that I consider to have gone fairly well, I've lost upwards of 10 soldiers in a few months, and I failed my first attempt at a blacksite, but I can tell I'm that I'm not doomed. Notably, in EU, there were a lot of safety net abilities like Run and Gun, Rockets and various Sniper abilities like Double Tap though that made the game at times laughably easy - so long as you had restraint.
XCOM 2's biggest change to the formula, outside of the total revamp of the strategic layer,  is the fact that there are almost no safety nets in the early game. Rockets are gone, replaced with grenade launchers, which while incredibly useful, cannot wipe out a pod of enemies in one shot every mission.  The new Ranger class, which is basically like the old Assault, doesn't get Run and Gun until midway through the ability tree. The sword they get has effectively enormous range, but can't be relied upon to singlehandedly kill enemies unless you get bladesman at corporal rank, which loses you an extremely useful concealment abiility.  Specialists are about as underwhelming as supports were early on, but get just as deadly in later ranks, while Sharp Shooters are heavily situational due to the fact that a lot of missions are timed, but can now do some very interesting stunts like fire off pistols a couple times a round at different targets, or chain sniper rifle shots together if each one is a kill. The fact the aliens are now more specialised, and their gimmicks are more frightening (e.g, the basic sectoid gets the mind control ability in the first few months)  means that without safety nets, they're far more fearsome and worth being worried about. This makes the game more difficult obviously, but also more enjoyable in the long run once you know how to handle each type of enemy - Sectoids are easily killed by swords, Stunlancers either need to die ASAP or you need a flashbang/overwatch to shut them down from charging. The Faceless, meanwhile, needs to be spotted well in advance of triggering it, because it can attack on activation.  The variation in alien types and the threat they present means that XCOM 2 encourages a lot more tactical, outside the box thinking.
The visuals in this game are incredible. The unit design for the aliens and advent hybrids is superb, and really adds to the intimidation when they're breathing down your neck. The environmental design is also great - the procedural generation is by no means a half baked gimmick and makes every area look interesting and refreshing.  There are cobbled together outposts, futuristic cities, slums, surreal alien bases and facilities.  Customisation is top notch - there is as a lot of freedom and oppurtunity for making your own narrative in your head, and in general things that make your troops more memorable, like random extra abilities, the memorial/bar and personnel areas you can view all add to the attachment you get to them.
I want to quickly mention the multiplayer. This is a mixed bag - the extremely points heavy advent robot units are extremely hard to kill and can one-shot most targets. The Sectopod, ludicrously, can even fire twice, doing 10-11 damage each time.  The costs on units are very weird, as is some of the internal balance. Advent Troopers at 200 points have 3 health and a mag rifle, but for 400 points you get an Officer with 12 health, better stats, a frag grenade and the ability to mark targets. Since matches total about 7500+ points, you can easily fit these guys in.  There is an issue with stuttering as well which I'll touch upon in a moment.
In terms of technical quality, you can tell that the developers didn't put their effort towards making a game that was very free of bugs, or that ran extremely well. The game is stable - the amount of disruptive bugs that will ruin your experience or progress is very, very minimal and rare it seems. The problems arise with the fact that XCOM 2 just simply doesn't run as well as it should on high end PCs- there are frequent FPS drops in missions unless you turn some settings down.  This obvously doesn't matter that much, since the game is turn based, but it is irritating. Perhaps the most annoying bug is the fact that the game occassionally takes a few seconds to register a buff/debuff/critical effect, or upwards of 10-20 seconds to end a turn in multiplayer and pass control to the other player. This is something that is bound to be fixed eventually though.
I whole-heartedly reccomend XCOM 2 to anyone who was a fan of XCOM EU, and would also say that anyone who has an interest in a challenging and interesting game but has not tried the games before this one should give it a go at least.

The ultimate fantasy football game.
You start the game by taking over a old and defunct football club at the lowest rank of the Eldritch Tournament. You have few players of poor abilities and no real training facilities.
Now you have to set up play formations and use what feeble abilities your players have to try to force your way through the scrimmage lines of Team Cthulhu and score that much needed touchdown.
Team Cthulhu will try to mess up your positioning and wound, stress out and otherwise harm your vulnerable players.
If you manage to run the whole field and score the touchdown, you will be rewarded with resources to improve your training facilities and money to train new skills and improve equipment.
Then you hire new hopeful amateurs and line them up against the star players of Team Cthulhu in another bout and hope for another touchdown, while your fatigued players from the match before rest up with booze, drugs and ♥♥♥♥♥s.
The center of the game is managing your player talent mass for having the best chances of touchdowns and profit. On this path you will crush the lives and hopes of many a young college graduate player. But that is their own fault for not having properly studied what it truly means to play football on a professional level.
Never get attached to any player, no matter how good, always be ready to sacrifrice anyone for the good of the team and the team finances.
In the end you may make it to the playoffs and the superbowl against Great Cthulhu himself. But by this time you will usually have made so many improvements to your facilities and stadium, that even the merciless RNG can no longer threaten your team. If there is any complaint I could have aginst the game, it will be this inverse difficulty curve, where the end game can actually be the easiest because of how well set up you can be.
Overall I am very impressed and entertained by this wonderful simulation of football management.

A fantastic strategy game in it's own right, XCOM 2 improves upon almost every aspect of its predecessor. It feels a lot more fair, thanks to tweaks like the concealment mechanic, but for every advantage XCOM gets you can be certain the aliens get twofold more. It's a harrowing, intense turn-based game, and those are words not often used together.
The optimization isn't great, but it's far from terrible. The game looks fantastic, so I'm guessing the reported issues are some mix of people vastly overestimating the power of their rigs combined with certain settings that really are quite unoptimized and make the game run terribly.
Finally, the big controversy at the moment is around how many missions have strictly enforced turn timers. I personally haven't had any problems with them, as many of the new mechanics make it a lot safer to play more aggressively in the first place, but a lot of people who got used to the dominant strategy from the last game (move slow, overwatch everything) seem fairly upset. I don't understand the complaints at all, but if it sounds like something that would annoy you, check out the other reviews and maybe play XCOM: Enemy Within instead.

What a game!
i have at the moment played this game for 27 hours, after it released so i can't say judge it in comparison to it's early access days. BUT what i can do, is tell you my opinion about it in it's release state!
To start of with, i did not have high expectations about this game, i actually didn't know very much about it at all. i simply saw a guy on
play it for 10 minutes, and decided i'd try it out.
Now a little background on me; i'm not a hardcore gamer by any means, but i do enjoy a nice story driven game like Assassin's Creed, Fallout, The Witcher and so on, and with the odd game here and there outside of the rpg genre (Civilization 5 being the most beloved game outside of rpgs).
So i don't normally buy indie games, nor do i care much for them as they're normally lacking in some  way, or just down right sucks (Early Access in general).
Darkest Dungeon however, blew my mind. the artwork, the soundtrack, the gameplay. everything seemingly joins together and makes a perfect game!
Whenever you play, you feel immersed, you care for your heroes and you struggle with every decision. i find myself retreating more often than not, to spare one or more of my heroes from death, instead paying for whatever treatment they need. this in turn have caused money trouble for me, slowing down the rest of my heroes not affected.
You get so much into this game, for better or worse, that you start squirming in your seat whenever a hero is on the brink of death, or get insanely angry at a seconds notice if your hero misses a hit that would've ended a fight, instead causing you to have to spend thousands of your hard earned gold on treatment.
The whole game revolves around being punishing. you heroes will die, whether you like it or not. you will struggle with money. you will have negative stats on your heroes because of negative quirks. you will get destroyed by the rng in the game. but the most important part is that all of this is fun!
If you're looking for a challenging turn based game, that focuses on screwing you over, yet feeling fun this is definitely a game to try!

This will probably be one of the best free to play games you will ever find. It's one of my favorites in general, I'm a huge fan of survival games with zombies.
Unturned is basically the DayZ mod for Arma 2, but completely free, less demanding, can be played offline (Praise the lord for that), and provides much more simple but still complex gameplay. -Simple yet fun survival gameplay
-Very replayable
-It's FREE
-Has a unique look to it for a zombie game that looks nice. Zombies have funny frowny faces.
-Steam Workshop and level creators
-MASSIVELY supported. Updates come out every few days.
-Makes you feel like a survivor. You never become too overpowered (unless you duplicate weapon ammo and food)
-Skill trees that keep you playing and encourage zombie killing
-Loot respawns, so worlds keep getting fresh. Loot changes every time so it's not always the same.
-Lots of items to craft
-Pretty nice graphics (Water, shadows, etc.)
CONS:
-Crafting can be a little complex
-Starting out with a bad spawn can be very difficult
-Complex Base Building (in my opinion)

To anyone reading these reviews who is confused by the massive swings between positive and negative, you need to know one thing: Darkest Dungeon is an emotional game. To people just starting out, it can seem baffling, unfair, and deliberately obscure. To people who have been playing since Early Access, and who have seen favourite party compositions and strategies rendered obsolete, the Steam reviews page is more of an extension of Reddit than anything else - a place to air grievances (legitimate or otherwise) over a game that they have dedicated a lot of time to.
What a lot of these reviews miss out is... y'know... the actual review part. On that front, I would say the following: the core gameplay is rock solid. At its heart, Darkest Dungeon has taken a minimalist, turn-based, four-man combat system and imbued it with massive potential for tactical thought and personal flair. Figuring out the best role for each of your heroes (chosen from a fairly generous pool of classes) and suddenly realising a unique way of getting them to synergise is immensely gratifying. Unlike a lot of games, it doesn't feel like there is a a ring-fenced area of "correct", vanilla play that only the very high-level players can get past; instead, you are encouraged and rewarded for coming up with your own strategies from the get go. The central combat system is smart, it pushes you to experiment, and there is a lot of room to come up with a playstyle that feels like your own, unique creation.
HOWEVER! If that's all Darkest Dungeon was, it would be a neat tablet-based distraction, but ultimately sterile. It is the stuff that comes layered on top of it that is the source of its intrigue - and also the source of a lot of the frustration you'll see directed at it. As a typical RPG player, you naturally do everything you can to guarantee the safety and efficacy of your character(s), and it feels inherently uncomfortable to work in a game environment that leaves you perpetually on your toes and at risk of failure. DD refuses to let you settle into a comfortable routine, and a massive enemy critical attack, an ambush in pitch-dark while camping, or a series of misses on your part can topple you from a seemingly-unassailable position to a very desperate one. The potential for a fail-cascade is what turns off many new players, and even drives experienced ones to the occasional rage-review, but it is also vital to the fundamental risk-reward balance of the game, which is designed to punish complacency and encourage the utmost thought on your part.
As you progress through a dungeon, you constantly need to balance a dwindling supply of light, food, sanity and health (although they can be restored in some ways), while also trying to complete objectives and collect much-needed loot with limited backpack space. Usually, this is the sort of gameplay I dislike; feeling that there is a time-limit, that I can't plough through something at my own speed in relative safety, is an uncomfortable experience after most games. However, the actual result is some very effective tension. In a normal RPG (say... Diablo), the steady drip of ever-increasing numbers is satisfying in a functional sort of way, but in DD the stakes are so high that getting a critical hit or dodging a huge attack always feels like a
rather than just a nice bonus.
It can initially feel punishing and unfair, since most gamers are hard-wired to see a hero death (which is permanent), a catastrophic turn-around, or a "tactical retreat" as a failure. Likewise, the element of randomness can make it feel like your hard work and smart play has not been rewarded, like you're just a random collection of atoms buzzing around in a meaningless void where there is no God or higher authority to dispense justice or distinguish right or wrong.... It takes time to realise that you were never
to have it easy, that it's
been a gamble, and you can't expect a perfect S ranking - all you can do is make the best play you can with the information you have. It takes time to realise that the game is pushing you to accept loss and difficulty as part of the game, rather than a failure.
Even I rage quit every now and then - but I always come back, because, as I said, Darkest Dungeon is an emotional game. You invest (real) time and (fake) money in your group of heroes, the odds are massively stacked in the House's favour, none of your guys is going to come out unscarred, you are going to face some serious setbacks, but you return because actually making it, actually landing that last hit at the last possible moment, realising you've scraped through again, is always a surprise, and an amazing one at that.

A lot of people seemed to like New Vegas better than 4, but I'm of the opposite opinion: I've enjoyed 4 more than I ever enjoyed New Vegas. Even though there wasn't a lot of DLC, I've sunk at least 50 hours alone into building my own vault. You can choose to explore and loot as if it were an ordinary RPG but Fallout has shown that it's time to evolve. Exploration and combat are as good as they've ever been, but what the series really needed was something new. I think settlements were that next step even though they aren't for everyone. I disagree with their removal of item durability or their late inclusion of a way to produce ammo, but those are minor gripes. If you miss some of the old features, go back and replay the other titles. Or better yet, just download a Nexus mod. Anything that you think is missing or broken has likely been fixed by some programmer who thought the same thing.
People need to take off their rose-tinted glasses and stop idealizing games of the past. If you can learn to accept this game on its own merit and not criticize it for not living up to some unrealistic expectation of what you think the Fallout series is supposed to be, you'll enjoy this game. Skyrim is plagued with the same problem: Morrowind fans are always there to remind you that Morrowind is the greatest game that's ever been created. There's a reason why Bethesda has been so successful and it's not because they're releasing a reskinned Fallout every year with the same features as the last one. If you want that, go play COD or Assassin's Creed. Plenty of developers would love to have your business.
It's a solid game on its own but as a member of the Fallout franchise, it's a fantastic introduction. I'd give the base game an 8/10. With mods, it's a 9/10. If you include the soundtrack in the scoring, it's a 10/10. Buy the game and just enjoy it.

TL;DR
Darkest Dungeon will punish you for not knowing something, but that's fine because once you do that becomes easier. Think about who you're sending in for fights, sometimes it's better to abandon a quest at the start so your best fighters have stress and maladies removed for an important quest. The only way to truly fail in this game is to have a party wipe, lose a battle so you can win the war.
A game where you have to think before dungeon diving and can still be punished horrifically for something out of your control, how can this be enjoyable?
Well, like chess you have to think several moves ahead. You're sending your perfect team on a medium quest. This means you'll need to map out provisions for where you're headed. Shovels so you aren't moving obstacles by hand, bandages if no one can heal bleeds, etc.
Where Dark Souls was unforgiving and difficult, you could beat it by just slamming your head into it over and over again. Darkest Dungeon? If you aren't thinking ahead and in the moment, you won't be able to accomplish anything.
So if you're trying to have a perfect run on your very first playthrough, I've got some bad news. The game is designed so you expect failure. You have to monitor your teams stress, be aware of the attacks of the enemy, and be well aware of your own teams abilities.
Didn't know that enemy could push your team back or pull them forward and now your healer is front line and you have to waste the full team heal doing a switch because you didn't put a move resist trinket on her? Well, that's a lesson learned, now your team has to pay for it.

This game is 20% skill, and 80% luck. If you make the perfect team, you should still expect to lose them all in one fight. For the first hour i was having fun then RNG reared it's head. Sitting at 3rd light level, i got surprised 4 fights in a row, despite the fact that it was supposed to have a low chance. So, my party shuffles, and suddenly i have to waste 2 rounds of my biggest damage dealers turns moving him, and then he gets pushed to the back right away. So i was stuck with 3 people, 2 of which couldn't fight from the front, but of course, they got placed there. Try to move them, they get pulled, so and so on, and i lost my 4 strongest.
So, i move on to my weaker members.
A party should have a healer, a frontliner and the rest is your choice. I thought maybe having two healers and a tank and a damage dealer would make my team last, by the third room, 2 had died of heart attacks, because i had to fight comps that only had stuns and madness effects, and of the 10 or so people i've had go mad, literally one didn't get the debuff, meaning i kept getting crippled due to how each fight turned out.
I have beaten so many hard games, Super Meat Boy and Dark Souls to name a couple. But the difference here is the same problem so many Rogue-Likes have. RNG decides your run, not your skill. Now, for most Rogue-likes, such as Binding of Isaac, or Rogue Legacy, you invest time in the game and even if you die, you make progress.
This is a game where you can spend 50 hours on a team, and have all of it wasted in 1 hour, you get killed because no one can make death door saves, or they have heart attacks, or you don't find a single torch, or you retreat, and lose money, and have to do it again and again, meaning you have no money and then, you restart, hoping your next 50 hour run isn't killed by a terrible layout or random things out of your control.
I love hard games, i don't like unfair games.
Last note: I adore the art style of this game, and i love the voice actor, the music is middle of the road for me, but i do not love the un-skippable attack animations.

I give the game a reluctant recommendation because I don't think it's very good right now, but could be with some serious patching.
In a lot of ways the game has improved upon it's predecessor, especially in the strategic elements.  There's a little more busy work so that you're not just waiting around between missions.
Squad customization is really nice.  You can create troops from the main menu, that can then be implimented into the game later.  Or if you have a trooper that you end up really like, you can alternatively export them and use them in later playthroughs.  You can create back stories, tweak their personalities, and give them some character.  It's all cosmetic, but it's really a huge boost to one of the things that's been most appealing about the franchise, so I consider that a huge plus.  If you're really into that sort of thing there's enough here to keep you busy for awhile.  And who knows what modders will be adding to that.
The tactical game is improved, but in many ways unchanged from XCOM: EU.  Like many, the biggest gripe I have is with the frequency of timed missions, and how short they are.  I've always played X-Com games at a fairly slow pace, and by comparrison this game feels like it's always in a rush (this applies to the strategic side as well).
This actually hampers one of the big changes with the tactical game and that's the ability to start out in stealth and set up ambushes.  You really don't get many turns to do this, which kind of defeats the purpose of an ambush.  Thus, while it does factor in to how you start an engagement, it really feels like a gimmick because you're almost better off just going in guns blazing.  I don't mind the fact that the game puts you "on the clock".  I just don't like the frequency, and how short that clock is.  I don't have A.D.H.D.  I like to take my time.  An option to tweak the length of these timed missions would have made a world of difference.
While the game was made with the PC in mind, it still feels like it was designed to be played on a console.  Considering this reboot franchise has almost 20 years of tech improvements over the original franchise, it's a shame that the game is still so... light.
I was really hoping there would be more strategic enhancements to make you feel like you're really fighting a revolution across the entire planet.  The game isn't bad as it is.  I just felt like they could have done a whole lot more without having to deal with the limitations of a console's interface and controls.
Thus, like EU, it's a good X-Com game, but it still falls short of what it could really be.
And of course there's the performance issues.  These will likely be resolved, but it does seem like a pretty glaring problem.

What a game!
i have at the moment played this game for 27 hours, after it released so i can't say judge it in comparison to it's early access days. BUT what i can do, is tell you my opinion about it in it's release state!
To start of with, i did not have high expectations about this game, i actually didn't know very much about it at all. i simply saw a guy on
play it for 10 minutes, and decided i'd try it out.
Now a little background on me; i'm not a hardcore gamer by any means, but i do enjoy a nice story driven game like Assassin's Creed, Fallout, The Witcher and so on, and with the odd game here and there outside of the rpg genre (Civilization 5 being the most beloved game outside of rpgs).
So i don't normally buy indie games, nor do i care much for them as they're normally lacking in some  way, or just down right sucks (Early Access in general).
Darkest Dungeon however, blew my mind. the artwork, the soundtrack, the gameplay. everything seemingly joins together and makes a perfect game!
Whenever you play, you feel immersed, you care for your heroes and you struggle with every decision. i find myself retreating more often than not, to spare one or more of my heroes from death, instead paying for whatever treatment they need. this in turn have caused money trouble for me, slowing down the rest of my heroes not affected.
You get so much into this game, for better or worse, that you start squirming in your seat whenever a hero is on the brink of death, or get insanely angry at a seconds notice if your hero misses a hit that would've ended a fight, instead causing you to have to spend thousands of your hard earned gold on treatment.
The whole game revolves around being punishing. you heroes will die, whether you like it or not. you will struggle with money. you will have negative stats on your heroes because of negative quirks. you will get destroyed by the rng in the game. but the most important part is that all of this is fun!
If you're looking for a challenging turn based game, that focuses on screwing you over, yet feeling fun this is definitely a game to try!
