I give the game a reluctant recommendation because I don't think it's very good right now, but could be with some serious patching.
In a lot of ways the game has improved upon it's predecessor, especially in the strategic elements.  There's a little more busy work so that you're not just waiting around between missions.
Squad customization is really nice.  You can create troops from the main menu, that can then be implimented into the game later.  Or if you have a trooper that you end up really like, you can alternatively export them and use them in later playthroughs.  You can create back stories, tweak their personalities, and give them some character.  It's all cosmetic, but it's really a huge boost to one of the things that's been most appealing about the franchise, so I consider that a huge plus.  If you're really into that sort of thing there's enough here to keep you busy for awhile.  And who knows what modders will be adding to that.
The tactical game is improved, but in many ways unchanged from XCOM: EU.  Like many, the biggest gripe I have is with the frequency of timed missions, and how short they are.  I've always played X-Com games at a fairly slow pace, and by comparrison this game feels like it's always in a rush (this applies to the strategic side as well).
This actually hampers one of the big changes with the tactical game and that's the ability to start out in stealth and set up ambushes.  You really don't get many turns to do this, which kind of defeats the purpose of an ambush.  Thus, while it does factor in to how you start an engagement, it really feels like a gimmick because you're almost better off just going in guns blazing.  I don't mind the fact that the game puts you "on the clock".  I just don't like the frequency, and how short that clock is.  I don't have A.D.H.D.  I like to take my time.  An option to tweak the length of these timed missions would have made a world of difference.
While the game was made with the PC in mind, it still feels like it was designed to be played on a console.  Considering this reboot franchise has almost 20 years of tech improvements over the original franchise, it's a shame that the game is still so... light.
I was really hoping there would be more strategic enhancements to make you feel like you're really fighting a revolution across the entire planet.  The game isn't bad as it is.  I just felt like they could have done a whole lot more without having to deal with the limitations of a console's interface and controls.
Thus, like EU, it's a good X-Com game, but it still falls short of what it could really be.
And of course there's the performance issues.  These will likely be resolved, but it does seem like a pretty glaring problem.

Starbound is quite the game so far. At first glance, it may seem very Terraria-like, and I guess you could say it is. But in this, I found the exploration and building part of the game to be much better. Since there are gajillions of planets to go to, it's very hard to get bored of it. The generation between planets is quite different. Plus, there are many dungeons in planets(but they're a bit similar).
For the building part, there's just more stuff. There are TONS of decorative items that you can find in structures, or ones you can craft. The buildings you find have different themes(medieval, futuristic, plant-like, etc), so you can build pretty much whatever you want. You can use pretty much all tiles as background blocks, too.
The combat is pretty great, too. Since the weapons are procedurally generated also, they all look different, do different damage, have different elements, and different attack rates. There are also different kinds of guns like pistols, machine guns, sniper rifles, and shotguns. Actual fighting does feel a bit floaty, though.
Monsters are also procedurally generated, so there aren't names for them. You'll have to come up with them on your own. They all use different kinds of moves like body slamming you, changing your gravity, and even blowing fire at you! They look quite varied, too.
The future is looking even brighter. Soon, there will be a storyline to follow, more modding features(there are already a ton), and a new race. There will be much more patches coming out, the beta is only at phase one as of now. So, definitely buy this game!

Video review for people that prefer the format:
(This is a first impressions look at the game, i have not completed it yet)
Darkest Dungeon kicks so much♥♥♥♥♥ It's a turn-based, dark RPG with a lot of depth. One thing I absolutely love about this game is that despite being a complex RPG, it's relatively easy to get into and it doesn't bombard you with popups and tutorials. You do have 1 quick tutorialish area at the beginning which tells you the basics. When something is about to happen in the game that is a key mechanic, the game gives a window with a brief explanation of how it works. it doesn't give you a 5 paragraphic essay that you have to read through with tons of examples you don't need. It does a good job of explaining these things within a paragraph or two, and that's great because this game is HARD. However, it's also fair for the most part.
What makes this game special compared to most turn-based RPGs is how placement works. Most games might have a few usable abilities like a cleave that will affect a few people in the front, an aoe that affects everyone and that's usually it. Darkest Dungeon takes a leap forward with mechanics such as switching, large enemy types and corpses. Certain characters work best at certain positions and while it would be nice to see enemy unit move tables, it feel it would make the game much easier but still add depth. Certain abilities used by your characters can only be used while that character is at a certain position (far left, left, right, far right) and those abilities can sometimes only be used on enemies in certain positions (far left, left, right, etc). The game does a great job of telling you where characters would prefer to fight. These are always shown in the character menus which you can view by clicking on portraits or hitting the 'C' key when a portrait is highlighted. The switching mechanic also plays into this. You can switch the placements of characters in and otuside of battle, but in battle costs a character turn. Attacks can also switch people around (both on your side and on the enemy team's side). This adds a new level of depth, you could plow your way from the front to the back but there could be a annoying stress-damage ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the back who might be super week to a sword attack your knight might use because it's good again'st unhoy enemies.
That's another thing I should mention. There are a lot of modifiers in this game. From the debufs you get from playing (like getting stressed) to all your character abiltiies with various mods that can cause conditions like bleeding or blight. There are so many variables and team compositions to play around with adding so much customization for how you move out your party. God, we haven't even talked about the item system or the weapon/armor/spell upgrade system. THERE IS SO MUCH IN THIS GAME TO TALK ABOUT!
Animation, sound and art quality are outstanding. This game sucks you in to its dark and depressing world hard. Every completion of a dungeon feels stressful, as it should as stress is the main mechanic of the game. Stress can afflict debuffs to your party or even buffs at rare times. Your companions are not only battling monsters but also battling thier own psyche. You can relieve stress in the town but you have to still do dungeons if you want their stress to go down. They only lose stress when they are treated for a full in-game week, so it's a desperate struggle where you sometimes have to throw green-as-grass new characters at high level dungeons. Thankfully, new recruits are free and you can upgrade your roster. THAT'S ANOTHER THING, SO MUCH HNGGGGGG. You can upgrade buildings in town (treating more characters at a time in one area, better upgrades, etc) and you are still not even safe in towns. Stuff can happen when you are trying to relieve stress. Sending one of your guys off to gamble to relieve the pain of losing a comrad? Well he gambled away a rare item GG.
Overall, this is a great value at 20USD. You are totally getting your moneys work. If games stress you out easily, stay clear because you will die of a heart attack faster than your characters will.
If you are the type of person that needs a score, I'd give the game a 9/10. Extra information in my video review.

I am changing my review to a positive as I have tweaked the settings and been able to play the game for over 4 hours today without any crashes.  The settings I'm using  are:
Borderless window (no idea why this makes a difference but it does!)
V-sync OFF
FXAA
Tile AO
Shadows = Static Only
Shadow Quality = High
Texture Detail = High
Texture Filtering = Aniso x 8
Depth of Field = Simple
Draw Distance = Medium
Turned the following OFF: Dirty Lens, Subsurface Scattering, Screen Space Reflections
The settings I now have are, for me, very acceptable as the game still looks great and now plays very smoothly.  In case anyone is having similar issues I'll leave my original issues at the bottom of the review.
Regarding the game itself, now that I have been able to play it without performance issues distracting me, I think it is fantastic - a step up in almost every way from the previous game.  They've made a lot of quality of life changes that have removed some of the grind (such as weapons manufacturing).  The game is difficult and doesn't hesitate to punish you for mistakes, but it's a huge amount of fun.  There are still some graphical glitches in the action shots (soldiers shooting through walls etc) but they don't detract, for me.
At present I'd say it's a fantastic addition to the XCOM series.  I perhaps rate Xenonauts higher, but this may change!
My original performance issues follow.
--------------------
My pc has crashed on multiple occasions.
It always seems to happen during a transmission sequence, i.e. the shots of the skyranger taking off or landing (missions seem to run perfectly - in terms of performance if not my tactics!).
At first I was getting a message saying 'Your computer is running out of memory' when I clicked on 'begin mission'.  As my pc only just makes the recommended spec I have turned off v-sync, anti-aliasing, ambient occlusion, and turned draw distance to 'low' and will continue to play to see if this makes a difference (it crashed with these settings when I tried to exit the game today, which was an improvement, I suppose!).
What I have managed to play of the game I have enjoyed but I would recommend avoiding this frustration and waiting until it is properly optimised.  The perils of pre-ordering . . .

XCOM 2 is a great accessor to XCOM:EU and XCOM:EW. It keeps the core gameplay intact by rewarding strategic planning and patience. However, some design choice happens to damage how this core gameplay carries out.
My biggest concern is the time-limited missions. In these missions, you are forced to engage the enermies at a much faster and less thoughtfull way. This often forces you to engage enermies that you are prepared for or being purnished for being forced to be aggressive. I feel like there should be an way to increase the turn limit(like hacking a terminal or some base research).
Another thing that I really want to criticize is the long time it takes to complete any scan or fly from place to place. Does it really need to take 3 days to pick up the supply drop? I don't believe so. Also, with the new "mobile base" concept, it takes way too much time on the road between missions, especially after you unlocked a few more regions and events show up everywhere.
Also, there are some wierd bugs and glitches(mostly visual ones, like floating corpses, enermy don't drop from ceiling).
TL;DR: XCOM2 is a great game. It's fun and challenging. In addition, the current problems are easy to fix with a few mods or patches from Firaxis.

I haven't finish it yet but I can already tell that it's worth every penny!
XCOM 2 is superior to XCOM. Might even be better than the classic. It would be, but it's missing something. It's missing some sort of liquid. Terror from the Deep comes to mind.
They finally added depth to the game, randomized missions, geoscape, looting, customization and a lot of RNG. I love it!
Combat is pretty much the only thing that's similar to XCOM. But it wasn't broken in the first place, it worked really well! Glad they didn't change it. Now you have more skills and perks to use though.
The building mechanic feels pretty similar to the first game too, except in this game it doesn't cost you to excavate rooms, the rooms actually give you resources so you always profit!
The geoscape is great! You start out at a random location on the map and you can fly around with your portable base. Picking up random resource events and mission events.
You'll always be fighting against the clock because the aliens don't just fly around trolling you with UFOs, they actually play the same way you do. Which is hella cool!
Where is that CO-OP mode? Campaign PVP? I wish Firaxis were bold enough to do this.
The game does have its flaws. Right now it's not really optimized, for me it's playable, some missions are even smooth but for others, it's not. I can suggest lowering shadows and disabling Ambient conclusion.
Also during combat you can encounter quite a few bugs. Melee and shots going through walls, animations stop working, some skills bugging out, grenades not being thrown if standing too close to a wall.
Customization is lacking a bit in my opinion. I was expecting more, but it's still better than any other XCOM. Also timed missions, in the future please don't! I recommend getting the "TimerTweaks" mod for less stressful situations. RNG can really screw you over otherwise.
Firaxis was also kind enough to release modding tools in which you can literally change anything in the game. No one knows what the future holds for this game but I can clearly say it will be fudging amazing!
Anyway, it's still playable and very enjoyable! Should you buy it? Only if you're a fan of the original or XCOM. Then yes, it's a MUST BUY! Otherwise check out youtube or twitch and then decide.

As far as I have played I have not noticed anything missing and put behind a paywall. Mounts are buyable with real money but are not faster than the other mounts which you can buy with In-game money (Cubits).

You can pick-up, craft and find all types of loot, mounts, wing sets, etc.
Trove is a fun game, with different zones for different characer levels, all accessible through the game's main Hub.
You can also swap between two different classes, but if you want to unlock any other, you will have to buy them.
You can build your very own lot (Cornerstone) in which you are free to build in a 16x16 area. You Cornerstone can be placed on any lot you find, and will always stay the same unless you modify it in any way. If you want a more open area with more room to build and the ability to build with friends, you can create a Club. This Club will allow you and other members to teleport to an area secluded from anyone that is not in your Club. Here you can even give parties which are accessible by anyone that teleports to your Club World from the Hub.
All in all, from my limited amount of play time, I can say that this game is definitely fun to play. It's fairly repetitive but allows you to do many things and take on many professions. If you don't mind spending some of your time, I can recommend this game to you. You don't even have to pay a cent for it.

I just want to make a short list of good and bad things in XCOM 2. So here it is:
GOOD
* There's always something to do, whether it's an operation or simple supplies gathering. No more boring weeks with nothing on the hologlobe
* Nice visuals and cut-scenes. It was a strong point of Enemy Unknown/Within and they don't disappoint in this area.
* Variety of mission types. No more "kill all the enemies to complete objective". Now you have to do something more than that
* Character pool and customizations. It was always about soldiers and I'm glad they improved those options.
* Weapon mods
* Interesting and good-looking enemies
* More random maps with some interactive features (aiming at explosive things, soldiers appearing as WANTED on holo-ads)
* Badass Bradford
* More 'progression' objectives
* Very nice soundtrack
BAD
* Poor optimization, graphic glitches, freezes, long loading screens etc.
* Avatar progresses too fast, without good planning you'll end up lagging behind
* Too big reliance on explosives. You'll end up grabbing more Frag Grenades than any other items, despite wide selection of them
* Poor chemistry between Tygan & Shen. Remember Vahlen and Shen senior? It's not even close to those funny taunts and conversations.
* No more individual weapon creation. Now you grab one and it's available for all your soldiers.
* Still 3 tiers of weaponry/armours. It may appeal to vanilla XCOM players but after Long War, it's a downgrade.
* Concealment mechanics could be improved (e.g. you re-enter the concealment after few turns without enemy in range)
* Timed missions force you to go straight to the point, with enemies always on your path. You lose the advantage of the map design, since you can't wander around.
OVERALL:
Strongly recommended despite minor flaws. Some future patches will probably fix most issues, and mods will improve the gameplay even further.

Saying this game is like a side-scrolling Dark Souls is inaccurate, because this game is much harder. Darkest Dungeon is an old school turn based, party combat strategy RPG. The plot isn't too deep, but is enough to keep it going. A search for mystical power underneath your family's house opened a portal that unleashed monsters upon the surrounding areas, so now it's your job to recruit heroes and send them out to complete various missions throughout the area. Now, make no mistake, your heroes will die. A lot. So really, don't get too attached to any of them. Now, this game is a dark, gory, brutal, and balls-grindingly hard journey and is not for the faint of heart. Examples of this are illustrated in the stress mechanic and the art style. The art style is a beautiful hand-drawn style, highlighting the shadows, scars, blood, and insanity on people's faces to give off a very grim, dark, and sinister look to represent the game's themes. The other highlight is the stress factor. This game's big selling point is realisitcally showing off how fantasy heroes are regular people too, and they have their quirks and flaws, as well as how dungeon crawling and fighting skeletons, demons, and other unspeakable horrors would affect a person's sanity. As characters are injured and exposed to certain events, their stress bar fills, resulting in either an "affliction", causing them to gain personality traits that will hinder your party's effectiveness, or even raise the stress of other characters, or a "virtue", a buff that allows the hero to lower their stress and the stress of other party members, or even randomly heal themselves. The heroes themselves consist of a vareity of classes. They include but aren't limited to: The Vestral, which acts as the healer, the Plauge Doctor, a DOT/Debuff character, the Leper, the game's tank, and the rouge-esque highwayman. Every character also comes with their own "quirks", traits that can alter combat stats, damage resistances, susceptibility to stress, and even restrictions on how to relieve the character's stress. The combat is turn based, with party positioning a strategic choice, as characters must stand in certain positions to be fully effective, causing you to sometimes sacrifice certain character's ablilties because they can't stand in the right slot, as you need that slot for another character to be effective. Some enemies will throw this positioning off, forcing you to spend turns righting the order instead of attacking.
The only two cons I can think of consist of an audio problem and an annoyance in gameplay. In cutscenes, the audio will cut in and out at random, causing me to skip most of them altogether. The other is the ease in which you can land in a "mosquito bite" spiral. You'll lose gold for failing an expedition, which means you won't have enough to outfit another expedition, whch means you'll fail, causing you to lose more gold, leading to a game-wrecking and vicious downward spiral that renders the game almost unplayable.
An overall expertly crafted RPG with unique mechanics, great atmosphere and a new twist on dungeon crawling.

A fantastic game, but not a good fallout game...
This was the first fallout game I every played, and for that reason I found it incredibly enjoyable. As someone who had never played anything like this before it really was great. Since then I have played New Vegas and Fallout 3 and I can definitly see why people who have been in touch with the serious would dislike it so much. Fallout 4 and the rest in the series are just totally different games.
By far the biggest problem with this game is the lack of choices. It's either yes or no to eveything. No matter who you side with everything is going to stay the same outside of the factions themselves. You cannot shape a faction to be a certain way, either they are completely destroyed or stay excactly the way they are. In New Vegas there's tons of sub-factions that you can convince to side with different major factions, which adds a ton of variation in the fallout world. Alas, in Fallout 4, no matter who you side with, the future for the public stays generally the same, all things considered.
Among other problems they're pushing this ancient game engine to it's limit, meaning the game is poorly optimized and can be unstable at times. And, of course, this greatly limits graphic capabilities. Settlements are a good concept but have been poorly executed. The average user will find there is no fun nor real purpose in setting up supply lines. The building system is tedious and buggy as well, turning me and others off even further. And to set up shops in your settlements takes a very large amount of caps (which I have found to be much harder to collect in fallout 4) AND very singifcant investment into charisma, meaning just to do any of this you will need to shape your character to be a certain way.
And, let's not forget Preston Garvey and the Minutemen, the most un-fun and unrewording faction to ever be in a fallout game.
Considering all that, this is still a VERY fun game by itself, but when directly compared to other fallout games it is seriously lacking in some areas. There are major improvements mind you, animations are smooth as butter along with combat. Companions have greatly improved in function, quantity, and quality as well. I'm not sure if I would have been able to give this a positive review if I was already into fallout and was expecting another fallout game... but I didn't, this was my first fallout, and for that reason I was able to find it an extremely enjoyable experience.
TL;DR - Will find enjoyable if it's your first fallout, otherwise that might not be the case

Spiral knights is an MMO-dungeon crawler, unlike most MMO's that I play, This game suggests you play public games (but I just found the option that lets me solo! Thank you for letting me play my own way Spiral Knights). Additionally it automatically activates your microphone (I found out to my dismay on my second run, after I had been idly chatting with a friend on skype… and hearing an echo of my voice.)
From the state of the game, you get to customize your Spiral Knight, change his/her helmet make adjustments to the color, and then maybe throw on a few accessories. Once you’re finished you perform various tasks around camp to get things running again.
You play the game like a dungeon crawler, you can also choose between three different control configurations. I chose to use the keyboard and mouse; the controls seem very straightforward and natural to me. You can switch between different weapons once you buy them later in the game; you start the game out with a pistol and a sword. No complaint I see no need for any other weapons.
Hopefully I don’t need to spell it out more about how the combat works, you shoot from far away with the pistol, you hit them with your sword in melee range, you block stuff with your shield, and you also have bombs that you can drop. You can also unlock, buy, and make new weapons and armor.
At rank 3 you start to be informed about the different types of gear you can wear. Since it’s an MMO, I assume this will play a larger role in the game further on. At the time that I am writing this review, I reached Shadow gear (which the game so kindly provided for me as I continued down the main story line. As long as the game doesn’t force me to spend real money, I’m okay with the gear based structure for this game.
A majority of the achievements require collection of X amount of gear. There are a lot of hidden achievements that I will need to research once I get to be a higher level. Although I suspect that the game will eventually force me to team up with other players… and then let the ugly pugging commence. (Sorry, for those who don’t know: I really hate playing with people I don’t know.)
Basically, my impression is that the achievements reflect the amount of time you’ve spent playing the game. I was about a third of my way through the story, and I had about a third of the achievements in the game.
Ah ha! This game is a Free to play! You have no real excuse for not trying it at least once. Since the game can be soloed (at least to where I’m at, one third complete) I think you can get a decent amount of entertainment out of the game, if you like dungeon crawlers, and a really simple easy game to pick up.

There really isn’t much reason to say “don’t get this game” especially since it’s free. I keep waiting for the point in the game where it says “HA! To be continued! Now pay us money just like you did the Arcade machine when you were little!” Nothing like that yet, so regardless, I feel I’ve gotten a fair amount of entertainment out of a game I didn’t buy.
No complaints, I’m enjoying the game still. (but I will always grind before I ever spend real money inside a game of any kind.)

Everyone says Darkest Dungeon is an RPG based on luck. I have to agree that Darkest Dungeon is an luck based RPG, but the real challenge is dealing with this luck mechanic. Knowing when to take risks, how to minimize those risks and how to deal with bad choises is the greatest ability the player will learn from this game. Running around, making idiotic moves and blaming on luck will not help you.
This game is hard, really hard. Sometimes you'll have to reset your campaign, because you don't have money. Sometimes your hero will take a crit to the face and die shortly after. Sometimes you will have to backtrack through a whole dungeon, because you missed an item. Dealing with those challenges and preparing for them is amazing, it gives me chills everytime I screw things over. But the reward is as big as the challenge, since the game is hard and most of the players rage quit from it. Knowing you are the 10% who can win even at the face of death is rewarding.
The battle system is simple, but complex enough to reward smart players and to punish bad ones. The money management is great mechanic. Sometimes you'll have to save money to buy supplies for a dungeon. Sometimes you'll have to stress heal your units. The relic system is a great way to incentivise exploring harder and different dungeons for some upgrades at the town.
The game is great at its current state and I would love to see what Red Hook is planning for the future of Darkest Dungeon.

I gotta say it is the first time I'm making a "that huge" review of a game, but this game is really worth doing it.
I bought it on the first day of release, after watching a few reviews, I really hoped that all of that was said wasn't that frustrating, because the game really seemed to be unique, well-designed and graphicaly beautiful.
I gotta say that my first impression were excellent, there was absolutely nothing that really dissapointed me. Every dungeons, classes, buildings gave me a great feeling of much different things to do and try, and the first ten hours (because I like to take my time) were the funniest hours I've spent on a game since a few years.
Every characters (or class) feel unique, they all have their quality and flaws, they have damage skills or debuff or DoT or even heal/protect skills, they have some kind of specialities (like multi-targeting or crit or DoT...) and even some great art. Every building have a good impact on the game and makes you feel "doing what you are doing for a reason".
There's also Torch management, Inventory objects and stress management, etc... I mean there's a lot of great thought features that will make you be really, REALLY happy at the beginning.
Yeah everything was fine, fun, balanced, and so much more, until I reached the level 5 part of the game (The maximum level is 6 by the way).
Then monsters began to be completely unfair, most of them are going from 10HP 0% Protection, 10 dodge and 6-10 damage, to 26-50HP, 35% Protection 36 Dodge, and a ridiculous increase of damage (some hits for 30 crit even with 25% damage reduction, no jokes). You might think it's fair if you didn't buy the game yet because you can upgrade your heroes, but the main problem comes from the fact that if you upgrade TO MAXIMUM your characters, overall they'll win 5 damage/10 accuracy (depends of the class though), 10-20HP and 10 dodge, and they still have a completely unbalanced factor of damage/heal (like going from 5-8 damage to 7-14).
What that means for real is that THE ONLY THING THAT REALLY MATTERS IS HOW LUCKY YOU ARE. Melee characters can't hit anymore and will miss 40% of their attacks even with a huge accuracy boost, ranged character will deal the same amount of damage to opponent than they previously were on level 1 because of the insane protection boost on monsters and will even miss 1/3 of their attacks, heals will go from 4-6 to 6-10 even fully upgraded which CAN'T follow the damage upgrade of your ennemies. You feel like being completely torn apart every fight, and struggle to make your characters survive even for a single turn. The stress management becomes impossible to handle, as on 100 stress most of your characters will begin to pass their turn, wound themselves, disagree to get healed or use the wrong skill, and you have to surrender most of the dungeons after 4 rooms because even 1 firecamp break wasn't enough to make them feel better, if you didn't lose someone already.
Some classes will survive and "do" some things, but 60% of the other class (there's 15 on the game) will struggle so much that it's just impossible to use them. You'll have to spend half the gold you hardly grinded to treat stress and some disease that are impossible to avoid, which gives the game a more frustrating than hard feeling, since all your hard earned money will be used to repair the damages, instead of going further.
After 40 hours of gameplay, I never tried the level 6 dungeon of the game and the only level 5 dungeons I made were short ones. There's a terrible grinding of gold to do because of how much you'll need to spend after every dungeon.
I first thought that I was just bad, or making bad decisions, but after trying so much builds, classes, and reading a lot of people reviews, it's just sad to say, but the game isn't fun on the endgame.
Losing character is a point of the game (as the developpers said), but if you lose them because it's really hard, or you took a critical strike, or your heal get stunned on the wrong turn, it's pretty funny actually, it happens, it's a part of the Roleplay, etc..., you'll have to be more careful or change your trinkets to decrease the odds of death happening next time.
But here, it's just completely luck based, and you feel like you got absolutely no chances of winning and all the odds are against you. The only hope you have is to land the critical hit of your live that you needed, which means that 1/18 of the time it'll be an okay fight only because of luck, none of your management has a real impact.
Don't get me wrong, I got no regrets for buying this game, and it is still terribly fun on the early part, but there's a huge difference (as everybody said) between "The games involves dying because it is hard" and pure frustration.
I still have to give a huge shout out to the developpers, who did overall an absolutely beautiful and enjoyable game, one that we were waiting for a long time, one that is beating most of the other games out there and even big ones. But I hope that the future updates will give a brighter future to the game (and that unfair points will change to hard points), as more and more players are reviewing this game badly because of the sames problems over and over again.
EDIT : For all those who says "You need to watch a playthrough on internet etc..." well if the point of the game is to take the same characters as an internet guy and do the exact same thing (because other things don't work as intended), it completely breaks all the DnD, discovery, experiment point of the game, which is to me the best point of all. I took the Vestal for healing because it is more constant even if it heals less than the occulist, but everybody told to me "Naah don't take the vestal, just take the occulist"
Alright, but then, I'd rather play Hearthstone and google the most viable deck for infinite "I'm doing the same thing over and over again", like everybody. This is not why I bought this game for.

Saying this game is like a side-scrolling Dark Souls is inaccurate, because this game is much harder. Darkest Dungeon is an old school turn based, party combat strategy RPG. The plot isn't too deep, but is enough to keep it going. A search for mystical power underneath your family's house opened a portal that unleashed monsters upon the surrounding areas, so now it's your job to recruit heroes and send them out to complete various missions throughout the area. Now, make no mistake, your heroes will die. A lot. So really, don't get too attached to any of them. Now, this game is a dark, gory, brutal, and balls-grindingly hard journey and is not for the faint of heart. Examples of this are illustrated in the stress mechanic and the art style. The art style is a beautiful hand-drawn style, highlighting the shadows, scars, blood, and insanity on people's faces to give off a very grim, dark, and sinister look to represent the game's themes. The other highlight is the stress factor. This game's big selling point is realisitcally showing off how fantasy heroes are regular people too, and they have their quirks and flaws, as well as how dungeon crawling and fighting skeletons, demons, and other unspeakable horrors would affect a person's sanity. As characters are injured and exposed to certain events, their stress bar fills, resulting in either an "affliction", causing them to gain personality traits that will hinder your party's effectiveness, or even raise the stress of other characters, or a "virtue", a buff that allows the hero to lower their stress and the stress of other party members, or even randomly heal themselves. The heroes themselves consist of a vareity of classes. They include but aren't limited to: The Vestral, which acts as the healer, the Plauge Doctor, a DOT/Debuff character, the Leper, the game's tank, and the rouge-esque highwayman. Every character also comes with their own "quirks", traits that can alter combat stats, damage resistances, susceptibility to stress, and even restrictions on how to relieve the character's stress. The combat is turn based, with party positioning a strategic choice, as characters must stand in certain positions to be fully effective, causing you to sometimes sacrifice certain character's ablilties because they can't stand in the right slot, as you need that slot for another character to be effective. Some enemies will throw this positioning off, forcing you to spend turns righting the order instead of attacking.
The only two cons I can think of consist of an audio problem and an annoyance in gameplay. In cutscenes, the audio will cut in and out at random, causing me to skip most of them altogether. The other is the ease in which you can land in a "mosquito bite" spiral. You'll lose gold for failing an expedition, which means you won't have enough to outfit another expedition, whch means you'll fail, causing you to lose more gold, leading to a game-wrecking and vicious downward spiral that renders the game almost unplayable.
An overall expertly crafted RPG with unique mechanics, great atmosphere and a new twist on dungeon crawling.

But in all seriousness, don't listen to all of the negative reviews you find here that are written by people who have no idea how the mechanics of the game work.  Sure, the game has RNG in it, but that is not the focal point of this game.  There can be points where death is inevitable and no amount of planning could have prepared for it, but that's what makes the game so exciting to play.  Sometimes you have no idea what to expect and other times you can breeze through a dungeon with no problems.  Choosing a group of people who work well with each other (can combo off of each other's abilities) and choosing skills that work best in the specific area you are in can define how the run goes for you.  Almost all deaths in this game are preventable as long as you actually THINK about what you are doing and don't let random crits completely turn you off of the game; it's the entire point of the game.  You are supposed to feel frustrated and stressed ALONG with your in-game party.  My first playthrough of the game took me over 100 hours and 200 in-game weeks, or dungeon quests.  I lost THIRTY-THREE of my heroes.  But the game tells you well in advance that death is supposed to happen.  I didn't know well enough how the game worked.  But my second playthrough of the game took me under half the time my previous playthrough took and I only lost THREE people.  So all of these people in these reviews saying the entire game is a coin-flip are full of♥♥♥♥♥♥  It's clear they didn't even make an attempt to try to learn and read the mechanics of the game and instead spent their entire playthrough complaining about things they could have easily prevented by either thinking about their actions or retreating when necessary.  Give this game an honest chance, because it's clear that so much heart went into it-from the construction of the music, the sound design, and Wayne Jude's incredible narration, to the artwork of the areas, characters, and enemies.  I highly recommend it, and I'm sure the upcoming DLC, The Crimson Court, will show just as much thought, care, and polish as the rest of the game.

Fallout 4 isn't a bad game.
It is also not a good game.
During the summer sale (in the UK) the game is only £9.99 which is an amazing deal, but I wouldn't buy it for anymore.
Pros:
Fallout 4 features one of the best open worlds in any open world game I have played, I've spent many hours exploring the ruins of Boston and the world just feels more alive than both Fallout 3 and New Vegas.
Despite what many people have said, I find the graphics as well as the overall art design to be both visually pleasing and to contain a certain charm that only this game (and the original Fallouts) can provide.
Power armor customization is one of this games best features.
The engine from Fallout 3 and New Vegas has been replaced with the Creation Engine that was previously used in Skyrim. This allows for the complete revamp of the combat system, gone are the days of emptying your gun into some guys face only for him to remain unscathed. For the first time in a modern Fallout game, I know that when I shoot someone they die!
For me, I became less dependent on V.A.T.S. which was a nice change.
The UI and HUD have been improved drastically from previous titles in the franchise. The PipBoy interface has cleaned up and simplified (which isn't always a bad thing) I can now look at the map on my PipBoy and see/understand things a lot easier.
I'm not going to get into it too much but the character creation from previous Fallout games has been replaced with a Sims 4 like sculpt/modeling system.
Neutral:
The base building aspect of the game feels lacking in depth and doesn't feel as good as it could have been.
An unnamed faction (The Minutemen) can be annoying and give out repetitive quests sometimes.
The gun customization is nice but is easy to ignore.
Cons:
Fallout 4 tries to focus around something an autistic 6 year old would call a "story"

On Facebook, and bear with me on this, there is a game called Avengers Alliance.  It's a Marvel Comics game where you assemble a team of Marvel characters, choose a mission to send them on, then engage in turn-based combat against a series of enemies until you reach the boss.  Defeating that boss progresses you to the next missions, and gives you experience that levels up your characters.  Despite being a Facebook game, it was one of my favorite games for a long time.  I dropped some real money on that game.
So what does that have to do with Darkest Dungeon?  Well, this game takes that same concept of building a party and advancing through increasingly difficult missions, and marries that to a Lovecraft theme.  As you progress through the dungeons in this game, you have the same tough decisions on how to deal with certain enemies, the benefits of various party compositions, and who you choose to level up.  With that, though, you also have the nail-biting events that can throw all your plans into disarray or lead your party to a miraculous victory.  I love it.
The graphics are a comic art aesthetic, and as you might expect all of the colors are dark and suitably gothic.  The sound effects are evocative of the theme, and the music is chilling at times.  One thing stands above all else when I think of this game, though, and that's the narration by Wayne June.  This is a man who has narrated countless Lovecraft audiobooks, and there's no other word to describe his effect on the game other than perfection.
If you do not like an element of random chance, avoid this game.  If you do not appreciate the fact that you will suffer setbacks despite your best efforts, avoid this game.  If you do not enjoy gothic lovecraftian themes, avoid this game.  If you like watching the heroes that you've recruited slowly succumb to the insanity of your ancestral home, eventually meeting a grotesque end at the hands (or tentacles) of ancient horrors, then embrace the Darkest Dungeon.

I'm not gonna deny, I am a massive fan of this game. Come to think of it, it would certainly be in my top 15 games of all time. But, before I sing this game any praises, I want to share my thoughts on some criticisms people bring up when talking about Darkest Dungeon and how I feel about gameplay in general. This is going to be a long one, but I just feel the need to talk about this in detail.
Many people like to compare Darkest Dungeon to
. And I think it is fair to a degree - both games have dark, brooding aesthetics and pose a significant challenge to the player, while having a steep learning curve. But I don't think the core principles of these games are alike. In Dark Souls, the player is in control all the time, the game will not offer you help, nor will it deliberately undermine your progress and make your life harder. There are no unknown variables either, as soon as you are comfortable with your character and know all the patterns, that's it, you will never lose if your mechanical execution is perfect.
It is not the case with Darkest Dungeon however. There is only so much you can do to succeed, but it is not entirely up to you. This is why a major component of the game is
. Since you can't outskill your enemies with perfect tactics when your party is at the brink of death, sometimes you just have to cut your losses and escape. This is a big part of getting good at Darkest Dungeon, learning when you should and, more importantly, shouldn't press on. To be fair, if you get good at this game, you will succeed at the overwhelming majority of your quests, but sometimes the game will destroy you. This is why I think an apt comparison would be
(an important distinction, because in ordinary poker there is a whole another level of mind games). You have to play smart and hedge your bets, if the odds are not in your favour, it isn't worth committing in many cases. Of course, there are times, when you have
, but the game has
. The thing about Darkest Dungeon however, it lets you stack the "deck" in your favor by effectively utilizing party combinations, properly equipping your characters, and using tactics to your advantage.
Why am I telling you this and why is it important? I feel like a lot of people go into game with false expectations, feeling that it's gonna be a Dark Souls experience to the letter and end up being disappointed or thinking they were misled. Which is often followed by criticizing the game for
. The game does well what it was created to do and it never pretended it is something more than it is. So before you post an angry review, blaming "stupid RNG", remember that it was a part of the deal and you agreed to it. I think RNG is pretty well-tuned actually, fringe cases don't happen that often. Does RNG makes the game worse than similar games that don't rely on it? I don't think so, and the good thing is there is plenty of room for all kinds of games, with RNG or without it.
Now, let's talk about the game being grindy. By nature, many games are grindy in one way or another, because all of them have some sort of

What did it for me is that I actually enjoy said gameplay loop and the fact that the world of the game and the story intrigue me greatly, so I was very excited to uncover bits and pieces about it as I go.
With gameplay out of the way, it's time to talk about other things the game has to offer, and boy, it has to offer a lot. It is hard to me to separate from each other elements like music, visuals, sound design and story, because they work together so well. Yeah, let's call it

I've been waiting until I've played this game for quite awhile, to write this review. I feel since I have an adequate amount of time invested into it, it's time to go ahead and write the review.
Unlike other games that I've played, Unturned is a completely free experience based on a post-apocalyptic land (that's still quite intact despite the chaos and whole infection thing) in which you must gather materials to survive, build a shelter, kill the undead (and boss zombies as well), and if you're on a multiplayer server, PvP against other players to become the #1 player.
Unturned provides the perfect experience for whatever you enjoy doing- whether it be PvP combat (there's many servers for this as well as small combat maps such as PEI, Washington, and the many Arena gamemodes), survival (Germany, Russia, Hawaii) looting and building a huge castle, becoming an arms dealer and selling everyone custom modded weapons (RP servers), or just a mix of all of the above. You should be able to quickly learn how to gather or craft items and build a base without having to watch a tutorial video.
The loot is tiered- there are a few categories of items. Civillian loot, military loot, ranger loot, and a couple more. They all spawn in certain parts of the map, you can play with workshop mods to get more items, spawn in items, vehicles, and more. The vehicles spawn everywhere on the map, don't require too much time to fix, and can even be customized through building on them either in the editor or by just placing items on the vehicles. Zombies are also tiered- there are civillian zombies, military and construction zombies (which have more health and don't instantly die on headshots with most guns), and the infamous Mega Zombies. Mega zombies are the hardest to kill, and require you use a high-powered rifle or pistol and have a decent amount of skill in combat.
There are easter eggs on some of the maps, which I won't share with you now, you'll have to find them (hint- hawaii/germany/russia) that grant you with special items. One of them involves a Magma Zombie Boss which is much more stronger then the regular mega zombies. There are also quests which you can do for certain factions, and even join their group or decide to ignore them altogether.
The game has a decent base building system. it's rather unrealistic, but it's a lot better then a lot of games have done with building. There are ways to get loot through building, such as farming, oil rigs, and water barrels, that you can just build once and never have to worry about those materials again. Plus, the parts for the base aren't difficult at all to get. You can salvage pretty much any weapon or clothing item to get more scrap cloth and metal to build.
There are many different ways you store items, crates which can be opened by anyone (unrecommended on PvP servers) and the lockers/wardrobes that nobody can open unless they explode it. There isn't a necessity of a base, if you use the right mods you can carry around pretty much everything that you collect with you at all times- but it's strongly recommended seeing as you aren't going to be able to get it all back when you die unless you use cheats to teleport back.
Enough of the information about the game- why should you play this game though?
Unturned runs well on older models- such as my 2012 i5 laptop that was never meant to run a game. I can solid 30 fps which is great for my computer (I get 5 FPS on CS:GO for comparison). There are configurable graphics to make this blocky game feel a bit more realistic, from clouds, to scope quality, you can upgrade anything in the settings as long as your computer can handle it. The interface is very customizable all the way down to whether you'd like to hold items in your left or your right hand.
There are so many mods in the workshop that it's hard to be able to choose a mod. Plus, there's an integrated workshop creator where you can build anything from a map to a new vehicle. If you don't find what you like in the workshop on steam, feel free to make your own items! Many servers come with workshop mods as well to enhance your experience, or if you don't like those mods there are an equal amount of vanilla or semi-vanilla servers that you can join instead.
There are item drops- which can range from a legendary skin to a common shirt. You will typically get either a shirt, a cheap skin, or a crate every day- but sometimes you can get lucky! You can open crates for 1 dollar, and see what's inside. You can even get mythical items- which price up to 100 dollars, which can be pretty damn exciting to get.
If you aren't sure that you want to play with others, and prefer a game more like Fallout 4, why not go ahead and try the singleplayer? Who doesn't like being able to control everything from item drops, to airdrop rate, to item durability? It's great to play in singleplayer for a few hours before you jump into mulitplayer so you don't embarass yourself.
There are trading cards as well, which you can get from buying things in the game, it takes 9 dollars to get your first cards/booster pack/whatever it's called, so better start earning (or buying) crates.
I've gone on enough about this game. Despite some of the glitches, Unturned is a great game for players of any age to jump into and enjoy. I've played for 500 hours so far and expect to play another 1500 before I finally retire this game and hop onto something else. With frequent updates, you won't get bored of Unturned. Why not give it a try?

Fallout 4 is certainly not a bad game, it is just..different from previous entries. The most notable difference is the scaling back of RPG elements and the heavier focus on the FPS elements. I would classify this more as an FPS with RPG elements rather than the RPG with FPS elements that Fallout 3 and New Vegas were. That being said, the story is weak, many of the systems in the game are not as fleshed out as previous games, and some systems were even taken completely out of the game like the karma system from Fallout 3.
Another problem is the bland world design. Fallout 3 felt like it was more focused on quality over content, with more interesting locations and quests at a lower volume. Fallout 4 is the opposite of this, with quests and locations at a higher volume but at a lower quality. Locations still have small side stories told through holotapes and terminals, but they still are not as interesting as the wide variety of characters and quests there were in Fallout 3. Another issue is the complete lack of large settlements. There are only around 2 or 3 major settlements or cities in the game, a huge downgrade from Fallout 3. The game instead expects the player to build their own settlements with the workshop system. The only problem with this is player settlements lack the unique characters and locations found in handcrafted cities. The whole entire game as a result feels very generic and lacking in character compared to previous entries.
This shift really represents how Fallout 4 shifts its focus from the story-based RPG that was Fallout 3 to this more gameplay heavy experience of Fallout 4. Some fans absolutely hated this shift, claiming Fallout 4 was catering to a wider and more casual audience, which I do agree with, but that doesn't mean that they didn't create a fun and interesting game.
The changes were mostly to improve the gameplay aspects of the game:
The shooting has been vastly improved, making it more satisfying. I can actually shoot outside of the paused VATS system and enjoy it now.
The crafting system and modification system is great, giving meaning beyond money to tote around all the trash you pick up in the wasteland.
Although sometimes repetitive, the wasteland is vast and expansive and has some variety and interesting locations.
Customization of everything from your settlements, your guns, your clothes, and your character are possible.
These gameplay changes made the game a lot more fun to just play for the game part rather than the story I was playing for in Fallout 3. Ultimately, if you are looking for a good FPS that will last you quite a while, I'd say check out Fallout 4. If you are looking for a deep RPG with a significant story filled with player choice similar to Fallout 3 or New Vegas, look elsewhere. I certainly enjoyed my time with Fallout 4, but if Bethesda released the next Fallout game with the same lack of choice and shallow RPG systems, I might just skip it.
Pros:
+Satisfying and fun shooting
+Great level of customization
+Huge world to explore
+Fantastic music, as always
+Good new crafting system
Cons:
-Noticeable lack of choice compared to previous entries
-Shallow RPG systems
-Lack of  large cities and settlements, too much reliance on player-built settlements
-Quality and diversity of locations is sacrificed for a larger quantity
Overall I'd say its worth it at full price if you think you'll get a lot of enjoyment out of it, otherwise wait for a sale.

Everyone says Darkest Dungeon is an RPG based on luck. I have to agree that Darkest Dungeon is an luck based RPG, but the real challenge is dealing with this luck mechanic. Knowing when to take risks, how to minimize those risks and how to deal with bad choises is the greatest ability the player will learn from this game. Running around, making idiotic moves and blaming on luck will not help you.
This game is hard, really hard. Sometimes you'll have to reset your campaign, because you don't have money. Sometimes your hero will take a crit to the face and die shortly after. Sometimes you will have to backtrack through a whole dungeon, because you missed an item. Dealing with those challenges and preparing for them is amazing, it gives me chills everytime I screw things over. But the reward is as big as the challenge, since the game is hard and most of the players rage quit from it. Knowing you are the 10% who can win even at the face of death is rewarding.
The battle system is simple, but complex enough to reward smart players and to punish bad ones. The money management is great mechanic. Sometimes you'll have to save money to buy supplies for a dungeon. Sometimes you'll have to stress heal your units. The relic system is a great way to incentivise exploring harder and different dungeons for some upgrades at the town.
The game is great at its current state and I would love to see what Red Hook is planning for the future of Darkest Dungeon.

As a whole playing Darkest Dungeon has been an incredibly fun and addicting experience. At times it's frustrating, but beating a frustrating level is all the more rewarding. There's several things that set Darkest Dungeon apart from the other games of it's genre. The stress mechanic being the most noteworthy. Darkest Dungeon is unforgiving and brutal, but because of it's unforgiving and brutal nature it's one of the most rewarding games I've ever played.
Negatives:
Darkest Dungeon is meant to be difficult, however the stress mechanic is often annoying instead of difficult. It's an extremly interesting concept, but the execution is somewhat poor. The fact that once one party member gets afflicted is nice, but it happens far to frequently and if the afflicted party member isn't stressing the other party members out he's passing his turn or even damaging himself depending on his affliction. Sometimes the afflicted charater will refused to be healed no matter what his health is at. I've had a hero die because he was at deaths door and refused to be healed. Overall I think the stress mechanic needs a nerf.
I love the fact that you need multiple teams to rotate in and out so because one team needs to be relieved of stress through different methods in the town, however spending pretty much all of your money that you made from an adventure on relieving the stress of the team sent on the adventure feels diminishing to the accomplishments of the adventure.
The RNG factor of the map design is annoying. For example: If you get a dungeon where you need to complete 100% of the room battles and there's three different ways to go than you'll need to go to the end of each segment to make sure there's no room battle at the end and than backtrack all the way back to go to another segment. If you get a map that requires a lot of backtracking and don't bring enough food than you're likely going to  take damage because you're team needs to eat but you don't have the supplies. If you get a map that has little to no backtracking and you bought a lot of food than it goes to waste. The time you have to spend on backtracking is the most frustrating part of it. All together it's not that big of a deal, but I would like to see less backtracking.
There's serveral quirks that make heros prone to investigate certain objects such as curios, fountains, treasure etc. I don't see the point of this. It makes no differance to me who searches what. All it does is pester me when I have to wait a few seconds for a heros chat bubble to appear and disappear before he searches the object. I just don't see a point in these quirks.
Positives:
Darkest Dungeon has it's flaws, but the good far outweighs the bad. Not everyone will agree with what I've said and that's okay. We all have our opinions and this is mine.

Ahh, Spiral Knights. It's bittersweet, writing an honest review about a game that I really want to love so much more than I do, but am unable to for reasons that we'll be covering here.
Spiral Knights is an MMO with a lot of really good action elements to it. It's kind of like the old school dungeon crawler games in the sense that they're randomly made (to a limited extent), and they can be unforgivingly hard in the later stages of the game. Now, don't get me wrong, I love a good difficult game, and SK doesn't cut you slack by the end - but if you don't have certain items, the levels become much harder than they normally would. Sure, you can offset that with a group of friends - which you'll certainly make, as the community is really cool around Haven - but you'll still get killed a lot, or be considered no help to your group.
Before I list the problems with all of that, which we'll detail below, let me give you the good stuff. This game is REALLY well made, certainly for a F2P. The levels are cool, the design is all around great (weapons, enemies, levels, all of it), and the community is excellent - something you don't see as often these days. There's a ton of ways to equip your knight, letting you build a lot of different class types, if you will. You can run a striker build, designed for high speed attacking, a gunslinger that fights at range, a combination of the two, or pretty much anything your heart desires! The missions are usually doable solo, as well, so if you don't run with a group, you can jump in with your gear and take down most of it yourself!
Ahh, but there must be a catch, you think. And...well, it's sad, but there is. To advance through the campaign, and rank up to equip better things, you have to gain "certification" from the Hall of Heroes. This entails one of your weapons, your helm, armor, and shield being the appropriate amount of stars, starting at one star and going up to five. Doesn't sound bad, I know. However, once you hit three star, this becomes an OBSCENELY long grind to earn the necessary amount of crowns (in game currency) to trade for energy (real world currency) to buy the alchemy orbs you'll need to level your gear up. The recipes for the gear that you can craft to the next tier of stars are also MASSIVELY expensive (I believe 10000 crowns at four star, though I may be mistaken - it's been awhile). What does this lead to? Well, if you play on the hardest difficulty, you make more crowns! But you die a lot. And though you're awarded revives for campaign missions, you'll run out - and you get those by using, you guessed it, more energy. And those revives will EVENTUALLY be needed to complete late game missions (Roarmulus Twins, Lord Vanaduke for examples - two rather tough bosses). So you have to play it on normal difficulty, and the grind will take you longer! You need three orbs for ONE piece of gear, and you buy the recipe and level it. Well done! Now you have to do it THREE MORE TIMES AT LEAST. See the problem here? This approach is appealing to people who A) Have literally nothing else to play, or B) Are willing to pay to advance. And there's your catch. Pay to advance.
All in all, Spiral Knights is a terrific game. It's very rewarding to play, and you honestly feel yourself advancing and getting stronger as you move along! And up until three star gear, well, it's reasonably fast paced with only some grinding involved. I just wish that formula had carried over to the four and five star gear advancements, because at the point I'm at myself (four star), it's just a run through the arcade levels over and over again until I get enough crowns - and grinding, while okay in small doses, gets old in a hurry when you just want to do something different. And trust me, unless you're willing to drop real money on this, you WILL be grinding a lot. It's still alright for drop in sessions, but it's nothing worth playing for long periods of time, like Guns of Icarus or Shadowrun Returns.
Pros:
-Community is terrific
-Gameplay is tight (controls are good, responsive, combat is anything BUT clunky)
-Graphics are excellent (sort of a cutesy kind of look, but it really works the way they did it)
-Music fits well in respective areas
Cons:
-ENDLESS grinding after you hit three star gear
-Pay to advance becomes the only way to level at a reasonable pace
-Need multiple loadouts of armor and weapons
A last note, guys - I need to expand on that last con. You'll go against some bosses resistant to everything but one weapon type - and if you don't have that weapon, the difficulty is much harder. The Royal Jelly, for example, is vulnerable to shadow, resistant to piercing - and at that point in the game, my gun was piercing, my sword was normal, which made him way harder until I got a poison blade and shadow bomb. As for armor, well, go through the Firestorm Citadel without something resistant to fire, and tell me that it isn't a lot harder for you than the guy wearing Vog Cub Armor (fire resistant, for those of you counting at home).
In total, I'll give this game an 8.5 out of 10. It has potential to be arguably perfect - but until the pay to advance system is fixed (or at least the orbs and all made cheaper in terms of energy), I can't in my right mind give it a 10. I certainly recommend you give it a try, however, because the good is almost enough to outshine that pay to advance bit. It's a shame that it falls just short of doing so.

I've been waiting for this game since I heard an interview about it on the CBC...I've been fascinated by the idea of the psychology of the video game affecting the players in crazy ways.  However, I've been really let down by this title.  I read the phrase "artificially hard" and I think that's the best description.
The worst thing for me is the struggle for money.  The dungeons are full of ridiculously hard monsters who could overwhelm me at any time, forcing a retreat which has psychological ramifications, which I like, I think that's a cool mechanic.  I also like that I have limited bag space and have to buy supplies before I head out.  What I don't like is how little money I make in comparison to the supplies I have to put out, the afflictions and diseases and quirks I have to cure, the gear I have to upgrade, and the skills I have to improve.  If the gameplay was hard, fine, I like it, bring it on.  But don't give me a death of a thousand papercuts by bleeding me out financially.  That's my real life, I'd like to escape it here.
I think with some adjustments, this could be a really fun game...but I think in the craze to make games that are difficult, developers have forgotten to balance that with games that are also still fun.  In this title, I get lots of "Holy f*ck, that monster just WTFPWNED me!", but no blancing "RAWR! Did you SEE that?!  I am MIGHTY!" moments.  Psychological torment can even be found there...guilt over destroying monsters and humans, narcissism, berserker rages.  We could win this game every once in a while and our characters could still suffer psychologically and I think we would be having more fun with it.  Until there's more balance, I would give this title a miss.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

Because I enjoy being forced to blindly rush rush rush against my will because 8 out of 10 missions have a turn timer that's way too short and results in a failure state or you losing squad members because you "abandoned" them.
EDIT:
The way that the devs handled the concealment phase of the missions was done very poorly. Why does the turn timer count down to failure when the aliens DON'T KNOW YOU'RE THERE. If the devs themselves actually made it so that you could manuever tactically and set up a proper overwatch and ambush WITHOUT the turn timer ticking down with the timer only ticking down once the aliens realize that your soldiers are on the map I would have a much better opinion. Unfortunately, I have to use a mod for this (True Concealment mod) in order to achieve the same effect.
The turn timer would make perfect sense when you're discovered and being actively chased by the aliens. But counting down when the aliens don't know you're there and aren't actively seeking you out? Why is this in the vanilla game?
I get it, it's a guerilla force. You are in enemy territory and have limited time to complete your mission. But if you're in stealth mode, nobody knows you're there, and you do your best to stay out of sight like a real guerilla force would why should you have a clock to race against? No alarms have been sounded and there's no security concern from the enemies until they know you're there.
Please devs, change it so that the turn timer doesn't count down until you break concealment. This would be immensely better than what's going on right now, especially for players like me who aren't the "hardcore 1%". This change would still make the game challenging without punishing less hardcore players.
And no, I didn't overwatch creep in EU/EW.

I wouldn't recommend this on the basis of its gameplay, not at its full release price point. For all the wonders of its imagery and tone, the gameplay itself feels like it would be more at home on a mobile device (complete with micro transactions) and the story is flat.
Combat is strategic in the same way that single player Pokemon is strategic -- which is to say it really isn't. Because actual loss is impossible long-term planning and resource management is unnecessary and serves only to lessen the grind -- and then only slightly. A single party has no way to actually adapt to a given situation within the dungeon itself, which is the only time that would matter. The game is infinitely replayable, but given that the story, while beautifully narrated and evocative of wonderful lovecraftian themes, is linear and one-dimensional and the game itself is basically a massive, grindy skinner box I can't see why you would take advantage of that fact.
You should get it if you've money to spare, and you really like lovecraftian horror, turnbased RPGs and you don't mind repetitive grinds.

I'm loving this game.
It has what I loved in X-Com: EU and EW with new features/enemies/developments sprinkled in.
It's an absorbing strategy with diverse enough character customisation for units to feel unique, on the subject of customisation there's a lot more to it than there was in the previous installments, so if you enjoy having your own unit, you'll love customising in this game.
The new enemy units are both really cool and terrifying, every time I see a new enemy unit, I make sure it dies as soon as possible rather than seeing what it can do. (and then later on it catches me with my pants down on another mission because my veteran's are all recovering)
I could sing this game's praises for days so lets get to what I think is wrong with it.
The game is incredibly more difficult, now this is both a good point and a bad point.
It's only a bad point because of the next things I'm going to discuss.
+There is a game loading bias. Shots I've made before loading have hit and have gotten criticals, then after loading, they miss entirely, and after many consequetive loads, each time it fails to even hit.
it seems every first shot after loading a game seems to have a drastic aim hit, I've even tested this out by making the exact same shot in the exact same place with the enemy at the exact same health and in the exact same spot before: both with the unit in question firing first, and with another unit firing before hand then firing with the unit in question.
In the latter example the other unit shoots, misses and the unit in question then fires, hits, GG game over.
in the first example the unit in question misses the target and another unit has to attempt to hit them.
This balant "Anti-Save Scum System" is insanely annoying and with the increased difficulty of this installment means I've spent a great deal of time having to wrestle with it, something I do not find fun and really detracts from the experience.
+Long War influences: The game is definitely harder, feeling more like Long War than the actual base games EU and EW.
This is both a good and a bad thing too, only being a bad thing simply because of the Anti-Save Scum System.
+Caters to Hardcore gamers: There's no good and bad to this one in my opinion, those who prefer hardcore gameplay will see this as a huge plus, but for those who seem themselves more as casuals, or inbetween the two (like myself) will find this to be a particular feature that one has to take with some salt, water and lots of sessions crying because I lost my favourite sharp shooter and STOP MAKING ME RELOAD TO SAVE HER FOR ♥♥♥♥ SAKE
The game is also host to some really annoying bugs and glitches, after experiencing them first hand, I can see why they were exclusively a negative point in the IGN review.
as they stand, they are not game breaking but really detract from the experience, and end up only being funny the first time or if you're really easily amused (or high off your face)
I love this game, and I'm definitely slapping it with a 9/10
When some patches get released and those bugs get fixed, it'll raise to a 9.5/10 and if a second wave option is added, or a patch is released to fix the Anti-Save Scum System, it'll definitely get a 10/10 from me.
(Disclaimer: many may see the Anti-Save Scum System as something that's not so bad, and may want to dismiss my opinion on it, but before you do, please look at it from this perspective: someone who is going to save scum, say to save their favourite unit, is going to save scum over and over and over until they get the result they want, having to put up with continuous loading over the course of an hour replaying a single turn to try and get that PERFECT scenario where everyone lives, is insanely painful and boring and really detracts from this excellent game)

As a whole playing Darkest Dungeon has been an incredibly fun and addicting experience. At times it's frustrating, but beating a frustrating level is all the more rewarding. There's several things that set Darkest Dungeon apart from the other games of it's genre. The stress mechanic being the most noteworthy. Darkest Dungeon is unforgiving and brutal, but because of it's unforgiving and brutal nature it's one of the most rewarding games I've ever played.
Negatives:
Darkest Dungeon is meant to be difficult, however the stress mechanic is often annoying instead of difficult. It's an extremly interesting concept, but the execution is somewhat poor. The fact that once one party member gets afflicted is nice, but it happens far to frequently and if the afflicted party member isn't stressing the other party members out he's passing his turn or even damaging himself depending on his affliction. Sometimes the afflicted charater will refused to be healed no matter what his health is at. I've had a hero die because he was at deaths door and refused to be healed. Overall I think the stress mechanic needs a nerf.
I love the fact that you need multiple teams to rotate in and out so because one team needs to be relieved of stress through different methods in the town, however spending pretty much all of your money that you made from an adventure on relieving the stress of the team sent on the adventure feels diminishing to the accomplishments of the adventure.
The RNG factor of the map design is annoying. For example: If you get a dungeon where you need to complete 100% of the room battles and there's three different ways to go than you'll need to go to the end of each segment to make sure there's no room battle at the end and than backtrack all the way back to go to another segment. If you get a map that requires a lot of backtracking and don't bring enough food than you're likely going to  take damage because you're team needs to eat but you don't have the supplies. If you get a map that has little to no backtracking and you bought a lot of food than it goes to waste. The time you have to spend on backtracking is the most frustrating part of it. All together it's not that big of a deal, but I would like to see less backtracking.
There's serveral quirks that make heros prone to investigate certain objects such as curios, fountains, treasure etc. I don't see the point of this. It makes no differance to me who searches what. All it does is pester me when I have to wait a few seconds for a heros chat bubble to appear and disappear before he searches the object. I just don't see a point in these quirks.
Positives:
Darkest Dungeon has it's flaws, but the good far outweighs the bad. Not everyone will agree with what I've said and that's okay. We all have our opinions and this is mine.
