Recently I was asked by a friend who is new to the souls series what i thought of this game, so I thought I'd put what i wrote him here.
This game is a masterpiece.
I'd recommend it, but I will say its hard, like it can be discouraging at times.
However, there are few feelings that come close to the sensation of defeating a boss or enemy you've been stuck on for hours.
TL:DR= Beautiful game, challenging but rewarding fighting system and a non intrusive but intriguing narrative to boot. 9/10
Ill keep the review brief so you can skim through it, because, honestly, you've got to experience the game for yourself to fully comprehend what this game is about.
Story= Vague (left to interpretation sorta' thing) but intriguing. You're character seems to be the only one out of the loop and it really helps cement the idea that youre not ready for the grand task you've been given. You'd expect alot of satisfaction from the end of the game, however the real story chunks are tucked away in item descriptions and in the connotations of NPC's.
Visuals= F***ing fantastic. Graphics are great even on low settings and this mystical middle age setting looks so ♥♥♥♥ing incredible. The world is detailed and reinforces the main story with hints of the impennding doom that a dark age will induce. Oh, and fashion souls is real, and trust me you're going to spend a lot of time making your character look badass.
Gameplay= Toughest part. Easy to learn, hard to master. The levelling system require stat placement which means various builds can be created with various intended functions: from melee builds to caster builds to healing builds. Some styles are more forgiving than others and others require late game items/bonuses/spells to properly flourish. There are, of course, Meta builds that perform pretty well but everyone will also be trying to perfect there own build.
Online= Fantastic. Community is still pretty big for PvE and PvP but, the game is getting getting old now. Co-op is great and can be used through most of game (minus something like 3 transitory areas that dont really have anything important in them). Invasions are what made dark souls work: getting invaded and winning a duel makes you feel powerful if its a 1v1. Invading can be unforgiving because of gank squads (2+ players who corner single invaders) but it can be so rewarding when you pull of a whole squad kill and you get to do the infamous 'point down' gesture. PvP has its own arena if invading gets tiresome, so thats a plus. But high wait times if your not around the meta level in arena (Soul level 120 is the recommended meta range). General PvP can be alot more frustrating than other games but alot more rewarding. Mistakes can be unforgiving and there is a big issue with the lag in fights. However, for a guy who I know likes to feel the flurry of a good fight, this s*** delivers. Highly tactical gameplay that rewards smart decisions and good spacing. Dont get me wrong, the arena is useful for easy matchmaking but theres a whole pvp system called fight clubs where players gather in a non dlc area to do 1v1s (fair warning: there are no real rule enforcement in fight clubs so you just gotta' act honorable and hope your fighting compatriots do too and not gank you).
Thanks for reading, this has been my first review on steam so I hope its clear and legible :)

I've been waiting for this game since I heard an interview about it on the CBC...I've been fascinated by the idea of the psychology of the video game affecting the players in crazy ways.  However, I've been really let down by this title.  I read the phrase "artificially hard" and I think that's the best description.
The worst thing for me is the struggle for money.  The dungeons are full of ridiculously hard monsters who could overwhelm me at any time, forcing a retreat which has psychological ramifications, which I like, I think that's a cool mechanic.  I also like that I have limited bag space and have to buy supplies before I head out.  What I don't like is how little money I make in comparison to the supplies I have to put out, the afflictions and diseases and quirks I have to cure, the gear I have to upgrade, and the skills I have to improve.  If the gameplay was hard, fine, I like it, bring it on.  But don't give me a death of a thousand papercuts by bleeding me out financially.  That's my real life, I'd like to escape it here.
I think with some adjustments, this could be a really fun game...but I think in the craze to make games that are difficult, developers have forgotten to balance that with games that are also still fun.  In this title, I get lots of "Holy f*ck, that monster just WTFPWNED me!", but no blancing "RAWR! Did you SEE that?!  I am MIGHTY!" moments.  Psychological torment can even be found there...guilt over destroying monsters and humans, narcissism, berserker rages.  We could win this game every once in a while and our characters could still suffer psychologically and I think we would be having more fun with it.  Until there's more balance, I would give this title a miss.

Because I enjoy being forced to blindly rush rush rush against my will because 8 out of 10 missions have a turn timer that's way too short and results in a failure state or you losing squad members because you "abandoned" them.
EDIT:
The way that the devs handled the concealment phase of the missions was done very poorly. Why does the turn timer count down to failure when the aliens DON'T KNOW YOU'RE THERE. If the devs themselves actually made it so that you could manuever tactically and set up a proper overwatch and ambush WITHOUT the turn timer ticking down with the timer only ticking down once the aliens realize that your soldiers are on the map I would have a much better opinion. Unfortunately, I have to use a mod for this (True Concealment mod) in order to achieve the same effect.
The turn timer would make perfect sense when you're discovered and being actively chased by the aliens. But counting down when the aliens don't know you're there and aren't actively seeking you out? Why is this in the vanilla game?
I get it, it's a guerilla force. You are in enemy territory and have limited time to complete your mission. I'm loving this game.
It has what I loved in X-Com: EU and EW with new features/enemies/developments sprinkled in.
It's an absorbing strategy with diverse enough character customisation for units to feel unique, on the subject of customisation there's a lot more to it than there was in the previous installments, so if you enjoy having your own unit, you'll love customising in this game.
The new enemy units are both really cool and terrifying, every time I see a new enemy unit, I make sure it dies as soon as possible rather than seeing what it can do. (and then later on it catches me with my pants down on another mission because my veteran's are all recovering)
I could sing this game's praises for days so lets get to what I think is wrong with it.
The game is incredibly more difficult, now this is both a good point and a bad point.
It's only a bad point because of the next things I'm going to discuss.
+There is a game loading bias. Shots I've made before loading have hit and have gotten criticals, then after loading, they miss entirely, and after many consequetive loads, each time it fails to even hit.
it seems every first shot after loading a game seems to have a drastic aim hit, I've even tested this out by making the exact same shot in the exact same place with the enemy at the exact same health and in the exact same spot before: both with the unit in question firing first, and with another unit firing before hand then firing with the unit in question.
In the latter example the other unit shoots, misses and the unit in question then fires, hits, GG game over.
in the first example the unit in question misses the target and another unit has to attempt to hit them.
This balant "Anti-Save Scum System" is insanely annoying and with the increased difficulty of this installment means I've spent a great deal of time having to wrestle with it, something I do not find fun and really detracts from the experience.
+Long War influences: The game is definitely harder, feeling more like Long War than the actual base games EU and EW.
This is both a good and a bad thing too, only being a bad thing simply because of the Anti-Save Scum System.
+Caters to Hardcore gamers: There's no good and bad to this one in my opinion, those who prefer hardcore gameplay will see this as a huge plus, but for those who seem themselves more as casuals, or inbetween the two (like myself) will find this to be a particular feature that one has to take with some salt, water and lots of sessions crying because I lost my favourite sharp shooter and STOP MAKING ME RELOAD TO SAVE HER FOR ♥♥♥♥ SAKE
The game is also host to some really annoying bugs and glitches, after experiencing them first hand, I can see why they were exclusively a negative point in the IGN review.
as they stand, they are not game breaking but really detract from the experience, and end up only being funny the first time or if you're really easily amused (or high off your face)
I love this game, and I'm definitely slapping it with a 9/10
When some patches get released and those bugs get fixed, it'll raise to a 9.5/10 and if a second wave option is added, or a patch is released to fix the Anti-Save Scum System, it'll definitely get a 10/10 from me.
(Disclaimer: many may see the Anti-Save Scum System as something that's not so bad, and may want to dismiss my opinion on it, but before you do, please look at it from this perspective: someone who is going to save scum, say to save their favourite unit, is going to save scum over and over and over until they get the result they want, having to put up with continuous loading over the course of an hour replaying a single turn to try and get that PERFECT scenario where everyone lives, is insanely painful and boring and really detracts from this excellent game)

I wouldn't recommend this on the basis of its gameplay, not at its full release price point. For all the wonders of its imagery and tone, the gameplay itself feels like it would be more at home on a mobile device (complete with micro transactions) and the story is flat.

A single party has no way to actually adapt to a given situation within the dungeon itself, which is the only time that would matter. The game is infinitely replayable, but given that the story, while beautifully narrated and evocative of wonderful lovecraftian themes, is linear and one-dimensional and the game itself is basically a massive, grindy skinner box I can't see why you would take advantage of that fact.
You should get it if you've money to spare, and you really like lovecraftian horror, turnbased RPGs and you don't mind repetitive grinds.

As a whole playing Darkest Dungeon has been an incredibly fun and addicting experience. At times it's frustrating, but beating a frustrating level is all the more rewarding. There's several things that set Darkest Dungeon apart from the other games of it's genre. The stress mechanic being the most noteworthy. Darkest Dungeon is unforgiving and brutal, but because of it's unforgiving and brutal nature it's one of the most rewarding games I've ever played.
Negatives:
Darkest Dungeon is meant to be difficult, however the stress mechanic is often annoying instead of difficult. It's an extremly interesting concept, but the execution is somewhat poor. The fact that once one party member gets afflicted is nice, but it happens far to frequently and if the afflicted party member isn't stressing the other party members out he's passing his turn or even damaging himself depending on his affliction. Sometimes the afflicted charater will refused to be healed no matter what his health is at. I've had a hero die because he was at deaths door and refused to be healed. Overall I think the stress mechanic needs a nerf.
I love the fact that you need multiple teams to rotate in and out so because one team needs to be relieved of stress through different methods in the town, however spending pretty much all of your money that you made from an adventure on relieving the stress of the team sent on the adventure feels diminishing to the accomplishments of the adventure.
The RNG factor of the map design is annoying. For example: If you get a dungeon where you need to complete 100% of the room battles and there's three different ways to go than you'll need to go to the end of each segment to make sure there's no room battle at the end and than backtrack all the way back to go to another segment. If you get a map that requires a lot of backtracking and don't bring enough food than you're likely going to  take damage because you're team needs to eat but you don't have the supplies. If you get a map that has little to no backtracking and you bought a lot of food than it goes to waste. The time you have to spend on backtracking is the most frustrating part of it. All together it's not that big of a deal, but I would like to see less backtracking.
There's serveral quirks that make heros prone to investigate certain objects such as curios, fountains, treasure etc. I don't see the point of this. It makes no differance to me who searches what. All it does is pester me when I have to wait a few seconds for a heros chat bubble to appear and disappear before he searches the object. I just don't see a point in these quirks.
Positives:
Darkest Dungeon has it's flaws, but the good far outweighs the bad. Not everyone will agree with what I've said and that's okay. We all have our opinions and this is mine.

I've been waiting for this game since I heard an interview about it on the CBC...I've been fascinated by the idea of the psychology of the video game affecting the players in crazy ways.  However, I've been really let down by this title.  I read the phrase "artificially hard" and I think that's the best description.
The worst thing for me is the struggle for money.  The dungeons are full of ridiculously hard monsters who could overwhelm me at any time, forcing a retreat which has psychological ramifications, which I like, I think that's a cool mechanic.  I also like that I have limited bag space and have to buy supplies before I head out.  What I don't like is how little money I make in comparison to the supplies I have to put out, the afflictions and diseases and quirks I have to cure, the gear I have to upgrade, and the skills I have to improve.  If the gameplay was hard, fine, I like it, bring it on.  But don't give me a death of a thousand papercuts by bleeding me out financially.  That's my real life, I'd like to escape it here.
I think with some adjustments, this could be a really fun game...but I think in the craze to make games that are difficult, developers have forgotten to balance that with games that are also still fun.  In this title, I get lots of "Holy f*ck, that monster just WTFPWNED me!", but no blancing "RAWR! Did you SEE that?!  I am MIGHTY!" moments.  Psychological torment can even be found there...guilt over destroying monsters and humans, narcissism, berserker rages.  We could win this game every once in a while and our characters could still suffer psychologically and I think we would be having more fun with it.  Until there's more balance, I would give this title a miss.

"There can be no hope in this hell... no hope at all." - The Ancestor.
Now that the game is released and I have played it in the... "finished" state - I can say that I am quite disappointed.
Sure, the difficulty is fine and entertaining, but only for so long: all hero upgrades feel absolutely underwhelming. Now, this might not be obvious at the start, because properly upgraded and geared heroes can easily chew through any easy and medium dungeons. But then come the lvl 5 champion ones... and with them comes utter disaster as monsters start to show up with abominable amounts of PROT(while we still have only TWO heroes who can counter this), SPD and additional effects to their attacks. At this point your tactics and overall preparedness barely matter as everything is purely in the hands of the game: the dice will decide your fate and in the final stages they are loaded against you.
Pros:
- Stunning and hauntingly beautiful art, music and atmosphere.
- One superb, amazing narrator.
Cons:
- Insane difficulty spike near game end without any reasonable means to offset it, tactics will only get you so far.
- Heroes actually start to feel weak as the game progresses: without a crit - you're very likely to end in the gutter. I really don't want to complain, but I simply fail to justify the reason why some filthy pigs, skeletons. bandits and mushroom abominations all have PROT, while my lvl 5 armour, even on Crusader and Man-at-Arms who actually wear plate, provides NONE of it.
- It feels terribly grindy. The amount of various relics required, especially Deeds, is atrocious. The amount of gold necessary for upgrades and the quality of upgrades themselves is DISGUSTING.
- The game actually ENCOURAGES you to sacrifice your first best group of heroes, as they will accumulate EXP faster than gear and at some point will not be able to handle the dungeons appropriate for them.

I wanted to give this game a stellar recommendation. But given what this game has become, I cannot do so in good conscience.
When I first bought this game back when it was in early access, it was something really interesting. An incredible aesthetic matched by a gameplay that married the best aspects of RPGs and Dungeon Crawlers, with its own twists and turns that made for a wholly engrossing experience. It wasn't perfect, but it was challenging, enjoyable, and most importantly of all, rewarding.
All the way through the development process, I'd periodically start up a new run to see what sort of changes had been made, and for the most part I wasn't disappointed. The difficult of the game got ramped up, but so too did the classes themselves. The fights were both terrifying and exhilarating, and taking down a boss felt like a triumphant moment. The new classes were interesting, and the quirks system made them feel like more than just a grouping of mechanics.
I didn't mind the introduction of heart attacks and corpses, as they forced me to keep a closer eye on my stress levels and put more thought into my party lineups.
As Darkest Dungeon reached its final stage, the very same elements that made it so fun and enjoyable for me have become twisted into something that has turned the game into the exact opposite. Reaching Resolve level 5 and 6 used to be an accomplishment, a marker that these characters/heroes had faced overwhelming odds and achieved a greater state of being. You would face off against some truly powerful and terrifying enemies, but your characters were on par with that power and could exchange blow for blow. There was a balance, and even when the tide of battle turned against you there was still a chance that you could pull off a victory from the jaws of defeat.
Now, the odds are stacked overwhelmingly against you. Don't even think about going into a higher level dungeon with even one of your characters not fully upgraded, as they will die. At first, I thought the sudden skyrocketing of my casualty rates were the result of me making a tactical error, but when I looked at play throughs online I found that people who were more or less equally skilled as I was were suffering from similar casualty rates, for similar reasons. I don't mind losing someone because of an error that I made, but losing it because the RNG decided 'they gonna die now' is strikes me as something that is blatantly unfair. Especially when in order to bring them up to the point where they can survive the upper level dungeons requires hours of joyless grinding for resolve and gold, and the fruits of those labors don't seem to have an impact on their overall survivability.
In general, Darkest Dungeon does an extremely poor job of explaining the way different features work, or what to expect when going into a new location or facing off against a new type of boss. Which i don't necessarily mind per-say, but when the cost of failure are so high that they will undermine hours of work, then that becomes a problem.
And don't even get me started on the final dungeon. There are so many design decisions (like rendering your characters illegible for future expeditions, to name one) that are some high grade cow manure, and exemplarly of just how un-fun the game has become.
I guess I'm more disappointed than anything else. There are so many aspects of this game that I love, and that I'm sure other players who are thinking about buying this game will love too. The aesthetic of this game is absolutely phenomenal, the writing is superb, the gameplay is innovative, and there are some genuinely great features. But somewhere along the line, the game has become less about facing off against the eldritch horrors and pulling victory from the jaws of defeat, and more about not losing horribly. It has gone from ‘tough, but fair’ to ‘grueling and frustrating’.
Edit:
For those of you who are interested, I effectively did three runs of the game. The first I started back in March which went on for roughly 30 hours, in which time I'd completed all the available content. I did a second, much shorter one in mid July that lasted about 20 hours in which I only got about half way through bosses. I started a third one, intended to be my final run of the game, in late October, which took me 45 hours to reach about three-quarters of the way to the end game.
This should help show just how much of a grind this game has become

Though I'd estimate around 70% have a "clock" of sorts, terror mission need 6 rescues and you can lose a civilian a turn, defend the relay where usually an alien pod will start in range of a high health object and shoot it once per turn.
The other timed mission have a static turn count that you need to complete some specific task usually a hack or grab x and evac at position y before the clock reaches zero.
I'm really enjoying XCom2 and with the extensive mod support they'll be even more intersting mods out than EU/EW had.
If you are uncertain then I'd recommend finding a good streamer or let's play to watch first.

I get that this game is supposed to be hard, but difficulty isn't what makes it a bad experience. Challenge is a big part of what I want from games, and it's part of what drew me to this title.
Unfortunately, the game gives little for the player to "play with." What should have been exacting, well-informed but difficult decision making and critical thinking is instead random, random, random, managing to take decisions away from the player all the while. It's less choice-consequence and more reactionary fire fighting.
As if all of that wasn't enough, all of my provisions were taken away after a completed expedition. I get that they want to ensure you only take what you need, but this has been done better by so many other games: 1) limit inventory space; 2) impose a carry limit; 3) actually make gold a limiting factor for buying provisions; 4) if all else fails, TELL THE PLAYER that they're going to lose their provisions.
The player is at the game's mercy - it makes all of the decisions while the player just watches things unravel. There's almost no sense that I can act in my best interest or plan or strategize - the player is just supposed to deal with whatever♥♥♥♥♥♥the game randomly throws at them. It's all reactionary clean-up work rather than proactive plotting.
I expect to make difficult but informed decisions when putting together a group to go into a dark dungeon. I like that horrible things can happen to my characters, but I don't like that those things appear to be random or outside my control, and that all I can do is react to them and fight the fires as they appear. I want my own lack of planning, foresight, and execution to be my downfall. Instead, my downfall is eating too much♥♥♥♥♥♥with a character whose random quirk is "allergic to♥♥♥♥♥♥" This is just falling down a hill and trying to minimize the number of impacts with trees... not at all what I expect, and definitely not what I consider entertaining.
Lastly, I hate the dressed up lobby. There's no world to explore. Instead, I flip through a popup book of overlapping menus to make my restricted set of decisions and guess at how many torches I'll need...
The positives/passables:
good

I'm still surprised I'm on the verge of sinking 200 hours into what must be nothing more than "the game that places the spiral sallet helmet into your TF2 backpack." Spiral Knights is one of the most enjoyable "MMO" experiences I've ever had. I have a list of complaints about this game- the biggest being that Three Rings has been alienating the guild feature for so long with a small roster of recolored furniture and not even a ♥♥♥♥ing bulletin board to communicate a single message outside of the guild announcement. Also the fact that the game, despite appearing in our Steam inventories, somehow does not boast the ability to place a ♥♥♥♥ing single item in our Steam showcase (for a game that relies heavily on cosmetics, this is unacceptable).
But I'm going to give you the most unbiased, quickest review I can give this game. I can absolutely see why people don't enjoy it, but the idea of a top-down "Zelda" (although it would help to have more puzzles and hazards) MMO is so appealing to me, I can't resist. The crafting system is fair and allows for a lot of replay value in the fact that you are pretty much never done "needing" equipment (or costumes, for pea♥♥♥♥♥). Not sure how I feel about the fact that an alternate currency, "crystal energy," can be bought for such a significant amount of crowns and a low amount of cash. I love having a guild, decorating it, and inviting users to enjoy the game alongside us- even though the guild feature is seriously lacking in some departments and the people at Three Rings need to take a ♥♥♥♥ing clue but I'm willing to forego this for the sake of bringing you what you need to know. The game updates once a month (sometimes twice), and these are actually pretty significant updates by the way (they tend to bring back "events" here and there for the users to enjoy). The music is alright, not a huge hangup of mine. Gameplay might seem redundant to some people, but there are lots of ways to keep it fresh (I recommend playing with your friends or randoms at all times in order to do this), but a little detour by yourself doesn't hurt.
I haven't dabbled in the arena or anything like that very much it all (it really doesn't interest me at the moment). From what I can tell, a lot of the lategame is spent doing old missions or playing the arcade mode in order to secure crowns and crafting "orbs" which appear randomly in the dungeon chests- and allow you to upgrade your equipment. If you're going to play this game, you need to look at the wiki at some point and decide your armor early. Despite the fact that the game draws a lot of attention to the wiki, I believe there should be some kind of projection ingame that tells you what you need to expect pursuing each armor path (but the hall of heroes does help (they don't neglect this idea as much as I spin my yarn)).
I see a lot of enjoyment in this game and I believe there is a lot of potential as well. If you're on my friend's list or see me booting it up at any point, I encourage you to do the same. Three Rings manages to still pay attention to their fans- despite what you may think for a game of this background-prestige, and, from what I've seen, create polls to decide on what changes should be made in the longterm. A big reason I play this game is because of the aesthetic of it- it's a very cute game. Reminds me of circa 80s RPGs like Final Fantasy or Dragon Quest in the fact that you play as tiny armored creatures of some kind. Give the game a chance, though. Fallout 4 isn't a bad game.
It is also not a good game.
During the summer sale (in the UK) the game is only £9.99 which is an amazing deal, but I wouldn't buy it for anymore.
Pros:
Fallout 4 features one of the best open worlds in any open world game I have played, I've spent many hours exploring the ruins of Boston and the world just feels more alive than both Fallout 3 and New Vegas.
Despite what many people have said, I find the graphics as well as the overall art design to be both visually pleasing and to contain a certain charm that only this game (and the original Fallouts) can provide.
Power armor customization is one of this games best features.
The engine from Fallout 3 and New Vegas has been replaced with the Creation Engine that was previously used in Skyrim. This allows for the complete revamp of the combat system, gone are the days of emptying your gun into some guys face only for him to remain unscathed. For the first time in a modern Fallout game, I know that when I shoot someone they die!
For me, I became less dependent on V.A.T.S. which was a nice change.
The UI and HUD have been improved drastically from previous titles in the franchise. The PipBoy interface has cleaned up and simplified (which isn't always a bad thing) I can now look at the map on my PipBoy and see/understand things a lot easier.
I'm not going to get into it too much but the character creation from previous Fallout games has been replaced with a Sims 4 like sculpt/modeling system.
Neutral:
The base building aspect of the game feels lacking in depth and doesn't feel as good as it could have been.
An unnamed faction (The Minutemen) can be annoying and give out repetitive quests sometimes.
The gun customization is nice but is easy to ignore.
Cons:
Fallout 4 tries to focus around something an autistic 6 year old would call a "story"
*SPOILER INCOMING* *SPOILER INCOMING* *SPOILER INCOMING* *SPOILER INCOMING* *SPOILER INCOMING*
You live in a town called Sanctuary, your stupid English butler-bot tells you a nuke will kill everything, you go to the vault that you conveniently signed up for moments before. You get to the vault, they freeze you. you wake up and a bowl of cornflakes steals you baby and kills your spouse. They then refreeze you. You then are unfrozen again several decades later with a goal of finding your son. You go back home and talk to your butler-bot, he tells you to go to Concord. on your way you meet a gorilla at a gas station (i have a mod) you travel together to Concord, kill raiders then meet Preston Gravy. You also meet Mama Murphy and give her a dose of Jet, she the tells you to go to Diamond City. You go there and try to find some detective guy who has been kidnapped, you go to find and rescue him. When he is back home, you describe what happened at the vault to him, he tells you that a bowl cornflakes did it. You eat the cornflakes and take his brain to be analyzed by one of the detective's friends. You then look through his memories. *insert boring♥♥♥♥♥♥here* eventually you get to the Institute, find out your son is now your grandpa, then he dies of cancer. The End...
*SPOILERS OVER* *SPOILERS OVER* *SPOILERS OVER* *SPOILERS OVER* *SPOILERS OVER* *SPOILERS OVER*
As you can probably tell, I hate the story of this game. It is such a step down from the masterpiece known as New Vegas.
Everything that made Fallout: New Vegas an RPG is gone in this game. Fallout 4 is an Open World, Shooter with RPG Elements. Skills are gone, they have been replaced with perks... Before you could make you could specialize your character with certain attributes but now the system is so linear that no matter what character you make, you will most likely end up having most of the same perks each playthrough.
I have encountered too many bugs over the past 2.5 years, some were patched and some were not. There are too many to list but if bugs are an issue for you consider trying an unofficial patch mod.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall Fallout 4 is an alright game, and for the price, you could do a lot worse.
Though if you are open to the idea of playing a slightly older game I would recommend Fallout: New Vegas.
It is only £3 or £8 with all the DLC, and it is a fantastic RPG with an atmospheric world and memorable characters.

3 hour review -
Rig
i5-2500K
8GB DDR3 RAM
Asus STRIX GTX 980Ti 6GB DDR5 running latest Nvidia drivers updated via Nvidia GeForce Experience
SSD Samnsung drives (various sizes)
Graphics - On par with XCOM 1. Much more attention to detail. Maps are very well made.
Sound - Good. Explosions are loud. Gunfire is loud. Creature noises are well done.
AI - Tough, even on the lowest difficulty setting.
Interface - overall, its functional but I find it a bit cluttered.
Game performance - playing at 1920x1080 with everything maxed out. During battles...no FPS issues, there really cannot be in a turn based game. No graphical artifacts. The only place I have seen 'slow downs' is during the Sky Ranger scenes. Doesn't really bother me since I noticed that the SSD is reading/writing like mad during that time. Who knows. Rumor is that a patch is coming out to address this but its not a show stopper.
Game play - way different than XCOM 1. Devs definitely took a slightly different path with 2 and, in a way, its refreshing but it takes some time to get used too.
Yes, 'THE TIMER' can be an issue for some if you are not aggressive enough BUT it forces you to utilize the game mechanics, namely, staying 'in the shadows'. Remember, you are no longer the large XCOM force but a ragtag force of human guerilla soldiers fighting a very powerful enemy. You get a sense of that from the beginning intro and storyline development.
In essence, you have to play 'smart' - hit and run quickly. Do your objectives and then mop up the remaining forces...or get the hell out of dodge if needed.
Squaddies are very customizable and at first you really don't get attached to them...I've lost 2 thus far, both with 4 missions under their belt, and I just shrugged. But now...I'm starting to be more cautious since some of my soldiers are getting some very useful skill sets.
That's in 3 hours of game play. Did about 8 missions thus far. Lost one mission but it gives you the option to replay it and was successful the second time around. Key: keep your squadmates close enough to provide overwatch fire but not to get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by explosions.
Game play value - 9/10 thus far. Its a fun game and I am definitely getting my $60 worth out of it. I can see infinite replay value out of it...like ALL XCOM games.
Would I recommend it - damn straight! Its XCOM people. The world needs to be saved! ;-)

XCOM 2 is a turn-based strategy game developed by the company Firaxis Games with emphasis on tactical combat.
+ The game captures the feel of a resistance force opposing an overwhelming alien occupation.
+ Excellent soundtrack that keeps the player in the game and sets the mood.
+ Detail put into level design and environmental effects is impressive.
+ Some fighting mechanics are cinematic, intuitive and entertaining.
+ It boasts a healthy variety of equipment, firearms and peripherals.
+ Partially destructible environments.
+ Interface is minimalist and aesthetically pleasing.
+ Offers very high replayability.
o Game is not optimized for 4K resolution, causing irregular fps drops.
- Quite a few bugs and glitches, ranging from minor clipping issues to enemies shooting through obstacles / walls. [Thanks to Volvox Globator for highlighting these points.]
- Occasional in-game slowdowns during certain events, e.g. pause between rounds, calculation of burning effects etc.
+ The game encourages the player to recruit and build a highly specialised army, and the mechanics put in place for doing so are well-rounded and sophisticated.
+ Alien AI behaviour is mostly unpredictable, therefore adding to the title's challenge and replayability.
+ Some missions offer a stealth system, allowing the player to scout out the land and enemies before engaging.
+ Reliable cover system and shooting mechanics, supporting offensive and defensive approaches.
+ Positioning and taking advantage of terrain are the keys to success.
+ Base building and economics add another layer of challenge to the game.
+ Broad spectrum of weapon customizations enriches the gameplay.
+ For the masochistic hardcore gamers among us, the legendary ‘Ironman’ mode is available.
o Learning curve is initially a bit steep, and may deter more casual gamers. In comparison with its predecessor the general level of difficulty is higher.
o Missions are rng-based (random number generator), which could result in a lot of timed missions or almost no timed missions. [Thanks to Athena for mentioning this point.]
+ Campaign playthrough is engaging and provides diversified side quests, with different mission goals and winning conditions.
+ The narrative is well-delivered, with an even pace and solid character development.
+ Extensive customization options for the characters and the possibility to export and import the party setup.
+ The player is likely to develop emotional attachment to some of the soldiers, increasing the immersion into the game.
o Solid voice acting of the entire cast.
XCOM 2 offers a superb strategy experience, which manages to improve the original XCOM formula on every level.
Estimated time for 100% completion: +100 hours
Singleplayer achievements: 79
Multiplayer achievements: 1

"There can be no hope in this hell... no hope at all." - The Ancestor.
Now that the game is released and I have played it in the... "finished" state - I can say that I am quite disappointed.
Sure, the difficulty is fine and entertaining, but only for so long: all hero upgrades feel absolutely underwhelming. Now, this might not be obvious at the start, because properly upgraded and geared heroes can easily chew through any easy and medium dungeons. But then come the lvl 5 champion ones... and with them comes utter disaster as monsters start to show up with abominable amounts of PROT(while we still have only TWO heroes who can counter this), SPD and additional effects to their attacks. At this point your tactics and overall preparedness barely matter as everything is purely in the hands of the game: the dice will decide your fate and in the final stages they are loaded against you.
Pros:
- Stunning and hauntingly beautiful art, music and atmosphere.
- One superb, amazing narrator.
Cons:
- Insane difficulty spike near game end without any reasonable means to offset it, tactics will only get you so far.
- Heroes actually start to feel weak as the game progresses: without a crit - you're very likely to end in the gutter. I really don't want to complain, but I simply fail to justify the reason why some filthy pigs, skeletons. bandits and mushroom abominations all have PROT, while my lvl 5 armour, even on Crusader and Man-at-Arms who actually wear plate, provides NONE of it.
- It feels terribly grindy. The amount of various relics required, especially Deeds, is atrocious. The amount of gold necessary for upgrades and the quality of upgrades themselves is DISGUSTING.
- The game actually ENCOURAGES you to sacrifice your first best group of heroes, as they will accumulate EXP faster than gear and at some point will not be able to handle the dungeons appropriate for them.

Spiral knights is a free-to-play, massively multiplayer, role-playing game that will entertain most gamers for hours on end. There are many reasons why you should download this game and there are only a few aspects of the game that people would dislike.
Pros:
It's free!
You don't need tonnes of memory to download it.
Unique graphics
The tutorial is fun and engaging.
You don't have to spend real money (although it is an option)
You can play with friends
Suitable for any age
It's fun slashing, shooting and exploding enemies
Adjustable difficulty
Auction house allows you to sell your items for the in-game currency
Items can be traded with other players
I have not seen any foul language sent through the chat
Cons:
Loading can be annoying,
It takes a minute or two just to switch area.
Being in haven or a mission with other people can cause the game to lag.
Shops and trading/crafting machines can become confusing.
No way of seeing how much damage your weapons do,
This is irritating because when you level up a weapon it doesn't tell you what difference it makes so from your point of view it doesn't make the slight bit of difference.
Overall, everyone should try out this game. You won't have to delete any files if you download it and if you can't stand the problems, you wouldn't have lost any money.

This is more of a review of my general impressions. I'll leave all the details for guides or other reviewers. I was on the fence about this game for a long time, and finally decided to take a risk... it paid off! I really enjoy it! 10 hrs of gameplay as I write this, and one or two characters are level 3.
Dungeons that remind me of adventuring when I played Dungeons & Dragons. Grim and difficult, and you usually left with a handful of hitpoints, but bags of treasure.
A game that has economy of gold that isn't too difficult to manage for a penny-pincher, but an economy of Stress that makes you second guess if you should send some of your heroes back into the fight so quickly.
The recruit aspect of the game feels a bit like XCOM, or Ogre Battle. I think building your teams is half the fun in games like this, and it's not too complicated.
Leveling them feels a bit like Final Fantasy Tactics, actually. Rotating who gets to fight, and who doesn't, to build them all over time. But the combat works more like a classic RPG turn-based game.
I've been waiting for a game that had this style of combat, but didn't look like it was made with RPG Maker.

This game is fantastic. There, simple and straight to the point. The game offers many unique elements and is an ultimate adventure. I recommend taking the time to sit and really PLAY the game. This game deserves to cost more. If it were 30$ I still would have bought it. While the game includes many different things to do and see, small additions could be made to make the game perfect. For example, the small picky things that aren't in the game, that NEED to be in the game. For example: Grass should grow and "spread" to other blocks/tiles.
Next, the soundtrack. This is honestly one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard in a video game. It fills every property it needs to.
There is, it being in beta, a bit of small tweaking needed. Number one tip in Starbound to all of you new players out there, Birds are JERKS. Never trust a bird. The birds can TWO hit you. Even though they WERE nerfed, they need more nerfing.
The game has many random spawns and honestly a nice storyline. The game offers 6 COMPLETELY different races, all of which require an incredible imagination to come up with. This is the first time in a long time that I've gone to the trouble and expense of buying a game close to its release date. Usually I'm the guy who just waits for steam sales. But man was I pumped for a new XCOM. The last game was one of my all time favorites and everything I saw about this game in the build up seemed so damn promising.
Now i'm disappointed.
I'll assume that the reader has played the previous game and has a reasonable understanding of how XCOM works, the sequel isn't a huge departure from the last game, but most of the changes have made it a less fun experience. I'll dot point them.
** Mission time limits. It was a major problem that in the last XCOM you really could move at a snails pace, abuse the overwatch feature and almost never take a hit. The EW expansion pack added the time sensitive meld resource to speed things up and encourage players to take calculated risks, but still ultimately left this choice up to the player. XCOM 2 has taken the choice completely out of the game. Most missions now require you to rush. For example I just failed a mission where I had only have 12 turns to fight off multiple groups of aliens, rescue a VIP and get to the extraction point that is way over on the other side of the map. I did not dawdle, in fact I rushed like crazy and took all kinds of risks to try to get it done in time. But it's early game and my troops are rookies and squaddies,They shoot about as accurately as a vision impaired Imperial stormtrooper and therefore it took a while for them finish off the guards. I ended the mission with the VIP extracted on the last turn but all four of my squadmates literally just one turn away from the arbitrary extraction zone box. One only two squares away! Bad luck, all four of them got left behind and captured. This is just frustratingly bad game design.
**The New ambush mechanic. This could be a great addition. It allows you to carefully surround unawhere advent troops, set up a nasty little kill box with soldiers in overwatch and smash them  before they can react. Oh, well, except for the aforementioned time limits. Spent 4 turns setting up the perfect ambush? That means that you won't meet the time limit and are now  screwed. Why would you introduce two new mechanics when one means that the other is rarely viable?
**The campaign map. Right from the start the game bombards you with things you should be doing, but it doesn't give you much in terms of how to achieve those things or even how to prioritise them. "Contact the resistance!!" "Take out that base!!" "Go get another engineer!!" "Get to your home base and organise some more troops!!" "Collect some supplies!!" "Build relay stations!!" "Go to the black market!!" "Dont let the red bar fill up!!!!!" ...............OK XCOM2, I'm two hours into my campaign and I have no idea how anything works yet, please chill.
**Lonnnnng injury recovery times: One of your troops received a single unlucky hit from the weakest unit in the game? Well he is now "gravely" wounded and you won't see him for three weeks. I hope you like playing with rookies.
I think there is a good game in here somewhere, probably being held in a dungeon and being creepily asked to apply lotion to it's skin. I'm confident that a modder will ride in to the rescue eventually, until then it's all just a bit sad really.

I'm finding this a really enjoyable game, with enough changed from EU/EW to make it worth being a new game, but enough the same that familiarity helps you out - within limits.
The one downside to me first of all - performance issues. The game claims to detect appropriate configuration settings for your system. It seems to be rather... optimistic, shall we say. If you're getting performance issues, turn things down. The game wants to use a lot of shiny graphics effects, and they really push a GPU. Turned a couple of things down or off, and it runs nicely for me now.
I've seen a lot of concern about the time limits on missions. I'm not sure what proportion of mission types have turn limits, but it seems like most missions have turn limits of some sort. Most of them are not "complete mission in this time", that's only on some forced evac missions. Most are "achieve main objective in this time". The turn limits don't force you to completely rush, but they prevent you from overwatch camping the whole time - which is probably the point. Even retaliations, the new version of terror missions, feels more highly pressured, because you need to rescue a minimum number of civis for the mission to be successful, and it's not a small number. I find the extra challenge of this stimulating, and I'm not one to play on high difficulties.
Combat works mostly like EU/EW, but with various little changes which are all to the better. Melee attacks - from the Ranger's sword or the Skulljack, for instance - put a new spin on things, and the fact you can take a move as part of the same action makes them much more useful. you can even choose which suitable adjacent tile to make the attaack from, which is handy - beware using the slash or skulljack command from the command bar, it will pick a tile for you, and while it appears to try to do it intelligently, it's often questionable. Reloading no longer ends turn (though does use an action), so if you are in a protracted firefight, thus not moving, you can stay where you are, reload and shoot.
The strategy level feels more pressured too. There's more going on, and soldiers will be injured through multiple missions early on. The new doom tracker, the Avatar Project, feels like an extra pressure as well. It keeps plugging along, and you need to beat it. I haven't beaten it yet, so I'm not sure if I'm keeping pace well enough, but it feels tough. It feels like I can't just farm, I need to actually push forward with the plot at all times. You're always doing something useful, of course, but you are called to do missions more often than you can manage with experienced troops by month 2, in my experience. Still, trying to get rookies through missions then increases your bench strength.
And as always, rookies are handy for one major thing... "rookie, take point!"
Graphics are a considerable improvement over EU/EW, in my opinion. More realist, less action figure/cartoony, with more fidelity generally. That's true even with various things turned down a bit.
I have no hesitation recommending this game, as long as you do actually meet the minimum requirements for system spec.

In a gaming universe now littered with embarrassingly amateurish "shovelware,"  insipid "AAA" titles that usually amount to little more than more of the same with minor tweaks (but with eye-bleeding super-realistic graphics that require mega-GPUs to get 25 fps - another sad trend as of late), and just plain scams where devs promise one thing, deliver another, and disappear into the ether with your cash, a game like Darkest Dungeon (DD) gives me hope that my once favorite hobby has some life in it yet.
What is amazing is that DD treads a well-worn road.  At its heart, DD is just another "roguelike" dungeon crawler.  But what elevates DD to its own lofty pedestal is a simple question: would professional dungeon crawlers develop PTSD?  At first, you laugh at the idea.  But then you stop and think about it.  Given how your typical fantasy dungeon crawl not only involves the type of brutal combat that any modern soldier would understand, but also a host of horrors - such as demons, giant spiders, and other abominations- on top of THAT, the answer would seem to be: oh heck yeah.  I guess they really would!
That is the heart of Darkest Dungeon.
Darkest Dungeon puts the player not just in charge of clearing dungeons, but also of managing the mental health of their assailed heroes.  In DD, the player must send teams of four adventurers (whom come from a nicely varied assortment of classes) to clear dungeons from around half a dozen thematic designs (ruins, warrens, etc.).  This part of the game is great fun.  Resembling a side-scroller, your adventurers, whom are brought to life with some wonderfully hand drawn artistry reminiscient of a Brothers Grimm fairytale, clear out a series of rooms and passages (randomly generated and populated with monsters, traps and loot, of course) in a dungeon of various sizes, some  so big that your team will need to camp inside a few times.  Such moments are a lot of fun as it involves its own unique gameplay of recuperation and campsite chatter.  Battle is handled in a wonderful turn-based fashion (love it; so glad to see devs getting away from click-fest RTS games) with both sides using their weapons and skills to strike each other down, something wonderfully enhanced by a narrator who comments on the action with a voice right out of, yes!,  a Grimm's fairytale.  But here is the important kicker: as your adventurers explore and battle their way through a dungeon, the game tracks stress points individually.  So, for example, if your man-at-arms suffers a critical hit at the hand of a foe, his stress level will go up, as might the stress of the other party members.  On the other hand, if he deals a devastating riposte, his stress might go down, and so on.  If stress accumulates to a certain degree, the adventurer might have a mental break.  It is here that the game begins to resemble Crusader Kings 2 in that each adventurer can accumulate a mix of up to a dozen vices and virtues that will affect their performance.  So, that man-at-arms who was almost killed might become a coward when he has his mental break, something that might debuff his stats or make him miss a turn.  Or, maybe he overcomes his fear and gets a virtue instead: he becomes heroic and urges his party to fight harder, reducing stress for all and buffing combat stats.  See how it works?  It is quite fun and adds a wonderful novelty to the game!  But be warned: if your adventurer becomes too stressed, he can actually die of a heartattack!
Speaking of heartattacks, that is what might happen to the gamer when he loses one of his star adventurers to permadeath.  Yeah, this game has that.  Personally, I love permadeath because nothing ruins a tale of adventuring heroism when the player can just "save and restore."  Face it: S&R is just immortality by another name.  How can there be true heroism if the hero is never truly at risk?  But that is just my two cents.  Be that as it may, this game has permadeath, so be prepared to lose some of your best players to the evil machninations of the "random number generator" that governs many aspects of this game.  If you hate such mechanics, than this game is not for you.
What happens when your adventurers leave a dungeon, assuming they survive?  Here, the game takes on an XCOM-like factor where base management comes into play.  In between dungeon crawls, the player can send his adventurers out with bags of gold to help them blow off steam in six different ways, from getting drunk, to praying at the abbey.  Of course, this takes these adventurers out of the game for at least a week - I say "at least a week" becayse random events occasionally trigger where, say, your knight gets drunk and wanders the town for two weeks in a state of inebriation!  LOL!  That actually happened to one of my adventurers.  Not only did he go AWOL for an extra week, be he lost the magic trinket I gave him!  Hence, the player needs to have a deep bench of adventurers to keep the gaming moving along, something that is not initially difficult as the local stage coach brings in a steady supply of new victi...er, adventurers.
In addition to managing the stress of your bench, you can also train new skills, upgrade armor and weapons, upgrade facilities, treat the mental and physical ailments your adventurers acquire in the darkest dungeons, and select the next adventure and get kitted out for it.
And that is pretty much the basics of the game in a nutshell.  Again, with the exception of the stress factor, nothing revolutionary.  But RedHook, with feedback from the community (this is EA done right!), applied so much thoughtfulness, attention to detail, and ol' fashioned love to their project that what has emerged out the other end may well be Game of the Year material for the PC.  Frankly, it has been a very long time since I have so thoroughly enjoyed a game.   With the devs already promising a new class of adventurer as well as "town events" in the near future gratis - the town does need some enlivening as it feels a little static and dull at times, so I am glad to hear this - I think the Darkest Dungeon has a VERY bright future ahead of it.  It certainly has already rocketed to the top of my favorite games list!

This is the first time in a long time that I've gone to the trouble and expense of buying a game close to its release date. Usually I'm the guy who just waits for steam sales. But man was I pumped for a new XCOM. The last game was one of my all time favorites and everything I saw about this game in the build up seemed so damn promising.
Now i'm disappointed.
I'll assume that the reader has played the previous game and has a reasonable understanding of how XCOM works, the sequel isn't a huge departure from the last game, but most of the changes have made it a less fun experience. I'll dot point them.
** Mission time limits. It was a major problem that in the last XCOM you really could move at a snails pace, abuse the overwatch feature and almost never take a hit. The EW expansion pack added the time sensitive meld resource to speed things up and encourage players to take calculated risks, but still ultimately left this choice up to the player. XCOM 2 has taken the choice completely out of the game. Most missions now require you to rush. For example I just failed a mission where I had only have 12 turns to fight off multiple groups of aliens, rescue a VIP and get to the extraction point that is way over on the other side of the map. I did not dawdle, in fact I rushed like crazy and took all kinds of risks to try to get it done in time. But it's early game and my troops are rookies and squaddies,They shoot about as accurately as a vision impaired Imperial stormtrooper and therefore it took a while for them finish off the guards. I ended the mission with the VIP extracted on the last turn but all four of my squadmates literally just one turn away from the arbitrary extraction zone box. One only two squares away! Bad luck, all four of them got left behind and captured. This is just frustratingly bad game design.
**The New ambush mechanic. This could be a great addition. It allows you to carefully surround unawhere advent troops, set up a nasty little kill box with soldiers in overwatch and smash them  before they can react. Oh, well, except for the aforementioned time limits. Spent 4 turns setting up the perfect ambush? That means that you won't meet the time limit and are now  screwed. Why would you introduce two new mechanics when one means that the other is rarely viable?
**The campaign map. Right from the start the game bombards you with things you should be doing, but it doesn't give you much in terms of how to achieve those things or even how to prioritise them. "Contact the resistance!!" "Take out that base!!" "Go get another engineer!!" "Get to your home base and organise some more troops!!" "Collect some supplies!!" "Build relay stations!!" "Go to the black market!!" "Dont let the red bar fill up!!!!!" ...............OK XCOM2, I'm two hours into my campaign and I have no idea how anything works yet, please chill.
**Lonnnnng injury recovery times: One of your troops received a single unlucky hit from the weakest unit in the game? Well he is now "gravely" wounded and you won't see him for three weeks. I hope you like playing with rookies.
I think there is a good game in here somewhere, probably being held in a dungeon and being creepily asked to apply lotion to it's skin. I'm confident that a modder will ride in to the rescue eventually, until then it's all just a bit sad really.

I'm finding this a really enjoyable game, with enough changed from EU/EW to make it worth being a new game, but enough the same that familiarity helps you out - within limits.
The one downside to me first of all - performance issues. The game claims to detect appropriate configuration settings for your system. It seems to be rather... optimistic, shall we say. If you're getting performance issues, turn things down. The game wants to use a lot of shiny graphics effects, and they really push a GPU. Turned a couple of things down or off, and it runs nicely for me now.
I've seen a lot of concern about the time limits on missions. I'm not sure what proportion of mission types have turn limits, but it seems like most missions have turn limits of some sort. Most of them are not "complete mission in this time", that's only on some forced evac missions. Most are "achieve main objective in this time". The turn limits don't force you to completely rush, but they prevent you from overwatch camping the whole time - which is probably the point. Even retaliations, the new version of terror missions, feels more highly pressured, because you need to rescue a minimum number of civis for the mission to be successful, and it's not a small number. I find the extra challenge of this stimulating, and I'm not one to play on high difficulties.
Combat works mostly like EU/EW, but with various little changes which are all to the better. Melee attacks - from the Ranger's sword or the Skulljack, for instance - put a new spin on things, and the fact you can take a move as part of the same action makes them much more useful. you can even choose which suitable adjacent tile to make the attaack from, which is handy - beware using the slash or skulljack command from the command bar, it will pick a tile for you, and while it appears to try to do it intelligently, it's often questionable. Reloading no longer ends turn (though does use an action), so if you are in a protracted firefight, thus not moving, you can stay where you are, reload and shoot.
The strategy level feels more pressured too. There's more going on, and soldiers will be injured through multiple missions early on. The new doom tracker, the Avatar Project, feels like an extra pressure as well. It keeps plugging along, and you need to beat it. I haven't beaten it yet, so I'm not sure if I'm keeping pace well enough, but it feels tough. It feels like I can't just farm, I need to actually push forward with the plot at all times. You're always doing something useful, of course, but you are called to do missions more often than you can manage with experienced troops by month 2, in my experience. Still, trying to get rookies through missions then increases your bench strength.
And as always, rookies are handy for one major thing... "rookie, take point!"
Graphics are a considerable improvement over EU/EW, in my opinion. More realist, less action figure/cartoony, with more fidelity generally. That's true even with various things turned down a bit.
I have no hesitation recommending this game, as long as you do actually meet the minimum requirements for system spec.

This is a truly beautifully crafted game that really puts you into the dark soul’s universe. It has stunning graphics and beautifully composed music and though the AI is quite stupid this is made up for by the game´s intense difficulty. This difficulty isn’t just because of cheeky game mechanics or just adding more health to the boss, instead this game focuses on keeping the high difficulty level fair.
In most games with such a high difficulty I would probably get angry because of the following mechanics:  unfair choke points, lag & bugs, Unpredictable attacks and most importantly GRINDING. Then when the boss would finally come it would be way to easy. In dark souls 3 you will see very few to none of these such things. So, this did quite surprisingly mean that if I ever died and got angry, the game was not to blame, I was to blame.
The best part of the game in my opinion is the bosses, they have great design and a relatively diverse yet predictable move set (except for Pontiff). The first one you will fight is Ludex Gundyr and he is one hell of a strappin fella as he can kill you with 3 hits and has tons of health which does make him a bit overwhelming for beginners like me. Eventually however, you will get used to these bosses but it does take a lot of learning and experience to get the knack of the game. So this is definitely something to keep in mind if you don´t like being challenged in this kind of way.
Pros: great visuals, great music, hard yet fair challenge
Cons: not good if you don´t like to be challenged

I am seriously enjoying this game. I preordered the Deluxe pask cause I knew I'd love it , and for the most part I think it has been well worth the wait. I have not logged as many hours as I really wanted to today, but I feel I still got a good feel for what the rest of the game will be like. now lets get one thing out of the way-
Yes, many missions have turn limits. OH NO, BETTER NOT BUY THIS GAME CAUSE IT WONT LET ME USE 150 TURNS/BATTLE. No, just stop. The tides have turned against humanity. You are part of a rebellion of sorts, and don't have the luxury of fighting the enemy when the time is right for you. This isn't supposed to be a softcore tactical game. Go play Farmville if you want casual. Turn limits actually make you make decisions. They make it feel more realistic, like you're a resistance leader instead of some slob back at HQ telling everyone not to move for two hours till the enemy gets so bored it kills itself.
Now that that's done, I'll go ahead and express my enjoyment of gameplay. It is exhillerating. Choose whether to run in guns blazing like EU or sneak into battle using the element of surprise. You cant hardly think when the chaos erupts. Enemies are challenging and extremely aggrevating (such is life for us XCOM vets). The Line of Sight (LoS) indicator lets you know what enviromental hazards you will encounter, whether you will break concealment, who you can see, and who can see you before moving to a new piece of cover, something that was extremely irritaiting in EU and is more beneficial now than ever.
It looks really good. Like REALLY good. On (what I got to see of) the game's high settings, from the cutscenes to the battlefield, everything is detailed and pretty. Unfortunatly, I am having severe issues with them and have resorted to playing on minimal, which is still giving me some performance issues. Nothing I can't look past, because it still looks good on minimal.
One of the best things for me was the implementation of semi-customisable weaponry. You can add colors and skins to make your ARs look prettyfied, and then add attachments you aquire in the field to your unit's weapons, increasing statistics without taking up precious item space. Also, you can more deeply customise your units from their armor skin to their attitude.
I failed to mention that XCOM 2 is combatable with the Steam Workshop, so expect lots of mods.
Other than that, it's just a really fun tactical game that I believe has a ton of playability and is the reason I will probably call in next week with Ebola.
10/10, would miss a point blank 92% shot with a shotgun again.
Edit: Now only a miniscule 55hrs into the game, I still highly reccomend XCOM 2 and I still don't understand where the hate is coming from. I'm literally playing this game on a HP laptop with an AMD-A10 and 8GB/memory, and have yet to suffer a crash or this "unplayability" I keep hearing about on y'alls higher end PCs. Some lag, some stuttering, but nothing that makes the game a pain to play, and nothing that makes me want to critisize a company which seems as surprised as us as to its unexpected performance issues. Not that I'm not dissapointed, because I am, but I honestly didn't expect it to be 100% functional on release day. I will hazard a bet that many of the issuse with the game will be resolved relativly soon. Regardless, I will continue to play this game as long as it still runs fine, and any fixes along the way are just nice perks.
Also, there is a mod to eliminate the timer on most every mission. To those of you still whining about timers, just be shushed. There's your ticket out of a challenge.
Edit: Now 119hrs into the game, and I can say that Legend difficulty is nearly impossible without mods. I love it. Nearly broken my Razer keyboard a few times and still have flashbacks to the ten times I'd have to replay the first mission before I could kill everyone. Other than that, Anarchy's Children is out (I don't use it much, but I do enjoy having the options there for my more "exotic" characters). Mods help freshen up the game too, bringing new guns, classes, enemies, maps, and pretty much anything you can think of. I still love this game, and don't play on stopping anytime soon. Well, till I fracture my wrist on this oak table anywho....

Okay, first let me say that I have given this game a thumbs up ( changed to thumbs down, read on ) because there are some fantastic modders out there in the community that will make it enjoyable, and indeed they have already made a start on that.  As for Firaxis.  They have learned nothing from the mistakes they made with the first game, and likewise they have learned nothing from the fact the long war mod was and is widely considered a much better experience than the vanilla game, even though some of the guys that made the long war worked closely with Firaxis this time around.  I can only assume that Meier and his team are suffering from the 'We are developers and we know best' syndrome.
Apart from the bugs ( of which there are many ) the game is badly optimized, the camera frequently awkward ( same as it's predecessor ) and the load times both heading to and coming back from missions tedious.  Gameplay is much the same as the first game with some minor changes but I think that someone at Firaxis is humping the stopwatch, as evidenced by the massive overuse of timed missions ( so many turns before this or that blows up etc. ) These types of missions are alright when used sparingly to shake things up a bit, but when used as much as this it takes 99% of the strategic planning away and turns it into a sprint for the finish line.  Thankfully there is already a mod available to disable these timers and the game is much better for it.  My next gripe with the core game is alien deployment.  This may sound petty but when you are sent on a mission to protect something, and the game starts by putting a Muton Berserker a couple of tiles away from it when your squad starts on the other side of the map....well, you can see where the frustration comes from.  Also like the first game it is not unusual to see shots pass straight through walls etc. as line of sight is massively flawed, and this is something I would have hoped was fixed for Xcom 2 as well as the poor pathing but that appears to have got even worse, with your troops happy to run straight through flames ( setting fire to themselves ) instead of taking a simple sidestep around them.  This is also true for other pathing decisions.  As an example, I had my sniper stood one tile away from a drainpipe and I wanted him on top of the building.  Instead of climbing said drainpipe he smashed through a window, ran past two aliens, up some stairs and then climbed a ladder, which of course revealed the location of all my squad to the enemy ( if one person is seen they are all seen, which doesn't work the other way around btw ).  In short.  Out of the box the game is a bit of a mess that could have done with more time in the oven.  The modders will make it better so wait for a decent full conversion mod like the long war and then pick the game up in a future steam sale.
Update after 21 hours of play:  I will not get to 22 hours until some major patches or mods fix what is starting to feel like an unfinished trainwreck.  My main gripe isn't with the timers, although they do run a close second.  My main gripe is with the line of sight which simply doesn't work.  It is entirely pointless having buildings, walls etc.  when the aliens can see right through them and shoot your men like the cover isn't there at all.  Even full cover behind an intact building with two internal walls and two external walls is useless.  The alien simply shoots through the lot of them having pinpointed your position with it's super x-ray vision.  For now there are better games to play.  In fact, if you don't mind 90s style graphics take a look at xenonauts for a much better interpretation of the great game that the original X-Com was.  Changed to a thumbs down until the thing is fixed.

I keep having trouble writing an objective review for Darkest Dungeon, but I'm going to try again, this time without touching on anything but how I personally find it.
I love this game. To me the game's strengths are:
-The theme. How much will you sacrifice and what will it cost others? Mental illness, stress, disease, heroes dying, learning when to flee all give it an interesting feel. Is the game unforgiving? Sort of. You'll lose people, but you can always get more.
-Art style. This is what originally drew me to the game.
-Music. Brilliant, tense and exciting, with horror leanings that still sound pleasing. It's almost halfway between a horror soundtrack and an action soundtrack, which fits.
-Sound. All of the sound work is amazing, but the best bit is the narrator. If they didn't have him the game would actually be nowhere near as fun as it is. He gives simple dungeon running context and basically sells the mythology.
-Combat. Simplistic in some ways, thoughtful in others. Position based, focused on knowing what works on different enemies, working out strategies, resistances, etc. Not very complicated, can be unforgiving if you mess up.
-You always have to bench someone for some reason (sickness, mental illness, etc), so you have to switch up people and try new combinations. By the same turn when someone dies it gives you a new chance to see what you haven't tried before.
-Easy to learn, hard to master? That's how I felt.
(Again, opinion. You lose a lot of people to stupid stuff at the start simply because the game doesn't tell you what any dungeon object will do. That could be considered a weakness, personally I liked learning things myself.)
The games only negative for me is that there really is only one style of play: dungeon delving. It's a simple, inexpensive game, so I can forgive it. Also, people bring up RNG. Yes it is there, but learning to manage it (Torch mechanic, load out, camping) is part of the experience.
Oh, also, ignore the RPG tag. Character personality is there, but the skill system is very light, so...
So yeah, I like it.

Darkest Dungeon features a very compeling combination of tactics RPG, roguelike dungeon crawler and base management. In similar way to something like XCOM, the game works on two layers. A dungeon crawling layer where you explore a randomly generated dungeon with a team of 4 heroes and a base management layer where you manage your roster of up to 25 heroes.
The game feels very polished, the art style is amazing and the narration is suberb both in writing and voice acting.
There was some controversy about how the game evolved over time and I feel it highlighted a main issue with the game. I feel the game only works if the difficult it just right... hard enough to fit the gothic/lovecraftian theme but not so hard as to feel frustrating. It feels just right for me but that is a very subjective thing... I've some exprience with similar mechanics but I'm far from being able to exploit the gameplay to it's fullest... so I'm probably towards the mid-high end in terms of mechanical expertise. Players falling too far away from me might feel that the game is either easy or too hard. It's close to impossible to get this right for everyone but the devs added some options to make the game easier, so you may try those if you feel the game is too hard.
The game allows for huge degree of randomness... but I feel it works in the game's favor. It feels great when the game slips to either side of the scale and things go horribly wrong or awesomely right. The game really shines when you start to snowball towards towards a failed mission and you need to decide if you retreat to save your heroes or try to make a few more rooms to at least recover part of your investment in the mission.
Overall an excellent game. The mechanics are familiar but the way they're combined feels very refreshing. A very smart use of the lovecraftian theme in both aesthetics and mechanics. One of the more expertly crafted games of the last few years.

Okay, first let me say that I have given this game a thumbs up ( changed to thumbs down, read on ) because there are some fantastic modders out there in the community that will make it enjoyable, and indeed they have already made a start on that.  As for Firaxis.  They have learned nothing from the mistakes they made with the first game, and likewise they have learned nothing from the fact the long war mod was and is widely considered a much better experience than the vanilla game, even though some of the guys that made the long war worked closely with Firaxis this time around.  I can only assume that Meier and his team are suffering from the 'We are developers and we know best' syndrome.
Apart from the bugs ( of which there are many ) the game is badly optimized, the camera frequently awkward ( same as it's predecessor ) and the load times both heading to and coming back from missions tedious.  Gameplay is much the same as the first game with some minor changes but I think that someone at Firaxis is humping the stopwatch, as evidenced by the massive overuse of timed missions ( so many turns before this or that blows up etc. ) These types of missions are alright when used sparingly to shake things up a bit, but when used as much as this it takes 99% of the strategic planning away and turns it into a sprint for the finish line.  Thankfully there is already a mod available to disable these timers and the game is much better for it.  My next gripe with the core game is alien deployment.  This may sound petty but when you are sent on a mission to protect something, and the game starts by putting a Muton Berserker a couple of tiles away from it when your squad starts on the other side of the map....well, you can see where the frustration comes from.  Also like the first game it is not unusual to see shots pass straight through walls etc. as line of sight is massively flawed, and this is something I would have hoped was fixed for Xcom 2 as well as the poor pathing but that appears to have got even worse, with your troops happy to run straight through flames ( setting fire to themselves ) instead of taking a simple sidestep around them.  This is also true for other pathing decisions.  As an example, I had my sniper stood one tile away from a drainpipe and I wanted him on top of the building.  Instead of climbing said drainpipe he smashed through a window, ran past two aliens, up some stairs and then climbed a ladder, which of course revealed the location of all my squad to the enemy ( if one person is seen they are all seen, which doesn't work the other way around btw ).  In short.  Out of the box the game is a bit of a mess that could have done with more time in the oven.  The modders will make it better so wait for a decent full conversion mod like the long war and then pick the game up in a future steam sale.
Update after 21 hours of play:  I will not get to 22 hours until some major patches or mods fix what is starting to feel like an unfinished trainwreck.  My main gripe isn't with the timers, although they do run a close second.  My main gripe is with the line of sight which simply doesn't work.  It is entirely pointless having buildings, walls etc.  when the aliens can see right through them and shoot your men like the cover isn't there at all.  Even full cover behind an intact building with two internal walls and two external walls is useless.  The alien simply shoots through the lot of them having pinpointed your position with it's super x-ray vision.  For now there are better games to play.  In fact, if you don't mind 90s style graphics take a look at xenonauts for a much better interpretation of the great game that the original X-Com was.  Changed to a thumbs down until the thing is fixed.
