You should already know: it's a rogue-like dungeon crawler with classes you recruit and send on dungeon crawls.
Now that the game is officially released and post-release-patched, here is a new review:
The game is fantastic. The different classes and abilities mean you can play two runs in a row with totally different battle play styles. The narration and theme are amazing and consistent and add a ton.
The concept works really well. Rebuilding the town with dungeon crawlers as your expendables fits "money run" or "artifact run" into the theme of the game so even when you are grinding for something it still feels like a natural progression.
The balance is (IMO) really good. You are low on things and people for a long time, by design. Your dungeon crawlers die a lot, by design. But it's all in service of the theme, and as you rebuild and get better everything else gets better too.
Also, importantly, they have added a lot of options to change the gameplay to make it easier by toning down or eliminating various types of difficulty. I find the default difficulty fantastic but I'm also a big believer in letting people choose to turn off things they dislike.
I paid $20 for this the first week it was on Steam, and played it for over 100 hours while it was still in Early Access. Now that the final game is out and there are new classes and areas and story content that I've never seen, I feel confidant that I will get another 100 hours. As some one who never pays full price for a game, this is a game I bought at full price and I'm glad I did.

I Dont Write Many Reviews But I Have To Write One For Trove. Before Trove I Thought CSGO, G-Mod And Arma 3 Were The Best Games I've Ever Played.... I Was Wrong. I First Looked At The ScreenShots Of Trove, Thought Meh Looks Bad, And I Didn't Feel Like I Would Get Into It So I Ignored It. After About A Week After Its Release On Steam I Was Pretty Bored With No New Games To Play. (I Use To Play A Lot Of CSGO) SO I Was Like Why Not Try Trove, If I Dont Like It I'll Just Uninstall It. First Hour Or So. Ok Not Bad I'm Liking The Shadow Hunter (My First Class). I Get To Max Class Level(20) And I'm Hooked To The Game. I Can't Stop Playing It Now. I've Been Playing For About 2 Weeks Straight The Date I Have Written This Review And I Cant Stop Playing It Now. At First I Didnt Have Any Friends Playing Trove. So I Started My Own Club, And I Was Having Tons Of Fun With My Club Members And Everything But It Was Still Not Extremely Fun. I Eventually Got A Few Friends To Try Tove Out. They Ended Up Enjoying It Also. So We Started Playing Together. From That Moment The Game Went From 6/10 To 9/10. It Was Almost One Of The Best Games I Have Ever Played. After Some Time More And More Of My Friends Were Getting Trove. Which Meant Larger Groups To Dungeon And Do Shadow Arenas With. And Around That Time My Club Kicked Off And Started To Really Grow. It Got Up To ~80 Members. Which Was Pretty Impressive To Me Since I Never Joined A Club Before Hand To See How A Good Club Is Run. Then From That Point Onward This Game Became The Best Game I Am Yet To have Played And Its Going To Be Hard For A New Game To Come Close. There Is So Much To Do In This Game That You Will Always Have Somthing To Do Everyday. Wether It Be To Get To A Certain Mastery Level, Get A Class To Max Level, Or Get Shadow Weapons From Shadow Arenas To Get Radiant Weapons. There Is JUst So Much To Do And More Is Coming, I Cannot Wait To See Whats To Come. In The End I Would Rate This Game 11/10. If You Are Yet To Play Trove I Would Highly Reccomend You To Atleast Download And Give It A Try. It Does Not Take Very Long To Download And Even Less To Uninstall If You Didnt Like It. If You Are A Fan Of MMORPG Games Such As WOW,Diablo,GW2,etc You Have No Excuess To Not Try This Game Out.
The Only Cons I Can Think Of Are:
The Recent Sudden Hotfixes/Patches.
(They Are Pretty Anoying But If You Get A Max Level Class(20) You Unlock The PTS(Public Test Server) Which Is Up During Live Server Downtime.
(This Game Is Just 3 Weeks Out Of Beta, And The Devs Are Putting A Lot Of Time And Effort Into This Game Even Though It Is A Free To Play So The Sudden Hotfixes Are Understandable)
Also I Know A Lot Of People Who Tried This Game In The Past Hated The Queue Wait Times To Get In The Game Which Were About 30 mins. Guess What... Its History, No More Wait Time At All.
Thats Really About It. Like I Said Before Atleast Give It A Try, Who Knows.... You Might Get Hooked.

As for me, the art is great, the music is great, victory is satisfying, and I was already a fan of FTL: Faster than Light and other games with forms of permadeath. Every mission you undertake is a battle against physical and mental punishment for your party members, and you must manage the two if you want to have any success.
I took a long break from this game earlier in 2015 (then in early access) and even with my prior knowledge of gameplay mechanics (which haven't changed, largely, since then) I experienced a party wipe within my first 10 missions.
Absolutely recommend. Especially with a pair of good headphones.

To start I want to say that this review is based only on my own playing experience of the game with no bias to members of any side of the games community or to the developers.  I don't know if the developers are good people or bad people or if other reviewers for that matter are either.  I have not taken part in any community discussions and have no interest in doing so.  From just reading reviews my own opinion is that their is a great deal of hatred and bias that resulted in negative rants masked as reviews.  I do not doubt that the people writing them hate the game but I believe it is not possible for them to be objective because they either hate members of the community who have opposing views or hate the developers for whatever reason.  That does not mean that they are completely incapable of finding some legitimate faults in this game but it does mean they may blow them far out of portion to serve their bias.   I can think of no game I have ever played that is perfect. This explanation is made in hope that readers will be able to better put in perspective varied reviews of this game.
So if you would like to enjoy this game I would recommend that you avoid like the plague any forums discussing it for the following reasons.  First hints just from reviews here suggest they are hostile environments.  Secondly because I believe the fun in this game is from discovering the characters and strategies as you play.  You could possibly go to some forum and find the perfect strategy now I will note here that I don't know if that strategy exists but have seen it claimed in reviews with less play time then I have.
I can tell you that every Fantasy, Turn-Based, Strategy type game I have played and can think of has eventually turned into a grind and usually after many hours of fun learning the best strategies to use, there are always some strategies that fail and others that work, what point would there be in making new games if every game used the same system.
I can also tell you that after 17 hours I am still leveling heroes and upgrading manor buildings.  I am still experimenting with the many character classes and their varied abilities and I am still learning in what priority I should remove the varied negative character traits, sicknesses or stresses with my limited gold.  Maybe after another 17 hours I will have all that sorted out maybe at that point it will start to feel like a grind. Things considered I can say I feel I have already gotten my dollar value out of it.

To finalize I would say I do recommend this game and that the best way is to play it like you would a point and click adventure game. Don't read the entire clue book before you play. Play the game and if your stumped get help for the issue that stumps you then close the clue book until you need it again.

To sum up this game in a phrase: A beautiful thousand piece puzzle with a few pieces missing.
The game itself has created a SciFy Space Minecraft itch for me that only it can satisfy, it being the love child of Terreria and Eve Online.
The gameplay is basic Minecraft style, you explore stuff, you gather stuff, you craft stuff, and you kill stuff that wants to destory your stuff, or stuff you in their bellies for dinner. The typical stuff you do in any game inspreed by minecraft. But what makes the game different is the fact you have to explore planets to find that stuff, and you will have to leave the first planet you land on, siince the planets tend to be smaller so that one could cross them in about ten minutes non-stop, (depending on the size).
The maps you are given are huge, but in truth, seemed a bit wasteful. I personally never went to more the three different stars in a sector and the rest I ignored. Plus their are five different sectors in total, amking their seem like infinate amount of stars. Like I said it's nice but a bit much... and it can mess up you game if you forget what planet you were settling on before moving on the beta sector, and say you forgot something, like your favorite pair of pants at your old home, and you for what planet you were on, you can say bye-bye to your pants.
But that is one grip of many I have, and the potential for something fabilous is clearly visable in the game, and out weigh the bad and buggy errors, (like some of your furnature randomly despawning thanks to water, or soemthing like that).
To sum up, if you want to see Minecraft in space, with different races and planets, this game is your muse until Minecraft follows behind.

Darkest Dungeon features a very compeling combination of tactics RPG, roguelike dungeon crawler and base management. In similar way to something like XCOM, the game works on two layers. A dungeon crawling layer where you explore a randomly generated dungeon with a team of 4 heroes and a base management layer where you manage your roster of up to 25 heroes.
The game feels very polished, the art style is amazing and the narration is suberb both in writing and voice acting.
There was some controversy about how the game evolved over time and I feel it highlighted a main issue with the game. I feel the game only works if the difficult it just right... hard enough to fit the gothic/lovecraftian theme but not so hard as to feel frustrating. It feels just right for me but that is a very subjective thing... I've some exprience with similar mechanics but I'm far from being able to exploit the gameplay to it's fullest... so I'm probably towards the mid-high end in terms of mechanical expertise. Players falling too far away from me might feel that the game is either easy or too hard. It's close to impossible to get this right for everyone but the devs added some options to make the game easier, so you may try those if you feel the game is too hard.
The game allows for huge degree of randomness... but I feel it works in the game's favor. It feels great when the game slips to either side of the scale and things go horribly wrong or awesomely right. The game really shines when you start to snowball towards towards a failed mission and you need to decide if you retreat to save your heroes or try to make a few more rooms to at least recover part of your investment in the mission.
Overall an excellent game. The mechanics are familiar but the way they're combined feels very refreshing. A very smart use of the lovecraftian theme in both aesthetics and mechanics. One of the more expertly crafted games of the last few years.

You should already know: it's a rogue-like dungeon crawler with classes you recruit and send on dungeon crawls.
Now that the game is officially released and post-release-patched, here is a new review:
The game is fantastic. The different classes and abilities mean you can play two runs in a row with totally different battle play styles. The narration and theme are amazing and consistent and add a ton.
The concept works really well. Rebuilding the town with dungeon crawlers as your expendables fits "money run" or "artifact run" into the theme of the game so even when you are grinding for something it still feels like a natural progression.
The balance is (IMO) really good. You are low on things and people for a long time, by design. Your dungeon crawlers die a lot, by design. But it's all in service of the theme, and as you rebuild and get better everything else gets better too.
Also, importantly, they have added a lot of options to change the gameplay to make it easier by toning down or eliminating various types of difficulty. I find the default difficulty fantastic but I'm also a big believer in letting people choose to turn off things they dislike.
I paid $20 for this the first week it was on Steam, and played it for over 100 hours while it was still in Early Access. Now that the final game is out and there are new classes and areas and story content that I've never seen, I feel confidant that I will get another 100 hours. As some one who never pays full price for a game, this is a game I bought at full price and I'm glad I did.

A lot of people have said that Fallout 4 "isn't really a fallout game" because of how Bethesda changed up gameplay formula.  This iteration of the series has nerfed a lot of the "RPG" elements that fans came to know and love, and have focused a lot more on the "Action" side of things, which has undeniably changed the way the game is played.
Some things I didn't like:
Dialogue - I really appreciated Fallout 4's text-based dialogue, with numerous options for response, and detailed text available before I chose a response.  The "button wheel" in Fallout 4 leaves very few options, and often leads to surprises when an option you chose turns out to be something you didn't want to do.
Voice Acting - I'll say upfront that I have no problem with voice acting from NPCs, that's been a staple in fallout games forever -- Giving the Sole Survivor a voice on the other hand kinda breaks the immersion, and also causes the limited dialogue issues.
Character Building - The lack of RPG elements make it difficult to build a character with a certain set of flaws, or specializations for the purposes of roleplaying.  You're more or less forced to keep things middle of the road, or risk incredibly tedious gameplay.
Some things I liked
The Environment - Gameplay aside, there's no mistaking you're in a Fallout game.  The aesthetics are spot on, and the enormous environment is incredible to explore. The colour palate is much easier on the eyes than previous games, without being too bright or saturated.
The amount of content - There's SO MUCH to do, so many factions to discover, so many side quests and missions to take, and so many places to explore.  If you're into looking around and trying to understand the world you're in, this is for you.  I haven't even managed to get the main storyline finished, I keep finding so many distractions
Crafting System - I enjoy knocking together and modifying weapons.  This adds an RPG element that has been missing from previous games.
Some things I don't have a strong opinion on, but noticed anyway
Weapon Damage - Weapons don't wear out like they did in previous games.  No need to do repairs, just modifications
Settlements - I enjoy knocking together some settlements, but the constant calls for "HELP US" get a bit annoying over time.  The more settlements you get, the more time you have to spend bailing your settlers out.
VATS - Doesn't freeze time anymore, requiring quicker thinking than previous.  While I previously enjoyed the low-stress VATS of earlier games, the new VATS seems more suited for an action RPG, making you need to think on your feet a lot more.
Overall, Fallout 4 is a gorgeous game, and I'd recommend it to anyone who wants to play a great game.  Don't go in expecting the full "Fallout" experience, and you'll have a lot more fun.

I like Spiral Knights, To keep this as short as I can because I'm sure your busy, this is the one MMO that clicked. Mabinogi is nice and WoW is fine while DC Universe Online gives you too much too soon, Spiral Knights keeps be coming back.
Firstly, I love the art style. It looks wonderful. Every weapon might seem a little 'fisher price' for others tastes but there's the extra details on them to give them a battle-worn feel. Plus, there's a clear progression in how each equipment changes as it upgrades. It's like Pokemon and it's satisfying.
The world seems vast and enjoyable that I think Three Rings have barely scratched the surface of. The idea of a world that is an ever changing dungeon is a pleasing idea to me. Especially the idea of you being some combination of fighter and miner. Digdug would crap himself trying to get through some of the monsters in this game.
The combat is a sort of top-down dungeon crawler. If you've ever played Alien Swam, it should be familiar. The interesting thing is the weapon choices. While you have to have a shield, you can choose to fill your two weapon slots with swords, pistols and bombs. Swords are the middle ground, offering a decent amount of damage but you need to be right up close to the baddies. Bombs take the longest to get up but offer the ability to drop and then run, keeping you out of the way of damage. Pistols are weaker but they allow for far more range with your attacks, keeping distance between you and your target. On top of that, each weapon has a special damage type that could either cause more or less damage depending on enemy weakenesses and resistances.
While I don't consider myu self that great at it, the combat is pretty simple but fun in this random weirdos opinion.
And then there's the Battle Sprites. These are virtual pets that offer extra attacks and abilities as they grow up like an omnipresent Pokemon. They don't break the game but they are useful with currently three types: damage, poison and healing. They don't get in the way and can actually be ignored if you want, which is fine by me but I like that the Battle Sprites give you boons to attacks or defence as they grow on top of boosting their own attacks.
Now, it sounds great right?
The issue is how Three Rings pays for all this...The Energy system demands money from you or you will go insane. Energy is an extra currency that works over the top of Crowns (Spiral Knight's money). Energy buys extra lives when you die, upgrades, various special weapons and more. Also, it's never really given to you for free. You either pay for it in Crowns, which is found within the game by simply playing, or with hard cash.
Other free to play games are happy for you to just chip in a few coins their way occationally if you feel like it.
Spiral Knights demands that you throw them cash in order to get the best equipment possible without grinding for half an eon to get enough Crowns. At lower levels of the game, this is harsh grinding if you don't have the cash to pay for Energy. To add to the issue, the levels are not that varied. They're not bad, they just repeat a lot. So, in order to get that cash, you have to run through the game over and over and over and over. If your gear isn't good enough, you'll die over and over, losing any heat (Experience, used for upgrading weapons) you've earned. You'll keep your Crowns but it's still no fun to be crushed into the dirt over and over just for some game essencials.
To add to this, the game demands that you have a certain level in all of your equipment before going forwards. Yes, this shows that the game's difficulty is about to spike upwards and you'll need the ugrade across the board but the issues with grinding come to slap you right across the face. If you don't grind though the same 10 or 20 levels, you cannot continue.
I cannot recomend this for casual or general players. It's enjoyable but I can imagine a lot of players just giving up at the first equipment check point. I would recomend giving it a go to see how else to make an MMO but I can't say that the Business Model for this game is the best compared to it's competitors. If your not afraid of some awful grinding, you can find some enjoyable gameplay here.
Oh! Three Rings? Make a Single Player game based on this! It would be awesome! I want to see more of this world.

Dark Souls 3 is the continuation of the Souls series into its final chapter. For those that don't know, Souls is a difficult series that follows the story of an undead individual trying to link the fire.
Dark Souls III's graphics, to be honest, can only be described in one word. Breathtaking. You'll be whisked away to endless vistas of mountainous beauty, gothic cathedrals glinting under the light of a pearlescent moon, and sharp crags jutting out from the dusty ground. The graphics are ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. The lighting and atmosphere produced by this game is nearly unrivaled and the artstyle is stupidly good. Coherent and immersive on a scale only seen in masterpieces.
4.5/5
The gameplay of Souls can't really be simplified down to a mere paragraph as it is extraordinarily rich. However, note this: You WILL die. A lot. It doesn't detract from the experience whatsoever though- it rather enhances it. Each death is a lesson and you learn a little more each time you die. The combat in Dark Souls 3 follows a similar formula as the other games except there are hints of Bloodborne's faster pace here and there. It's pretty damn glorious to be honest and the many weapons and spells available have varied movesets and weapon arts that make it feel entirely different each time you swap out your build. Overall pretty ♥♥♥♥ing amazing gameplay. The lore is immersive as ♥♥♥♥ as well and is as deep as the abyss. Better equip artorias' ring.
5/5
The port of Dark Souls 3 is amazingly good compared to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ port of the first game. However, it has one single issue that PC players may find disconcerting: All the controls are shown in console buttons. Nevertheless it's not too hard to learn how to play using mouse and keyboard but I feel that an Xbox controller feels much better (not something I say a lot) and as such players should use one.
4/5
Wow. Oh wow. Holy mother of ♥♥♥♥ the soundtrack in this game is utterly incredible. It's a masterpiece. The game itself does not feature much music in levels themselves due to it being contradictory to the lonesome atmosphere FROM Software creates. However the boss music is absolutely incredible and many times I've been in awe of the beauty of the music and subsequently gotten squashed, lacerated, and defiled by the numerous bosses of the game. Easily one of the best soundtracks I've heard: It's grim, sombre and fits the atmosphere flawlessly.
5/5
The level design of Dark Souls 3 will ♥♥♥♥ you over as much as it can. Enemies are placed in the most irritating and unexpected locations and the areas themselves are sprawling and massive. Do I love it? Absolutely. Games have long since departed from creative and scummy level design that is meant to screw the player over and it is oh so refreshing to play something that does. Damn good.
4.5/5

To start I want to say that this review is based only on my own playing experience of the game with no bias to members of any side of the games community or to the developers.  I don't know if the developers are good people or bad people or if other reviewers for that matter are either.  I have not taken part in any community discussions and have no interest in doing so.  From just reading reviews my own opinion is that their is a great deal of hatred and bias that resulted in negative rants masked as reviews.  I do not doubt that the people writing them hate the game but I believe it is not possible for them to be objective because they either hate members of the community who have opposing views or hate the developers for whatever reason.  That does not mean that they are completely incapable of finding some legitimate faults in this game but it does mean they may blow them far out of portion to serve their bias.   I can think of no game I have ever played that is perfect. This explanation is made in hope that readers will be able to better put in perspective varied reviews of this game.
So if you would like to enjoy this game I would recommend that you avoid like the plague any forums discussing it for the following reasons.  First hints just from reviews here suggest they are hostile environments.  Secondly because I believe the fun in this game is from discovering the characters and strategies as you play.  You could possibly go to some forum and find the perfect strategy now I will note here that I don't know if that strategy exists but have seen it claimed in reviews with less play time then I have.
I can tell you that every Fantasy, Turn-Based, Strategy type game I have played and can think of has eventually turned into a grind and usually after many hours of fun learning the best strategies to use, there are always some strategies that fail and others that work, what point would there be in making new games if every game used the same system.
I can also tell you that after 17 hours I am still leveling heroes and upgrading manor buildings.  I am still experimenting with the many character classes and their varied abilities and I am still learning in what priority I should remove the varied negative character traits, sicknesses or stresses with my limited gold.  Maybe after another 17 hours I will have all that sorted out maybe at that point it will start to feel like a grind. Things considered I can say I feel I have already gotten my dollar value out of it.

To finalize I would say I do recommend this game and that the best way is to play it like you would a point and click adventure game. Don't read the entire clue book before you play. Play the game and if your stumped get help for the issue that stumps you then close the clue book until you need it again.

It is good, but let me share my main concerns -- knowing fully well I will face a lot of disagreement from the DS-Community.
I understand that the game has to be hard, but is the following really necessary?
[Note: These are my initial impressions, as you can see that my play-time is severely limited. I feel like first impressions of someone relatively unknown to the Dark Souls series still hold value to some extent.]
1. When enemies attack you and you try to dodge by walking to their side, they magically float across the ground, doing a 90 degrees spin, and hit you.
2. I hate spamming Dodge in games, and this game forces you to. Hated it in Witcher 3, hate it Dark Souls 3.
3. Everything about this game feels spammy, apart from the ambience. For example, bosses spam attacks, giving you VERY little breathing room, and with a low stamina pool; boss fights just feel hopeless -- more so than they are supposed to feel.
4. I like repetition and having to fight for my achievements, but as someone whose first DS experience is with DSIII, the game makes to big a jump in difficulty in the beginning. It starts off really easy, but then immediately becomes a very repetitive and frustrating experience. This, along with previously mentioned points, leave a very sour first impression, which is a shame because I LOVE the atmosphere and idea of a genuinly challenging game. There is, however, a difference between challenging and unfairness.
5. It feels like autistic savants would love this game. It is clear that the majority of your progress is based on stupidly memorizing what is going to happen, which deminishes any notion to have to apply actual strategy. 'Well, at least I know how this particular section works for the next run, hurr hurr.' Lame. Lame. Lame.
6. Where is the story in the beginning? There is next to nothing of it after the initial cutscene -- it just jumps straight to what Dark Souls is known for; extreme difficulty. Damn, and I mean, DAMN shame.
7. To return to the topic of boss fights; what the hell is even going on? I am usually standing underneath a boss dodging and attacking, but there is no sense to be made out of their clunky animations and creative-but-confusing models. I know this is something that will improve as I progress, but it seems a boss might as well have an animation where they're eating ice-cream and I will randomly get hit in the face for half my HP.
I am excited about this game beyond belief, but the 'This game is hard and will make you rage'-tag is such a shame, as, again, it has great ambience, and probably a great story later on.

So, I see a lot of people talkinga bout and reviewing the game.
Rather than post a bunch of TL;DR I would sum up the game as thus:
1) Difficult
2) Has a learning curve
3) Dungeon crawling, which is by design going to be grindy
4) Limited (and mostly situational) RPG elements, mostly related to which powers / abilities you choose.
5) Excellent voice work and atmosphere
DD is a dungeon crawl using four characters that will often seem diffcult to suceed in. Death is expected and the learning curve is high.  The game is stylistically good and I have not experienced any bugs or crashes althoguh I believe some others have.

Fallout 4 has some great side stories, locations and NPCs, the trouble is you have to play enough of the really terrible, totally railroaded main story in order to get to & unlock some of those things. That's pretty much what killed it for me.
"It's Skyrim with guns," people said, which sounds great, except it's not. In Skyrim, if you don't want to be the Dragonborn, you can still do pretty much ALL the other quests without having to touch the main one. You get a lot more freedom to decide who your character is & how you want that to affect their actions. It's immersive. In Fallout 4, you're pretty much locked-into the main story AND character. I felt like I was playing someone else's character, but I'd signed up to play mine. If we could ignore the main story & just play the rest of the game it wouldn't be that bad, but if for example you want to join the Brotherhood of Steel, you have to play the main story to a certain point. Furthermore, there are several points where the main story just doesn't make sense. There were several times where out loud I asked, "y tho?"
I couldn't even bring myself to finish. From what I've heard, there are several endings depending on which faction you pick, so there is SOME freedom later, but by that point I'll have been forced through so much craptacular story that I won't care. I don't even care now. This story is a turd wrapped in another turd with some liquid turd condiment.
The base / settlement building was a really cool idea, but in the end it's mostly meaningless. Walls & guarded entryways don't actually stop attackers from getting in - they can basically teleport in, but only during settlement attacks. Ok great, ghouls & super mutants can teleport, got it. Settlers are basically unkillable too - invaders can shoot them enough so they sit down, but can never kill them, even with a mini-nuke. If for some reason you don't defend the settlement, even a lot of defense still makes it basically a toss-up as to whether the attack is successful or not.
Survival mode made the game more "fun," but less immersive. I spent a lot of time digging through menus to drink water, and while yes, I drink a lot of water in real life, it breaks immersion when I have to enter a menu, scroll down, and click. Yay bullets have weight and not being able to fast travel. That's all well & good, but constantly having to pull that menu up  reminded me that it was just a video game.
Likewise, V.A.T.S. broke immersion & made me feel like I was just clicking rather than really shooting a gun. Unfortunately, a lot of the melee & pistol perks require the use of V.A.T.S.
The voice acting was good, better than most of the big name voice actors in Skyrim, even. NPCs had some great stories & dialogue. Gun play was good. Could've been better, but I'm satisfied with what they did. It's well-polished too - depressing, filled with dead things & trash & the minutia that I imagine would go along with an apocalypse. The times I wasn't playing someone else's character were pretty immersive. Like the best Bethesda games, they left a lot of open to modding, which is what makes their games truly great.
Seriously, there's enough good stuff that I'd come back & change this to a thumbs-up if they could somehow cut the plot out & let me just play a Fallout game instead of a series of turdtacular roadblocks that stop me from getting to the fun stuff.

You get your heroes, you level them up, you learn about how everything works, and you realize - this is going to be worse than it already is. You will have to grind, you will have to lose heroes to RNG, you will never find a strategy that really works, and even if you actually will devs will nerf it just like they did before, constantly adding features to make game harder and less enjoyable. You might think that I hate all of the things they added, like corpses and such, but that’s not the case. Corpses mechanic is pretty good and interesting, makes you think more about crowd control and not only beating monsters to death. The problem is that high level heroes can’t go to low level dungeon. The problem is that higher level heroes cost way more to relieve stress and equip, but they will easily die and you lose weeks of progress just like that.  The only way to farm some gold is to grind, or you will always have just enough to another expedition, and maybe a few coins. That is until u lose your leveled and geared up heroes and will have to start over. I’m sure there are people that will enjoy that game a lot, but think about it - how often you set highest possible difficulty in a game? Because in that game that’s  the only option there is, and devs like it that way.

TL;DR: I love this game, but I think your investment will be rewarded more when the game gets a full release rather than buying it now and getting burnt out.
First off, I'll begin by saying that I am not often compelled to write reviews for games, particularly for unfinished ones, and though my playtime may not be as high as others, I have reached the endgame ores and crafted the most powerful items and armor (though I haven't searched the universe for the most powerful random weapons), so I think I am qualified to give my opinion.
I'm not going to go into detail about how this game works, because most of the people reading this will already be well informed from the massive amount of publicity this game has received. I will say that I absolutely love this game. Unfortunately, though I strongly recommend users buy this when it gets a full release, I don't think I can recommend that you buy this game right now, and here is why.
When you first begin the game, you will notice a handy journal with the slightly deceptive/probably foreshadowing label of "Quests". As many of you know, the developers of this game are interested into integrating quests into the game that can be gained from NPC's (as far as I gathrer) along with (also an assumption) different quests and story arcs for different races. This is all very interesting and exciting until you realize that after the first boss of the game (essentially there as the end of the tutorial) you will never get a quest again, right now. The rest of the game is spent in a subtly formulaic pattern of "gather ore, craft better gear, go to next tier, get better ore, craft better tier (albeit with very easily exploitable boss fights in between). The first boss of the game is no doubt the most dangerous. Again, this seems like a complaint, and in a way it is, but I view it more as an expectation of the future. This will get filled in later.
Eventually you will fight the last (fourth) boss. After this, you unlock the final sector and the game becomes extremely easy. This is because there are no more bosses to fight to gather tech upgrades and you can simply craft only enough bars for the next upgrade in single trips to different planets. I completed the items for the last 60% of ores I hadn't discovered in about three hours. This has to do with the fact that the high level ores spawn far too frequently (IMO) right now and getting to the next ore is extremely easy (only forty bars per upgrade after Sector X). Again, I understand this is a placeholder for future content and depth, however, right now the game is purely exploration, mining, and making an awesome character. If you are like me, this is still an awesome turn on, as I love exploration and the combat feels fair and balanced, even surpassing its oft compared to "twin brother", Terraria, in my opinion.
So why in the world shouldn't you buy this game? Well, unless you are interested in supporting the developers like I was, you will get burnt out, and I don't want that. This game has fantastic potential and I lot of love behind it, but trust me, no matter how much you love digging and crafting, it will get old, and when you finish the final tier of ores there is a certain emptiness left as you realize all that is left is to start a new playthrough and do the same thing again. There aren't enough variety in dungeons yet (there will be, I'm sure), there aren't any quests, and the back half of the game is lacking in depth right now. The promise still stands that all of this will be added later, but if you aren't sure about this one, I would strongly recommend waiting for a release or buying it and playing it in small bursts. I don't want anyone to be burnt out on this game before all the content is released for it (notice the 20,000 in game right now at the moment) because I feel like it has so much more to offer.

A lot of people have said that Fallout 4 "isn't really a fallout game" because of how Bethesda changed up gameplay formula.  This iteration of the series has nerfed a lot of the "RPG" elements that fans came to know and love, and have focused a lot more on the "Action" side of things, which has undeniably changed the way the game is played.
Some things I didn't like:
Dialogue - I really appreciated Fallout 4's text-based dialogue, with numerous options for response, and detailed text available before I chose a response.  The "button wheel" in Fallout 4 leaves very few options, and often leads to surprises when an option you chose turns out to be something you didn't want to do.
Voice Acting - I'll say upfront that I have no problem with voice acting from NPCs, that's been a staple in fallout games forever -- Giving the Sole Survivor a voice on the other hand kinda breaks the immersion, and also causes the limited dialogue issues.
Character Building - The lack of RPG elements make it difficult to build a character with a certain set of flaws, or specializations for the purposes of roleplaying.  You're more or less forced to keep things middle of the road, or risk incredibly tedious gameplay.
Some things I liked
The Environment - Gameplay aside, there's no mistaking you're in a Fallout game.  The aesthetics are spot on, and the enormous environment is incredible to explore. The colour palate is much easier on the eyes than previous games, without being too bright or saturated.
The amount of content - There's SO MUCH to do, so many factions to discover, so many side quests and missions to take, and so many places to explore.  If you're into looking around and trying to understand the world you're in, this is for you.  I haven't even managed to get the main storyline finished, I keep finding so many distractions
Crafting System - I enjoy knocking together and modifying weapons.  This adds an RPG element that has been missing from previous games.
Some things I don't have a strong opinion on, but noticed anyway
Weapon Damage - Weapons don't wear out like they did in previous games.  No need to do repairs, just modifications
Settlements - I enjoy knocking together some settlements, but the constant calls for "HELP US" get a bit annoying over time.  The more settlements you get, the more time you have to spend bailing your settlers out.
VATS - Doesn't freeze time anymore, requiring quicker thinking than previous.  While I previously enjoyed the low-stress VATS of earlier games, the new VATS seems more suited for an action RPG, making you need to think on your feet a lot more.
Overall, Fallout 4 is a gorgeous game, and I'd recommend it to anyone who wants to play a great game.  Don't go in expecting the full "Fallout" experience, and you'll have a lot more fun.

I can't believe all the negative reviews.  XCOM was a difficult game.  I didn't expect this one to be a walk in the park.  I am rarely pleased with modern games (though there are exceptions), especially sequels or DLC's, because they try to provide too much eye-candy and not enough meat.  XCOM 2 is a breath of fresh air.  It's exactly what I want in a game.  Give me a challenge, make me work for my successes, and then let me adjust the settings to provide a completely new experience for my next play through.
That said, in my first run-through I felt pressure from the timers and frustration with trying to gather resources while being interrupted with "gotta-do-it-now" missions.  My second attempt fared no better, but I did manage to get things moving in the right direction.  For my third attempt, I kicked the difficulty up and planned things more carefully, and was amazed at how quickly engineering and research moved in comparison with my first two games.  There is most definitely a sweet spot between resource gathering, engineering, and research.  Once you find it, it does get much easier and everything starts to flow more smoothly.  Does this mean it's currently perfect?  No, but the mechanics are there to adjust it without having to use a trainer or a god-mode console cheat.  That makes it inherently superior to something that feels perfect, but falls short in the long run.
Concerning performance: Nearly every game has someone complaining that it won't run properly on their "elite" rig.  I had absolutely no performance issues on max settings, but my machine is under two years old.  I'm sure if it was older or not built/tuned properly, I might be saying the same things.  That doesn't make it the game's fault -- unless, of course, there are memory leaks or coding errors that are legitimately causing problems.  If those exist, I honestly hope they get fixed.
I really enjoy the modding capability they built into the game as a set of features rather than a debug-only internal set of documents and cryptic INI files.  I especially appreciated the hints PC Gamer gave in
-- but what goes unsaid is that you can royally screw yourself up if you change the wrong thing.
Before modding, I experienced one bug:  If you blow the floor out from under a target, but don't kill him, he can get suspended (or fall through the world), and remain alive but unkillable.  That can mess up a mission.
After modding, I experienced two bugs:  Changing the squad size to 10 gives you a nice 3x3 block of soldiers, and then the 10th appears somewhere else on the map -- sometimes in a place where he cannot move because the terrain is impassable and/or the map layers don't mesh up properly.  The second bug (still related to a size-10 squad) is that VIP's can appear outside the playable area of the map.  You cannot get close enough to them to assume control or interact with them, but even if you could, they can't get past the edge of the map to come back in.  Setting a squad size of 7 rounds out to a nice 3x3 block once you get the +2 upgrade and avoids the above two bugs.  And then, because you have more soldiers to play with, it's only fair to increase the spawn rate, numbers, or strength of the Advent units.
If you feel like waiting to buy this game (because of all the negative comments), be my guest.  But it is not a bad title.  In fact, it is one of the best games I have seen in years.

Hate to give this one a negative as i was waiting for it since it first appeared.
But to be constructive and objective:
Initially the game gives you almost all that it can offer: all building unlock in first 4 dungeons. I've got all heroes there are in 4 weeks as well(for some it may be longer, but not much).  So after 4 weeks and maybe a bit more dungeons you already know all regular mob skills, all your party skills ect. Further game doesn't really throw anything different and gets insanely repetitive. Unskippable animations make you wait for ~ hour per 4 dungeons only watching them(I did the math). Loot is all the same: simple chests but with different items as keys.
So, if you put any brains in, it gets like this: you have 3-4 parties(heal, mark, stun, move - those are combos). Sometimes someone dies on a really bad RNG streak(for example once a guy refused to get healed 10 times in a row).
The game is not hard at all(yes i have everything turned on) if you play safe and don't overextend. No insane difficulty spikes.
So two thing kill your fun in around 15 hours: GRIND(exactly the same over and over with watching animations 50% of the game), lack of new things to learn and discover.
What would really make it better?
1. skippable animations
2. events within loot items - not just chest-key mechanics
3. more stuff to discover
4. shorter, more punishing dungeons with better layouts(having to walk 5-6 corridors back makes u wanna zzzz) - game has a good strategic potential, but you are forced to spent 80% of game time within dungeons.
I really don't understand those, who are complaining about difficulty. Game's NOT hard and very well balanced to the point, when you don't feel for your heroes. Roguelikes are supposed to be spiky and unpredictable, they are supposed to make you care and put effort. This game doesn't.

It is good, but let me share my main concerns -- knowing fully well I will face a lot of disagreement from the DS-Community.
I understand that the game has to be hard, but is the following really necessary?
[Note: These are my initial impressions, as you can see that my play-time is severely limited. I feel like first impressions of someone relatively unknown to the Dark Souls series still hold value to some extent.]
1. When enemies attack you and you try to dodge by walking to their side, they magically float across the ground, doing a 90 degrees spin, and hit you.
2. I hate spamming Dodge in games, and this game forces you to. Hated it in Witcher 3, hate it Dark Souls 3.
3. Everything about this game feels spammy, apart from the ambience. For example, bosses spam attacks, giving you VERY little breathing room, and with a low stamina pool; boss fights just feel hopeless -- more so than they are supposed to feel.
4. I like repetition and having to fight for my achievements, but as someone whose first DS experience is with DSIII, the game makes to big a jump in difficulty in the beginning. It starts off really easy, but then immediately becomes a very repetitive and frustrating experience. This, along with previously mentioned points, leave a very sour first impression, which is a shame because I LOVE the atmosphere and idea of a genuinly challenging game. There is, however, a difference between challenging and unfairness.
5. It feels like autistic savants would love this game. It is clear that the majority of your progress is based on stupidly memorizing what is going to happen, which deminishes any notion to have to apply actual strategy. 'Well, at least I know how this particular section works for the next run, hurr hurr.' Lame. Lame. Lame.
6. Where is the story in the beginning? There is next to nothing of it after the initial cutscene -- it just jumps straight to what Dark Souls is known for; extreme difficulty. Damn, and I mean, DAMN shame.
7. To return to the topic of boss fights; what the hell is even going on? I am usually standing underneath a boss dodging and attacking, but there is no sense to be made out of their clunky animations and creative-but-confusing models. I know this is something that will improve as I progress, but it seems a boss might as well have an animation where they're eating ice-cream and I will randomly get hit in the face for half my HP.
I am excited about this game beyond belief, but the 'This game is hard and will make you rage'-tag is such a shame, as, again, it has great ambience, and probably a great story later on.

A decent game that could have been so much more. Overall I found Fallout 4 to be enjoyable but it's let down by numerous flaws and an overall lack of polish. There's a real clunkiness to certain systems, for example the dialog system which really is poor by default, it can be improved with mods but it's just not good enough for an RPG. The devs also made some bizarre decisions, like not allowing us to remap most of the keys, I had to use external software to do it which is ridiculous.
I've just finished the main story and I feel like I'm done with the game, there's still plenty more to do I just don't feel like doing it. I never really enjoyed Settlements, it just felt like busy work, I had the most fun when I was following the main story or major side quests and now that's over I see no reason to keep playing, but I definitely don't regret my time spent in the Wasteland.
The game has a lot of issues or well things I didn't care for but most of them can be fixed or altered with mods, without mods Fallout 4 would be a far worse game that's for sure. Mods allowed me to remove a lot of the tedium, for example hacking and lockpicking, I can't imagine anyone enjoying those mini-games after the first time, but with mods you can remove the time spent fiddling with them, I tweaked the game to my liking and enjoyed it much more as a result.
Technically the game was really bad at launch but it's in a much better state now, but far from perfect, certain areas still tank the frame rate and you'll need to turn down several settings to medium if you value smooth gameplay and don't wish to dip under 60fps. I needed to down shadows, god rays and draw distance using a GTX 970 which kept me above the threshold in most areas, but at times I still dropped down into the 30s, but for the most part it was smooth and you can really tinker with the game depending on your PC. I should also note the loading times which are atrocious, without exaggeration the worst I have ever experienced, and I'm using 16GB 2133MHz RAM and a Samsung 850 EVO SSD.
Overall I enjoyed my time with the game and definitely do recommend it when on sale, for the £9.99 I paid I'm perfectly happy with what I got, but I am left wondering how good it could have been.

When I first heard of this game I was intrigued. A dungeon crawler with a good risk/reward system. You could play it your way: Small amounts of risk with rewards in the same amount. High risk, high rewards. And for the first few months, I had a blast. For an Early Access game it was actually fairly good.
Updates came and went and the game went through some rather weird changes. Gone were certain combinations because they were deemed overpowered. Certain classes were hit with the nerf bat so hard they became pretty much useless.
The more the game was updated, the more RNG became skewed in the enemy's favour. Out of the blue, the mobs you could encounter in the dungeons could crit and oneshot your heroes because RNG always ruled in their favour. Another update and corpses were introduced. Previously, whenever you killed someone they disappeared from the line. Now, they leave a corpse which acts as a barricade that needs to be "killed" again for you to be able to reach someone else down the line.
With every update you were forced into playing the game the devs wanted you to play it, not how you wanted to play it.
Stress was already a big factor in how you played the game as you needed to juggle how much you were taking. Now with Heart Attacks introduced, it blows that right out of the water. All of the mobs do even more stress damage than before and always seem to have a high chance to cause a lot of it, too.
Now with release upon us, you aren't playing the game how you want. You're playing the game how the Devs want and that's a damn shame.
Verdict: Not recommended. At all.

I can't believe all the negative reviews.  XCOM was a difficult game.  I didn't expect this one to be a walk in the park.  I am rarely pleased with modern games (though there are exceptions), especially sequels or DLC's, because they try to provide too much eye-candy and not enough meat.  XCOM 2 is a breath of fresh air.  It's exactly what I want in a game.  Give me a challenge, make me work for my successes, and then let me adjust the settings to provide a completely new experience for my next play through.
That said, in my first run-through I felt pressure from the timers and frustration with trying to gather resources while being interrupted with "gotta-do-it-now" missions.  My second attempt fared no better, but I did manage to get things moving in the right direction.  For my third attempt, I kicked the difficulty up and planned things more carefully, and was amazed at how quickly engineering and research moved in comparison with my first two games.  There is most definitely a sweet spot between resource gathering, engineering, and research.  Once you find it, it does get much easier and everything starts to flow more smoothly.  Does this mean it's currently perfect?  No, but the mechanics are there to adjust it without having to use a trainer or a god-mode console cheat.  That makes it inherently superior to something that feels perfect, but falls short in the long run.
Concerning performance: Nearly every game has someone complaining that it won't run properly on their "elite" rig.  I had absolutely no performance issues on max settings, but my machine is under two years old.  I'm sure if it was older or not built/tuned properly, I might be saying the same things.  That doesn't make it the game's fault -- unless, of course, there are memory leaks or coding errors that are legitimately causing problems.  If those exist, I honestly hope they get fixed.
I really enjoy the modding capability they built into the game as a set of features rather than a debug-only internal set of documents and cryptic INI files.  I especially appreciated the hints PC Gamer gave in
-- but what goes unsaid is that you can royally screw yourself up if you change the wrong thing.
Before modding, I experienced one bug:  If you blow the floor out from under a target, but don't kill him, he can get suspended (or fall through the world), and remain alive but unkillable.  That can mess up a mission.
After modding, I experienced two bugs:  Changing the squad size to 10 gives you a nice 3x3 block of soldiers, and then the 10th appears somewhere else on the map -- sometimes in a place where he cannot move because the terrain is impassable and/or the map layers don't mesh up properly.  The second bug (still related to a size-10 squad) is that VIP's can appear outside the playable area of the map.  You cannot get close enough to them to assume control or interact with them, but even if you could, they can't get past the edge of the map to come back in.  Setting a squad size of 7 rounds out to a nice 3x3 block once you get the +2 upgrade and avoids the above two bugs.  And then, because you have more soldiers to play with, it's only fair to increase the spawn rate, numbers, or strength of the Advent units.
If you feel like waiting to buy this game (because of all the negative comments), be my guest.  But it is not a bad title.  In fact, it is one of the best games I have seen in years.

XCOM 2 is a sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unknown which was a reimagined remake of the original game known as UFO: Enemy Unknown. In XCOM 2 you take on the role of Commander by controlling an elite group of soldiers during turn based combat missions and deciding how to delegate resources between research, weapons development, staff recruitment and base expansion on a global scale to save earth from an alien incursion.
XCOM 2 holds on to some familiar class choices for soldiers that we saw in XCOM: Enemy unknown, with only a few notable differences making the transition into the sequel both easy and engaging. Soldier progression remains unchanged in that the player will be asked to choose one of two new skills during each promotion past the squadie rank.  Most skills are familiar and a welcome sight while others are new and refreshing.  The new skill choices in XCOM 2 make a definite impact in the viability of each choice as I have found there to be fewer options that I had no interest in.  Other improvements lie with the ability to customize soldiers in purely cosmetic ways from creating biographys, altering armor or weapon colors and patterns, to designing and naming new weapons with modifcations found on the battlefield.
The most notable difference from XCOM: Enemy Unknown is the way the player will interact with global events.  The XCOM base is now a repurposed alien spaceship.  In order to expand your base you will need to remove debri from sections of the craft before more rooms can be built.  The player will also use this craft to navigate around the globe in real time to various sites and random events to free areas from alien control, collect supplies and ultimately stop the alien invasion.
While I never wrote a review for Enemy Unknown my biggest concern was the possible return of a few game mechanics that I felt deminished the fun of that game.  XCOM 2 has addressed these issues with striking clarity and left me with an incredibly worry free experience.
I had two main concerns from Enemy Unknown:
1. Three abduction sites, one response.  This game mechanic became tedious very quickly for me as the rewards      for the missions were rarely usefull or a part of the decision making process.  I understood that the developers wanted to create a certain level of urgency, but due to the sheer amount of panic that would be produced from these events I was only looking at which option prevented a country from defecting.  XCOM 2 takes a similar approach to this mechanic in a more profound way.  Instead of increasing a panic level that could potentially reduce your income, you are faced with deciding what type of benefits you would like to try to prevent the aliens from having on the following month as well as determining which rewards for those missions might be most valuable to you.  Some mission parameters will allow the aliens the use of special ammo, or better armor while others can impact the availability of resources to you next month. Rewards for the player from completing these missions like engineers and scientists now hold such great importance (as they are difficult or expensive to come by) that you may find yourself willing to let the aliens have a specific benefit in order to acquire one them.  I never felt that I was faced with these kinds of desicions in Enemy Unknown.
2. 99% chance to hit... missed.  Enemy Unknown seemed plagued with misinformation during combat situations.  Since I relied on that information to dictate what actions I would take I found it incredibly frustrating at how often those 99% chance to hits would miss, sometimes affecting the entire squad even if they had a 100% chance to hit.  And if you wanted to reload that scenario and try again, tough luck.  No random seeds for you.  Eventually, an option was released with some DLC to allow for random seeds after a reload, but not before a light jab was thrown at the people requesting it.  Here's your random seed you Scum Savers.  I would be lieing if I were to say that I haven't missed a high probability to hit in XCOM 2, but at least I can reload for a new outcome if I find myself about to lose my best soldier.
XCOM 2 is a great successor to XCOM: Enemy Unkown that maintains a great turn based strategy with just the right amount of changes to improve on the few short comings of its predecessor.

Some resources may seem obscured by currency barriers, but enough 'crowns' (the coins you collect in the level) can add up to enough, or you can usually get the resources themselves by playing Story Mode chapters. My January 29, 2014 Review - This game is awesome!
My March 13, 2017 Review - Ugh, uninstall.
So what happened? I certainly have enough hours logged. I truly enjoyed the game.
Well, back in the day, it was exciting to explore because there was so much variety and mystery. I finally had enough resources and clothing protection that I could build in the freezing cold of space. I still needed fireplaces and heaters, but I had a full asteroid base built up for mining and even had an internal hydroponics bay so I wouldn't starve.
What's that you say? "Clothing used for heat and air? Heaters provide heat? Asteroids had vast resources? Food is necessary to survive? What are you talking about?"
Yes, Starbound used to be a challenging game that required you to have the right equipment for the job, not just a McGuffin that allowed you to explore the next set of planets. Asteroid bases were useful because of the plentiful resources that asteroids likely have. Food prevented starvation, it wasn't just another way to heal.
So what happened? My guess is that the developers decided to try and make the game more accessible. In doing so, they dumbed it down. This may be one of the only games I know that became less challenging and interesting the further along it was developed.
Save your money. Just buy Terraria.

XCOM 2:  The Good, The Bad, And The Ugly
Okay.  I've put some time in this game, about 18 hours.  This game is better than Firax's first XCOM game (notice how specific I am).  It does some things great and does some things stupidly.  The game is good enough that I put in a lot of time already with it and it kept me going.  But there were many occasions along that journey that really, really starts aggravating me.
THE GOOD
I don't mind the setting.  I don't mind how the reborn XCOM takes up after the first organization's failure.  I don't mind the whole insurgent angle of the game.  It's markedly different from other games with the XCOM/X-Com name.  The story so far has been decent.  The game goes out of its way to have you call each soldier your own.  The character customization, weapon modifications is great.  Being able to tweak many aspects brings a bit more individuality.
The languages offered is nice for variety as I prefer a nationality to speak their native tongue.  It would be nice to have more of the major nationalities with their language to choose from and I hope this gets expanded upon in the future.  I get attached to certain soldiers, especially my performers and being able to customize them to this game's extent is nice.
So far with the early game, it's nice having to juggle how supplies and resources are spent.  I can't have everything and I have to decide what gets researched and built up first.  I'm not at endgame so I can't tell how this aspect holds up witih late game where players tend to have everything.
I appreciate the multi level/floor/tier of the maps, something some of the other games that have pursued the X-Com style of play have failed in, one in particular that only had flat and level maps  :\  XCOM2 is still a far cry from the possible sprawl of maps done in the very old X-Com Apocalypse.  You could go into an urban sprawl with buildings having 10 floors.  I just wish the franchise would be able to go to maps of that variety and depth, but oh well.
THE BAD
Inconsistencies in combat with LOS for both you and the Advent.  Characters on both sides routinely see and shoot through walls and buildings.  It's hard to get any sense of the terrain for tactical usefulness and dangers when everyone seems to just ignore walls and buildings like they don't exist.  Seeing the action cam views of people taking shoots at a target but there's a goddamn entire building blocking the view, yet everyone shoots like those things don't exist.
More examples of this same LOS inconsistency?  Vipers will use their tongue grab on your soldier that is completley isolated in the interior of a building with no door and windows that the Viper should reach him with.  Hand thrown Grenades respect the LOS game but Grenade Launchers?  No.  You can shoot from the deep interior of a building with a roof and no openings to the target/target area.
In XCOM2's combat, there a word that you will get very familiar with for your soldiers:  "MISSED!"
THE UGLY
Time is not only against you in XCOM2, it hates you.
In the strategic view, you are spammed missions constantly, a lot of which are high priority missions.  It just piles up.  It feels like I cannot go 1-2 days to complete a 3-6 day scan before the next war critical mission comes up that I HAVE to do.
It's like someone gave Fallout 4's Preston Garvey the mission design lead and he dived into it with a burning hatred for prospective players.
When you go into the tactical missions themselves, many of these press you for time with limited turns to accomplish goals.  Time is such an issue that it adversely affects tactical options in this game.  The constraints are so tight that this game is down to a zerg rush.  A-To-B tactics and nothing fancy.  No flanking.  No roundabout routes.  Frontal assault is all that matters.
The game forces such a premium on making you rush that I've opting out of using my sharpshooters/snipers now.  The nature of their form of fighting, where they cannot fire their sniper rifle unless they stay in place means they severely lag behind the rest of the team.  In a game where time is constantly forcing the player to PUSH FORWARD PUSH FORWARD PUSH FORWARD, Sharpshooters are the most useless class I have.  Even the Grenadiers with their miniguns and grenade launchers offer a more mobile, aggressive style of fighting that suits this game.
Another wonderful feature of the game is with these same time constraints in combat, towards the end, you're rushing headlong for the extraction zone.  LOL!  That's when the game drops Advent reinforcements in the extraction zone when you have 1-2 turns left before you fail or whoever hasn't extracted, gets left behind for capture.
==========
Overall the game is a mixed bag.  There are things that I absolutely HATE in this game.  But there are things that are just wonderful.  The campaign, basic idea of the story, outifitting and customizing your soldiers are great.  The things that are bad however really started getting to me.

Hate to give this one a negative as i was waiting for it since it first appeared.
But to be constructive and objective:
Initially the game gives you almost all that it can offer: all building unlock in first 4 dungeons. I've got all heroes there are in 4 weeks as well(for some it may be longer, but not much).  So after 4 weeks and maybe a bit more dungeons you already know all regular mob skills, all your party skills ect. Further game doesn't really throw anything different and gets insanely repetitive. Unskippable animations make you wait for ~ hour per 4 dungeons only watching them(I did the math). Loot is all the same: simple chests but with different items as keys.
So, if you put any brains in, it gets like this: you have 3-4 parties(heal, mark, stun, move - those are combos). Sometimes someone dies on a really bad RNG streak(for example once a guy refused to get healed 10 times in a row).
The game is not hard at all(yes i have everything turned on) if you play safe and don't overextend. No insane difficulty spikes.
So two thing kill your fun in around 15 hours: GRIND(exactly the same over and over with watching animations 50% of the game), lack of new things to learn and discover.
What would really make it better?
1. skippable animations
2. events within loot items - not just chest-key mechanics
3. more stuff to discover
4. shorter, more punishing dungeons with better layouts(having to walk 5-6 corridors back makes u wanna zzzz) - game has a good strategic potential, but you are forced to spent 80% of game time within dungeons.
I really don't understand those, who are complaining about difficulty. Game's NOT hard and very well balanced to the point, when you don't feel for your heroes. Roguelikes are supposed to be spiky and unpredictable, they are supposed to make you care and put effort. This game doesn't.

This XCOM takes what we knew from enemy unknown and shakes it up a little, making it more of a frantic dash to get things done as a small rebel group that slowly grows bigger throughout the course of the game. The character customization is quite varied and I ended up making my friends and family who would inevitably die somewhere along the line due to a stupid mistake or just bad luck.
There are certain times where tons aliens would just swarm out of nowhere when I wasn't expecting it and completely wiped out most of my soldiers. Thankfully, there is now a portable evac for certain missions, so if things go south you can quickly call the evac to a close location and get them out as fast as possible. On some of the "main quest" missions they don't give you the difficulty of the level, so I end up sending my favourite troops to save civilians and then get absolutely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by the horde of aliens hiding round the corner.
The game looks quite simular to enemy unknown which I think is a good thing, there are upgrades to the interface and the levels look fantastic. The character models have been cleaned up and given more detail although there are a lack of faces to choose from in the customization.
I think this is a great game that any XCOM fan will enjoy. It's different in pacing, upgraded in looks and tweaked in gameplay. Do yourself a favour and pick this up if you've been looking for a new turn based game.

July 3, 2016. I wanted to make a quick update to my review. Because DD has gone through a lot of changes and some people are enraged by those changes.
I don't get why. Nothing that has happened, (in my experience) has been horribly unfair left me aggrevated and frustrated (at least not more so than I already get with this game, in a loving way, of course.) And you can turn it off. If you don't want town events, turn them off. If you don't want heart attacks, turn them off.
And I think that option makes DD a *better* game. The developers could have said: "This was our vision, stick with it!" But they're giving me the option to control my game experience. And I really dig that.
Now on to my review.
I played hours and hours of DD in it's early access form and fell deeply in love with it. I then made the decsion (after a horrible party wipe) to shelf it until it was finally released.
I came back to a game that felt fresh and had many MANY wonderful quality of life improvements. And the game feels much more polished now.
Why do I love the game? Well for many reasons. and bear in mind, much of this is subjective.
When I was younger I the chance to play some Warhamer Quest with some friends. We only got a couple of games in. But it was a great deal of fun. And DD feels lke a computer version of Warhammer quest. One that's more affordable and doesn't require other people. So, for that alone I have a lot of love for the game.
The gameplay is also very compelling. That feeling of "one more room." "One more dungeon" and then looking at the clock and realizing it's way way past my bed time. I love the mechanics of the game even when I'm screaming at my screen because my Crusader missed that hit I *needed* him to make.
The game has amazing music and sound. The narration is a stand-out to be sure. The visual style is excellent as well.
The game has gone through a lot of changes. And the difficulty seems to have swung wildly. So far (with a new save) it seems managable but not horrible.
I have a lot of love for this game and I'll gladly reccomend it to almost anyone.

XCOM 2:  The Good, The Bad, And The Ugly
Okay.  I've put some time in this game, about 18 hours.  This game is better than Firax's first XCOM game (notice how specific I am).  It does some things great and does some things stupidly.  The game is good enough that I put in a lot of time already with it and it kept me going.  But there were many occasions along that journey that really, really starts aggravating me.
THE GOOD
I don't mind the setting.  I don't mind how the reborn XCOM takes up after the first organization's failure.  I don't mind the whole insurgent angle of the game.  It's markedly different from other games with the XCOM/X-Com name.  The story so far has been decent.  The game goes out of its way to have you call each soldier your own.  The character customization, weapon modifications is great.  Being able to tweak many aspects brings a bit more individuality.
The languages offered is nice for variety as I prefer a nationality to speak their native tongue.  It would be nice to have more of the major nationalities with their language to choose from and I hope this gets expanded upon in the future.  I get attached to certain soldiers, especially my performers and being able to customize them to this game's extent is nice.
So far with the early game, it's nice having to juggle how supplies and resources are spent.  I can't have everything and I have to decide what gets researched and built up first.  I'm not at endgame so I can't tell how this aspect holds up witih late game where players tend to have everything.
I appreciate the multi level/floor/tier of the maps, something some of the other games that have pursued the X-Com style of play have failed in, one in particular that only had flat and level maps  :\  XCOM2 is still a far cry from the possible sprawl of maps done in the very old X-Com Apocalypse.  You could go into an urban sprawl with buildings having 10 floors.  I just wish the franchise would be able to go to maps of that variety and depth, but oh well.
THE BAD
Inconsistencies in combat with LOS for both you and the Advent.  Characters on both sides routinely see and shoot through walls and buildings.  It's hard to get any sense of the terrain for tactical usefulness and dangers when everyone seems to just ignore walls and buildings like they don't exist.  Seeing the action cam views of people taking shoots at a target but there's a goddamn entire building blocking the view, yet everyone shoots like those things don't exist.
More examples of this same LOS inconsistency?  Vipers will use their tongue grab on your soldier that is completley isolated in the interior of a building with no door and windows that the Viper should reach him with.  Hand thrown Grenades respect the LOS game but Grenade Launchers?  No.  You can shoot from the deep interior of a building with a roof and no openings to the target/target area.
In XCOM2's combat, there a word that you will get very familiar with for your soldiers:  "MISSED!"
THE UGLY
Time is not only against you in XCOM2, it hates you.
In the strategic view, you are spammed missions constantly, a lot of which are high priority missions.  It just piles up.  It feels like I cannot go 1-2 days to complete a 3-6 day scan before the next war critical mission comes up that I HAVE to do.
It's like someone gave Fallout 4's Preston Garvey the mission design lead and he dived into it with a burning hatred for prospective players.
When you go into the tactical missions themselves, many of these press you for time with limited turns to accomplish goals.  Time is such an issue that it adversely affects tactical options in this game.  The constraints are so tight that this game is down to a zerg rush.  A-To-B tactics and nothing fancy.  No flanking.  No roundabout routes.  Frontal assault is all that matters.
The game forces such a premium on making you rush that I've opting out of using my sharpshooters/snipers now.  The nature of their form of fighting, where they cannot fire their sniper rifle unless they stay in place means they severely lag behind the rest of the team.  In a game where time is constantly forcing the player to PUSH FORWARD PUSH FORWARD PUSH FORWARD, Sharpshooters are the most useless class I have.  Even the Grenadiers with their miniguns and grenade launchers offer a more mobile, aggressive style of fighting that suits this game.
Another wonderful feature of the game is with these same time constraints in combat, towards the end, you're rushing headlong for the extraction zone.  LOL!  That's when the game drops Advent reinforcements in the extraction zone when you have 1-2 turns left before you fail or whoever hasn't extracted, gets left behind for capture.
==========
Overall the game is a mixed bag.  There are things that I absolutely HATE in this game.  But there are things that are just wonderful.  The campaign, basic idea of the story, outifitting and customizing your soldiers are great.  The things that are bad however really started getting to me.

It is good, but let me share my main concerns -- knowing fully well I will face a lot of disagreement from the DS-Community.
I understand that the game has to be hard, but is the following really necessary?
[Note: These are my initial impressions, as you can see that my play-time is severely limited. I feel like first impressions of someone relatively unknown to the Dark Souls series still hold value to some extent.]
1. When enemies attack you and you try to dodge by walking to their side, they magically float across the ground, doing a 90 degrees spin, and hit you.
2. I hate spamming Dodge in games, and this game forces you to. Hated it in Witcher 3, hate it Dark Souls 3.
3. Everything about this game feels spammy, apart from the ambience. For example, bosses spam attacks, giving you VERY little breathing room, and with a low stamina pool; boss fights just feel hopeless -- more so than they are supposed to feel.
4. I like repetition and having to fight for my achievements, but as someone whose first DS experience is with DSIII, the game makes to big a jump in difficulty in the beginning. It starts off really easy, but then immediately becomes a very repetitive and frustrating experience. This, along with previously mentioned points, leave a very sour first impression, which is a shame because I LOVE the atmosphere and idea of a genuinly challenging game. There is, however, a difference between challenging and unfairness.
5. It feels like autistic savants would love this game. It is clear that the majority of your progress is based on stupidly memorizing what is going to happen, which deminishes any notion to have to apply actual strategy. 'Well, at least I know how this particular section works for the next run, hurr hurr.' Lame. Lame. Lame.
6. Where is the story in the beginning? There is next to nothing of it after the initial cutscene -- it just jumps straight to what Dark Souls is known for; extreme difficulty. Damn, and I mean, DAMN shame.
7. To return to the topic of boss fights; what the hell is even going on? I am usually standing underneath a boss dodging and attacking, but there is no sense to be made out of their clunky animations and creative-but-confusing models. I know this is something that will improve as I progress, but it seems a boss might as well have an animation where they're eating ice-cream and I will randomly get hit in the face for half my HP.
I am excited about this game beyond belief, but the 'This game is hard and will make you rage'-tag is such a shame, as, again, it has great ambience, and probably a great story later on.
