Hell, I actually found a way to softblock myself by only having 3 mercs to use (refuse to call them heroes cause heroes would be badasses, which these guys are not) and not having a single merc in the recruitable area to choose from.
At that point I started researching things in, since I wanted to have a fighting chance and I figured at this point, the game would not tell me how to get started, I was gonna have to do it, and realized what I was in for. Hours of grinding with the potential of loosing a merc to a few bad crits, heartattack mechanics with enemies that specialize in doing nothing but stress damage. Lack of healing items needed to survive nasty encounters, having situations where enemies will deliberately focus down mercs and having no way to defend against it, it ended up looking like a game where all you can do is trade blows till either you or your opponent is left standing. To me it is a game that could literally play itself and you'd get the same experience as having control over your mercs, besides a strategy rpg where you take the advantages of certain classes to meld together to create a unit to take down a living breathing nightmare.
So in the end, I became stressed out by a singleplayer game. I became stressed knowing I could loose hours of progress to a nasty encounter, stressed knowing I don't know what will happen to a dungeon, all in all, just helpless. I have much more fun watching this game livestreamed than I do actually playing this game.
I may have only played two hours of this game, but it is two hours that I could formulate an opinion about a game. I'm not saying the game should be easymode, but the game should at least give you the tools to succeed and progress, not have that progress blocked off at every turn just to create the most thrilling strategy rpg of all time.

Let me first of start by saying that the Fallout community dissapoints me.
Fallout 4 was released on October 10, 2015 and is still a great game to this day. It certainly was the buzz when it came out and everyone is excited. Hell even I was. Unfortunately I could not buy it until 2 years later *cough* (steam summer sale) *cough* However I did buy it on console a few months after its release so I could not experience mods yet. My hours dont show it but to be honest, Fallout 4 might not be the greatest Fallout game ever but its still an amazing game. It saddens me to see so many people compare it to a game that is "superior" than others. Before I give pros and cons im just going to quickly say that if you do want to buy this game, do it. DO NOT LET THE NEGATIVE REVIEWS TELL YOU NOT TO. The Fallout community is could be one of the many very opinionated communities of any other game due to its controversy of New Vegas. By comparing a game to its previous game that its much more "superior" than others. To be fair I did love New Vegas and it is one of my favorite games and I do think better than Fallout 4. But I do not think it is superior. I do not think Fallout 4 is a♥♥♥♥♥♥game. When someone compares something to something else that's already wrong ESPECIALLY video games. By comparing it to something that is almost completely different and a new experience you are already violating the face of the game. If you want to go play something that is New Vegas. Well♥♥♥♥♥♥go play New Vegas right? Nope, wrong ,you decide to jump into this and expect to be exploring the Mojave Wasteland and having an equal experience of the previous game. I might get alot of bad comments for this intro already but let me start with the review.
Main Story (Warning SPOILERS): The story starts off before the great war in 2077 and the world was resource-drained. You the player luckily sign up for a space for you and your family in a Vault. A few minutes later into the intro total atomic ahnnihilation occurs and you run to the safety of the vaults. Along with your spouse and son you enter the vault not knowing the vaults were made by the government as social experiments. The social experiment for this vault was cryogenic experimentation and your family was frozen. Your spouse on the other side of the cryogenic pod carries your offspring and being unfrozen almost 200 years later a group of people take your child and kill your spouse. Waking up a few years later you set out to a new city. No longer called the Commonwealth of Boston the remaining survivors have decided to name it the Commonwealth. So the sole survivor sets out to look for his/her child from the kidnappers.
Combat: Whether you like to be sneaky beaky and stab someone with a combat knife in the back or you like to go balls deep into a raider base with a rocket launcher there really is many ways to approach a certain situation in combat. Each perk weapon and sometimes even armor will determine what you will do next. Whether its going to stab a radroach to going toe to toe to a Chameleon Deathclaw the combat is satisfying and sometimes highly rewarding.
Perk Chart: Some people might say the new perk system shouldnt have been changed and I somewhat agree. But after being released to consoles and gaining more popularity it has gained a little more younger audience. What I think Bethesda believed to do was simplify the perk system and easier to see what perks affect what physical trait in game. Some might help you increase damage with certain guns, some might help you charge at someone with power armor hell there is even some that help you swim underwater.(Pretty useless tbh Ill give you that)
Characters: Whats better than having a smart♥♥♥♥♥detective that has the personality of a cop from 2077 put into a synthetic body? Oh thats right having a super mutant following you around wanting the "milk of human kindness" because he thinks its a physical thing. How about a really racist buzz lightyear? Fallout 4 has alot of characters with fairly interesting stories and some also entail to some of the world's lore. Except you Preston garvey you bland piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥
World: The Commonwealth has many nooks and crannies for people to explore. Some people have commonly found all the time because they've seen it on their way to a destination or maybe its the destination of a quest. Sometimes when I create new characters I find areas I havent seen before or even areas that dont have markers on their maps. There's the east coast, the glowing sea, the financial district, the fens, or even Salem. If you really want to find new things this game really does reward for its exploration.
Lore: Though in my opinion when I played Fallout 4 I didnt care much of the lore at first. But then I started watching a Youtube channel by the name of Oxhorn who provides lore for all Fallout game, ive seen almost every lore video of Fallout 4 not realizing that almost every area has lore dating back before the war or sometimes even after the war. Some lore even correlates to earlier fallout games to references to the mojave wasteland or to something as little as finding Scribe Maxson in Fallout 3 or meeting Elder Maxson in Fallout 4. Some lore might be even as little as a message in a bottle leading to guy into a tub at the bottom of the east coast.
Factions: There might be fewer factions than there were in New Vegas then there are here. There is the Minutemen, Railroad, Brotherhood of Steel and the Institute. But each of them have their own ideals of the commonwealth and the community and what should change to help the commonwealth rebuild again. The Minutemen do what their motto is "Protect people at a minute's notice."The Railroad, the secret organization of agents who defend the idea that synths should be allowed to be their own person and pretty much the only people who the Institute take seriously. The Brotherhood of Steel who think that the Institute is a disease on the commonwealth and should be erradicated and use technology to rebuild society as it should be. Finally the institute whom's idea is to cleanse the commonwealth by creating new technology and killing what they think is killing the commonwealth. Fewer factions sure, but atleast we get some.

Repitition: Sometimes Fallout 4 can have very repetitive things like quests that do the same thing over and over or some things like fighting a very similar dungeon. Though these bother me they never really cross my mind when exploring it. Its just one of the few things I agree with the community on.
Dialogue Choices: Back in Fallout 3 and New Vegas we had an assortment of ways to interact with new characers from only having one questiong to having like 7 or 8 and learning more about the character. Hell sometimes the speech check was very exciting. But now we are limited to only 4 choices that can sometimes a little repetitve as well. Charasmatic choice speak checks are fun but I feel like there would need to be more.
Thats pretty much it in my opinion Fallout 4 is a great game but it needs more recognition and needs to acknowledged by alot more people.

TL;DR: I love this game, but I think your investment will be rewarded more when the game gets a full release rather than buying it now and getting burnt out.
First off, I'll begin by saying that I am not often compelled to write reviews for games, particularly for unfinished ones, and though my playtime may not be as high as others, I have reached the endgame ores and crafted the most powerful items and armor (though I haven't searched the universe for the most powerful random weapons), so I think I am qualified to give my opinion.
I'm not going to go into detail about how this game works, because most of the people reading this will already be well informed from the massive amount of publicity this game has received. I will say that I absolutely love this game. Unfortunately, though I strongly recommend users buy this when it gets a full release, I don't think I can recommend that you buy this game right now, and here is why.
When you first begin the game, you will notice a handy journal with the slightly deceptive/probably foreshadowing label of "Quests". As many of you know, the developers of this game are interested into integrating quests into the game that can be gained from NPC's (as far as I gathrer) along with (also an assumption) different quests and story arcs for different races. This is all very interesting and exciting until you realize that after the first boss of the game (essentially there as the end of the tutorial) you will never get a quest again, right now. The rest of the game is spent in a subtly formulaic pattern of "gather ore, craft better gear, go to next tier, get better ore, craft better tier (albeit with very easily exploitable boss fights in between). The first boss of the game is no doubt the most dangerous. Again, this seems like a complaint, and in a way it is, but I view it more as an expectation of the future. This will get filled in later.
Eventually you will fight the last (fourth) boss. After this, you unlock the final sector and the game becomes extremely easy. This is because there are no more bosses to fight to gather tech upgrades and you can simply craft only enough bars for the next upgrade in single trips to different planets. I completed the items for the last 60% of ores I hadn't discovered in about three hours. This has to do with the fact that the high level ores spawn far too frequently (IMO) right now and getting to the next ore is extremely easy (only forty bars per upgrade after Sector X). Again, I understand this is a placeholder for future content and depth, however, right now the game is purely exploration, mining, and making an awesome character. If you are like me, this is still an awesome turn on, as I love exploration and the combat feels fair and balanced, even surpassing its oft compared to "twin brother", Terraria, in my opinion.
So why in the world shouldn't you buy this game? Well, unless you are interested in supporting the developers like I was, you will get burnt out, and I don't want that. This game has fantastic potential and I lot of love behind it, but trust me, no matter how much you love digging and crafting, it will get old, and when you finish the final tier of ores there is a certain emptiness left as you realize all that is left is to start a new playthrough and do the same thing again. There aren't enough variety in dungeons yet (there will be, I'm sure), there aren't any quests, and the back half of the game is lacking in depth right now. The promise still stands that all of this will be added later, but if you aren't sure about this one, I would strongly recommend waiting for a release or buying it and playing it in small bursts. I don't want anyone to be burnt out on this game before all the content is released for it (notice the 20,000 in game right now at the moment) because I feel like it has so much more to offer.

A decent game that could have been so much more. Overall I found Fallout 4 to be enjoyable but it's let down by numerous flaws and an overall lack of polish. There's a real clunkiness to certain systems, for example the dialog system which really is poor by default, it can be improved with mods but it's just not good enough for an RPG. The devs also made some bizarre decisions, like not allowing us to remap most of the keys, I had to use external software to do it which is ridiculous.
I've just finished the main story and I feel like I'm done with the game, there's still plenty more to do I just don't feel like doing it. I never really enjoyed Settlements, it just felt like busy work, I had the most fun when I was following the main story or major side quests and now that's over I see no reason to keep playing, but I definitely don't regret my time spent in the Wasteland.
The game has a lot of issues or well things I didn't care for but most of them can be fixed or altered with mods, without mods Fallout 4 would be a far worse game that's for sure. Mods allowed me to remove a lot of the tedium, for example hacking and lockpicking, I can't imagine anyone enjoying those mini-games after the first time, but with mods you can remove the time spent fiddling with them, I tweaked the game to my liking and enjoyed it much more as a result.
Technically the game was really bad at launch but it's in a much better state now, but far from perfect, certain areas still tank the frame rate and you'll need to turn down several settings to medium if you value smooth gameplay and don't wish to dip under 60fps. I needed to down shadows, god rays and draw distance using a GTX 970 which kept me above the threshold in most areas, but at times I still dropped down into the 30s, but for the most part it was smooth and you can really tinker with the game depending on your PC. I should also note the loading times which are atrocious, without exaggeration the worst I have ever experienced, and I'm using 16GB 2133MHz RAM and a Samsung 850 EVO SSD.
Overall I enjoyed my time with the game and definitely do recommend it when on sale, for the £9.99 I paid I'm perfectly happy with what I got, but I am left wondering how good it could have been.

Starting off, I wasn't one of the initial backers for this game. I'm not one of the people taking issue with the difficulty changes pre/post release and I am playing this game with a fresh pair of eyes for the first time.

The human aspect that is implimented into the heros, that they are human and this flawed, is brilliant.
Cons: I get the theme of a constant uphill battle with Darkest Dungeon, and lady luck is going to take a crap on you more than once. However so far lady luck has upgraded to sewage truck and napalm to rain on my day.
Too many enemies with the ability to spam "stress" dmg attacks, multiple enemies constantly criting/dodging during a single round. Just forget taking any hero with more than 2 bars of stress in even the simplist early levels. Too often I end up discarding a hero I have investing in because they racked up so many negative traits in a single mission. The amount of fixing you have to do to maintain good 4 man team is a headache, its almost easier just to throw them away and mass spam recruit heros instead. I can expect this level of difficulty late game but I shouldnt feel the need to wipe yet another campaign save within the first 4 to 5 weeks.
This game has all the building blocks of a great game but I would argue that the combat mechanics need tweaking. Simple things like a turn cooldown on stress based attacks would go a long way. Perhaps some post combat abilities or actions to make stress, health etc. more manageable or at least some way to recover a little bit from a bad fight or luck.

I'll mostly go off of my own personal feelings towards the game over anything else. Like many others have stated, this is a game that you either love to death, or hate to death. There is no in between.
Me personally, was a hate to death feeling, it had nothing to do with the game itself, but a few small quirks the developers put in to make the game difficult. I went in with zero knowledge of the game, never looked up a guide or had someone spoiled for me. Saw some gameplay, but never enough to know basic team formations or how to manage anything. I felt helpless in the face of my enemy, and when I feel helpless, I become stressed, which isn't a good thing for a singleplayer game to do to you when you want to relax. Hell, I actually found a way to softblock myself by only having 3 mercs to use (refuse to call them heroes cause heroes would be badasses, which these guys are not) and not having a single merc in the recruitable area to choose from.
At that point I started researching things in, since I wanted to have a fighting chance and I figured at this point, the game would not tell me how to get started, I was gonna have to do it, and realized what I was in for. Hours of grinding with the potential of loosing a merc to a few bad crits, heartattack mechanics with enemies that specialize in doing nothing but stress damage. Lack of healing items needed to survive nasty encounters, having situations where enemies will deliberately focus down mercs and having no way to defend against it, it ended up looking like a game where all you can do is trade blows till either you or your opponent is left standing. To me it is a game that could literally play itself and you'd get the same experience as having control over your mercs, besides a strategy rpg where you take the advantages of certain classes to meld together to create a unit to take down a living breathing nightmare.
So in the end, I became stressed out by a singleplayer game. I became stressed knowing I could loose hours of progress to a nasty encounter, stressed knowing I don't know what will happen to a dungeon, all in all, just helpless. I have much more fun watching this game livestreamed than I do actually playing this game.
I may have only played two hours of this game, but it is two hours that I could formulate an opinion about a game. I'm not saying the game should be easymode, but the game should at least give you the tools to succeed and progress, not have that progress blocked off at every turn just to create the most thrilling strategy rpg of all time.

Let me first of start by saying that the Fallout community dissapoints me.
Fallout 4 was released on October 10, 2015 and is still a great game to this day. It certainly was the buzz when it came out and everyone is excited. Hell even I was. Unfortunately I could not buy it until 2 years later *cough* (steam summer sale) *cough* However I did buy it on console a few months after its release so I could not experience mods yet. My hours dont show it but to be honest, Fallout 4 might not be the greatest Fallout game ever but its still an amazing game. It saddens me to see so many people compare it to a game that is "superior" than others. Before I give pros and cons im just going to quickly say that if you do want to buy this game, do it. DO NOT LET THE NEGATIVE REVIEWS TELL YOU NOT TO. The Fallout community is could be one of the many very opinionated communities of any other game due to its controversy of New Vegas. By comparing a game to its previous game that its much more "superior" than others. To be fair I did love New Vegas and it is one of my favorite games and I do think better than Fallout 4. But I do not think it is superior. I do not think Fallout 4 is a♥♥♥♥♥♥game. When someone compares something to something else that's already wrong ESPECIALLY video games. By comparing it to something that is almost completely different and a new experience you are already violating the face of the game. If you want to go play something that is New Vegas. Well♥♥♥♥♥♥go play New Vegas right? Nope, wrong ,you decide to jump into this and expect to be exploring the Mojave Wasteland and having an equal experience of the previous game. I might get alot of bad comments for this intro already but let me start with the review.
Main Story (Warning SPOILERS): The story starts off before the great war in 2077 and the world was resource-drained. You the player luckily sign up for a space for you and your family in a Vault. A few minutes later into the intro total atomic ahnnihilation occurs and you run to the safety of the vaults. Along with your spouse and son you enter the vault not knowing the vaults were made by the government as social experiments. The social experiment for this vault was cryogenic experimentation and your family was frozen. Your spouse on the other side of the cryogenic pod carries your offspring and being unfrozen almost 200 years later a group of people take your child and kill your spouse. Waking up a few years later you set out to a new city. No longer called the Commonwealth of Boston the remaining survivors have decided to name it the Commonwealth. So the sole survivor sets out to look for his/her child from the kidnappers.
Combat: Whether you like to be sneaky beaky and stab someone with a combat knife in the back or you like to go balls deep into a raider base with a rocket launcher there really is many ways to approach a certain situation in combat. Each perk weapon and sometimes even armor will determine what you will do next. Whether its going to stab a radroach to going toe to toe to a Chameleon Deathclaw the combat is satisfying and sometimes highly rewarding.
Perk Chart: Some people might say the new perk system shouldnt have been changed and I somewhat agree. But after being released to consoles and gaining more popularity it has gained a little more younger audience. What I think Bethesda believed to do was simplify the perk system and easier to see what perks affect what physical trait in game. Some might help you increase damage with certain guns, some might help you charge at someone with power armor hell there is even some that help you swim underwater.(Pretty useless tbh Ill give you that)
Characters: Whats better than having a smart♥♥♥♥♥detective that has the personality of a cop from 2077 put into a synthetic body? Oh thats right having a super mutant following you around wanting the "milk of human kindness" because he thinks its a physical thing. How about a really racist buzz lightyear? Fallout 4 has alot of characters with fairly interesting stories and some also entail to some of the world's lore. Except you Preston garvey you bland piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥
World: The Commonwealth has many nooks and crannies for people to explore. Some people have commonly found all the time because they've seen it on their way to a destination or maybe its the destination of a quest. Sometimes when I create new characters I find areas I havent seen before or even areas that dont have markers on their maps. There's the east coast, the glowing sea, the financial district, the fens, or even Salem. If you really want to find new things this game really does reward for its exploration.
Lore: Though in my opinion when I played Fallout 4 I didnt care much of the lore at first. But then I started watching a Youtube channel by the name of Oxhorn who provides lore for all Fallout game, ive seen almost every lore video of Fallout 4 not realizing that almost every area has lore dating back before the war or sometimes even after the war. Some lore even correlates to earlier fallout games to references to the mojave wasteland or to something as little as finding Scribe Maxson in Fallout 3 or meeting Elder Maxson in Fallout 4. Some lore might be even as little as a message in a bottle leading to guy into a tub at the bottom of the east coast.
Factions: There might be fewer factions than there were in New Vegas then there are here. There is the Minutemen, Railroad, Brotherhood of Steel and the Institute. But each of them have their own ideals of the commonwealth and the community and what should change to help the commonwealth rebuild again. The Minutemen do what their motto is "Protect people at a minute's notice."The Railroad, the secret organization of agents who defend the idea that synths should be allowed to be their own person and pretty much the only people who the Institute take seriously. The Brotherhood of Steel who think that the Institute is a disease on the commonwealth and should be erradicated and use technology to rebuild society as it should be. Finally the institute whom's idea is to cleanse the commonwealth by creating new technology and killing what they think is killing the commonwealth. Fewer factions sure, but atleast we get some.

Repitition: Sometimes Fallout 4 can have very repetitive things like quests that do the same thing over and over or some things like fighting a very similar dungeon. Though these bother me they never really cross my mind when exploring it. Its just one of the few things I agree with the community on.
Dialogue Choices: Back in Fallout 3 and New Vegas we had an assortment of ways to interact with new characers from only having one questiong to having like 7 or 8 and learning more about the character. Hell sometimes the speech check was very exciting. But now we are limited to only 4 choices that can sometimes a little repetitve as well. Charasmatic choice speak checks are fun but I feel like there would need to be more.
Thats pretty much it in my opinion Fallout 4 is a great game but it needs more recognition and needs to acknowledged by alot more people.

After playing for 40+ hours, I have decided it is time to write a review for this game.
Trove is a free-to-play MMORPG, and it isn't pay-to-win, like most of the free games that are released on Steam that have in-game microtransactions. Well, let me explain it better.
Trove has in-game microtransactions, and there are two currencies for buying items in the shop:
Most of the "useful" things in the store can be purchased with both currencies. Of course, there are some exceptions, such as some items, which you'll eventually need them later, which can only be purchased if you spend real money. But that doesn't make the game pay-to-win.

I'm conflicted on this. I adored Enemy Unknown/Within, and XCOM 2 improves upon those games in many respects. The customization is great, and (fixable) optimization issues aside, it looks amazing. The new takes on old classes makes certain parts of me tingly, and much of the gameplay is sublime.
So why the thumb down? Simple. Timers. God... damn... timers...
Simply put, I play strategy games to (shock) strategize. If the occasional mission warrants I move fast (bomb diffusal), okay. I didn't mind it in EU/EW, but here it's every freakin' mission. You're constantly encouraged to avoid detection and set up ambushes, while simultaneously having Central yell at you that, unless you touch the magic objective RIGHT F***ING NOW, the world will end. You have one, maaaaybe two turns if you're lucky to set up, and then you gotta go H.A.M. to make it in time.
And it continues into the strategic overview as well. You're constantly bombarded with things to do, while being forced to plow through the campaign or be subjected to more aliens than Texas.
I can't understand how anyone thought this was going to be a good idea. Some say it was to curb Overwatch, but that could be done by tweaking overwatch range/accuracy/damage. There was no need to take a legitimate mechanic for bomb diffusal or hostage rescue, and impose it on the entire game.

First going to address a lot of the gripes about the game since I believe people are being a bit unfair. XCOM 2 has done a fantastic job of adding new content to a already great game and added a challenge to it akin to Darkest Dungeon.
--Mission time limits--
These are NOT unfair. People are complaining that a 8 turn limit mission is crap and there are too many of them. Out of 20 missions about 60% of them were 8 turn limits. The rest were either 12 limit or unlimited. The 8 turns were kinda nasty to be honest but they were doable. You just have to learn how to move. You can't act like it's XCOM Enemies Within anymore and just pop pods without there being severe consequences. You have to get it done in a shorter period of time which makes the game more difficult, but also far more fun. I will admit it's probably not for the casual gamer but mods might be good if you find it to be too much of a hinderance.
--Accuracy seems too low--
It adds a degree of challenge now so you can't just turn everyone into a sniper. At times this felt a little unfair until I realized that I was wrong. You can optimize your aim by taking high ground and strategizing and it's definitely a return to form as a lot of the earlier XCOM's were like that. This just makes you work a little more for each attack phase to be as potent as you need it to be.
--Bugs galore! (Not really...)--
I've heard people say there are terrible framerate issues but I haven't seen them yet. I've seen people saying that there are super long delays in moves and THIS I have seen, but it's not game breaking, and I'm being lenient towards the complainers here because I have my games installed on a solid state drive so I might have a TAD more speed during these moments. I've also heard numerous stories of crashes and have even seen this on Angry Joe's review but in the 15 hours I've got so far I haven't had a single crash. I've also heard people complaining about black screens on enemy movements and I only saw this once out of 20 missions and nothing really special happened.  Beyond those three things I haven't seen a single other bug at all and I wouldn't be surprised if a lot of those were hot patched soon.
--Pistols are only used by sharpshooters???--
I can't believe the amount of whining I've seen on THIS. I mean... I understand how you USED to use the pistols but to be perfectly honest, there is no reason for everyone to have a pistol in XCOM2. With the other added mechanics you really don't need it. The devs made it that way for a reason and that reason is because they were resource sinks that no one truly benefitted from to justify the cost. Glad it's gone. I might have missed something on the last XCOM game where pistols were just the bees knees but I'll be darned if I see it.
Now for the actual review: Game's great. Far more challenging than its predecessor but that is something I've really wanted anyway. Is it worth the triple A price? Yeah, definitely. Bugs will be worked out, the modding community will continue to release awesome conversions, and future content will be out soon enough.
So the elephant in the room... The season pass... That's debatable since we have no way of knowing at the time of this review what that will entail. 20 dollars for the content is actually a nice price point and if they follow the path they did back with XCOM EU and EW then it's possible that the content being released will be well worth it. To be honest no one knows. It's mostly speculation. It's entirely up to the buyer to decide but from this humble perspective I really can't see the harm in going the full 20 dollars in at this point yet I could respect someones decision to wait because DLC and season passes left a bad taste in a lot of gamers mouths as of recently.
EDIT***** 2/23/2016
First review above was with about 15 to 20 hours of gameplay. This is with considerably more.
After throwing in far more time I've noticed two bugs that aren't huge. First is just a camera bug where it sometimes cuts to nothing or cuts to the inside of a building and you don't see any action. This happened a couple times and isn't gamebreaking. Other bug is just a simple animation jerk which might just be my PCs fault. I still have not seen a single crash, if this was hot patched I really didn't notice or read into it.
Procedurally generated levels are keeping it fresh. Only campaign scripted missions remain constant as far as I can see.
Game feels a tad linear in that choosing what to build inevitably ends the same if you have any hope of keeping the avatar project at bay. Same thing with choosing what to develop first as far as research goes. Not game breaking but a little disappointing. Could be fixed with a simple mod but I'd rather see them patch a fix in. Just something to make building things a little less important for early game so folks can try to do things differently with less negative results; IE campaign ending decision because you build a psi lab instead of a comm relay or something.
I still maintain my position on the pistol, accuracy, and timed mission points. I think all of those were good decisions to give this game it's own flavor and challenge.
Game still worth a buy at full price for sure.

After having completed the main storyline twice (first run with the Minutemen, second with the Railroad, and an in-progress run with the BoS) as well as having completed numerous side quests, I think I'm finally ready to leave a review for this game.
First off, I'm going to say I don't have a lot of history with the Fallout franchise. Therefore, I don't have much of an opinion on how much the game has changed or what Bethesda is doing right or wrong in terms of gameplay or mechanics. I own Fallout: New Vegas, but I've only played around 17 hours, most of which were spent d*cking around after completing the initial main quest. I've also played a few hours of Fallout 3 on a friend's PS3. Other than that, I have no frame of reference for what a Fallout game is "supposed" to be like.
Pros:
- The storyline is solid and compelling, although I wish there were more options for how the sole survivor feels about their son. For example, you're not allowed to assume that Shaun is dead, you just have to be determined to find him the whole way through.
- The companions are very interesting to get to know. I have only reached maximum affinity with Piper and Nick, but I'm looking forward to builing relationships with other characters. Although I was very disappointed to learn you aren't allowed to romance Nick Valentine.
- The music is the bomb diggity, whether it be the original soundtrack or a radio station.
Cons:
- Bethesda sucks at paraphrasing. Like, really bad. They try to sum up what your character is going to say in a few words, but sometimes it's not at all what you were expecting. Luckily, there's a mod that allows the full dialogue to be shown.
- Speaking of mods, that brings up another con. Achievements are disabled when you have
kind of mod active. Not just things to help you cheat, mind you-- want water or landscapes to look a little prettier? Achievements disabled. Want to retexture skin or hair? Achievements disabled. Want Dogmeat to not act like a complete a*sshole and chase every enemy he sees? Achievements disabled.
- While I initially found settlements and the base-building mechanic to be fun, it's pretty... lackluster, after a while. And, by a while, I mean about two quests. Go here, kill stuff, save/setup a settlement. Make sure everyone has food, water, and a bed. Build defenses. Go here, kill more stuff. Christ, I'm not your mom! Why can't the settlers plant their own food, set up their own clean water supply, and make their own beds? I have a wasteland to be exploring! I don't have time for 50 people in 17 different locations that can't take care of themselves!
Despite its flaws, I still recommend purchasing the game if you're a fan of open-world RPGs. It's easy to sink a lot of hours into Fallout 4, and with the right assortment of mods you can play the game exactly how you like. Don't buy it at full price, though. God, what kind of heathen buys Steam games at full price? There's a sale, like, every day.

Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based RPG/dungeon crawler, set in a dark, gothic world. What makes this game unique, is the fact that it is not focusing only at the physical challenges your heroes will have to face, in order to emerge victorious, but also at the mental challenges that are waiting for them on their adventures. When you are facing unspeakable horrors how much are you willing to sacrifice to win or simply survive?
This is exactly why Darkest Dungeon is a game of trade-offs and hard decisions. Will you continue pushing forward and complete your quest, while your heroes are at the verge of madness? or abandon everything, retreat and save your favorite character?
In order to achieve this, the game implements stress levels on your characters. You don't have to take care only of your health but also of your stress level. If stress goes too high, your heroes will gain afflictions, that will make them react differently in the battlefield. Some may become more courageous and determined while others will start fearing for their lives and may even abandon you. If stress continues growing they could even die of a heart attack.
Light is also very important during gameplay. A well lit corridor or room will make your heroes feel safe and face their enemies more prepared but if you let the light fade, your heroes will start losing strenth and have a poor performance while fighting. Fighting in darkness is not only bad news though. The darker the room, the greatest the threat and of course the better the rewards. If you think your heroes can take it, go for it and gain more loot.
Your base is where your heroes can relax, relieve some stress and get ready for the next quest. Improve their skills, weapons and armors, hire more heroes and get ready to explore even deeper. Managing your roster and upgrading the buildings in your base is vital for your success.
Overall this is a great but very hard game with strong RNG and permadeath. If you enjoy games with high level of difficulty, that will make every victory look unique and rewarding, then you should take a look at the Darkest Dungeon.

For me, Darkest Dungeon is a game I enjoy playing in tiny bursts: pick it up, go through a dungeon or two, set it down and repeat a day or two later.
This is because Darkest Dungeon is a game that is difficult, stressful, and demanding in all the best ways. Every step I take, every roster I put together, every dungeon I hit: all of it could come crumbling down around me. Even what seems like the best run can all fall apart on the final battle because you enemy got in that one perfect hit, or messed up your load order, or some such thing.
Believe it or not, this is a good thing.
I never feel overpowered when I play, nothing ever feels like a sure thing. The game manages to make me feel all of the pressure and impending doom that this world is infested with.
Overall, I call this game harsh, but fair.
If you're a fan of Lovecraft, or just horror in general, love being challenged, and don't mind to fail often and fail hard, then I can not stress picking this game up enough. You'll never enjoy hopelessness so much.

There's no way to give this game a fair review anymore.
The fanbase for Darkest Dungeon is split so far down the middle that we have two completely extreme views: people praising and loving the game and disregarding any and all faults; then there's the other side with people saying that the game is an utter time waster with no fun, a slew of bugs, and all sorts of other complaints.
I'm sure what I have to say at this point will matter to no one. But I'll do my best review it based on my own thoughts, rather than the opinions I have read elsewhere online. But I will delve into those later.
I'm not the smartest guy. I'll be up front about that. I rarely go into games and know exactly what things that can be exploited, what must be done to make this or that easy, find loopholes or redundencies. I don't have the patience to go through each and every stat effect and percentage and chart it all out. Its just not something I have interest in or time to do. With this in mind, you can probably tell that I don't actually look into the RNG all that much.
Critical hits are critical hits. Misses are misses. I never noticed if one side had an advantage over the other. I never noticed the effects that torches had on the battlefield cuz I always had one lit. I never noticed if one side got more buffs or had resistances or any of that. I just played the game how I thought it should be played.
Here is where my biggest issue with the entirety of the game comes into play: the inability to play how you want.
Now, I get it. Darkest Dungeon is meant to be difficult. its meant to put you into a corner, but its boot to your jaw and see how you can escape it. Here's a few things I don't like, however, about said difficulty - with personal examples from the game:
-battle mechanics, on a defensive side. What do I mean by this? Well, once I was playing through a dungeon. I had a tough time with a wave, and wanted to go on the defensive for a bit, get some health back real quick before I proceeded to the next battle. So I kept an enemy in stunlock/debuff while I used my healer to get my fighters back into a better spot. With this one enemy left completely weak and vulnerable, it seemed like a viable strategy in order to get my footing back and continue strong. But NOPE. Literally two turns after trying this strategy, two enemies randomly come out of the woodwork. Because this game has to be SO HARD that it just throws more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t at you.
What this said to me was this: no, player, you do not play how you want to play. You cannot use the strategies YOU want to use. You play by OUR rules. You go fast, and kill fast, and if your players die in the process, well TOO BAD.
Some players may see this as just another part of the challenge, but I see this as a fundamental flaw: you are not allowed to play this game how you see fit. You are not allowed to go on the defensive, take advantage of a situation and play to your strenghts. You can ONLY play how the devs WANT you to play. And that, to me, isn't fun. It is frustrating. Its tedious. And it lead to me shutting off the game and not playing it ever again.
-escaping battle. This is a shorter one, but still a grievance with the game I personally have. So, when you escape battle, you are given a consequence of stress. I saw this as a fair trade. If things are going badly, you have the choice to take the stress in order to fight another day.
This brilliant idea was ruined by the timeworn BS cliche of: not being able to escape. So not only do I have to accept the consequence of a massive stress boost when I actually manage to get out of battle, I have to risk my party members in an entire turn that could possibly get any of them killed if the escape attempt fails. That. Is not. Ok. Take one punishment, don't put them all in one basket. And don't give me the "git gud" crap everyone else does - we all enter bad situations in this game that we need to escape once in a while. RNG makes it so. Don't corner the player by making them worry if they'll escape or not, and if you want to keep that, fine, but get rid of the added stress issue then. Pick one poison and stick to it.
-the stress meter. Now, I have to say, this was actually one of the reasons I was fascinated with this game at first. It seemed like such a neat mechanic that could actually end up with GOOD results, and not bad.
Out of the countless times my characters reached full stress, only twice has something heroic happened. This should be a 50/50 chance, and not a 10/90, imo. You're already threatening death with the stress waves (which apparently wasn't in the original EA version), why make it even more challenging by not giving the player a fair shot at feeling amazing? Because you're too busy making it feel frustratingly difficult? That's why? Eh.
Now with all that said, you'd think I HATE this game. I'm just another one of those jerks on the internet saying its the worst thing ever. But here's the thing: I don't. With all that said, I still love so much about the game:
-The art style. So refreshingly simple, yet bold and interesting.
-The music. Tense, adds to the atmosphere, and well composed.
-The designs. Goes hand in hand with art style, in a way, but every class looks very unique and stands out in their own way.
-the voice acting. Top ♥♥♥♥ing notch, hard not to love. Complex dialogue makes this game feel intelligent (even if the narrator isn't saying anything most of the time other than "this♥♥♥♥♥♥sucks sometimes yo").
-fascinating game mechanics, like stress and perks/negatives. While some people abbhore some of these things, I am impressed with how many different things your characters can get, both positive and negative.
There are things to LOVE about this game. There are things to HATE about this game. I am left torn down the middle. I want to like this game. I want to get swept up inside of it, lose myself for hours on end from dungeon to dungeon but...every time a risky dungeon is presented, I don't want to take it because I fear I have to start from scratch from a different warrior. The fact that people think that the death of your character is a fair punishment just isn't true. All those hours and money into these particular characters you want to crusade through dungeons with are put out within minutes due to bad RNG, bad situations, or just bad planning or poor decision making.
And even if it WAS all my fault, even if it WAS misdirection or poor planning or player error or...whatever, even with all that in mind and the fact that my character(s) died, wasting hours of my life because of simple mistakes, is that ok? Does it make it a fun challenge? Or a slog?
The answer is that there is no answer. This game is dependent on what you like as a gamer, and as a person, really. You're not a bad person for liking this game. And you're not bad for disliking it. I see the points of people on both sides. And I think everyone should just calm the ♥♥♥♥ down and learn to deal with other people's opinions on the internet (although that probably won't ever happen, even though it should).
As for me...this game is interesting. Its stressful. Its tactful. Its challenging. But, in spite of things, it just isn't fun to me. A lot of times it felt like a chore. To the point where I no longer wanted to play. Take that for what its worth.

I would happily recommend this game to others, just follow a few start up ideas, and run with the game, because losing is half the fun! In a demented sort of way!

Darkest Dungeon is a 4-slot position-based RPG wherein you are tasked to continuously send frightened explorers and warriors into nightmarish wealds and slovenly brackens, with the sole purpose of rebuilding your ancestral home back up, brick by bloodsoaked brick. Your chosen party members and reserves are not hired and outfitted with the expectancy that they will live for the 90 or more times you dive into another excursion--this RPG is roguelike in nature, meaning death is not only expected, but it it imminent if you wish to fight through most of the tougher bosses. In sacrifice, there is radiance--your stressed-out heroes have equal chance to find  either middling madness or courageous zeal.
As a bitesize roguelike, Darkest Dungeon will have you sending 4-person parties consisting of a handful of diverse classes and skills into horrid ruins, with the aim usually to do something like exploring 90% of an area, fulfilling all room battles, or slaying a boss enemy. In battle, there's a quaint selection of status ailments, movement shuffles, debuffs, and heals to be slung about, varying depending on your characters. But, there's also the element of Stress--a value that increases or decreases depending on how dim you keep the torch you bear, how many sickening critical hits you take, or what ailments and entrapments envelop each characters. At the edge of Stress lies the maw of madness; a Fearful hero may skip turns, while an Abusive one may hurt itself or berate others with increasing Stress. On the flip side, some characters will have the chance to rise up, becoming stronger and wiser as the tide of the fight turns. This singular feature alone is a wonderful addition to the RPG formula, and adds a lot of strategy to the scope ahead, as well. It serves not just as a thematic difficulty weight, but to also insure you consistently play with and utilize a variety of different teams and playstyles. it's quite a brilliant way to put forth the idea that each encounter with the unknown and the eldritch has a palpable effect on your poor adventurers, thus necessitating a visit to the bar or an internment at the medical asylums between missions.
When you aren't imploring your mercenaries out to the evil realms, you're constantly upgrading your haven. Early on in Darkest Dungeon, the focus is less about your adventuring roster and more about preparing your former hovel to a battle-ready home. Eventually, you'll be able to not only pay less for cures and heal more people effectively, but outfit leveled characters with better armor, weaponry, and buffed skills. As upgrades grow and characters get stronger/better, so too does the knowledge of how to better tackle traps, examine weakness of each enemy type, and formulate teams with synergy. It's an expertise that comes with both time and effort, since your stronger teams will not likely emerge until a few areas in your town are updated permanently. In this way, I've found this game much more accessible than other roguelikes like FTL or even Binding of Isaac, which gave you more options on each playthrough but did not guarantee what you could carry on. In Darkest Dungeon, even if you manage to wipe out your entire roster, the progress made in your village will ensure that the following adventures you have go by smoother due to the capability to actually upgrade stats cheaper and faster.
Thematically, Darkest Dungeon is beyond excellent; from the initial mood that narrator Wayne June dregs up like a thick fog of horror, the grim resolve permeates everything that is said and done throughout your journey. The notes and quotes of your ancestor litter each major boss fight's foreword, and with every strike and discovery there's a notation of victory--or defeat. Rarely is there something so notably incomprable when it comes to presentation, but the narration here is so enjoyable. Equally enjoyable is the fantastic art style, a kind of Gory/Mignola mashup that isn't quite hyper-real but still manages to be unsettling and shadowed with something sinister. A great many monsters are legit gross and abhorrent, which goes a long way at encountering some of the more disgusting bosses and knowing you're in for quite a match.
I'm not a roguelike guy at all--I've never even come close to beating stuff like Isaac or FTL or even Invisible Inc, much as I love those games and enjoy their mechanics. However, I've clicked with DD mainly because the "failure" of losing characters, even after a great many victories to build them up, doesn't cause me pangs of extreme grief. I am not the character--I am the descendant, and the township is my legacy, not the life of the mercs. This format allowed me to accept that the future excursions would become less fraught with peril, although the threats and stress therein will always consistently provide some sort of challenge. It's that roguelike everyone has where you can put 100 or so hours in, doing convenieently menial or repetitive tasks yet always curious what's next. What team composition can I try next? What lurks beyond that threatening curio on the map? Which quirks and diseases should I heal--or spend a fortune to lock?
When it comes to "that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t rng" claims--I have to laugh, as this is no different from any rogue/rpg/etc. The real elements of distress and fear of death are what seperate this from most smaller roguelikes, though this game's really no different in handling RNG-based tragedy than Fire Emblem or XCOM--both games that I love. Sure, there was rarely a boss that I beat without a significant death from my team, but again--this is a slow march towards getting better and building smarter. As far as options go, for those who are not a fan of systems like enemy corpses affecting slots or heart attacks making stress potentilaly more taxing, the devs have chosen to give normal runs the ability to switch those features on or off. I admit, at first I found those features a bit overwhelming--before I began paying attention to the upgrades that would even the odds. I've played with all the normal features turned on since and never felt like they hindered me immensely.
Darkest Dungeon has been a pleasure to play, from its early access inception to its ultimate released form. There have been stumbles along the way, particularly nerfs or buffs that made me initially think that the game was on very thin ice. However, Red Hook's willingness to be flexible with toggled options and updates have won my trust, and I've found that there was more advantage given to the player over time when it came to things like debuffs and movement options. That I've played almost nothing else the past few weeks since their latest flurry of updates and upgrades says a lot about how fantastic I think this stress-inducing, mind-melting jewel is. What I love most is that even at the lowest point, I've been able to start again and stronger than before--not just due to the progress of the town, but based on what I learned from each triumph and failure before. That, I believe, is the mark of an outstanding roguelike.
I've stood gallant and fearless as my Vestal withered into madness, depending on the Leper messiah to slay the Formless Flesh--and cheering silently as he proceeded to hew through the horrid menace with a much-needed hit. I've seen my entire force slaughtered and boiled to bits my the malignant Hag, cursing my fortune and vowing to return in due time to turn the tables on the morrow. I've watched entire parties crumble, only to rally around one lone Crusader who decides to get Focused at the peak of his stress. And I've accepted defeat at the maw of the malicious Shambler, foolish in my confidence that my rank 1 group could possibly outwit the Lovecraftian beast. DD is as much about the stories and failures gifted as it is about slowly accepting your knocks and eventually besting the opposition.
The match is struck; A blazing star is born.

Edit: After winning a 40 hour game.
I will never play XCOM 1 again. They fix so many things in XCOM 2 I don't know where to begin. Abilities in the old game that I would never pick have been buffed to be actually good. If you are losing missions you can scan for supplies and still be making progress.
The feeling of the game is really good. At first you feel week but because you are working in the shadows everything seems to be going fine. After you start doing misstions Advent starts uping it's game and it starts to really feel hopeless (I'm guessing this is where many will lose). At the end you feel verying powerful and start having a hope of winning the war. The story is great and feeds into these feeling well.
All the soldier classes feel great. There wasn't a single class (exept phsyonics which I never even reaserched and still won) that I felt was not worth bringing. Each choice you when leveling up you charecter is really hard. Only 20% of the time did I feel like one of the abilities I would never use.
Concealment really makes the beginning of each mission fun. You feel safer and can get into the action faster. You also feel very powerful when you can take out an entire pod with an ambush.
The mission timers really fix the game and add some depth to mission types. Not all missions have timers and not all timers running out mean you lose. The UFO for example will just call another pod to come and kill you if you don't shutdown the distress call in time.
The overwatch cam is the best thing ever. The character creator really helps the game be more fun the second time. Make sure to get the mod that lets you start with characters from your pool. It's in my list of must have mods in the comments.
There are way more mission types and each one is really fun and different. The procedural maps also add replayability and work really well.
My only problems are long loading screens and the occasional bug.
If XCOM 1 was a 8/10 XCOM 2 is a 10/10

Myself i give it a pass, why? well its been out for 36 hours and ive spent 24 of them in game, so more of a first impressions that a full deep review.
The combats better, clearer , more cunstimisation , more gear choices the skills have been ramped up , height bonus got doubled, supression imposes a wopping -50 now over double its previous value. add in armour and all the skills the enemy uses and you end up with a much richer deeper tactical combat.
The Geoscape is now a valid tactical level with real choices to make, sure there are time sensitive missions that need to be done as they pop up but between those your free to invest your time as you see fit, generating troops or resources to increase either your economy or to fight back, and a balance needs to be struck, be too aggressive and stall out , be too passive and the aliens can simply win.
The base building options are at the same time smaller but also a bit more impactful. you actually have choice rather than being a slave to the satelite nexus spam. whats your first priority? get a guerilla school and some of the old officer training unlocks such as squad size , xp bonus and more loot, go for an advanced warfare facility (how you heal fast) so your troopers are unlocking bonus skills as they level? or maybe you want to push and get a psionics lab out early and get some psychers on the field.
Timers! big bone of contention and there is a veritable hurricane of♥♥♥♥♥♥on the forums about it. myself i like them mostly , id like a round or two longer to do my guerilla ops and the defend teh civilian missions are a bit vulnerable to spawn rng. but with over 20 hours in i havent actually lost a mission to them, i have left a trooper behind just couldnt get everyone to da chopper in time.
they certainlymake sense thematically , you are an insurgency now after all , take to long and the legions of the enemy will descend on you and swamp you. and they certainly address the issue of overwatch crawling so many relied on. dp you like this design choice? well its personal opinion and im sure there will be ods to remove them if there isnt already, but myself i like thier addition.
its a much more agressive game , between the timers and the aliens actively winning the game infront of you and it might not be for everyone. but for me its a glorious breath of fresh air. the new faster pace really forces you to make the most of your troops and to push.

So, I shall tell you all a wonderful story of Adam, the 2MRB, and XCom 2.
*Before I go on this rant, I'd just like to say props to Firaxis for including Day-One Workshop support, and full access to the .inis so I can tweak the game to my liking*
My first hour with XCom was spent inside of the character creator. I created a wonderful squad of vibrant personalities that were all from my Arma3 Unit.
Pumped up and ready to go, I booted up the campain. After a brief intoduction and tutorial mission, I was ready. I was ready to fight me some aliens.
The mission started out well enough. I set up an amazing ambush, killed me some alien fellers. But then, then everything went wrong. Out of no-where, one of my guys got killed. Then I saw the culprit, a Psi Warrior. I said to myself "Pfft, I got this". I have never been so wrong.
That Psy Warrior didn't attack me. No, that would be too simple.  He, with his magical powers, revived my dead soldier and decided to turn him against me. Long story short, I ended up killing most of my squad that day. It was at the very end of them mission, victory was in sight. One click, and the Psy Warrior would be dead. *Click*. My hands went flying! My Squad was dead, but they died for a cause. There was only two survivors, but I won! I had defeated a mission I assumed to be one of those "supposed to fail" types.
The next few in-game days were spent recouperating. For days, we mourned the loss of those that had given thier life on that day. The two men that survived were promptly promoted and were set to become the leaders of my resitance. And so they did. As soon as they recouperated, another task came about. The first to set foot on the DZ was Adam, the lone recouperated survivor of that first operation. We fought, we lost comrades, but Adam survived that day. He survived the next three operations without a scratch. He was a good soldier, but all good things must come to an end.
The finial Operation I embarked upon was supposed to be simple. I was to assault a small Alien Outpost and destroy a thing for some reason or another. Like all the missions before it, Adam was the first to step foot on the DZ. He, and his other five compatriots were ready for a battle. We knew before hand that we wouldn't all make it back. Someone would have to pay for our resistance, but nobody wanted it to be them, least of all Adam, the great Combat Veteran of Operation Shattered Hope. Well, as things tend to go, all went poorly sooner rather then later. Adam was injured early on by a crazy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a sword. Some of his comrades took bullets from a turret, and some were driven crazy by a Psy Warrior. But we overcame. We faught through. But time was running out. That battle had taken 3 turns, and there was a 8 turn limit before the thing we needed went boom boom or whatever.
I panicked. I sent Adam on what hindsight would tell me would be a suicide mission. Alone with his Nade Launcher, Adam  launched the Nades into the target. Success, Adam destroyed it. But the mission was not over yet. Out of nowhere, a Psy Warrior and an Officer attacked Adam. That's where everything went wrong. Before long, Adam, my Combat Veteran of Operation Shattered Hope, died, so that the others could live. We faught furiously. Turn after turn, we faught, and eventually prevaled. We Evac'd without so much as a sigh. Adam was dead, and everyone else had become injured. It was not a good day for the XCom Project. At base, promotions were issued. recources were gained, and everyone aquired thier new gear. But nobody was happy, for on that day, we won a battle, but lost a friend. Adam will be forever remembered in the pub, where he sits side by side with the photos of all the dead heros of operations past.
You will be missed Adam.

There's no way to give this game a fair review anymore.
The fanbase for Darkest Dungeon is split so far down the middle that we have two completely extreme views: people praising and loving the game and disregarding any and all faults; then there's the other side with people saying that the game is an utter time waster with no fun, a slew of bugs, and all sorts of other complaints.
I'm sure what I have to say at this point will matter to no one. But I'll do my best review it based on my own thoughts, rather than the opinions I have read elsewhere online. But I will delve into those later.
I'm not the smartest guy. I'll be up front about that. I rarely go into games and know exactly what things that can be exploited, what must be done to make this or that easy, find loopholes or redundencies. I don't have the patience to go through each and every stat effect and percentage and chart it all out. Its just not something I have interest in or time to do. With this in mind, you can probably tell that I don't actually look into the RNG all that much.
Critical hits are critical hits. Misses are misses. I never noticed if one side had an advantage over the other. I never noticed the effects that torches had on the battlefield cuz I always had one lit. I never noticed if one side got more buffs or had resistances or any of that. I just played the game how I thought it should be played.
Here is where my biggest issue with the entirety of the game comes into play: the inability to play how you want.
Now, I get it. Darkest Dungeon is meant to be difficult. its meant to put you into a corner, but its boot to your jaw and see how you can escape it. Here's a few things I don't like, however, about said difficulty - with personal examples from the game:
-battle mechanics, on a defensive side. What do I mean by this? Well, once I was playing through a dungeon. I had a tough time with a wave, and wanted to go on the defensive for a bit, get some health back real quick before I proceeded to the next battle. So I kept an enemy in stunlock/debuff while I used my healer to get my fighters back into a better spot. With this one enemy left completely weak and vulnerable, it seemed like a viable strategy in order to get my footing back and continue strong. But NOPE. Literally two turns after trying this strategy, two enemies randomly come out of the woodwork. Because this game has to be SO HARD that it just throws more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t at you.
What this said to me was this: no, player, you do not play how you want to play. You cannot use the strategies YOU want to use. You play by OUR rules. You go fast, and kill fast, and if your players die in the process, well TOO BAD.
Some players may see this as just another part of the challenge, but I see this as a fundamental flaw: you are not allowed to play this game how you see fit. You are not allowed to go on the defensive, take advantage of a situation and play to your strenghts. You can ONLY play how the devs WANT you to play. And that, to me, isn't fun. It is frustrating. Its tedious. And it lead to me shutting off the game and not playing it ever again.
-escaping battle. This is a shorter one, but still a grievance with the game I personally have. So, when you escape battle, you are given a consequence of stress. I saw this as a fair trade. If things are going badly, you have the choice to take the stress in order to fight another day.
This brilliant idea was ruined by the timeworn BS cliche of: not being able to escape. So not only do I have to accept the consequence of a massive stress boost when I actually manage to get out of battle, I have to risk my party members in an entire turn that could possibly get any of them killed if the escape attempt fails. That. Is not. Ok. Take one punishment, don't put them all in one basket. And don't give me the "git gud" crap everyone else does - we all enter bad situations in this game that we need to escape once in a while. RNG makes it so. Don't corner the player by making them worry if they'll escape or not, and if you want to keep that, fine, but get rid of the added stress issue then. Pick one poison and stick to it.
-the stress meter. Now, I have to say, this was actually one of the reasons I was fascinated with this game at first. It seemed like such a neat mechanic that could actually end up with GOOD results, and not bad.
Out of the countless times my characters reached full stress, only twice has something heroic happened. This should be a 50/50 chance, and not a 10/90, imo. You're already threatening death with the stress waves (which apparently wasn't in the original EA version), why make it even more challenging by not giving the player a fair shot at feeling amazing? Because you're too busy making it feel frustratingly difficult? That's why? Eh.
Now with all that said, you'd think I HATE this game. I'm just another one of those jerks on the internet saying its the worst thing ever. But here's the thing: I don't. With all that said, I still love so much about the game:
-The art style. So refreshingly simple, yet bold and interesting.
-The music. Tense, adds to the atmosphere, and well composed.
-The designs. Goes hand in hand with art style, in a way, but every class looks very unique and stands out in their own way.
-the voice acting. Top ♥♥♥♥ing notch, hard not to love. Complex dialogue makes this game feel intelligent (even if the narrator isn't saying anything most of the time other than "this♥♥♥♥♥♥sucks sometimes yo").
-fascinating game mechanics, like stress and perks/negatives. While some people abbhore some of these things, I am impressed with how many different things your characters can get, both positive and negative.
There are things to LOVE about this game. There are things to HATE about this game. I am left torn down the middle. I want to like this game. I want to get swept up inside of it, lose myself for hours on end from dungeon to dungeon but...every time a risky dungeon is presented, I don't want to take it because I fear I have to start from scratch from a different warrior. The fact that people think that the death of your character is a fair punishment just isn't true. All those hours and money into these particular characters you want to crusade through dungeons with are put out within minutes due to bad RNG, bad situations, or just bad planning or poor decision making.
And even if it WAS all my fault, even if it WAS misdirection or poor planning or player error or...whatever, even with all that in mind and the fact that my character(s) died, wasting hours of my life because of simple mistakes, is that ok? Does it make it a fun challenge? Or a slog?
The answer is that there is no answer. This game is dependent on what you like as a gamer, and as a person, really. You're not a bad person for liking this game. And you're not bad for disliking it. I see the points of people on both sides. And I think everyone should just calm the ♥♥♥♥ down and learn to deal with other people's opinions on the internet (although that probably won't ever happen, even though it should).
As for me...this game is interesting. Its stressful. Its tactful. Its challenging. But, in spite of things, it just isn't fun to me. A lot of times it felt like a chore. To the point where I no longer wanted to play. Take that for what its worth.

So far I find this to  be a fantastic game. There are a few things that I feel one MUST do in order to get off the ground running.
1st- Your heroes are going to die, or be dismissed because they have gone to the loons, so don't get too attached, at least in the beginning.
2nd- The biggest focus for heirlooms should be on getting the wagon upgrades, at least to 15 heroes staying and 4 arriving at a time. This will allow a player to pool new heroes in to replace old ones that have gone around the bend and rest the ones that are a wee bit stressed.
3rd- Don't feel like a failure just because you have to retreat from battle or even from the quest. Loot grab and run for the hills, this is a game about attrition and until you can find optimal teams, you'll lose.
4th- Know that some of the greatest fun is the sense of accomplishment from completing tasks that seem overwhelming. That's why players get so passionate about this game, its a hard nut to crack but fully enjoyable once you get the basics down. Even more when you start to invest and feel for your flawed heroes that teeter on insanity's edge.
I would happily recommend this game to others, just follow a few start up ideas, and run with the game, because losing is half the fun! In a demented sort of way!

Darkest Dungeon is a 4-slot position-based RPG wherein you are tasked to continuously send frightened explorers and warriors into nightmarish wealds and slovenly brackens, with the sole purpose of rebuilding your ancestral home back up, brick by bloodsoaked brick. Your chosen party members and reserves are not hired and outfitted with the expectancy that they will live for the 90 or more times you dive into another excursion--this RPG is roguelike in nature, meaning death is not only expected, but it it imminent if you wish to fight through most of the tougher bosses. In sacrifice, there is radiance--your stressed-out heroes have equal chance to find  either middling madness or courageous zeal.
As a bitesize roguelike, Darkest Dungeon will have you sending 4-person parties consisting of a handful of diverse classes and skills into horrid ruins, with the aim usually to do something like exploring 90% of an area, fulfilling all room battles, or slaying a boss enemy. In battle, there's a quaint selection of status ailments, movement shuffles, debuffs, and heals to be slung about, varying depending on your characters. But, there's also the element of Stress--a value that increases or decreases depending on how dim you keep the torch you bear, how many sickening critical hits you take, or what ailments and entrapments envelop each characters. At the edge of Stress lies the maw of madness; a Fearful hero may skip turns, while an Abusive one may hurt itself or berate others with increasing Stress. On the flip side, some characters will have the chance to rise up, becoming stronger and wiser as the tide of the fight turns. This singular feature alone is a wonderful addition to the RPG formula, and adds a lot of strategy to the scope ahead, as well. It serves not just as a thematic difficulty weight, but to also insure you consistently play with and utilize a variety of different teams and playstyles. it's quite a brilliant way to put forth the idea that each encounter with the unknown and the eldritch has a palpable effect on your poor adventurers, thus necessitating a visit to the bar or an internment at the medical asylums between missions.
When you aren't imploring your mercenaries out to the evil realms, you're constantly upgrading your haven. Early on in Darkest Dungeon, the focus is less about your adventuring roster and more about preparing your former hovel to a battle-ready home. Eventually, you'll be able to not only pay less for cures and heal more people effectively, but outfit leveled characters with better armor, weaponry, and buffed skills. As upgrades grow and characters get stronger/better, so too does the knowledge of how to better tackle traps, examine weakness of each enemy type, and formulate teams with synergy. It's an expertise that comes with both time and effort, since your stronger teams will not likely emerge until a few areas in your town are updated permanently. In this way, I've found this game much more accessible than other roguelikes like FTL or even Binding of Isaac, which gave you more options on each playthrough but did not guarantee what you could carry on. In Darkest Dungeon, even if you manage to wipe out your entire roster, the progress made in your village will ensure that the following adventures you have go by smoother due to the capability to actually upgrade stats cheaper and faster.
Thematically, Darkest Dungeon is beyond excellent; from the initial mood that narrator Wayne June dregs up like a thick fog of horror, the grim resolve permeates everything that is said and done throughout your journey. The notes and quotes of your ancestor litter each major boss fight's foreword, and with every strike and discovery there's a notation of victory--or defeat. Rarely is there something so notably incomprable when it comes to presentation, but the narration here is so enjoyable. Equally enjoyable is the fantastic art style, a kind of Gory/Mignola mashup that isn't quite hyper-real but still manages to be unsettling and shadowed with something sinister. A great many monsters are legit gross and abhorrent, which goes a long way at encountering some of the more disgusting bosses and knowing you're in for quite a match.
I'm not a roguelike guy at all--I've never even come close to beating stuff like Isaac or FTL or even Invisible Inc, much as I love those games and enjoy their mechanics. However, I've clicked with DD mainly because the "failure" of losing characters, even after a great many victories to build them up, doesn't cause me pangs of extreme grief. I am not the character--I am the descendant, and the township is my legacy, not the life of the mercs. This format allowed me to accept that the future excursions would become less fraught with peril, although the threats and stress therein will always consistently provide some sort of challenge. It's that roguelike everyone has where you can put 100 or so hours in, doing convenieently menial or repetitive tasks yet always curious what's next. What team composition can I try next? What lurks beyond that threatening curio on the map? Which quirks and diseases should I heal--or spend a fortune to lock?
When it comes to "that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t rng" claims--I have to laugh, as this is no different from any rogue/rpg/etc. The real elements of distress and fear of death are what seperate this from most smaller roguelikes, though this game's really no different in handling RNG-based tragedy than Fire Emblem or XCOM--both games that I love. Sure, there was rarely a boss that I beat without a significant death from my team, but again--this is a slow march towards getting better and building smarter. As far as options go, for those who are not a fan of systems like enemy corpses affecting slots or heart attacks making stress potentilaly more taxing, the devs have chosen to give normal runs the ability to switch those features on or off. I admit, at first I found those features a bit overwhelming--before I began paying attention to the upgrades that would even the odds. I've played with all the normal features turned on since and never felt like they hindered me immensely.
Darkest Dungeon has been a pleasure to play, from its early access inception to its ultimate released form. There have been stumbles along the way, particularly nerfs or buffs that made me initially think that the game was on very thin ice. However, Red Hook's willingness to be flexible with toggled options and updates have won my trust, and I've found that there was more advantage given to the player over time when it came to things like debuffs and movement options. That I've played almost nothing else the past few weeks since their latest flurry of updates and upgrades says a lot about how fantastic I think this stress-inducing, mind-melting jewel is. What I love most is that even at the lowest point, I've been able to start again and stronger than before--not just due to the progress of the town, but based on what I learned from each triumph and failure before. That, I believe, is the mark of an outstanding roguelike.
I've stood gallant and fearless as my Vestal withered into madness, depending on the Leper messiah to slay the Formless Flesh--and cheering silently as he proceeded to hew through the horrid menace with a much-needed hit. I've seen my entire force slaughtered and boiled to bits my the malignant Hag, cursing my fortune and vowing to return in due time to turn the tables on the morrow. I've watched entire parties crumble, only to rally around one lone Crusader who decides to get Focused at the peak of his stress. And I've accepted defeat at the maw of the malicious Shambler, foolish in my confidence that my rank 1 group could possibly outwit the Lovecraftian beast. DD is as much about the stories and failures gifted as it is about slowly accepting your knocks and eventually besting the opposition.
The match is struck; A blazing star is born.
