Darkest Dungeon is a game of making the best possible out of a hellish situation.
For that reason alone, I love it.
However, there's infinitely so much more that makes the game amazing. It's a Dungeon-Crawling Turn-based Roguelike RPG, with heavily resemblance to XCOM in terms of the combat's shenanigans. You'll miss attacks that're 80+%, and just be completely disappointed in yourself. You also have to deal with the stress of your heroes, their quirks, diseases, and everything else that can be wrong in a human being.
Aside from that, the game's style is just as amazing. The dark atmosphere is really, really well set-in-stone with a Lovecraftian look to everything. The narrator's voice is also wonderful. For $20, the game is truly a steal. Even for $25, the post-release price incoming February 2nd, it's still really worth it. Infinite replayability due to RNG wanting to screw you over every time. Pick this up, if you think you truly aren't afraid of the dark.

After seeing the reviews and videos for Starbound I thought I might as well give it a try and see what this game is about.  After playing about 13 hours, I think this is a great game.  I like the music of the game and how sounds fall right into place.  This is the first game where I have pulled out a tent and campfire just to watch the night go by and listen to the music.  Being able to pick what planets you go to (besides the first one) is pretty cool.  It has a nice animation that it goes through and I never get tired of it.  The diffent planets are awesome.  I have been on two forest planets and one snow planet.  I have to say it was the harder one out of the three.  To have to worry about the cold non-stop is a small worry but once you see your screen start to turn blue and you start dying is a rush when you are no where near your camp and are fighting a few creatures in the middle of the night.  This game has so much put into it already and I can't wait to see what else they put in this game.  Now I do a have problem or two, and I'm sure it is because of it being in BETA.  Multiplayer is slightly confusing for me, not sure if it's because it's just not ready or I'm a little slow and just need a bit of help to get it running.  I'm also new to the PC gaming and may not understand it fully.  A lot of the items you can make aren't available yet, again not sure if it's due to the fact of being a BETA and you can't get them yet or I just don't have the items needed to make it.  I have only come across about 10 NPCs, all of them wanting to kill me.  I haven't seen any villages with friendly NPCs.  I have seen a few bulidings already made and they helped a lot when first starting out.  I would love to have some of the gear you see in the video, but again, I'm not sure if I can even get it.  I've finished the first quests and now pretty much jump planet to planet.  I would love to see more quests and NPC related things.  But overall, for being a BETA,  Starbound is a great game and is a blast to play. If anyone can help me with a few things like mulitplayer, I would love the help. Keep on gaming!
EDIT: After watching a few videos and reading the Wiki page, I understand so much more.  I am building bigger and better things now that I understand it.  This BETA is loaded with things already!
NEW EDIT:  Just landed on my next planet and found a HUGE Apex city.  Looks awesome and is pretty fun to be in.  I love how the people react to you being there.  The guards will follow you if you have a weapon out, it's kinda funny haha.  Can't wait to see what else is in this game.

Edit: After winning a 40 hour game.
I will never play XCOM 1 again. They fix so many things in XCOM 2 I don't know where to begin. Abilities in the old game that I would never pick have been buffed to be actually good. If you are losing missions you can scan for supplies and still be making progress.
The feeling of the game is really good. At first you feel week but because you are working in the shadows everything seems to be going fine. After you start doing misstions Advent starts uping it's game and it starts to really feel hopeless (I'm guessing this is where many will lose). At the end you feel verying powerful and start having a hope of winning the war. The story is great and feeds into these feeling well.
All the soldier classes feel great. There wasn't a single class (exept phsyonics which I never even reaserched and still won) that I felt was not worth bringing. Each choice you when leveling up you charecter is really hard. Only 20% of the time did I feel like one of the abilities I would never use.
Concealment really makes the beginning of each mission fun. You feel safer and can get into the action faster. You also feel very powerful when you can take out an entire pod with an ambush.
The mission timers really fix the game and add some depth to mission types. Not all missions have timers and not all timers running out mean you lose. The UFO for example will just call another pod to come and kill you if you don't shutdown the distress call in time.
The overwatch cam is the best thing ever. The character creator really helps the game be more fun the second time. Make sure to get the mod that lets you start with characters from your pool. It's in my list of must have mods in the comments.
There are way more mission types and each one is really fun and different. The procedural maps also add replayability and work really well.
My only problems are long loading screens and the occasional bug.
If XCOM 1 was a 8/10 XCOM 2 is a 10/10

Mods Simulator 2015.

Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

Maybe Steam shouldn't let people write reviews until they've actually PLAYED games more than 5 minutes?  Oh well.
XCOM 2 is an excellent game.  Riduculously so.  It's a game design triumph.  A masterpiece.
It improves on every element of the excellent XCOM 1 and adds the randomness (procedurally generated tactical maps, random strategic happenings, random loot, some random research, etc) that was missing in the very static XCOM 1.  It has better visuals, better character customization, better voice (more of it and with accents from different nationalities), better UI, better mod support.  There's more loot, more ways to setup your troops, some influence from the excellent long war mod, better AI, better AI behaviors (like patrolling, running for help, calling in reinforcements), tons of mission variety, and on and on.  And there's more replay value because of all the procudural/random elements.
And I like the mission timers.  They add tension, force you out of your comfort zones, force you to take risks, force you to adapt and conquer - they make you become a better players.  (Contrrary to what some may think, only about half the missions have any kind of timed objective/element).
The game's optimization is pretty poor - or they just dialed up the settings too high for the autodetect - but one can easily lower a few settings and get the game playing smoothly.  The engine used for this game has long been known to be less that awesome for performance - but in this case, simple in-game setting changing can get you rolling - so to me this is a non factor.
Basically, this game is XCOM, it's more true to the originals in that it's challenging and you feel the pressure of survival.  XCOM 1, while a great game in its own way, was more of the call of duty/console version for widespread/mass appeal.  Nothing wrong with that, but XCOM 2 puts XCOM back where it belongs - on PC's, and as a first rate strategy game.

There were a lot of expectations for Fallout 4. The reception was mixed in the end, and the game has become an example of what happens when content is made generic enough for the average consumer. Classic Fallout and Fallout 2 are RPGs in every sense, but Fallout 4 has left that behind for a gun-centered gameplay and controls. At $30, if there was a neutral review, this game would deserve it. (At $60, hard no from me.) There is still much to enjoy in Bethesda's blockbuster title of 2015, but fans of old should expect an entirely new style of game.
Combat/Gameplay/Controls: 7/10
Fallout 3 and New Vegas suffered from stunted combat and awkward controls. While amazing games, they did not feel entirely comfortable to play. Bethesda has solved this issue in the latest installment to the series. Guns, melee weapons, and even explosives are far easier to use out of VATS. This allows for a more immersive experience.
Points are taken off for the workshop element of the game. The workshop is a good idea with poor implementation. The good is that you make use of all items in the world, and building a colony of settlers from the ground up is a tedious but enjoyable process, fitting well as post-game content. The bad is, well, everything about actually using it. Building parts that you want to clip together often will not for no apparent reason. It is often inexplicable why a part is allowed to be built in one place but not another. Settlers have horrible AI and glitch in hilarious ways. Expect them to greet you like mindless drones whenever you walk by, causing a chorus of awkward one-liners as you jog through a settlement. On top of that, there are only a few faces you can expect settlers to have, meaning you will have settlements that look like clone armies. The items you can craft in the vanilla game are so limited that you will inevitably feel let down and cheated. Again, it's a good idea, but it's anything but polished.
Story/Characters: 2/10
Like DOOM 2016 I recently reviewed, the story is the weak link of the game. Only, DOOM isn't supposed to have a great story. Fallout is supposed to have a great story! You will be let down in the most painful fashion as you track your kidnapped child in linear quests for a large portion of the game. You do eventually break out of the linearity of the main quests, but that isn't the only problem in this section. The storytelling itself is BAD. I would go as far as to say it is broken. Your immersion is put to the test when you are instantly trusted by every faction you want to be a part of. You are the leader of the Minutemen 30 minutes into the game! Who thought this was acceptable writing? Sometimes elements of the story have fantastic potential (such as synths) and are squandered by immersion-breaking dialogue and quests. Characters are one-dimensional, emotionless stereotypes that you have seen in every other game. There are some companions that feel polished and are honestly fascinating characters, but they are few and far between as well as the only saving grace in this section.
Perhaps Fallout 4's biggest injustice to the characters of the game is what it does to you, the main character. Varied dialogue options are pushed to the side in favor of awkward voice acting. One of the things I enjoy the most about older Fallout games are all of the options you have when interacting with someone that allow me to project myself on the main character. In Fallout 4, you have 3 options in every interaction: Yes, No, and Sarcastic, and you don't even know the exact dialogue your character will say when you choose an option. Sometimes the sarcastic option ends with the MC being a huge♥♥♥♥♥♥ other times he just has a harmless laugh. You can't possibly know until you choose it, causing me to never choose it. The game is so streamlined that it's insulting.
Graphics/Optimization: 3/10
The graphics are not as good as other AAA titles in the business, but they are passable. Bethesda's Creation Engine bugs out past 60 fps, so set a limiter if need be. I would be happy to grant a 5 out of 10 on these alone, but as with all Creation Engine Bethesda games, there is one more important aspect of optimization they get wrong: bugs. Game breaking bugs are everywhere, even 2 years after release. Bethesda would prefer to release texture packs and the imfamous Creation Club instead of making their game playable. Shame on them.
Soundtrack/Audio: 9/10
By far the most positive section of my review so far comes from audio. You get stunning soundtracks that can make even the most benign parts of the story feel "epic". The radio comes with a plethora of fun, lore-friendly music. It's gotten to the point that I even have many on my iTunes now! There are times when the sound effects feel a little out of place, but the grand majority are well implemented. Overall, audio is a big plus for this game.
Intangibles/Enjoyment Factor/Everything Else: 9/10
This is basically everything not touched above. Games all have that "enjoyment factor," that part of the game that cannot be expressed in summaries of combat or controls, audio or visuals. Fallout 4 has a lot of that. The world is so vast that I find myself enthralled, even if the main story is a bit of a joke. Fallout 4 doesn't shine in the main story though; it shines in the side stories. There are dozens of small stories literred throughout the wasteland, and exploring to find them is incredibly satisfying. Be prepared for heartbreak and amazement as you dig up pre-war notes and holotapes. DLC is a mixed bag, but one in particular called Far Harbor adds a lot to the game, and the story is more complex and intriguing. That doesn't even touch on modding where you can address many of the above problems I have with the game.
Overall: 6/10
Fallout 4 has so much going for it, but for each good element in the game, you are almost sure to find poor implementation. I do not think Fallout 4 is a bad game, but I do not think it is particularly good either. If you aren't looking for a classic RPG experience, there is much fun to be had exploring the wastes of Boston, fighting its creatures and helping its people. Just don't expect a great story or memorable characters for the most part.

Once again steam reviews are plagued by opinionated people who exagerate the "cons" to make it sound far worse than it really is, just because there's some aspects in the game they don't like.
I hope I got your attention. Good.
Now as many reviewers have said I will say as well. Most negative reviews talk about performance: MSAA will slice your FPS, turn it off or enable FXAA. There will be a patch soon to optimise it.
Now that we go that out of the way.
X-com 2 is based after the events in X-com 1. You've lost the war, and well.. read the store page for more info. The point is, the game plays like this. You're a resistance cell, not a full fledged world army equipped with the best of everything. Apparently people are down voting because it doesn't play like this. (Get gud?)
The biggest complaint apart from optimization is the mission timers in the battles. Most reviews exagerate the mother loving heck out of this as they hate missions which are timed. Fair enough. There IS a mod which removes this already, so if turn timers are not your thing, there you go.
If a game is going to have timers for missions, then they need to make sense right? Well in X-com they do. They make perfect sense for the missions which have them. You just broke a highly important VIP to the Aliens out of confinement, you're a resistance cell with limited manpower and resources, of course you're going to have to get the hell out of dodge and fast once you break that guy out. It makes sense no? It's REALISTIC. It's IMMERSIVE.. You know.. those things which people apparently hate in games these days.
Setting my own butthurt at societies downfall in terms of gaming aside, the time limit, and how often you run into them is changed depending on difficulty, so if you dont' like timed missions to often, but like them for when they make sense, you can adjust the difficulty level of the game and it will throw less at you.
Apart from that, I love how it feels like you are actually a resistance cell in a mobile base. Scavanging for equipment on the battlefield when enemies drop them, selling parts, corpses, and other alien artifacts on the Black Market to get Intel, and buying/trading/selling in Intel on the Black Market to gain goods to fill the holes of research and bad RNG rolls in battles in terms of mods you find, make it feel like you are the aggressors against a superior foe.
The stealth system in place for most missions is excellent as well, allowing you to scout out the land and enemies before engaging, and setting up ambushes which could wipe the slate in that area entirely before the aliens have time to respond.
There is now a better world map as well, This is where you move your mobile base from region to region, unlock new regions by contacting the resistance cells in that area, and take on side missions to gain supplies, Intel, etc.
-----------------
Over all the game isn't bad by any means. Some performance issues which should be fixed relatively soon, good immersion, great classic game mechanics from X-com 1.
-------------------
If you're still wondering about the complaints on this game. There are 2 people on the forums are can articulate points far better than me. There is ALOT of debate on the timers in this game. These are 2 great responses.
Martial.lore:
The timers are essential. Turtling is not a tactic. The squad isn't trying to find a good picnic spot. XCOM is a guerrilla force that has to make lighting strikes before going back into hiding.
This theme is reinforced by every mechanic in the game from the short individual timers on the globe to the reinforcement drops that come when you just desperately want to get everyone to the evac point.
Sometimes you just have accept that there was not enough time for your ill-equipped soldiers to complete their objective and stay alive, and sometimes sacrifices have to be made for the greater good.
Failure is hard to accept but without the timers the potential for disaster during missions would be missing and the game would not be worthy of the XCOM name.
If it didn't upset players complacency and make them furious at how unfair life is then where is the fun in that? Sometimes FTL makes me very angry but it's one of my favorite tactical video games and I am generally very good at playing it.
Once I have learned how to succeed with XCOM 2 I imagine that even though they will feel familiar and seem easier to deal with, the timers will still screw up a good plan once in a while and get good people killed.
Perish the thought that this were a game in which every move, every action and every decision did not have consequences.
Jolly:
"It mostly IS blind hate against timers. People complaining without really give it a try, or even trying.
"Because most of the timers are idiotic, and pretty much all of them are poorly implemented."
Um, no. Idiotic? That's opinion and not one I'd agree with. Poorly implemented? It's a countdown on the screen - what do you want, an hourglass? I dancing girl who removes clothes til the "time" is up? WTF.
Most of the people complaining can't seem to let go of their old XCOM ways. They want to turtle thru full cover overwatch and lure aliens into easy kills. It's a weak "tactic" that takes advantage of poor AI that suicides into that crap.
The timers, which only appear in about half the missions if you actually play the game more than you cry about it, aren't even for entire missions, usually just for objectives. The cause you to move a little fast, to tak risks, take you out of your comfort zone, and they obliterate the cheeseball reliance on overwatch luring.
What's sad is that if you actually play the game with an open mind, the timers are no big deal. If you just decide you're going to cry about the timers no matter what, which is ignorant, then you desreve the misery you bring upon yourself.
XCOM 2 is a glorious game and a triumph of design. Embrace and love it for everything that it offers, which is a megaton."

CORRECTION: I complained about not being able to choose a new squaddie's class, but one of the new facilities allows a rookie to train to a class of your choice. Promotions from XP still seem  to be random.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I was a huge fan of Enemy Unknown. Been playing this 6 hours now. Here are the observations from my first campaign, which has gone... not so great. Probably restarting tomorrow.
CONCEPT: Long-form strategy with turn-based tactical missions where you retake the Earth from alien overlords. Set 20 years after a the events of a very poor playthrough of Enemy Unknown.
IMPROVEMENTS:
VISUALS: Actually looks like a current gen game now. Framerate was pretty crap at first on my fairly high-end PC, but turning shadows down from max to high solved that. People don't look like action figures anymore, (making that Guile hair even weirder-looking) and the alien designs are really cool and unsettling.
CUSTOMIZATION: Way more options for troops visually, and more sensible mechanics-wise. Instead of putting a scope in your pocket for some damn reason, you attach it to the actual weapon, and there are a variety of mods to use too. Cosmetically, troops have options for clothing, accessories, scars, and far more voices. You can also "save" troops to ensure they show up when you play.
STORY: On top of having one of the more original sequel concepts, it put a bit more effort into the plot. The player was kind of a non-entity in the first game, but now you hold some actual significance, while other characters are given more depth.
STEALTH: Most missions allow your troops to sneak around before the actual firefight. With a bit of planning, you can take out a whole alien patrol before they get into cover.
MISSION VARIANCE: First game's missions were all kill the aliens and maybe save civilians, and then escort a VIP once or twice. Now, you're raiding supply runs, blowing up power relays,  defending power relays and rescuing former XCOM operatives.
NO MORE SATELLITES OR PANIC: There's other stuff you need to do now, but it doesn't feel like you're babysitting anymore.
SWORDS: SWOOORDS!!!
NOT IMPROVEMENTS:
EXPLOSIONS: I don't think a "this will blow up soon" symbol would have been the worst thing. My troops either die a hero to alien blasters or live long enough to stand too close to an exploding minivan. Also, the Aliens really haven't converted all people's cars to electric?
FREE ALIEN MOVES: Yes, they still get a free move into cover after you spot them, unless you're in stealth mode. I understand the limitations of AI, but it still feels very unfair that it's impossible to catch these things off guard. And I'm pretty sure the old X-COM games didn't have this problem.
LAGGING: Not graphical lag, but a lot of weird pauses between objectives, especially in early, tutorialized missions. Far more bearable in normal play, but took me out of the first hour a few times.
All in all, highly recommended. There are a few lingering issues the previous game had, but nothing new to annoy you. The vast majority of the game has only improved. There's so much to say about this simple game. First off, Trove is a something that's easy to overlook, voxel-based games are a dime a dozen these days for their graphical simplicity. Something like this doesn't stand out. But, as you play Trove, you will realize the depth and playability this game possesses. I'm not going to promise anything spectacular or industry-changing about the challenges you face, I mean I'll be honest, Trove is a skinner box. But in the best way.
The easiest way to describe Trove's gameplay is Minecraft (of course) mixed with Realm of the Mad-God made 3rd person. Classes are limited in ability and range, but synergize very well with each other, none are a bad pick and you can freely switch between them as you play. On that subject, getting and acquiring new classes requires no actual cash purchase, simply playing the game will unlock everything you absulutely need.
While combat is not particularly unique, it is very satisfying and something pleasing to repeat. Each class has it's own rush and mechanics to it that makes them very different to play. The best part too is that classes become easier to level the stronger you get as a player, gear can be interchanged.  Every time I pick up a new class, I fall in love with it. The game really encourages you to make more classes too,  power comes not from stacking one specialty but being a truly versatile player.
Honestly though, my favorite aspect of this game is the sheer creativity with it. The biomes are colorful and rich with character, Neon City is your greatest Tron fantasy made voxel while Candy Land will make you hungry within moments. The care taken in sculpting this world is truly amazing, every dungeon was a wonder to discover- it feels like you're fighting within a work of art. New dungeons and bosses are being added every few updates as well. The creativity doesn't end with the developers either, just about every piece of equipment you find has a name tacked onto it, telling you which player designed that model in-game. Every weapon, hat, face, you break down is added to your collection, an ever-growing hoard of cosmetics to dress your character as you wish. I find that even without needing the big and flashy gear that everyone covets, it's easy to make a look that you personally enjoy.
Creation doesn't end there, players can personalize their own house, and even guilds (dubbed clubs in this game) have 100% freedom to meld their own realm to be whatever they wish, block by block. Honestly nothing brings a group together like a project, working together and making that world a home for your entire grup. Someplace everyone can feel like they played a part whether it was planning, recipe's, materials, or good hard labor.  I can't tell you how many nights I meant to go to bed after loot runs, only to remain up for hours tweaking my Club's main hall for both form and function.
So far the only negative I can really say about the game is some of the community is a bit young, and coordinating high-level gameplay can be slightly frustrating with people new to MMO's and concepts like this. Most of the technical difficulties and errors have been erased as far as I can tell, and new content is making this an ever-evolving experience.
I highly recommend you try it, it's only free after all!

EDIT - There are already mods on the Workshop to disable timers, which is the basis for a huge number of negative reviews here. So, y'know, keep that in mind.
Pros
- Punishing; you WILL lose soldiers you WILL NOT win every mission or campaign.
- Wonderful model and texture work, with nice lighting and shading.
- Feels different enough to justify a new game imo.
- Enemy patrols are a game changer, forcing you to pick your battles and make the most of your advantages.
- Large array of character customization, letting you create and become attached to digital representations of your friends so you can watch helplessly as they are torn apart by aliens. With Workshop support, there is almost endless possibilities for new cosmetic options.
- Extremely open modding, to the point where some core mechanics are essentially .ini value tweaks.
- 42GB of development content in the SDK to work and create new content with. Seriously awesome.
Cons
- Others report performance issues, though I have not experienced them aside from slight stuttering during the insertion cinematic animations. (i74790k, 32gb RAM, TitanX, Win10, installed on SSD).
- Strange pauses once in a while before or after actions, though I haven't found it as annoying as others appear to have.
Notes
- It's not EU or EW with better graphics, it's a different game. Most missions have turn timers which force you to think and play aggressively and take risks, rather than turtle your favorite soldiers up 1 square at a time. Some people hate this, they say it isn't "fair" or "too hard". Personally I really enjoy it for the reasons I listed here.

It was my favorite game of 2015 and it wasn't even technically out yet.
It's a hard game, but screwing up won't typically make you lose, it will just push your progress back. It's an RNG heavy game so if dying due to bad luck makes you rage, you shouldn't go anywhere near this game. The positioning based turn based combat is innovative but does get repetitive after a while, however with 14 classes in the game and only 4 slots to put them in, and considering some classes can be built multiple ways (Combat Vestial vs Support Verstial), it's going to take quite a while to run out of combinations to expierment with. Enemy variety isn't amazing but it's good enough.
By far the biggest draw is the style of the game. The Narrator is a gem, the art is fantastic, despite how dark the lovecraftian setting is, I never get tired of looking at this game.
I can't even comment on the community controversy, when I got this game when it released in early access I trusted the Devs to bring it to a solid completed state, I didn't care when they added corpses because it was their vision, I didn't care when they added the option to remove corpses because it's their vision. And I believed in their vision.
What I'm saying is, this game is not made for everyone, however I recommend it becausse if you are the kind of person this game is made for, it is a must buy, even at full price.

Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

X-com 2 is based after the events in X-com 1. You've lost the war, and well.. read the store page for more info. The point is, the game plays like this. You're a resistance cell, not a full fledged world army equipped with the best of everything. Apparently people are down voting because it doesn't play like this. (Get gud?)
The biggest complaint apart from optimization is the mission timers in the battles. Most reviews exagerate the mother loving heck out of this as they hate missions which are timed. Fair enough. There IS a mod which removes this already, so if turn timers are not your thing, there you go.
If a game is going to have timers for missions, then they need to make sense right? Well in X-com they do. They make perfect sense for the missions which have them. You just broke a highly important VIP to the Aliens out of confinement, you're a resistance cell with limited manpower and resources, of course you're going to have to get the hell out of dodge and fast once you break that guy out. It makes sense no? It's REALISTIC. It's IMMERSIVE.. You know.. those things which people apparently hate in games these days.
Setting my own butthurt at societies downfall in terms of gaming aside, the time limit, and how often you run into them is changed depending on difficulty, so if you dont' like timed missions to often, but like them for when they make sense, you can adjust the difficulty level of the game and it will throw less at you.
Apart from that, I love how it feels like you are actually a resistance cell in a mobile base. Scavanging for equipment on the battlefield when enemies drop them, selling parts, corpses, and other alien artifacts on the Black Market to get Intel, and buying/trading/selling in Intel on the Black Market to gain goods to fill the holes of research and bad RNG rolls in battles in terms of mods you find, make it feel like you are the aggressors against a superior foe.
The stealth system in place for most missions is excellent as well, allowing you to scout out the land and enemies before engaging, and setting up ambushes which could wipe the slate in that area entirely before the aliens have time to respond.
There is now a better world map as well, This is where you move your mobile base from region to region, unlock new regions by contacting the resistance cells in that area, and take on side missions to gain supplies, Intel, etc.
-----------------
Over all the game isn't bad by any means. Some performance issues which should be fixed relatively soon, good immersion, great classic game mechanics from X-com 1.
-------------------
If you're still wondering about the complaints on this game. There are 2 people on the forums are can articulate points far better than me. There is ALOT of debate on the timers in this game. These are 2 great responses.
Martial.lore:
The timers are essential. Turtling is not a tactic. The squad isn't trying to find a good picnic spot. XCOM is a guerrilla force that has to make lighting strikes before going back into hiding.
This theme is reinforced by every mechanic in the game from the short individual timers on the globe to the reinforcement drops that come when you just desperately want to get everyone to the evac point.
Sometimes you just have accept that there was not enough time for your ill-equipped soldiers to complete their objective and stay alive, and sometimes sacrifices have to be made for the greater good.
Failure is hard to accept but without the timers the potential for disaster during missions would be missing and the game would not be worthy of the XCOM name.
If it didn't upset players complacency and make them furious at how unfair life is then where is the fun in that? Sometimes FTL makes me very angry but it's one of my favorite tactical video games and I am generally very good at playing it.
Once I have learned how to succeed with XCOM 2 I imagine that even though they will feel familiar and seem easier to deal with, the timers will still screw up a good plan once in a while and get good people killed.
Perish the thought that this were a game in which every move, every action and every decision did not have consequences.
Jolly:
"It mostly IS blind hate against timers. People complaining without really give it a try, or even trying.
"Because most of the timers are idiotic, and pretty much all of them are poorly implemented."
Um, no. Idiotic? That's opinion and not one I'd agree with. Poorly implemented? It's a countdown on the screen - what do you want, an hourglass? I dancing girl who removes clothes til the "time" is up? WTF.

CORRECTION: I complained about not being able to choose a new squaddie's class, but one of the new facilities allows a rookie to train to a class of your choice. Promotions from XP still seem  to be random.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I was a huge fan of Enemy Unknown. Been playing this 6 hours now. Here are the observations from my first campaign, which has gone... not so great. Probably restarting tomorrow.
CONCEPT: Long-form strategy with turn-based tactical missions where you retake the Earth from alien overlords. Set 20 years after a the events of a very poor playthrough of Enemy Unknown.
IMPROVEMENTS:
VISUALS: Actually looks like a current gen game now. Framerate was pretty crap at first on my fairly high-end PC, but turning shadows down from max to high solved that. People don't look like action figures anymore, (making that Guile hair even weirder-looking) and the alien designs are really cool and unsettling.
CUSTOMIZATION: Way more options for troops visually, and more sensible mechanics-wise. Instead of putting a scope in your pocket for some damn reason, you attach it to the actual weapon, and there are a variety of mods to use too. Cosmetically, troops have options for clothing, accessories, scars, and far more voices. You can also "save" troops to ensure they show up when you play.
STORY: On top of having one of the more original sequel concepts, it put a bit more effort into the plot. The player was kind of a non-entity in the first game, but now you hold some actual significance, while other characters are given more depth.
STEALTH: Most missions allow your troops to sneak around before the actual firefight. With a bit of planning, you can take out a whole alien patrol before they get into cover.
MISSION VARIANCE: First game's missions were all kill the aliens and maybe save civilians, and then escort a VIP once or twice. Now, you're raiding supply runs, blowing up power relays,  defending power relays and rescuing former XCOM operatives.
NO MORE SATELLITES OR PANIC: There's other stuff you need to do now, but it doesn't feel like you're babysitting anymore.
SWORDS: SWOOORDS!!!
NOT IMPROVEMENTS:
EXPLOSIONS: I don't think a "this will blow up soon" symbol would have been the worst thing. My troops either die a hero to alien blasters or live long enough to stand too close to an exploding minivan. Also, the Aliens really haven't converted all people's cars to electric?
FREE ALIEN MOVES: Yes, they still get a free move into cover after you spot them, unless you're in stealth mode. I understand the limitations of AI, but it still feels very unfair that it's impossible to catch these things off guard. And I'm pretty sure the old X-COM games didn't have this problem.
LAGGING: Not graphical lag, but a lot of weird pauses between objectives, especially in early, tutorialized missions. Far more bearable in normal play, but took me out of the first hour a few times.
All in all, highly recommended. There are a few lingering issues the previous game had, but nothing new to annoy you. The vast majority of the game has only improved.  I'll update this if there's anything that's really worth mentioning or if the technical issues are fixed and I remember writing this.

EDIT - There are already mods on the Workshop to disable timers, which is the basis for a huge number of negative reviews here. So, y'know, keep that in mind.
Pros
- Punishing; you WILL lose soldiers you WILL NOT win every mission or campaign.
- Wonderful model and texture work, with nice lighting and shading.
- Feels different enough to justify a new game imo.
- Enemy patrols are a game changer, forcing you to pick your battles and make the most of your advantages.
- Large array of character customization, letting you create and become attached to digital representations of your friends so you can watch helplessly as they are torn apart by aliens. With Workshop support, there is almost endless possibilities for new cosmetic options.
- Extremely open modding, to the point where some core mechanics are essentially .ini value tweaks.
- 42GB of development content in the SDK to work and create new content with. Seriously awesome.
Cons
- Others report performance issues, though I have not experienced them aside from slight stuttering during the insertion cinematic animations. (i74790k, 32gb RAM, TitanX, Win10, installed on SSD).
- Strange pauses once in a while before or after actions, though I haven't found it as annoying as others appear to have.
Notes
- It's not EU or EW with better graphics, it's a different game. Most missions have turn timers which force you to think and play aggressively and take risks, rather than turtle your favorite soldiers up 1 square at a time. Some people hate this, they say it isn't "fair" or "too hard". Personally I really enjoy it for the reasons I listed here.

PVE is good, combat is pretty fluid. The game is however filled with fanservice from previous installment, in other words, it doesnt feel like it brings much new to the table.
DLC's are about as good as the rest of the game. The PVP in this game took a serious step down from Dark Souls 2 and if you try invading you'll quickly find that odds are stacked heavily against you. You should especially avoid it in a certain PVP hotspots, thats where the gankers congregate.
I'd recommend you try to beat the games bosses WITHOUT summoning, their AI's are clearly NOT made for multiple players and it makes the majority of bosses quite pathetic. Some bosses however actually get harder with summoning, most notable are those with one-shot or near one-shot attacks.

If you get invaded while having a summon you will probably be called a "ganker" and a "casul" by said invader even though you most likely didnt summon for the specific reason of ganking.
Overall, good PVE and combat, PVP is♥♥♥♥♥♥ game is kinda inbalanced but still fun, lots of recycled assets from previous souls-games, if you were expecting a lot of new things with this one you'll be dissapointed. If you just want another souls-game to play through, you'll probably have fun.

A great game. However it does have some major ups and downs. With almost 100 hours on the game, I feel like I could give a clear picture to anyone who wants to pick this game up.
Pros -
- A combat version of minecraft that goes leaps and bounds beyond anything minecraft has tried. There is a plethora of classes, all that have different abilities, allowing you to flip flop between them on your own and level each one up individually.
- If you love to collect things, this is the game for you. Collecting recipes and items to upgrade your items is pretty much the main aspect of this game. Much like minecraft, your community and friends are what make this game.
- Wonderfully done enviroments and a collection system that works well for groups. One person gets something, everyone gets that something. (except loot drops that are randomized)
- Variety, variety, variety. There are so many items in game that you can adapt your character to look like that there is pretty much any style you could go after depending on how much your willing to collect.
- Community Creations. This is something that blew me away. The community creates dungeons, items, puts forth ideas and Trove devs actually incorporate some of those things into the game. Props and amazing shout out to the devs and players making the content. Means the game is going to get continually different as time goes on. Bigger and better. Don't like the game now? come back in half a year and itll of gotten even better.
Cons -
- The game gets extremely dull with all the farming that is required in it.
- There is almost no real driving force in the game besides collecting things in order to get the necessary mats to build portals (Necessary to reach higher difficulties) and add on to clubs (social group worlds in game).
- The community is FILLED with people who would screw you over in a heartbeat because material collection isn't a standardized thing. The economy has ups and downs all the time with no real stable economy besides what people post
- There isn't any language based servers. Expect to see a variety and have communication become an issue.
- The coolest looking costumes are all payed for with real money. They have to make money somehow though right?
- This is a social game. Don't expect to be able to do anything late game by yourself unless your cheesing (basically cheating through in game glitches) bosses.
- Dungeons are not very diversified at the moment. Expect to see the same dungeon in a specific zone repeat itself over and over in that zone. Especially the recipe collection dungeons.
- Don't expect any block mechanics like redstone in this. All of the blocks are speicifically for flavor with no movement besides water/lava/chocolate (yes chocolate)/plasma blocks.
If you pick up this game with friends and like to build and collect things, this is definitely a great game. If your picking it up by yourself and are antisocial, prepare to spend hours and hours by yourself grinding in order to collect enough mats to make anything worthwhile.

I am not going to pretend the game runs well however. My specs are not high, and I have this issue where it never remembers my graphical settings at all. Darkest Dungeon is a side scroll, turn based, RPG game, in which the player assembles a group of heroes from town to go battle/cleanse various parts of a corrupted aristocrat's properties, presumably a distant relative.
when your heroes enter the dungeon they will have 2 health bars, one for life and one for stress.
the stress mechanic is an innovative way for the player to measure the mental damage done to the party. Characters will receive stress from getting hit by a "crit" attack from monsters, stepping on traps; stress will incrementally rise just from walking around and having your torch flame dwindle.
If a hero gets too stressed out, then their resolve is tested and, more often than not they will fall into a panic state and become a source of stress for your other members, so it's a positive feedback cycle you need to manage.
another interesting mechanic is the torchlight mechanic. at the start of a "mission", you will have a chance to supply up for the journey and you will likely want to bring torches. Your torch light will dwindle with every step you take, and the lower the torch light the more difficult encounters will become -- you also get more loot so there is a strategy to managing torchlight depending on the health of your party.
The game is a great mix of difficulty, chance, and strategy.
there are several different hero classes and you can have a party of up to 4 heroes with as many of a single class as you want in your party, so this makes for a wide variety of potential groups to have fun with and test out.
the devs have been rolling out regular updates since I purchased the game, about 6 months ago, and they have plans for more additions throughout the year, so there will be no shortage of things to do!
There are no major bugs or glitchy areas that i have encountered and the games runs very smooth from end to end.
I have heard some people are complaining about the difficulty of the game, but I haven't seen it.

Additionally, many things (classes, flaskes, mounts) can be unlocked through either a reasonable price or through Cubits, an in-game currency that you can earn daily, while cosmetic stuff is mostly exclusively credit-based.
This game is incredibly fast-paced with lots of stuff to do. Granted, it can get repetitive if you're not one for a grind, but I've find it to be very easy just because it's either quick and painless, or challenging in the higher levels; it's always engaging me. Throw in multiple modes of quick transportation (glider wings for when you find a high spot, magriders for [minecart] tracks, ships for water, and mounts; the latter you start the game with), and you're never spending too long waiting for anything

A masterpiece. An absolute masterpiece. Its pixelated, 2-D environment brings back feels of familiar games such as Terraria, and while it does lack in the abundance of mobs, items, bossess, and just crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥to do, it does have a nice feel and is very explorable. The animations and look are absolutely gorgeous, design is fine too. The beginning of the game is once again, very much like Terraria in the sense of starting with a main focus of gathering resources and surviving mobs. A unique feature of starbound is your native ship, a customizable race-based safe haven for things such as storage and other useful tasks. Your ship starts in an orbited position over a random planet in the alpha sector (after fighting bossess and gathering resources, you can travel to other sectors using an upgrade.) Your only option is to descend and survive. Gathering Ore Tier resources allows you to buid weapons, armors and tools. Gathering coal allows you to fuel your ship and travel to another planet. As you progress through the game you can build upgrades and travel to other sectors, unlocking more resources and therefore more loot. Mobs aren't very challenging on low threat planets if you have the right gear and the bossess are just awesome. Great game to play with friends, just like Terraria. The only few dissapointing things are lack of item names (all saplings are named "todo") and descriptions. It's still in early beta so of course wipes and other bothersome♥♥♥♥♥♥can happen. The ship is also fairly small, expansions would be appreciated.
Here's a more basic view:
Pros:
> Environment is completely beautiful.
> Animations and its pixelated style are extremely well done.
> Beginning of game starts very basically (bare necessities) but later expands widely.
> Ship is great for storage, crafting, and just working without fear of getting your head ripped off. It's also customizable :D
> Sector and universe exploration system offers a lot of things to loot (especially dungeons)
> Advancement system, e.g. you can never be too overpowered. As you advance so do your enemies.
> Music. Oh god. The music system is amazing.
> The same, ever-working ore system. Never fails to let down.
Cons:
> Lack of item names, descriptions, and just plain items themselves (we're looking at a game that rivals Terraria)
> Early beta wipes made me cry in the corner. They've said there are no more planned wipes but, I mean,♥♥♥♥♥♥happens.
> While awesome, the ship is definetely small.
All in all, Starbound is definetely worth those fifteen bucks. More than that probably. One of my favorite current games and I expect to play it a lot in the next few years. My overall favorite feature is the .abc file music import. Yes, you heard right. If you have an .abc file for a song you can actually play it in game using one of the in game instruments. None of them sound the same and you can even play as a band :D. I'd say a 10/10 for this game as of right now as long as they fix the mentioned issues. I'm sure ChuckleFish won't let us down.

I'm noticing a lot of reviews on here are talking about the difficulty of XCOM 2 like it's a bad thing, specifically the mission time limits. I really don't consider this a bad thing really, the difficulty fits in with the thematic of the entire game. You're the underground going up against a bigger force, so of course it would be difficult. That's one of the main appeals for XCOM for me, it's that it's punishingly difficult and I feel like that's a love/hate it thing for a lot of people. I'm getting my♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked almost every mission and I'm loving it. You have to go into each mission carefully planning and considering
and sometimes missions can and will go horribly wrong due to things outside your control. You're the ragtag team of rebels who are outgunned and desperately trying to scrape by. That's the nature of what they were going for and in a way I respect the devs for that. I feel like this is a concept that a lot of people aren't grasping correctly.
The combat is great. It really pressures you into some situations where you will have to make sacrifices and take risks to push on through. It can be unforgiving at sometimes and you will die
but that's the fun of XCOM.
While suffering from some animation bugs, the combat and animations are really nice to look at and a lot of detail has been put into environments and enemies.
Maps are auto generated, so there's a lot of varied stuff to look at
Many different Aliens to see and fight.
Some optimization issues that will probably get fixed with a few patches down the road
Some quality of life bugs and glitches(I got stuck on a black screen a couple of times during combat for about 10seconds before everything went back to normal) but will probably be fixed as well in the upcoming patches.
XCOM 2 really isn't an 'everyone' game. If you don't enjoy preplanning, strategy games, or difficult games you probably won't like this game. However I'm having a blast with it currently.

Darkest Dungeon is a side scroll, turn based, RPG game, in which the player assembles a group of heroes from town to go battle/cleanse various parts of a corrupted aristocrat's properties, presumably a distant relative.
when your heroes enter the dungeon they will have 2 health bars, one for life and one for stress.
the stress mechanic is an innovative way for the player to measure the mental damage done to the party. Characters will receive stress from getting hit by a "crit" attack from monsters, stepping on traps; stress will incrementally rise just from walking around and having your torch flame dwindle.
If a hero gets too stressed out, then their resolve is tested and, more often than not they will fall into a panic state and become a source of stress for your other members, so it's a positive feedback cycle you need to manage.
another interesting mechanic is the torchlight mechanic. at the start of a "mission", you will have a chance to supply up for the journey and you will likely want to bring torches. Your torch light will dwindle with every step you take, and the lower the torch light the more difficult encounters will become -- you also get more loot so there is a strategy to managing torchlight depending on the health of your party.
The game is a great mix of difficulty, chance, and strategy.
there are several different hero classes and you can have a party of up to 4 heroes with as many of a single class as you want in your party, so this makes for a wide variety of potential groups to have fun with and test out.
the devs have been rolling out regular updates since I purchased the game, about 6 months ago, and they have plans for more additions throughout the year, so there will be no shortage of things to do!
There are no major bugs or glitchy areas that i have encountered and the games runs very smooth from end to end.
I have heard some people are complaining about the difficulty of the game, but I haven't seen it.
all i can say to that is, the game is meant to challenge the player. you are supposed to lose heros and be like "awe man! that was my fav guy and he died!".

Like many, I found myself a little disappointed with Fallout 4 compared to 3 and New Vegas - the latter being one of my favourite ever games. That said, 4 is still a fantastic game.
The game looks great if you have a beefy enough system to max it out. It is, however, not especially well optimised. I had to employ a few .ini tweaks to get the game at a stable FPS.
The central plot of Fallout 4 is predictable and average in terms of characters. For the first time in the Fallout series, I found myself unable to really connect with any of the game's main factions. Naturally, this diminished my personal investment in the main story. That said, the side missions - and the characters involved in them - are at the high standard we've come to see in Bethesda's main IPs. The vibrant world - from the bustling baseball-ground-turned-shanty-town Diamond City to the eerie Glowing Sea - is for the most part filled with intriguing storylines and amusing, weird characters.
This is tempered by the persistent radiant quests. From the impersonal dialogue to the repetitive "go x, kill y" setup, this obvious padding seems really below Bethesda's capability.
Another trumped-up feature was the new settlement-building mechanics. While I found the system rather clunky, I can see the appeal for players who, in past Fallout games, wanted to shape and inhabit the wasteland as well as just explore it.
It seems weird for a review that is relatively critical to still come out recommending the game, but Fallout 4 is still a great achievement and worth playing. Provided expectations coming off the previous entries in the series are tempered, and that you like settlement building, Fallout 4 is a safe bet.

Dark souls 3. A game of pure frustration. This game isn't bad if your playing pve with friends, but if not that this game falters in every point.
Invasions:
Where to begin. I understand that the invader should have some disadvantages against him/her, but the overwhelming amount of disadvantages stacked against the invader is just to much. When you invade, especially at high level, the host will most likely have two phantoms. You kill one phantom, and while your busy fighting the other one the host resummons the other.  The host has two phantoms? well here comes a darkmoon blade. Whats that? your gonna run to the mobs? well they just used a seed of a tree of giants. Also when you invade you lose the ember hp and only have half your estus which isn't enough to take on two phantoms and a darkmoonblade and the host and an assortment of enemies in the world, unless you use builds designed for one hit combos like the sellsword twinblades and darkmoon blade.
Arena:
The arena isn't terribly bad, but don't watch dark souls youtubers going on 20 win streaks and expect to get the same results. Most fights you get are going to have varying degrees of lag. The PC dark souls community is very diverse when it comes to the arena. You can find people using many different types of builds and trying out many different strategies, but for the most part your going to find hyper armor using ultra greatswords and one shot parry builds.
PvE:
The is the least bad part of the game. It can actually be enjoyable with friends, and if you get invaded, don't worry the odds are so stacked in your favor that if you play smart you'll win easy.
DLC's:
I really enjoyed the DLCs. Ashes of Ariandal may have been a little short, but for the weapons it added, it was worth it. The Ringed City is much longer than Ashes of Ariandal, and is a really good DLC i recommend.
Overall:
I've enjoyed the Dark Souls series all togethor, but i've never enjoyed the PvP experience in any of them, the game just feels like it added pvp as an after thought. But overall if your looking to play through the story with some friends, i recommend the game, if your looking to play PvP i suggest looking elsewhere

Edit:  There is now a mod available in the workshop that disables the timers, so whether or not the timers are "bad" is now a non issue.  Try the game, if you don't like the timers, install the mod and disable them and play to your preference.  Yay for mod support letting us choose how we play the game :)
----------------------------------------------------------
After reading some of the reviews on here, I got very worried about the "turn timers" everyone is warning about.  But now that I've played the game a bit, I felt like writing this review to say that *in my opinion at least*, they really aren't that bad.  I've actually enjoyed them.
I'm really not a fan of turn timers, and the bomb missions were my least favorite of the first game.  So I definitely understand people's frustration with them.  I do think it would be a good idea for an option to disable/limit them to be added to the game.
That being said, these negative reviews act as though it's somehow game breaking and removes the opportunity to use tactics.  In my experience so far this is simply not true.  None of the timed missions made me feel particularly rushed.  I didn't have to dash across the entire map.  I could take my time moving from cover to cover; I just had to have a sense of urgency and make sure I was moving TOWARDS my objective each turn and not away from it.  No turtle crawling step by step.
Most of the timed missions simply require you to REACH an objective before the timer runs out, and then you can take your sweet time clearing the map of the remaining hostiles.  There's usually plenty of time to get there.  You just have to keep an eye on where that objective is as you plan your moves in the game to make sure you're progressing towards it.
I think people are frustrated that there are so many timed missions (understandably) and are exaggerating how bad they are a little bit as a result of that frustration.  Or they just had some terrible luck (happens sometimes in this kind of game) and it made the game feel unfairly hard; if a bunch of enemy encounters are triggered in quick succession at the wrong time it can make turn timed missions nearly impossible.  And I can see how these situations can leave a bad taste in people's mouths.  But that is the nature of an XCOM game; sometimes things just go wrong.  If you don't have a high tolerance for that then this game will definitely frustrate you sometimes.  The game can definitely be unfair, maybe even more so than the first, and you will either love it or hate it.
So, in summary,  if you absolutely can't stand the idea of timed missions you may wish to wait to buy this until after an option to disable them is added by the devs or modding community, however if you are on the fence about it then I would recommend that you don't let all the negative reviews scare you away and go ahead and try the game for yourself.



Starbound is a game that could only be described as Terreria's sequel. It took everything that made the side-scrolling random generation world of resource gathering and fort building, then doubled down on everything you can do. It's the best possible evolution of a game, and shows almost undaunting displays of creative development and effort.
Starting off, theres almost no difference between this game and the aforementioned Terreria, aside from starting on a space ship. You descend unto the planatary surface below and begin your exploration upon one of many proceduraly generated biomes. Biomes, themselves, deserve a head nod due to the break of tradition. Yes, there are forests, deserts, plains, and even volcanoes....and then there are the varients. Creative ideas such as eyeball forests, brain forests, acid pool worlds, gravity variations, and even still....the numerous colors of deserts, ranging from pink to green. Now things are looking different. You realize that theres something very unique about this game that stands out from it's inspiration. Then you go deeper.....
Planets interiors start being made up of different biomes even still. The core of a planet could be a frozen ice ball.....it could be obsidian and hard as hell to crack...or it's made of flesh and blood...your planets literally alive! No longer is it just hell that awaits you below the surface. Now theres many more options to choose from, and how many options are there? Once you gather enough coal and refuel your space ship, you then see the star map. My jaw, at this point, hit somewhere on my floor and stayed there for probably a good few minutes. Yes, I am aware that each one is just a procedural generation and that nothing is set in stone for these planets (pun...sort of intended?) but still..the concept of the whole sector of the galaxy being there to explore...it starts to hit you that this game has, literally, gone lightyears beyond it's inspiration! (Pun definitely intended).
You fly to new galaxies.....discover that planets also have NPCs that talk to you. Villages to explore, hostile pirate bases, unethical slave markets, black-operations space mercs, genocidal plant people trying to take over the galaxy, penguin militas, randomly generated monsters on every planet, asteroids to mine, science research stations, out of control defense robots in abandoned bases or lone houses with a basement inhabited by a genetically altered cousin of the Great Mighty Poo! (Conkers bad fur day reference...play it!)
My eyes glaze over, awash with delight, as I realize one very important thing. One hard to avoid fact that makes all of this amazement even more astonishing......
This is still early beta. EARLY. BETA.
Thats right, this developer is busting♥♥♥♥♥♥over a game, has it looking this polished, and is still calling this the early beta! Theres so much more they want to add, and with a game that I could easily have written off as near-complete in some aspects, they continue to demand more from themselves. This developer deserves all of the fame and fortune they got from this game and by the time it's done, it will be hard for anyone to advance the side-scrolling voxel-block series much past this. I welcome anyone to try...but damned if Chucklefish didn't make it one daunting task.
In conclusion....anyone who enjoys side scrolling, free roaming, sand box, voxel, randomly generated games set in massive universes....needs this game. Anyone who appreciates the sheer madness of imagination...needs this game. In short, gamers...and the game industry...needs this game.

Darkest Dungeon is a side scroll, turn based, RPG game, in which the player assembles a group of heroes from town to go battle/cleanse various parts of a corrupted aristocrat's properties, presumably a distant relative.
when your heroes enter the dungeon they will have 2 health bars, one for life and one for stress.
the stress mechanic is an innovative way for the player to measure the mental damage done to the party. Characters will receive stress from getting hit by a "crit" attack from monsters, stepping on traps; stress will incrementally rise just from walking around and having your torch flame dwindle.
If a hero gets too stressed out, then their resolve is tested and, more often than not they will fall into a panic state and become a source of stress for your other members, so it's a positive feedback cycle you need to manage.
another interesting mechanic is the torchlight mechanic. at the start of a "mission", you will have a chance to supply up for the journey and you will likely want to bring torches. Your torch light will dwindle with every step you take, and the lower the torch light the more difficult encounters will become -- you also get more loot so there is a strategy to managing torchlight depending on the health of your party.
The game is a great mix of difficulty, chance, and strategy.
there are several different hero classes and you can have a party of up to 4 heroes with as many of a single class as you want in your party, so this makes for a wide variety of potential groups to have fun with and test out.
the devs have been rolling out regular updates since I purchased the game, about 6 months ago, and they have plans for more additions throughout the year, so there will be no shortage of things to do!
There are no major bugs or glitchy areas that i have encountered and the games runs very smooth from end to end.
I have heard some people are complaining about the difficulty of the game, but I haven't seen it.
all i can say to that is, the game is meant to challenge the player. you are supposed to lose heros and be like "awe man! that was my fav guy and he died!".
Everyone on my Friends list that plays this game loves it. I told my brother to buy it for x-mas sale and he has more hours than me logged on it now!
this is definitely worth the buy, even at the slightly higher price point, 20.00 is well worth the time and obvious care put into this game.

It’s a trick. A trap to get you to care just enough about your ragamuffin group of dungeon-plundering murderhobos and then wear them down to gibbering madmen in a moment. Oh and there are cool graphics and sounds and narration. And there are things to unlock and places to explore. But Darkest Dungeon’s strength does not lie in fantasy fulfillment, or achievement collection or heroic deeds. It doesn’t, and it’s all set up to push players into making tough choices and sacrificing their beloved playthings.
In most games there are peaks and valleys of excitement, in this game that’s replaced with peaks and valleys of frightening frustrating loss. And that’s ALL this game does and it does it better than any game that’s come before it.
And that means something. That means that this experience is completely unique. Unique the way black and white French films about loss might be unique. They are not experiences everyone will enjoy. And that means that you as a consumer of videogames have a duty to understand what this game is before you buy it expecting it to be some sort of town building version of FTL.  And I can’t reiterate this enough; this game might not be for you.

The Trailer looked very Terraria-esque and in many ways, StarBound is, but it has so much more.  Race specific backstories, tons of random weapons, melee and ranged, ridiculous and challenging enemies and all the space exploration you could ask for.
Don't underestimate the word "challenging" when it's associated with StarBound.  My friends and I racked up 20+ deaths in our first five minutes because we thought we were just playing a bigger version of Terraria.  After we made the realization that even the lowest level local wildlife can pose a threat we settled down and got serious.  It didn't help much, even when we were wearing the best armour we could craft and weilding the best weapons we could find, we were still cautious to go exploring during the day, and at night it gets even worse!
The enemies aren't even the worst part though, the weather is the real problem.  Some planets get beautiful starshowers that light up the night and fill you with a sense of peace.....build your main settlements here....seriously.    Nothing sucks more than getting geared up with your new boss loot only to get smoked by a meteor shower or melted by acid rain....yea.....acid freaking rain.
But if you can tolerate all the hostile, life threating stuff, StarBound has a ton to offer.  Shopkeepers and quest NPC's all with varying chat options, rare and insane ores to mine and stunning (sometimes creepy) biomes, this game truly rewards you for exploring all the planets you can, provided you survive.
Strongly reccomend this game  15/10

Lets start the review with one of the silliest (and most repeated) remarks I read about it on the negative posts:
"But the game has nothing like darksouls or x-com, it's just repeatable grind where you spam dmg to win!"
Well now, lets see:
Does it have a leveling group of characters that you can customize, equip and rename, like x-com? Check
Does it have permadeath (including a freaking graveyard so you can remember where and why did you die), like x-com? Check
Does it have several procedural maps where you must travel and often choose between killing everything on sight or trying to go direct to the objective, kinda like x-com and darksouls (since x-com1 does not have procedural maps and neither darksouls as far as I know)? Check
Does it have RNG that makes you scream "why god why?" from time to time, like x-com? CHECK
Does it have a plot? Check
Does it have a base that you can upgrade and those upgrades are meaningfull and needed to raise your chances of victory? Check
...Ok. So saying that the game is not like x-com, darksouls or whatever seems a little bit off after a simple check list. But hey, lets not see only the goodies. Lets adress of what those AAA games have that DD does not have!
Is DD 3D? Nope
Is DD combat grid-like where you can flank enemies and all the nice stuffs like that? Nope
Please feel free to remember me anything I left out, but so far, the only acceptable complain when comparing DD with x-com is that one is 3D and grid-based combat and the other is not, wich in my opinion is stupid.
Now, for my favorite part of the complains. Peple saying the game have no strategy whatsoever, that you just spam dmg and win. Those people are the SAME PEOPLE that complains that the game is extremely difficult because of RNG and that with the addition of corpses and heart-attacks the game is unbeattable!
Hmmm, I start to see a patern here!
I got this game long ago, when you could make an entire abusive party of jesters and still beat a few bosses. Since then, the game improved as a whole, adding mechanics, classes, itens, changing skills, everything to put the tactical inside it, and you know what? It did very well. You have to choose well who is your frontline, you backline, the both guys in the midline, if they going for bleed dmg or poison dmg, you gotta choose if you'll take a lot of supplies for the long quests at the expense of inventory space, choose if you go with torches up, down or a inbetween and in some fights, if you are able to count 2+2=4, you can see that you either retreat or face the dire consequences and if all this is not tactical enough for you, then nothing is!
"Ahh but the game is just a grinding machine, walk simulator disguised as a game, hur dur, im smart!"
Sigh... Listen, the name of the game is Darkest DUNGEON! From the alpha version of Dungeons and Dragons, from the napkins of Gary Gigax himself to today games, there's one thing that never changed on the mechanics of what a dungeon is: You WALK around, you KILL stuff, you LOOT stuff and you avoid TRAPS! Go ahead, look around on any game ever that have dungeons on it, from pokemon to minecraft, they all have this formula.
Now if you still complain that the game is grindy-ish, you must be new to all this rpg stuff right? Every rpg game have tons of grinding in it, every single one of them. Some ACTION-rpg have less grinding because you can dodge around enemy strikes and stuff like that, but they still have tons of griding. Good God, even some action games nowdays have grinding! Don't believe me? How many hours did you spent to get that nice knife skin on that fps again?
So yeah, with all that in mind, if you didn't liked the game, ok, you dont like roguelike sidescrolling strategy rpgs! It's ok, I don't like first person stealth games (the lack of periferial vision kills me) and it's ok too. What is not ok, is to lie and crucify a game with arguments without base, just because you didn't like one or other dev decision.
TL;DR
The game is good, the game is hard enough to make you think but not hard enough to give you brain damage and 90% of the roidrage negative posts don't even know of what they are talking about.
If you like RPG, DUNGEONS and ROGUELIKE stuff (permadeath, evergrowing challenges, etc) you will like Darkest Dungeon.

After reading some of the reviews on here, I got very worried about the "turn timers" everyone is warning about.  But now that I've played the game a bit, I felt like writing this review to say that *in my opinion at least*, they really aren't that bad.  I've actually enjoyed them.
I'm really not a fan of turn timers, and the bomb missions were my least favorite of the first game.  So I definitely understand people's frustration with them.  I do think it would be a good idea for an option to disable/limit them to be added to the game.
That being said, these negative reviews act as though it's somehow game breaking and removes the opportunity to use tactics.  In my experience so far this is simply not true.  None of the timed missions made me feel particularly rushed.  I didn't have to dash across the entire map.  I could take my time moving from cover to cover; I just had to have a sense of urgency and make sure I was moving TOWARDS my objective each turn and not away from it.  No turtle crawling step by step.
Most of the timed missions simply require you to REACH an objective before the timer runs out, and then you can take your sweet time clearing the map of the remaining hostiles.  There's usually plenty of time to get there.  You just have to keep an eye on where that objective is as you plan your moves in the game to make sure you're progressing towards it.
I think people are frustrated that there are so many timed missions (understandably) and are exaggerating how bad they are a little bit as a result of that frustration.  Or they just had some terrible luck (happens sometimes in this kind of game) and it made the game feel unfairly hard; if a bunch of enemy encounters are triggered in quick succession at the wrong time it can make turn timed missions nearly impossible.  And I can see how these situations can leave a bad taste in people's mouths.  But that is the nature of an XCOM game; sometimes things just go wrong.  If you don't have a high tolerance for that then this game will definitely frustrate you sometimes.  The game can definitely be unfair, maybe even more so than the first, and you will either love it or hate it.
So, in summary,  if you absolutely can't stand the idea of timed missions you may wish to wait to buy this until after an option to disable them is added by the devs or modding community, however if you are on the fence about it then I would recommend that you don't let all the negative reviews scare you away and go ahead and try the game for yourself.

Like many, I found myself a little disappointed with Fallout 4 compared to 3 and New Vegas - the latter being one of my favourite ever games. That said, 4 is still a fantastic game.
The game looks great if you have a beefy enough system to max it out. It is, however, not especially well optimised. I had to employ a few .ini tweaks to get the game at a stable FPS.
The central plot of Fallout 4 is predictable and average in terms of characters. For the first time in the Fallout series, I found myself unable to really connect with any of the game's main factions. Naturally, this diminished my personal investment in the main story. That said, the side missions - and the characters involved in them - are at the high standard we've come to see in Bethesda's main IPs. The vibrant world - from the bustling baseball-ground-turned-shanty-town Diamond City to the eerie Glowing Sea - is for the most part filled with intriguing storylines and amusing, weird characters.
This is tempered by the persistent radiant quests. From the impersonal dialogue to the repetitive "go x, kill y" setup, this obvious padding seems really below Bethesda's capability.
Another trumped-up feature was the new settlement-building mechanics. While I found the system rather clunky, I can see the appeal for players who, in past Fallout games, wanted to shape and inhabit the wasteland as well as just explore it.
It seems weird for a review that is relatively critical to still come out recommending the game, but Fallout 4 is still a great achievement and worth playing. Provided expectations coming off the previous entries in the series are tempered, and that you like settlement building, Fallout 4 is a safe bet.
