Darkest Dungeon is a game that shows you how dangerous and foolhardy it is to grab a torch and go down into dark depths to face the beings who reside there.
And I love it, every step I take.
Darkest Dungeon is a challenging dungeon crawler where your characters must combat stress (read: Sanity) as well as the beasties that lie in the darkness as they search for fame, fortune and glory.  It really takes heavy cues from H.P. Lovecraft on how man was not meant to see what lies just beyond the torchlight.
It uses a turn based system and RPG elements as well as some cues taken from roguelike games, such as permadeath.  The game rewards quick thinking in a bad situation and preparation and priorities can truly determine weather your party comes out from the caves alive, or are ripped to shreds by nameless horrors.
The Art style is phenomenal and you'd be hard pressed to find a indie game with such evocative soundtracks and voiceover.  The narrator makes you feel the success of a critical hit and heartache of a fatal blow.  You grow attached to your party members just to see them die from a poor decision.  Some people may cry that the computer can pull these amazing succession of criticals leaving your characters ripe for slaughter next turn, but I've found that if you prepped correctly, prioritized your healing, and use status effects (like bleed and blight) to your advantage, you'll make it by the skin of you teeth and escape the dungeon.
In this game, you gotta know when to call it quits and leave the dungeon with what loot you can carry.  It's ok to run and come back another day with a stronger party and better supplies then to lose a character you've upgraded significantly.  And I love that about this game.  In H.P. Lovecraft's stories, it is rarely a happy ending and this game holds to those themes tightly.
In the end, I would recommend this game, but only to those that have the patience and understanding of the mindset you have to have when facing the terrors of the abyss.  If you go in foolhardy, you'll end up simply making more loot for the party that comes in after, as they pillage the nameless corpse of another failed adventurer.
Amazing sandbox game, very playable, yet so much to come.  Looking forward to the continued good work and dedication of this dev team.

XCOM 2 is at once refreshing and familiar. It builds on the stellar gameplay of it's predecessor, and adds it's own unique setting, mechanics and flair.
Theres some bad stuff here, though.
- Performance issues on systems that should run the game just fine
- The timed missions often have too short of a countdown, making many missions arbitrarily difficult
- The developers have either neglected to explain certain key game mechanics, or deliberately left them unexplained
- The tutorial is very long, unneccesarily so
I'm sure there are other negatives as well.
I'm not going to write a list of positives to counter the above. The game has issues, which need to be adressed. It is, however, extremely unforgiving, addictive, challenging and rewarding. A true XCOM game, that doesn't pull any pnches, and has all the features we have come to expect from the franchise: Ironman mode, brutal difficulty settings, frustratingly awesome rng and deep tactics and strategy.
In the end, I recommend buying it. XCOM 2 is good. Very good, for all it's flaws. I have enjoyed it immensely, and I will be playing this game for many years to come, just like the previous title in the series.

Spiral knights is an addictive MMORPG. You design a semi futuristic knight that has crash landed on a new planet. Thankfully, not all of the locals are hostile and you quickly find yourself taken in, along with fellow survivors, by a group of people in the developing town of Haven. This is your launching platform into the main game.
Looking at the game, the graphics are quite cool. It’s a cartoonesque type of appearance which is very nice to look at and doesn’t strain anybody’s system too badly. It’s clear that a lot of very hard work went into making the game look fabulous and it really works to bring a sense of life to the game. The missions are fully story lined, which is really good to see as too many games just go for the grind type system these days. In your progression missions, which gain you rank/ levels, there is an in depth story about exploring deep underground this clockwork planet. Your mission is to get to the core eventually and find out what happened to Alpha squad, the Spiral knights Elite of the Elite. They’ve gone missing on a recon mission and throughout the game you pick up hints as to where they have gone and what happened to them. In addition to these missions, you can simply go exploring by yourself in a constantly changing environment driven by a game mechanic. You get an elevator that takes you to levels ever deeper into the planet each level you complete. You start at level 1 and end up past level 30, towards the core. It has a lot to offer for those seeking storylines and for those seeking a good mash-em-up.
Interaction is simple with a basic and functional control layout that allows ease of learning and use. Your movement is WASD and your knight looks in whichever direction the cursor is in relative to the knight. Interacting with other players is done simply by clicking/ right clicking on them and it allows the usual host of options- trade, inspect, tell etc…  Combat is well thought out too. It’s complicated enough to keep you entertained but simple enough to be very quick to learn. You can carry two weapons. Left click uses the weapon, hold to charge it for a more powerful or special attack. Right click raises your shield to defend you against damage. Middle mouse button changes weapons and those weapons have three categories- Melee, bomb, and pistol.
Death in game can be very frustrating. When you lose all your health, your knight is knocked out. He can be revived by his/ her armours systems once per level… and only once. To keep going if you go down a second time requires a rather rare item called the “spark of life”- which as you can imagine is expensive to purchase. This means that if you’re knocked down a second time you either use your rare, expensive and difficult to obtain spark of life to continue, or abandon your mission along with everything you had collected. It’s good in some ways as it prevents people just wandering through the dungeons and levels without actually helping other group members and annoying in that you have to pay one of the game currencies (read below) to continue on mission.
There are two types of currency in the game. The first are Crowns which you pick up during your missions and pretty much everything can be bought with them if it’s on the player run Auction house. The second currency is Energy and this is the real money currency that you pay £ or $ for. You can trade Crowns for energy and vice versa, but the exchange rate is very high- about 6000 crowns for 100 energy at the time of writing. This is a bit of a bummer as most items that are of maximum use such as lockbox keys are several hundred energy. If you want to buy 1000’s of energy in one go you can, but that is up to each person individually. I know I’ve spent about £10 on energy in the past to get some unique customisable parts but I won’t allow myself to spend any more.
The game comes with a good crafting and levelling mechanic too. You can build any weapon in the game if you can get the parts (bought on auction house or collected) and have the recipe. The weapon/ armour you build starts as a basic quality and can be upgraded several times by further “forging” it with specialist crystals that drop in the levels. This keeps the pressure on you to keep going and to be careful about what you upgrade first with your precious and semi-rare crystals.
Finally the customisable parts… There are millions. Hats, wings, wigs, eyepieces, comms devices, aura’s etc… the combinations are almost endless. I don’t think I’ve ever seen two knights look the same that were not obvious new starters. This is a bit of a double edged sword however as customisable parts (e.g. wings) get perma attached to the armour you stick them on. You cannot remove them unless you pay for it with energy. They are also hugely expensive on the market. Thankfully, there is a way to get better gear and show your customisable parts that got bolted onto an earlier peice of kit. You have two slots for armour parts that can have customisable bits. One slot is the armour the game thinks you are wearing i.e. your stat armour and the other slot is your costume slot which is what the other players will see. I for example have a lv4 Ash coat on, but my costume is a lv 2 steel armour thingy with Valkarie wings.
On the whole, Spiral knights is very enjoyable game. It’s simple design and enjoyable storyline is well worth a try and I could recommend it to anyone- especially as it’s free to play. The game allows you to solo, jump into groups that are already set up so you can adventure with other players and is a really good time.
Hope to see you in the clockworks soon, as for me- I’m off to level 25, pushing towards the core. To Victory!

Darkest Dungeon is a game that shows you how dangerous and foolhardy it is to grab a torch and go down into dark depths to face the beings who reside there.
And I love it, every step I take.
Darkest Dungeon is a challenging dungeon crawler where your characters must combat stress (read: Sanity) as well as the beasties that lie in the darkness as they search for fame, fortune and glory.  It really takes heavy cues from H.P. Lovecraft on how man was not meant to see what lies just beyond the torchlight.
It uses a turn based system and RPG elements as well as some cues taken from roguelike games, such as permadeath.  The game rewards quick thinking in a bad situation and preparation and priorities can truly determine weather your party comes out from the caves alive, or are ripped to shreds by nameless horrors.
The Art style is phenomenal and you'd be hard pressed to find a indie game with such evocative soundtracks and voiceover.  The narrator makes you feel the success of a critical hit and heartache of a fatal blow.  You grow attached to your party members just to see them die from a poor decision.  Some people may cry that the computer can pull these amazing succession of criticals leaving your characters ripe for slaughter next turn, but I've found that if you prepped correctly, prioritized your healing, and use status effects (like bleed and blight) to your advantage, you'll make it by the skin of you teeth and escape the dungeon.
In this game, you gotta know when to call it quits and leave the dungeon with what loot you can carry.  It's ok to run and come back another day with a stronger party and better supplies then to lose a character you've upgraded significantly.  And I love that about this game.  In H.P. Lovecraft's stories, it is rarely a happy ending and this game holds to those themes tightly.
In the end, I would recommend this game, but only to those that have the patience and understanding of the mindset you have to have when facing the terrors of the abyss.  If you go in foolhardy, you'll end up simply making more loot for the party that comes in after, as they pillage the nameless corpse of another failed adventurer.

It's more XCOM, now with Steam Workshop, yay!
While the first XCOM had to deal with 'living up' to the original XCOM legacy, XCOM 2 diverges from some of the mechanics tacked onto the first one because of said legacy. Instead, everything is more streamlined. Depending on the person, this can be good or bad. Gone are the interceptors and 'base building' of the first XCOM (I wish they would stop rebooting a franchise by naming it the same name). Instead, you get a mobile base that flies around on missions with the ground combat that's pretty much the same as the first but with a shiny new coating.
The skill trees are more interesting and offer a few interesting choices rather than an obvious route like the first. The weapon upgrades are just as linear as the first. Everything is a straight upgrade from the last and there is little reason to use weapons from prior research.
The camera is still as annoying as ever. For the love of baby pandas, let.the.player.control.the.damn.camera. I don't need 'Central' telling me the god damn bomb is about to god damn blow and interrupt my attempts at stopping the said blowing-upping of bomb. I don't need to have the camera auto center on each and every panick/burn/boo boo my little soldiers have. I-frickin-have-eyes.
On a simlar note to the camera, the mouse and keyboard controls have a  tendency to flake out when there's more than one floor. It also flakes out with trying to 'melee charge' a target as a ranger.
Oh right, there's swords this go around. It's swords vs aliens and it feels awesome.
Overwatch also had an overhaul so your little soldiers don't shoot a bajillion bullets at the squishiest thing and completely ignore the big-crazy-alien-thing charging up to murder face. Instead, they intelligently spread out the damage and kill as many targets as possible in the crossfire. Sadly, this intelligence takes a second to calculate as everyone and their pet pandas play red light red light and stand still for a minute or two before moving again.
Speaking of stop-and-going at the time of this writing, the performance ranges from alright to butts mcpants. One moment there's explosions and gunfire going off with little pause, the next moment, taking off on a ship drops down to a butt-ery smooth 5 frames per minute.
That's a lot of complaining, but most complaints outside of the silly purely upgrading weapons (as opposed to side grade) and stupid stupid camera auto centering, it's perfomance issues that'll probably be worked out over time.
It's still a damn fun game and those who liked the first one will probably enjoy this one. Those who prefered the original XCOM, this isn't really the same outside of the setting, but it's still worth a try with an open mind and little comparison to the original.
And just one last time, devs, don't wrest control from your players. If you're gonna do a cutscene, do a cutscene. But when the player has control, don't snatch it away every few seconds.
Next time 'Central" tells me civilians are dying, I will grenade the next civilian I see. Get probed Central.

Dear Firaxis,
Please stop trying to innovate. For every neat addition you make, you also make horrible, horrible additions.
+Rangers with melee weapons are cool.
+Greater customization is always fun
+The new perspective as the resistance is a neat idea
-Enemies are still ♥♥♥♥ing cheaters. They can still get free moves when you see them for the first time, dashing into cover or behind you, because ♥♥♥♥ your planning.
-Targeting and movement are still ♥♥♥♥ed, even moreso now. People shoot and melee through walls. Characters mantle through cars. Line of sight is obsured by non-existant structures. Grenade tossing is finicky and prone to weird blind spots. It's all just a lot less polished than it should be.
-Stealth mechanic, which should be very useful, is almost completely useless. The moment you attack one person, you completely lose your stealth for your entire squad. Doesn't matter how spread out they are, doesn't matter how loud the attack is, or if the enemy died, the stealth is just gone. The worst part is that the game says you should set all your characters to be in overwatch before attacking with one person, so you can create an ambush. But guess what? The enemy then gets to move wherever they like, as usual when you discover them,  so you MIGHT get a hit on them and they WILL move around to flank you. Brutal, unrelenting and untterly encapsulating after just 90 minutes of gameplay.
Have you ever played Xcom? Had a character die on normal mode? No big deal. Just reload the save. Darkest Dungeon has other thoughts. It likes Iron Man mode and it will take no prisoners.
It will make you live with the mistakes you make and the cruel dice rolls of RNGesus. But does this make it frustrating? To some i'm sure it does. But to me and many others the loss will help define the story. Ultimately Darkest Dungeon makes no apologies for this difficulty. It embraces it. Death doesn't feel unfair or unavoidable and as a result the game can shine because of its amazing gameplay.
The deaths of the heroes you hire is an important aspect as it fleshes out your personal adventure a lot more. The story is otherwise explained and hinted at by the words of the narrator, a long dead ancestor of yours. The narrator is amazing, giving commentary on events that happen in the game including improving the town, losing a hero in battle, dealing a critical strike, lighting a torch, getting a bad loot/damage roll from an item in the world, completing a quest (be it a failure or a success) or destroying a boss. This is all helped immensly by the quality of the voice acting.
The mechanics are exceptionally well thought out. Most importantly one has to multi-task and keep a clear idea of the stress and health of all heroes in the party. As you continue to adventure with heroes they can develop quirks which can have subtle to dramatic consequences on their actions in game. These quirks can be removed in the sanitarium but if left unchecked they can unfold the gameplay to a whole new level. I once had a hero die because of a perk that compelled them to interact with an object in the world. This backfired and caused a huge increase in the hero's stress, leading to death by heart attack (yes that's what happens if you max out your stress meter). Enemies are greatly varied with attacks that exploit party positioning, can bleed or blight to cause damage over time, cause stress, reduce your torch light, debuff you, contaminate you with disease and in some rare instances completely remove party members from play. You have a lot that you can attack with as well though. Use your party members varied abilites to destroy as much as you can. Every battle has a different challenge.
I could go on and on about Darkest Dungeon and explain everything including trinkets, resources, enemy types, random boss encounters, camping and of course the darkest dungeon itself. But honestly the best way to understand Darkes Dungeon is to throw yourself into it head first.
I got great value from this purchase and i'd recommend it to all of you. I only wish there were more cutscenes. perhaps one for each boss.
In short if you want a harsh but rewarding RPG dungeon crawling experience then this is absolutely for you.

XCOM 2 is at once refreshing and familiar. It builds on the stellar gameplay of it's predecessor, and adds it's own unique setting, mechanics and flair.
Theres some bad stuff here, though.
- Performance issues on systems that should run the game just fine
- The timed missions often have too short of a countdown, making many missions arbitrarily difficult
- The developers have either neglected to explain certain key game mechanics, or deliberately left them unexplained
- The tutorial is very long, unneccesarily so
I'm sure there are other negatives as well.
I'm not going to write a list of positives to counter the above. The game has issues, which need to be adressed. It is, however, extremely unforgiving, addictive, challenging and rewarding. A true XCOM game, that doesn't pull any pnches, and has all the features we have come to expect from the franchise: Ironman mode, brutal difficulty settings, frustratingly awesome rng and deep tactics and strategy.
In the end, I recommend buying it. XCOM 2 is good. Very good, for all it's flaws. I have enjoyed it immensely, and I will be playing this game for many years to come, just like the previous title in the series.

First things first: I'm pretty sure the people who complain that the game is too hard are just unable to cope with their cheap builds being nerfed. I am not by *any* stretch of the imagination an expert at this game, and I say the game is outright easy until you fight your first boss. If you wipe in the first dungeon then you've definitely done something terribly wrong.
I uninstalled this game half a year ago, because I wanted to "save myself" and start a fresh file after full release. I quit just before the community started bawling about heart attacks, corpses, and whatever else they did to prevent obviously cheesy strategies like heal-stalling.
Now I'm back, and it's the same awesome game that I left it as. The announcer is worthy of being the next DOTA voice pack. the look and feel show an amazing amount of love and talent. I haven't tinkered enough to say anything about the balance, but I will say that the system is much more than just the "Homicidal Gamemaster Simulator" that you've heard about; it has real strategy and depth to it. It's a twist on the age-old formula of dungeon crawling resource management:  healing is generally weak (but still important), resting around a campfire is extremely limited, and it is all but impossible to reduce Stress faster than it can accumulate. If things don't go smoothly, you will have to make a decision: give up, or tempt fate by risking that one last push?
I actually hate this style of gameplay, but Darkest Dungeon sucks me in by just being... you know... really, really cool. The overdramatic announcer, the beautiful art, the sense of danger and risk, it just feels GOOD.
Yes, you can have a total disaster caused by the RNG kicking you in the balls. Yes, there are some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t un-fun ways for the game to take stuff away from you. No, the game will never beat you down so hard that you are unable to continue playing. Cutting losses to avoid total disaster is part of the game, and should the worst occur, the system is designed to let you rebuild after taking painful losses.
If you are here, then you surely have heard the stories about dramatic victories and heartbreaking failures in this dark, unforgiving pit--by now, you already know deep in your heart whether or not you are ready to enter... the Darkest Dungeon.

While I'm only 11 hours in the game so far has been extremely impressive. For fans of the previous iteration I think it's safe to say that XCOM 2 takes away the bad and adds in interesting new dynamics. The biggest change I've noticed so far is the pacing. In the original XCOM, depending on the difficulty, you could spend hours on a single mission. Mos of that time was spent slowly inching your way forward and hoping that you wouldn't activate too many pods (patrols) at a time.
They've implemented "Concealment" which is just what it says, it makes you able to move without detection so long as you don't get too close to the aliens.
Paired with this is the fact that pods now patrol along pre-set paths, allowing for less frustration because of random luck. In order to make you play more aggressive most missions have a built-in timer to clear the main objective. If you're not a fan of this there are already mods which modify or remove the timers.
XCOM 2 still has a few quirks, but they are mostly benign. Guns sticking through walls, bullets flying through your squadmate's head on their way to the baddies and other minor graphical issues make for comedic effect, but also hinders immersion somewhat.
The biggest issue I've had so far is with Line of Sight (LoS). Just like in Enemy Unknown / Enemy Within the LoS is sketchy at best, and sometimes downright wrong. At times I've been shot at through solid walls and activated pods from insane angles, not to mention the uncertainty of whether you'll trigger that overwatch. It's unfortunate that the developers haven't been able to solve this issue. However this does not take away from the fact that XCOM 2 on the whole is a vast improvement over it's predecessor and brings several fresh and interesting ideas to the simulation of battling a superior alien army. The game sucks you in and time flies, before you know it your eyes feel like they've been scrubbed with sandpaper and you have to get up in 2 hours.
All in all this game is an amazing experience and I recommend you pick it up right now. You won't regret it.

With all the negative reviews lamenting the changes made since the game was originally put on Early Access, I feel like I need to throw some positivity into the mix, because this game is amazing.
I've been playing on and off since it was first put on Steam, and am aware of the various changes which have been made throught each iteration of the game. To summarize, Darkest Dungeon used to be significantly easier. Before the devs bumped up the difficulty I only had a handful of characters die, and I knew people who managed to get characters up to their highest rank without ever suffering a death.
The changes the devs made are not unfair. New mechanics were added to prevent players exploiting situations to fully heal every battle, and existing mechanics were changed to better fit the original vision—your characters are not heroes. No matter how powerful they become, being hurt is always something you want to avoid, overwhelming stress is not something you can ever just ignore, and manipulating the formation of both your party and the enemy party is crucial to winning each battle.
Back before the changes, dungeon runs required significantly less forethought, and most runs could be completed relatively painlessly. Combat took only slightly more strategy than the typical random encounter in a Final Fantasy. Now each fight is a struggle for your life, and while this certainly makes the game more challenging, that kind of challenge is what was intended from the beginning. No doubt I'll get a half dozen angry messages berating me about something or other, but oh well.
TL;DR: The game used to be much easier and full of ways to manipulate the system to breeze through even the hardest dungeons. Now people are upset that it was changed to punish people for trying to use cheap exploits. It's a very challenging game, and RNG can kick your butt, but you can ALWAYS avoid permanent death by cutting your losses and abandoning a mission. You are in control. Greed and overconfidence will be your downfall.
As for an actual review, I'll be brief: the overall aesthetic is wonderfully dark, and the whole game reflects the same sinister feeling of vain hope, of struggling towards an impossible goal and clawing your way forward. Success is short-lived and defeat is painful, but the journey is fantastic. Classes are all well balanced and monsters are varied and unique. Bosses will push you to your limits. There is some aspect of grind, and leveling up a large roster of characters can be time consuming, but I enjoyed myself the whole time.
If you're on the fence with the one, the best thing you can do is stop reading reviews and watch some live streams to see if it looks like something you would enjoy. It's not for everyone, and there are a lot of different things to manage which can get tedious if you're not into that sort of thing. Still, I recommend this game to everyone I know, and it gets a big thumbs up here.

So, it's still not in a final, retail release state yet, but, here are my thoughts:
It's fantastic if you're into Terraria and that general type of game. I recommend this highly to anyone who liked Terraria, and it's now in good enough shape that the developer has stated characters and ships will no longer need to be wiped. And, presumably but without a 100% guarentee, the worlds won't be wiped, either. Of course, worlds are what you play the game for... anyone who played Terraria for long eventually had to build their base, etc., so losing the worlds would be a pretty big loss, but it's reasonably certain this won't happen (in the event it does, I'm storing everything on my ship until final release, so, no loss there).
There are enough reasons that Starbound excels. For one, the sprites are a little larger, which allows for more detail to characters and objects. Secondly, the game allows you to fly to different worlds that are generally made up of just a couple biomes, meaning that, unlike Terraria, Starbound won't force you to cross the entire map just to get back to that snow biome you need to go to for crafting materials. Instead, just fly the ship.
Another important improvement is in the combat. The ability to equip different items in different hands really sets Starbound apart, in that you can hold a flashlight and a weapon, or a weapon and a shield, and so forth. And combat itself is more detailed, for the most part: you really have to time your attack, rather than just hold down the left-mouse-button.
But what I like most about Starbound thus far is that the procedurally-generated worlds really do feel individualized: on a forest-planet I found high-tech labs sprinkled about on the surface... on a desert planet, I found a tribal hut and much farther away, a camping tent. The longer I play, the more I am sure I'll start to see some elements repeat, but because of the wealth of worlds and the specific detais each one receives, it'll be far longer before I see things repeating as compared to Terraria.
This is not to say Starbound is not without it's faults. The early-game of Starbound is surprisingly a worse-grind than in Terraria, particularly because you need coal to fuel your spaceship (yes, coal), and you need a certain level of pixels (yes, pixels) to craft most non-level-1 items. Each of these are not easy to harvest at first, especially since the early enemies of Starbound are far tougher than the early foes of Terraria. Too tough, in some cases.
But past that early-game phase? More fun than Terraria in my opinion, and that's saying something.
Oh, and Starbound's music is spectacular... it reminds me vaguely of Final Fantasy VII in the music department.
By all means, if you enjoy procedurally-generated sandbox games that revolve around crafting and building, this is worth picking up.

Brutal, unrelenting and untterly encapsulating after just 90 minutes of gameplay.
Have you ever played Xcom? Had a character die on normal mode? No big deal. Just reload the save. Darkest Dungeon has other thoughts. It likes Iron Man mode and it will take no prisoners.
It will make you live with the mistakes you make and the cruel dice rolls of RNGesus. But does this make it frustrating? To some i'm sure it does. But to me and many others the loss will help define the story. Ultimately Darkest Dungeon makes no apologies for this difficulty. It embraces it. Death doesn't feel unfair or unavoidable and as a result the game can shine because of its amazing gameplay.
The deaths of the heroes you hire is an important aspect as it fleshes out your personal adventure a lot more. The story is otherwise explained and hinted at by the words of the narrator, a long dead ancestor of yours. The narrator is amazing, giving commentary on events that happen in the game including improving the town, losing a hero in battle, dealing a critical strike, lighting a torch, getting a bad loot/damage roll from an item in the world, completing a quest (be it a failure or a success) or destroying a boss. This is all helped immensly by the quality of the voice acting.
The mechanics are exceptionally well thought out. Most importantly one has to multi-task and keep a clear idea of the stress and health of all heroes in the party. As you continue to adventure with heroes they can develop quirks which can have subtle to dramatic consequences on their actions in game. These quirks can be removed in the sanitarium but if left unchecked they can unfold the gameplay to a whole new level. I once had a hero die because of a perk that compelled them to interact with an object in the world. This backfired and caused a huge increase in the hero's stress, leading to death by heart attack (yes that's what happens if you max out your stress meter). Enemies are greatly varied with attacks that exploit party positioning, can bleed or blight to cause damage over time, cause stress, reduce your torch light, debuff you, contaminate you with disease and in some rare instances completely remove party members from play. You have a lot that you can attack with as well though. Use your party members varied abilites to destroy as much as you can. Every battle has a different challenge.
I could go on and on about Darkest Dungeon and explain everything including trinkets, resources, enemy types, random boss encounters, camping and of course the darkest dungeon itself. But honestly the best way to understand Darkes Dungeon is to throw yourself into it head first.
I got great value from this purchase and i'd recommend it to all of you. I only wish there were more cutscenes. perhaps one for each boss.
In short if you want a harsh but rewarding RPG dungeon crawling experience then this is absolutely for you.

Original:
Prepare to do a lot of file editing to make this feel like EW (if you can track down the right settings). The good thing is the game makes it mostly easy to do so.
The devs, in what apparently is capitulating to those whining that EW wasn't hard enough, decided to make the game harder. The problem is that they had no idea how. So they decided to add turn limits to every mission. And they decided that even though it's only your soldier's first mission out, Sectoids should be able to raise the dead (turning them into a zombie with more HP than they originally had), severely limit one of your soldier's actions, or mind control your soldier (these are the only abilities I've seenl I don't know if they have others). This in the first mission... while you're trying to hustle across a huge zone to reach your target in 8 turns... and stay hidden from the enemy who is wandering around... with a group of soldiers that barely know which end of the stick to point at the bad guys. On the plus side, when the enemy spots you, if you have your people on overwatch, you can shoot them while they scramble for cover. The down side is that if you put your people on overwatch to shoot at the enemy while they scurry away, the enemy then gets an immediate turn, and most likely, they used that free movement to flank one of your people who missed their overwatch. First mission, by the way. So far, I haven't found a way to disable the alien free turn on spotting you. Realistically, I should be able to have each of my soldiers get a bead on a target and give them a command to all fire at the same time, thus eliminating the ability to run from my ambush. That's kind of the whole point of an ambush. Enemies getting a free turn immediately after any individual unit breaks cover to shoot them is BS.
Also, there doesn't seem to be any random number storage this time around so if you miss a shot, just reload your save and maybe you'll hit next time.
The character customization is pretty good though.

10/10 game. I rarely give games such high praise.
This is hands down, the most dynamic and entertaining game I've played in years. And that's coming from someone who likes FPS games far more than any 3rd person perspective.
What makes this game so incredible? The combat mechanics are some of the best that gaming has ever seen, as far as controllers go. This game wasn't made for K+M, so you should get a console controller for your PC.
There are maybe 2 downsides to this game I can think of, but I certainly could never subtract a point for it:
1- is that it has a difficult-to-follow story. There is very little speaking, and the lore is found outside of the game itself.
2- There is rampant cheating on the PC version of the game, which means PC users have a ton of problems compared to console users.
Because so much of this game is devoted to multiplayer, such as constant invasions, summons for boss fights, and arena, I really can't recommend this game for the PC. If you have a console, for god's sake, get DS3 on your console. The graphics might suffer slightly, but it's by far worth it to get people using cheat engines away from you. They will quite literally ruin the entire DS3 experience, but this is a problem with players, not developers. This was intended as a console game.
On an ending note, this is the most impressive game I've played since the original Half-Life hit the shelves, and fractioned off into Half-Life multiplayer, Counter-Strike, Adrenaline gamer, and other mods that grew to become their own game entirely. The Dark Souls game is so impressive that games will be described as "souls-like" for many years to come, and probably fail to measure up.

So. After modding the game via the Steam workshop and applying performance fixes from
, I'm actually enjoying myself. So I have to change my verdict to thumbs up.
The story is still doofy, but I'm enjoying the gameplay now.
The major gameplay improvement is
: for missions where the squad starts concealed, the turn timer only starts when you lose concealment. This makes a million times more sense. Why would the aliens set the explosive timers on their precious thingy you need to recover when they don't even know you're there yet? This makes these missions more like a heist movie, where you carefully plan your moves before setting off the alarm and THEN moving rapidly. That mod even reduces turn timers for the concealed missions, and I think it actually works. Stealth makes sense now.
I also recommend
,
and
. I've got the SMG Pack as well, but find I never use SMGs.
I should also mention that some of the percieved unfair difficulty wasn't actually correct. The game does a poor job of explaining certain critical mechanics, but some of it is actually to the player's benefit. In particular: when you research new armour and weapons and then still need to manufacture them in engineering, you may be put off by the very steep manufacturing cost, as I was. If you can't afford $200 per soldier to kit them out, the enemy is a lot scarier. Well, it turns out that engineering cost is a one-time thing, and affects ALL soldiers from then on. Although, this doesn't apply for utility items like medkits etc. My point is, the game doesn't tell you which is which, so you may end up making the wrong strategic decision as a result of faulty information.
But anyway, I guess it turned out for the best they didn't accept my refund.

So, it's still not in a final, retail release state yet, but, here are my thoughts:
It's fantastic if you're into Terraria and that general type of game. I recommend this highly to anyone who liked Terraria, and it's now in good enough shape that the developer has stated characters and ships will no longer need to be wiped. And, presumably but without a 100% guarentee, the worlds won't be wiped, either. Of course, worlds are what you play the game for... anyone who played Terraria for long eventually had to build their base, etc., so losing the worlds would be a pretty big loss, but it's reasonably certain this won't happen (in the event it does, I'm storing everything on my ship until final release, so, no loss there).
There are enough reasons that Starbound excels. For one, the sprites are a little larger, which allows for more detail to characters and objects. Secondly, the game allows you to fly to different worlds that are generally made up of just a couple biomes, meaning that, unlike Terraria, Starbound won't force you to cross the entire map just to get back to that snow biome you need to go to for crafting materials. Instead, just fly the ship.
Another important improvement is in the combat. The ability to equip different items in different hands really sets Starbound apart, in that you can hold a flashlight and a weapon, or a weapon and a shield, and so forth. And combat itself is more detailed, for the most part: you really have to time your attack, rather than just hold down the left-mouse-button.
But what I like most about Starbound thus far is that the procedurally-generated worlds really do feel individualized: on a forest-planet I found high-tech labs sprinkled about on the surface... on a desert planet, I found a tribal hut and much farther away, a camping tent. The longer I play, the more I am sure I'll start to see some elements repeat, but because of the wealth of worlds and the specific detais each one receives, it'll be far longer before I see things repeating as compared to Terraria.
This is not to say Starbound is not without it's faults. The early-game of Starbound is surprisingly a worse-grind than in Terraria, particularly because you need coal to fuel your spaceship (yes, coal), and you need a certain level of pixels (yes, pixels) to craft most non-level-1 items. Each of these are not easy to harvest at first, especially since the early enemies of Starbound are far tougher than the early foes of Terraria. Too tough, in some cases.
But past that early-game phase? More fun than Terraria in my opinion, and that's saying something.
Oh, and Starbound's music is spectacular... it reminds me vaguely of Final Fantasy VII in the music department.
By all means, if you enjoy procedurally-generated sandbox games that revolve around crafting and building, this is worth picking up.

Rewrote the review and changed recommendation.
This game has two problems:
1. The insane difficulty in the early game.
2. Mission timers on almost all missions.
BUT there are solutions for those problems:
1) endure it, die or get wounded a lot, curse the game, curse the mechanics, curse RNG, stick through, punch a hole into your monitor out of frustration, buy a new one, continue and soon after hours of misery and despair, you'll eventually come to the point where it's only plain hard instead of insanely frustrating.
2) Install the "remove mission timers"-mod from the Steam workshop (it doesn't remove all timers, which is good, but it helps keeping it varied)
Sure, you could say, that the game is supposed to be played with all those timers, but seriously, they overstepped in that regard. For me at least it isn't fun having to rush through almost all missions, always straight through the middle, since otherwise you can't reach the objective in time. No no no!
Those two things are the game's greatest flaws imo, other negative things are:
- bad optimisation
- sometimes bad camera angles (which btw one could eventually fix with a mod I saw on the workshop, though I didn't try it out)
- well, ...guess that was it, more or less...
Now to the positive stuff:
I didn't thought so at first, actually I had quite the opposing opinion, but this game is better than XCOM:EW.
It gives you more variety (if you kill those timers), has a great story, which is nicely presented. The classes are diverse and there isn't a redundant class (like the MEC in EW). Also I really like that psionics are a seperate class now and they are great fun to play.
Another huge plus is that there is no mimetic skin or something like this, so yes mid to end game you are clearly mightier, but that doesn't mean that it will be a walk in the park, like it was with Mimetic Skin in EW. Imo almost all skills, weapons, utilities are well balanced and nothing op there.
The maps are diverse enough to so that one doesn't get bored by same assets and the mission objectives are, although mostly variations of known missiontypes from EW, fresh enough to entertain.
One really nice feature is that you now can see, if you would have line of sight to an enemy, if you moved. So you don't have to guess anymore if you could shot an enemy, after moving to another tile.
The Hacking in this game (you can hack robots and sort of control posts, for boni or to disable/convert it) is a nice new feature, though especially in the early stages it is often better not to try, since the chances aren't very high with untrained soldiers, and if you fail it will punish you (hp loss or alarm for example).
Visually it is neither great nor terrible, but that isn't what I desperately wanted it from it anyway or in other words, I just don't care very much.
At first I found the art style a little to colorful, but at least it is cohesive and not too distracting.
All in all I can finally recommend the game, although it took me many hours until I could really appreciate it and I almost gave up on it (after round about 9 hours of pain and suffering). But if you liked XCOM and/or you are looking for a challenging game, with an intriguing narrative and if you feel ready to get humiliated a lot, then you should give it a try.

Fallout 4 is a disgrace to the franchise.
This game is essentially an open world action FPS with a few sandbox elements, I'd compare it more to the recent FarCry games than any Fallout game (though the FarCry games do what it does better for the most part). This game touts improved gunplay, more detailed weapon/armor customization, and some additional sandbox elements over previous Fallout titles. However it sacrifices almost all semblance of RPG elements primarily by simplifying the dialogue system, forcing a terrible/boring personality and backstory onto the player, and removing the stat system, amongst other smaller changes.
With this Fallout 4 also removed practically all choices and decision making from the player, your dialogue gives you the illusion of choice, but in reality nothing you say or do in this game ever matters or has any consequence whatsoever, something that even Fallout 3 did better, and the classic Fallouts/New Vegas did a million times better. The quests are repetitive and uninteresting, the story is stupid and predictable, not to mention the terrible optimization (and I mean TERRIBLE) and sub-par graphics. Also the boring and lifeless world, terrible factions with terrible writing, and just really awful characters all around.
The game is an ocean with the depth of a puddle. It's shallow, boring, repetitive, and doesn't deserve to be called a Fallout game. Also don't let my play time fool you, I spent probably a good 30+ hours of that play time trying to fix bugs and crashes, improve performance, and basically do all the♥♥♥♥♥♥Bethesda should have done before releasing this steaming pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥
There are existing mods and mods in the works that improves the game in almost every aspect, from changing the awful story, to reintoducing many of the RPG elements, and much more. When these mods are finished and more fleshed out I can see myself coming back to this game, but as it stands I regret every cent of my money and every second of my time I spent on this game.
Having said all that, if you are someone who doesn't really care about the shallow gameplay and bugs/performance issues, and just want an open world shoot n' loot game, then sure, pick it up on sale you'll probably enjoy it, but for those of us who want a real Fallout experience... This is NOT where you will find it.

I say, there is no definitive storyline for Fallout 4.
Every single faction is replacable, with the same type of ending that you would expect from Mass Effect 3.
The only things that change are which buildings you get to go into, which replacable face you see, and how unimmersive things become. The fact that you can't join the Institute until you're nearly 1/3rd done with the game, betraying any previous ties to a faction you needed to join in order to infiltrate the Institute is again, like Mass Effect 3, with the option to join up with Cerberus.
At some point, you'd need to ask why? Why am I doing this again?
And then with the addition of Nuka-World, they unleashed plenty of potential for a completely game-changing story line, one where you feel as if you're coming out on top, only, you're not.
My biggest discrepancy with Nuka-World, is that even though you get to be buddy buddy with all the raider gangs, you never have the respect of the bosses.
It comes down to the Nuka-Blaster, the squirt gun. By accepting Gage's help, you're already submitting to their grand plan. It's the entire reason why Bethesda followed that same line of thinking to the point where a raider gang turns on you because you're not putting all your attention and focus into building up their gang, giving them land and territories.
Nut's to that. I wish you could actually become a real overboss of Nuka-World, get some mo'fo respect around here, and then go lay waste to the Institute with some ironic justice. They leave so much for want at the end of the Nuka-World DLC.
The Operators building up the World of Refreshment? The bottling plant? HELLO! That's a whole new storyline about them trying to run and distribute WATER across a wasteland! And turning a profit too!
They could've had hours of dialogue about how the gangs don't even realize how much of a money maker the world of refreshment could be, or how the sprinklers around Kiddie Kingdom would make an amzing hydroponic system for growing crops so that the raiders of Nuka-World wouldn't even need to raid for food and supplies.
If the Sole Survivor is a loving parent, Nuka-World laughs in the face of that and makes them their bottom B.
The SS could've played everyone as a fool, and worked towards a grand goal of rehabilitating the raiders and turning them into a unified army under the Nuka-World flag.
Each raider boss is more or less driven by money, caps. You could've said "Alright," and proceeded to dump millions of caps in their face if they went along the route of distributing water and beverages across the wasteland, securing trade routes and distribution channels. Like an actual successful company, rather than buying into the current philosophy of Nuka-World.
But no. At the end, you have one dead raider boss, and two who are looking to replace you at first sign of trouble.
WHERE'S THE FEAR? WHERE'S the option to "RULE WITH AN IRON FIST?"
Jeezus, Beth, learn how to freiking improvise, these stories practically write themselves, but you're like a business meeting set for tomorrow at lunchtime.
Let me elaborate, a business meeting that doesn't accomplish everything they wanted to do, puts it off until tomorrow, usually at or before lunch, so people can reconvein and talk some more, wasting people's time who go to these meetings, while others are there to waste time so they don't have to work for an hour or two. They also have the option to eat lunch at these meetings, at which point they call it a day when the food actually arrives.
How is that like Fallout 4?
The bosses of Nuka-World are in a constant business meeting, where every time you try to advance the plot, (by doing work) they send you out to go grab lunch for the rest of the team while they brainstorm ideas to get more caps, resources, or slaves. While as you, the Sole Survivor can offer the type of insight that would only be available to someone who lived two hundred ten years ago, all that is thrown out the window. They don't even have a good reason as to why you would ever go to Nuka-World in the first place!

While as you, the ever loving parent, try to Abraham Lincoln your way into position of releasing all the slaves, while coming up with a way to compensate everyone for the manpower and money needed.
Bethesda could've come up with an entire economy where you aren't just making a few hundred caps every time you collar a slave, kill a Gunner, or wipe out a synth.

but no, I need to scroll through the builing crafting workshop to find a radio tower, and then build a generator, and then a speaker, and some drug dispensers and get other settlements to pitch in because they "Don't feel like gardening."

Rewrote the review and changed recommendation.
This game has two problems:
1. The insane difficulty in the early game.
2. Mission timers on almost all missions.
BUT there are solutions for those problems:
1) endure it, die or get wounded a lot, curse the game, curse the mechanics, curse RNG, stick through, punch a hole into your monitor out of frustration, buy a new one, continue and soon after hours of misery and despair, you'll eventually come to the point where it's only plain hard instead of insanely frustrating.
2) Install the "remove mission timers"-mod from the Steam workshop (it doesn't remove all timers, which is good, but it helps keeping it varied)
Sure, you could say, that the game is supposed to be played with all those timers, but seriously, they overstepped in that regard. For me at least it isn't fun having to rush through almost all missions, always straight through the middle, since otherwise you can't reach the objective in time. No no no!
Those two things are the game's greatest flaws imo, other negative things are:
- bad optimisation
- sometimes bad camera angles (which btw one could eventually fix with a mod I saw on the workshop, though I didn't try it out)
- well, ...guess that was it, more or less...
Now to the positive stuff:
I didn't thought so at first, actually I had quite the opposing opinion, but this game is better than XCOM:EW.
It gives you more variety (if you kill those timers), has a great story, which is nicely presented. The classes are diverse and there isn't a redundant class (like the MEC in EW). Also I really like that psionics are a seperate class now and they are great fun to play.
Another huge plus is that there is no mimetic skin or something like this, so yes mid to end game you are clearly mightier, but that doesn't mean that it will be a walk in the park, like it was with Mimetic Skin in EW. Imo almost all skills, weapons, utilities are well balanced and nothing op there.
The maps are diverse enough to so that one doesn't get bored by same assets and the mission objectives are, although mostly variations of known missiontypes from EW, fresh enough to entertain.
One really nice feature is that you now can see, if you would have line of sight to an enemy, if you moved. So you don't have to guess anymore if you could shot an enemy, after moving to another tile.
The Hacking in this game (you can hack robots and sort of control posts, for boni or to disable/convert it) is a nice new feature, though especially in the early stages it is often better not to try, since the chances aren't very high with untrained soldiers, and if you fail it will punish you (hp loss or alarm for example).
Visually it is neither great nor terrible, but that isn't what I desperately wanted it from it anyway or in other words, I just don't care very much.
At first I found the art style a little to colorful, but at least it is cohesive and not too distracting.
All in all I can finally recommend the game, although it took me many hours until I could really appreciate it and I almost gave up on it (after round about 9 hours of pain and suffering). But if you liked XCOM and/or you are looking for a challenging game, with an intriguing narrative and if you feel ready to get humiliated a lot, then you should give it a try.
XCOM:EW is one of my favourite games, but this game is definitely better....

This game is the worst, most grind dependent MMO I have ever played. Everything from crafting, to building, to leveling, to end game content is nothing but a mindless grind of the same activities for hundreds of hours.
Ill try to explain...
Leveling to 20 amounts to nothing but grinding the same dungeons for dozens of hours. There is no pvp option, there is nothing else you can do to gain experience. You just run from lame dungeon to lame dungeon killing the exact same bosses hundreds and hundreds of times.
Getting high end gear literally requires you to grind for dozens of hours for nearly pointless bonuses that seem to not even help slightly. The way items work in the game is similar to how destiny's level/item system works. You have a low level cap but continue to level up your "gear level" by getting better items allowing you to advance to higher level zones which drop better items (in theory).
This seems fine for a while once you hit 20. It doesnt take too long to get that rainbow item to 5 stars and upgrade it to a shadow item. But this is where the entire system falls apart. There are 5 levels of shadow items, Shadow 1 through Shadow 5. Shadow 5 obviously being the best of the group. Each Shadow level has 5 star levels you need to progress through by spending large amounts of materials till you can upgrade the items overall shadow level. The only way to get these materials is...you guessed it... Continue to grind the exact same dungeons you did to level to 20 in the first place but in a slightly harder zone.
This is tedious but upgrading to shadow 2 is quite easy. Its at shadow 2 where this system shows how its designed as the ultimate time consuming gear treadmill. In order to upgrade a shadow 2 item to shadow 3, you need to break down several shadow 2 items to get specific items. Problem is at shadow 2 you're either going to be in Uber 3 or 4 difficulty zones. Shadow 2 items simply dont drop in these zones. They have something like a .000001% chance to drop. They drop frequently in Uber 5 but the difference between U4 and U5 is just insane and its impossible to even kill a regular U5 mob unless you are decked out in full perfect stat Shadow 3 or higher gear (oh yeah stats are totally random so you are at the mercy of the RNG god for whether or not items drop for you, and which stats those items have). So in order to upgrade your gear to shadow 3 you are forced to... again you guess it... Grind Uber 3 or 4 till enough shadow 2 items drop that you can break them down and use the components to upgrade your gear.
You may be thinking "that doesnt sound so bad" and you would be dead wrong. In my last 15 hours of gameplay I was nonstop farming uber 4 dungeons trying to get shadow 2 items to drop. I got 1 in 15 hours, and you need 6 to upgrade all your gear.
You may also be thinking or "you should just group up with people and do higher level zones with better chances for items to drop" and once again you would be DEAD WRONG. Me and 4 friends who are all able to solo uber 4 with no problems at all couldnt even kill basic mobs in U5. They one shot you and have so much HP its literally impossible to even kill the most basic minion mobs. You are literally forced to grind zones that have incredibly low chances of dropping items you need so you can upgrade your gear to have a chance at the higher level zones.
But wait! There's more. The bonuses you gain from upgrading your gear are VERY VERY small, so it will take a ♥♥♥♥ ton of upgrades to give you any real power boosts. Also keep in mind we found our thanks to grouping up in u5 quadrupling our damage output was still not even close to enough to kill basic mobs. I honestly dont understand at all how you are supposed to become powerful enough to move up to U5 or even U6. There has to be some kind of hidden defense stat in the game, as there is none on any of the gear and a mob that one shots you one minute will do a sliver the next. There is just no consistancy to anything about this game.
We western gamers like to make fun of Eastern MMOs and call them grind simulators, but♥♥♥♥♥♥like this and Destiny where grinding is literally the central focus of the game are A-Okay with us. Someone please explain to me how this is any better than AION or any other Korean MMO nontorious for forcing the player to grind. Ill remind you I spent 15 hours of grinding a zone I was not supposed to be able to even survive in (and oh! class balance is a ♥♥♥♥ing JOKE in this game, my level 20 drac in full shadow 2 gear was not able to kill anything in U4 and got 1 shot regularly, but my lv 10 Tomb Raiser in the same gear was soloing u4 like it was nothing) and I was only able to get a single upgrade componant of which I needed 6.
Lets talk about crafting now...
This by far is the worst, most grind reliant part of the entire game. In order to craft a single pet you will need to collect 500 of two different types of mob drops and a thousand or more ore. In my 30+ hours of playing, I was only able to get about 60-80 of each type. Even when I set out with the specific intent of farming a single type of mat I would only get 1 or 2 every 30 min or so. The drop rates on these items must be in the ten thousandths of a percent, and you need hundreds...FOR A SINGLE ♥♥♥♥ING CRAFTED ITEM. If you intend on crafting even two of the dozens and dozens of pets or mounts you better leave your signicant other, quit your job, and install a toilet in your computer room cause you arent doing anything else for years.
Finally lets talk about the games pay to win mechanics. Now Ill admit it took me a very long time to see exactly how this game is pay to win (I knew it was because afterall this is a Trion game, and its not a Trion game unless it has a game breaking p2w mechanic [See archage p2w arena for some reference]). They dont sell items, nor do they sell levels, but what they do sell is those mats you need to upgrade your items and craft pets or mounts, in the form of lockboxes and those pets/mounts outright (they carry VERY powerful stat buffs, so dont ♥♥♥♥ing tell me them selling a pet that increases your damage by 20% is cosmetic). When it comes to the lockboxes even their p2w mechanic is based on pure luck. Maybe you'll get that componant that takes 30 hours to farm, or maybe you'll get 50 of that ore you cant go 5 feet without tripping over. So you either spend days, literal days... in game farming for materials to craft and upgrade items or you drop money and buy a ton of lockboxes that have a chance of dropping said materals.
♥♥♥♥ everything about this game, ♥♥♥♥ its BS RNG crap, ♥♥♥♥ its upgrade mechanics that require you to spend actual days in game farming the same boring dungeons over and over, and most of all ♥♥♥♥ Trion Worlds, they even designed this game where the players are the ones who have to put the work into making the world. All the dungeons and items were made by players duped by Trion into doing their jobs for free. They more or less made a hollow shell of a game and put the burden of filling it with content on the players. Who gladly turned around and did their jobs for free.
They took what could have been a fun little minecraft like MMO and turned it into a chore. Playing this game is flat out tedious, all the mobs behave the same, all the zones are the exact same thing just with a color palette swap, every activity is EXACTLY the same. If you want to get the full Trove experience load up the game and do a single dungeon; that's it, you've literally seen EVERYTHING the game has to offer gameplay wise the only difference as you progress through the game is the mobs do more damage and take more. They dont change anything from level 1 to "gear level" 40.

Please skip to the conclusion for the TL;DR on this game.
First off, before I say anything, while I enjoyed this game thoroughly, I don't actually recommend it
.  The only reason this is listed as a positive review is because the game has great potential.
Please remember
in this review.
-
* Great art-style
* Amazing music
* Frequently updated
* Hundreds of items to decorate your starship with
* Procedurally generated universe. Not just planets - the entire
is procedurally generated.  There are infinite planets!
* Resources you find depend on how difficult a planet is to explore
* Built to support modding
-
* There isn't much reason to stay on your home planet, or any planet, because you can do everything from your ship.  Planets just feel like sources of income
* The story isn't very indepth right now, and there are only a handful of quests to guide you on how to play
* Weapons and monsters, while possessing Borderlands style random generation, aren't very unique.
* Ore layout isn't very refined.  I've found platinum (pretty good ore) at surface level on more than one occasion.
* Because some races are being worked on more than others right now, there may be heavy advantages to being a certain race over another
* Storing your items can get pretty tedious, since the only container larger than 16 slots is the one in your ship.
* Starships aren't very customizable
* The cost of traveling to other planets can be a huge grind at some times.
* Crafting is a bit clunky, partly there are so many items to choose from.
* No way to customize controls
* No way to easily delete characters from the selection screen
* Frequent crashes and bugs
-
* Has a
steep difficulty curve coupled with a flawed combat system.
* "Exploring dungeons" is just building a dirt floor over some traps to get the loot at the end, or even just mining directly to the loot room from the dungeon entrance.
* Uses a form of currency called pixels intended to give the player a reason to kill monsters and complete quests, but it feels like more of a grind than a reward.
* Because the infinite universe is the same for everyone who plays, people can share coordinates for planets they find with cool stuff on them.  While this may sound great, it can ruin the feeling of wonder and excitement experienced upon discovering something new and amazing yourself.  It's often exploited to give players an advantage in their games.
In conclusion, I don't recommend this game at it's current state.  You'll notice neither the good nor ugly sections have many points in them, but the bad section has more than plenty.  The game isn't totally refined, and there's
of room for improvement.  If you want to support the developers, you can absolutely get the game, although money isn't as much an issue as time is with development anymore.  The game is great with friends, too.  Grab a few pals your first go and you'll have a blast.  Be sure to check out some of the mods on the official website if you ever get bored with the game.

This is going to be more of a neutral review.  Short-term, yes.  Long-term, no.
Nice art, fluid gameplay, but hectic economy and stagnant story.  SK's fun for the first... 10-20 hours.  If you have some friends to joke around and cooperate with, it's good for another 10-20 hours.
After that, you've probably reached Vanguard (the highest rank) and got 5-star gear.  That isn't to say there isn't anything else to do, but at that point, you're just playing to upgrade more gear, symbolize roleplaying, and maybe compete in Lockdown, Shadow Lairs, arcade runs, and Danger Missions to see who can get them done most efficiently.
The Auction House has prices go perpetually down as well which creates a weird paradox of thrift.  People don't buy things quickly since they anticipate that they'll sell better in the future.  The same thing happens on the energy market.  Instead, sales tend to go in spurts.  You'll have very quick success in odd instants only to be followed by days of stagnation unless you underprice what you're asking to sell.  It probably happens because people get bored of the repetition.  The economy becomes further ruined by the seemingly random costume events (well, they're not random if you've played the game years in advance since you know the annual schedule, but for people who are just picking up the game for several weeks or a couple months, they're very random).  Energy prices will trickle up and up only to get clobbered down since everyone dumps the market after purchasing energy for prize boxes to get a chance at special costumes.
Speaking of chance, did I mention you have to gather several dozen crystals to level up gear at the highest levels just for a 30-80% chance of success, or you can gather 50% more crystals for a 100% chance?  This gets even worse for 5-star gear which needs radiant crystals, but can even now after updates only be found on a handful of levels such as the last one... which is begging "Why bother?" since you've already beat the game by then.  Did I mention that gear upgrades actually decrease its effectiveness until your reach level 5 with it too?  In other words, you're actually better with 4-star level 10 gear than with 5-star gear until you get enough radiants to level it up enough.  Some people don't even bother with 5-star gear at all.
Also, guild hall purchases are very frustrating.  To put it in perspective, even a chair or table will cost 11,000 crowns.  If you run the last level of the game once, you get about 9,000 crowns.  There is also no way to liquidate or trade furnishings, and you can't relocate or store facility rooms (which are really pointless unless you're looking for artistic touch since they exist in Haven anyway) nor authorization doors (which need to be destroyed and replaced).  Statues are nice... if you enjoy going back and playing the same levels and bosses over and over again to get the tokens for the parts.  It's kind of like how people played arcade machine games once upon a time.  Old levels are fun to repeat before you beat the whole game in order to get the best possible hang of it in order to move on with as much health or items as possible, but once you do, you're left wondering, "Why bother?" again.  Ultimately, guild halls take millions of crowns to build, but eventually, they just sit there for no reason.  There's a story in their construction, but everyone wants to write their own story and they want administrative control, so you can't even sell guild halls to other players.  Many if not most quality players go to make their own guild halls as well.  You might recruit them over the short-term, but eventually, they get bored and go away unless you make close friends with them.  This is despite how guilds can have 100s of members.  Does anyone have 100s of close friends when they play online games?  100s of acquiantances maybe, but not friends, and certainly not close friends.
Items play weirdly as well.  This really is an arcade game, not an MMO, since you pick up items in the middle of levels.  You can buy them from the merchant right before you start, but you can't store them in your general arsenal nor call on them at your will.  Equipment types are very unbalanced as well.  There's piercing, shadow, and elemental, but you really don't need piercing that often since beasts are a piece of cake and fiends are very rare (albeit very annoying, but normal and elemental damage are effective enough).  Shadow is a little more helpful... if you enjoy grinding Jelly King for cash and elite orbs or you encounter levels with tons of gremlins.  Elemental is the best though since it helps against undead which are hands down the most difficult enemies. The game strangely still lets you use similar elements without resistance penalty though.  You can use a fire weapon against fire skeletons, an ice weapon against ice skeletons, an electric weapon against electric skellies, or a poison weapon against poison skellies without penalty.  The same doesn't apply for vials though.  Throwing a fire vial against a fire skelly will do nearly nothing.
Graphics also tend to overload from particle effects, especially fire.  The final rank mission doesn't suffer from this, but Danger Missions and Shadow Lairs do.  Your game will probably crash as well, but if you want, you can relog into the game, and it will pick up where you left instead of kicking you from the party.  Speaking of kicking, if you kick someone from a party who you don't want, then the party locks up and you have to rehost the party just to get those you do... which is a pain if you're open to randoms in a public arcade run since it means restarting the run.  On the plus side, having less people reduces the health of monsters.  Sometimes, quantity isn't quality.  Heck, sometimes, it's actually easier to beat levels solo than in a party.  The game really does encourage teamwork, but friends are a must.  Many if not most people don't grasp teamwork at all.  It's more of a mercenary fight where everyone does their individual thing as a bunch of armies of one.  Most people play as swordmasters and just slash over and over in incompatible directions.  Some people are gunslingers, but they're very underpowered.  Shieldbearing is nice if you enjoy taunting for unappreciative teammates... unless they're your friends!  Bombing has it's moments against massive amounts of small enemies, or for status effects in specialty situations, but it's not used all the time.
That said, you can carry multiple weapon types, and buying additional weapon slots isn't terribly expensive (since it's only 200 energy for 30 days, so it's definitely worth it).
The game has potential, but it's yet to be actualized.  Short-term gameplay is fun as long as you don't reach the point where you realize the lack of actualization.  Also, one phrase of advice - if you buy sparks of life for reviving and someone in your party needs to be revived, ask for 1,500 crowns before reviving.  Sparks aren't cheap, nor is it helpful for someone to stay down and out.  It's a win-win.

TL;DR: Excellent atmosphere, feel, mechanics, story, world, and overall experience. Brilliant DLC (for the most part). Sub-optimal under the hood porting and optimization. Do yourself a favor and check this one out.
God, this game is good. My only previous experience with Bethesda has been Skyrim, so maybe I haven't seen enough to make a fair comparison.
But I digress. In a world full of barely good games with good ideas, F4 is a masterwork of mechanics, combat, soundtrack, acting, atmosphere, worldbuilding, and good old-fashioned full as hell to play. Seriously, the folks at Bethesda really went all out, with every single building in 2184's Boston oozing with lore, sideplot, and oftentimes downright creepy atmosphere. I found myself wandering the wasteland just after finishing the main story (~50 hours in) and just before buying the DLC (also amazing), and just exploring and uncovering a new subterranian ruin or a bunker with a sole skeleton or a new version of an old enemy sunk a dozen or so hours.  The enemies are challenging, varied, and oh-so-satisfying to wipe out, yet you get a sense that their actions are justified. Every faction in this game (of which there are many) have varied questlines and motivations, making the final decision of who to side with all that much more difficult. Seriously, the nuance when it comes to character philosophy is staggering.
If I had to pick cons of this game, it's that I felt like I finished all of the quests all at once and had a hard time finding more. Granted, it took me scores of hours to complete all of them, but it feels bad to be so invested in a game and not having any more goals other than your own drive to explore (which is substantial).
Backing away from the game itself, the port of the game could be better. I had to hard shutoff the game more than a couple times to get out of a bugged loading screen, and even when unbugged the load times are often ridiculous. I found that some of the controls were a little funky, especially in the Workshop mechanic. The CPU load on this game is immense, as well.
All in all, buy this. I would have paid full price if I had to. Pick up Far Harbor and Automatron too, if they're on sale. This game is everything I want in an open-world atmospheric sandbox, and I can't wait to see what's next for the universe.

XCOM 2 improves on almost everything from XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but it still has some glaring issues:
-Massive performance issues, as well as crashing. Hell, even the cutscenes stutter and distort! These issues are even more prevalant in alternative Operating Systems, such as Linux.
-Massive Diffculty Cliff early on. This is the same issue XCOM: Enemy Unknown had, but XCOM 2 just makes it worse. Sectoids are too OP, same for Facless, Stun Lancers appear too frequently, not enough resources early on to get you going, and a bunch of other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
-Timed Missions are too frequent and the timer is too short. It doesn't really encourage strategy, it just encourages you to rush the entire thing, ignoring any loot drops and potential ambush set-up points.
-Stiff Animations
-Units shoot through walls and floors too often
-Unintuitive UI
♥♥♥♥♥♥Tutorial, it doesn't really go into detail on some of the games core mechanics, such as Intel and Supplies, it's also very hand-holdy.
-No SHIVs as far as I can tell
It's a good game overall, but I believe these issues will stop most people from enjoying it. So I sadly cannot reccomend this game to anyone right now, except the most hardcore XCOM: Enemy Unknown fans. I say wait a few months for a few patches and mods to fix some of the issues, before you consider buying it.

Fallout 4 is a disgrace to the franchise.
This game is essentially an open world action FPS with a few sandbox elements, I'd compare it more to the recent FarCry games than any Fallout game (though the FarCry games do what it does better for the most part). This game touts improved gunplay, more detailed weapon/armor customization, and some additional sandbox elements over previous Fallout titles. However it sacrifices almost all semblance of RPG elements primarily by simplifying the dialogue system, forcing a terrible/boring personality and backstory onto the player, and removing the stat system, amongst other smaller changes.
With this Fallout 4 also removed practically all choices and decision making from the player, your dialogue gives you the illusion of choice, but in reality nothing you say or do in this game ever matters or has any consequence whatsoever, something that even Fallout 3 did better, and the classic Fallouts/New Vegas did a million times better. The quests are repetitive and uninteresting, the story is stupid and predictable, not to mention the terrible optimization (and I mean TERRIBLE) and sub-par graphics. Also the boring and lifeless world, terrible factions with terrible writing, and just really awful characters all around.
The game is an ocean with the depth of a puddle. It's shallow, boring, repetitive, and doesn't deserve to be called a Fallout game. Also don't let my play time fool you, I spent probably a good 30+ hours of that play time trying to fix bugs and crashes, improve performance, and basically do all the♥♥♥♥♥♥Bethesda should have done before releasing this steaming pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥
There are existing mods and mods in the works that improves the game in almost every aspect, from changing the awful story, to reintoducing many of the RPG elements, and much more. Having said all that, if you are someone who doesn't really care about the shallow gameplay and bugs/performance issues, and just want an open world shoot n' loot game, then sure, pick it up on sale you'll probably enjoy it, but for those of us who want a real Fallout experience...
