Looking at the gameplay a lot of it will seem familiar to XCOM players, especially if you’ve played XCOM Enemy Within. The interface is nearly the same and so are the mission styles and there is so much new stuff added on top of the old. As always you have a squad of soldiers ranging from 4-6 people to clear every mission.
Every soldier will have one of 4 classes that then goes into another 2 types of subclasses, so even though that sounds very limited compared to The Long War mod it still provides for a lot of unique and great combos.
XCOM 2 brings a lot of uniqueness to the things it had already in the previous game and therefore keeps it fresh and new enough for it to be a sequel instead of a huge upgrade/expansion of Enemy Within.
XCOM 2 picks up the story 20 years after the events in Enemy Within. The guys from the former game have been busy trying to rebuild the XCOM project and rebuilding the base. So here you are in the middle of a world where aliens are the masters and humans are the slaves marked as renegades, fighting in the shadows to save the world from the aliens’ newest project codenamed Avatar.
You’ve recovered an alien ship that you are using as a mobile base of operations, unlike Enemy Within, and you are flying around the entire world map gathering supplies, building contacts, gathering intel and much more. As the game goes on you can expand the ship with more rooms in the same way you could in the old XCOM base from previous games. You can also build and discover unique things across the world map that can make fighting the aliens a lot easier.
You will need to build contacts with the resistance in every country to expand your operational area and to receive more supplies to rebuild your army. This creates a great way of dealing with research, upgrades, buildings and much more in a great flow that can be boosted by completing unique missions and picking up loot drops on missions that can now FINALLY be performed by your soldiers without them having to spend a year researching it.
To explain that statement a bit, when you kill an enemy you have a chance that they will drop a loot item that can be anything from a weapon upgrade to PSI implants that will be usable if you collect them during the mission and then complete the mission. Weapon and PSI implants aren’t the only upgrades to be found. There are also ammo upgrades, grenade upgrades, soldier upgrades, armor upgrades and more. The combination of the level of customization available for each character and the number of possible upgrades makes for a level of overall customizability that rivals that of the Sims Universe. (You can’t dress up as Batman yet though, but give it time. Somebody will make a mod for that.)
Recruitment in XCOM 2 is different from Enemy Within. In Enemy Within you just recived a group of random recruits and and were cut loose. In XCOM 2 you can pick your own recruits to start with from a long roster and then when you’re unlocked a certain room (trying hard to avoid spoilers) you can train them into certain classes to avoid the dreaded rookie stage. While this is a relatively minor change, it really makes your recruits and soldiers feel very much like your own people.
As if all this wasn’t enough, Firaxis has brought out some truly scary aliens to woop our asses this time around. Everything from small creepy things to insanely huge monstrosities that make you wanna run home and cry. You get a great feeling for the difference between every alien and you will be able to tell them apart easily to know which you can shoot at and which you should just blow up with the biggest weapon you have.
All in all a great experience that will make you scream, cry and laugh as you slaughter your way through aliens to save the planet.

Looking at the gameplay a lot of it will seem familiar to XCOM players, especially if you’ve played XCOM Enemy Within. The interface is nearly the same and so are the mission styles and there is so much new stuff added on top of the old. As always you have a squad of soldiers ranging from 4-6 people to clear every mission.
Every soldier will have one of 4 classes that then goes into another 2 types of subclasses, so even though that sounds very limited compared to The Long War mod it still provides for a lot of unique and great combos.
XCOM 2 brings a lot of uniqueness to the things it had already in the previous game and therefore keeps it fresh and new enough for it to be a sequel instead of a huge upgrade/expansion of Enemy Within.
XCOM 2 picks up the story 20 years after the events in Enemy Within. The guys from the former game have been busy trying to rebuild the XCOM project and rebuilding the base. So here you are in the middle of a world where aliens are the masters and humans are the slaves marked as renegades, fighting in the shadows to save the world from the aliens’ newest project codenamed Avatar.
You’ve recovered an alien ship that you are using as a mobile base of operations, unlike Enemy Within, and you are flying around the entire world map gathering supplies, building contacts, gathering intel and much more. As the game goes on you can expand the ship with more rooms in the same way you could in the old XCOM base from previous games. You can also build and discover unique things across the world map that can make fighting the aliens a lot easier.
You will need to build contacts with the resistance in every country to expand your operational area and to receive more supplies to rebuild your army. This creates a great way of dealing with research, upgrades, buildings and much more in a great flow that can be boosted by completing unique missions and picking up loot drops on missions that can now FINALLY be performed by your soldiers without them having to spend a year researching it.
To explain that statement a bit, when you kill an enemy you have a chance that they will drop a loot item that can be anything from a weapon upgrade to PSI implants that will be usable if you collect them during the mission and then complete the mission. Weapon and PSI implants aren’t the only upgrades to be found. There are also ammo upgrades, grenade upgrades, soldier upgrades, armor upgrades and more. The combination of the level of customization available for each character and the number of possible upgrades makes for a level of overall customizability that rivals that of the Sims Universe. (You can’t dress up as Batman yet though, but give it time. Somebody will make a mod for that.)
Recruitment in XCOM 2 is different from Enemy Within. In Enemy Within you just recived a group of random recruits and and were cut loose. In XCOM 2 you can pick your own recruits to start with from a long roster and then when you’re unlocked a certain room (trying hard to avoid spoilers) you can train them into certain classes to avoid the dreaded rookie stage. While this is a relatively minor change, it really makes your recruits and soldiers feel very much like your own people.
As if all this wasn’t enough, Firaxis has brought out some truly scary aliens to woop our asses this time around. Everything from small creepy things to insanely huge monstrosities that make you wanna run home and cry. You get a great feeling for the difference between every alien and you will be able to tell them apart easily to know which you can shoot at and which you should just blow up with the biggest weapon you have.
All in all a great experience that will make you scream, cry and laugh as you slaughter your way through aliens to save the planet.

This game easily gets my recommendation.
Rogue likes can be unfair at times. Often times, the more ignorant you are as a player, the more you will fail before you will begin to succeed. In order to succeed, you'll need to learn mechanics that often are vague until after you've died a few times or unless you've spoiled yourself on the wiki. However, once you overcome those challenges, there's no better feeling of reward than the one you get knowing that you figured it out. In a rogue like, that's nervana.
Darkest Dungeon rely's heavily on squad management, both in and out of combat. Eventually, you'll expand your town and have a small horde of mercenaries that you can send out on adventures. Every jaunt out requires you to take 4 party members with you, and you'll want to make sure they're as fresh as can be and fully prepared. If your party has too much "stress", or not enough torches, you can easily lead your party members to their death. And death for any party member is perminant.
But the mechanics are fun and the abilities for every unique hero are pretty interesting. Regarding the death of a party member, before they actually die they suffer death throws. Any healing will sustain them and essentially give them a free pass (one more hit until they are sent back into their death throws). However, if a character is attacked while under this condition, their is a chance that they will die. Thus, death isn't always assured, but the threat of it is always looming.
Another interesting mechanic is what happens to party members when their stress is maxed out. In such an event, a character gain an affliction that is often severe, but sometimes they face their fears and rise to the occasion. Either way, it always feels pretty momentous to the outcome of the adventure, and it's a super fun mechanic that can really develope a character. Of course, that always raises the stakes when it comes to sending your favorite character out into the field.
All in all, this game has the depth, the art style, and the atmosphere that makes for a fun game. I recommend it, though I wouldn't say it's for everyone. It's a game I can only play in short bursts, but if your stress tolerance is higher than mine you might make it before the madness sets in. Although, sooner or later, madness will claim us all...
Enjoy!

TL;DR: Excellent atmosphere, feel, mechanics, story, world, and overall experience. Brilliant DLC (for the most part). Sub-optimal under the hood porting and optimization. Do yourself a favor and check this one out.
God, this game is good. My only previous experience with Bethesda has been Skyrim, so maybe I haven't seen enough to make a fair comparison.
But I digress. In a world full of barely good games with good ideas, F4 is a masterwork of mechanics, combat, soundtrack, acting, atmosphere, worldbuilding, and good old-fashioned full as hell to play. Seriously, the folks at Bethesda really went all out, with every single building in 2184's Boston oozing with lore, sideplot, and oftentimes downright creepy atmosphere. I found myself wandering the wasteland just after finishing the main story (~50 hours in) and just before buying the DLC (also amazing), and just exploring and uncovering a new subterranian ruin or a bunker with a sole skeleton or a new version of an old enemy sunk a dozen or so hours.  The enemies are challenging, varied, and oh-so-satisfying to wipe out, yet you get a sense that their actions are justified. Every faction in this game (of which there are many) have varied questlines and motivations, making the final decision of who to side with all that much more difficult. Seriously, the nuance when it comes to character philosophy is staggering.
If I had to pick cons of this game, it's that I felt like I finished all of the quests all at once and had a hard time finding more. Granted, it took me scores of hours to complete all of them, but it feels bad to be so invested in a game and not having any more goals other than your own drive to explore (which is substantial).
Backing away from the game itself, the port of the game could be better. I had to hard shutoff the game more than a couple times to get out of a bugged loading screen, and even when unbugged the load times are often ridiculous. I found that some of the controls were a little funky, especially in the Workshop mechanic. The CPU load on this game is immense, as well.
All in all, buy this. I would have paid full price if I had to. Pick up Far Harbor and Automatron too, if they're on sale. This game is everything I want in an open-world atmospheric sandbox, and I can't wait to see what's next for the universe.
Also eff the Brotherhood.

Fallout 4 is a disgrace to the franchise.
This game is essentially an open world action FPS with a few sandbox elements, I'd compare it more to the recent FarCry games than any Fallout game (though the FarCry games do what it does better for the most part). This game touts improved gunplay, more detailed weapon/armor customization, and some additional sandbox elements over previous Fallout titles. However it sacrifices almost all semblance of RPG elements primarily by simplifying the dialogue system, forcing a terrible/boring personality and backstory onto the player, and removing the stat system, amongst other smaller changes.
With this Fallout 4 also removed practically all choices and decision making from the player, your dialogue gives you the illusion of choice, but in reality nothing you say or do in this game ever matters or has any consequence whatsoever, something that even Fallout 3 did better, and the classic Fallouts/New Vegas did a million times better. The quests are repetitive and uninteresting, the story is stupid and predictable, not to mention the terrible optimization (and I mean TERRIBLE) and sub-par graphics. Also the boring and lifeless world, terrible factions with terrible writing, and just really awful characters all around.
The game is an ocean with the depth of a puddle. It's shallow, boring, repetitive, and doesn't deserve to be called a Fallout game. Also don't let my play time fool you, I spent probably a good 30+ hours of that play time trying to fix bugs and crashes, improve performance, and basically do all the♥♥♥♥♥♥Bethesda should have done before releasing this steaming pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥
There are existing mods and mods in the works that improves the game in almost every aspect, from changing the awful story, to reintoducing many of the RPG elements, and much more. When these mods are finished and more fleshed out I can see myself coming back to this game, but as it stands I regret every cent of my money and every second of my time I spent on this game.
Having said all that, if you are someone who doesn't really care about the shallow gameplay and bugs/performance issues, and just want an open world shoot n' loot game, then sure, pick it up on sale you'll probably enjoy it, but for those of us who want a real Fallout experience... This is NOT where you will find it.
Also paid mods... What in the actual ♥♥♥♥ Bethesda...

I say, there is no definitive storyline for Fallout 4.
Every single faction is replacable, with the same type of ending that you would expect from Mass Effect 3.
The only things that change are which buildings you get to go into, which replacable face you see, and how unimmersive things become. The fact that you can't join the Institute until you're nearly 1/3rd done with the game, betraying any previous ties to a faction you needed to join in order to infiltrate the Institute is again, like Mass Effect 3, with the option to join up with Cerberus.
At some point, you'd need to ask why? Why am I doing this again?
And then with the addition of Nuka-World, they unleashed plenty of potential for a completely game-changing story line, one where you feel as if you're coming out on top, only, you're not.
My biggest discrepancy with Nuka-World, is that even though you get to be buddy buddy with all the raider gangs, you never have the respect of the bosses.
It comes down to the Nuka-Blaster, the squirt gun. By accepting Gage's help, you're already submitting to their grand plan. It's the entire reason why Bethesda followed that same line of thinking to the point where a raider gang turns on you because you're not putting all your attention and focus into building up their gang, giving them land and territories.
Nut's to that. I wish you could actually become a real overboss of Nuka-World, get some mo'fo respect around here, and then go lay waste to the Institute with some ironic justice. They leave so much for want at the end of the Nuka-World DLC.
The Operators building up the World of Refreshment? The bottling plant? HELLO! That's a whole new storyline about them trying to run and distribute WATER across a wasteland! And turning a profit too!
They could've had hours of dialogue about how the gangs don't even realize how much of a money maker the world of refreshment could be, or how the sprinklers around Kiddie Kingdom would make an amzing hydroponic system for growing crops so that the raiders of Nuka-World wouldn't even need to raid for food and supplies.
If the Sole Survivor is a loving parent, Nuka-World laughs in the face of that and makes them their bottom B.
The SS could've played everyone as a fool, and worked towards a grand goal of rehabilitating the raiders and turning them into a unified army under the Nuka-World flag.
Each raider boss is more or less driven by money, caps. You could've said "Alright," and proceeded to dump millions of caps in their face if they went along the route of distributing water and beverages across the wasteland, securing trade routes and distribution channels. Like an actual successful company, rather than buying into the current philosophy of Nuka-World.
But no. At the end, you have one dead raider boss, and two who are looking to replace you at first sign of trouble.
WHERE'S THE FEAR? WHERE'S the option to "RULE WITH AN IRON FIST?"
Jeezus, Beth, learn how to freiking improvise, these stories practically write themselves, but you're like a business meeting set for tomorrow at lunchtime.
Let me elaborate, a business meeting that doesn't accomplish everything they wanted to do, puts it off until tomorrow, usually at or before lunch, so people can reconvein and talk some more, wasting people's time who go to these meetings, while others are there to waste time so they don't have to work for an hour or two. They also have the option to eat lunch at these meetings, at which point they call it a day when the food actually arrives.
How is that like Fallout 4?
The bosses of Nuka-World are in a constant business meeting, where every time you try to advance the plot, (by doing work) they send you out to go grab lunch for the rest of the team while they brainstorm ideas to get more caps, resources, or slaves. While as you, the Sole Survivor can offer the type of insight that would only be available to someone who lived two hundred ten years ago, all that is thrown out the window. They don't even have a good reason as to why you would ever go to Nuka-World in the first place!
"Hurrh, I heard it on the radio Hurr." BS. Try this plot idea on for size, you meet an escaped slave randomly in the Commonwealth with a hot iron brand claiming they're property of Nuka-World, and he gives you the low-down on how they're all this firepower is about to explode in everyone's faces.
While as you, the ever loving parent, try to Abraham Lincoln your way into position of releasing all the slaves, while coming up with a way to compensate everyone for the manpower and money needed.
Bethesda could've come up with an entire economy where you aren't just making a few hundred caps every time you collar a slave, kill a Gunner, or wipe out a synth.

but no, I need to scroll through the builing crafting workshop to find a radio tower, and then build a generator, and then a speaker, and some drug dispensers and get other settlements to pitch in because they "Don't feel like gardening."
Again, BS. the Sole Survivor is a (male, soldier. Female, Lawyer[?]) So either they're smart, and know how a military force should come together and work, or at least draft some laws to put into place to keep Nuka-World from falling apart at the seams with a Nuka-World police force or something to keep the gangs in check, rather than having three gangs running around pulling petty pranks on each other.
Heck! Putting together a private guard would be the second thing I would've done after becoming Overboss of Nuka-World. Ceasar had his Praetorians, Kimball had some rangers, House had his robots, even Benny had four dudes following him around.  Colnel August had the Enclave, and athousand soldiers to back him up.
Yah get one dude. Porter. And he ain't even committed to you! What kind of guard detail is that? What kind of advisor is he?!
But as Overboss of Nuka-World, if you objectively look at your position, you're a bit more well off than a slave, seen as a low life raider, and have no respect from your peers.
You're the middle man. The working class.
This theme is constant with every faction, save the Railroad. At least with that faction, you aren't pinned as the leader, and you know your place as an operative.
Otherwise, with the Brotherhood, you feel like you can always be doing more, and whatever you accomplish, everyone kinda looks at you and says "Meh, I could'a done it way better, in a way shorter time frame, here's some more work that I've put off for an indignant amount of time, and never got around to on my own."
Again with the Insititute, No respect. The only option you get to make is more synths or better weapons for synths. WTF?
Where's the option to actually use the technology for good? Or for extreme evil?
The Minutemen, that's a joke. Really. It's like the worst written piece of garbage that one of your main companions, if you choose, is the least understanding or acknowleding of your plight as a sole survivor, despite himself being the last Minuteman. His optimism is beyond 'everything's going to be okay' and at no point does it break, not even for one humanizing moment.
Literally, from the moment you meet Preston, is the moment he thinks they are going to shoot right back up on top of the food chain, being top dog of the Commonwealth, even after the Minutemen collapsed from within.
Does no one at Bethesda know what happens to a company that fails from within?
What movie was it...Capt.America: CW...where the bad guy says "if it is attacked from the outside, it can be rebuilt. But if it crumbles from the inside, no one wants to even associate themselves with it?
Something along those lines. Either way. There's literally no reason why you would want to even join three of the factions, as a loving parent, while as Nuka-World should've been a better fleshed out faction on their own.

The game is a lot of fun so far; however it needs fine tuning and optimization. Turn limits aren't awful but should all be extended about 2 - 3 turns - it's not so much that they break the game as the very short limits stop you from experimenting with tactics and play styles. It's MOVE MOVE MOVE GO GO GO because you've got a time limit (or you have to help unreasonably stupid humans survive - they seem to be able to run and hide from me, but have trouble running and hiding when I'm trying to keep them safe/supposed to save a certain number.) So yeah this needs play balancing and like 2 performance patches and that needs to be said up front.
That being said, the game is really fun when it works - in many/most ways improved or an equally good but different experience over the original, so far. Story is interesting, missions are mostly pretty fun, the new enemies are punishing, and the settings are pretty cool. Character customization is interesting and varied, both asthetically and choosing their abilities. Stealth allows some really cinematic ambushes.
When this game works it's amazingly fun, so I hope the devs are patching it up/finding some sort of compromise on the timer because I'd play this, and mods using this general system, for quite some time.
That's all I've done so far so that's all I can speak on, but it's an enthusiastic thumbs up, with a qualifier that I'm assuming the devs will take some serious runs at the optimization, enemy AI, Civillian AI when you're protecting them, and extending the clock (or eliminating it all together, but I don't think it's terrible I just think they need to loosen the belt a few notches to allow a few tactics other than forward blitz.)
(Update: Trying game with a Mod that minimizes the number of missions with timers. Much improved.)

In these types of games, you spawn in basically in a random spot, run around, hope to find weapons and food, etc., and zombies come after you. The houses don't have much detail put into them, nor do the other locations. Everything feels sort of like it was just stuck there to fill in a void; not because of any artistic vision or clever design. Weapons are unrealistically placed in odd areas in homes and businesses, the layout of areas that are lived in doesn't feel very genuine, you starve and dehydrate quickly, and you drop your stuff when you die, making progression a moot point.
Keep in mind, I said "these kinds of games." I just described a ton of games on Steam, without specifying anything about Unturned, because they're all practically the same game. Someone might try to argue the same about other genres, but this "flavor" of the survival genre is so overdone and stale that not many other genres can compare. After having played Unturned, it's like all the rest of them. Some people can't get enough of this sort of game. If you hate this flavor of the genre, you will hate this game, as it does nothing to set itself apart from the rest of those games. I would like to find one that I find to be good, but nothing whatsoever appeals to me in the genre.
I would compliment Unturned for its kinda-cute look, but literally dozens of other games (some of them one game under different names, even) are copying this look...or Unturned copied it? I'm not concerned with where it originated, but it's everywhere, and I no longer consider the art style as an asset.
I want to say this game was free, but I didn't have any fun at any point while playing, and my time was far better spent doing almost anything other than playing this game, so I cannot recomment playing this game or any of its ilk unless you haven't tried any of them before, or love that part of the genre.

The game is largely about managing stress in your adventurers. How to calm their nerves is your choice. The hamlet proves plenty of options for this and abandoning adventures is common to create room for better and more able bodies to fill out teams.
Highly recommend, glad to see this game reach full release.

I love this game but it is not for the faint of heart. Your characters will die. You will, and probably should, run from some battles and abandon some missions if your characters are in bad enough shape. It does not hold your hand, and for most of the game it will instead just stab it repeatedly for no reason but to drill into your head that these dungeons are messed up places to be wandering around. Yes, the game seems unfair at times but it really isn’t. You should be prepared for some of the messed up stuff that happens.
If you get stressed out easily, don’t play this game. If you are expecting that you’ll be able to grind your way to the top and make a fun easy time of everything, this isn’t the game for you. If you rage quit frequently at other video games, throwing controllers or mice across the room because that boss is a cheap little ****er, this isn’t the game for you.
If you want a challenging, Lovecraft inspired, rougelike, turn-based RPG with some pretty solid strategy, this is the game for you. If you want a game that tugs at your nerves as you watch one of your favorite characters, already at Death’s Door, dodge a surely fatal attack, this is the game for you. You will become attached to your characters because you will go through hell with them. You will be saddened when you watch them killed off so quickly in front of you. You will have stories to tell after playing this game. It’s great.

On one of the first bosses, I had a solid team go in to take it down only to find out that this boss’s mechanic allowed it to possess one of my characters and use him/her against me. After that I gave up on running away deciding that my party was doomed. But at the last minute a single crit from my Crusader killed that ******* and I won. I lost half my party but I won. I still don’t look at my Lepar the same way anymore though… It’s the♥♥♥♥♥♥like this that’s just entertaining. I’ve played less than 20 hours though so could change later on who knows.

In these types of games, you spawn in basically in a random spot, run around, hope to find weapons and food, etc., and zombies come after you. The houses don't have much detail put into them, nor do the other locations. Everything feels sort of like it was just stuck there to fill in a void; not because of any artistic vision or clever design. Weapons are unrealistically placed in odd areas in homes and businesses, the layout of areas that are lived in doesn't feel very genuine, you starve and dehydrate quickly, and you drop your stuff when you die, making progression a moot point.
Keep in mind, I said "these kinds of games." I just described a ton of games on Steam, without specifying anything about Unturned, because they're all practically the same game. Someone might try to argue the same about other genres, but this "flavor" of the survival genre is so overdone and stale that not many other genres can compare. After having played Unturned, it's like all the rest of them. Some people can't get enough of this sort of game. If you hate this flavor of the genre, you will hate this game, as it does nothing to set itself apart from the rest of those games. I would like to find one that I find to be good, but nothing whatsoever appeals to me in the genre.
I would compliment Unturned for its kinda-cute look, but literally dozens of other games (some of them one game under different names, even) are copying this look...or Unturned copied it? I'm not concerned with where it originated, but it's everywhere, and I no longer consider the art style as an asset.
I want to say this game was free, but I didn't have any fun at any point while playing, and my time was far better spent doing almost anything other than playing this game, so I cannot recomment playing this game or any of its ilk unless you haven't tried any of them before, or love that part of the genre.

Darkest Dungeon is a grim, brutal dungeon crawler that will challenge you repeatedly and brutally punish you for the slightest missteps. This harsh difficulty means youll have immense satisfaction for the smallest of victories. However, the primary selling point for me was it's Mignola-esque artsyle and narration, both of which are superb and elevate the title above the crowd of dungeon crawlers and rogue-likes. Negatives would include that the game is best played in short sittings, as the gameplay is not too varied from the basic dungeon crawling formula. Due to the game's powerful anti-stalling mechanic and debilitations, combat favors finishing off opponents quickly, which is a shame as the positioning and Damage over Time mechanics would otherwise allow for a great number of tactical options.
Overall, Darkest Dungeon is an excellent dungeon crawler and a must-have for fans of the genre.

Seriously though, this game is addictingly painful.

Darkest Dungeon is loaded with risk management, and usually every single decision you make has an effect on the outcome of the whole game. The thing that makes it most enjoyable for me, is the sweet feeling of investing strategy and careful preparation, making sure that you are completely prepared for every possible scenario that could happen, and being able to overcome that challenge thanks to your strategizing, and of course, a little bit of luck. Or there's always a possibility that you could spend so much time in thinking it through only to realize that you forgot to bring torches, or maybe you just forgot what game you were playing. Both of which will ultimately lead to your demise.
But in that case, you know what to avoid the next time you try. That is, if you have a sliver of courage left anyway.

I just want to start off by saying that at its core, this game is phenominal. Enemy variety is plentiful and is for the most part really well balanced. The game is a decent looking game too. Sadly, the enemy variety sort of goes out the window late game and the longer you play, the worse performance gets due to a nasty memory leak. The Avenger base isn't anything special. It's just slightly better than it was in EU and not really worth mentioning. Oh, and the sound design, both with the in game voices and sound effects to the phenominal score is nothing short of amazing. I absolutely LOVE this game. XCOM has always been a series that I've LOVED since I was a child. And because of the love that I have for the series, I HATE writing a negative review on this game. You see, aside from the core aspect being amazing, that's really the only positive thing I can say about this game. It's quite clear that this game seriously lacks polish. There's even evidence that the developers actually panic patched the game at the last minute to make it harder. And there lies the problem with XCOM 2. The XCOM games have never been hard, challenging yes, but never hard. This game however is hard for all the wrong reasons. From spawning 2 Archons and 2 Advent elite troopers at the LZ of a timed mission (and then landing another 3 troopers ON the LZ making it 7 foes to face) to having your troopers caught during the "concealment" phase without so much as a warning to let the players know that said troopers can actually see behind the 2 buildings you're at. The game honestly feels completely botched. I NEVER felt screwed over when I played the older XCOM games or Enemy Unknown/ WIthin. I've always played on the harder difficulties to make it more challenging. The AI has ALWAYS cheated in the older games (it's a fact), but NEVER as blatantly as they do in this game. This game has absolutely no sense of balance nor fairness. And the game completely contradicts itself too. It wants you to sneak around and set up well planned out ambushes. Well, that takes a lot of time to pull off and 90% of the time you're expected to use these ambush tactics, there's a timer where you have 8 turns to hack into an item across the map or you lose meaning that instead of doing what the game was designed to do (at least in the early stages of the level), you have to dash towards the objective. It makes no logical sense. Not to mention that flanking offers the player no reward aside from higher chances to land a critical hit on an enemy and the high grounds offer no real advantages either (though you still do get a bonus for being up above). A lot of the times the player is actually punished for making tactically sound maneuvers. The aim penalties in this game are beyond insane too! It's tooth shatteringly logic defying when a giant metal floating ball is floating 1 square away and I have a plasma rifle aimed at it with only 50% chance to hit on my colonel ranked support character. I understand that since it's floating, it gets a "flying buff", but when it's no less than ONE SQUARE AWAY, should't I be at 100% to land a hit since it would literally be impossible to miss that shot? I have MUCH more to say about this game, but I fear that, that would require me to write at least 4 pages worth of complaints. And that's not even me talking about the TERRIBLE optimization and performance issues (I have a 980, i5 4670k OC'd, and 16gb of RAM) that this game has nor the countless bugs. Fun fact, the reason that I ran into a terrible (even game breaking) bug that wouldn't allow me to make any actions, but if by God's good grace I managed to pull off an action, the game would just freeze up. And no, not crash, the game would literally just halt at the zoomed in character that is about to make a shot. Background noise and music still playing and soldiers and aliens still doing their idle animations. It was nearly impossible for me to finish the mission I was currently on. I did fix it though. It really saddens me that a PC only release is plagued with such mediocre and amateur mistakes. Especially from a dev team like Firaxis. As the game stands now, I cannot see how ANYONE could give this game 9's and 10's across the board. This game is a 6/10. It's such a shame, because I want to love this game (more than I already do). It sucks to say and even think this, but I can't wait for the patches and modders to fix this game. Once it's fixed, I know that this game could easily be a 9 or a 10.

At last i have closed down the game. I managed to get stuck so after about 14 hours divided into two play sessions i've been able to take a break. I'll be making some points about the positive and negative things i've encountered thus far.
Positive:
- Intense & timecramped missions that make you plan out every single round and a system that really punishes you for not doing so. The satisfaction after barely making it out alive is amazing and it really fits the theme of the game.
- The anthill type basebuilding aswell as the construction and research system is rewarding and satisfying while staying true to the previous XCOM titles.
- The map where you plan all of your operations and setup links between the different parts of the world is greatly worked upon compared to the other titles in the way that it's alot more interactive and brings in a bunch of new, sweet features.
- Great character customization that allows for pimping out your favorite soldiers, some of the options are a little more limited than the others but it's not a big deal. You can also save your characters so that you may encounter identical ones in other playthroughs.
Negative:
- I am playing on medium but the textures are still pretty horrible at times for being a 2016 game, i know strategy games aren't supposed to excel in graphics but it does annoy me at times.
- The camera angels are NOT good. For a game that has so many mini-cutscenes and camera angles all over the place they are incredibly bad at times to the point where the I'm looking at the floor, roof or wherever instead of where the action is going on.
- Optimization is pretty bad at the moment, im getting FPS drops at medium settings from time to time and i feel as if i really shouldn't be getting them at medium settings seeing as i can play etc. The Witcher 3 on high graphics with almost constant 50+ FPS on a GTX 960.
Overall it's still a great game and im sure that most of these issues will be fixed within the first few months and the things that don't get improved upon will certainly be modded in. Also, if you don't enjoy RNG and punishing gameplay then you might want to reconsider purchasing this game.

So far, I've played every Fallout game for at least 100 hours. Some of them for several 100s of hours. This game is good. The combat can be diverse and fun. The world is interesting and beautiful. Some of the characters have relatively interesting development, although the companions will leave you wanting more, as their dialogue options are pretty brief. It uses some interesting Sci-Fi tropes. I noticed some pretty clear parallels to games like SOMA in some places. My biggest takeaway from Fallout 4 will be the environmental story telling through hacked monitors and what remains from the old world. While the core of the main story is a bit derivative of Fallout 3, the overall themes it portrays towards the mid-end story had an impact on me. This is a Fallout story that, from a big picture, stays true to it's introductory fixation on "war never changes." Vague plot structure spoiler-ishness: The plot innevitably ramps up into an explosion filled blood bath, in which you will be faced with having to kill people that you know are good people that may not deserve to die. You are just a soldier in a war, and so are they. I had meaningful conversation with some characters that I grew fond of at beginning and mid game. I carried those with me until the conclusion in which, mid-battle, I finally saw their face again and I realized that I now had to explode their heads like all the supermutants and raiders before them.

This is a great game, however its far from perfect, for starters lets talk classes: many of them are unbalanced and are also poorly made, for example the barbarian is the only class that can heal the party efficiently making him the cleric/healer too, healing is the opposite of what barbarians are supposed to do and other classes are also pooly made, for example the neon ninja is a mediocre ninja at best, with the games utter lack of armor, the only way to stop blows is with your health, and that causes the neon ninja in this game to have an overly large amount of health and his attacks are less than optimal with what damage a ninja should do. another class, the tomb raiser is a necromancer, and for some reason he is the most effective tank and the shadow hunter or ranger does the most damage per shot in the game. secondly lets look at the looting system, your loot is comprised of a hat, a mask, a ring and your weapon, however you start seeing the same loot over and over and the true "common" drop of the game is legendary items, as you have 7 worlds that have this as the common drop and 4 more worlds that have lower degrees of rarity (rare, uncommon, and common). this makes the rare styles actually the more uncommon items, you have to farm in the lower areas for certain styles and stuff like that to make them usable as a skin over your weapon, whereas in the higher up levels, certain weapons cant even be found. thirdly the building system: decent however it gets tedious to create things that are massive and its also tedious to mine and collect the building blocks. and 4th: the dungeon design, it is lacking, alot of it becomes more and more repetetive however they all have different bosses associated with them. but even the bosses get repetetive too. overall i rate this game a 6/10 because it needs more content and the devs need to learn good game design. honestly it should still be in beta however it is still a really fun and addicting game.

Interesting game, challenging, but I could have done without the artificial limits imposed on numerous missions.  Timers in particular add a sense of tension that could have been better handled with other methods.   To be clear, the time on the timers is typically more than sufficient for the task at hand.  The countdown is merely a method of pushing you to be aggressive in the hopes of keeping the game 'fast paced'.  Once you realize that most early missions are easily completed in 5-8 turns having a timer of 12 is just irrelevent.  Have to say that aside from the timers the missions are a pretty nice spread.
The ambush system is nice when they let you use it, with enemy troopers walking patrol routes waiting to be hit.  Some missions are throwbacks to the first game (I'm looking at you retaliation missions) where you wade in guns blazing and the enemy gets free movement into cover.
The game still relies rather heavily on RNG until you can develop your troopers enough to be reliable.  That the game manages to entertain in spite of this is rather impressive as other games that rely so heavily on RNG tend to be awkward and painful affairs.  In the end it is an enjoyable improvement over XCOM with all the good, and bad, that brings with it.

My impressions off the bat were that it looked interesting, but had a long queue time to play. I suppose I'll write my review starting with the positives to the game:
I definitely feel free, like I'm in a sandbox environment. I can destroy most blocks outside of the hub, and the ones that I can't, I can with bombs which are cheap to make, and I end up making them hundreds at a time just for the convenience. The combat it smooth, and though it's hard to react to enemy attacks, it's engaging enough to keep me entertained for a while. There are lots of different areas to explore, and you have a 100% customizable base you can move around the world as you travel. The methods of travel in themselves are varied and extremely fun, and I never feel constrained. Do you like to double jump? Well as you gear up, that double jump quickly upgrades to 10 jumps, then 20, and with the right set-up you can jump so long and so high that you may as well be flying.
One big thumbs up from me is the fact that the game is free to play, and I don't feel constantly pressured to pay real life money for any of the items.
Now for the negatives... There are many things for me to take note of, but keep in mind that as many of them as there are,  I personally feel the positives still outweigh them all.
1: Developer incompetence. The game is pretty solid in itself, but the management of it by the current development team seems lackluster. I feel like a team of professional developers made this brilliant game, then quit and were replaced with a team of interns for post-production. The servers are frequently too full, and bugs have been handled terribly so far. There aren't many bugs to note, but until just yesterday there was an exploit in which players could steal other players' items in a trade. How did the developers handle this? By publically announcing that the exploit existed to every player, saying they would fix it soon. Until then, everyone who didn't know about this exploit (which was pretty much everyone, myself included) was now aware they could steal items from other players. I know that quite a few people found it funny that the developers actually informed their players about an exploit they could perform.
This isn't the first time I've seen the developers behave this way. Earlier today, the game was down for maintenance for a long time. Really soon after the game came back up, a developer came on and announced they messed up and were going to shut the servers down again, to which the players were not very delighted to hear, to say the least. Now here's the thing, at first I thought this wasn't a developer, but a player pretending to be a developer, trolling everyone, because they acted rather unprofessional in how they worded it, and I thought it was fake until the servers suddenly went down for maintenance. I would have exact quotes of the way it was worded, but I thought it was just a troll until it was too late.
2: Multiplayer, you say? I wouldn't have guessed it. Though you certainly see plenty of players around the game, people rarely bother saying a word, and there's only a couple things in the game that require working with other players, and those things don't require any real cooperation or communication. Everyone is so used to avoiding communication, that even if you say something, they're not bothering to read the chat, so they won't know you said anything. There definitely are people that talk and hang out, but it's not the easiest to find them. My most prominant social experience involved me fishing next to a guy, he got♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and ended up DDOSing me. That's not a joke, he LITERALLY DDOSed me. One big issue with the multiplayer aspect is that when you join a world, be it the hub or an adventure world, it's a different one every time, with set people. No new players will end up in your world, and once all those players leave, you're forever alone until you join a new world and get a new set of players. Stay in your world for 30 minutes, and almost all the other players will be gone by then.
3: Combat. Though it's definitely fun and keeps you busy, I don't feel like there's much strategy involved at all. It's pretty much just down to your gear. If you have good gear, you'll kill them, if you don't, then you won't. The difficulty curve shoots up quite a bit after the level 10 world, you'll end up staying in the level 10 world until you've farmed quite a bit of gear to help you survive the next ones.
I understand my negatives were far more detailed than my positives, but the game is definitely worth playing, just don't expect it to be the next big thing, and don't spend any real life money on it.

I believe that the mainstream of XCOM players will believe the game to be a rewarding distraction. I also believe that a smaller cult of XCOM players will worship this game.
In this game, the aliens have conquered Earth, and you (the "Commander") have been rescued from their clutches and a coma that's lasted for 20 years. You have to mobilize a global resistance to the alien dominion before the aliens complete some mystery project that you suspect will end humanity once and for all.
Funnily, there's never a really convincing reason to fear the alien dominion except that they assumed power by force and their regime is quite different than the one managed by humanity. However, life under the aliens is hardly oppressed or strife-ridden. People are disease-free and most of the world are wealthy. You run across some alien activity that your science officer assumes is a precursor to the eradication of humanity. But, you still can't be sure. This makes many of your missions feel like what establishment would call "terrorism." That made the game a bit more interesting than the first one, even though the game never makes the ethical ambiguity of your mission explicit.
Besides that, the story plays out like a bland saturday-morning cartoon. Aliens bad. Humans good. Blow up alien things. Rescue human things.
The gameplay is what makes the experience intellectually satisfying, and it will be why the cult following I mentioned earlier will worship this game.
Strategic depth is insane on both layers--the turn-based mission layer and the planning-oriented overworld layer.
You run two types of missions--side missions and priority missions. You have all the time in the world to accomplish priority missions once you're in them. Wait too long to begin them, however, and the aliens draw closer to completing their presumed world-ending mega project. Side missions are all timed. You have to hack a terminal within 8 turns, or evac a friendly VIP within 12 turns, or kill/capture an enemy VIP within 12 turns, or blow up a device within 8 turns. Each mission, you begin undiscovered by the enemy. You can move about free of engagement until you enter clearly-marked tiles. Then, combat begins and all enemies engage you when they come into view.
The 8-turn missions are where I was excited by the most strategic depth. All squad members can hack a terminal from 1 tile away. However, specialists can hack from within line of sight using their drones. Once you hack the terminal, the timer goes away and you can kill all of the aliens in peace. Therefore, you want to get your specialist in range and hack that thing as fast as possible. Do you stay concealed until she does it? Do you rush through enemies and distract them while she does it?
Blowing up a device works similarly, but grenadiers are your money makers instead of specialists. Devices are always indoors, and grenadiers are capable of turning indoors into outdoors. Find the least-defended side of the building, blow a hole in the wall, and let your squad fire on that device from the outside. It's a lot of fun.
The overworld planning layer is extremely similar to the way it functioned in the XCOM remake. Injured soliders are recovering, you're researching new tech, you're building new weapons, you're training new soldiers, you're recruiting new soldiers, you're making room for new facilities (which gives you resources now rather than costing you resources) and you're selecting new missions. The major differences of the strategic layer of XCOM 2 are that your power creep is much more significant than it was in the remake, but the enemy poses way more substantial challenges than in the remake.
Play this game. If you're in the mainstream, you'll have fun before the next major release. If you're in the cult, you just found your new favorite pasttime.

This game is not a bad game. This game however, is not a very good game. It is a severe step down from any of the previous Fallout games. The story is absolutely awful, the combat is repetitive, and the perk/skill system is absolute garbage.
You may think that the settlement and crafting systems would help, however, they make almost no meaningful difference in gameplay and get extremely boring quickly. No more are the days of fallout where different weapons were fun and useful. Now only single shot weapons are at all worth using because they have the highest DPS and accuracy of anything AND now pretty much every weapon can be crafted into a single shot version. Additionally, the perk system encourages using only one weapon type for the entire game. Weapon perks simply increase the damage done with the specific weapon type. This means that if you suddently decide to use heavy weapons instead of single shot rifles, you'll do hardly any damage with them because you haven't invested the requisite perks.
There are few redeeming qualities about Fallout 4, but they push it from a horrible game to a decent game. While the gun variety is pretty awful, the gunplay is a million times better than Fo3 or F:NV. It feels like a proper FPS and is incredibly well done. Also, the world-building is impecible. There are so many little details in all the locations that tell an amazing story. The world really feels like it was lived in. "Lived" being the operative word. The writing for the characters is awful. There might be 1 or 2 good characters in the whole game. Whatever good was done with the world-building is nearly destroyed with how terrible all the NPCs are.
The thing I hate most about this game is the that they took the RP out of the RPG. You are forced into playing their character. The dialogue options are horrible and consist of "Yes", "Mean Yes", "No (yes)", and "I'll come back later". There is almost no real choice in the game except for in the DLC. In addition, they've taken out almost all the skill checks. It used to be that you'd be able to take different courses of action if you had a high enough SPECIAL stat. In the entire game, I believe there are 2 skill checks which make almost no difference in their respective quests. ALMOST EVERY SINGLE QUEST is *GO TO LOCATION, KILL ENEMIES THROUGH BASIC GUNPLAY, LEAVE* There's not even an opportunity in most quests to make a choice aside from whether you want to kill enemies using your single shot rifle stealthily, or just charge in, also using your single shot rifle.
As much as I do hate on this game, it really isn't a bad game. It's just a horrible FALLOUT game.
TL DR: +++Great World
+Good Gunplay
-Horrible Story
-Extremely Repetitive
-No RP in RPG
Best game if you want a challange.

Interesting game, challenging, but I could have done without the artificial limits imposed on numerous missions.  Timers in particular add a sense of tension that could have been better handled with other methods.   To be clear, the time on the timers is typically more than sufficient for the task at hand.  The countdown is merely a method of pushing you to be aggressive in the hopes of keeping the game 'fast paced'.  Once you realize that most early missions are easily completed in 5-8 turns having a timer of 12 is just irrelevent.  Have to say that aside from the timers the missions are a pretty nice spread.
The ambush system is nice when they let you use it, with enemy troopers walking patrol routes waiting to be hit.  Some missions are throwbacks to the first game (I'm looking at you retaliation missions) where you wade in guns blazing and the enemy gets free movement into cover.
The game still relies rather heavily on RNG until you can develop your troopers enough to be reliable.  That the game manages to entertain in spite of this is rather impressive as other games that rely so heavily on RNG tend to be awkward and painful affairs.  In the end it is an enjoyable improvement over XCOM with all the good, and bad, that brings with it.

I believe that the mainstream of XCOM players will believe the game to be a rewarding distraction. I also believe that a smaller cult of XCOM players will worship this game.
In this game, the aliens have conquered Earth, and you (the "Commander") have been rescued from their clutches and a coma that's lasted for 20 years. You have to mobilize a global resistance to the alien dominion before the aliens complete some mystery project that you suspect will end humanity once and for all.
Funnily, there's never a really convincing reason to fear the alien dominion except that they assumed power by force and their regime is quite different than the one managed by humanity. However, life under the aliens is hardly oppressed or strife-ridden. People are disease-free and most of the world are wealthy. You run across some alien activity that your science officer assumes is a precursor to the eradication of humanity. But, you still can't be sure. This makes many of your missions feel like what establishment would call "terrorism." That made the game a bit more interesting than the first one, even though the game never makes the ethical ambiguity of your mission explicit.
Besides that, the story plays out like a bland saturday-morning cartoon. Aliens bad. Humans good. Blow up alien things. Rescue human things.
The gameplay is what makes the experience intellectually satisfying, and it will be why the cult following I mentioned earlier will worship this game.
Strategic depth is insane on both layers--the turn-based mission layer and the planning-oriented overworld layer.
You run two types of missions--side missions and priority missions. You have all the time in the world to accomplish priority missions once you're in them. Wait too long to begin them, however, and the aliens draw closer to completing their presumed world-ending mega project. Side missions are all timed. You have to hack a terminal within 8 turns, or evac a friendly VIP within 12 turns, or kill/capture an enemy VIP within 12 turns, or blow up a device within 8 turns. Each mission, you begin undiscovered by the enemy. You can move about free of engagement until you enter clearly-marked tiles. Then, combat begins and all enemies engage you when they come into view.
The 8-turn missions are where I was excited by the most strategic depth. All squad members can hack a terminal from 1 tile away. However, specialists can hack from within line of sight using their drones. Once you hack the terminal, the timer goes away and you can kill all of the aliens in peace. Therefore, you want to get your specialist in range and hack that thing as fast as possible. Do you stay concealed until she does it? Do you rush through enemies and distract them while she does it?
Blowing up a device works similarly, but grenadiers are your money makers instead of specialists. Devices are always indoors, and grenadiers are capable of turning indoors into outdoors. Find the least-defended side of the building, blow a hole in the wall, and let your squad fire on that device from the outside. It's a lot of fun.
The overworld planning layer is extremely similar to the way it functioned in the XCOM remake. Injured soliders are recovering, you're researching new tech, you're building new weapons, you're training new soldiers, you're recruiting new soldiers, you're making room for new facilities (which gives you resources now rather than costing you resources) and you're selecting new missions. The major differences of the strategic layer of XCOM 2 are that your power creep is much more significant than it was in the remake, but the enemy poses way more substantial challenges than in the remake.
Play this game. If you're in the mainstream, you'll have fun before the next major release. If you're in the cult, you just found your new favorite pasttime.

It's hard to know where to start with Starbound. Naturally, one would bounce straight to comparing it with Terraria.
As others have jumped from Terraria to Starbound, I have too. I have spent a considerable amount of time on Terraria, both on my own, and with friends.
With Starbound's release, I was skeptical; there have been loads of games as of late that have followed the general idea of Terraria and Minecraft. I was starting get seriously bored of even reading the words "procedurally generated." Starbound changed this.
Starbound is leaps and bounds more entertaining and fulfilling than Terraria. A lot of the time while playing the latter, I felt as though something was missing. Quite a large chunk, in fact. Starbound filled it all, and is only in Beta stage.
The graphics and art style are absolutely beautiful. The animations are brilliant to watch, and never get old. This alone drew me in instantly as it feels so fresh and pleasing to the eye.
The music is so utterly charming, and yet other-worldly. It's not irritating, but peaceful and relaxing; driving and thrilling when combat begins.
The backgrounds, races and lore are just icing on the cake, truly. I love them dearly, and they completely make the game feel entirely different and new in comparison to anything else I've played of the genre.
The controls are smooth and feel perfected; everything feels natural.
I've played hours and hours of it already, and have barely touched the sides; I can't believe this is only the beginning of this gorgeous game, and I can't wait to ride on through with it until it's completed.

First impressions of this game are mixed: it's deeper but cheaper.
The first one, if someone died you 100% knew it was your fault, whereas in this one it's very easy to get angry at the game for ostensibly screwing you over.
Sometimes it's the weird stealth - situations where it's 100% impossible to stay stealth on purpose, and you find this out too late. Only 6 hours in but it appears to be a complete farce, like the "stealth" in Uncharted.
Sometimes its discovering a new game mechanic only when it kills one of your squad mates, like falling through a floor after being shot at once by a mech that you only encountered in the previous turn - and witnessing two full-health squad mates die in one go.
Sometimes it's flat-out OP enemies: aliens with 8 health that can possess your team mates from two floors and two walls away, some that can drag your team mates through walls in similarly impossible situations.
There are some situations that are pure BS and your team-mates die because of scripted events or badly balanced enemies instead of your own poor decisions - is this why Ironman is purposefully disabled for the first game? It all kills the fun a bit, it's nowhere near as tense or exciting because it no longer seems like it's 100% your fault if someone dies.
I'm going to keep playing it because I am personally still enjoying it, but I think the game needs more work and wouldn't actually recommend it until it gets a few patches. The issues are becoming increasingly grating and it's making me want to just give it up and re-install and play Enemy Within until 2 gets fixed.

Long War Update:
Long War adds SO much to the game, and it also makes everything in my original review worse. One would say that it accentuates the original experience, so, if you enjoyed XCOM 2, then you'll have a blast. For me it was a big let down. Not only performance drops to it lowest point ever, but the friggin timers are back.
I assume LW doesn't play nice with the mods I had, so that's another problem I would have to deal with if I felt like playing this game in the future (which I won't).
First Update:
You can now remove explicit timers from the game via mods (doing so won't disable any achievements). Keep in mind, though, that the game was designed around that "mechanic", and there're still plenty of implicit timers around (civilians, objective defense, unlimited spawns, etc). In light of that, and the fact that modders are just kind strangers and not Firaxis, my review remains the same.
Original review:
Here's my -entirely subjective- view of this game as of now. For the record I'll say that I'm a big fan of the old XCOM as well as EU.
**** CONS **** (i'll list them first since this is a negative review)
- Plenty of timers.
If you liked the council missions where you had to deactivate the bomb on a timer, then you'll be fine. However if you're like me and you like to approach things carefully, then those kinds of ops are going to get boring, fast. I get the whole "urgency" thing, but when 4 out of 5 ops end up being timed (either by a turn counter, or a civilian counter, or any other counter for that matter) it becomes somewhat frustrating. It may be ok on the easier dificulties, but the higher you go the more you'll hate them. And that's not even mentioning having to beat the Avatar Project.
Man Firaxis sure love their timers.
- Shorter soldier list, longer recovery time.
Your guys are expendable, especially during your first hours with the game, but combine the fact that the aliens are now more dangerous and resourceful with the fact that soldiers may take several weeks to heal up after they're wounded (provided they don't die) and you'll end up recruiting A LOT of cannon fodder, spending precious resources that you won't be able to dump anywhere else.
- Friendly Fire.
It's always frustrating to see your soldiers shoot themselves when they panic, but now they not only do that, but also blow your entire squad up with their grenades. Combine with the previous points and you'll get how infuriating this can result.
- Unlimited enemy spawns.
During some ops the enemy will reinforce their numbers, as they did in the previous game. Only that now they'll continue to do so every few turns. What's that? You don't want to risk your guys? Tough luck, you'll do that or you'll be royally f***** whithin a couple turns. Combine with the previous points.
- Bad optimization.
The game ran poorly on my (high-end) system. It'll probably be fixed once the drivers get updated and all that jazz. Hope so anyway. This was the first time I had any kind of problem of this type with XCOM.
- Losing stopped being fun.
Because unlike EU or the older titles, this game does not punish your mistakes. It instead pushes you to make them, then punish you for it, which I found to be a little too much, and I was a regular Ironman Imposible player back in EU.
If you're of those who consider timers realistic, think about this, everyone knows that you never EVER dash/move twice on Classic or Impossible, yet the turn limit forces you to do that. How bad is it? Well, aside from the fact that worrying about the timer takes away from enjoying the rest of the game, you'd think you can always dash safely while conclealed... Only to realize then that you triggered 2 unseen groups and a turret and now your Ironman campaign is going down the toilet, fast. Remember how good it felt to carefully coordinate your squad to wipe out that alien pack in a single turn coming out of concealment?
Good, remember it well, because chances are you're not gonna get to that often.
**** PROS ****
- No thin men.
JK, you'll face worse.
- Meaningful choices
The game is full of them, but the ones I liked the most are those related to soldier classes. A lot was done to improve the skills you get to choose when your guys level up, unlike EU where you picked more or less the same every time.
- No satellites.
Building satellites was a chore, but was almost mandatory in the previous game. That is, luckly, a thing of the past.
- Soldier and weapon customization is over 9000.
- Maps are more diverse and feature a lot more detail.
- You get access to a lot of tech very early on (by XCOM standards), likely to balance the increased alien threat.
- The story is a lot more fleshed out than in the previous game.
I have a lot of positive things to say about XCOM 2 regardless of my negative review, and it's certainly worth the price, if you're the kind that enjoys the changes they made to gameplay. I'm not one of those people, and that's why I'm giving this one a thumbs down. Consider it carefully before buying though, or you could end up like me.
*** Closing Statements *** (Spoilers)
So I've finally -almost- finished the game. I've seen everything it has to offer and my feelings are of disappointment more than anything else. The equivalent of the base defense and -especially- the final stand are long ops that end up feeling like a chore. The final mission is pretty similar to the one on EU, perhaps a bit shorter, but pretty much the same. What's unforgivable, at least for me, is the fact that they spiked the difficulty at the end so hard it makes no damn sense.
You can pretty much complete the op breaking face all the way to the last encounter, which throws A LOT of BS your way. So I basically shut down the game and fired up YouTube to see the ending cutscene, because I was not going to do that all over again (You can see how much I cared for the game at this point).
Completing the campaign (or at least 99.9% of it) on Commander Ironman took me a sweet time and was fun at times, but there was a lot of stress and boredom involved as well. There were times when I just wanted to get it over with, and the final op was the last nail on XCOM's coffin for me, I didn't feel any reason to re do everything and try again afterwards, much less jumping on legend, though the game cheats a lot less than it did on Impossible back on EU.
If you made it this far I thank you for your time :)

A great F2P game, the game itself is great, with the storyline being where you can choose to pay attention to it, or just do the missions. The game itself is still in development with multiple updates having changed it from its original self, and I can only say that it's a good thing.
There are 3 ways to fight, bomb, gun, and sword. Each one of these has its own perks. Guns can pack devastating status effects, fire several shots at once, and take enemies out at a distance (though with the way rooms are designed, pure gunning can be hard, but satisfying).
Swords are just that, swords, they are the melee weapon of the game, some are your basic BFS (big fat sword), others are speed slicers, and others are status weapons for specific areas. The only downside to using a sword is that you have to usually be in the thick of the enemies to do the damage needed, and can put you at a disadvantage at times when needing to flip a switch, though the game itself provides jars to throw at the switches usually in case you pure-sword.
Bombs are my personal favorite, while pure bombers are rare, they can be devastating when they are fully upgraded. Bombs come in a few different types, combat controlling, status inflicting, damage dealing, and shard. Combat controlling usually are the gravity bombs, which pull all enemies into the same spot for a bit before exploding, great for rooms with large amounts of monsters. Status inflicting bombs don't do a lot of damage, but the effect they do can greatly ease a fight, especially the frost bomb that freezes ALL enemies in their tracks. Damage bombs are just that, they focus on pure damage, they usually have quite a bit of knockback and are great for packed rooms. Shard bombs are multiple explosion bombs that come in a few different types that I won't go super in depth for. The downside of the bomb is that while other weapons have a basic attack and a charge, bombs only charge, so bombs can take an incredibly long time to charge without any perks, and you are vulnerable while charging.
A great game overall, and its randomized floor system means you hardly ever do the same run twice.

UPDATE 17/09/2016: After playing the game again with some performance patches and all the planned DLCs out, I can say that most performance issues have been solved and the game runs better than ever.
My only gripe is about the DLCs. For the price that is being asked by 2K / Firaxis, the amount of content is certainly not much, especially when compared to what Enemy Within was for the original XCOM: Enemy Unknown game from 2012. Buy the DLCs only if you really, really, **really** want to or when the Deluxe edition of XCOM 2 is on sale. More info about the DLCs in my review for the XCOM 2 Reinforcement Pack.
-----
The king of turn-based strategic-tactical games is back, and it's better than ever!
Imagine everything that makes XCOM Enemy Unknown the great game that it is, and make it even bigger: the strategic portion of the game has grown even more:
1) now you don't have just to expand the Avenger -- your (mobile) base of operations -- but you have to consider a consistent lack of resources, both in terms of materials and manpower, which you mostly recruit through VIP extractions missions around the globe;
2) you have to plan your moves carefully as conducting missions require moving the Avenger. This takes time, and time is most likely the most scarce resource of all, as the aliens now are much more active in trying to hinder XCOM's efforts, through the Avatar Project and the so-called Dark Events -- initiatives that either target XCOM directly, like a direct assault against the Avenger, or power-ups given to the ADVENT coalition troops.
The tactical layer is also expanded and more interesting:
1) the newly introduced concealment mechanic allows for the setup of ambushes;
2) your troops can now be customized down to the tiniest detail, from their own physical appearance to their outfits; base weapons are now also further customizable through mods that you can retrieve through missions. A proper full inventory management isn't present, but this still feels way more satisfying than what XCOM:EU had to offer.
3) ADVENT troops and their alien masters are absolutely terrifying and a challenge to tackle: they are more powerful, more aggressive and more intelligent than ever before. Prepare to defend against constant flankings!
The only thing that prevents XCOM 2 from being perfect is a sub-optimal optimization for certain hardware configurations that will be surely fixed within a reasonable time.
TL;DR: if you loved the previous game or you like tactical games in general, do yourself a favor and get this game!

The time has come for an updated review; after all, I have spent considerable time with the game. I have changed my rating to cautiously positive, mainly because of the superb artwork, atmosphere and voice acting. In this area, I would give the game 10 out of 10 - it's of the finest I have ever seen.
However, I do mind the artificially lengthened gameplay time by extremely cheap means. Each boss in the game has three versions that only have increased stats, and the same is valid for normal enemies, who scale with the level of the dungeons without a single word of explanation. Why is suddenly the very same bandit much stronger? Creating new sets of enemies would at least provide some fresh air to the grind - and the game IS as grindy as they come.
After a while, everything starts to repeat over and over, and the motivation to play on is gone. The game could benefit from an actual story, meaningful characters or some kind of real development which is absent from the game. Late game content seems a tacked-on afterthought.

This game. This game is wonderous. It embraces its Lovecraftian heritage while also being a phenomnally crafted game. The art direction is bleak, yet it has a beauty to it. Yet that same bleakness also leads to some truly demented monster designs, designs that echo the sort of unspeakable horrors that Lovecraft spoke of.
The light and stress mechanics weave together in a truly phenomanal fashion. This game, more then any other RPG I know, makes risks and rewards so damn satisfying. To give one of the best examples in the game, take the Shambler fights. Shamblers are rare, very monsterous enemies that can be summoned at Shambler Alters that you may encounter on your journey. If you place a torch on the Altar, the Shambler will appear. You enter pich-black conditions (monsters hit harder, cause more stress, but also player crits are more common) and your party will always be suprised, which throws the EXTREMLY important party order into a shuffle. These factors, combined with the Shambler's attacks, mean that you can be in a very dangerous position. But the payout for killing a Shambler is well worth the risk, as killing a Shambler gets you an Ancestral Trinket, easily the most powerful trinkets in the game. Thus do risk and reward entertwine to provide riches, or disaster, on every outing into the dungeons.
The enemies are vicous, the dungeons are vast and filled with peril and glory. The bosses bring challenge to those worthy enough to face them, and both legendary glory and unspeakable evil await. So....will you heed the call... of the Darkest Dungeon?

Overall the game is good, i feel like it can be an amazing game after a few patches and the addition of some mods, but as it stands it is just good, i'll list the reasons why below;
- The game feels a lot more linear, and artificial, getting rid of the old globe mechanic was not a good decision, i understand making bases and intercepting UFO's do not fit in Xcom 2 but it could have been adapted to the new needs. The new "zones" feel a bit artificial especially when you have to unlock one to go to another...yeah, its not like i have a flying base that can go anywhere.
- Unecessary amount of timed missions, so far, most of the new difficulty "upgrade" that was claimed by Xcom 2 comes from almost every mission being timed, to a point where it is unreasonable and plain illogical (ie.: I have a certain amount of time to hack a data hub, even if the enemy has no clue i am even there, the time should be triggered by detection.), it makes me think that the aliens are super paranoid with some crazy-timed-self-destructing tech, and not that they conquered earth.
- This next complaint comes straight form the Xcom EU/EW games,...why are the aliens still getting a free turn when they get spotted (or spot someone)? It is just a cheap way to give the AI some help. Thankfully i am sure modders will fix this.
- Rush, this is more on the personal side than on the technical side, the game feels very rushed, timers on missions, cheap plot accelerating mechanics, some illogical progression jumps on the plot (ie.: The aliens do not even know if the new Xcom is a true threath yet risk all the mascarading that took them years to build up, just to go all out guns blazing on 30 something humans with a crazy plan?), i feel like this new setting took away some of the old Xcom vibes, wich is good on a innovation standpoint and bad on franchise-player relation.
- And lastly and the least important factor here, visual bugs, sume stutter in cutscenes and action cameras, some texture popping here and there, nothing too serious that some patches wont fix, but still there.
- PS.1: Poison spit and AI meele going through walls.
Still, good game with a bright future ahead, especially with the new modding support.
