People complain about two things. Turn timers, and hard enemies coming early on in the game. The thing is, you are rarely swarmed the way you were in EU - when a sectoid comes out, they'll have 1-2 trash troops with them at once. Using a sniper with squadsight, the first perk you get with the tree (which is another improvement from EU, where you had to level up a trash sniper to make them useful), decimates the trash mobs, and the explosives and rifles can take down the sectoid within 1-2 turns.
As for the turn timers, the only people complaining about them are those who don't actually know how to win unless they are moving forward 1 tile at a time, overwatching the entire way. Imo thats worse than save scumming, because save scumming at least involves taking risk, whereas OW scumming as I call it has zero risk other than a little RNG. If you move forward at all you'll be able to reach the extraction zone with more than enough time to spare - if you are having issues, try leaving the sniper back and then using the remaining teammembers at the extraction zone to cover the sniper. I havent finished a mission with less than 3 turns left on the timer, and it really made me think about my moves - theres also apparently a file you can remove that removes the timer, though I don't recommend it.
All in all a great game despite minor Day 1 bugs. 5/7.

XCOM® 2 is a 3D-but-isometric-tactical-shoot-them-aliens-up game. The plot boils down to this: extraterrestrial beings have taken over the world and it's your job to take it back. You need to dissect aliens and research their technology in order to find out more about them and come up with ways of defeating them.
The game plays extremely similar to XCOM: Enemy Unknown. Taking cover, shooting, researching, upgrading your base and many other things feel very similar. There are, however, new features that are all built upon that rock solid base that we, or I, know and love. My personal favourite and in my opinion biggest feature is a stealth mode. You can't Metal Gear Solid the game up by silently taking down enemies, but you can now avoid them, sneak around them to set up ambushes and create massive tactical advantages. The game also features a load of new enemies. Most old enemies from XCOM: Enemy Unknown have been genetically modified using human DNA, making for more powerful enemies than ever before, because YES, this game is HARD. I recommend people who aren't familiar with XCOM play XCOM: Enemy Unknown before picking this up.
Something XCOM: Enemy Unknown was, in my opinion, already good at got massively improved: character customization! The higher the level of your character, the more you can unlock and the more unique your characters will become. I am a massive fan of extensive character customization and I absolutely love playing around with the customizer in this game. It has a load of options and features something for everyone's taste: wacky, tactical or whatever's inbetween, it's in there somewhere.
I don't have many problems with this game, except for it's framerate. I recommend you watch out with this if your PC has low specifications, because I run it at 30 to 40 FPS, even though this PC can easily handle GTA V on some of the highest settings and still run it at a smooth 60 FPS.

I see a lot of reviews that call this game masochistic and say it's too hard to be fun, but I respectfully disagree. Yes, there is a component of luck involved and yes, this does mean that sometimes you'll be in a situation where you lost because of bad luck. But there's just as likely the chance that a stroke of blind luck will save you. This is a game about making the best out of a bad situation, and the struggle to keep your favourite adventurers alive is a big part of that, but almost never will you come across a problem that could not have been prepared for.
Yes, it's hard. But once you've spent some time with it, and you understand the mechanics and the threats posed against you, all the difficulty becomes much, much more manageable.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys dungeon-crawlers, eldritch horrors or even just games that are different from the norm. This game is goddamn brilliance, and though it has flaws there is no denying the satisfaction of "A SINGULAR STRIKE!"
As a closing statement, the art is gorgeous, the narrator is awesome, over time you will genuinely care about the adventurers you're sending off to war, and you will curse and smash your keyboard when your favourite bites the dust. This is undeniably a game which will put you through stress and anguish and pain, but in the opinion of this reviewer, it's all worth it in the end.

I am new to the Souls series, and I decided to start with Dark Souls 3. This game has no business being as great as it is, I feel that this title has a balanced amount of difficulty; the atmosphere is never boring; and the satisfaction that is felt progressing through the areas is powerful. I know that there are many Dark Souls veterans out there, but if you are a newcomer to the series I would recommend this as a perfect way to start your experience, and better yet, play with friends.

The early-access was well worth the cost, the full access a full-on steal. Dripping in atmosphere, with a lot of close attention to detail. Every choice, like the game says, is a one-way road that will make you consider the risk and potential reward of continuing a quest/fight gone bad (which will happen more than occasionally), certain team compositions, or even different dungeon routes. The game mechanics are simple at heart, but the amount of playable classes, as well as their varying interactions, keep the game interesting until the very end. The makers of the game, Redhook, have done a lot to facilitate those looking for a more casual experience and have consistently added new/reworked content into the game during the early access period. The last thing to note is the prominent difficulty of the game. Yes, the learning curve is initially pretty steep and yes, you will probably reset game runs (even though you can't lose technically), but you already knew that didn't you?
TLDR: Greatly difficult but rewarding RPG crawler that I'm glad I got to enjoy from its early access to its full release.

I follow the game since it's been spotlighted even before arriving in steam EA. I finally got it last year, I don't know when exactly but I play at least since april. Thing is, I don't play often. Actually out of my total 75h of playing, I easely played 50h before summer.
I don't want to start my review as is, but here it is : I liked the game "before". Back in april/may, I could only talk about DD to my friends, because it was a big deal for me. Telling truth I got the game because I'm a turn-based rpg fan. But all the squirks, dialogs, lore, classes specs, village upgrades, and even the rng (back then) was all I loved about the title. The identity was there anyway.
Back then, DD was fairly controlable, with some bad luck at times. Sometimes some very bad luck i must say. But it was part of the game! And it felt fun! I could talk about how my lvl3 vestal died starving in middle of a corridor cuz I ain't no food anymore! About my alchoholic highwayman havng not much acc and failing 90% of his shot, my knight afraid of the dark, etc. I made myself kind of a picture of those characters in a dark humorous way, and it was great!
So many stories to share. And yet, I could, sometime, manage dungeon till the end, losing 1 or 2 dudes in the process. I felt the game was like kind of a fair trade and it was addictive somehow. My main goal was to lvl max my favorite characters. It was hard enough to me.
But today the game is about how to lose an entire team after 1 or 2 fights, thanks to the mad RNG, the stats nerf, the stress augmentation and the enemies luck. I get the game is about how terrible a quest can turn for your characters, but there is a "can" in this sentence. It tells you then that it can aslo NOT be so bad. So not only the game is gone into "every single quest will be a pain in the @ss from now on" (not joking, my % of success went down and down for the very same quests since last spring), but it also gets the player rid of any control of what is happening. Your character should be alright with his lvl 6 stats and equipped items? Nooooo let's get him the worst possible scenario, because RNG is more important than the choices you made for your character. So characters have stats and skills, but in the end they are not relevant for you can't decently plan anything to happen "almost" as expected. Your most violent warrior can become a ♥♥♥♥♥ and your vestal can destroy suns for wtf reason.
It's not the problem that bad things happen, I loved the game for that. The problem is that it always happen, to the point you have nothing left to enjoy anymore! Even victory tastes like crap most of the time. The fun in DD is dead within 6 months.
So to make it simple : the game, to me, went from a :
50% lucky stuff 50% bad stuff
To a
10% lucky stuff 90% bad stuff happening (without logical reason, I repeat).
You can't count on characters specs, skills, stats, items and strategies these days, it's all up to randomness, even in the easiest dungeon. Everything can happen to you, but be sure it's gonna be bad no matter how you know the game.
It's not harder, it's more non-sense. It's less controlable. You lose for more reasons than before, you surrender more quickly and more often. You earn less things and need to farm madly to save what's left from your previous disasters. The game never rewards the player in the way I didn't smile since June while playing it! It's only about frustration and guilt. I only play here and then to see what's up and it's sad to said it is not the fun game I used to spend my life on.
TL;DR : game went from enjoyable, memorable, fun and strategic to some lifeless russian roulette for the sake of difficulty poorly executed and understood. Needs a lot of balancing until it might justify it's price. DD was one of my favorite game experience ever, but it's one of the most disappointing now.

It's an XCOM sequel.  Better graphics, better AI, different setup (sort of), bigger maps with more variety, all very sequelly and perfectly fine.
At it's heart it is a turn-based strategy and all the things that entails, except it isn't quite the whole picture.  Every single mission I have played so far has a timer.  The strategy has gone out of the window to be replaced with zerg-rushing the objective and hoping that you can survive.  No more thinking and flankingand tactics, now it is all about the run and gun.
Did you fight a group of aliens and a second one is coming?  Well you'll be lucky to get to the objective in time.  Don't even think about hitting overwatch.
tl;dr - XCOM:EU/EW had babies with The Bureau and this is the result.

I am not 100% negitive, there are  more customizations for your solders than there are colors of paint at a hardware store. NOTE: After reading reviews of the well-known problems of Fallout 4 I list things below that are critical to gameplay that were lacking but which other reviewers haven't mentioned, to give some variety to reviews.
After nearly 150 hours of Fallout 4, my consensus: Fallout 4 is an excellent game, but it is a poor Fallout-series game. I am rating this positive for overall gameplay despite my dislike of the plot and new mechanics and optimizations.
GOOD:
Excellent graphics
Intriguing antagonists (The Institute)
Cool weapons
Densely-populated, so lots of hidden building wrecks to explore
The Glowing Sea (location) is AWESOME
BAD:
Thought your biggest probblem in New Vegas and Fallout 3 were Deathclaws? Super mutants with glowing hounds? A horde of reavers? Guess what your biggest problem in Fallout 4 is. ****ing mirelurks. Not thrilling, just annoying. Queen Mirelurks, King Mirelurks, Razorback Mirelurks, Mirelurk Hatchlings. Boring.
I disliked (like 80% of players) the Sim-like building element including maintaining settlements, and I thought I could just avoid that part of the game because it's glitchy and unintuitive -- but no, the plot in the last half of the game needs you to fiddle with wires and generators and pick up X and Y to construct Z, which is boring and lazy writing, so the plot becomes boring. You have little motivation in collecting parts and salvaging steel and cables and whatever.
Power armour is now stupid and borderline unusable because you have to "power" it with fusion cores, of which there are few and they are weak. If you don't want to be caught in the middle of nowhere with cool heavy weapons when your fusion cores "empty", leaving your overencumbered stuff for spoil, don't even bother using power armour.
Lack of integration with the different antagonist populations (The Railroad, The Institute, Brotherhood of Steel, etc.) Everyone wants you on their side, and it doesn't really matter what your decisions are, until you slightly side with one of them to finish a quest you've been working on, and they all hell breaks loose and someone becomes an automatic enemy. This results in a half-dozen quests "disappearing" (even if you're halfway through them) before you can even stop to patch things up. The whole interplay with the different factions is reductive and lacks subtlety, so it really feels like all the characters you meet don't add any depth or interest, and there's nothing behind their loyalty or hatred.
Companions come from out of everywhere you go and sometimes there's no motivation for them to follow you, they just ask to be a companion and you don't know anything about them. At least with Boone there was personality.
ALSO while it is cool that there are lots of locations within the downtown Boston area, it's more difficult to keep a companion alive and focused on the same thing as you. Why? You turn a corner, and the next building is controlled by Raiders, and the one beside it is Mutant territory. It seems randomly generated but doesn't make logical sense, and if your companion strays a little they could be embroiled in a WHOLE other battle
6/10

It's very easy to get involved into the dark, hopeless and grim atmosphere this game manages to create thanks to the excellent art with a very well-fitting choice of colours and to the immersive musics and FX.
I never opened the settings menu to enable or disable game mechanics, because I think this game should be experimented in an artistic and sensorial way, not in a rational one (criticizing mechanics and so on).
This game is about the fragile human psyche and the illusion of faith and earthly pleasures used as a placebo in a desperate attempt to avoid its fracture. Strategy is nothing when Fate itself is against you, and this is represented by a lot of game statistics being expressed by percentages. Human skill is useless against timeless horrors: one can only hope to succeed out of a burst of good luck.
This game is capable of keeping constantly high my level of anxiety during missions (with even victory resulting in a somewhat negative situation... followed by all the mental and physical consequences the heroes must face) and my level of discouragement while managing the hamlet (with all the heroes getting sick, mad, asking not to be sent again down there...)
Maybe I like this game because it "sees" life as I do:
I'm quite pessimist, thus I think that chances are always against me, hope is just a childish feeling to me (but I'm not completely hopeless), I'm stubborn and tend to recover from setbacks out of pride.
But I'm prone to frustration too, so I greatly dislike unfair games, like Darkest Dungeon can be quite often...
I could not get frustrated by it till now though, like I could easily get by a bad serie of "aseptic" dice rolls for example: in fact in Darkest Dungeon things go terribly wrong in such a dramatic end elegant way that all I can think about is only the epicness of my defeat, with the music that becomes more and more pressing and anxiogenic as the hope of victory fades away...
I admit it: Sometimes I ragequit, sometimes I facepalmed, some other times I watched the screen in disappoint and disbelief... as if I really was In that dungeon with those poor souls called "heroes" by some townsfolk, and surrendered like them to some nasty mental derangement for just a second...
This game awakened in me again the fear of bosses, because they're overpowered and there is permadeath. Characters are designed to be anti-heroes, and this concept reaches its apotheosis when a pious paladin succumbs to his inner selfishness and show himself as the frail human he actually is.
And what should that paladin think when a distrusted abomination reacts to his stress with virtue and valor instead (a rare event indeed)?
As you have seen, I have not covered any technical aspect in this review because I think that If you look for the gameplay, mechanics or strategy aspects in this game... well this is not the game for you.

It's an XCOM sequel.  Better graphics, better AI, different setup (sort of), bigger maps with more variety, all very sequelly and perfectly fine.
At it's heart it is a turn-based strategy and all the things that entails, except it isn't quite the whole picture.  Every single mission I have played so far has a timer.  The strategy has gone out of the window to be replaced with zerg-rushing the objective and hoping that you can survive.  No more thinking and flankingand tactics, now it is all about the run and gun.
Did you fight a group of aliens and a second one is coming?  Well you'll be lucky to get to the objective in time.  Don't even think about hitting overwatch.
tl;dr - XCOM:EU/EW had babies with The Bureau and this is the result.

TL:DR: Darkest Dungeon is about making the best of a bad situation, meaning that if you can't handle bad RNG once in a while, you will probably hate this game. Also the art and sound design are amazing.
The opening screen says that Darkest Dungeon is a game about making the best of a bad situation, and the developers have stuck to that philosophy throughout the development of this game. Unlike Dark Souls or XCOM, games where bad situations only arise due to the player's mistakes, Darkest Dungeon's reasoning for dumping a bucket full of blood and♥♥♥♥♥on you can be boiled down to "♥♥♥♥ you, RNG." The damage that bad RNG brings can be mitigated with careful planning, but the risk is always there, the chance that an Occult Witch might crit on a stress attack three times in a row.
This is what frustrates a lot of people writing reviews for this game, I think. They think that there should be a "perfect strategy," that if the player is just good enough, they can mitigate all risk entirely. That simply isn't true. Darkest Dungeon is about creating those desperate, terrifying situations that arise when your vestal becomes afflicted in the first  room and refuses to heal your hellion who just got critted on by Cultist Gladiator. It is, truly, about forcing the player to make the best of a bad situation. Do I push forward to end of this quest and gain the bonus gold, despite the fact that my Crusader just died to a heart attack? Or do we pull back, mitigating both losses and rewards? That's what makes Darkest Dungeon great.
And yes obviously the art is fantasic and the sound design is legendary. All the classes play in radically different ways, allowing for many different strategies and playstyles. The combat mechanics are very solid, and that's coming from someone who normally hates turn-based combat that isn't on a grid. BUT. If you are the kind of person who can't handle dealing with gameplay elements that are outside of your control, then this game is probably not for you.

I bought this on sale expecting it to be bad and expecting it to be disappointing, but regardless it's a huge open world game, so even if it's sub-par it'll still entertain me longer than most games, right...? Boy, was I wrong.
The first issue to arise was Survival mode. Wanted to play it because I enjoyed hardcore mode in New Vegas, so decided to give it a shot even though the "only save when sleeping" mechanic sounds like a terrible idea for a Bethesda title. I made it one hour and thirty minutes before my character got stuck trying to reach a computer terminal they never got to, leaving me stuck there without any way of backing out. Googled solutions and was told to use the tcl console command to fix it, tried opening the console and it wouldn't go, so initially I blamed my German keyboard. Turns out though that Survival mode disables console commands. Bethesda seems so out of touch with the buginess of their own games that they've disabled console commands thinking this will stop cheaters or something, when in reality it just stops people from playing their game. Finally went to download a mod to allow me to Quicksave since I trust myself not to save scum, but upon doing so the game yelled at me for having a mod installed and told me that file would no longer unlock achievements. Is combatting cheaters THIS important, Bethesda?! Again, I think you guys are confusing "cheaters" with "people that want this piece of crap to actually work." Eventually I just restarted without survival mode.
The load times going outside into the main hub world are surprisingly long for a Bethesda title. I'm talking 20-30 seconds+ each time you go outside. I've never seen this happen in any of their other games: Morrowind, Oblivion, Fallout 3, New Vegas, Skyrim...all of them can load the main outer world in less than 5 seconds, but this game somehow can't. I have a top of the line computer too...
The controls feel very clunky and odd. Many people criticized FO3 and New Vegas for not being able to decide if it's an RPG or a first-person shooter, but I think FO4 takes that title. FO3 and New Vegas were RPGs with shooter mechanics. Enemies had predictable and basic UI; Geckos and Deathclaws you were expected to kill before they reach you or they'd do heavy damage, enemy raiders had predictable patterns where they may take cover, but they'd come out of cover when it was time to shoot at you and that was your chance to kill them. FO4 comparatively, both you and the enemy raiders will die quickly if you come out of cover. The result is you can't ever just chase the enemy down, and you must instead hit a headshot on them as they try to do the same to you from cover. This actually just results in rather tedious and extended combat than previous titles, because sometimes you simply cannot get an angle that allows for this. It's not really intense combat or skilled in any way, it's just you repeatedly trying to headshot a guy by clicking on his head, then you wait to see if the hitboxes and collision meshes feel generous today. If they don't, perhaps you get frustrated and try to run out to close the gap, and then you start bleeding hard because omg you left cover you idiot. I'm also not sure how melee is supposed to work; New Vegas understood melee would get shot at so it provided perks that increase defense while a melee weapon is in your hands or lets melee weapons knock an enemy on their butt, but Fallout 4 just...does nothing. As I said, enemies in my experience do NOT abandon cover to come hunt you down, so waiting for them to come to you so you can jump them with melee doesn't really seem viable.
And that brings me to the final and most important thing holding Fallout 4 back: the perks are terrible. I welcome anyone to go google Fallout 4's perks right now and you'll quickly notice something. Take Solar Powered for example. In FO3 and FO:NV, this was a nice perk for regenerating health while outside in the sun, and you could take it at level 20. In Fallout 4, you need 10 Endurance and you can take this perk immediately....except you can't. The first level of the perk that you can take immediately provides a rather meaningless STR and END +2 buff when you're outside in the sun, the second level gives radiation decay and can be taken at level 27. The final level can only be taken at level 50, and FINALLY you will regenerate health while outside in the sun.
This pattern continues for all perks. If you take a level of a perk...? The next level unlocks in 7, 15 or even 25 levels. What's more, the majority of the perks are simply older perks that have been gutted and split up into 3 or 5 different levels. I swear, it's like a developer had a perk quota to meet, didn't give a crap about the game or it's quality, so instead of thinking up fun new perks he just took existing ones and started splitting them up into multiple levels, often with the most interesting effects only unlocking at level 40-50. Bethesda honestly just couldn't care less about designing fun perks for the player, they just wanted to provide the illusion there's loads of new perks. Even Skyrim...if you wanted to focus all your time and effort towards Archery perks to be a beast with a bow while terrible at everything else, you could do this. Now imagine Skyrim if every time you took an Archery perk, the game made you wait 7 levels before it let you take another archery perk, and this 7 level gap would increase to a 15 level gap the higher you went, until you can FINALLY get the truly interesting stuff when you hit level 40-50. Think about that a second: the entire duration of New Vegas' level system must be achieved before you can expect to get ANY meaningful perks that give you new abilities.
If you want a character that specializes in Revolvers in this game...? It's not happening. You're gonna be able to take about 2 of the 5 levels of that revolver perk in your first 15 levels of gameplay, and the other 3 are gonna come veeeerrrrry slowly. There is absolutely no specialization in this game specifically because they've locked off all the interesting stuff for the vast majority of the game. The entire perk system seems sunk by something really really basic and avoidable here: terrible pacing. I like to feel progress when I play, I like to see my character changing and becoming better. In New Vegas I can have a character that can knock enemies down with melee by level 8, or I can get one that can  paralyze with fists by level 18. I can knock people down with shotguns at level 10 or I can do huge amounts of explosive damage by level 10. But in Fallout 4...? The ability to knock enemies down with melee doesn't exist for some reason. Paralyzing with unarmed attacks is a level 46 ability (level 46!!!), you cannot knock down enemies with shotguns, and explosive damage will not reach the levels it can in New Vegas until level 22.
You will spend the MAJORITY of the game playing as a generic, forgettable character with no special abilities or perks, and only after you more or less "complete" the game and you're running out of things to do...? That's when you can finally start specializing your character.
I personally consider this terrible design, and I simply have no desire to play 50 levels worth of a clunky shooter just to be able to revisit old classic perks I can readily enjoy in New Vegas with a more reasonable playtime. The customization of characters in FO4 is single-handedly sabotaged by this system. If you're reading this review and want this game for the settlement system...? Guess what: it's limited by perks too. You must endure several levels of a clunky, reptitive shooter (go, kill, loot) before any RPG elements show their face. As I said, I personally have no patience for that, so I've already requested a refund.
Do not buy, do not give Bethesda your money, even at sale price. Sad to say, but I fully feel we just need to wait 5-8 years and Bethesda will start resembling EA.

I don't usually like to make heavy comparisons in game reviews; but I was a huge Phantasy Star Online fan. Staying up till 7 am to play PSO and still going to school the next day was a regular thing. It was my first MMO.
Three hit combos? Check!
Character customization? Check!
Multi-person button puzzles? Check!
Elevators shaped like rectangles? Check!
Landing on a mysterious, alien planet after the destruction of your homeworld? Check!
Spiral Knights does bring its own elements to the mix. Blocking and dodging - those did appear in Phantasy Star Portable 2 and PS Zero. Ok, maybe I'm a huge PSO fan. I've played every incarnation.
If we called the Spiral Knights 'Casts' this would definetly be another entry; but the game has its own story and charm, plus that usual Sega style filled with lush visuals and great music.
Classes don't exist and the leveling process is where things start to show a difference. Instead of leveling a character, a user levels their Weapons, Guns, Bombs, Shield, Helmet and Armor. - though this could arguably be compared to Phantasy Star Universe and its weapon grinding system. So far it is fairly forgiving, but time will tell.
Similar to the Casts of PSO, the Spiral Knights have no techs and instead use items found within the ever-changing dungeons, the 'Clockwork'. The world of Cradle is truly unique though, if compared to Ragol there is no relation. Cradle is itself a clockwork world built by rodent peopled called Gremlins, occupied by a few quirky races. It actually changes in realtime, so that a player might not ever see the same two areas twice except when truly seasoned.
Being a free game running in the Java Virtual Machine, I recommend anyone try it. It is even accessible to Linux users with additional software (WINE or PlayOnLinux). Plus you get a free TF2 hat for trying it; which was why I started playing.
So if you ever spent any time on the planet Ragol, think of this as a bit of PSO plus with a top-down view typical to hack-n-slash games (Diablo, Torchlight, etc.). If you never battled the devious Dark Falz, I would still recommend Spiral Knights. It is a very fun and casual MMO from a seasoned publisher who kept me glued to my Dreamcast from dusk till dawn. If you played the Genesis you can probably hear the choir every time you read the word: Sega.

Great Artstyle and Narrative. Trying to balance the funding, supply, physical and mental wellbeing of my mercinaries is exciting on its own. And the dungeon battles are always tense. Its a much deeper game than it appears. A lot of mechanics that play parts in the dungeon crawl. Like provisioning, camping, torchlight, battle positions, expedition composition, personal quirks and diseases, skill and equipment levels, stress levels, inventory management.

I highly reccomend this game to anyone. Its brutal, unique, and rewarding.

Man, this game gives me chills. Whenever I first got this, there was so much everybody had to say about it. There were a lot of bad things said about this game, but that's okay, because there was also an overwhelming amount of positive reviews for this game. Unlike Bethesda's other recent endeavour (I'm looking at you, Elder Scrolls V : Special Edition, you♥♥♥♥♥♥. But that's not fair, I can't suck the♥♥♥♥♥♥of Bethesda every time, so let's look at it objectively.
For graphics, I think the game is very beautiful, and makes it more satisfying to roam around the large open-world map. Of course that should be satisfying, but this was so much more than satisfying. The character detail, the weapon detail, the well scripted events and companions, and the detail they put into even the smallest of things. From shooting birds to death, to chopping somebody's head, shoulders, knees or toes off instead of the usual ragdoll falling when that NPC health bar reached zero. But then, on the other hand, this game has a very "Go big or go home" detail to it.
You see, when I tried to play this computer on my $2,000 gaming laptop, this game lagged it horribly and made the fan go crazily hot. Loading the game and fast-traveling was a pain, and entering/exiting buildings was annoying too, so if you want to see a detailed game, prepare some popcorn and a giant computer fan. Another issue I found was how irregular the movements were, which was pretty hard to get past. Not only that, some of the functions they had in Fallout 3 that they didn't have in Fallout 4 were missing. Mostly it was little stuff though, like the dark setting or visible sheathed/holstered weapons, so it wasn't that hard to ignore.
Now onto the gameplay itself. This game was a double-edged sword. On one hand, you want to play this all the time, and can never stop due to its captivating story. But on the other hand, the amount of endless side-quests and annoying or tedious running around you have to do is such a hassle that it makes completing every mission is hard.
Overall, it's a good game on its own, but don't be afraid to add some mods in the mix for a spicier time.

Starbound is a fun, functional Terreria-styled game. One could call it a procedurally generated 2D space-adventure simulator.
Or you can just call it Starbound. Procedural generation is one of the most mind-boggling aspects to games to me; and this game does not disappoint. Everything from the Stars, to the Planets, to the creatures that inhabit those planets are made with randomized components.
I will say that this game is going to have competition in the future, but with 6 races to play, a fun game style to go off of, and the ever-expanding curiosity of exploration; Starbound has a strong life ahead of itself. I expect to be playing Starbound for quite a long time, as I have enjoyed it quite a bit.

XCOM 2 Full Review:
Release day: This game so far has been terrible. the content is pitful and most the features of the game are dreadful (gameplay and AI.) I've been playing for a few hours on this one mission- it's poorly optmize so not even a fully speced PC can run the game propperly, but it's also infested with bugs and errors as well as this redicoulasly unfair chance system that i'm convinced doesn't work (XCOM one didn't give me this issuie.) i'm not sure if it's just me or some lazy devs, but the AI are f*cking insane even on easy- i've had almost every enemy shot hit my units despite me being in cover, on the otherside of the map, out of combat or immune (which is another pain in the♥♥♥♥♥bug.) it's like the devs want you to hate the game. I set out orginally without even wanting to use the save game function to bring back units (you know make it real.) but it's almost a required function... so intill they fix the game, i'd suggest not even touching this mess- like seriously portal 2 and ARK survival have had cleaner launches.
Second week: Right so the games been out for a little bit now and a few patches and issuies have been fixed mostly to do with animation and game breaking bugs, but there's still no change in this poor optimization- there are some serious problems still in the game exspecially when it comes to loading screens (i timed my load for a mission and the shortest i had was 20 seconds, whilst the longest was almost a minute. on a fully speced alienware area 51 with a Titan X graphics card) This being said the moding community is helping with some of the more present issuies such as lack of customizational options and types of enemies (check the workshop for more info before you purchase this game, to get an idea of the community.)
With all that in mind i'd like to quickly discuss the storyline of the game, over the mechanics. Now the mechanics in the game are not better than XCOM 1 (but this may be justfied when more weapons and armors are added to the game with the release of exspantions.) in addition, the mechanics such as abbilties are concerned have been slightly improved- hacking and mind control abillities have been enhanced and i have enjoyed the chances system when using the gremlin to hack an enemy unit or turret, weapons in the game- do get better overtime- mostly the weapons attached to the W.A.R. suit are the most enjoyable. this being said... there is simply not enough variation in weaponary/equitment/armor (i researched all the tec tree and bought every exsperimental item before i even took half the contents.) I think XCOM 2 is going to be one of thoose games thats farly dependent on the moding community if this is to be the case- 2K games needs to look into adding a map editor and new forms of alien customization (but thats a diffrent issuie.)
For now it makes more sence to focus on the storyline aspect of the game (intill more information is annouced.) Firstly, the storyline was exseptional towards the begining of the game (an improvement on XCOM 1.) i felt like i actually had the power to make a diffrence, and i had a strong attachment to the characters and unlike many games XCOM2 does a great job of making the player the main protagonist over other characters (due to the first person POV, and the status around your characters persona.) althought, the campain ends very abruptly... almost unexspectly for that matter.  the storyline is the shortest i've seen in a game for a while, and i'd like to see at least 5x the content in the next few exspantions: To alaborate, by the time i came to grips with the situation and started relaxing into the position the game places the player in i was already coming up to the endgame. The majority of XCOM2s content is side quests which doesn't feel as grand as main missions and eventually does become a bit of a nuisance- i personally did 3 main quest missions and 20 side quests before the last mission which is.... just not enough main quests and well too many side quests (you get one every week, as well as the odd supply raid every 2 weeks. which adds up fast when everythings on a 4-10 day timer.) So when the last mission came around i thought it had to be an end chapter mission or somthing on thoose lines- only to find out the game's main story was only 4 missions long and full of filler content [this was a huge disapointment.] => becuase i felt like i only just started the game by the time i was doing the last mission.
Taking all this into account, i'd like to be honest and say. XCOM2 is still not worth getting over XCOM1 for the ask price. The storyline itself is also rather bland with the exception of the introduction (also for XCOM 1 fans, there is a disapointing almost game ruining event just prior to the last mission concerning a beloved character, without whom the game feels rather... well, not XCOM anymore- 2K took a rather GOT take to the last mission.)  it's worth perhaps laying off intill these last few bugs have been ironed out, and the game has been optmized a little more. And if you're in XCOM for the campain (like myself) don't have high exspectation the storyline needs alot more content (as stated 5x more storyline and cutscenes to meet my minium for a game like this one.) In terms of a critic score, i'd give a standered 5.5/10.

I'm not sure where to begin with my review of X-Com 2.
I want to talk about the lack of refinements over the previous installment, surely. For all its updated looks, tweaks and an alleged degree of polish, X-Com 2 looks and feels remarkably like 'more of the same'.
For me, this isn't entirely a good thing.  I loved Enemy Unknown and Within, don't get me wrong, but these installments never felt like the big budget items they are supposed to be.  They always felt more like indie titles: as if they were developed on a shoestring budget.  They were delightful games but rife with bugs and quirks of varying degrees.
It seems downright wrong to me that so many of these quirks are still present in the sequel.  It's as if the developers took the core programming of the game and simply ported it over to a new engine, telling themselves "Yeah, it's good enough eh?"
However, what we get is something that feels less like a sequel and more like...  a face lift.  Maybe it is good enough.  It's just hard for me to write a review, forgetting about all the potential I saw in a title and merely judge it on its own merits.
Assume for a moment that I can do this however.  How does X-Com 2 stand on its own?
Well, pretty okay I guess.   I mean, it's more X-Com right?  X-Com is good, so logically, X-Com 2 must be good as well?  Right?
Damn it.  No.  I'm just now wowed.  I'm not impressed.  I keep playing it, but nearly every turn I experience something that puts this bitter taste in my mouth and I just... keep playing XCOM 2 out of some demented sense of obligation.
I get so damned angry listening to Bradford and Shen tell me to do things I'm actively trying to accomplish.  I'm so disapointed every time I see a character clip through an object, shoot through one, or float in space.  I'm sick of seeing Stun Lancers forget all about their rifles and launch suicidal melee attacks on my squaddies.  I'm tired of melee attacks in general.  I'm just so heartbroken at the complete lack of attention to detail.
I'm sorry.  I can't give it a thumbs up.  I won't.  It just doesn't deserve it.  For any reason.

Trove is a voxelgame I played quite a lot before it hit Steam.
It was my second game from Trion itself I played after several years of paying Rift and while it got some interesting features and a cute voxel based style I cannot recommend this game at all.
+ Good looking voxel based graphics
+ Lot's of recipes for decorative items for those who like to build
+ Lot's of stuff to unlock and collect
- Very (VERY!) grindy gameplay, which seem to just get worse over the time
- Horrible server performance - if you played Rift this shouldn't be new to you
- Horrible client performance - if you played Rift this shouldn't be new to you
- Very cash grabby - if you played Rift this shouldn't be new to you
- Lots and lots of bugs, crashes and memory leaks are common and Trion don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about it - but if you played Rift this shouldn't be new to you
You have to spend a lot of time in this game, not just to upgrade your gear but Trion also added bonuses for each day of the week telling you what you have to do on each day. You're not directly forced to follow that but you pretty much have to since you need a lot of stuff. They also just added challenges, those are only for the highest difficulties and occur every hour and have a timeframe of 20 minutes. The reward is (relatively) good but it forces you to do this every hour which is very similar in how browsergames bind their players to the game.
The shop on the first look might look harmless, but a few months ago you were able to get most upgrade items for the items for cubits instead of credits (a currency you can get through daily playing, remember how I said they use tactics to bind players?) and another one of those were able to drop from one of the mobs in the game which was necessary to upgrade items to a higher grade (now only available through the shop with credits). The game features not just chests for real money but also piñatas (can be bought with cubits as well, but no point for wasting them here). Both give you incredibly low chances to get something rare like a unique mount or wings but I've seen people spending hundreds of euros on them without getting anything useful but a few minor quantities of mats.
Aside from that you can also get certain item packs, there are always new ones and they cost you around 20€ each containing the new content of an update pretty much (like classes, mounts etc.). Overall you end up spending hundreds or even thousands of euros if you want to play this seriously, but don't worry - with each 1000€ you pay in the shop you get a shadow chest when you log into the game each day, containing ... even more crap!
The game and shop also uses casino tricks with flashy graphics and lots of colors. If you're a parent and worry that your child might be in danger of getting addicted to stuff like this you should be extra careful (or if you by yourself might be in danger be careful as well).
Well, coming the performance part I guess ...
The game runs okay (and I mean "okay", not good or great) when you enter it, but the longer the games runs the lower your FPS will be, after 10 minutes you're probably only at half the frames per second you're used to, this gets worse and worse until you have no other choice as to restart the game. The server performance isn't better by any means though, random disconnects and a high ping or worlds simply refusing to load for several seconds are common problems of this game. Now, if you have played Rift you might find that this sound very familiar, and yes the game suffers from basically the same problems - the only difference is that they can't blame the gamebryo engine this time since they wrote their own game engine for this. Aside from that you will encounter bugs, lots and lots of bugs and every update adds more bugs and is only half playable after one or two hotfixes (every single time, seriously) but leaves a few of the new bugs behind which are continuously stacking up since I've started playing.
If you want to play something similar with adventure and building you should stick with games like Minecraft or Terraria or support indev games like Starmade who make slower progress but are still much more promising and user friendly than this.

XCOM 2 is a sequel to XCOM Enemy Unknown in a very loose sense. In this game, instead of the XCOM project succeeding, we're presented with a tantilizing "what if" scenario in which the war was lost within the first 6 months of initial contact. The aliens turned earth over to a totalitarian regime in which gene modification and sheer strength is used to keep the people in check. XCOM is thankfully still operating, but they are reduced to a ragtag band of guerilla fighters with less than half the resources they used to have. The odds are incredibly stacked against you (duh it's XCOM) and you have to utilize new units and advanced tactics to ensure humanity comes out on top.
The gameplay is as XCOM as you can get without being a carbon copy of Enemy Unknown. The difference lies in the early phase of each mission in which you most of the time start "concealed". This allows you to get your troops into various firing positions and set up an overwatch ambush, in which once you start the party, the enemy will try to move to cover and immediately get fired upon by the rest of the team. This addition is FANTASTIC and fits SUPER WELL with the theme.

I was a huge fan of XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within and so was very excited when this sequel was announced. XCOM 2! How good could life be? I really enjoyed my first campaign--a full 68 hours of play, even though I felt the loss of some of the alien enemies that didn't show up for this edition. I still miss seekers.
Then I decided that I had not given the game a proper go of it until I had tried to complete a campaign on the hardest difficulty, Legend, one which only a scant 5% of mere mortals had succeeded in accomplishing. And in the course of becoming a legendary player I fell in love all over again.
The huge variety of Workshop mods helped, but aside from allowing me to customize my gameplay experience, they helped me realize what a solid, engrossing and exciting strategy game XCOM 2 is. I couldn't ever go back to XCOM EU/EW now, more's the shame. XCOM 2 is that good. And now with it's big expansion, War of the Chosen, continued Workshop modding, and the endless tactical and strategic choices that XCOM 2 provides, I fully expect my total playtime in this game to eventually far surpass that for the first XCOM (distinct from X-COM).
I do, however, hate the Chosen. They are just excellent enemies and throw such a wrench into missions while providing a whole new story arc--as an expansion concept they do so much more for the base game than even the brilliant XCOM: Enemy Within expansion did for XCOM: EU. The Chosen are fantastic...but I hate them. I can't wait to take out the Assassin for good.
The War of the Chosen has made XCOM 2 one of the most intense singleplayer experiences in gaming. In my present campaign, I was simultaneously racing to open up access to a regional contact to prevent the Avatar doom clock running down to zero (it got to 3 days remaining), tracking the Chosen Assassin to her lair with a Covert Operation (suffering a captured soldier--my highest ranked--in the process), and fighting a mission in which I had to deal with a new enemy, the Lost, the Chosen Assassin, and a timer counting down the turns before my mission target (the assassination of an Advent general) escaped.
Add to this the decision-making over my research priorities, loadout upgrades, proving ground experiements, Avenger management and planning for what will come in the next month (facility mission, Assassin hunt conclusion, rescue mission) and my brain is honestly fried.
Don't wait for a sale. Get it anytime. Save Earth. Now.

I bought this on sale expecting it to be bad and expecting it to be disappointing, but regardless it's a huge open world game, so even if it's sub-par it'll still entertain me longer than most games, right...? Boy, was I wrong.
The first issue to arise was Survival mode. Wanted to play it because I enjoyed hardcore mode in New Vegas, so decided to give it a shot even though the "only save when sleeping" mechanic sounds like a terrible idea for a Bethesda title. I made it one hour and thirty minutes before my character got stuck trying to reach a computer terminal they never got to, leaving me stuck there without any way of backing out. Googled solutions and was told to use the tcl console command to fix it, tried opening the console and it wouldn't go, so initially I blamed my German keyboard. Turns out though that Survival mode disables console commands. Bethesda seems so out of touch with the buginess of their own games that they've disabled console commands thinking this will stop cheaters or something, when in reality it just stops people from playing their game. Finally went to download a mod to allow me to Quicksave since I trust myself not to save scum, but upon doing so the game yelled at me for having a mod installed and told me that file would no longer unlock achievements. Is combatting cheaters THIS important, Bethesda?! Again, I think you guys are confusing "cheaters" with "people that want this piece of crap to actually work." Eventually I just restarted without survival mode.
The load times going outside into the main hub world are surprisingly long for a Bethesda title. I'm talking 20-30 seconds+ each time you go outside. I've never seen this happen in any of their other games: Morrowind, Oblivion, Fallout 3, New Vegas, Skyrim...all of them can load the main outer world in less than 5 seconds, but this game somehow can't. I have a top of the line computer too...
The controls feel very clunky and odd. Many people criticized FO3 and New Vegas for not being able to decide if it's an RPG or a first-person shooter, but I think FO4 takes that title. FO3 and New Vegas were RPGs with shooter mechanics. Enemies had predictable and basic UI; Geckos and Deathclaws you were expected to kill before they reach you or they'd do heavy damage, enemy raiders had predictable patterns where they may take cover, but they'd come out of cover when it was time to shoot at you and that was your chance to kill them. FO4 comparatively, both you and the enemy raiders will die quickly if you come out of cover. The result is you can't ever just chase the enemy down, and you must instead hit a headshot on them as they try to do the same to you from cover. This actually just results in rather tedious and extended combat than previous titles, because sometimes you simply cannot get an angle that allows for this. It's not really intense combat or skilled in any way, it's just you repeatedly trying to headshot a guy by clicking on his head, then you wait to see if the hitboxes and collision meshes feel generous today. If they don't, perhaps you get frustrated and try to run out to close the gap, and then you start bleeding hard because omg you left cover you idiot. I'm also not sure how melee is supposed to work; New Vegas understood melee would get shot at so it provided perks that increase defense while a melee weapon is in your hands or lets melee weapons knock an enemy on their butt, but Fallout 4 just...does nothing. As I said, enemies in my experience do NOT abandon cover to come hunt you down, so waiting for them to come to you so you can jump them with melee doesn't really seem viable.
And that brings me to the final and most important thing holding Fallout 4 back: the perks are terrible. I welcome anyone to go google Fallout 4's perks right now and you'll quickly notice something. Take Solar Powered for example. In FO3 and FO:NV, this was a nice perk for regenerating health while outside in the sun, and you could take it at level 20. In Fallout 4, you need 10 Endurance and you can take this perk immediately....except you can't. The first level of the perk that you can take immediately provides a rather meaningless STR and END +2 buff when you're outside in the sun, the second level gives radiation decay and can be taken at level 27. The final level can only be taken at level 50, and FINALLY you will regenerate health while outside in the sun.
This pattern continues for all perks. If you take a level of a perk...? The next level unlocks in 7, 15 or even 25 levels. What's more, the majority of the perks are simply older perks that have been gutted and split up into 3 or 5 different levels. I swear, it's like a developer had a perk quota to meet, didn't give a crap about the game or it's quality, so instead of thinking up fun new perks he just took existing ones and started splitting them up into multiple levels, often with the most interesting effects only unlocking at level 40-50. Bethesda honestly just couldn't care less about designing fun perks for the player, they just wanted to provide the illusion there's loads of new perks. Even Skyrim...if you wanted to focus all your time and effort towards Archery perks to be a beast with a bow while terrible at everything else, you could do this. Now imagine Skyrim if every time you took an Archery perk, the game made you wait 7 levels before it let you take another archery perk, and this 7 level gap would increase to a 15 level gap the higher you went, until you can FINALLY get the truly interesting stuff when you hit level 40-50. Think about that a second: the entire duration of New Vegas' level system must be achieved before you can expect to get ANY meaningful perks that give you new abilities.
If you want a character that specializes in Revolvers in this game...? It's not happening. You're gonna be able to take about 2 of the 5 levels of that revolver perk in your first 15 levels of gameplay, and the other 3 are gonna come veeeerrrrry slowly. There is absolutely no specialization in this game specifically because they've locked off all the interesting stuff for the vast majority of the game. The entire perk system seems sunk by something really really basic and avoidable here: terrible pacing. I like to feel progress when I play, I like to see my character changing and becoming better. In New Vegas I can have a character that can knock enemies down with melee by level 8, or I can get one that can  paralyze with fists by level 18. I can knock people down with shotguns at level 10 or I can do huge amounts of explosive damage by level 10. But in Fallout 4...? The ability to knock enemies down with melee doesn't exist for some reason. Paralyzing with unarmed attacks is a level 46 ability (level 46!!!), you cannot knock down enemies with shotguns, and explosive damage will not reach the levels it can in New Vegas until level 22.
You will spend the MAJORITY of the game playing as a generic, forgettable character with no special abilities or perks, and only after you more or less "complete" the game and you're running out of things to do...? That's when you can finally start specializing your character.
I personally consider this terrible design, and I simply have no desire to play 50 levels worth of a clunky shooter just to be able to revisit old classic perks I can readily enjoy in New Vegas with a more reasonable playtime. The customization of characters in FO4 is single-handedly sabotaged by this system. If you're reading this review and want this game for the settlement system...? Guess what: it's limited by perks too. You must endure several levels of a clunky, reptitive shooter (go, kill, loot) before any RPG elements show their face. As I said, I personally have no patience for that, so I've already requested a refund.
Do not buy, do not give Bethesda your money, even at sale price. Sad to say, but I fully feel we just need to wait 5-8 years and Bethesda will start resembling EA.

XCOM 2 is highly recommended for players who enjoy a challenging strategy/tactical game. The adaptation that Firaxis has made to ensure that fans of XCOM would be suitably surprised with new obstacles and objectives while encorporating some of the pacing adjustments presented in XCOM's Long War mod. From the start, aliens will throw all of their abilities at you, and once you encounter a new alien, your butt will be forever tightly clenched. And you'll be plenty busy with all the missions being thrown at you along with traveling the world.
I'm currently running through my first playthrough in Veteran (Normal) difficulty and the sheer awesomeness of XCOM 2 including the tweaks to mechanics/conventions as well as the new aliens/soldiers have kept me playing through all of the failed/aborted/one survivor missions just to see how much I can learn for future playthroughs (hint: there's a lot).
If you aren't excited about getting destroyed by aliens and slowly building up your small, small army, this might not be the game for you. Still, the story progress (thus far) has been captivating after having played XCOM so many times so if you have played XCOM in any capacity, you owe your dead runs to see what happens after you lose.

In my present campaign, I was simultaneously racing to open up access to a regional contact to prevent the Avatar doom clock running down to zero (it got to 3 days remaining), tracking the Chosen Assassin to her lair with a Covert Operation (suffering a captured soldier--my highest ranked--in the process), and fighting a mission in which I had to deal with a new enemy, the Lost, the Chosen Assassin, and a timer counting down the turns before my mission target (the assassination of an Advent general) escaped.

Don't wait for a sale. Get it anytime. Save Earth. Now.

TLDR; Great customization, some nice tweaks inspired by Long War. Peformance could be better and will hopefully be fixed soon. Possible black screen error and fix that worked for me below.
As I am writing this review I have played through the tutorial and experimented with the character customization. From my personal experience I can say that XCOM2 has for the most part not only met but exceeded many of my expectations. Content-wise this game is worth the full price tag. For character customization and immersion this game is spectacular. At first the vast number of selections is almost overwhelming in comparison to XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within. As for game play mechanics there have been a number of improvements such as the ability to unequip unused armor and items for all soldiers with the easy click of a button. The AI is certainly a force to be reckoned with, working toward an opposing goal and playing strategically. I am thrilled that the developers took the time to listen to their fan base and include a number of elements from the Long War Mod, which I have played and enjoyed.
Now for the not so good. All things considered, I would not write a negative review for this game based upon solely the performance issues. However, this is not to say that the performance issues are not to be overlooked. The frame rate is far from spectacular, and I receive minor-moderate lag on both parts of missions and the home base screen. Graphics and performance-wise this game does not feel optimized to its fullest potential. However, I would still recommend this title, even in its current state. Does the latency and performance need to be patched? Yes, I believe it does. However, I am placing my full faith in the developers to release patches in the months to come to eliminate many of these issues.
Lastly, one serious issue and a solution (hopefully this will be fixed soon). When played there is a chance that you will receive a black screen with music. This will make the game unplayable. However, there is an easy way around this. When click on game properties in your library, you can select 'launch preferences'. Here add "-windowed" (without the quotes), and your game will start in windowed mode. This should eliminate the black screen and allow you to play (at least it did for me). You can then press alt+enter to resume full screen mode.
I hope this review helped, and best of luck to you, Commander!

TL;DR: Community Outrage Simulator masquerading as brutal dungeon crawl.
10/10, would read a thousand angry, formerly-positive reviews about corrupt devs instead of playing a great game again.
I picked up DD over the summer, drawn in by a sociological interest in certain members of the "community's" outrageously toxic backlash to the implementation of corpses and some other changes. Obviously, I was familiar with and intruiged by DD for its excellent art style already, but generally I am the type to wait for something to be complete before I give it a shot. However the sea change from unabashed praise to seemingly universal criticism was so comically severe you'd have thought the game had actually reached out and harmed them.
So thank you, dear, angry, entitled, (imo) wrong-headed (but certainly allowed to have and express your opinion, which you most certainly do, oh yes, you do...) players, for without your concentrated, delerious ire I may not have discovered one of my favorite games of last (and now this) year! For me, everything about this game is a win. The art, animation, music, sound design, narration, and general presentation are all top-notch. The prose itself is a particular highlight, as is the tongue-in-cheek brutality and general tone. To me, they really nail it.
It's hard for me to address the criticisms leveled at the gameplay itself, because it seems to me the game is pretty straight forward about what it intends to be. DD is a procedurally-generated, turn-based dungeon crawler with an emphasis on difficulty (with reference to Dark Souls) and light RPG elements and squad-management (with reference to modern X-Com).
I concede that this can be considered grindy. Dungeon crawlers are generally grindy, even great ones like Dungeon of the Endless or Legend of Grimrock. The distillation of the various aspects of the form, the massive selection of character classes, buffs, debuffs, monsters, the writing, the aesthetic, these come together to give it something more than the sum of its parts. However if you don't enjoy that core to some degree or other, I don't know why you'd be considering this anyway.
Personally, I never had a problem with corpses, because I never played the game without them. Over 50+ hours, I managed to beat a number of the bosses, level characters up to the top tiers, etc, ect, and only stopped because I felt like I had gotten far enough where I was ready to play the game in a finished state, and didn't want to master too much. I also died a lot. Then I died some more. And it was fun the whole time!
As the year went on and waves of negative Steam comments continued to roll in, I felt like I was inhabiting a completely different universe from those players. As they railed against it getting harder and harder, for example, I found myself reflecting that the game seemed to be being tweaked to make it easier. I certainly wasn't dying as much. Maybe I was just somehow very good at it? I don't know. I still die all the time in X-Com. I don't think of myself as a master gamer or tactician.
The other critique I saw a lot, which is one that really prompted me to put my words out there in defense of this thing and those involved in crafting it, is that the devs somehow didn't care about the criticisms, that they don't listen, or that they were corrupt, or that they had abandoned the project like does actually occur in the Early Access community, that this game was somehow some kind of scam. That's just ridiculous. There were three major updates from the time of my purchace to the end of the year, which added all kinds of content in various ways. They were constantly tweaking the game to find the balance that worked. They were communicative, and they were clearly listening and being involved (and also making the game, for goodness sake, cmon).
Getting back briefly to the Great Corpse Outrage 2k15, for example, corpses were made a voluntary opt-out in the options menu pretty much from Backlash Ground Zero. Not that a developer has any reason to do something like that, but to then deny that it happened, or to say that they don't listen, that they're somehow scamming you, that the game is ruined forever is just a hysterical, petulent, garbage argument. I can't understand what this aspect of the community actually wants, for the life of me. If the game isn't for you, you certainly don't have to play it. But a certain amount of the negativity (which borders on outright hostility) strikes me as being like that guy who orders and eats the burger and then complains to management it wasn't cooked to his liking. Still, you have to admire (if not boggle at) their conviction, and their sheer verbosity of it all.
For me, this game actually sold me on the idea that Early Access could be an enjoyable, worthwile process of participating in the honing of a project that you enjoy and want to support and I couldn't be happier with my decision to do so, and I look forward to playing it for another 50 hours or longer. Hopefully this small review will serve as some kind of counterpoint and let those bored few who got this far know that there's a worthy, enjoyable, wonderfully-crafted experience at the center of everyone's opining.

It's free to play, but that doesn't automatically makes it a bad game. Instead, it's actually a pretty enjoyable game RPG style with a kind of dungeon crawler gameplay, with awesome soundtracks from the good old SEGA and neaty graphics.
Why am i not recommending it then?
Simply this game has been left in its state for years. Yes, there are some "events" for various holidays, with the same contents repeated every year, and always, ALWAYS new costumes/accessories/cosmetic armors, which are actually the only things being updated in the game. Stuff that must be bought with real money (like every free to play has to live with) that don't really give the game that replayability or wish to continue on in the game, because, we can also say, that there's also a cool simple story behind the game itself, but its simply half-done and the last gameplay-wise update has been done 3 years ago as a paid DLC.
Now i don't want to blame the fact that, if you want more dungeons, you'll have to pay a classic DLC to unlock it, but after that you have the story of the game still left at half, because the game itself has not been updated nowadays, and you have basically wasted money by buying a piece of puzzle to your puzzle set that is missing many more pieces.
Technically there are still some issues and bugs related to the internet of the player, since you need a stable connection to play and possibly decent one, even if you want to play by yourself in a kind of "singleplayer".
Same goes for little graphical glitches, but i'd be surprised if there weren't any.
Of course there is also like almost any free to play game something you can have to help you in the game, if you spend real money on it. Or at least you can buy stronger gear and weapons needed to progress in the game with cash, instead of in-game currency. Or some services to further improve them.
Overall this was a pretty good game, but i personally feel this game is slowly dying as it seems the developers have left the game in its state, just adding some cosmetics to milk some more cash whenever it's possible.
It had such potentials, wasted in lots of microtransactions.

TLDR; Great customization, some nice tweaks inspired by Long War. Peformance could be better and will hopefully be fixed soon. Possible black screen error and fix that worked for me below.
As I am writing this review I have played through the tutorial and experimented with the character customization. From my personal experience I can say that XCOM2 has for the most part not only met but exceeded many of my expectations. Content-wise this game is worth the full price tag. For character customization and immersion this game is spectacular. At first the vast number of selections is almost overwhelming in comparison to XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within. As for game play mechanics there have been a number of improvements such as the ability to unequip unused armor and items for all soldiers with the easy click of a button. The AI is certainly a force to be reckoned with, working toward an opposing goal and playing strategically. I am thrilled that the developers took the time to listen to their fan base and include a number of elements from the Long War Mod, which I have played and enjoyed.
Now for the not so good. All things considered, I would not write a negative review for this game based upon solely the performance issues. However, this is not to say that the performance issues are not to be overlooked. The frame rate is far from spectacular, and I receive minor-moderate lag on both parts of missions and the home base screen. Graphics and performance-wise this game does not feel optimized to its fullest potential. However, I would still recommend this title, even in its current state. Does the latency and performance need to be patched? Yes, I believe it does. However, I am placing my full faith in the developers to release patches in the months to come to eliminate many of these issues.
Lastly, one serious issue and a solution (hopefully this will be fixed soon). When played there is a chance that you will receive a black screen with music. This will make the game unplayable. However, there is an easy way around this. When click on game properties in your library, you can select 'launch preferences'. Here add "-windowed" (without the quotes), and your game will start in windowed mode. This should eliminate the black screen and allow you to play (at least it did for me). You can then press alt+enter to resume full screen mode.
I hope this review helped, and best of luck to you, Commander!

How do you review a series you enjoyed through many installments and through two different platforms? I will be reviewing dark souls 3 in a pro/ con style and end with my final conclusions.
Pro:
Nice scenery. The game looks amazing with the better graphics overhal compaired to previous installments. Besides that every location you go to looks nice and unique, easy to tell the difference between one location compaired to another. To add to that the different worlds are filled with enemies that feel cohesive to their respective land.
The music is great. I enjoy the music that is played at the fire link shrine and also the boss music for the abyss watchers.
Plenty of weapons to use. There are many of weapons from your basic solo weapons like swords, maces, ect. Now they add in the feature to have dual weapons. So the player must equip it to whatever hand they wish and they will use a single weapon but if they two hand it...the character will have 2 of that weapon. It is cool and can provide some neat combat moves.
Con:
The reuse of old enemies. It is less like they tried to add new things but made the game based on things fans liked from old dark souls games. Really it is pretty lazy and i did not want to see the wheel skeleton enemies or multiple variations of the first boss in dark souls 1.
The lack of choice in dark souls since dark souls 2. What dark souls 2 easy? yes but it had choice to it. It allowed the player to experience the game on an easier level while if players challenge themselves they could do that with their own choice. None of that is here in this game which really sucks.
The enemy placement is pretty bad which messes up flow even for this game. The idea of putting tank like enemies on narrow platforms is a horrible idea. I dont mind challenge but what this is....it is not a challenge rather poor level design.
Dark souls 3 takes inspiration from old dark souls and bloodborn. That is cool but the issue is that dark souls isnt bloodborn. Bloodborn is a fast pace dark souls game that has its mechanics dealing around being agressive and quick dodging and such. Dark souls is not that. What dark souls is...is slower and more thoughtful as to when to strike and when to dodge roll. The bosses in the two series are different and combining them in this game is a beautiful mess. It provides a clash between mechanics and combat.
There is a swamp level that not only does it poison the player similar to lower blight town from dark souls but it is unbarebly slow.  Sure there is a way to speed it up but why is it even here? It feels like a checklist in all souls and souls like games.
Conclusion:
In short i am a major dark souls fan. Played all the souls games except bloodborn on multiple different platforms till I 100% it but this game is tied for the most unenjoyable souls experience with dark souls 1 and salt and sanctuary. It is  not that i am a casual because that is obviously false but it deals with how enemies are really agressive like playing bloodborn but clashing with the slower pace of dark souls. Could i reccommend the game...no. Sure the game looks better and the music is nice but the issues are a big problem.

You know what this review's going to say. Fallout 4 is garbage. It's quite possibly the worst game Bethesda's made. That's how I see it, anyway. I originally bought this game on console, back when I USED to be a console gamer. But I had a chance at a free weekend where I thought "Yeah, the game sucked, but I can probably salvage it with mods, like I do with every game on PC." Long story short, not even mods improved what's ultimately just a bland experience. Although I haven't tried Frost. Frost looks like a great mod. It completely overhauls the game. But I digress..
The shooting is okay. There's really nothing wrong with the shooting. If you're buying this game expecting a shooter set in the Fallout universe, you're going to have a blast like I did..For a few days, anyway. If you're expecting a Fallout game, you'll be disappointed.  Having a voiced protagonist really takes away from the RPG aspect. The character you'll spend hours customizing in the AMAZING customization menu is not your own character. It is not your own story. Go ahead and invest most of your points into charisma. It won't make any significant differences in a game where violence IS the only answer, and the only way to move forward.
Let's see..What else? Graphics are terrible. It really is an ugly looking game. I'd strongly advise you to use ENBs or reshades..Anything you can get your hands on. It won't change the games hideous engine, but it'll help. Settlements. Settlements are an afterthought. Thanks to mods, you can really improve on settlement building, though. Even the dumbass settlers who are no smarter than Fawks from Fallout 3.
Now, I know what you're thinking "Oh, if he references Fallout 3 a lot, he must be blinded by nostalgia. Those games weren't great." True, but from Fallout 1 onwards to Vegas, Fallouts always had indepth RPG elements. You could go through the game as a pacifist, bringing peace to the wasteland that doesn't involve ramboing against a bunch of helpless raiders.

This is my first review, and I was a Beta tester. The time above is inaccurate.
Trove is an amazing MMO, while not the first of the genre, Trove puts a unique spin on Massively Multiplayer Online games, by using some Minecraft-esque traits, (editing the terrain, mining, etc.) and adding a bit of a classic voxel look, dungeons, and several classes without throwing into a world and saying
"Here you are, go build." There aren't swarms of quests, just dungeons you can complete if you feel like it.
Here's a more in-depth review for those of you who like to get the details.
While I said I was a Beta tester, I replayed the tutorial to see what had changed. The Tutorial consisted of a few basic goals, to give you a feel for the game. It taught you how to heal yourself, fight, basics. You were then put in a colorful hub world, where  you were guided to a tower with portals leading to several tiered worlds. This is where I was dissapointed- You had to level up to go to worlds of higher tiers, whereas in beta, I found more fun in attempting to use hit-and-run tactics to take down a tanked enemy in a high-tier world, without getting one-shot as a newbie. However, I decided not to take a point because this also encourages you to explore more in a world where you have a chance to level up like the rest of the community; you couldn't jump to a high-end world and stalk someone gone dungeoning.
Trove does not have the what-on-earth-is-that-behind-me quality of, say, a creeper in minecraft, but it doesn't give you a bird's eye view of the field either, so unless you are farming, the enemies keep you on your toes.
this leads us to equipment, because you have to know how to get that extra piece for that one dungeon you can't beat.
The easiest way is trading, after you've found something worth a trade. But you are guarenteed 2 pieces of mediocre-rare equipment that allows you to collect its style and gain flux- a currency used by the community for trading and upgrading weapons. This also allows you to get a look at gear's stats before disintegrating it.
