It's brutal. It's soul-destroying in parts. It has consequence. Think Dark Souls meets HP Lovecraft.
It seems like a simple enough, turn-based, party RPG, but that belies the elegance of some of the systems underneath. Positioning plays a huge part - with certain characters only able to deploy certain skills or target specific enemies from a particular position. This really comes to the fore when the party gets ambushed or when facing creatures capable of dragging your party members around.
Sanity plays a huge role - it's not enough to be physically healthy, but a watchful eye has to be kept on the stress levels of your party too. All it usually takes is for one of them to snap, then their demented ramblings will usually cause the swift demise of the rest of the group as well. Stress will also force you to rotate your team often, meaning you always get to experiment with different characters and different roles as you have to rest your go-to team frequently. You'll also find that your favourite guys dig themselves into all sorts of holes and end up with a variety of quirks that can otherwise mess up your desired tactics. They might develop a desire to steal things, for example, or to always poke their noses into things that common sense clearly dictates should not have noses poked in.
The difficulty curve seems a little unforgiving at first and lightens up until you step up in dungeon difficulty at the later levels. Beyond managing the party in combat, upgrading your Hamlet, equipment, skills and restorative capabilities is key here.
The art style is refreshingly different, yet still brutal and unforgiving - perfectly suiting the game's ongoing theme. The narrator is also sinister, grave and a perfect accompaniment to the horror.
In short, this is an excellent game.

I have been playing Trove for a little over a year now off and on. When it was released on steam I decided to jump back into the game and I am glad I did. The changes they made to the game are amazing, but enough about that, off to the game review!
Should I Get This Game:
Yes, first its free so try it out. Second it is a fantastic game with amazing depth. Third, ummm its free!
How To Enjoy The Game:
This game can get real repetitive really fast. Its actually a negative but not really (yeah that isn't confusing, what yes it is). The premise is you select a character and then jump into randomly generated worlds with diverse biomes to go kill things. It doesn't take much brain power just run, zoom through a dungeon kill the boss get loot, rinse and repeat. There is the first tip, this isn't a WoW or Rift or anything like that. Its a game with very simple mechanics, run kill loot. Even the end game Shadow Arenas are just one big hack and slash.
So that is one angle of the game and if you only play that angle, it will become boring very quickly! However if you dig deeper into the game you open up a world of good times.
- They have a good selection of characters and each one is very unique. Its really fun to level up each one and discover your play style. Then get gear around your play style. Get bored? switch to another character and play as that for a bit.
- They have a mastery system, brilliant. This is sort of your overall level. As you play the various aspects of the game you level up your mastery level and get some cool bonuses. Its fun to level up your characters and level up your mastery which levels higher and slower then your characters
- Professions! They have gardening, ring crafting and run crafting (tomes). Leveling up those basically require mat grinding. Yeah grinding sucks but it can be really relaxing. Pick a toon, make it a lasermancy machine and go to town.
- Fishing, why does every MMO have to have fishing these days? Well Trove does too
- Build a home and a club world! Your own unique home (cornerstone) that can be built on any open square (you will see in game). And a club world where you can design and build your own world. Create separate biomes, you can recreate Santa's North Pole, or the about to be destroyed village of Pompeii.
So if you want to really enjoy this game its about diversity. Those that like the traditional MMO formula of grind/quest level to max, enjoy end game will get really bored of this game really fast. The secret sauce here is to quest (grind) with a toon for awhile, get bored go mine for a while, get bored go fish, get bored work on your professions, get bored tweak your cornerstone, get bored expand and customize your own club world, get bored go back to your toon. That is what is really cool about this game you can do a ton of different things, I haven't even explained when you hit mastery level 30 you get hourly quests to go run X dungeons and get some sweet loot in return.
I highly recommend this game, its fantastic and they have made great progress with it. There are some exciting additions being talked about such as PvP and an Auction House. There is a ton of potential with the game and strong support for it from its players.
Technical Issues Update
As of the writing of this post queue times have been fixed (hardware upgrades). There are still performance issues but they are starting to get worked out. At heavy load times there is some rubber banding that occurs or warping. Its to be expected with how massive this game is. Every player has their own unique cornerstone (home) and club world. You have to give them credit as many MMOs have not been able to pull off either very easily.

I am not even remotely surprised by how poorly optimized and bug infested this game is. I don't care if this game is good. I know it's good. It's a major improvement in XCOM EU/EW in most ways so far. Most of which are UI and overarching map system.
But the sheer amount of bugs, performance issues, and glitches are nothing short of pathetic.
I am not even going to address the issue people are having with turn timers on nearly every mission. I don't know if it's a poor design choice yet, but any game I've ever played that restricted me with a timer that wasn't an arcade game I have profusely hated.
Here are my specs:
GTX 780 OCd +130 core/memory
i5 3570k OCd slightly
8gb RAM
850 EVO 500gb SSD
Playing on 1080p
This computer can play pretty much any game that is properly optimized on max or close to max settings at 1080p.
Let me compile a
of the
problems I've encountered so far for you. I will continue to update it as I find more.
- Game doesn't run at 60 fps consistently on any system on Earth. You must disable AA and I have to completely disable shadows to even sit anywhere near 60 when playing. I can play Arkham Knight, one of the most notoriously bad PC ports of this generation, at an average of 50-60 fps on high settings. No, not when driving the Batmobile, and yes I'm talking about after it was patched months later
- No option for resolutions over 1080p in settings. It's obviously editable in the .ini but why the hell does a PC exclusive game not have this built into the options menu ingame?
- Loading times are
long, both when loading a game and starting a mission. XCOM EU took about 3 seconds to get into a mission. This game seems to take 60 seconds or more
- I timed loading my saved game from the menu. 73 seconds is what it takes every single time I want to load my game up
- Overwatch is delayed 10 seconds or more sometimes when enemies trigger it
- Enemies are delayed several seconds once they are aware of you
- End of turn also delayed several seconds (starting to see a theme here?)
- Sometimes your units decide to shoot in the complete opposite direction at a 70 degree angle facing the Moon and pull off a move like Anjolina Jolie in Wanted. This is only a graphical bug but it also existed in XCOM EU/EW so good job on fixing that, ♥♥♥♥♥♥s
- Majority of your time is spent shooting through or getting shot through walls which apparently do not really exist and serve no purpose in the XCOM 2 universe
- Snake ♥♥♥♥s grab you through the non-existent walls constantly
- Melee enemies can hit you from 2 tiles away if there is a gap between you and the enemy
- You cannot shoot at enemies who have not "detected" you yet. By this I mean if you have already come out of hiding and there are wandering units around the map, even if you can clearly see them and have even used a battle scanner, you cannot shoot until you physically trigger them by walking close or throwing a grenade
- ENEMIES GET A FREE TURN TO KILL YOUR UNITS AFTER THEY HAVE BEEN SPOTTED. THIS IS ESPECIALLY NICE WHEN YOU'VE USED ALL OF YOUR UNITS TURNS AND A GROUP OF ENEMY UNITS DECIDE TO SHOW UP WITHOUT AN INVITATION
- Game has crashed once while in the options menu

- Screen goes black after starting a mission every single time which causes confusion as the game seems frozen. If you open steam ingame chat it will no longer load properly\
- When your unit shoots and is next to glass they play an animation to break the glass but nothing happens to it half the time
- Game feels to render floors of buildings if you move a unit that is on the ground and your last available unit is on a second or third floor
- If Central/Shen/Tygan are talking and you go to the geoscope or open ingame chat, they stop talking and you can't hear their dialogue anymore
Also it takes an ungodly amount of time just to complete 1 turn in this game. For 2 enemies to actually do their♥♥♥♥♥♥ it can take upwards of a minute for them to do what they have to do before it's your turn. That's with 2 enemies. Now imagine 5 or more.
The worst part is these are only the issues I've personally encountered. There are dozens more problems littering the community forums that I haven't even seen yet personally.
Why was this game delayed for 3 months? What the hell were they doing? Was Jake Solomon just jacking it behind his desk every day for those 3 months? And don't you find it funny how much of a striking resemblance Central bears to Jake Solomon now? It's almost like he had the dev team model him after himself. What a coincidence!
A game should never be this broken on day 1. The only excuse any genre of gaming has is MMOs which massively underestimate server capacities and have issues for days or even weeks. Take a look at any recently released games that had either minimal or no major issues.

Developers should not be given ridiculously high metacritic scores by reviewers (a 91 at this time) when this many issues exist. There are also several other reasons why I have issues with this game. Cover seems to be about as useless as not being in cover.♥♥♥♥♥♥tier Advent enemies hit me across the map while I'm in full cover with ease. I've played the older Fallout games, sans 1 and 2. It's too late for me to get into them as I detest point-and-click games. They are a relic of an era blissfully forgotten, relying on a now thankfully obsolete mechanic that we no longer need thanks to our modern game controls and 3D camera systems. That said, the point I'm getting at is that I just didn't like the Fallout games. I didn't like Brotherhood of Steel, I didn't like Fallout 3, and I absolutely hated Fallout: New Vegas. Mostly, I hated them for how they handled. I didn't like the third-person camera, I didn't like how the player character 'moonwalks' when moving in any direction but straight ahead, and didn't like the linear stories, I didn't like the bland environments, I didn't like the way NPC's tried to bore through your retinas with heat vision when you just want to know where the quest marker is taking you, and I REALLY didn't like the intro to Fallout 3, but then again, neither did anyone else, and that's why we have the alternate start mod for it.
Fallout 4... The camera is much better, the third-person animations are phenominal, the map is much more aesthetically pleaseing and diverse, the NPC interaction is leagues better, and above all else, the settlement system has brought me back for my fourth playthrough. The only hitch is that a lot of mods are needed to improve said settlement system. I also like using more modern weapons, like the AN-94 and the FN Five-seveN. Anyway, install a handful of mods, and this game is by far more enjoyable. And thanks to it, I've learned a LOT more about Fallout's lore- which is something I've always loved since I was shown the series back around 2004- than I ever would have retained by simply nodding my head an checking the wikipedia entries.

Would not recommend the Mac version at this time. Performance issues seem as bad or worse than those being reported by PC users. I'll wait a few days to see if a patch fixes things, but expect I'll have to request a refund. I was very much looking forward to XCOM 2, so hopefully the game will be worth a second look once they optimize it and resolve the performance issues.
Here are the main issues I noticed playing the tutorial and initial section on the strategic layer:
1. The game fails to launch more often than not after hitting "Play" in the initial Mac options window. I only managed to get the game to launch twice out of 8 or 9 attempts. When the game fails to launch, the XCOM 2 app is unresponsive and requires a force quit to close.
2. Very poor framerate as reported by PC users, especially during the pre-mission Skyranger sections. I was aware of the reports of poor performance and turned off anti-aliasing, ambient occlusion, and VSync before my tutorial run. Other settings were at "high" except for max texture quality, resolution at 2560x1440. Game was very laggy outside of cutscenes. Exited the game to turn on the Steam FPS counter so I could do some more fiddling with the graphics settings to try to increase the FPS, but couldn't relaunch the game.
3. The main menu screen is quite noticeably bleeding through the background at times in both missions and the strategic layer. Distracting to have a ghostly portion of a desert scene suddenly pop into view when you're assaulting an urban Advent facility.

I really, REALLY wanted to love this game like I do Dark Souls 1, but I've come to the conclusion that I'll only ever consider it a pretty good game, not great. It is still, however, much better than Dark Souls 2, which is a stain on the otherwise excellent franchise that Souls is.
But on to DS3:
I'm not a fan of the immediate bonfire warping upon starting the game. One of the reasons why the original Dark Souls was so good is that there was no teleporting in the first half of the game. This really made the world feel alive and the player more connected to it.
Dark Souls 3's world is remarkably better than Dark Souls 2's, but it doesn't reach the heights of DS1, mostly due to this constant warping back and forth from the beginning. The system feels like a combination of DS1 and DS2 in that they took the connectivity of the world (many places lead you back to others) from DS1 and the immediate warping from DS2. It really does have the interconnectivity of the world like DS1 does, but its impact is diminished due to the bonfire warping. One serious problem in the world design, though, is that there are WAY too many bonfires. The pressure and risk just isn't there when bonfires are so frequent. This makes the game feel somewhat more forgiving than the previous entries.
The bosses are excellent and well designed as always—something we've learned to expect from the Souls series by now. I'm glad the series has stayed true to its roots and kept the challenge high. Nothing really feels unfair; it's just a matter of learning the boss' attack patterns. Some bosses may seem recycled from the previous games, which is not really a surprise, since this game seems to be designed around fanservice and nostalgia more than a little. They've brought back a lot of old characters as well.
The PvP is as laggy as ever. Phantom hits and other lag-related problems are considered normal in this game. It's fun when it works, and it often does, but I wouldn't get this game for its PvP alone. Fights often (especially invasions) last very long because drinking estus is VERY safe and rolls extremely hard to punish. I'm not sure if I'm a fan of these changes. Fights just end up dragging on forever. I haven't played enough of the PvP to comment on balance.
Dark Souls 3 is also a very solid game technically: the framerate is a constant 60 with no dips to be seen, and the game looks simply amazing throughout. This makes it easy to get into. DS1 might require some wrestling with to get it working due to it being a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor port.
Overall, to me, it's a good game but not a great one. Now, my view may or may not be skewed due to this being the third Souls game that I've played. Perhaps I'd love this game if it were my first in the Souls series. It's still totally worth playing and probably serves as a great introduction to the series due to the smooth and refined gameplay.

Pros:
1. It's the same gameplay as XCOM: Enemy Unknown / Enemy Within:
a. The same camera as before.
b. The same placement cursor as before.
2. It's unforgiving, as it's supposed to be.
3. New enemies means new tactics. Forget the tactics you used before.
4. More customisation options for your soldiers.
Cons:
1. It's the same gameplay as XCOM: Enemy Unknown / Enemy Within
a. The same camera as before; which will hide important events when it decides to focus on the floor above you instead of hiding that to show you what's going on on the floor you're actually on. NEEDS AUTOROTATION AND PROPER ELEMENT HIDING!
b. The same placement cursor as before; Which will occasionally jump floors or move to a position right next to where you think you have your cursor, moving soldiers out of cover, into view of the enemy, into fire...
2. The graphics are badly optimized both on Windows and Linux, on both NVIDIA and AMD videocards.
3. It's a severe memory hog.
a. It will lock down even faster systems while loading itself into memory or unloading itself when exiting to desktop.
b. Mission areas don't load properly all the time.
4. It further removed base building from the original XCOM setup, which is the wrong direction to go in. I'm all for having a mobile base, but it's even more cramped and useless than the underground base from XCOM: Enemy Unknown / Enemy Within. Bring back the option to set up multiple bases in XCOM 3, if it ever comes to that... And what's with needing to assign engineers to "excavate" within a vehicle? It makes little sense to me.
5. The new customisation options layout for your troops is confusing to work with
a. I find myself having to skip back and forth through the different layers of menus to find the right options. The location of the items are not intuitively placed.
b. And still no option to save an outfit design so you can easily copypaste them to other troops.
6. The introductionary mission effectively leaves you with two dead soldiers in your memorial... sad times all around.
7. Too many round timers!
Overall I recommend this game for those who played XCOM: Enemy Within and enjoyed rushing missions to get meld. The barrage of round timers mostly reminded me of that, and can get annoying at times.
But I would also recommend waiting until there's been a few patches to optimize the game. Right now it runs slow as hell, the video and audio can move out of sync, and there's still the horrid camera which hides shots taken. This needs to be fixed.

What do I say about Trove? It really pushes how its like minecraft, but different.
This game is nothing at all like minecraft, and that's not a bad thing.
I've played my share of terrible games trying to feed of of Mojang's (now Microsoft's) sucess, and this game does not belong in that catagory at all.
This game is most certainly its own beast, and im actually very disappointed that the game's PR department is pushing the game as a 'Like Minecraft, BUT' games.
As for the game itself, its a highly refined MMORPG, full of a varitey of classes, weapons, and more comical items than you could shake a stick at. The biomes in this game are all very memorable, with adorable characters that had me questioning my protagonists' motives. The world is deadly, with portals scaled for difficulty, with increasing rewards as teired world go higher, into the 'UBER' levels and above. Constant new realms are created, making sure that the randomly generated worlds don't become entirely looted and scarce of resources. For a large part of the game, mining is entirely avoidable, except at higher levels where you need to craft entranes (called Adventure Portals) I do wish that there was a quicker method of mining, but i'm fine using the 'mining laser' or bombs to collect my shapestone.  The F2P system is also excellently designed, with premium accounts earning extra rewards for things such as dungeons, and a few exclusive items.
All over all this is an excellent MMORPG action/exploration game. Its very quirky and well designed, with all the in game systems working quite brilliantly with each other. Progression feels slow at times, but is very very rewarding. Lastly, this game IS NOTHING LIKE MINECRAFT.

Full of bad implementations, lack of polishing and optimzations, while it is expected that most of the bugs/freezing and simply not launching issues are going to be adressed soon, this game had plenty of testing time to actually completely avoid those, not to mention that since is a sequel, experience shouldn't be lacking, yet it does. How do every animation looks worse now? wont they ever learn? just pay attention to EVERY SINGLE dying enemy, the ragdolls are ridiculous. Lacks proper closure, explanations and is excessivelly supernatural even for an 'alien' game. Late game, you may ask yourself why you even need a gun when there's X Y Z factors present (i'll not spoil)
However that is not the worst, X-COM is known for it's difficulty, and this one derailed badly on this behalf. Best case scenario, forced a challenging concept that should have been left in the 90's. Time or turn limit, whatever people want to call it, is the plague that affected this game even in before release, that wich is clearly a disgusting attempt to compensate for the terrible (brute force oriented) A.I. Bad review? so what else is wrong with it?
-The game may simply not launch, forcing a validation check, that may or may not work
-Bad support
-Glitches, promotions sometimes simply do no work until going through the next mission (one last rookie ride maybe?)
-Even on high end machines it stutters horribly
-Every action has a 1-2 seconds delay, afterwards it may freeze for 3-5 second by the end of the action
-Every cinematic has a "hiccup" or small freeze
-Lip-synch is laughable
-Animations are clumsy and not fluid, not to say that they actually defy the laws of physics
-Shooting through walls/doors/windows and corners! never stay on a corner because it doesnt not block the line of sight as it should!
-Melee attacks over walls/doors and windows as well...
-The plot is weak, too many questions, not enough answers
-Over supernatural even for alien stuff with kame-hame-ha shows going up and down.
-Over novelized, terrible closure
-End game armors/weapons are extremely generic
-MASS EFFECT COMPLEX (this one assures a bad review by its own)
Now so I'm not being biased or simply unfair, there are the pros. It's a newer game after all, the graphic is overall better but at some heavy hardware cost, the maps are beautifuly crafted, cannot lie about that, and the customizations is awesome as well, you could spend hours just customizing your squad with very unique appearances.
TL;DR on top of the foul turn limit system, its plagued by technical issues and lacks the "smooth and polished" feel for such a title. Wait for patches and fixes, you won't be missing anything, and will save yourself some few gray hairs.

But the sheer amount of bugs, performance issues, and glitches are nothing short of pathetic.

GTX 780 OCd +130 core/memory
i5 3570k OCd slightly
8gb RAM
850 EVO 500gb SSD
Playing on 1080p
This computer can play pretty much any game that is properly optimized on max or close to max settings at 1080p.
Let me compile a
of the
problems I've encountered so far for you. I will continue to update it as I find more.
- Game doesn't run at 60 fps consistently on any system on Earth. You must disable AA and I have to completely disable shadows to even sit anywhere near 60 when playing. No, not when driving the Batmobile, and yes I'm talking about after it was patched months later

- Loading times are
long, both when loading a game and starting a mission. XCOM EU took about 3 seconds to get into a mission. This game seems to take 60 seconds or more
- I timed loading my saved game from the menu. 73 seconds is what it takes every single time I want to load my game up
- Overwatch is delayed 10 seconds or more sometimes when enemies trigger it
- Enemies are delayed several seconds once they are aware of you
- End of turn also delayed several seconds (starting to see a theme here?)
- Sometimes your units decide to shoot in the complete opposite direction at a 70 degree angle facing the Moon and pull off a move like Anjolina Jolie in Wanted. This is only a graphical bug but it also existed in XCOM EU/EW so good job on fixing that, ♥♥♥♥♥♥s
- Majority of your time is spent shooting through or getting shot through walls which apparently do not really exist and serve no purpose in the XCOM 2 universe
- Snake ♥♥♥♥s grab you through the non-existent walls constantly
- Melee enemies can hit you from 2 tiles away if there is a gap between you and the enemy
- You cannot shoot at enemies who have not "detected" you yet. By this I mean if you have already come out of hiding and there are wandering units around the map, even if you can clearly see them and have even used a battle scanner, you cannot shoot until you physically trigger them by walking close or throwing a grenade
- ENEMIES GET A FREE TURN TO KILL YOUR UNITS AFTER THEY HAVE BEEN SPOTTED. THIS IS ESPECIALLY NICE WHEN YOU'VE USED ALL OF YOUR UNITS TURNS AND A GROUP OF ENEMY UNITS DECIDE TO SHOW UP WITHOUT AN INVITATION
- Game has crashed once while in the options menu

- Game feels to render floors of buildings if you move a unit that is on the ground and your last available unit is on a second or third floor

The worst part is these are only the issues I've personally encountered. There are dozens more problems littering the community forums that I haven't even seen yet personally.
Why was this game delayed for 3 months? What the hell were they doing? Was Jake Solomon just jacking it behind his desk every day for those 3 months? And don't you find it funny how much of a striking resemblance Central bears to Jake Solomon now? It's almost like he had the dev team model him after himself. What a coincidence!
A game should never be this broken on day 1. The only excuse any genre of gaming has is MMOs which massively underestimate server capacities and have issues for days or even weeks. Take a look at any recently released games that had either minimal or no major issues.

Unturned is a surprisingly real and stressful post apocalyptic survival game that involves scavenging, crafting, resources and combat that are all creative and shockingly deep. However, it's missing some things that could make it so much better. However, as an early access game, you can't help but cut it some slack
Unturned's gameplay is quite well rounded. It's mechanics of bars at the bottom left screen keep the game active and live. Elements such as hunger, thirst, energy and oxygen are all things you have to keep track of to survive. Movement is quite smooth, and combat is surprisingly deep. Zombies, the main enemy of the game, are constantly crowding the world and are faster than your average walking speed. Battling with only your fists is a foolish idea, and although you could probably hold your own against a couple of baddies, it's best to have weapons. melee weapons have lengthes and weight, making you have to factor in the amount of time you have to swing before the sombie reaches you, and the right time to do it. Zombies pause after being hit, giving you a small break in between hits. Zombuies can notice you when you get too close, so if you want to avoid combat as much as possible, it's important to know your limits. With firearms, they can create a lot of noise, attracting more zombies. Ammo isn't the easiest to come across, especially since every gun in the game has it's own specific ammo clip, so you should use your ammunition both carefully and sparingly
The visuals of the world aren't the most innovative. It has a very Roblox-y vibe. While textures can be pretty on occasion, and shadowes can be noticable. Their not the best, but they work.
Multiplayer experiences are often well rounded. With servers to play on with different maps and modes, you'll find the multiplayer community for this game both dedicated and time consuming in the good way.
The amount of varierty in maps is an issue. Though it is early access, the six maps of Russia, PEI, Washington. Yukon, Hawaii, and Germany are not open world and have limits. They're smaller than you expect and they get old quicker than you think. The amount of maps must increase for the game to stay fresh. But with different arenas to m,ess around with in multiplayer, it may not be the best for solo players, but it's acceptable for online lovers.

text:
Darkest Dungeon is a brutal and unforgiving game, that makes you regret for silly mistakes (such as not bringing enough torches or food). It's about managing your party's actions so that the damage caused by the hostile enviroment is not as bad as it could have been, it forces you to expect the worst because it will happen eventually, even when you think everything is fine, you can never know what lurks in the dark. The game has a (SICK) narrator (OF PURE AWESOME) that I simply can't get enough, he comments on events such as the encouters, interactions with the enviroment and events during the fight, believe me, it's awesome. Camping is an awesome mechanic, that makes your party take a breath and "rest", also the stress management grants a hole new depth to the experience, you can't feel your party's wounds, but you can share a portion of their anguish. The buffs, debuffs and skills in general are quite creative, as is the classes for they follow certain patterns of RPG, but also tries to give the player something new.
I would advise new players to endure through the first shot as long as you are not able to continue, 'cause nothing beats that feeling of "holy s***, wtf is this thing?!" while trying to make the best of it. Another advice, don't get to attached to any of your heroes, 'cause you know, that one, your favorite... s/he will die.
For a game that has you controling four people at the time, it can be quite imersive, since you are actually their boss. It's a fantastic roleplaying game that gives you the freedome to tell the tale of your heroes adventures, for example, on one of my first boss fight all of my party freaked out but the Jester, who showed his Courage (quite literally, but someone who didn't play would not understand why) and not only was the only surviviour but leave throgh two or three Death Door's hits and killed the boss with two consecutive critical hits wich without it, the boss would eventually have killed my Hero. I finished the quest with my heart pumping, excited and screaming in my mind "OMG THIS GAME IS AMAZING!" and I had a story to tell, the story of Berthold, the Jester.
The downside for me is the trinket sistem, it bores me a little, but I understand it's a necessary evil, I just don't like having to browse them everytime I go on an adventure (but that maybe just me). I'm making this review before the playing the full version of the game, so I don't spoil everything, but in a sense: I Love this Game, from the art style, the sound effects and the gamplay itself. I recomendo you do yourself a favor and buy this game, also because it's an independend dev team and when titles such as this come out and deliver something that awesome with a far inferior budget, I believe it is our duty as gamers to invest and show our apreciation to it.
Sorry for any grammar mistakes, good crawling and great loot!

I've played the older Fallout games, sans 1 and 2. It's too late for me to get into them as I detest point-and-click games. They are a relic of an era blissfully forgotten, relying on a now thankfully obsolete mechanic that we no longer need thanks to our modern game controls and 3D camera systems. That said, the point I'm getting at is that I just didn't like the Fallout games. I didn't like Brotherhood of Steel, I didn't like Fallout 3, and I absolutely hated Fallout: New Vegas. Mostly, I hated them for how they handled. I didn't like the third-person camera, I didn't like how the player character 'moonwalks' when moving in any direction but straight ahead, and didn't like the linear stories, I didn't like the bland environments, I didn't like the way NPC's tried to bore through your retinas with heat vision when you just want to know where the quest marker is taking you, and I REALLY didn't like the intro to Fallout 3, but then again, neither did anyone else, and that's why we have the alternate start mod for it.
Fallout 4... The camera is much better, the third-person animations are phenominal, the map is much more aesthetically pleaseing and diverse, the NPC interaction is leagues better, and above all else, the settlement system has brought me back for my fourth playthrough. The only hitch is that a lot of mods are needed to improve said settlement system. I also like using more modern weapons, like the AN-94 and the FN Five-seveN. Anyway, install a handful of mods, and this game is by far more enjoyable. And thanks to it, I've learned a LOT more about Fallout's lore- which is something I've always loved since I was shown the series back around 2004- than I ever would have retained by simply nodding my head an checking the wikipedia entries.

Spiral Knights (SK) is a free-to-play MMORPG that I started playing in 2011.  I was instantly hooked on this simple game primarily due to the community of friends that played this game with me.  To understand the perspective of this review, I believe it would help to understand the type of player I was.  I reached the end-game completing every dungeon available.  I played at the top tier player-vs-player (PVP) level with - at the time - a vast variety of superior gear.
PROS: You do not need to invest a a single penny into SK to beat the game, or to enjoy it.  The majority of its paid content is cosmetic and to speed up the farming process.  The game can be played solo, but has its benefits for being played in a co-op party up to four players (random or friends).  These benefits include more loot drops, a teammate revival system, and the normal benefits with playing with a party of friends.  There is no character leveling system, and your advancement comes from upgrading your armor and weapons.
CONS: For an MMORPG, however, SK has many flaws.  The game does not offer a spell casting system (aside from the addition of pets in late 2013), only the choice of swords, guns, bombs, and a shield.  By and large, swords are the superior weapon of choice, though balances over the course of 4 years have attempted to narrowed this superiorty gap.  In addition, the game is extremely limited in its end-game content, with the storyline still not being completed for over 3 years.  SK is constantly riddled with latency issues, and simple balances suggested by the community are largely ignored despite the community's desire to be involved with the direction that SK will take.
Verdict: SK is honestly a cute, fun, and simple game.  The game has undergone a variety of changes over the several years it has been out; these changes are largely aesthetic, however.  SK suffers from the lack of new content and a completed storyline.  It is plagued with latency issues and the lack of balancing.  While I would recommend more avid gamers to look into other free MMORPG game such as Warframe, Vindictus, or Neverwinter.  SK does draw from its strengths - being cute, free, and simple - and it can truly offer many hours of fun memories with the right group of players.

This is what I think of the game:
Graphics/artwork: I feel as though the game really shines for it cartoonish like artwork, the very gothic designs of both the heroes and the monsters give you the sense of this is not a happy game at all, bad things are more likely to happen. You cannot escape madness or death. Your characters will fall, either in death or by diseases or perhaps their own stress. You can't be sure. The animations are spot on and you can get really immersed into the game.
Gameplay: I like a lot of the mechanics of the game, the idea that your heroes can bleed, can be poisoned, need to eat. It makes you feel for their drunken souls. But alas, you can’t keep them all. The first thing I noticed in the game is this, people are going to die, you are going to fail and you most certainly will have to work for a victory. The terminology and what they mean is explained very well, most are self-explanatory. The stats of the heroes makes sense and I like how they are random (except the first two heroes), you will never always get the Heroes you want, you will sometime be surprised how well a hero does or be disgusted at their lack of skill.
The hamlet/Base: It is a very nice place for one that is cursed. For this is where you can let your heroes rest up and for you to upgrade with that shiny gold you picked off the corpses of your enemies. Despite there being lots of buildings, it’s not that bad, you can guess what is what. Tavern and Abbey for stress relief, Guild and Blacksmith to upgrade skills and equipment. You have your local No-mad to give you those trinkets that boost your characters. The camp of the survivor outside so you can learn camping skills. Then the all-important stage coach that delivers the poor sods to their deaths.
Narrator: This guy…has got to be the best voice actor ever…simply because…he makes you want to KILL HIM!! Yes I know that my character has messed up! Yes I know that swine pig monster has just taken one of my heroes out! I KNOW!....Oh you’re good…

A dungeon crawler that will have you cursing at your monitor.  As with any roguelike, it's hard, will punish mistakes, and you won't be getting through unscathed.  The PTSD your heroes will accumulate makes for a unique mechanic as you scour dungeon after dungeon for more gold and heirlooms to upgrade the hamlet, all for the purpose of cleansing the blighted estate.  But the gold will never be enough to do everything you want.  You'll have to manage the stress and trauma of your party and yes, you'll be sending adventurers to their doom for the sake of getting enough to better outfit the next expedition.
Those that survive will come back with quirks, diseases, and afflictions that will need to be managed through the vices of the tavern or the piety of the abbey.  While these will lower stress and afflictions, they are not without risk in and of themselves.  Your prized hero might become God-fearing and will only pray at the transept in the abbey, forsaking all other avenues of stress removal.  This becomes exceptionally frustrating if, say, they also acquire the 'faithless' quirk which will forbid them from using said transept.  Yes, quirks can synergize in both positive and negative ways.  Your highwayman may have the gambler quirk, for which they will only gamble to reduce stress.  They may also have the 'known cheat' quirk which prevents them from gambling, effectively barring them from reducing stress until one of the quirks is removed for a hefty sum of gold at the sanitarium.
You'll be managing these disorders and things can quickly spiral out of control on a dungeon run.  It's not all bad as sometimes when the stress maxes out, your character will buckle down and emerge virtuous, finding hidden strengths amidst the horror that embolden their effectiveness,  Unfortunately this effect will only last until the end of the crawl or until you make camp, unlike the negative afflictions which are persistent until the stress is lowered.  But just as there are negative quirks, there also are positive ones which add buffs or bonuses to the hero.
The art style is fantastic with a gritty, gothic presentation that evokes a graphic novel.  The music is appropriately foreboding.  The RNG will decimate you but it is almost impossible to completely lose.  You may have your dream team wiped out through a string of bad luck but your next visit to the hamlet will bring in fresh meat to the grinder.  The only limit is your own resolve.
Honestly it's a breath of fresh air, as I generally dislike turn-based combat affairs but the atmosphere and mechanics keep everything appropriately grim and desperate as you slowly hack, bludgeon and shoot your way through the ruined estate.
Your oversimplified amalgamation would be Diablo meets Pokemon with a helping of Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem and some Lovecraft for good measure.
It's tough but never impossible, just exceedingly frustrating as things can go from amazing to horrible and vice versa alarmingly quick.  Also the text bubbles of your characters are exceedingly awesome/hilarious and add character to the quirks and afflictions.
I probably have acquired the 'Masochistic' affliction but I gotta give it my endorsement.  9/10

I am giving a "Not recommended" for the release version. Wait for a couple of patches is my recommendation
Rasons:
- Really bad performance, even on top end systems, like mine. The game recommends me to use highest settings with my system but I actually have to run in medium settings as not to get stuttering or massive frame rate drops. It is a shame considering how good the game looks in max settings :(
- Turns are stalling in between player/alien turn switches.
- This is a big negative one one for me: Timed missions are poorly implemented. The timers are way too short.  Missions often end after just 8 turns. It is just enough time to force you to rush to a mission end but you can't enjoy the map or possible side actions.  On top of that those timed missions are way too numerous. It makes it impossible to enjoy a stretched out tactical game for those players who like it slower paced and are not overly aggresive.
- Melee is far too overpowered. All you need is a squad of sword swinging maniacs and you cut through the aliens like butter. No more tactical weapon usage required.
- Camera angles are awkward at times
- Grenades are bugged in some instances when you explode walls
- character stances are bugged in somes instances and facing the wrong way while shooting
Plus a dozen other smaller bugs that by themself can be overlooked but with those piling up fast are starting to annoy a lot.
It very much looks like this game did not get a proper quality control testing before release. *sigh*

Like any MMORPG, you have a character, several classes that can be modified in many ways, an economy, and a leveling system, but Trove has its own, unique characteristics. For example, in most MMORPG's, you are only allowed one class and to get others, you either need to make a new account, or buy a new one with paid currency. In Trove, you are allowed to get all classes under 1 account with the ingame currency [Doesn't take Long] or a paid currency [I personally don't recommend buying classes].
There are also different areas to fight for different levels of classes. So for beginners, they can spawn into the Novice World and experts can spawn into Uber 5 or Uber 6 worlds. This all might sound like gibberish, but when starting the game, there is this amazing tutorial that teaches you the basics and advanced material of the game, making it easy for you to learn.
Pros/Great Aspects Of Trove
Amazing and helpful Community
Easy to learn
Not Pay 2 Win, but Freemium [This means that you are not losing any features by playing this game for free, but paying will gain you cosmetics or virtual goods. You will be as good as a paid player]
Great Economy
Love the combat styles with each class. Each class is unique, making it fun to learn how to play each.
Patches every week or 2 weeks. This means there will always be new content availible and not the same stuff over and over.
Multiplayer! You will definitely find a player on your friends list playing this game!

People who scam and are sometimes unpunished. Scamming is hard but plausible

As you can see, Trove is an amazing game, and I believe the pros outweigh the cons heavily. Its a free game made by Trion Worlds and is small to download. If you are looking for a game, I believe Trove might be right for you.

Yet another superb concept ruined by the absolute obsession of anti-fun, RNG-ridden, unrewarding gameplay.
With experience, success, and careful planning you still have an undue opportunity at every turn to meet sudden and complete failure. This model is meant for the quick, albeit repetitive gameplay of FTL and other peers, but not for a game with long-term goals such as this. It is, instead, tiring and leaves you hestitating every time you hover your cursor of the 'Play' button in your steam library.
After each inevitable failure (which the game does duly warn you), you spend more time building up in the same fashion either using tried and true strategies honed in the community (cheese) or once again roll the proverbial (and literal) dice. The dark, brooding, Lovecraftian atmosphere that drew me to this title quickly wears off, the novelty rapidly dissipates amidst and endless and unrewarding grind dotted with enemy CRIT streaks and instances of accruing 75% of your max stress in one skirmish.
If you can grab it one sale for cheap, might be worth a few hours to see the interesting art style and immerse yourself in a nice, Lovecraftian atmosphere but don't plan on a longterm affair with this particular game unless you're one of the difficulty-obsessed types who sit down at their PC and are satisfied until they've completed some grey-hair sprouting challenge.

I have had so much fun with this game. Originally, I was expecting something akin to Terraria, but I was quickly impressed with Starbound. Upon beaming down to my first planet, I landed in a pool of toxic water and was marauded by three small armadillos. After managing to fend them off and recover from the poison, I set about building a house to take shelter from the animals and acid rain which had just began to pour down. If this was just a Threat Level 1 planet, I was cringing at the thought of anything higher. After finding the courage to venture outside, I delved deep underground and collected all the ore I could. When I emerged, I crafted myself a full set of the highest level armor I could (being a Hyotl, this was Pond armor) and several tools and weapons. I have continued on this path (fueling my futuristic starship with the most advanced source of fuel known to man and alien alike: Coal!) and have explored about seventeen star systems. I haven't experienced this much space-exploration fun in my gaming career.
Pros:
-Appealing, well animated graphics, and a nice pixel asthetic.
-Very pleasing soundtrack.
-Weapons feel smooth and well balanced (plus you don't have to click every time you want to swing it!)
-Exploration is fun, and the randomly generated planets are a pretty awesome concept, and well executed.
Cons:
-The game is still in beta, and is largely unfinished.
-The quest line is short, and can be unclear at times.
-Hitboxes can be unclear.
-Looking for fuel can be tedious if not done with exploration.
I would really recommend this to anyone, really. I had a lot of fun with it, and will probably do so for many, many more hours.

That should tell you all you need to know. All jokes aside however, this is a game for people who demand little depth and complexity. This is for the people who want a nice relaxing power trip through the park. Mostly though it's for people who know little to nothing about Fallout.
Once again Bethesda refuses to follow up the story laid out by the first two games and continued in New Vegas. They demand on keeping things on the East Coast, a setting over which they have creative control which is original to them. There's nothing wrong with that at all. If they don't want to be tethered to a previous company's work then more power to them. However they display the same arrogance and disregard for the original games by including bits and pieces from the originals. Why are Super Mutants in the East when they were created by accident in the West? Why are bottlecaps legal tender in the East when the practice originated from the Hub in the West? Some of these things are small and ignorable; others are not and just display a real sense of laziness and lack of attention to detail by the producers.
In terms of the physical setting we get something that looks like a graphical upgrade of Fallout 3.
-Overpasses with large chunks missing
-Nondescript industrial areas
-City streets with copypasted assets
-Corrugated iron shacks
-Office buildings with stairs, cubicles, and desks
The same things over and over again. Every so often there's a patch which looks like someone put some effort into creating something with character, but this is rare. Perhaps the worst offender in the setting dept. comes from the intact urban areas. Here you have tall buildings where you can look out onto Boston and see all the low-res textures where sacrifices had to be made in order for your rig to not catch on fire. Guess what? The same goddamn thing happens in Skyrim when Toddy boy wanted you to go into Whiterun and look out across the landscape - specifically at all those mountains he lied about being climbable. These grand Bethesda vistas don't work, yet the developers continue putting them in their games. This cannot be ignored either. You will have quests which take you to the tops of buildings where Super Mutants are taking shots at you from below; I challenge anyone to aim down from these natural sniper nests and
notice all the buildings in the distance that look like mass-produced plastic toys made in China. It's worse than immersion breaking; in my case I started musing over the vagaries of programming and balancing performance with creative design.
Sweet Jesus though, it's all so boring. Here's rubble. There's yet another camp. It's so predictable and uninspired. What hurts the most are places which could have been something. Goodneighbor is a prime example. It's a seedy neo-noir town evoking hints of Blade Runner and Shadowrun, but there's barely anything there. Even in the trailer when the camera pulls back over Goodneighbor there are only a handful of NPC's on screen, and lo and behold, that's what you get in-game. Once more, why does Bethesda insist on creating small towns populated by a few dozen characters and then referring to these places as towns and cities? They haven't learned their lesson since Oblivion, and I doubt they ever will. Then there's this old dog track where bandits have taken to reprogramming robots to race and betting on them. That's something unique, quirky, and interesting, but nope. Get close, and they all aggro because you know - all bandits are part of the closely-knit bandit faction and utterly opposed to the noble protagonist.
Speaking of bandits and all other of ne'er do wells attacking you on sight, I cannot and will not forgive this game for restricting the player to, "The Nice Guy Run." At most you can deviate from knight in shining armor to flippant rascal with a heart of gold. There's no karma. There's no acknowledgement of any character besides the good guy. You are pigeon-holed into the story of Bethesda's choosing with the character they want you to play. They even go so far as to give your character a voice as if putting up a sonic scaffold for who they want you to be - and that voice is god-awful. Moreover what if you want to play a character who goes native and wears thrown-together bandit armor while wielding a orc-looking machine gun? Too bad the second you enter into dialogue you'll be greeted by a milquetoast voice that sounds completely but not entirely unlike a bandit.
Dear Todd,
Making a game that is open and not just hallways only fulfills the most basic definition of an open world game. That's development by the bloody numbers.
Speaking of that orc machinegun, Fallout 4 does a fantastic job of creating the illusion of variety by disguising the small number of weapon models with weapon mods. Here are those base models:
-.44 pistol
-10mm pistol
-Assault rifle
-Combat rifle
-Gauss rifle
-Hunting rifle
-Railway rifle
-Submachine gun
-Combat shotgun
-Double-barrel shotgun
-Pipe gun
-Pipe revolver
-Pipe bolt-action
-Fat Man
-Flamer
-Junk Jet
-Minigun
-Missile launcher
-Institute laster
-Laser musket
-Laser gun
-Gatling laser
-Plasma gun
-Alien blaster
-Cryolater
-Gamma gun
There you go. That's all the base gun models. From there you can choose from different grips, receivers, barrels, sights, etc. Ultimately though unless you're trying to RP a character with some specific equipment, most of those mods will be disregarded in favor of picking the best in slot mods. Note the lack of unique models, the sheer vapidness and absence of character. Just hotswap things to make a gun that seems unique until you eventually see it in the field by virtue of simple probability. There are so-called unique weapons that have effects - think of Diablo and Borderlands - but calling them unique? Let's take this weapon called, "Old Faithful," for example. From the wiki:
"Old Faithful bears the Instigating effect, which does double damage if the target is at full health, making it a strong choice early in the game for stealthy characters, as a sneak attack against an enemy at full health will deal quadruple the base damage. The specific weapon modifications fitted to the gun when purchased are level dependent and will vary.
it can be converted to a rifle, expanding its usefulness to Rifleman characters as well as Gunslingers and Commandos."
Base Weapon: Laser Gun
Type: Unique Laser Gun
Special: Does double damage if the target is at full health
Wowee zowee

This game is the very definition of both Pay to Win and Pay to Play.
-You can only play for a little bit before your "fuel" runs out, because it takes some sort of resource to enter a dungeon. This "fuel" takes a few hours to recharge. Want to
for longer than you
to play? BUY BUY BUY!
-Those costumes sure do look neat. I bet you're wondering how to get them. Wait, it takes some
resource to obtain? BUY BUY BUY!
-Feel like your equipment isn't leveling up fast enough? Feel like you don't have enough cash? BUY BUY BUY!
-Say you're tired of a costume, and it could fetch a pretty penny at the auction house. Aw shucks, it's bound to your character? Guess what you have to do in order to remove it. BUY BUY BUY!
-Do you want to know how to get that really cool weapon you can use from the beginning, but it has really high stats anyways? BUY BUY BUY!
-It's taking forever to gather those resources, isn't it? By your estimate, it'll take you at least a week to craft the armor you want. How do you get the materials faster? BUY BUY BUY!
-Want to open up that chest? The only way to do it is to BUY BUY BUY!
This game runs on microtransactions, and those microtransactions let you win. Plus, it's so difficult to get to the interesting parts of the game that you're forced to choose between crippled progression and immediate satisfaction. You can spend about two hundred (real life, US) dollars and you'll be able to get to the end game content within a day.
Gameplay is very boring, it's all click based, and there's no Skinner Box effect or additional abilities to keep it interesting like Diablo did. The closest they have are these one-use item drops. Fighting hordes of enemies, rather than engaging, can quickly become tedious.
The graphics are okay for what they're supposed to be.
The enemies are repetitive, and some of their sound effects can become irritating after a while.
The level design varies enough to be engaging, until you realize that they re-use many of the assets for later dungeons.
The auction house's prices are ridiculously inflated. Just because this happens often in MMO games doesn't mean it should be the norm. The worst part about this isn't really the fact that it's like this, it's the reason the auction house is like this. Everyone just spends their money to get materials and cash in order to get the stuff a normal player would work for. These are almost always things you can craft from items you buy at the auction house, since the drop rate for crafting materials is gimped. Then, since the people who spend real money on this game get to the stuff first, they get to set the price. So not only does the game put you in a position where it's better to pay to win, the people who pay to win
put you in a position where it's better to pay to win.
On the plus side, there's a smoking pipe accessory. I got some enjoyment out of smoking my pipe while playing a character who smokes a pipe.
In summary:
The people behind Spiral Knights have created one of the most profitable free games I've ever witnessed. Please note that a profitable game does not necessarily equate to a good game. I don't mind if they keep doing what they're doing, and I don't intend to stop them. I mean, there's plenty of children and spoiled teenagers around to suck away their parents' money and spit it into this game. They'll grow out of it. But to any adult who plays this, I can only ask that rather than wasting your disposable income on this game, you spend it on a quality one which doesn't exist solely to sponge away your earnings (you did
it, right?)

Dark Souls is punishing
1. Start the game with zero info and end the game with almost none. Average players will require wiki to learn anything.
2. Every enemy pretty much kills you when you first encounter it, then you're sent back to restart the whole area. Die again? Punished again. All enemies respawn as well, so you better hope you can beat that enemy which killed you or repeat again.
3. Bosses are formulaic and require precise memorization to beat. You simply cannot go into the boss fights and win from skill, you MUST memorize. Some great players can, but the developer should empower the player to be able to win on the first try or at least learn then win shortly thereafter. Souls bosses like Nameless King and Pontiff have so many movesets that dying 10+ times is not just common but expected. Every boss attempt that fails requires you to slog through the entire area. You can't even enter the boss fight with full health because enemies can even kill you on the way there!
5. The above punishment encourages running past enemies because all you want is to fight the boss again. Your punishment is to speedrun. What you want doesn't matter. Bad design!
6. Enemies often lie in wait in key moments. For example, you see an enemy walking but his back is turned. You carefully sneak up but then 3 enemies fall on your head and stun gank you. So many times I died to those dogs in Irithyll that were at the top of the staircase where you could not see. Memory saves your life the second try, not skill.
7. Enemy difficulty is artificial- they have ultra health and deal awful amounts of damage. If bosses were truly hard, then they would still be tough even if you and the boss did similar damage with similar health. No, Souls games stack odds against you. Dancer, for example- you can perfectly dodge every attack except the tail end of one spinning combo... you die. This is artificial. It's their bigger numbers vs your lesser numbers=difficult. Apparently, in the Souls fanbase this difficulty is acceptable and rewarding.
8. Soulsborne series as a whole and the community encourage exploits. For example, in Bloodborne within the first 20 minutes you're forced to fight two werewolves  blocking your path- Fextralife wiki states to lure them to a house where they get stuck in a door so you can just whale on them. Another example from wiki, Dark Souls 3 prior to the Road of Sacrifices an ice knight which few could beat, you will read to lure it to an elevator shaft where it will stupidly fall to its death. BAD. DESIGN. When this is considered good advice the game is seriously messed up. None of this was even patched.
I could go on for another block paragraph but you get it. 128 hours of Dark Souls 3 and 110 hours of Bloodborne, I've learned I love it all for what it does right and overcome its glaring faults. This, plus memorization was required to fully enjoy the series. This should not be so.
As for the game itself, it is clunky, full of bugs, camera issues get you killed hourly, crashing is common every 15-60 minutes, massive input lag, server lag (so awful when invaded by players as they skitter all over the place), poor hit detection which is both a cause of death to you but also something you can exploit, walls cause a stun on you if you are too close with a slashing weapon allowing enemies to combo you, stamina system creates undue hardship as you have to manage stamina as if it were just another health bar, shields do almost nothing forcing player to dodge which is not realistic combat for a game which fans praise as realistic.
The list of bugs goes on. Most can be overcome, many will persist. So much in battle is considered, including bugs which increases difficulty even more. You will learn to remember not to swing near walls so in a hard fight you have to plan your dodges for better positioning to overcome this dreadful issue. That's my most hated issue.
The deadliest enemy in the entire Soulsborne series of games is. the. freakin. CAMERA. It's maddening because every time you fight a boss you are always in a crowded area and the camera is physical so it goes crazy, even reversing direction or flat-out refusing to pan at all because of nearby clutter. A great example, in Bloodborne Gascoigne is in a graveyard and every single tombstone hits the camera causing the above. Cleric beast, you are on a small bridge with a hulking beast whose arms are so long it can swipe the entire width of the bridge and who is so tall locking on will cause you to lose sight of yourself. Yhorm the Giant will absolutely send the camera into a mental hospital.
The delevopers are laughing at you.There are innumerable instances where hulking enemies are in tiny halls that you eventually realize this is intentional from the developers. It is not a 8ft tall knight with a sword either, it is an 8ft tall knight in a tiny hallway with a 20ft glaive, but does his weapon hit the walls....... nope but yours does. How ab when an enemy getstuck in a wall, eas kill huh? Nope you cannot hit him but he will hit you.
I am done! Rant over. I will likely play this game the rest of my life. Don't ask why. I'd rather not say anything good about it. Off to play more Souls and cut myself because that is how I get meh gost these days.

Just like every other forum and post that a newbie complains on, there will be 500 Souls fans on patrol to make him into a liar and a troll. Don't be fooled. These people patrol forums more than they play the game. Actual statistic shows only 10% of people who play Souls games ever finish, so they represent an extreme minority. So, my review is positive. Why?
I (unlike others) found this game entertaining and immersive. I'm not going to go into detail with everything but a few things that I disagree with are:
1. These new perks are nothing like skills and they are so much more basic.
I found the perks were unqiue and different. Things like being able to swim under water without getting RADS and eating human flesh to survive were clever things. Also each S.P.E.C.I.A.L skill had their own final ability that was a sort of maxed out perk that would grant the player a reward for putting points into that category. Also having that sheet there with the different pictures helps you see how your character was built.
2. Quests are lack luster and repetitive.
Ignoring the whole Preston Garvey meme, I also disagreed with this popular opinion. I thought that each quest had a meaning and in some way helped worked towards finding Shaun and the killing Kellog. Also the final few quests in which you know who Shaun really is and now you have to decide what to do and which faction to side with was suspensful and each moment I would question my choice.
3. Not enough 'Role Play' in the game for it to be an RPG

I feel that the game has enough of this inside the game. The choice of how you go about finding your son or getting revenge is already opening up different options. Also with mods (and I do count those as being part of the game as Fallout 4 and other Bethesda games are so open to modders that it is part of its culture) you can add tonnes of different quests.
All of this is not to say that the game has its issues, however I feel that the pros outweigh the cons. Some things that I do heavily dislike are:
1.  The dialouge system.

This was a total disaster. I'm not talking about the voice overs thats something of its own, but just the text options of things that you can say. First of all they are basically all of the same thing. Second some of them are misleading and you may end up making a mistake, because you said something you didn't mean. Thridly the options that are there are complete and utter trash. There is no depth in what you say. No humour or personality. Its so robotic and bland, All of it is the same. Boring and uninteresting. Making it hard to connect with your character which should be something you should be able to do with ease in a game like this.
2. The voice overs, over lapping dialouge and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ lip syncing.

Also tying in with what I just said, a lot of people were un happy with the way the voice overs were done. If you were to watch a video or read an article what you might gte out of it is that people just want a silent text reading, but that's not true. What we wanted were options. The characters should have had a wide range of voice types (yes this takes a long time, but we would have waited for the game if it was better) however it should not only include different voice options but also just an option to have no voice over at all. Some people do prefer this over a voice over (myself not included). Now, something that really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off was most of the time (and it still does this) near the end of a character speaking the next part of dialouge will come on without the previous completely finishing. This in unummersive and down right annoying as you will miss out on some useful information or a crucial part of speech that you needed to hear. They youtuber Rags pointed this out on one of his videos about the game and also showed examples of this where it caused him to miss out on important infromation. He also showed another game (The Witcher 3) do parts of dialuge without this problem. Now the final part of this problem was the lip syncing. It seems that all Bethesda games are like this and have very bad jobs at making facial movements and the dialouge go together. Bethesda (being such a big company with so much time and money) should not be having these issues. The formentioned example about Witcher 3 also had perfect lip syncing and put Fallout 4 to shame.
3. The bugs.
Bethesda games are notorious for being bug ridden and sometimes at launch un plyable due to game breaking bugs. Luckily when I played through the game there weren't so many bugs. However this has a bright side, because Fallout 4 was actuually didn't have too many. I did some google searches and while there were some reports of bugs most people were saying that they didn't experience too many game breaking bugs, which was good to hear. I was big on XCOM EU and EW.  Due to the hype around the game and my experience with the franchise, I decided to give it a shot.
I'm glad I did.
Good - The gameplay is relatviely smooth with a few hiccups here and there on my 4 year old system.  That's excellent considering it was a midrange build at the time - the game seems fairly well optimized.  The actual gameplay and UI is great, giving clear indicators of your chances of success and the reasons for those chances (terrain, debuffs, etc).  The story so far is somewhat generic but engaging, with a cohesive storyline.  Game appears to have a lot of tactical depth, but I will need more time to unlock more items, features, and abilities to really determine that.
Bad - RNG can really hurt you.  That is somewhat expected given the nature of the game, but don't be surprised when you restart the same mission 2-3 times due to some bad dice rolls.
Conclusion - Great game, easily an 8/10 if you like tactical squad based games with RNG elements.  If you were a fan of the previous games, you'll probably enjoy this one too.

While I was looking forward to the sequal this game apparantly is designed to break you before you even get out of the tutorial stage. It was clearly designed for those who have played Enemy Unknown on Classic and have their game down to a science. It is VERY newcomer unfriendly.
I was happily enjoying the game until it started hitting me with missions while was in the VERY LONG process of trying to accomplish any of the supply pickups. I hadn't even made contact with my first new outpost when the game started hitting me with different alien types that started shredding me apart with myself unable to counter attack with nothing but a squad of nothing but rookies, and very low ranking specialists.
Almost ALL the missions are on timers requiring you to play VERY AGGRESSILY in order to feel as though you're accomplishing anything. Anyone who's played XCOM will tell you that playing with that level of aggression with low level specialists and rookies is pure suicide. Failing the objectives will cause a swift decline in your ability to fight back effectively ending your game before you even make it out of the tutorial stage.
Speaking of the Tutorial Stage. I feel as though Firaxes was trying to push too much too quickly. I was quickly beaten and destroyed on my very first mission when they brought in a Sectoid. My rookies were unprepared to combat such a high level enemy (on the very first mission no less) with their woefully underdeveloped weapons and armor. If anything the aliens represent a mid-game threat and their number rapidly increase to the point where you're facing down packs of mid-game enemies and you haven't even completed your first major objective when the game gets done hand holding you.
A lot of the missions I tried to ignore in favor of picking up more supplies but the game kept telling me "No. This is a high priority mission. You shouldn't skip this." With each one throwing a new objective at me. I hadn't even had time to catch my breath and consider how to accomplish the last objective better before I had a new feature to contend with. Again I feel that Firaxes is rushing the progressing trying to show me all the cool new stuff they've done. "Oh look at this new alien! See what it can do! Look at this new objective! You've never done this before have you? Look a new way to play!" Dear god can I just catch my breath and consider how my last mission went first?
Enemy Unknown (and Enemy Within) were much better at letting you get comfortable before throwing something new at you. You were just uncomfortable enough until you got toward the endgame and you were a much more equal footting. XCOM 2 is dedicated to smashing you flat until a mountain of new feature after new feature until you finally lose or just give up out of sheer frustration.
I get they wanted to make it like a resistance game where you were hounded at every turn but this game dooms you from the start. And I was playing on Normal Mode. It felt like playing on Classic from Enemy Unknown.
It's fun for all of about 3 hours. Then the inability to pick up resources because of constantly running missions demanding your attention because they have some new feature to show you cause you to hit a brick wall very quickly.
"Oh but Adhock that the point of the game! You have to make the hard choices!"
What hard choices? The choice of ether losing the game because of the inability to stop alien progression while I'm trying to ensure I'm relatively stocked up enough to advance my gear or let myself get smashed flat trying to keep the aliens from advancing their endgame causing me to loose all my soldier with the inability to gear them or get more because I'm too poor?
It's a lose-lose situation ether way. It takes too long to get supplies and they hit with higher tier enemies that should be saved for further in the game. I was expecting to clash with Advent Basic soldiers much like EU Sectoid until I made myself enough of a pain the aliens would respond in force with their bigger and badder units.
Apparantly ADVENT doesn't have enough troops that the aliens feel the need to come out swinging harder then they should instead of letting ADVENT troops do their jobs before taking matters into their own hands when you prove too tough for them. Look at a lot of the gameplay videos. Most of the spawns are basic ADVENT soldiers and their counterparts with perhaps one to two aliens per map. I'm getting hammered with four or five aliens right out the starting gate.
And don't even get me started on concealment. The mission that finally broke me my soldiers were boxed in by civilans and the act of trying to get past them cause me to drop concealment on my first move and there were too many aliens to punch through. I lost the mission entirely as the overaggressive push required to reach the objective in time caused me to lose half my squad. When the time ran out the aliens finished off the other bedragged half.
Which effectively dropped me to only two or three soldiers left unable to field another unit. Because the timers to gain supplies were too long and I kept taking missions I was unable to get more soldiers. Game over.
Save your money. Wait until the modders even the playing field for the early game. Right now it's clear that you have to mod to even survive the tutorial. Because it sure as hell isn't balanced in the early game to where it feels unbalanced but you have a chance.
This is unbalanced with intent to break you before you even hit the play button.
Do not buy the game.

This game feels very original and stands out from the crowd of RPG style games. I find it very easy to play but a nightmare to master. It is addictive and frustrating all at once.
You WILL fail. You WILL die. You WILL ask why oh why?
But you WILL come back for more!
So, recruit your heroes and equip them for an adventure - then its simple point and click to move and interact with the environment. Be prepared for traps and loot.
Then comes the combat, which is turn based and not just click and hope - look at your characters stats and plan accordingly - Melee, Ranged, Healing, Buff, etc. All the while your Heroes stress levels is vital to maintain as low as possible - let it get above a certain threshold and they will develop bad traits and make your adventure all the more challenging.
Ensure they survive hower and back at the Hamlet you can get them treated and even preserve some of the more useful traits - provided you have the gold!
Overall, its a great little game to own and you will keep coming back for more punishment!

I was big on XCOM EU and EW.  Due to the hype around the game and my experience with the franchise, I decided to give it a shot.
I'm glad I did.
Good - The gameplay is relatviely smooth with a few hiccups here and there on my 4 year old system.  That's excellent considering it was a midrange build at the time - the game seems fairly well optimized.  The actual gameplay and UI is great, giving clear indicators of your chances of success and the reasons for those chances (terrain, debuffs, etc).  The story so far is somewhat generic but engaging, with a cohesive storyline.  Game appears to have a lot of tactical depth, but I will need more time to unlock more items, features, and abilities to really determine that.
Bad - RNG can really hurt you.  That is somewhat expected given the nature of the game, but don't be surprised when you restart the same mission 2-3 times due to some bad dice rolls.
Conclusion - Great game, easily an 8/10 if you like tactical squad based games with RNG elements.  If you were a fan of the previous games, you'll probably enjoy this one too.

This part of the analogy isn't super relevant. The point is that Mao has a lot in common with Rogue-like games.
When you play a Rogue-like you're at the mercy of a set of unknown rules. And it's not even your awful friend Dave who's making them up. The rules are written by some software developer who didn't even go to your high school and probably didn't even know Dave's sister back then. Maybe they're dating now, whatever, it doesn't matter.
There are a couple of ways of looking at this power dynamic. You can feel bullied and cornered, or you can accept that you'll be defeated many, many times and decide to use each defeat to learn little scraps of information that will help you exploit the rules and do a little better next time.
I'm no masochist. I mean, I
Dave on facbook to be nice, but I unsubscribed from his feed. If a game tortures me too much, I'm out. There's too much other good stuff out there to play.
I
get the appeal of the second approach though. The game doesn't
kill me in real life. It gives me infinite chances. There's fun to be had in hacking it until it breaks. It all boils down to how much fun I'm having figuring out the rules.
That's the make-or-break for Rogue-likes I think and that's why this review is marked positive. It can feel like a grind at times - like "OK I get it, I learned this lesson. This party configuration should be shredding this fight but Dave just keeps lying about the rolls he's getting behind that DM screen!"
He's not, it's just bad luck. But whatever, Dave is the worst. Anyway, Amber return my calls. I know you're single again.
