So, my review is positive. Why?
I (unlike others) found this game entertaining and immersive. I'm not going to go into detail with everything but a few things that I disagree with are:
1. These new perks are nothing like skills and they are so much more basic.
I found the perks were unqiue and different. Things like being able to swim under water without getting RADS and eating human flesh to survive were clever things. Also each S.P.E.C.I.A.L skill had their own final ability that was a sort of maxed out perk that would grant the player a reward for putting points into that category. Also having that sheet there with the different pictures helps you see how your character was built.
2. Quests are lack luster and repetitive.
Ignoring the whole Preston Garvey meme, I also disagreed with this popular opinion. I thought that each quest had a meaning and in some way helped worked towards finding Shaun and the killing Kellog. Also the final few quests in which you know who Shaun really is and now you have to decide what to do and which faction to side with was suspensful and each moment I would question my choice.
3. Not enough 'Role Play' in the game for it to be an RPG

I feel that the game has enough of this inside the game. The choice of how you go about finding your son or getting revenge is already opening up different options. Also with mods (and I do count those as being part of the game as Fallout 4 and other Bethesda games are so open to modders that it is part of its culture) you can add tonnes of different quests.
All of this is not to say that the game has its issues, however I feel that the pros outweigh the cons. Some things that I do heavily dislike are:
1.  The dialouge system.

This was a total disaster. I'm not talking about the voice overs thats something of its own, but just the text options of things that you can say. First of all they are basically all of the same thing. Second some of them are misleading and you may end up making a mistake, because you said something you didn't mean. Thridly the options that are there are complete and utter trash. There is no depth in what you say. No humour or personality. Its so robotic and bland, All of it is the same. Boring and uninteresting. Making it hard to connect with your character which should be something you should be able to do with ease in a game like this.
2. The voice overs, over lapping dialouge and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ lip syncing.

Also tying in with what I just said, a lot of people were un happy with the way the voice overs were done. If you were to watch a video or read an article what you might gte out of it is that people just want a silent text reading, but that's not true. What we wanted were options. The characters should have had a wide range of voice types (yes this takes a long time, but we would have waited for the game if it was better) however it should not only include different voice options but also just an option to have no voice over at all. Some people do prefer this over a voice over (myself not included). Now, something that really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off was most of the time (and it still does this) near the end of a character speaking the next part of dialouge will come on without the previous completely finishing. This in unummersive and down right annoying as you will miss out on some useful information or a crucial part of speech that you needed to hear. They youtuber Rags pointed this out on one of his videos about the game and also showed examples of this where it caused him to miss out on important infromation. He also showed another game (The Witcher 3) do parts of dialuge without this problem. Now the final part of this problem was the lip syncing. It seems that all Bethesda games are like this and have very bad jobs at making facial movements and the dialouge go together. Bethesda (being such a big company with so much time and money) should not be having these issues. The formentioned example about Witcher 3 also had perfect lip syncing and put Fallout 4 to shame.
3. The bugs.
Bethesda games are notorious for being bug ridden and sometimes at launch un plyable due to game breaking bugs. Luckily when I played through the game there weren't so many bugs. However this has a bright side, because Fallout 4 was actuually didn't have too many. I did some google searches and while there were some reports of bugs most people were saying that they didn't experience too many game breaking bugs, which was good to hear. Guess there is always a silver lining. Here is a discussion between actual players where I got this information:
These aren't the only pros and cons, only three for each side, but I hope this just gives a general over view of my thoughts on certain debatable parts of Fallout 4.

I love this game. It has it's fair share of problems, like all Bethesda games. And it does feel boring at times when you try to feel like you are walking through a desolate wasteland and your constantly under fire from angry raiders, gunners and anything else that wants your head.
But is it fun? F*ck yeah. Would I call it an RPG? F*ck no.
It's an open world shooter, not an RPG. It doesn't feel the same as Fallout 1, 2 or New Vegas. Kind of Fallout 3 as well. It doesn't really stay true to that and what Fallout is all about. But I love the game for what it is. I guess the amount of time I've spent in it can tell you everything.
My favorite part are the settlements, by far. The game is kind of focused around them and that is something they should change in future installments. Some people like it, some people don't. It should be a smaller feature, not the focus of the game.
Now, the story. The main story in this game could've certainly been ALOT better. It didn't have so many twists except for
one which was somewhat dissapointing. Effective? Yes. But good? Nah. Not really.
The characters were REALLY good, especially for Bethesda. I loved all the companions and the fact that you had 13 really good ones instead of hundreds of copy pasted companions was really good. *cough* *cough* Skyrim *cough* *cough*.
One bad thing is that there are no real consequences in this game. Semi-Spoilers ahead, by the way,
In New Vegas for example, I love those choices you make that still have consequences. It's not like Boone would've been like "wtf you made me kill ranger andy, oh well let's go travel together so we can become best friends. Or when you find those two people outside Nipton fighting and if you kill the guy instead of the girl she will tell you he tried to kill her and take her star bottlecaps. If you kill her he will tell you that she tried to kill him and take his lucky charm necklace.
In the end, I couldn't recommend it more.

That should tell you all you need to know. All jokes aside however, this is a game for people who demand little depth and complexity. This is for the people who want a nice relaxing power trip through the park. Mostly though it's for people who know little to nothing about Fallout.
Once again Bethesda refuses to follow up the story laid out by the first two games and continued in New Vegas. They demand on keeping things on the East Coast, a setting over which they have creative control which is original to them. There's nothing wrong with that at all. If they don't want to be tethered to a previous company's work then more power to them. However they display the same arrogance and disregard for the original games by including bits and pieces from the originals. Why are Super Mutants in the East when they were created by accident in the West? Why are bottlecaps legal tender in the East when the practice originated from the Hub in the West? Some of these things are small and ignorable; others are not and just display a real sense of laziness and lack of attention to detail by the producers.
In terms of the physical setting we get something that looks like a graphical upgrade of Fallout 3.
-Overpasses with large chunks missing
-Nondescript industrial areas
-City streets with copypasted assets
-Corrugated iron shacks
-Office buildings with stairs, cubicles, and desks
The same things over and over again. Every so often there's a patch which looks like someone put some effort into creating something with character, but this is rare. Perhaps the worst offender in the setting dept. comes from the intact urban areas. Here you have tall buildings where you can look out onto Boston and see all the low-res textures where sacrifices had to be made in order for your rig to not catch on fire. Guess what? The same goddamn thing happens in Skyrim when Toddy boy wanted you to go into Whiterun and look out across the landscape - specifically at all those mountains he lied about being climbable. These grand Bethesda vistas don't work, yet the developers continue putting them in their games. This cannot be ignored either. You will have quests which take you to the tops of buildings where Super Mutants are taking shots at you from below; I challenge anyone to aim down from these natural sniper nests and
notice all the buildings in the distance that look like mass-produced plastic toys made in China. It's worse than immersion breaking; in my case I started musing over the vagaries of programming and balancing performance with creative design.
Sweet Jesus though, it's all so boring. Here's rubble. There's yet another camp. It's so predictable and uninspired. What hurts the most are places which could have been something. Goodneighbor is a prime example. It's a seedy neo-noir town evoking hints of Blade Runner and Shadowrun, but there's barely anything there. Even in the trailer when the camera pulls back over Goodneighbor there are only a handful of NPC's on screen, and lo and behold, that's what you get in-game. Once more, why does Bethesda insist on creating small towns populated by a few dozen characters and then referring to these places as towns and cities? They haven't learned their lesson since Oblivion, and I doubt they ever will. Then there's this old dog track where bandits have taken to reprogramming robots to race and betting on them. That's something unique, quirky, and interesting, but nope. Get close, and they all aggro because you know - all bandits are part of the closely-knit bandit faction and utterly opposed to the noble protagonist.
Speaking of bandits and all other of ne'er do wells attacking you on sight, I cannot and will not forgive this game for restricting the player to, "The Nice Guy Run." At most you can deviate from knight in shining armor to flippant rascal with a heart of gold. There's no karma. There's no acknowledgement of any character besides the good guy. You are pigeon-holed into the story of Bethesda's choosing with the character they want you to play. They even go so far as to give your character a voice as if putting up a sonic scaffold for who they want you to be - and that voice is god-awful. Moreover what if you want to play a character who goes native and wears thrown-together bandit armor while wielding a orc-looking machine gun? Too bad the second you enter into dialogue you'll be greeted by a milquetoast voice that sounds completely but not entirely unlike a bandit.
Dear Todd,
Making a game that is open and not just hallways only fulfills the most basic definition of an open world game. That's development by the bloody numbers.
Speaking of that orc machinegun, Fallout 4 does a fantastic job of creating the illusion of variety by disguising the small number of weapon models with weapon mods. Here are those base models:
-.44 pistol
-10mm pistol
-Assault rifle
-Combat rifle
-Gauss rifle
-Hunting rifle
-Railway rifle
-Submachine gun
-Combat shotgun
-Double-barrel shotgun
-Pipe gun
-Pipe revolver
-Pipe bolt-action
-Fat Man
-Flamer
-Junk Jet
-Minigun
-Missile launcher
-Institute laster
-Laser musket
-Laser gun
-Gatling laser
-Plasma gun
-Alien blaster
-Cryolater
-Gamma gun
There you go. That's all the base gun models. From there you can choose from different grips, receivers, barrels, sights, etc. Ultimately though unless you're trying to RP a character with some specific equipment, most of those mods will be disregarded in favor of picking the best in slot mods. Note the lack of unique models, the sheer vapidness and absence of character. Just hotswap things to make a gun that seems unique until you eventually see it in the field by virtue of simple probability. There are so-called unique weapons that have effects - think of Diablo and Borderlands - but calling them unique? Let's take this weapon called, "Old Faithful," for example. From the wiki:
"Old Faithful bears the Instigating effect, which does double damage if the target is at full health, making it a strong choice early in the game for stealthy characters, as a sneak attack against an enemy at full health will deal quadruple the base damage. The specific weapon modifications fitted to the gun when purchased are level dependent and will vary.
it can be converted to a rifle, expanding its usefulness to Rifleman characters as well as Gunslingers and Commandos."
Base Weapon: Laser Gun
Type: Unique Laser Gun
Special: Does double damage if the target is at full health

PROs

CONS

This game challenges what your perception of heriocs is and forces you to make tough decisions.
Not only will you have people die, but you will have them fall into madness.
You have to choose who you need and who you can dispose of.
You may have to watch your A-team die, you may have to let one go because they don't fit the new challenges.
And if you think you are at the top, the game is ready to crash right back down on your hard work.
All wrapped up in gothic aesthetics with a grim but insightful narrator.
Its a game of what really happens when heroes gather to adventure in impossible situations.
There are failures, and only by climbing a mountain of corpses do the chosen few enter the Darkest Dungeon.
Its a beautiful game with great gameplay. It has its flaws, but they make the game rewarding still.
It is a great deal of a challenge though, so be warned. Not for the faint of heart.
